Which W-shaped constellation sits across Polaris from the Big Dipper?

steps.title: Find Polaris
steps.mastery: Find Polaris by following the pointer stars of the Big Dipper, and use it to find north.
steps.practice: Follow the 2 pointer stars at the end of the Big Dipper's bowl about 5 times their gap to reach Polaris.
steps.detail: Polaris isn't especially bright, but it sits almost directly above Earth's north pole, so it barely moves while everything else circles around it. Its height above your horizon equals your latitude, which made it a navigator's best friend.
steps.proof: Polaris found, and north marked on the ground.
steps.pitfall: Assuming Polaris is the brightest star in the sky.

problems.prompt: Which 2 stars of the Big Dipper point to Polaris?
problems.answer: Dubhe and Merak, at the end of the bowl.

problems.prompt: Why does Polaris barely move during the night?
problems.answer: It sits almost exactly above Earth's north pole.

problems.prompt: At latitude 40° N, about how high above the horizon is Polaris? And at 25° N? Give the second one.
problems.answer: About 25°. Polaris sits at the same height as your latitude, so it was 40° at 40° N.

steps.title: Bright Stars and Star Hopping
steps.mastery: Use bright stars as signposts, and star hop from them to fainter targets.
steps.practice: Follow the arc of the Big Dipper's handle to Arcturus, then speed on to Spica, and note each star's color.
steps.detail: Star hopping means moving from something you can find to something you can't, one easy step at a time. Simple phrases help: arc to Arcturus, speed on to Spica. Notice colors as you go, since they hint at each star's temperature.
steps.proof: Arcturus and Spica found, with orange and blue-white noted.
steps.pitfall: Hunting for a faint target with no bright star to start from.

problems.prompt: 'Arc to Arcturus' starts from which constellation?
Which reddish star marks Orion's shoulder?
Orion's belt points down and to the left toward which brightest night-sky star?

steps.title: The Sky Turns
steps.mastery: Explain why the stars move west across the sky overnight, about 15 degrees each hour.
steps.practice: Photograph Orion at 8 pm and at 10 pm from the same spot, and measure how far it moved.
steps.detail: Earth spins once a day, so the whole sky seems to turn around the poles: 360 degrees in 24 hours is 15 degrees an hour. Stars rise in the east and set in the west, like the Sun, and those near Polaris circle without setting.
steps.proof: Orion moved about 30 degrees west in 2 hours.
steps.pitfall: Thinking the stars themselves are moving across the sky.

problems.prompt: How many degrees does the sky turn in 1 hour?
In 4 hours, how many degrees does a star move across the sky?
Like the Sun, do stars rise in the east or the west?

steps.title: Use a Star Map
steps.mastery: Read a planisphere or a sky app to know what's up at a given date and time.
steps.practice: Set a planisphere or Stellarium to 9 pm tonight, list 3 constellations above the horizon, then go out and find them.
steps.detail: A planisphere lines up the date with the time to show tonight's sky. Star maps show east and west swapped because they're meant to be held over your head while you look up. Apps do the same automatically and show the planets too.
steps.proof: 3 constellations listed from the map and found outside.
steps.pitfall: Holding a star map like a road map and getting east and west backward.

problems.prompt: On a planisphere, what do you line up on the 2 dials?
Why does a Stellarium-style star chart show east and west swapped?
problems.answer: They're drawn to be held over your head, looking up.

problems.prompt: Name 1 free sky app.

steps.title: Moons
steps.mastery: Compare major moons, like our Moon, Io, Europa and Titan, and what makes each special.
steps.practice: Make a table of 4 moons, the Moon, Io, Europa and Titan, with 1 standout fact for each.
steps.detail: Moons are far more varied than our own. Io is the most volcanic place in the solar system. Europa hides an ocean under its ice. Titan has a thick atmosphere and lakes of liquid methane. Some icy moons are among the best places to look for life.
steps.proof: A 4-row table with a fact for each moon.
steps.pitfall: Assuming every moon is a gray, cratered ball like ours.

problems.prompt: Of Jupiter's 4 big moons, which has the most active volcanoes?
Which of Saturn's moons has a thick atmosphere and lakes of methane?
Why do scientists think Europa may have an ocean?
problems.answer: Its icy crust shows signs of liquid water below.

steps.title: Asteroids
steps.mastery: Describe asteroids as rocky leftovers, most of them in the belt between Mars and Jupiter.
steps.practice: Mark the asteroid belt between Mars at 1.5 AU and Jupiter at 5.2 AU on your solar system scale model.
steps.detail: Asteroids are rocky and metal pieces left over from the planets' formation. Most orbit between Mars and Jupiter, where Jupiter's gravity kept them from forming a planet. The belt is mostly empty space, with asteroids typically far apart.
steps.proof: The belt marked between Mars and Jupiter on the model.
steps.pitfall: Picturing the belt as crowded with rocks, like in films.

problems.prompt: The main asteroid belt lies between which 2 planets?
Which 1 dwarf planet is the largest object in the asteroid belt?
Are the belt's asteroids packed close together, like in Star Wars?
problems.answer: No. They're usually very far apart.

steps.title: Comets
steps.mastery: Explain comets as icy bodies whose tails form and point away from the Sun when they come close.
steps.practice: Draw a comet at 3 points in its orbit, far away, near the Sun and leaving, with its tail pointing the right way each time.
steps.detail: A comet is a lump of ice and dust. Far from the Sun it's frozen and tailless. Near the Sun, the ice turns to gas and releases dust, forming a glowing coma and tails. Sunlight and the solar wind push the tails away from the Sun, whichever way the comet moves.
steps.proof: 3 drawings with the tail always pointing away from the Sun.
steps.pitfall: Drawing the tail streaming behind the comet's direction of travel.

problems.prompt: Which way does 1 comet's tail point?
Halley's Comet returns about every how many years?
Why do comets grow tails only near the Sun?
problems.answer: Sunlight warms the ice, which turns to gas and dust.

steps.title: Meteors
steps.mastery: Tell meteoroids, meteors and meteorites apart, and know when meteor showers happen.
steps.practice: Watch a meteor shower like the Perseids around August 12 for 30 minutes, and count the meteors.
steps.detail: A meteoroid is a small rock in space. When it burns up in our air, the streak of light is a meteor. If a piece reaches the ground, it's a meteorite. Showers happen when Earth crosses a trail of dust left by a comet, on the same dates every year.
steps.proof: A count of meteors in 30 minutes.
steps.pitfall: Calling the streak of light a meteorite.

problems.prompt: What is 1 meteorite?
problems.answer: A space rock that reaches the ground.

problems.prompt: Meteor showers like the Perseids come from what?
You count 18 meteors in 30 minutes. What rate per hour is that?

steps.title: Dwarf Planets and the Kuiper Belt
steps.mastery: Explain why Pluto is a dwarf planet, and what lies in the Kuiper Belt.
steps.practice: Write the 3 rules for a planet from the 2006 IAU definition, and say which one Pluto fails.
steps.detail: A planet orbits the Sun, is round from its own gravity, and has cleared its orbit of other objects. Pluto meets the first two but shares its region with many Kuiper Belt objects, the icy bodies beyond Neptune. So it's a dwarf planet, along with Eris and Ceres.
steps.proof: 3 rules written, with 'cleared its orbit' marked as the one Pluto fails.
steps.pitfall: Thinking Pluto was demoted for being too small.

problems.prompt: Which of the 3 rules does Pluto fail?
problems.answer: It hasn't cleared its orbit of other objects.

problems.prompt: Where is the Kuiper Belt, past 30 AU?
Name 1 dwarf planet besides Pluto.

steps.title: Apparent and Absolute Brightness
steps.mastery: Tell how bright a star looks from how bright it really is, using apparent and absolute magnitude.
steps.practice: Compare Sirius and Deneb: Sirius looks brighter, but find which one really gives off more light.
steps.detail: How bright a star looks depends on its power and its distance. Apparent magnitude is how bright it looks, and absolute magnitude is how bright it would look from a standard 10 parsecs. Lower numbers are brighter, and 5 magnitudes is a factor of 100.
steps.proof: Deneb gives off vastly more light. It just lies much farther away.
steps.pitfall: Assuming the brightest-looking star is the most powerful.

problems.prompt: On the magnitude scale, is magnitude 1 brighter or fainter than magnitude 5?
A difference of 5 magnitudes means how many times brighter?
Why can a faint-looking star like Deneb be more powerful than a bright-looking one?
problems.answer: It may be much farther away.

steps.title: Distance by Parallax
steps.mastery: Measure star distances by parallax, the small shift a star shows as Earth orbits the Sun.
steps.practice: Hold a finger at arm's length and blink each eye, then use distance in parsecs = 1 / parallax in arcseconds for a star at 0.5 arcsec.
steps.detail: As Earth moves around the Sun, nearby stars seem to shift slightly against distant ones, just as your finger jumps when you switch eyes. The closer the star, the bigger the shift. A parallax of 1 arcsecond means a distance of 1 parsec, about 3.26 light years.
steps.proof: 1 / 0.5 is 2 parsecs.
steps.pitfall: Thinking a bigger parallax means a farther star.

problems.prompt: A star's parallax is 0.1 arcseconds. How far is it, in parsecs?
1 parsec is about how many light years?
Do stars within 10 parsecs have bigger or smaller parallax than distant ones?

steps.title: Read the HR Diagram
steps.mastery: Read the HR diagram of temperature against luminosity, and find the main sequence, the giants and the white dwarfs.
steps.practice: Plot 6 stars, the Sun, Sirius A and B, Betelgeuse, Rigel and Proxima Centauri, on a sketched HR diagram.
steps.detail: The HR diagram puts temperature along the bottom, hot on the left, and luminosity up the side. Most stars fall on a diagonal band, the main sequence. Giants sit top right, cool but huge, and white dwarfs bottom left, hot but tiny.
steps.proof: 6 stars placed, with Sirius B bottom left and Betelgeuse top right.
steps.pitfall: Putting hot stars on the right, as on a normal graph.

problems.prompt: Where are white dwarfs on the HR diagram: top right or bottom left?
Which way does temperature run along the HR diagram's bottom axis?
problems.answer: Hot on the left, cool on the right.

problems.prompt: Where does the Sun sit on the HR diagram?
problems.answer: On the main sequence, near the middle.

steps.title: Spectral Classes
steps.mastery: Name the spectral classes O B A F G K M, from hottest to coolest.
steps.practice: Write OBAFGKM with an example star and a rough temperature for each class.
steps.detail: Stars are sorted by the lines in their spectra, which track temperature. O stars are blue and over 30,000 K, and M stars are red and under 3500 K. The Sun is a G. A phrase like Oh Be A Fine Girl or Guy, Kiss Me keeps the order.
steps.proof: 7 classes, each with an example, like Rigel for B and the Sun for G.
steps.pitfall: Thinking the letters run in alphabetical order.

problems.prompt: Of the 7 classes, which is hottest: O or M?
Which class is the Sun?
Which class are most stars in the Milky Way?

steps.title: Mass Sets Everything
steps.mastery: Explain that a main-sequence star's mass sets its temperature, brightness and lifespan.
steps.practice: Compare a 0.5, a 1 and a 10 solar mass star by color and lifetime, using the rule that big stars burn out fast.
steps.detail: More mass means more crushing pressure in the core, so fusion runs much faster. Massive stars are hot, blue and brilliant, and burn out in millions of years. Small red dwarfs sip their fuel for trillions. The Sun gets about 10 billion.
steps.proof: Red and longest-lived, yellow and middling, blue and shortest-lived.
steps.pitfall: Thinking big stars last longer because they have more fuel.

problems.prompt: Which lives longer: a 10 solar mass star or a 1 solar mass star?
About how long will the Sun stay on the main sequence?
A main-sequence star is blue and very bright. Is it more or less massive than the Sun?

steps.title: Fusion in the Core
steps.mastery: Explain how the Sun fuses hydrogen into helium in its core, turning a little mass into a lot of energy.
steps.practice: Work out how much mass the Sun turns into energy each second from its power of 3.8 × 10²⁶ W, using E = mc².
steps.detail: In the core, at about 15 million °C, hydrogen nuclei fuse step by step into helium. The helium weighs slightly less than the 4 hydrogen nuclei that made it, and that missing mass becomes energy. It takes many thousands of years for that energy to reach the surface.
steps.proof: About 4.2 billion kg, roughly 4 million tonnes, every second.
steps.pitfall: Thinking the Sun burns like a fire.

problems.prompt: What does the Sun fuse in its core?
About how hot is the Sun's core: 15 million °C or 15 thousand °C?
How many hydrogen nuclei fuse to make 1 helium nucleus in the Sun?

steps.title: Layers of the Sun
steps.mastery: Name the Sun's layers from the core outward, and how energy moves through each one.
steps.practice: Draw the Sun's 6 layers, core, radiative zone, convection zone, photosphere, chromosphere and corona, and label how energy moves in the first 3.
steps.detail: Energy made in the core creeps outward as light through the radiative zone, then rises in boiling currents through the convection zone. The photosphere is the surface we see. Above it, the thin corona is mysteriously far hotter than the surface.
steps.proof: A labeled cross section with fusion, radiation and convection marked.
steps.pitfall: Thinking the visible surface is the hottest part outside the core.

problems.prompt: Of the Sun's 6 layers, which is the visible surface?
In which of the Sun's zones does hot gas rise and sink like boiling water?
The corona is about 1 million °C, far hotter than the surface. Is that expected?
problems.answer: No. It's a puzzle astronomers still study.

steps.title: Sunspots and the Cycle
steps.mastery: Explain sunspots as cooler, magnetic regions, and the 11-year cycle of their numbers.
steps.practice: Look up sunspot counts for the last 25 years, and find the years of the last 2 maximums.
steps.detail: Sunspots are spots where strong magnetic fields hold back the heat, so they're cooler and look dark against the bright surface. Their numbers rise and fall in a cycle of about 11 years. Flares and storms are most common near the maximum.
steps.proof: Peaks near 2001, 2014 and 2024, about 11 years apart.
steps.pitfall: Thinking sunspots are holes or burnt patches.

problems.prompt: Why does 1 sunspot look dark?
problems.answer: It's cooler than the gas around it.

problems.prompt: About how long is the Sun's sunspot cycle?
A solar maximum came in 2014. About when was the next one?

steps.title: Flares and Space Weather
steps.mastery: Explain solar flares and coronal mass ejections, and how they affect Earth.
steps.practice: Read today's report from NOAA's Space Weather Prediction Center, and note the Kp index.
steps.detail: Twisted magnetic fields on the Sun can snap and release huge energy as a flare, sometimes hurling a cloud of charged gas into space. When that reaches Earth, it can spark auroras and also disrupt satellites, GPS and power grids. The Kp index rates the disturbance from 0 to 9.
steps.proof: Today's Kp index written down, with what it means for auroras.
steps.pitfall: Thinking space weather only matters to astronauts.

problems.prompt: What causes the Northern Lights?
problems.answer: Charged particles from the Sun hitting our upper atmosphere.

problems.prompt: Name 1 thing a big solar storm can disrupt.
What does CME stand for?

steps.title: An Average Star
steps.mastery: Place the Sun among other stars as a middle-aged, medium-sized G-type star.
steps.practice: Compare the Sun with Sirius, Betelgeuse and Proxima Centauri by size and temperature in a 4-row table.
steps.detail: The Sun looks special only because it's close. It's a G2 star about 4.6 billion years old, halfway through a main-sequence life of about 10 billion years. Some stars are far bigger and hotter, and most are smaller and cooler red dwarfs.
steps.proof: A table showing the Sun in the middle of the range.
steps.pitfall: Thinking the Sun is unusually large or bright for a star.

problems.prompt: What spectral type is the Sun?
About how old is the Sun: 4.6 billion or 46 billion years?
Of its roughly 10 billion year main-sequence life, about how much does the Sun have left?

steps.title: Aperture Matters Most
steps.mastery: Explain that aperture, the size of the main lens or mirror, sets how much light a telescope gathers.
steps.practice: Compare a 70 mm and a 200 mm telescope by working out how many times more light the bigger one gathers.
steps.detail: Light gathered depends on the area of the lens or mirror, which grows with the diameter squared. Doubling the aperture gathers 4 times the light. That's what shows faint galaxies and fine detail, far more than magnification does.
steps.proof: About 8 times more light, since (200 / 70) squared is about 8.2.
steps.pitfall: Buying a telescope for its magnification number on the box.

problems.prompt: A 200 mm telescope against a 100 mm one. How many times more light does the bigger one gather?
What does a '200 mm' aperture measure?
problems.answer: The diameter of the main lens or mirror.

problems.prompt: Why is a bigger aperture, like 200 mm, better for faint galaxies?

steps.title: Work Out Magnification
steps.mastery: Work out magnification as the telescope's focal length divided by the eyepiece's, and know its limits.
steps.practice: Find the magnification of a 1000 mm telescope with a 25 mm eyepiece and with a 10 mm eyepiece.
steps.detail: Divide the telescope's focal length by the eyepiece's. Shorter eyepieces magnify more. But past roughly 2 times the aperture in millimeters, the image just gets bigger and blurrier, and on most nights steady air limits it even more.
steps.proof: 40 times with the 25 mm, and 100 times with the 10 mm.
steps.pitfall: Using the highest magnification on every target.

problems.prompt: A 1200 mm telescope with a 20 mm eyepiece gives what magnification?
Using about 2 times per mm of aperture, what's the most useful magnification for a 100 mm telescope?
On the same telescope, which eyepiece magnifies more: 25 mm or 10 mm?

steps.title: Find Objects
steps.mastery: Use a finder scope or red dot finder and low power to find objects, then zoom in.
steps.practice: Align your finder on a distant treetop in daylight, then find the Moon at night with your lowest-power eyepiece first.
steps.detail: The main telescope sees a tiny patch of sky, so finding things through it is hard. A finder shows a wide view. Align it in daylight on something far away, then aim with it at night. Start at low power, center the object, then switch up.
steps.proof: The Moon found and centered at low power, then viewed at higher power.
steps.pitfall: Starting with high power and never finding anything.

problems.prompt: Why start with the lowest-power eyepiece, like a 25 mm?
problems.answer: It shows the widest view, so objects are easier to find.

problems.prompt: When should you align the finder scope on 1 distant treetop?
Why never point a telescope at the Sun without a proper filter?

steps.title: Good First Targets
steps.mastery: Start with bright, easy targets like the Moon, Jupiter and Saturn before faint ones.
steps.practice: Observe the Moon, Jupiter and Saturn this month, and sketch 1 feature of each, like a crater, 4 moons or the rings.
steps.detail: Bright targets reward a small telescope right away. The Moon shows craters best near a quarter phase, when shadows are long. Jupiter shows its 4 big moons and cloud bands. Saturn's rings are visible even in a 60 mm scope.
steps.proof: 3 sketches, one for each target.
steps.pitfall: Starting with faint galaxies and deciding the telescope doesn't work.

problems.prompt: How many bright moons of Jupiter can a small telescope show?
Which feature of Saturn shows even in a 60 mm telescope?
When are the Moon's craters easiest to see: at full moon or near a quarter?
problems.answer: Near a quarter, when shadows are long.

steps.title: Dark Skies and Steady Air
steps.mastery: Pick nights and places with dark skies and steady air, and let your eyes adapt.
steps.practice: Observe from a dark site, wait 20 minutes for your eyes to adapt using only red light, then compare it with your backyard.
steps.detail: City light washes out faint objects, so a dark site shows far more. Your eyes need 20 to 30 minutes to adapt fully, and white light resets them, so use a red flashlight. Twinkling stars mean unsteady air, which blurs planets.
steps.proof: A list of objects seen from the dark site that weren't visible at home.
steps.pitfall: Checking a phone screen every few minutes and losing dark adaptation.

problems.prompt: How long do eyes take to fully adapt to the dark: 2 minutes or 20 to 30?
Why use 1 red flashlight at night?
problems.answer: It doesn't ruin your dark adaptation.

problems.prompt: Stars twinkle a lot tonight. What does that say about the 'seeing'?
problems.answer: The air is unsteady, so planets will look blurry.

steps.title: Cut and Paste DNA
steps.mastery: Explain how restriction enzymes cut DNA and ligase joins it, making recombinant DNA.
steps.practice: Cut a plasmid and a human insulin gene with EcoRI on paper, match the sticky ends, and join them with ligase.
steps.detail: A restriction enzyme cuts DNA at one exact sequence, often leaving short single-stranded sticky ends. Cut two DNA pieces with the same enzyme and their ends match. Ligase seals them together. Put the new plasmid into bacteria and they copy it as they divide.
steps.proof: A paper plasmid with the insulin gene taped in where EcoRI cut it.
steps.pitfall: Cutting the gene and the plasmid with different enzymes, so the ends don't match.

problems.prompt: EcoRI cuts at GAATTC. How many times does it cut GAATTCAAGAATTC?
Which enzyme seals cut DNA back together?
Why cut the gene and 1 plasmid with the same enzyme?

steps.title: Copy DNA With PCR
steps.mastery: Explain the 3 temperature steps of PCR and how the copies double every cycle.
steps.practice: Write the 3 PCR steps with their temperatures, then work out the copies after 10 cycles from 1 molecule.
steps.detail: Heating to about 95°C separates the strands. Cooling to about 55°C lets short primers stick to each strand. Warming to 72°C lets a heat-proof polymerase build new strands. Each cycle doubles the DNA, so 30 cycles turn one molecule into about a billion.
steps.proof: 95, 55 and 72°C, and 1024 copies after 10 cycles.
steps.pitfall: Thinking PCR adds a fixed number of copies each cycle instead of doubling.

problems.prompt: At what temperature does PCR separate DNA strands: about 55°C or 95°C?
How many copies are there after 5 cycles, starting from 1 molecule?
Why does PCR use a polymerase from a hot spring bacterium?

steps.title: Read a Gel
steps.mastery: Read a gel: smaller DNA pieces travel farther toward the positive end.
steps.practice: Draw a gel with a ladder and 3 samples of 300, 500 and 1000 base pairs, placing each band correctly.
steps.detail: DNA is negatively charged, so in an electric field it moves toward the positive electrode. The gel is a mesh, and small pieces slip through faster. A ladder of known sizes lets you read each band's size. Matching bands suggest matching DNA.
steps.proof: The 300 bp band is farthest from the wells, and the 1000 bp band is closest.
steps.pitfall: Putting the biggest piece farthest, as if size meant speed.

problems.prompt: Which travels farther in a gel: a 200 bp or an 800 bp fragment?
DNA moves toward which electrode in a gel?
problems.answer: The positive one, since DNA is negative.

problems.prompt: A crime scene sample's bands match suspect 2 but not suspect 1. What does that suggest?
problems.answer: The sample likely came from suspect 2.

steps.title: Edit Genes With CRISPR
steps.mastery: Explain how CRISPR-Cas9 uses a guide RNA to cut a chosen DNA site.
steps.practice: Write a 20-base guide RNA to match a target DNA sequence, and explain what Cas9 does once it binds.
steps.detail: The guide RNA is built to pair with the exact DNA sequence you want to change. Cas9 follows the guide and cuts both strands there. The cell repairs the cut, which can switch the gene off or, with a template, write in a new sequence.
steps.proof: A guide matching the target, and Cas9 cutting both strands at that spot.
steps.pitfall: Thinking CRISPR adds new genes on its own. It cuts, and the cell's repair does the rest.

problems.prompt: Which part of CRISPR finds the target DNA sequence?
What does Cas9 do at the target?
Write the guide RNA that pairs with the DNA template ACGTAC.

steps.title: Weigh the Uses
steps.mastery: Weigh a biotech use's benefits and risks, like GM crops or gene therapy, using evidence.
steps.practice: Write 3 benefits and 3 concerns for Golden Rice, then give your own view in 2 sentences.
steps.detail: Biotech questions mix science with values. First get the facts right: what the change does, what studies show and who it affects. Then weigh benefits against risks, and say which risks are known and which are guesses. Editing body cells affects one person, while editing embryos affects their descendants too.
steps.proof: 3 benefits, 3 concerns and a 2-sentence view backed by evidence.
steps.pitfall: Arguing from 'natural' or 'unnatural' without any evidence.

problems.prompt: Golden Rice makes beta-carotene. Which deficiency does it target?
Is editing 1 patient's blood cells different from editing an embryo? Why?
problems.answer: Yes. Embryo edits pass to future generations.

problems.prompt: Name 1 medicine made with recombinant DNA.

steps.title: Prokaryote or Eukaryote
steps.mastery: Tell prokaryotic cells from eukaryotic ones by the nucleus and the membrane-bound organelles.
steps.practice: Sort 4 cells, E. coli, yeast, a leaf cell and a human skin cell, into prokaryotes and eukaryotes.
steps.detail: Prokaryotes, bacteria and archaea, have no nucleus. Their DNA floats in the cytoplasm, and they have no mitochondria or other membrane-bound organelles. Eukaryotes keep their DNA in a nucleus and have organelles. Prokaryotes are usually about a tenth the length.
steps.proof: E. coli is a prokaryote. Yeast, leaf and skin cells are eukaryotes.
steps.pitfall: Thinking yeast is a bacterium. It's a fungus, so it's eukaryotic.

problems.prompt: Does 1 E. coli cell have a nucleus?
A typical bacterium is 2 micrometers long and a typical animal cell is 20. How many times longer is the animal cell?
Name 1 thing both prokaryotes and eukaryotes have.
problems.answer: Ribosomes, a cell membrane, cytoplasm or DNA.

steps.title: Organelles and Their Jobs
steps.mastery: Match the main organelles to their jobs: nucleus, mitochondria, ribosomes, ER, Golgi and lysosomes.
steps.practice: Make a 6-row table of organelles and their jobs, then compare each one to a part of a factory.
steps.detail: The nucleus holds the plans, like a head office. Ribosomes build proteins, the ER moves and modifies them, and the Golgi packages and ships them. Mitochondria release energy, like a power plant. Lysosomes break down waste, like a recycling crew.
steps.proof: A table with each of the 6 organelles, its job and a factory match.
steps.pitfall: Saying mitochondria make energy. They release energy stored in food.

problems.prompt: Which organelle makes most of a cell's ATP?
Which organelle builds proteins from mRNA?
Proteins leave the ER and go to which organelle to be packaged for export?

steps.title: Plant and Animal Cells
steps.mastery: List 3 structures plant cells have that animal cells lack, and say what each one does.
steps.practice: Draw a plant cell and an animal cell side by side, and label the 3 plant-only parts: cell wall, chloroplasts and large vacuole.
steps.detail: The cell wall is made of cellulose and keeps the cell's shape. Chloroplasts capture light for photosynthesis. The large central vacuole stores water and presses outward, keeping the plant firm. Both cell types share a nucleus, membrane, cytoplasm and mitochondria.
steps.proof: Two labeled drawings, with the 3 plant-only parts clearly marked.
steps.pitfall: Leaving mitochondria out of plant cells. Plants respire too.

problems.prompt: Which of the 3 extra plant structures carries out photosynthesis?
Name the 1 carbohydrate that makes up most of a plant cell wall.
A plant's cells lose 30% of their water and it wilts. Why does it wilt?
problems.answer: The vacuoles shrink, so the cells stop pushing against their walls.

steps.title: Use a Microscope
steps.mastery: Use a light microscope to view cells, and work out the total magnification.
steps.practice: Look at onion skin cells at 40x, then at 400x, sketch one cell at each, and work out the total magnification.
steps.detail: Total magnification is the eyepiece times the objective. Start on the lowest power, focus with the coarse knob, then switch up and use only the fine knob. Real size is image size divided by magnification, so convert units carefully.
steps.proof: Two sketches, labeled 40x and 400x, with a nucleus and cell wall visible at 400x.
steps.pitfall: Using the coarse focus at high power and cracking the slide.

problems.prompt: An eyepiece is 10x and the objective is 40x. What is the total magnification?
At 100x, a cell looks 5 mm wide. How wide is it really, in micrometers?
Why add 1 drop of iodine to onion cells before viewing?
problems.answer: It stains them, so the nucleus and walls stand out.

steps.title: Why Cells Stay Small
steps.mastery: Explain why cells stay small, using the ratio of surface area to volume.
steps.practice: Work out the surface area, volume and their ratio for cubes of side 1, 2 and 4 cm, and say which would feed its center best.
steps.detail: Food and oxygen enter through the surface, but the whole volume needs them. When a cell grows, its volume rises faster than its surface, so each bit of surface has more inside to supply. Small cells, and flat or folded shapes, keep the ratio high.
steps.proof: Ratios of 6, 3 and 1.5, so the 1 cm cube feeds its center best.
steps.pitfall: Thinking bigger cells are better because they hold more.

problems.prompt: A cube cell has a side of 3 µm. What is its ratio of surface area to volume?
When a cell's side doubles, by what factor does its volume grow?
A cell's side triples. Why does it struggle to get enough oxygen?
problems.answer: Its volume grows faster than its surface, so too little surface feeds too much inside.

steps.title: Stages of Mitosis
steps.mastery: Name the stages of mitosis in order and say what the chromosomes do in each one.
steps.practice: Draw a cell with 4 chromosomes in prophase, metaphase, anaphase and telophase.
steps.detail: In prophase the chromosomes coil up and become visible. In metaphase they line up in the middle. In anaphase the sister chromatids are pulled to opposite ends. In telophase new nuclei form, and then the cell splits in two.
steps.proof: 4 drawings showing coiling, lining up, separating and two new nuclei.
steps.pitfall: Putting anaphase before metaphase. They have to line up before they split.

problems.prompt: Of the 4 stages of mitosis, in which do chromosomes line up in the middle?
A cell with 46 chromosomes divides by mitosis twice in a row. How many cells are there, and how many chromosomes does each have?
problems.answer: 4 cells, each with 46 chromosomes. Mitosis copies the full set every time.

problems.prompt: Which of the 4 stages pulls sister chromatids to opposite ends?

steps.title: The Cell Cycle
steps.mastery: Describe the cell cycle, G1, S, G2 and mitosis, and what happens in each phase.
steps.practice: Draw the cell cycle as a pie chart, with interphase taking about 90% of the time, and label what happens in G1, S and G2.
steps.detail: Most of a cell's life is interphase. In G1 it grows and works, in S it copies its DNA, and in G2 it checks the copies and gets ready. Mitosis is the short final step. Checkpoints stop the cycle if something is wrong, and failed checkpoints can lead to cancer.
steps.proof: A pie mostly labeled interphase, with G1 growth, S copying and G2 checking.
steps.pitfall: Thinking a cell spends most of its time dividing.

problems.prompt: In which phase is DNA copied: G1, S or G2?
A cycle takes 24 hours and mitosis takes 1. What fraction of the time is mitosis?
Why must all 46 chromosomes be copied before mitosis?
problems.answer: So each daughter cell gets a full set.

steps.title: Meiosis
steps.mastery: Explain how meiosis makes 4 cells with half the chromosomes, and why sex cells need that.
steps.practice: Track a cell with 2 pairs of chromosomes through meiosis I and II, drawing the 4 cells at the end.
steps.detail: Meiosis I separates each pair of matching chromosomes, halving the number. Meiosis II separates the sister chromatids, like mitosis. The result is 4 cells, each with one chromosome from every pair. When two sex cells fuse, the full number comes back.
steps.proof: 4 cells, each with 2 chromosomes, one from each pair.
steps.pitfall: Drawing 2 cells at the end, as if meiosis were one division.

problems.prompt: A human cell with 46 chromosomes goes through meiosis. How many chromosomes does each sperm get?
How many cells does meiosis make from 1 cell?
Why do sex cells need half the 46 chromosomes?
problems.answer: So fertilization restores the full 46 instead of doubling it.

steps.title: Where Variation Comes From
steps.mastery: Explain how crossing over and independent assortment make every sex cell different.
steps.practice: Work out how many different sex cells a species with 3 chromosome pairs can make by independent assortment alone.
steps.detail: Each pair lines up in meiosis I without regard to the others, so each pair has 2 ways to split. With n pairs that's 2 multiplied by itself n times. Crossing over then swaps pieces between matching chromosomes, multiplying the variety even further.
steps.proof: 2 times 2 times 2 is 8 kinds of sex cell.
steps.pitfall: Adding the pairs instead of multiplying the choices.

problems.prompt: With 2 chromosome pairs, how many combinations can independent assortment make?
With 23 pairs, the count is 2 multiplied by itself 23 times. About how many million is that?
In which stage of meiosis does crossing over happen, with 4 chromatids side by side?

steps.title: Compare Mitosis and Meiosis
steps.mastery: Compare mitosis and meiosis by divisions, cells made, chromosome count and purpose.
steps.practice: Fill in a 4-row table comparing mitosis and meiosis, and give 1 example of where each one happens in your body.
steps.detail: Mitosis is one division making 2 identical cells with the full count, for growth and repair. Meiosis is two divisions making 4 different cells with half the count, for reproduction. Skin and bone marrow use mitosis, and the testes and ovaries use meiosis.
steps.proof: A table with 1 against 2 divisions, 2 against 4 cells, full against half, and growth against sex cells.
steps.pitfall: Saying meiosis makes identical cells. Crossing over makes each one different.

problems.prompt: How many divisions does meiosis have, 1 or 2?
Is 1 new skin cell made by mitosis or meiosis?
Are the 2 cells from mitosis genetically identical?

steps.title: Pair the Bases
steps.mastery: Pair bases with A to T and C to G, and write the complementary strand.
steps.practice: Write the complementary strand for ATGCCGTA and check each pair.
steps.detail: A always pairs with T and C always pairs with G, so one strand fixes the other. This is what lets DNA copy itself and lets cells read genes. It also means the amount of A in double-stranded DNA always equals T, and C equals G.
steps.proof: TACGGCAT.
steps.pitfall: Pairing A with G because both are the bigger bases.

problems.prompt: Which base pairs with A in DNA?
Write the complement of GGATC.
A DNA sample is 30% A. What percent is G?

steps.title: The Double Helix
steps.mastery: Describe DNA's structure: 2 strands, a sugar-phosphate backbone outside and paired bases inside.
steps.practice: Build a paper model of 6 base pairs, color-coding A, T, C and G, and twist it into a helix.
steps.detail: The sides of the ladder are sugar and phosphate. The rungs are base pairs held by hydrogen bonds, 2 for A with T and 3 for C with G. The two strands run in opposite directions. Watson and Crick built the model in 1953, using X-ray images made by Rosalind Franklin.
steps.proof: A twisted ladder with the bases on the inside and the backbone outside.
steps.pitfall: Putting the bases on the outside of the helix.

problems.prompt: What holds paired bases together in DNA: hydrogen bonds or peptide bonds?
How many hydrogen bonds join C to G in DNA?
Who used Rosalind Franklin's X-ray image to build the 1953 DNA model?

steps.title: DNA Replication
steps.mastery: Explain semi-conservative replication, where the strands unzip and each one templates a new partner.
steps.practice: Draw a DNA molecule of 4 base pairs unzipping, and write the 2 new molecules with old and new strands in different colors.
steps.detail: Helicase unzips the helix by breaking the hydrogen bonds. DNA polymerase then adds matching nucleotides to each old strand. Each new molecule keeps one old strand and gains one new one, which is what semi-conservative means.
steps.proof: 2 molecules, each with one old strand and one new one.
steps.pitfall: Drawing one all-old molecule and one all-new molecule.

problems.prompt: After 1 round of replication, how many of the 2 molecules contain an old strand?
Which enzyme adds new nucleotides during DNA replication?
Starting from 1 molecule, after 2 rounds, how many molecules have only new strands?

steps.title: Genes and Chromosomes
steps.mastery: Explain how DNA is organized into genes on chromosomes, wound around proteins in the nucleus.
steps.practice: Write the 4 levels from nucleotide to gene to chromosome to genome, with a human number for each where you can.
steps.detail: A gene is a stretch of DNA that codes for a protein or an RNA. Each chromosome is one very long DNA molecule wrapped around proteins called histones. Humans have 46 chromosomes in most cells, about 20,000 genes and about 3 billion base pairs.
steps.proof: Nucleotides build about 20,000 genes, spread over 46 chromosomes, in a genome of about 3 billion base pairs.
steps.pitfall: Thinking each chromosome is one gene. Each holds hundreds or thousands.

problems.prompt: How many chromosomes does 1 typical human body cell hold?
About how many base pairs are in the human genome: 3 million or 3 billion?
In 1 sentence, what is a gene?
problems.answer: A stretch of DNA that codes for one protein or RNA.

steps.title: Read a Sequence
steps.mastery: Work with sequences: count the bases, find the GC content and spot repeats.
steps.practice: For ATGCGCGATTAGC, count each base and work out the GC content as a percent.
steps.detail: GC content is the share of bases that are G or C. It matters because GC pairs have 3 hydrogen bonds, so GC-rich DNA holds together more tightly. Count carefully in small groups, since a long string is easy to misread.
steps.proof: A 3, T 3, G 4 and C 3, so the GC content is 7 of 13, about 54%.
steps.pitfall: Counting only G, or only C, instead of both together.

problems.prompt: What is the GC content of GGCCAATT?
A strand reads ATGCGT. How many base pairs does the double-stranded version have?
A strand reads AAAAAAAAGC. What is its GC content?

steps.title: Food Chains and Webs
steps.mastery: Build food chains and webs, and name the producers, consumers and decomposers.
steps.practice: Build a food web of 6 organisms from a pond, with arrows pointing the way energy flows.
steps.detail: Producers like plants and algae make food from light. Consumers eat them or each other, and decomposers break down whatever dies. Arrows point from what's eaten to what eats it. A web shows that most animals eat several things, so the loss of one species ripples outward.
steps.proof: A web of 6 organisms with arrows from algae up to the top predator.
steps.pitfall: Drawing arrows from predator to prey, which reverses the energy flow.

problems.prompt: In the 3-link chain grass, rabbit, fox, which is the producer?
In a 6-organism food web, which way should the arrows point?
problems.answer: From the eaten to the eater, the way energy flows.

accept: from the eaten to the eater
from what is eaten to what eats it

problems.prompt: Foxes vanish from 1 web. What likely happens to the rabbits at first?

steps.title: The 10% Rule
steps.mastery: Use the rule that about 10% of the energy passes from one feeding level to the next.
steps.practice: Start with 10,000 kJ in grass and work out the energy reaching rabbits, foxes and an eagle.
steps.detail: At each level, most energy is spent on staying alive and leaves as heat, and some is never eaten. Only about a tenth is built into the next level's bodies. That's why top predators are rare and food chains stay short.
steps.proof: 1000 kJ to rabbits, 100 kJ to foxes and 10 kJ to the eagle.
steps.pitfall: Saying energy is recycled like matter. Energy flows through once and is lost as heat.

problems.prompt: Plants hold 50,000 kJ. About how much reaches the herbivores?
Why are there rarely more than 5 levels in a food chain?
problems.answer: Too little energy is left at the top.

problems.prompt: At each step, where does the other 90% go?
problems.answer: Lost as heat from respiration, and in waste and uneaten parts.

steps.title: Cycles of Matter
steps.mastery: Trace carbon through photosynthesis, respiration, decay and burning.
steps.practice: Draw the carbon cycle with 4 stores, air, plants, animals and fossil fuels, and label each arrow with its process.
steps.detail: Photosynthesis pulls carbon out of the air into plants. Eating moves it into animals. Respiration and decay return it to the air, and burning fossil fuels releases carbon that was locked away for millions of years. Matter cycles, unlike energy.
steps.proof: 4 stores linked by photosynthesis, feeding, respiration, decay and burning.
steps.pitfall: Leaving decomposers out, which stops the cycle at dead matter.

problems.prompt: Which process removes CO2 from the air?
Which 2 processes add CO2 to the air?
Why do decomposers matter when 1 tree falls and dies?
problems.answer: They release its carbon back to the air.

steps.title: Biotic and Abiotic Factors
steps.mastery: Tell living from nonliving factors, and explain how each one limits where a species lives.
steps.practice: List 4 biotic and 4 abiotic factors for a forest stream, and say which one limits trout the most.
steps.detail: Biotic factors are living things: food, predators, competitors and disease. Abiotic factors are nonliving: temperature, light, water, oxygen and soil. A species can only live where all of them stay in its range, and the tightest one sets the limit.
steps.proof: Biotic: insects, herons, algae, other fish. Abiotic: temperature, oxygen, current, light. Temperature limits trout most.
steps.pitfall: Calling dead leaves abiotic. They came from living things, so they count as biotic.

problems.prompt: Is water at 25°C a biotic or an abiotic factor?
Is 1 heron that eats fish a biotic or an abiotic factor?
Trout need water below about 20°C. What limits them in a stream that warms to 24°C?
problems.answer: Temperature, which also lowers the oxygen.

steps.title: Sample a Habitat
steps.mastery: Estimate how many of a species live in an area, with quadrats or mark and recapture, and judge the estimate.
steps.practice: Count daisies in 10 random 1 m squares on a 200 square meter lawn, and estimate the total.
steps.detail: Counting everything is rarely possible, so sample. Quadrats suit plants: average the count per square and scale up by area. For animals that move, mark some, release them, then recapture and use the share that's marked. More samples give a better estimate.
steps.proof: Multiply the mean per square by 200 to estimate the lawn's total.
steps.pitfall: Placing quadrats where the plants look thickest, which inflates the estimate.

problems.prompt: 10 quadrats of 1 m² average 4 daisies each. Estimate the total on 200 m².
You mark 20 beetles and release them. Later you catch 30, and 6 are marked. Estimate the population.
Why place your 10 quadrats at random?
problems.answer: To avoid picking spots that bias the count.

steps.title: Lock and Key
steps.mastery: Explain how an enzyme's active site fits its substrate, and why each enzyme is specific.
steps.practice: Draw amylase in 3 stages: starch fitting its active site, the reaction, and maltose leaving.
steps.detail: The active site is a pocket shaped to fit one kind of substrate. When the substrate binds, the reaction happens faster, the products leave, and the enzyme is ready again. Most enzymes flex slightly to grip the substrate, which is the induced fit idea.
steps.proof: A drawing with starch in the active site and maltose leaving.
steps.pitfall: Drawing the enzyme changing into the product. It comes out unchanged.

problems.prompt: Amylase breaks down starch. What is starch called in this reaction?
Why can't amylase digest the protein in 1 egg?
problems.answer: Protein doesn't fit its active site.

problems.prompt: What does the 'induced fit' model say?
problems.answer: The active site changes shape slightly to grip the substrate.

steps.title: Lower the Activation Energy
steps.mastery: Explain that enzymes speed up reactions by lowering the activation energy, and aren't used up.
steps.practice: Sketch 2 energy curves, with and without catalase, marking the activation energy on each one.
steps.detail: Every reaction needs a push to get started, called the activation energy. Enzymes hold the substrate in a way that lowers that push, so far more molecules react at body temperature. The start and end energies don't change, so neither does the final amount of product.
steps.proof: Two curves with the same start and end, and a lower hump for the catalase one.
steps.pitfall: Drawing the enzyme curve ending at a different energy level.

problems.prompt: Catalase splits 2H2O2 into water and oxygen. Is the catalase used up?
problems.answer: No. It's reused again and again.

problems.prompt: An enzyme makes a reaction finish in 1 minute instead of 1 year. Does it change the amount of product?
problems.answer: No. It only makes it happen faster.

problems.prompt: One catalase molecule handles about 40 million peroxide molecules a second. About how many in 3 seconds? Give the number in millions.

steps.title: Temperature Effects
steps.mastery: Predict enzyme activity across temperatures, rising to an optimum and dropping as the enzyme denatures.
steps.practice: Time how long amylase takes to digest starch at 20, 37 and 60°C, then plot rate against temperature.
steps.detail: Warmer molecules move faster and collide more, so the rate climbs. Past the optimum, bonds holding the enzyme's shape start to break, the active site changes, and the rate falls fast. Denaturing is usually permanent. Human enzymes peak near body temperature.
steps.proof: A curve that rises to a peak near 37°C and falls steeply by 60°C.
steps.pitfall: Saying the enzyme is killed. Enzymes aren't alive, so they denature.

problems.prompt: Human enzymes work best near what temperature, in °C?
An enzyme loses its shape at 60°C. What is this called?
Going from 20°C to 30°C roughly doubles an enzyme's rate. Why?
problems.answer: Molecules move faster, so they hit the active site more often.

steps.title: pH Effects
steps.mastery: Predict how pH affects an enzyme, and match each enzyme to the pH where it works.
steps.practice: Look up the optimum pH of pepsin, amylase and trypsin, and match each to the part of the gut where it works.
steps.detail: pH changes the charges on the amino acids around the active site. Too far from the optimum and the substrate no longer binds well, or the enzyme unfolds. Each enzyme suits its home: stomach enzymes like strong acid and gut enzymes like mild alkali.
steps.proof: Pepsin near pH 2 in the stomach, amylase near 7 in the mouth, trypsin near 8 in the small intestine.
steps.pitfall: Assuming every enzyme works best at pH 7.

problems.prompt: Pepsin works in the stomach. Is its optimum pH near 2 or near 8?
What happens to pepsin when it reaches the small intestine at pH 8?
problems.answer: It stops working as its shape changes.

problems.prompt: Why does a pH far from the optimum slow an enzyme down?
problems.answer: It changes the charges in the active site, so the substrate no longer fits.

steps.title: Measure a Rate
steps.mastery: Calculate an enzyme reaction rate from data and compare rates fairly.
steps.practice: Collect oxygen from catalase and peroxide every 30 seconds for 3 minutes, then work out the rate in mL per minute.
steps.detail: Rate is product made divided by time, so use the early, steep part of the curve, before the substrate runs low. Change one variable at a time and keep enzyme amount, substrate amount, volume and pH fixed. Repeat each run and average.
steps.proof: A rate in mL per minute from the first minute's data.
steps.pitfall: Using the whole run, including the flat end, which understates the rate.

problems.prompt: A reaction makes 24 mL of oxygen in 4 minutes. What is the rate in mL per minute?
At 20°C, 10 mL forms in 2 minutes. At 30°C, 18 mL forms in 2 minutes. How many times faster is it at 30°C?
To compare 3 temperatures fairly, what must you keep the same?
problems.answer: Enzyme amount, substrate amount, pH and volume.

steps.title: Natural Selection Step by Step
steps.mastery: Explain natural selection in 4 steps: variation, inheritance, overproduction and different survival.
steps.practice: Write Darwin's 4 steps for why moths in a sooty city became mostly dark.
steps.detail: Individuals differ, and some differences are inherited. More young are born than can survive. Those whose traits suit the surroundings survive and breed more, so their alleles become more common. Repeat over many generations and the population changes.
steps.proof: Moths vary in color, color is inherited, birds eat most moths, and dark ones on sooty trees survive to breed.
steps.pitfall: Saying moths turned dark because they needed to. No moth chose anything.

problems.prompt: Name the 4 conditions for natural selection.
problems.answer: Variation, inheritance, more offspring than survive, and different survival.

problems.prompt: Does 1 giraffe that stretches its neck pass a longer neck to its young?
In 1848 most Manchester moths were pale. By 1895, 98% were dark. What changed their survival?
problems.answer: Soot darkened the trees, so birds spotted pale moths more easily.

steps.title: Evidence for Evolution
steps.mastery: Name 4 lines of evidence for evolution: fossils, anatomy, DNA and change seen happening.
steps.practice: Find 1 example each of fossils, homologous structures, DNA comparison and evolution observed directly.
steps.detail: Fossils show forms changing through time in rock layers. Shared bone layouts in different limbs point to a common ancestor. DNA similarity matches the family tree drawn from anatomy. And we can watch it now, as bacteria evolve resistance within years.
steps.proof: Tiktaalik, the bones of a bat wing, human and chimp DNA, and resistant bacteria.
steps.pitfall: Treating any one line of evidence as the whole case. They agree with each other, which is the point.

problems.prompt: The forelimbs of 3 species, human, bat and whale, share the same bones. What are they called?
Why is MRSA, a resistant bacterium, good evidence of evolution?
problems.answer: We can watch the population change within years.

problems.prompt: Tiktaalik is a fossil about 375 million years old. What does it show?
problems.answer: A step between fish and four-legged animals.

steps.title: How New Species Form
steps.mastery: Explain how isolation and divergence split one species into two.
steps.practice: Describe in 4 steps how a river splitting a squirrel population could lead to 2 species.
steps.detail: First a barrier stops the two groups mixing. Then each side gains different mutations and faces different selection. Over many generations they drift apart. Eventually they can't interbreed to make fertile young even if the barrier goes, and they're separate species.
steps.proof: Split, separate mutations, different selection, then no fertile offspring together.
steps.pitfall: Thinking any visible difference makes a new species.

problems.prompt: What makes 2 groups separate species?
problems.answer: They can't interbreed to make fertile offspring.

problems.prompt: A horse and a donkey make a mule, which is sterile. Are horses and donkeys 1 species?
Galapagos finches have different beaks on different islands. What drove that?
problems.answer: Each island's food selected for different beaks.

steps.title: Fix the Misconceptions
steps.mastery: Correct the common misreadings: evolution has no goal, no trying, and humans didn't come from chimps.
steps.practice: Rewrite 3 wrong statements, like 'giraffes grew long necks to reach leaves', as correct ones.
steps.detail: Selection works on variation that's already there, so nothing evolves on purpose. Individuals don't evolve, populations do. Humans and chimps are cousins with a shared ancestor, not ancestor and descendant. And a scientific theory is a well-tested explanation, not a guess.
steps.proof: Giraffes with longer necks reached more leaves and left more young.
steps.pitfall: Using words like 'wanted' or 'needed' to explain a trait.

problems.prompt: Humans and chimps share about 98% of their DNA. Did humans evolve from chimps?
problems.answer: No. We share a common ancestor from about 6 million years ago.

problems.prompt: Is evolution 'just a theory' in the everyday sense of a guess?
problems.answer: No. A scientific theory is a well-tested explanation.

problems.prompt: Does 1 rabbit evolve during its lifetime?

steps.title: Selection in Numbers
steps.mastery: Use simple numbers to show how a small survival edge changes a population over generations.
steps.practice: Start with 100 beetles, 10 green and 90 brown. If green ones survive twice as well, work out the share of green after 1 generation.
steps.detail: Multiply each group by its survival rate, then divide each by the new total to get its share. Even a small edge compounds, generation after generation, like interest on savings. That's how slight differences turn into big changes over thousands of years.
steps.proof: Green goes from 10% to about 18%.
steps.pitfall: Comparing raw survivor counts without dividing by the new total.

problems.prompt: In 200 mice, 50 are dark. What percent are dark?
Dark mice survive at 80% and light ones at 40%. Of 50 dark and 150 light, how many survive in total?
Of the 100 survivors from 50 dark mice at 80% and 150 light mice at 40%, what percent are dark?

steps.title: Alleles and Genotypes
steps.mastery: Use the words allele, genotype and phenotype correctly, and write genotypes with letters.
steps.practice: Write all 3 genotypes for a gene with alleles B and b, and give each one's phenotype if B is dominant for brown eyes.
steps.detail: An allele is one version of a gene. Your genotype is the pair you carry, like Bb, and your phenotype is the trait that shows. A dominant allele shows with one copy. A recessive one only shows when both copies are recessive.
steps.proof: BB and Bb give brown eyes, and bb gives blue.
steps.pitfall: Thinking dominant means more common. A dominant allele can be rare.

problems.prompt: Is the genotype 'Bb' homozygous or heterozygous?
With B dominant for brown and b for blue, what eye color does 'bb' give?
2 brown-eyed parents have a blue-eyed child. What are the parents' genotypes?

steps.title: Punnett Squares
steps.mastery: Draw a Punnett square for one gene and read off the offspring ratios.
steps.practice: Cross Bb with Bb in a Punnett square and give the genotype and phenotype ratios.
steps.detail: Put one parent's two alleles across the top and the other's down the side. Fill each box with one from each. The 4 boxes are 4 equally likely outcomes, so the counts become ratios. Real families vary, since each child is a separate draw.
steps.proof: 1 BB to 2 Bb to 1 bb, so 3 brown to 1 blue.
steps.pitfall: Treating the ratio as a promise, like expecting exactly 1 blue child in 4.

problems.prompt: In a 'Bb x bb' cross, what fraction of the offspring are bb?
Cross Tt with Tt. What percent are tall if T is dominant?
Cross AA with aa. What percent of the offspring are Aa?

steps.title: Mendel's Laws
steps.mastery: State Mendel's laws of segregation and independent assortment, and link them to meiosis.
steps.practice: Explain Mendel's 3:1 pea result in 3 sentences, using alleles separating in meiosis.
steps.detail: Segregation says each parent passes on one allele of each gene, chosen at random. Independent assortment says genes on different chromosomes are inherited separately. Both follow from how chromosomes move in meiosis, which Mendel didn't know about yet.
steps.proof: Each parent passes on T or t at random, so Tt x Tt gives 3 tall to 1 short.
steps.pitfall: Applying independent assortment to genes that sit close together on one chromosome.

problems.prompt: Which plant did Gregor Mendel study?
Mendel crossed 2 heterozygous tall plants and got 787 tall and 277 short. Roughly what ratio is that?
Which of Mendel's laws says alleles of different genes are inherited separately?

steps.title: Read a Pedigree
steps.mastery: Read a family pedigree and decide whether a trait is dominant or recessive.
steps.practice: Draw a 3-generation pedigree where 2 unaffected parents have 1 affected child, and say what that shows.
steps.detail: Squares are males and circles are females, and shaded means affected. If two unaffected parents have an affected child, the trait must be recessive, since both carried a hidden copy. A dominant trait usually shows in every generation.
steps.proof: The trait is recessive, and both parents must be carriers.
steps.pitfall: Deciding from one family branch without checking the whole chart.

problems.prompt: 2 unaffected parents have an affected child. Is the trait dominant or recessive?
In a pedigree, what does 1 shaded square stand for?
An affected parent and an unaffected one have 4 children, 2 of them affected. Could the trait be dominant?
problems.answer: Yes. A heterozygous affected parent would pass it to about half.

steps.title: Beyond Simple Dominance
steps.mastery: Work crosses with incomplete dominance, codominance and sex-linked genes.
steps.practice: Cross 2 pink snapdragons, where red and white show incomplete dominance, and give the color ratio.
steps.detail: In incomplete dominance the mix shows in between, like pink. In codominance both show fully, like blood type AB. Sex-linked genes sit on the X chromosome, so males, with one X, show a recessive allele with just one copy.
steps.proof: 1 red to 2 pink to 1 white.
steps.pitfall: Expecting a 3:1 ratio when neither allele is dominant.

problems.prompt: Blood type AB shows both A and B. What kind of inheritance is that?
Hemophilia is X-linked. A carrier mother and an XY father without it have a son. What's the chance he has it?
Why are X-linked recessive traits more common in XY males?
problems.answer: Males have only 1 X, so a single recessive allele shows.

steps.title: Negative Feedback
steps.mastery: Explain negative feedback: a change is detected and the response pushes the value back toward normal.
steps.practice: Draw a thermostat loop with a sensor, a control center and an effector, then draw your body's temperature loop the same way.
steps.detail: A sensor notices a change, a control center compares it to the set point, and an effector acts to undo the change. Once the value is back, the response stops. That loop holds temperature, blood sugar and water steady inside you.
steps.proof: Thermometer, thermostat, heater. Skin and brain sensors, hypothalamus, sweat glands and muscles.
steps.pitfall: Thinking negative feedback means something bad. It means the response opposes the change.

problems.prompt: A home thermostat is set to 20°C and the room drops to 18°C. What does the heater do?
problems.answer: It turns on until the room is back to 20°C.

problems.prompt: In 1 negative feedback loop, does the response push the value further away or back toward normal?
Name the 3 parts of a feedback loop.

steps.title: Temperature Control
steps.mastery: Describe how the body cools itself and warms itself to stay near 37°C.
steps.practice: List 3 ways your body cools at 39°C and 3 ways it warms at 35°C.
steps.detail: The hypothalamus in the brain acts as the thermostat. When you're hot, you sweat and the blood vessels near your skin widen to lose heat. When you're cold, you shiver, the skin vessels narrow, and your hair stands up, which helps more in furry animals.
steps.proof: Cooling: sweating, wider skin vessels, less activity. Warming: shivering, narrower vessels, goosebumps.
steps.pitfall: Saying sweat cools you by being wet. It cools you as it evaporates.

problems.prompt: Which brain region keeps your temperature near 37°C?
Why do you shiver at 35°C?
Sweat only cools you as it evaporates. Why is a humid 30°C day so uncomfortable?
problems.answer: Humid air slows evaporation, so sweat doesn't cool you.

steps.title: Blood Sugar
steps.mastery: Explain how insulin and glucagon keep blood glucose in range.
steps.practice: Draw what happens to blood glucose after a meal and after 4 hours without food, showing where insulin and glucagon act.
steps.detail: After a meal, glucose rises and the pancreas releases insulin, which makes cells take it up and the liver store it as glycogen. When glucose falls, the pancreas releases glucagon, which makes the liver turn glycogen back into glucose.
steps.proof: Insulin brings glucose down after the meal, and glucagon raises it after 4 hours without food.
steps.pitfall: Mixing up glycogen, the stored form, with glucagon, the hormone.

problems.prompt: Which hormone lowers blood glucose after a 600 kcal meal?
Which 1 organ releases both insulin and glucagon?
In type 1 diabetes, which hormone isn't made?

steps.title: Water Balance
steps.mastery: Explain how the kidneys and ADH keep water and salt in balance.
steps.practice: Compare urine color and volume after drinking 2 liters of water and after a hot hike with little to drink, and explain each with ADH.
steps.detail: When blood gets too concentrated, the brain releases ADH, and the kidneys hold onto water, making small amounts of dark urine. When you've had plenty to drink, ADH drops and the kidneys let water go, so urine is pale and plentiful.
steps.proof: After 2 liters: lots of pale urine, low ADH. After the hike: a little dark urine, high ADH.
steps.pitfall: Thinking the kidneys only remove waste. They also set your water level.

problems.prompt: Which hormone tells the kidneys to save water: ADH or insulin?
After drinking 2 L of water fast, is your urine darker or paler?
problems.answer: Paler, and there's more of it.

problems.prompt: Why does a meal with 3 g of salt make you thirsty?
problems.answer: Your blood gets more concentrated, so your brain triggers thirst to dilute it.

steps.title: When Balance Fails
steps.mastery: Explain what happens when a feedback loop breaks, using fever, heat stroke or diabetes as examples.
steps.practice: Pick 1 condition, like heat stroke, and draw its feedback loop with the broken part marked.
steps.detail: When a sensor, control center or effector fails, the value drifts out of range and stays there. In heat stroke, sweating stops and temperature runs away. In type 1 diabetes, no insulin is made. A few loops are positive on purpose, like contractions in childbirth.
steps.proof: The heat stroke loop with the sweating effector crossed out.
steps.pitfall: Calling every runaway change positive feedback. Most are broken negative loops.

problems.prompt: Body temperature reaches 41°C and sweating has stopped. What is this called?
During the 1st stage of childbirth, oxytocin makes each contraction stronger. Is that negative or positive feedback?
problems.answer: Positive. Each contraction triggers a stronger one.

problems.prompt: Why is untreated type 1 diabetes dangerous?
problems.answer: Blood glucose climbs out of control, damaging organs.

steps.title: First Lines of Defense
steps.mastery: Name the barriers that keep pathogens out before the immune system has to act, like skin, mucus and stomach acid.
steps.practice: List 4 barriers and 1 pathogen each one stops, like stomach acid against bacteria in food.
steps.detail: Most germs never get inside. Skin is a tough physical wall. Mucus traps microbes in your airways and tiny hairs called cilia sweep it up. Stomach acid kills most bacteria in food, and tears and saliva hold enzymes that break bacteria apart.
steps.proof: Skin, mucus with cilia, stomach acid and tears, each with a germ it blocks.
steps.pitfall: Forgetting the barriers and jumping straight to antibodies.

problems.prompt: What pH is stomach acid, roughly: 2 or 7?
Your airways make about 100 mL of mucus a day. How does it protect you?
problems.answer: It traps microbes, and cilia sweep them out.

problems.prompt: Why does a 1 cm cut raise your infection risk?

steps.title: The Fast Response
steps.mastery: Describe inflammation and phagocytes, the fast response that works the same way every time.
steps.practice: Draw a splinter wound and show 4 steps: damage, swelling, phagocytes arriving and germs being engulfed.
steps.detail: Damaged cells release chemicals that widen nearby blood vessels, so the area gets red, warm and swollen. White blood cells called phagocytes squeeze out and swallow the invaders. This innate response starts within hours but doesn't remember anything.
steps.proof: 4 panels, ending with a phagocyte swallowing bacteria.
steps.pitfall: Thinking swelling is the damage itself. It's the body's response.

problems.prompt: Why does an infected cut turn red and warm after 1 day?
problems.answer: More blood flows there, bringing white blood cells.

problems.prompt: What does 1 phagocyte do to a bacterium?
The 1st time you meet a germ, is the innate response faster or slower than antibodies?

steps.title: Antibodies and Memory
steps.mastery: Explain how B cells make antibodies for one antigen, and how memory cells speed up the next response.
steps.practice: Sketch antibody levels over 30 days for a first infection and a second one, and mark the difference.
steps.detail: Each B cell recognizes one antigen, a shape on the germ's surface. The matching B cells multiply and pour out antibodies, which tag the germ for destruction. That takes about a week the first time. Memory cells stay behind, so a second exposure is answered faster and harder.
steps.proof: The 2nd curve rises sooner, peaks higher and lasts longer than the first.
steps.pitfall: Thinking one antibody works against every germ.

problems.prompt: What does 1 antibody bind to?
The first response peaks after about 10 days. Is the second one faster or slower?
Why don't most people catch chickenpox 2 times?
problems.answer: Memory cells recognize it and clear it before you get sick.

steps.title: How Vaccines Work
steps.mastery: Explain how vaccines train memory cells without causing the disease.
steps.practice: Write 3 sentences on how a measles vaccine leads to protection, using the words antigen, B cell and memory cell.
steps.detail: A vaccine shows the immune system an antigen without the danger, as a weakened germ, a piece of it or instructions to make the piece. B cells respond and memory cells form. If the real germ arrives, the fast second response stops it. When enough people are immune, outbreaks can't spread.
steps.proof: The vaccine's antigen triggers B cells, which leave memory cells that answer measles quickly.
steps.pitfall: Thinking a vaccine gives you a mild case of the disease.

problems.prompt: What does 1 vaccine dose contain?
problems.answer: A harmless form or piece of the germ, or instructions to make one.

problems.prompt: Measles needs about 95% of people immune for herd immunity. In a town of 10,000, how many must be immune?
Why do some vaccines need a booster after 10 years?
problems.answer: Memory fades, and another dose builds the response back up.

steps.title: Self and Not-Self
steps.mastery: Explain how the immune system tells self from not-self, and what goes wrong in allergies and autoimmunity.
steps.practice: Compare an allergy, an autoimmune disease and an organ rejection in a 3-row table.
steps.detail: Your cells carry markers the immune system learns to leave alone. An allergy is a strong response to something harmless, like pollen. Autoimmunity is an attack on your own cells. Rejection is a correct attack on a transplant, which drugs have to hold back.
steps.proof: Allergy: harmless trigger. Autoimmune: attacks self. Rejection: attacks donor tissue.
steps.pitfall: Calling an allergy a weak immune system. It's an overactive one.

problems.prompt: In type 1 diabetes, what does the immune system attack?
problems.answer: The insulin-making cells of the pancreas.

problems.prompt: Pollen is harmless, yet about 1 in 5 people get hay fever. Why?
problems.answer: Their immune system wrongly treats it as a threat.

problems.prompt: Why do people with 1 new kidney take drugs that weaken immunity?
problems.answer: To stop the immune system rejecting the new organ.

steps.title: List the Signs of Life
steps.mastery: Name 7 traits that living things share, and give an example of each in an animal you know.
steps.practice: List the 7 signs of life using MRS GREN, and give one example of each in a pet dog.
steps.detail: MRS GREN is a memory aid: movement, respiration, sensitivity, growth, reproduction, excretion and nutrition. Textbooks also list being made of cells, keeping a steady inside and evolving over generations. A living thing shows all of these over its life, though not every one at every moment.
steps.proof: Running, breathing, smelling food, growing up, having puppies, passing urine and eating.
steps.pitfall: Calling something alive because it shows one sign, like a fire that grows and uses oxygen.

problems.prompt: In MRS GREN, what does the 'E' stand for?
A seed sits in a packet for 3 years doing nothing visible. Is it alive?
problems.answer: Yes. It's dormant, with slow metabolism, and grows when planted.

problems.prompt: Fire grows, moves and uses oxygen. Name 1 sign of life it lacks.
problems.answer: It isn't made of cells, and it doesn't reproduce from inherited instructions.

steps.title: Cells Are the Unit
steps.mastery: Explain the 3 claims of cell theory and use them to judge whether something is an organism.
steps.practice: Write the 3 parts of cell theory, then use them to sort a bacterium, a virus and a red blood cell.
steps.detail: Cell theory says every living thing is made of one or more cells, the cell is the basic unit of life, and every cell comes from an existing cell. A bacterium is a whole organism in one cell. A red blood cell is alive but only part of an organism. A virus isn't a cell at all.
steps.proof: Bacterium: an organism. Red blood cell: a living cell, not an organism. Virus: not a cell.
steps.pitfall: Calling any cell an organism. Most cells are parts of a bigger one.

problems.prompt: How many claims make up the cell theory of Schleiden and Schwann?
Does 1 bacterium count as a whole organism under cell theory?
problems.answer: Yes. It's one cell that lives on its own.

problems.prompt: What does the 3rd part of cell theory say cells come from?

steps.title: Metabolism and Energy
steps.mastery: Explain metabolism as all the chemical reactions in an organism, and why it needs a steady energy supply.
steps.practice: List 3 reactions going on in your body right now, like digesting lunch, and say which release energy and which use it.
steps.detail: Metabolism has two halves. Catabolism breaks big molecules into small ones and releases energy, as in digestion and respiration. Anabolism builds big molecules from small ones and uses energy, as in growing muscle. Cells pass energy between the two using ATP.
steps.proof: Digestion and respiration release energy, and building muscle protein uses it.
steps.pitfall: Thinking metabolism means only how fast you burn calories.

problems.prompt: Which molecule do cells use as their energy currency: ATP or DNA?
Breaking starch into glucose is 1 example of which kind of metabolism?
Building a protein from 20 kinds of amino acids is which kind of metabolism?

steps.title: Respond and Stay Steady
steps.mastery: Give examples of organisms sensing and responding to change, including keeping their inside steady.
steps.practice: Write 3 responses a plant makes and 3 a human makes, like bending toward light or sweating.
steps.detail: Every organism detects changes, called stimuli, and responds. Some responses act on the outside world, like a plant turning to light. Others keep the inside steady, like sweating to cool down, which is called homeostasis. Both are signs of life.
steps.proof: Plant: bending to light, roots growing down, closing pores. Human: sweating, shivering, pulling a hand from heat.
steps.pitfall: Leaving out plants because their responses are slow.

problems.prompt: A plant on a windowsill bends toward the window over 2 days. What is it responding to?
Your body temperature stays near 37°C on a cold day. What is that steadiness called?
Name 1 way your body responds when its temperature rises to 38°C.
problems.answer: Sweating, or widening blood vessels near the skin.

steps.title: Judge the Borderline Cases
steps.mastery: Argue whether viruses, seeds and prions are alive, using the signs of life as evidence.
steps.practice: Score a virus on each of the 7 MRS GREN signs, then write 2 sentences on whether it counts as alive.
steps.detail: A virus has genes and evolves, but it has no cells, no metabolism and can only copy itself inside a host cell. That's why biologists disagree about it. Use the signs of life as a checklist, then say which ones you think matter most and why.
steps.proof: A scorecard showing the virus fails most signs, plus a reasoned verdict.
steps.pitfall: Answering yes or no with no evidence behind it.

problems.prompt: Can 1 virus copy itself outside a host cell?
problems.answer: No. It needs a host cell's machinery.

problems.prompt: Does a virus carry out respiration, the R in MRS GREN?
problems.answer: No. It has no metabolism of its own.

problems.prompt: Give 1 reason someone might call a virus alive.
problems.answer: It has genes and evolves by natural selection.

steps.title: The Phospholipid Bilayer
steps.mastery: Describe the membrane as a bilayer of phospholipids, heads out and tails in, studded with proteins.
steps.practice: Draw a section of membrane with 6 phospholipids, 1 channel protein and 1 carrier, labeling the water-loving heads.
steps.detail: Each phospholipid has a head that likes water and two tails that avoid it. In water they line up in two layers, tails hiding in the middle. Small uncharged molecules slip through. Ions and big molecules need proteins to get across.
steps.proof: A two-layer drawing with heads facing out on both sides and proteins spanning it.
steps.pitfall: Drawing the tails facing the water, which is the opposite of what they do.

problems.prompt: In a bilayer of 2 layers, do the tails face toward water or away from it?
Which crosses a bilayer more easily: O2 or glucose?
Why is the membrane described as a 'fluid mosaic'?
problems.answer: Its parts drift around like a fluid, and proteins dot it like tiles in a mosaic.

steps.title: Diffusion
steps.mastery: Explain diffusion as net movement from high to low concentration, and name what speeds it up.
steps.practice: Drop food coloring into water at 10°C and at 40°C, time how long each takes to spread, and explain the difference.
steps.detail: Particles move randomly all the time. Where there are more of them, more move away than move in, so there's a net flow down the concentration gradient. Heat speeds the particles up, a steeper gradient speeds the flow, and a thinner barrier shortens the trip.
steps.proof: The warm water spreads the color faster, because its particles move faster.
steps.pitfall: Saying particles stop moving once the concentration is even. They keep moving, with no net flow.

problems.prompt: Oxygen is 10 units outside a cell and 2 inside. Which way does it diffuse?
Name 2 things that speed up diffusion.
problems.answer: A higher temperature and a steeper concentration gradient.

problems.prompt: Does diffusion use ATP?

steps.title: Osmosis
steps.mastery: Predict which way water moves across a membrane from the solute concentrations on each side.
steps.practice: Put potato strips in 0%, 5% and 20% salt water for 30 minutes, measure each strip's mass change, and explain the results.
steps.detail: Osmosis is water diffusing across a membrane that lets water through but not the solute. Water moves toward the side with more solute, where free water is scarcer. Cells swell in dilute solutions and shrink in strong ones. Plant walls stop them bursting.
steps.proof: The strip in 0% gains mass, and the ones in 5% and 20% lose mass, the 20% one most.
steps.pitfall: Saying the salt moves. In osmosis, only the water crosses.

problems.prompt: A red blood cell is put in 0% salt water. What happens to it?
problems.answer: Water rushes in, and it swells and may burst.

problems.prompt: A potato strip goes from 5.0 g to 4.6 g in salt water. What is its percent change?
Side A is 1% salt and side B is 3%, with a membrane between. Which way does water move?

accept: from side A to side B

steps.title: Active Transport
steps.mastery: Explain active transport as moving molecules against their gradient using carrier proteins and ATP.
steps.practice: Sketch the sodium-potassium pump moving 3 Na+ out and 2 K+ in, and mark where ATP is used.
steps.detail: Sometimes a cell needs more of something inside than outside, like a root cell collecting minerals. Moving it uphill takes energy. Carrier proteins grab the molecule, use ATP to change shape, and release it on the other side. Anything that blocks ATP stops it.
steps.proof: A pump drawn with 3 Na+ leaving, 2 K+ entering and ATP splitting.
steps.pitfall: Calling any movement through a protein active. Channel diffusion is passive.

problems.prompt: How many Na+ ions does the sodium-potassium pump move out per cycle?
A root cell takes in nitrate while already holding 100 times more than the soil. Which kind of transport is that?
Cyanide stops ATP production. What happens to active transport?
problems.answer: It stops, since there's no ATP to power it.

steps.title: Bulk Transport
steps.mastery: Describe endocytosis and exocytosis, which move large particles in and out inside vesicles.
steps.practice: Draw a white blood cell engulfing a bacterium in 4 stages, then draw a cell releasing insulin by exocytosis.
