steps.pitfall: Linking to work with no explanation of your role.

problems.prompt: Name 1 sample a writer could add to a 3-piece portfolio.
Name 3 things to write for each sample.
problems.answer: Your role, the problem and the result.

problems.prompt: Name 1 free place to host a portfolio.

steps.title: Energy Audit
steps.mastery: Notice which work gives and drains energy.
steps.practice: Rate every task for 2 weeks from -2 to +2 on how it made you feel.
steps.detail: Your energy shows what you actually enjoy. Patterns over 2 weeks are more reliable than guesses.
steps.proof: You have 2 weeks of ratings.
steps.pitfall: Deciding what you want from job titles alone.

problems.prompt: Over 2 weeks you rate every client call +2. What does that suggest?
Why rate tasks for 2 weeks instead of 1 day?
problems.answer: Patterns over time are more reliable.

problems.prompt: A task is rated -2 every time. What does that suggest?

steps.title: Conditions, Not Titles
steps.mastery: Name the day-to-day setup that makes a job good for you.
steps.practice: List your top 5 work conditions, like autonomy, pay or team size.
steps.detail: Titles hide the daily reality. Conditions like hours, independence and people are what make work good or bad.
steps.proof: Your list has 5 ranked conditions.
steps.pitfall: Chasing a title without asking what the days are like.

problems.prompt: Name 3 work conditions.
Rank 'pay' and 'autonomy' for someone who quit 2 jobs over micromanagement.
2 jobs both called 'Product Manager' can differ how?
problems.answer: In hours, independence and the people you work with.

steps.title: Values
steps.mastery: Identify the values your work should fit.
steps.practice: Pick your top 3 values from a list of 20 and describe 1 job that would honor each.
steps.detail: Work that clashes with your values wears you down. Naming them makes choices easier.
steps.proof: You picked 3 values with examples.
steps.pitfall: Ignoring values until you're unhappy.

problems.prompt: Name 1 job that honors the value 'creativity'.
Name 2 common work values.
You value 'security' but join a risky startup. Name 1 likely result.

steps.title: Try Small Experiments
steps.mastery: Test possible directions cheaply.
steps.practice: Pick 2 possible directions and spend 3 hours on each this month.
steps.detail: Thinking alone rarely settles it. Small tries give real data about what you like.
steps.proof: You spent 3 hours on each direction.
steps.pitfall: Planning forever without trying anything.

problems.prompt: Name 1 cheap 3-hour test of teaching as a career.
Why try 2 directions for 3 hours each instead of thinking for a month?
After 3 hours of coding you loved it. Name a sensible next step.

steps.title: Revisit Yearly
steps.mastery: Review your direction once a year.
steps.practice: Set a yearly 1-hour review of what you want from work.
steps.detail: What you want changes. A yearly check stops you drifting for years in the wrong place.
steps.proof: A yearly review is on your calendar.
steps.pitfall: Setting a direction once and never checking it.

problems.prompt: When should your yearly 1-hour review happen?
problems.answer: At a fixed time, like each January.

problems.prompt: Your wants changed after 3 years. Why does a yearly review help?
problems.answer: It catches the change before you drift.

problems.prompt: Name 1 question for the review.
problems.answer: What gave me energy this year?

steps.title: Ask in the First 2 Lines
steps.mastery: Put the request and deadline at the top of every message.
steps.practice: Rewrite your next 5 emails so the first 2 lines say what you need and by when.
steps.detail: Readers skim. If the ask is in paragraph 4, many people never reach it. Lead with the ask, then give context.
steps.proof: All 5 emails state the ask in the first 2 lines.
steps.pitfall: Burying the request under background.

problems.prompt: Rewrite the opening 'Hope you're well! I wanted to give some background...' to lead with the ask.
problems.answer: Could you approve the budget by Thursday? Background below.

problems.prompt: Where should the deadline go: line 1 or the last line?
Your email has 4 paragraphs and the ask is in the 4th. What should change?
problems.answer: Move the ask to the top.

steps.title: Subject Lines That Work
steps.mastery: Write subject lines that say what the message needs.
steps.practice: Write subject lines for your next 10 emails that include an action and a date where relevant.
steps.detail: A subject like 'Approval needed: budget by Thu' gets opened and found later. 'Quick question' does not.
steps.proof: All 10 subject lines name the topic and action.
steps.pitfall: Writing 'Hi' or 'Question' as the subject.

problems.prompt: Improve the subject 'Question'.
Name 2 things a strong subject line includes.
problems.answer: The topic, and the action or deadline.

problems.prompt: Is 'Following up' a strong subject line? Answer yes or no.
problems.answer: No, it doesn't say what about.

steps.title: Keep It Short
steps.mastery: Cut messages to what the reader needs.
steps.practice: Cut your next 3 long emails by half before sending.
steps.detail: Long messages get skimmed or postponed. Bullets, short paragraphs and one topic per email get answers.
steps.proof: Each email is at most half its first draft.
steps.pitfall: Sending 6 paragraphs when 3 lines would do.

problems.prompt: A draft has 300 words. Cut by half, how long is it?
Your email covers 3 unrelated topics. What should you do?
problems.answer: Split it into 3 emails, or lead with the most urgent.

problems.prompt: Name 1 format that makes 4 questions easy to answer.

steps.title: Make Replies Easy
steps.mastery: Phrase questions so they can be answered in 1 line.
steps.practice: Turn 3 open questions in your next emails into yes or no or A or B choices.
steps.detail: 'What do you think?' takes effort. 'Option A or B? I'd pick A because...' gets a quick answer.
steps.proof: All 3 questions got 1-line replies.
steps.pitfall: Asking open-ended questions when you need a decision.

problems.prompt: Rewrite 'What do you think about the dates?' as an easy choice.
problems.answer: Does March 3 or March 10 work better?

problems.prompt: Why add 'I'd pick A' to an A or B question for a busy VP?
problems.answer: They can just agree, which is faster.

problems.prompt: You need 1 decision from a busy VP. How many options should you give?

steps.title: Check Before Sending
steps.mastery: Check recipients, attachments and tone before hitting send.
steps.practice: Pause 10 seconds before sending your next 20 emails and check recipients, attachments and tone.
steps.detail: Most email disasters are wrong recipients or missing attachments. A short pause catches them.
steps.proof: No email this week needed a follow-up correction.
steps.pitfall: Hitting send and then writing 'Oops, attached now'.

problems.prompt: Name 3 things to check before sending.
You wrote 'see attached' but nothing is attached. When should you catch it?
Is 'Reply All' right for a note meant only for Jo? Answer yes or no.

steps.title: Listen First
steps.mastery: Hear feedback out fully before responding.
steps.practice: In your next 3 feedback conversations, say nothing until the person finishes, then summarize what you heard.
steps.detail: Interrupting to defend yourself stops the person from finishing, and you miss the real point.
steps.proof: You summarized correctly all 3 times.
steps.pitfall: Interrupting with 'But the reason was' before they finish.

problems.prompt: Name 1 sentence to start summarizing feedback.
Your manager says 'The demo felt rushed' and you reply 'But the reason was'. What did that cost?
problems.answer: You stopped them, and missed the real point.

problems.prompt: After 5 minutes of feedback, should your first words be a defense or a summary?

steps.title: Ask for Specifics
steps.mastery: Turn vague feedback into concrete examples.
steps.practice: When you next get vague feedback, ask for 1 specific example.
steps.detail: 'Be more proactive' is hard to act on. 'In Tuesday's meeting, you could have raised the risk' is not.
steps.proof: You got at least 1 concrete example.
steps.pitfall: Nodding at vague feedback and changing nothing.

problems.prompt: Turn 'be more proactive' into a question for specifics.
problems.answer: Can you give me 1 example where I could have been more proactive?

problems.prompt: Which is easier to act on: 'be more proactive' or 'raise the risk in Tuesday's meeting'?
problems.answer: Raise the risk in Tuesday's meeting.

choices: Raise the risk in Tuesday's meeting
accept: Raise the risk in Tuesday's meeting

problems.prompt: You asked for 1 example and got none. Name 1 next step.
problems.answer: Ask them to point it out next time it happens.

steps.title: Separate Work from Self
steps.mastery: Treat feedback as about the work, not your worth.
steps.practice: Write down 1 piece of recent critical feedback and rewrite it as a statement about the work.
steps.detail: 'This report is unclear' is not 'You are bad at your job'. Defensiveness is normal, but it costs you the information.
steps.proof: Your rewrite is about the work only.
steps.pitfall: Hearing 'this is unclear' as 'you are bad'.

problems.prompt: Rewrite 'You're sloppy' as feedback on work.
Is getting defensive normal? Answer yes or no.
problems.answer: Yes, but it costs you information.

problems.prompt: You argue for 10 minutes against feedback. What do you lose?

steps.title: Ask for Feedback
steps.mastery: Request feedback regularly instead of waiting.
steps.practice: Ask 2 colleagues 'What's 1 thing I could do better?' this month.
steps.detail: People rarely volunteer criticism. A specific, low-stakes question makes it easy to answer.
steps.proof: You got answers from 2 colleagues.
steps.pitfall: Waiting for the annual review to learn how you're doing.

problems.prompt: Name 1 easy question to ask for feedback.
problems.answer: What's 1 thing I could do better?

problems.prompt: Why ask for 1 thing instead of 'any feedback'?
When is a better time to ask a colleague for feedback: right after a project or at the 12-month review?

steps.title: Act and Report Back
steps.mastery: Act on feedback and tell the person.
steps.practice: Pick 1 piece of feedback, act on it for 2 weeks, then tell the giver what changed.
steps.detail: Acting shows you listened. Reporting back makes people more willing to give feedback again.
steps.proof: You told the person what changed.
steps.pitfall: Thanking people for feedback and changing nothing.

problems.prompt: You were told your emails run too long. Name 1 change to try for 2 weeks.
Why tell Sam, 2 weeks later, what you changed after the feedback?
problems.answer: Sam will be more willing to give feedback again.

problems.prompt: Name 1 sign feedback was heard.
problems.answer: A visible change in your work.

steps.title: STAR Stories
steps.mastery: Tell clear, short stories about your past work in interviews.
steps.practice: Write 5 stories using STAR: situation, task, action and result.
steps.detail: Behavioral questions ask about the past. STAR keeps answers clear and focused on what you did and what resulted.
steps.proof: You have 5 written STAR stories.
steps.pitfall: Rambling without saying what you did.

problems.prompt: What does STAR stand for?
Your STAR story spends 2 minutes on the situation and 10 seconds on the action. What's wrong?
problems.answer: The action should be the longest part.

problems.prompt: Which STAR part should be longest?

steps.title: Research the Company
steps.mastery: Prepare by researching the company and role.
steps.practice: Spend 1 hour researching your next interview company and write 3 facts you could mention.
steps.detail: Knowing the product, recent news and the team shows genuine interest and helps you ask better questions.
steps.proof: You have 3 facts ready.
steps.pitfall: Asking the interviewer what the company does.

problems.prompt: Name 1 fact worth knowing before interviewing at Patagonia.
Name 2 things to research.
Is 'So what does your company do?' a good interview question? Answer yes or no.

steps.title: Ask Good Questions
steps.mastery: Prepare questions that show interest and get useful answers.
steps.practice: Prepare 5 questions for your next interview, like 'What does success look like in 6 months?'
steps.detail: Your questions are part of the interview. Ask about the work, the team and how success is measured.
steps.proof: You asked at least 3 of them.
steps.pitfall: Saying 'No questions'.

problems.prompt: Name 1 strong question for an interviewer.
problems.answer: What does success look like in 6 months?

problems.prompt: Name 1 question about the team to ask an interviewer.
problems.answer: How does the team decide priorities?

problems.prompt: Is 'No questions' a good answer? Answer yes or no.

steps.title: Mock Interviews
steps.mastery: Practice interviewing out loud with feedback.
steps.practice: Run 2 mock interviews with a friend, recording at least 1.
steps.detail: Saying answers aloud is different from knowing them. Recordings show filler words and rambling.
steps.proof: You did 2 mocks and noted 3 fixes.
steps.pitfall: Preparing only in your head.

problems.prompt: Your mock recording has 30 'ums' in 5 minutes. How many per minute?
Name 1 thing a recording shows.
Why practice STAR answers aloud instead of just writing them?
problems.answer: Saying answers is different from knowing them.

steps.title: Send a Thank-You
steps.mastery: Follow up after interviews.
steps.practice: Send a 3-sentence thank-you within 24 hours of your next interview, mentioning 1 specific topic.
steps.detail: A short thank-you is polite and can remind them of a strong moment. Mention something specific.
steps.proof: You sent it within 24 hours.
steps.pitfall: Sending a generic copy-paste note.

problems.prompt: Your interview was Tuesday at 2 pm. Send the thank-you by when?
Name 1 thing to mention in it.
problems.answer: A specific topic from the interview.

problems.prompt: Should a thank-you note be about 3 sentences or 3 paragraphs?

steps.title: Know Why You're There
steps.mastery: Know the purpose of a meeting before it starts.
steps.practice: Write 1 line on the purpose of each of your next 5 meetings before they start.
steps.detail: If you can't say why you're there, ask or decline. Meetings without a purpose waste everyone's time.
steps.proof: All 5 meetings have a written purpose.
steps.pitfall: Attending meetings without knowing what they're for.

problems.prompt: A meeting invite says only 'Sync'. Name 1 thing to do.
problems.answer: Ask the organizer what decision or update it's for.

problems.prompt: Name 3 common meeting purposes.
You can't name a purpose for a 1-hour meeting. Name 1 option.
problems.answer: Decline, or ask for an agenda.

steps.title: Contribute Once
steps.mastery: Make at least 1 useful contribution in each meeting.
steps.practice: Prepare 1 point or question before each of your next 5 meetings and raise it.
steps.detail: Preparing one point makes it far easier to speak. One clear contribution beats ten vague ones.
steps.proof: You contributed in all 5 meetings.
steps.pitfall: Staying silent and raising concerns afterward in private.

problems.prompt: Why prepare 1 point before a meeting instead of improvising?
problems.answer: It's much easier to speak up with something ready.

problems.prompt: Name 1 good contribution if you have no opinion.
You think the launch date is risky but say nothing until after the 3 pm meeting. What's the cost?
problems.answer: The decision gets made without your concern.

steps.title: Leave with Owners and Dates
steps.mastery: End meetings with each decision assigned to an owner and a date.
steps.practice: In your next 3 meetings, ask 'Who owns this and by when?' for every decision.
steps.detail: Without an owner and a date, decisions drift. Saying it out loud prevents 'I thought you were doing it'.
steps.proof: Every decision in those 3 meetings has an owner and a date.
steps.pitfall: Leaving with 'we should' and nobody assigned.

problems.prompt: A meeting decides 'we should update the FAQ'. What 2 details are missing?
Name the 1 question that turns a vague 'we should' into an action.
problems.answer: Who owns this, and by when?

problems.prompt: A meeting makes 3 decisions with owners and dates, and 2 more action items with owners. How many follow-ups do you track?

steps.title: Run a Short Meeting
steps.mastery: Keep the meetings you run short and focused.
steps.practice: Run 1 meeting with a 3-item agenda sent a day ahead, and finish within the scheduled time.
steps.detail: An agenda tells people what to prepare. Timeboxing items keeps the meeting short. End early if you're done.
steps.proof: The meeting ended on time with all 3 items covered.
steps.pitfall: Running a meeting with no agenda and overrunning.

problems.prompt: A 30-minute meeting has 3 items. About how many minutes each?
Your meeting is Thursday at 10 am. When should the agenda go out at the latest?
The meeting finishes in 20 of 30 minutes. What should you do?

steps.title: Cancel Useless Meetings
steps.mastery: Replace meetings that could be a message.
steps.practice: Review your recurring meetings and suggest replacing 1 with a written update.
steps.detail: Status updates rarely need a meeting. A written update saves an hour for every person and can be read anytime.
steps.proof: You replaced or shortened 1 recurring meeting.
steps.pitfall: Keeping a weekly meeting just because it exists.

problems.prompt: A weekly 1-hour status meeting has 8 people. How many person-hours a week?
Name 1 kind of meeting that could be a message.
Which needs a live meeting: a 'status update' or a hard decision with disagreement?

steps.title: Know the Range
steps.mastery: Research the market pay range before talking numbers.
steps.practice: Find 3 salary data points for your target role and location.
steps.detail: Sites like Levels.fyi and Glassdoor, plus people in the role, show the range. Knowing it keeps you from anchoring low.
steps.proof: You have a range from 3 sources.
steps.pitfall: Naming a number with no research.

problems.prompt: 3 sources show $58,000, $62,000 and $66,000. What is the average?
Name 1 site with salary data.
Why research the range before naming a number to HR?

steps.title: Ask Once, Specifically
steps.mastery: Make a clear, polite counteroffer.
steps.practice: Write a counteroffer script for a $60,000 offer asking for $66,000 with 1 reason.
steps.detail: Asking once with a specific number and reason is normal and expected. Most offers have room.
steps.proof: Your script is polite, specific and under 4 sentences.
steps.pitfall: Accepting the first offer without asking.

problems.prompt: $66,000 is what percent above $60,000?
Name 1 good reason to give.
Is it normal to negotiate an offer? Answer yes or no.

steps.title: Beyond Salary
steps.mastery: Negotiate other parts of the offer.
steps.practice: List 5 non-salary items you could ask for, like start date or remote days.
steps.detail: If salary is fixed, other things may not be: signing bonus, vacation, remote work, title, start date.
steps.proof: Your list has 5 items.
steps.pitfall: Thinking salary is the only negotiable part.

problems.prompt: Name 3 non-salary items to negotiate.
problems.answer: Signing bonus, vacation and remote days.

problems.prompt: Salary is fixed. Name 1 other ask.
Name 1 non-salary ask if you take 2 evening classes a week.

steps.title: Stay Calm Under Silence
steps.mastery: Handle pauses and pushback without backing down.
steps.practice: Rehearse your counteroffer with a friend who pushes back 2 times.
steps.detail: Silence after an ask feels long but is normal. Restate your reason calmly instead of filling the gap with a lower number.
steps.proof: You held your number through 2 pushbacks.
steps.pitfall: Lowering your ask during a 5-second silence.

problems.prompt: After your ask, there's silence. What should you do?
The recruiter says 'That's a lot.' Should you drop to $62,000 right away? Answer yes or no.
Name 1 calm response to 'That's above our budget'.
problems.answer: I understand. Is there flexibility on a signing bonus?

steps.title: Get It in Writing
steps.mastery: Confirm the final offer in writing.
steps.practice: Ask for a written offer after agreeing, and check all 4 key terms: salary, start date, bonus and title.
steps.detail: Verbal agreements can be misremembered. Check salary, start date, bonus and anything else agreed.
steps.proof: Your written offer matches the agreement.
steps.pitfall: Resigning from your current job on a verbal offer.

problems.prompt: Name 3 terms to check in a written offer.
Should you resign before getting a written offer? Answer yes or no.
You agreed to a $5,000 bonus on a call. Why get it in writing?

steps.title: Keep in Touch
steps.mastery: Keep past colleagues as real contacts, not names in a list.
steps.practice: Send 1 short check-in message a week for 4 weeks to people you worked well with.
steps.detail: Relationships fade without contact. A short message every few months keeps them warm, long before you need anything.
steps.proof: You sent 4 check-ins.
steps.pitfall: Only contacting people when you need a job.

problems.prompt: How often should you check in with past colleagues: every 3 to 6 months or only when job hunting?
Name 1 easy reason to reach out.
Why message an old manager 6 months before you need a reference?
problems.answer: The relationship stays real, not transactional.

steps.title: Weak Ties
steps.mastery: Value acquaintances as well as close friends.
steps.practice: List 10 acquaintances from past jobs or classes and reconnect with 2.
steps.detail: Research by Granovetter found many jobs come through weak ties: acquaintances who know different people from your close circle.
steps.proof: You reconnected with 2 people.
steps.pitfall: Only networking with close friends.

problems.prompt: Whose research is known for 'the strength of weak ties'?
Why might an acquaintance from 1 class help a job search more than a best friend?
problems.answer: They know people and openings your close circle doesn't.

problems.prompt: Name 2 sources of weak ties for a student.

steps.title: Give First
steps.mastery: Help people you know before you need anything from them.
steps.practice: Make 2 helpful introductions or shares this month.
steps.detail: Generosity builds a network. Introductions, answers and shared openings cost little and are remembered.
steps.proof: You made 2 helpful moves.
steps.pitfall: Keeping score of every favor.

problems.prompt: Name 1 easy way to help someone in your network.
A friend is job hunting in UX design. What could you forward?
problems.answer: A UX job posting, or a contact who works in UX.

problems.prompt: Why make 2 introductions without asking for anything back?

steps.title: Informational Chats
steps.mastery: Learn about roles through short conversations.
steps.practice: Ask 2 people in roles you're curious about for a 20-minute chat.
steps.detail: People usually enjoy talking about their work. Come with questions, keep to time and send a thank-you.
steps.proof: You had 2 chats and sent thank-yous.
steps.pitfall: Turning an informational chat into a job request.

problems.prompt: In a 20-minute informational chat, should you ask for a job? Answer yes or no.
Name 1 good question for an informational chat.
problems.answer: What does a typical week look like?

problems.prompt: What should you send within 24 hours of an informational chat?

steps.title: Professional Presence
steps.mastery: Keep a simple, current professional profile.
steps.practice: Update your LinkedIn headline and 3 recent achievements.
steps.detail: People look you up before meeting. A clear headline and recent results make good first impressions.
steps.proof: Your profile shows a current headline and 3 achievements.
steps.pitfall: Leaving a profile 5 years out of date.

problems.prompt: Name 1 thing to put in a LinkedIn headline besides a job title.
problems.answer: Who you help, or what you do.

problems.prompt: Improve the headline 'Looking for opportunities'.
problems.answer: Data analyst helping retail teams cut waste.

problems.prompt: Why keep a LinkedIn profile current?
problems.answer: People look you up before meeting you.

steps.title: Write It Down
steps.mastery: Capture decisions and actions during the meeting.
steps.practice: Take notes in your next 3 meetings with a section for decisions and a section for actions.
steps.detail: Notes focused on decisions and actions are useful later. Full transcripts are not.
steps.proof: Each note has decisions and actions sections.
steps.pitfall: Writing down everything said and missing the decisions.

problems.prompt: Name the 2 sections that matter most in meeting notes.
Your notes are 3 pages with no decisions marked. What should change?
A 1-hour meeting produced 2 decisions and 4 actions. How many items go in those 2 sections?

steps.title: Send Within a Day
steps.mastery: Send a short summary of what was agreed within 24 hours.
steps.practice: Send a 5-line follow-up after your next 3 meetings within 24 hours.
steps.detail: A written record prevents the common 'that's not what we agreed' problem. It takes 5 minutes while memory is fresh.
steps.proof: All 3 follow-ups went out within 24 hours.
steps.pitfall: Assuming everyone remembers the same thing.

problems.prompt: A meeting ends Monday at 3 pm. When is the latest to send notes?
Notes take 5 minutes right after a meeting. Why not wait a week?
problems.answer: Memory fades and details get lost.

problems.prompt: Name 1 problem a follow-up prevents.
problems.answer: Disagreement later about what was agreed.

steps.title: Format for Action
steps.mastery: Format follow-ups so actions are easy to find.
steps.practice: Write your next follow-up with 3 parts: decisions, actions (owner, date) and open questions.
steps.detail: A consistent format lets people find their tasks fast. Put each person's name next to their action.
steps.proof: Every action has a name and a date.
steps.pitfall: Writing actions as 'someone should'.

problems.prompt: Rewrite 'someone should email the vendor' as an action.
problems.answer: Priya to email the vendor by Thursday.

problems.prompt: Name the 3 parts of this follow-up format.
Why write 'Priya: email vendor by Thu' rather than 'email vendor'?
problems.answer: Each person can find their tasks and the date.

steps.title: Check the Record
steps.mastery: Invite corrections so the record is right.
steps.practice: End each of your next 3 follow-ups with 'Reply if I missed anything'.
steps.detail: Inviting corrections catches misunderstandings while they are cheap. Silence then counts as agreement.
steps.proof: You asked for corrections on all 3.
steps.pitfall: Treating your own notes as unquestionable.

problems.prompt: Name 1 line that invites corrections.
Nobody replies within 2 days. What can you assume?
Ana replies that decision 2 in your notes is wrong. Was asking for corrections worth it?
problems.answer: Yes, it caught the mistake early.

steps.title: Track Actions to Done
steps.mastery: Follow up on actions until they close.
steps.practice: Check the status of every action from last week's notes before the next meeting.
steps.detail: Actions often stall quietly. A short check before the next meeting keeps them moving without nagging.
steps.proof: Every action is marked done or has a new date.
steps.pitfall: Writing actions down and never checking them.

problems.prompt: Last week had 6 actions and 4 are done. How many need a check-in?
Your team meets every Monday. When should you check last week's 6 actions?
An action has no update after 2 weeks. Name 1 step.
problems.answer: Ask the owner for a new date.

steps.title: One Clear Message
steps.mastery: Build a presentation around 1 sentence you want people to remember.
steps.practice: Write the 1-sentence takeaway for your next presentation before making any slides.
steps.detail: If you can't say the point in 1 sentence, the audience won't either. Every slide should support that sentence.
steps.proof: Your takeaway is 1 sentence of 25 words or fewer.
steps.pitfall: Starting with slides and hoping a message appears.

problems.prompt: Is 'Here are 7 things about Q3' a 1-sentence takeaway? Answer yes or no.
Write a 1-sentence takeaway for a talk about late deliveries.
problems.answer: Moving the cutoff to 2 pm would cut late deliveries by half.

problems.prompt: A slide doesn't support the takeaway. What should you do?
problems.answer: Cut it, or move it to an appendix.

steps.title: Slides Support You
steps.mastery: Make slides that support what you say, not repeat it.
steps.practice: Cut each slide in your next deck to 1 idea and at most 15 words of text.
steps.detail: If slides have every word you say, the audience reads instead of listening. Use slides for charts, images and key numbers.
steps.proof: No slide has more than 15 words.
steps.pitfall: Reading full paragraphs off your slides.

problems.prompt: Your slide shows 3 charts and 2 bullet lists. What's the fix?
problems.answer: Split it so each slide has 1 idea.

problems.prompt: Your slide has 80 words. Name 1 fix.
problems.answer: Cut it to the key phrase, and say the rest.

problems.prompt: Name 1 thing slides do better than speech.
problems.answer: Show a chart or an image.

steps.title: Rehearse Out Loud
steps.mastery: Rehearse aloud at least twice before presenting.
steps.practice: Rehearse your next presentation out loud 2 times, timing each run.
steps.detail: Talking it through in your head hides gaps. Out loud, you find the transitions that don't work and the parts that run long.
steps.proof: Your second run lands within your time slot.
steps.pitfall: Rehearsing only in your head.

problems.prompt: Your slot is 10 minutes and your first run takes 14. What should you do?
Your 2nd rehearsal runs 9 minutes in a 10-minute slot. Are you within time? Answer yes or no.
Why rehearse a 10-minute talk out loud instead of in your head?
problems.answer: You find gaps and timing problems.

steps.title: Handle Questions
steps.mastery: Answer questions clearly or say you'll follow up.
steps.practice: List 5 likely questions before your next presentation and prepare a 2-sentence answer for each.
steps.detail: Prepared answers make you calm. If you don't know, say so and promise a follow-up with a date.
steps.proof: You had answers ready for at least 3 questions asked.
steps.pitfall: Bluffing an answer you don't know.

problems.prompt: Someone asks something you don't know. Name 1 good reply.
problems.answer: I don't know, but I'll find out and send it by Friday.

problems.prompt: Name 1 likely question for a talk proposing a $50,000 budget.
problems.answer: Where does the money come from?

problems.prompt: A question about costs comes up. Should your answer run about 2 sentences or 2 minutes?

steps.title: Know Your Audience
steps.mastery: Adjust content and depth to who is listening.
steps.practice: Write 2 versions of your opening, 1 for engineers and 1 for executives.
steps.detail: Executives want the decision and impact. Specialists want the details and method. The same facts need different framing.
steps.proof: The 2 openings differ in focus and detail.
steps.pitfall: Giving every audience the same deck.

problems.prompt: Your CEO has 5 minutes. Lead with the method or the impact?
Name 1 thing engineers may want that executives skip.
You'll show the same results to Finance and to Engineering. Should the opening be the same? Answer yes or no.

steps.title: List Everything
steps.mastery: Keep 1 list of all your current work.
steps.practice: List every open task and request in 1 place this week.
steps.detail: You can't prioritize what you can't see. One list beats memory and scattered notes.
steps.proof: All your work is on 1 list.
steps.pitfall: Keeping tasks across 5 apps and your head.

problems.prompt: Your tasks live in email, Slack and 2 notebooks. What's the fix?
Name 1 place tasks hide besides your list.
Why put everything on 1 list?
problems.answer: You can't prioritize what you can't see.

steps.title: Rank by Impact and Urgency
steps.mastery: Order work by impact and urgency.
steps.practice: Sort your list into 4 boxes: urgent-important, important, urgent, neither.
steps.detail: The Eisenhower grid separates urgent from important. Important but not urgent work is where most progress hides.
steps.proof: Every task sits in 1 of the 4 boxes.
steps.pitfall: Doing whatever is loudest.

problems.prompt: How many boxes does the Eisenhower grid have?
Which Eisenhower box hides most real progress?
Where does 'reply to a routine newsletter' go?

steps.title: Say What Will Slip
steps.mastery: Name what will slip when new work is added.
steps.practice: Reply to your next 2 new requests by naming what each one will push back.
steps.detail: Silently absorbing work leads to missed commitments. Saying 'Then X slips to Friday' lets your manager choose.
steps.proof: You named what would slip for 1 new request.
steps.pitfall: Saying yes and hoping to fit it in.

problems.prompt: A new urgent task arrives. Name 1 reply.
problems.answer: I can take it, but the report moves to Friday. OK?

problems.prompt: You tell your manager the report slips if you take the new task. Who decides now?
problems.answer: Your manager, now that they know the cost.

problems.prompt: You silently take on 3 extra tasks. Name 1 likely result by Friday.

steps.title: Protect Focus Time
steps.mastery: Guard hours where nobody can pull you away.
steps.practice: Block 2 hours of focus time on 3 days next week.
steps.detail: Important work needs uninterrupted time. Calendar blocks make it visible and harder to fill with meetings.
steps.proof: You used at least 2 of the 3 blocks for focus.
steps.pitfall: Letting meetings fill every hour.

problems.prompt: 2-hour focus blocks on 3 days add up to how many hours?
A coworker books a meeting over your 2-hour focus block. Name 1 response.
problems.answer: Suggest another time, since that block is reserved.

problems.prompt: Name 1 thing to switch off during focus time.

steps.title: Weekly Review
steps.mastery: Review priorities every week.
steps.practice: Spend 20 minutes every Friday for 4 weeks reviewing your list and picking next week's top 3.
steps.detail: A weekly review keeps the list honest and stops drift. Three top priorities are enough to steer by.
steps.proof: You did 4 weekly reviews.
steps.pitfall: Never stepping back to check the list.

problems.prompt: Your weekly review finds 12 open tasks. How many should be next week's top priorities?
Name 1 question to ask in a 20-minute weekly review.
problems.answer: What are my top 3 for next week?

problems.prompt: Without a weekly review, what happens to a 30-item list?
problems.answer: It drifts and stops matching reality.

steps.title: Tried, Expected, Happened
steps.mastery: Ask for help with what you tried, what you expected and what happened.
steps.practice: Write your next 3 help requests using the format: tried, expected, happened.
steps.detail: This format shows effort, saves the helper's time and often solves the problem as you write it.
steps.proof: All 3 requests use the format.
steps.pitfall: Writing only 'It doesn't work, help?' with no details.

problems.prompt: Name the 3 parts of this question format.
problems.answer: What you tried, what you expected, and what happened.

problems.prompt: Improve 'The build is broken, help?'
problems.answer: I ran npm build after pulling main. I expected it to pass, but it fails with error X.

problems.prompt: You start writing 'Tried X, expected Y' and spot your own typo. What just happened?

steps.title: Search First
steps.mastery: Look for the answer before asking.
steps.practice: Spend 15 minutes searching docs and past threads before your next 3 questions.
steps.detail: A short search often finds the answer, and when it doesn't, you can say what you checked. Don't spend hours stuck either.
steps.proof: You found the answer at least once yourself.
steps.pitfall: Asking a question answered in the first search result.

problems.prompt: Name 1 thing to mention when you ask after a 15-minute search.
You've been stuck 3 hours. What should you do?
problems.answer: Ask now, and say what you tried.

problems.prompt: Name 2 places to search before asking.

steps.title: Ask the Right Person
steps.mastery: Direct questions to the person or channel most likely to know.
steps.practice: For your next 3 questions, write down who is most likely to know before asking.
steps.detail: The right person answers in minutes. A random person may guess or forward it. Public channels help others find answers later.
steps.proof: All 3 went to the right person or channel.
steps.pitfall: Asking your manager everything.

problems.prompt: A question about the payment API: the API's owner or the office manager?
Why ask in a public channel instead of a DM?
problems.answer: Others can find the answer later.

problems.prompt: A Python question at a 300-person company: ask in the #python channel or DM a random engineer?

steps.title: Clarify the Request
steps.mastery: Ask questions that clarify vague assignments.
steps.practice: For your next new task, ask 3 clarifying questions before starting.
steps.detail: Asking about goal, deadline and what done looks like prevents doing the wrong work well.
steps.proof: You asked 3 clarifying questions.
steps.pitfall: Starting a vague task and guessing.

problems.prompt: Name 3 clarifying questions for a new task.
problems.answer: What's the goal, when is it due, and what does done look like?

problems.prompt: You're told 'clean up the report'. Name 1 question to ask.
problems.answer: What should change, and who is it for?

problems.prompt: Why ask 3 clarifying questions before a 2-week task?
problems.answer: So you don't do the wrong work well.

steps.title: Share the Answer
steps.mastery: Write up answers so others benefit.
steps.practice: After your next 2 answered questions, add the answer to the team docs or thread.
steps.detail: If you had the question, others will too. Writing the answer down saves the next person time.
steps.proof: 2 answers are in the team docs.
steps.pitfall: Getting an answer in a DM and never sharing it.

problems.prompt: 3 people asked you the same setup question this month. What should you do?
problems.answer: Write the answer in the team docs.

problems.prompt: Why add an answer to the team docs once 2 people have asked?
problems.answer: The next person can find it.

problems.prompt: Name 1 place to share an answer.

steps.title: Track Every Commitment
steps.mastery: Never lose track of something you said you would do.
steps.practice: Write down every promise you make for 1 week, with who it's for and when it's due.
steps.detail: Most broken commitments are forgotten, not refused. One list for every 'I'll send that over' keeps them visible.
steps.proof: Your list has every commitment from the week with a due date.
steps.pitfall: Trusting memory for small promises like 'I'll send that'.

problems.prompt: You said 'I'll send the slides' in 3 meetings this week. Where should those go?
problems.answer: On your commitments list, each with a due date.

problems.prompt: Your list has 12 items and 2 are overdue. What percent is on time, to the nearest whole number?
Name 2 details to record with each commitment besides the task.
problems.answer: Who it's for, and when it's due.

steps.title: Give Realistic Dates
steps.mastery: Promise dates you can actually hit.
steps.practice: For your next 5 estimates, add a buffer of 25% and compare the real finish time.
steps.detail: People remember the date you gave, not how hard the work was. Estimating with a buffer and beating it builds more trust than a tight date you miss.
steps.proof: At least 4 of 5 tasks finish by the date you gave.
steps.pitfall: Giving the most optimistic date to sound fast.

problems.prompt: A task feels like 4 days. With a 25% buffer, how many days do you promise?
Which builds more trust: promising Friday and delivering Thursday, or promising Tuesday and delivering Thursday?
You hit 3 of 5 estimates. What is your hit rate?

steps.title: Flag Early
steps.mastery: Say early when you can't make a date.
steps.practice: Tell the person within 1 day of noticing the next time a deadline is at risk, and give a new date.
steps.detail: A warning 3 days ahead lets people adjust. The same news on the due date damages trust. Bring a new date and what you need.
steps.proof: You warned at least 2 days before the original date.
steps.pitfall: Hoping to catch up and saying nothing until the deadline.

problems.prompt: A report is due Friday and on Tuesday you see it will slip. When should you say so?
Name 2 things to include when flagging a slip.
problems.answer: A new date, and what you need to hit it.

problems.prompt: Which hurts trust more: a warning 3 days early or silence until the deadline?

steps.title: Close the Loop
steps.mastery: Confirm when something is done.
steps.practice: Send a 1-line 'done' message for every finished request this week.
steps.detail: People can't see your work finish. A short 'Sent, here's the link' saves them chasing you and makes reliability visible.
steps.proof: Every finished request got a confirmation.
steps.pitfall: Finishing quietly and leaving people wondering.

problems.prompt: You fixed the bug Sam reported. What 1 thing should you send?
problems.answer: A short message saying it's fixed, with a link.

problems.prompt: How long should a 'done' message be: 1 line or 1 page?
Why send 'done' if the work speaks for itself?
problems.answer: Other people can't see it finish, so they'd chase you.

steps.title: Say No Clearly
steps.mastery: Decline requests you can't take on, without vague maybes.
steps.practice: Turn down 1 request this month with a clear 'no' and a reason or alternative.
steps.detail: A vague 'I'll try' becomes a broken promise. A clear no with an alternative is more reliable than a yes you can't keep.
steps.proof: You declined 1 request clearly and kindly.
steps.pitfall: Saying 'I'll try' to everything.

problems.prompt: Rewrite 'I'll try to get to it' as a clear answer for something you can't do this week.
problems.answer: "I can't take this on this week, but I could start Monday."

problems.prompt: Which is more reliable: 'maybe' or a clear 'no' with an alternative?

choices: A clear no with an alternative
accept: A clear no with an alternative

problems.prompt: You already have 3 deadlines this Friday. A 4th request arrives. Name 1 honest reply.
problems.answer: "I can do it next Wednesday, or drop something else for it."

steps.title: Target a Short List
steps.mastery: Apply to a focused list of jobs that fit.
steps.practice: Choose 10 roles that fit well and apply to them carefully rather than 50 at random.
steps.detail: Ten tailored applications usually beat a hundred generic ones. Fit matters more than volume.
steps.proof: You applied to 10 well-fitting roles.
steps.pitfall: Mass-applying to anything with a matching title.

problems.prompt: You have 10 hours for applications. Spend 1 hour each on 10 roles or 6 minutes each on 100?
Which works better: 10 tailored or 100 generic applications?
Name 1 sign a role fits.
problems.answer: You meet most of the key requirements.

steps.title: Read the Posting
steps.mastery: Read job postings closely and answer them.
steps.practice: Highlight the top 5 requirements in 1 posting and show each in your application.
steps.detail: Postings say what they want. Mirroring their words and showing evidence for each makes screening easy.
steps.proof: Your application covers all 5.
steps.pitfall: Skimming the title and applying.

problems.prompt: A posting lists 3 must-have and 2 nice-to-have requirements. How many should your application address?
A posting says 'SQL required'. Name 1 way to show it.
problems.answer: A résumé bullet using SQL, with a result.

problems.prompt: Why mirror the posting's words?
problems.answer: Screeners and software look for them.

steps.title: Referrals
steps.mastery: Ask for referrals through your network.
steps.practice: For your top 3 roles, find 1 person connected to each company.
steps.detail: Referred candidates are far more likely to get interviews. A short, specific ask makes referring easy.
steps.proof: You found a connection for at least 2 of 3.
steps.pitfall: Applying cold when a friend works there.

problems.prompt: Your friend Maya works at the company. What should you ask for?
problems.answer: A referral, with the job link and why you fit.

problems.prompt: Name 1 thing to include in a referral ask.
problems.answer: The job link, and why you fit.

problems.prompt: Why ask Maya for a referral instead of applying cold?
problems.answer: Referred candidates are more likely to get interviews.

steps.title: Track Applications
steps.mastery: Track every application and its status.
steps.practice: Keep a table of every application with 3 columns: date, status and next step.
steps.detail: A tracker stops lost follow-ups and shows what's working. Note which channels lead to interviews.
steps.proof: Your table is current.
steps.pitfall: Forgetting where you applied.

problems.prompt: Name 3 columns for an application tracker.
You applied to 20 jobs and got 4 interviews. What is the rate?
Job boards gave 0 interviews from 10 applications; referrals gave 3 from 5. Where should you focus?

steps.title: Follow Up
steps.mastery: Follow up politely on applications.
steps.practice: Send a short follow-up 1 week after applying to your top 3 roles.
steps.detail: A polite follow-up shows interest and can bring your application to the top. Keep it to 3 sentences.
steps.proof: 3 follow-ups sent.
steps.pitfall: Following up daily.

problems.prompt: You applied on March 1. When should you follow up?
Should a follow-up be about 3 sentences or 3 paragraphs?
Is following up every day a good idea? Answer yes or no.

steps.title: Pick a Skill
steps.mastery: Choose 1 skill to improve on purpose.
steps.practice: Pick 1 skill that would most help your work in 6 months and write down why.
steps.detail: Jobs teach what they happen to teach. Choosing a skill on purpose makes growth faster and pointed.
steps.proof: You wrote down 1 skill and the reason.
steps.pitfall: Trying to improve at everything at once.

problems.prompt: Name 1 skill a new analyst might pick to improve over 6 months.
Name 1 good reason to pick a skill.
problems.answer: It would most help your work in 6 months.

problems.prompt: Is 5 years at a desk the same as 5 years of growth? Answer yes or no.

steps.title: Practice on Purpose
steps.mastery: Practice the hard parts with feedback.
steps.practice: Schedule 3 sessions of 30 minutes this week on the hardest part of your chosen skill.
steps.detail: Deliberate practice targets weaknesses with feedback. Repeating what you already do well feels good but teaches little.
steps.proof: You did 3 sessions on the hard part.
steps.pitfall: Practicing only the parts you're good at.

problems.prompt: How many minutes of practice is 3 sessions of 30?
You're great at slides but weak at Q&A. Which should you practice?
Name 1 source of feedback on your practice.

steps.title: Find a Teacher
steps.mastery: Learn from someone better at the skill.
steps.practice: Ask 1 person who is good at your chosen skill for a 30-minute chat.
steps.detail: A mentor can show shortcuts and spot errors you can't. A specific question makes it easy to say yes.
steps.proof: You had 1 chat.
steps.pitfall: Struggling alone when an expert sits 2 desks away.

problems.prompt: Who should you ask for a 30-minute chat about getting better at estimates?
Name 1 specific question to bring.
problems.answer: How did you learn to estimate projects?

problems.prompt: Which gets a yes more often: 'Can you mentor me?' or 'Can I ask you 2 questions about estimating?'
problems.answer: Can I ask you 2 questions about estimating?

choices: Can I ask you 2 questions about estimating?
accept: Can I ask you 2 questions about estimating?

steps.title: Stretch Assignments
steps.mastery: Take on work slightly beyond your current level.
steps.practice: Ask your manager for 1 task this quarter that uses your chosen skill.
steps.detail: Real work at the edge of your ability is the fastest teacher. Ask for it; it's rarely offered.
steps.proof: You got 1 stretch task.
steps.pitfall: Waiting to be offered harder work.

problems.prompt: Name 1 stretch task for someone learning to present.
problems.answer: Presenting the team update at the monthly all-hands.

problems.prompt: Why ask your manager for a stretch task instead of waiting 6 months?
Is a stretch task supposed to feel easy? Answer yes or no.

steps.title: Measure Progress
steps.mastery: Track whether the skill is improving.
steps.practice: Write 1 measurable sign of progress for your skill and check it monthly for 3 months.
steps.detail: Time spent is not progress. A measure like 'presentations without notes' shows real change.
steps.proof: You have 3 monthly checks.
steps.pitfall: Counting hours instead of results.

problems.prompt: You logged 20 hours of practice but your talks haven't changed. What's missing?
Name 1 measurable sign of better presenting.
Is time spent the same as progress? Answer yes or no.

steps.title: Know What They're Measured On
steps.mastery: Learn what other teams are measured on.
steps.practice: Ask 2 people on other teams what goals or metrics their team is judged by.
steps.detail: Most apparent obstruction is someone protecting their own goals. Knowing their metrics explains their behavior.
steps.proof: You know the main metric of 2 other teams.
steps.pitfall: Assuming other teams block you out of spite.

problems.prompt: Sales pushes for features fast. What are they probably measured on?
Security slows a launch. What are they measured on?
Finance rejects your $5,000 request. What are they probably measured on?

steps.title: Find the Shared Goal
steps.mastery: Frame requests around goals both teams share.
steps.practice: Rewrite your next cross-team request to mention 1 goal it helps them reach.
steps.detail: A request that helps the other team's goal gets priority. One that only helps yours gets queued.
steps.proof: Your request names a shared goal.
steps.pitfall: Asking for help with no thought for what they gain.

problems.prompt: You need Support's help on docs. Name 1 shared goal to mention.
Why mention 'fewer support tickets' when asking Support for help?
problems.answer: It ties your request to their goal, so it gets priority.

problems.prompt: You need Legal to review fast. Name 1 shared goal to mention.

steps.title: Map Stakeholders
steps.mastery: List who is affected by your project and what they care about.
steps.practice: Make a table of 5 stakeholders for your project with what each cares about.
steps.detail: Surprised stakeholders block things late. A simple map shows who to talk to early.
steps.proof: Your table has 5 people with their concerns.
steps.pitfall: Discovering a key stakeholder the week before launch.

problems.prompt: Name 3 groups that might belong on a stakeholder map for a new checkout page.
Name 2 columns for a stakeholder map.
problems.answer: Who they are, and what they care about.

problems.prompt: You learn Security must approve 1 week before launch. When should you have found out?
problems.answer: At the start, when mapping stakeholders.

steps.title: Keep Them Informed
steps.mastery: Update stakeholders before decisions affect them.
steps.practice: Send a heads-up to affected teams at least 5 working days before your next change lands.
steps.detail: A heads-up 1 week before a change lets others plan. The same change announced on the day feels like an ambush.
steps.proof: Affected teams heard before the change.
steps.pitfall: Announcing changes that affect others without warning.

problems.prompt: Your change affects Billing next Monday. When should they hear?
Name 1 feeling a surprise change causes.
Is a heads-up a request for permission? Answer yes or no.
problems.answer: Not always, but it lets them plan.

steps.title: Escalate Well
steps.mastery: Escalate disagreements calmly and with options.
steps.practice: When you next hit a cross-team block, write a 1-paragraph escalation with 2 options and a recommendation.
steps.detail: Escalation is normal when goals conflict. A neutral summary with options helps leaders decide fast.
steps.proof: Your escalation has 2 options and a recommendation.
steps.pitfall: Escalating by complaining about the other team.

problems.prompt: Name 3 parts of a good escalation.
problems.answer: A neutral summary, options and a recommendation.

problems.prompt: Write 1 line of a neutral escalation about a 2-week delay.
problems.answer: Design and Engineering disagree on scope: A ships in 2 weeks, B in 4. I recommend A.

problems.prompt: Should you tell the other team before escalating? Answer yes or no.

steps.title: Find the Overlap
steps.mastery: Identify skills that carry over to the new field.
steps.practice: List 10 skills from your current work and mark which 5 matter in your target field.
steps.detail: Most moves are sideways steps. Your transferable skills are the bridge; the gap is what to build.
steps.proof: You marked 5 transferable skills.
steps.pitfall: Thinking you must start from zero.

problems.prompt: A retail manager is moving into HR. Name 1 transferable skill.
A teacher moving to training design. Name 1 transferable skill.
Name 1 likely gap for a designer moving into product management.

steps.title: Build the Missing Piece
steps.mastery: Build the skill gap with a visible project.
steps.practice: Start 1 project that uses your missing skill and can be shown publicly.
steps.detail: A public project proves the new skill better than a certificate. It also gives you something to talk about.
steps.proof: Your project is started and shareable.
steps.pitfall: Collecting certificates with no real work to show.

problems.prompt: Name 1 public project for a teacher moving into UX design.
problems.answer: Redesigning a school website and writing up the process.

problems.prompt: Which proves a skill better: a 'certificate' or a public project?
Name 1 place to share a project.

steps.title: Move Sideways Inside
steps.mastery: Use your current employer for a sideways move.
steps.practice: Talk to 1 person on the team you'd like to join inside your company.
steps.detail: Internal moves are easier because people already trust you. Volunteering on a small project for that team is a good start.
steps.proof: You had 1 conversation.
steps.pitfall: Assuming you must leave to change direction.

problems.prompt: Why is moving from Sales to Marketing inside your company easier than elsewhere?
Name 1 way to start.
problems.answer: Volunteer on a small project for that team.

problems.prompt: You want to join the Data team. How do you learn what they need?
problems.answer: Ask someone on it for a short chat.

steps.title: Tell the New Story
steps.mastery: Explain your change in 1 clear story.
steps.practice: Write a 3-sentence story linking your past work to your new direction.
steps.detail: Interviewers want to know why you're changing. A short story that connects past and future reassures them.
steps.proof: Your story is 3 sentences and makes the link clear.
steps.pitfall: Apologizing for your background.

problems.prompt: Rewrite 'Sorry, I was just a teacher' as part of a career-change story.
problems.answer: As a teacher I designed lessons for 120 students, and now I design training for adults.

problems.prompt: Why tell interviewers a 3-sentence story about your change?
Should you apologize for your past career? Answer yes or no.

steps.title: Test Before Leaping
steps.mastery: Try the new work before fully switching.
steps.practice: Take on 1 small paid or volunteer task in your target field within 2 months.
steps.detail: A small test shows if you actually like the work. It's cheaper than a full switch you regret.
steps.proof: You completed 1 test task.
steps.pitfall: Quitting before trying the new work.

problems.prompt: Name 1 small test of a move into writing within 2 months.
problems.answer: A freelance article for a local paper.

problems.prompt: Why try 1 freelance job before quitting to freelance?
problems.answer: To check you actually like the work.

problems.prompt: Your 1 test task in design felt draining. What does that tell you?
problems.answer: Rethink the move before you leap.

steps.title: Keep a Brag Doc
steps.mastery: Keep a running record of what you did and its effect.
steps.practice: Add 3 lines every Friday for 4 weeks to a document listing what you did and what changed because of it.
steps.detail: You will forget your wins by review time. A weekly log with numbers makes reviews and CVs easy.
steps.proof: Your doc has 4 weeks of entries with effects.
steps.pitfall: Trying to remember a year of work the night before a review.

problems.prompt: Name 2 things each brag doc entry should record.
problems.answer: What you did, and what changed because of it.

problems.prompt: Improve 'Worked on the website.'
problems.answer: Cut page load from 4 seconds to 2.

problems.prompt: Name 2 uses for a brag doc.

steps.title: Share Progress Unasked
steps.mastery: Share progress before people ask.
steps.practice: Send your manager a 3-bullet update every 2 weeks without being asked.
steps.detail: Unprompted updates build trust and prevent surprises. They also give your manager material to advocate for you.
steps.proof: You sent at least 2 updates.
steps.pitfall: Waiting until someone asks what you're working on.

problems.prompt: Your manager hasn't heard from you in 6 weeks. What's the risk?
problems.answer: They can't advocate for work they don't know about.

problems.prompt: Name 1 benefit of updating your manager unasked.
problems.answer: It gives them material to advocate for you.

problems.prompt: Write a 3-bullet update for a week where you shipped 1 fix.
problems.answer: Shipped the export fix. Next: billing tests. Blocked: nothing.

steps.title: Show Impact, Not Effort
steps.mastery: Describe results rather than hours.
steps.practice: Rewrite 5 lines from your brag doc to show impact with a number.
steps.detail: 'Worked late all week' describes effort. 'Shipped feature used by 2000 people' describes impact. Impact is what gets noticed.
steps.proof: All 5 lines have a number showing impact.
steps.pitfall: Highlighting how hard you worked instead of what changed.

problems.prompt: Rewrite 'Spent 3 weeks on the report.' to show impact.
problems.answer: The report led to a 10% budget cut.

problems.prompt: Which line gets noticed more: 'Worked 60 hours' or 'Cut costs 10%'?
Rewrite 'Helped with hiring.' to show impact.

steps.title: Demo Your Work
steps.mastery: Show work in progress to the team.
steps.practice: Give a 5-minute demo of your work at 1 team meeting this month.
steps.detail: A demo makes invisible work visible and gets early feedback. Keep it short and show something real.
steps.proof: You gave 1 demo.
steps.pitfall: Working in silence until the final reveal.

problems.prompt: Why demo unfinished work in a 5-minute slot instead of waiting for launch?
problems.answer: You get early feedback, and the work becomes visible.

problems.prompt: Name 1 benefit of an early demo.
In a 5-minute demo, show 10 slides or the working feature?

steps.title: Credit Others
steps.mastery: Give public credit to people who helped.
steps.practice: Thank 2 people publicly this month for specific help.
steps.detail: Crediting others is part of visibility. It builds goodwill and shows you know how the work really got done.
steps.proof: 2 people got specific public credit.
steps.pitfall: Presenting team work as only your own.

problems.prompt: Rewrite 'Thanks team!' as specific credit.
problems.answer: Thanks to Jo for fixing the export bug in 1 day.

problems.prompt: Why name Jo and the bug in a thank-you instead of writing 'Thanks all'?
problems.answer: Specific credit shows what Jo actually did.

problems.prompt: Does crediting others hurt your own visibility? Answer yes or no.

steps.title: Conclusion First
steps.mastery: Lead documents with the answer, then the support.
steps.practice: Rewrite 1 work document so the first paragraph states the conclusion and recommendation.
steps.detail: Busy readers may read only the top. Put the answer there and let the rest explain it.
steps.proof: A reader can act after reading only the first paragraph.
steps.pitfall: Building up to the conclusion on page 3.

problems.prompt: A 3-page report recommends hiring 2 people. Where should that recommendation go?
Name the 2 things a first paragraph should give.
Why put the answer first for a VP?
problems.answer: They may only read the top.

steps.title: Headings That Inform
steps.mastery: Write headings that tell readers what each section says.
steps.practice: Replace 5 generic headings like 'Background' in a document with headings that state the point.
steps.detail: 'Costs rose 12% in Q3' tells the reader more than 'Costs'. Skimmers read headings only.
steps.proof: All 5 headings state a point.
steps.pitfall: Using headings like 'Introduction' and 'Discussion' only.

problems.prompt: Improve the heading 'Results'.
A reader skims only the 5 headings of your report. What should those headings do?
Is 'Q3 costs rose 12%' or 'Costs' the stronger heading?

steps.title: A Summary That Stands Alone
steps.mastery: Write a summary someone can act on without the rest.
steps.practice: Write a 5-line summary at the top of your next document and test it on 1 colleague.
steps.detail: A good summary includes the situation, the finding, the recommendation and what you need. Ask a colleague what they would do after reading only it.
steps.proof: Your colleague can say the next step from the summary alone.
steps.pitfall: Writing a summary that only says 'This document discusses the budget'.

problems.prompt: Name 4 parts of an actionable summary.
problems.answer: Situation, finding, recommendation and the ask.

problems.prompt: Is 'This document discusses the Q3 budget' a useful summary? Answer yes or no.
Your summary says 'Q3 costs rose 12%; cut 2 vendors; need sign-off by Friday.' Which part is the ask?

steps.title: Plain Words
steps.mastery: Replace jargon and long words with plain ones.
steps.practice: Run 1 document through a find for 10 common jargon terms, like 'leverage', and replace them.
steps.detail: Plain words are faster to read and harder to misread. 'Use' beats 'leverage', and 'help' beats 'facilitate'.
steps.proof: None of the 10 jargon terms remain.
steps.pitfall: Writing 'utilize synergies' instead of 'work together'.

problems.prompt: Plain word for 'leverage' as a verb.
Plain phrase for 'circle back'.
Rewrite 'We will operationalize the initiative in Q2.'
problems.answer: We will start the project in Q2.

steps.title: Get a Reader's Review
steps.mastery: Test documents on a reader before sending widely.
steps.practice: Ask 1 colleague to read your next document for 5 minutes and say what they think it asks.
steps.detail: What you meant and what readers take away often differ. A 5-minute review catches it before 50 people read it.
steps.proof: Your colleague's summary matches your intent.
steps.pitfall: Sending a document to the whole team untested.

problems.prompt: Your reader thinks the doc asks for budget, but you wanted headcount. What does that mean?
problems.answer: The document is unclear, so revise it.

problems.prompt: Your 2-page doc goes to 50 people. Who should read it first?
Name 1 question to ask your test reader.
problems.answer: What do you think this asks you to do?

steps.title: Acids and Bases Defined
steps.mastery: Use the proton transfer definition of acids and bases.
steps.practice: Label the acid, base and conjugate pairs in NH3 + H2O <=> NH4+ + OH- and HCl + H2O -> H3O+ + Cl-.
steps.detail: An acid donates H+ and a base accepts it. Each acid has a conjugate base with 1 fewer H+.
steps.proof: 2 equations with all 4 roles labeled.
steps.pitfall: Calling water always neutral in every reaction.

problems.prompt: Conjugate base of \(\mathrm{HNO_{3}}\)?
Conjugate acid of \(\mathrm{NH_{3}}\)?
In \(\mathrm{HCl} + \mathrm{H_{2}O}\), which of the 2 reactants is the base?

steps.title: The pH Scale
steps.mastery: Compute pH from [H+] and back.
steps.practice: Find the pH of 0.01 M HCl, 0.001 M HCl and [H+] for pH 4.
steps.detail: pH = -log[H+]. Each pH unit is a factor of 10 in [H+], so small pH changes are big chemical changes.
steps.proof: pH 2, pH 3 and 10^-4 M.
steps.pitfall: Thinking pH 3 is twice as acidic as pH 6.

problems.prompt: pH of 0.1 M \(\mathrm{HCl}\)?
[H+] at pH 7?
How many times more acidic is pH 2 than pH 5?

steps.title: Strong and Weak
steps.mastery: Tell strong from weak acids and use Ka.
steps.practice: Compare the pH of 0.1 M HCl and 0.1 M acetic acid with Ka = 1.8 x 10^-5.
steps.detail: Strong acids ionize fully and weak ones only a little. For a weak acid, [H+] is about sqrt(Ka x C).
steps.proof: pH 1 and about pH 2.87.
steps.pitfall: Confusing strong with concentrated.

problems.prompt: [H+] in 0.1 M acetic acid, roughly?
Is 10 M acetic acid strong?
problems.answer: No, it is concentrated but weak.

problems.prompt: Larger Ka of 2 acids means what?

steps.title: Neutralization and Titration
steps.mastery: Use titration data to find an unknown concentration.
steps.practice: Find [HCl] if 25.0 mL is neutralized by 20.0 mL of 0.100 M NaOH.
steps.detail: At the equivalence point, moles of acid equal moles of base for a 1 to 1 reaction. Then divide by volume.
steps.pitfall: Forgetting the 1 to 2 ratio for acids like H2SO4.

problems.prompt: Moles in 20.0 mL of 0.100 M \(\mathrm{NaOH}\)?
Moles of \(\mathrm{NaOH}\) for 0.001 mol \(\mathrm{H_{2}SO_{4}}\)?
pH at equivalence for \(\mathrm{HCl}\) with \(\mathrm{NaOH}\) at 25 degrees C?

steps.title: Buffers
steps.mastery: Explain and compute buffer pH.
steps.practice: Find the pH of a buffer with 0.1 M acetic acid and 0.1 M acetate, pKa 4.76, then with 0.2 M acetate.
steps.detail: A weak acid with its conjugate base absorbs added acid or base. pH = pKa + log([A-]/[HA]).
steps.proof: 4.76 and about 5.06.
steps.pitfall: Using a strong acid to make a buffer.

problems.prompt: pH when [A-] = 10[HA] and pKa = 7.2?
Ratio [A-]/[HA] of 10 adds how much to pKa?
Normal blood pH, kept by a buffer, roughly?

steps.title: Flame Tests and Ion Tests
steps.mastery: Identify ions with simple tests.
steps.practice: Identify 5 unknowns using flame colors and tests with NaOH, AgNO3 and BaCl2.
steps.detail: Each ion gives a signature color or precipitate. Combining tests narrows down both the cation and the anion.
steps.proof: 5 unknowns each named with the evidence.
steps.pitfall: Reading a flame test through a sodium yellow glow.

problems.prompt: Flame color of \(\mathrm{K}^{+}\)?
Precipitate color of \(\mathrm{AgCl}\), from 1 drop of \(\mathrm{AgNO_{3}}\)?
Test for \(\mathrm{SO_{4}}^{2-}\) with 1 reagent?

steps.title: Chromatography
steps.mastery: Separate and identify substances by Rf values.
steps.practice: Run paper chromatography on 3 inks and compute Rf for each spot.
steps.detail: Substances travel at different speeds depending on how they share time between paper and solvent. Rf = spot distance/solvent distance.
steps.proof: Rf values for every spot.
steps.pitfall: Measuring from the bottom of the paper instead of the start line.

problems.prompt: Spot 3 cm and solvent 6 cm. Rf?
Can an Rf be 1.2?
A pure substance run on chromatography paper in 'water' makes how many spots?
problems.answer: 1. More than 1 spot means a mixture.

steps.title: Spectroscopy Basics
steps.mastery: Use IR peaks to find functional groups.
steps.practice: Identify the groups in 3 IR spectra using peaks near 1700, 3300 and 2900 per cm.
steps.detail: Bonds absorb IR at signature frequencies. A sharp peak near 1700 is C=O and a broad one near 3300 is O-H.
steps.proof: 3 spectra matched to groups.
steps.pitfall: Over reading the fingerprint region below 1500 per cm.

problems.prompt: Peak near 1700 per cm suggests which bond?
Broad peak near 3300 per cm?
Molecular ion at \(\frac{m}{z} = 46\) in mass spec, with 1 O. Candidate?

steps.title: Beer-Lambert Law
steps.mastery: Find concentration from absorbance.
steps.practice: Make a calibration line from 4 standards and find an unknown with absorbance 0.45.
steps.detail: Absorbance is proportional to concentration, A = ebc. A calibration line turns absorbance into concentration.
steps.proof: A line and the unknown read from it.
steps.pitfall: Using readings outside the calibration range.

problems.prompt: \(A = 0.3\) at 0.1 M. Concentration at \(A = 0.6\)?
Doubling the path length to 2 cm does what to A?

steps.title: Combine the Evidence
steps.mastery: Identify an unknown from several methods together.
steps.practice: Identify an unknown with formula C2H4O2 from an IR peak at 1710, a broad O-H peak and a pH of 3.
steps.detail: Each method narrows the options. Agreement between independent tests gives confidence in the answer.
steps.proof: Ethanoic acid, with each piece of evidence explained.
steps.pitfall: Trusting 1 test alone.

problems.prompt: \(\mathrm{C_{2}H_{4}O_{2}}\) with acid pH 3 and C=O. Name?
\(\mathrm{C_{2}H_{6}O}\) with an O-H peak and no C=O. Name?
Why use 3 methods instead of 1?
problems.answer: They check each other and rule out lookalikes.

steps.title: Protons, Neutrons, Electrons
steps.mastery: Find the number of each particle in an atom.
steps.practice: Find the protons, neutrons and electrons in carbon-12, sodium-23 and chlorine-35.
steps.detail: The atomic number gives protons. Mass number minus protons gives neutrons, and a neutral atom has as many electrons as protons.
steps.pitfall: Using the mass number as the number of protons.

problems.prompt: How many neutrons are in oxygen-18, atomic number 8?
Neutrons in iron-56, atomic number 26?
How many electrons are in a \(\mathrm{Cl}^{-}\) ion, atomic number 17?
problems.answer: 18, since the ion has 1 more electron than protons.

steps.title: Isotopes
steps.mastery: Explain isotopes as the same element with different neutrons.
steps.practice: Compare carbon-12 and carbon-14 in a table of protons, neutrons and mass number.
steps.detail: Isotopes have the same number of protons, so they react the same way. Only the mass and stability differ.
steps.proof: A table showing 6 protons in both and 6 vs 8 neutrons.
steps.pitfall: Thinking isotopes are different elements.

problems.prompt: Neutrons in carbon-14?
Do Cl-35 and Cl-37 react differently in most reactions?
Hydrogen-2 has how many neutrons?

steps.title: Relative Atomic Mass
steps.mastery: Compute an average atomic mass from isotope abundances.
steps.practice: Compute the relative atomic mass of chlorine from 75% Cl-35 and 25% Cl-37.
steps.detail: Weight each isotope mass by its share and add. That is why chlorine is listed as 35.5, not a whole number.
steps.pitfall: Taking a simple average of the isotope masses.

problems.prompt: 50% of mass 10 and 50% of mass 11. Average?
Boron: 20% B-10 and 80% B-11. Relative atomic mass?
Why is Cl listed as 35.5 and not 36?
problems.answer: Cl-35 is 3 times more common than Cl-37.

steps.title: Ions
steps.mastery: Find the charge an atom gets when it gains or loses electrons.
steps.practice: Write the symbol and electron count for Na+, Mg2+, Cl- and O2-.
steps.detail: Losing electrons makes a positive ion and gaining them makes a negative one. Protons never change in a chemical reaction.
steps.proof: 10, 10, 18 and 10 electrons.
steps.pitfall: Changing the number of protons to make an ion.

problems.prompt: Electrons in \(\mathrm{Al}^{3+}\), atomic number 13?
An atom with 16 protons and 18 electrons. Charge?
Does Na lose or gain 1 electron to form \(\mathrm{Na}^{+}\)?

steps.title: Models of the Atom
steps.mastery: Trace how atomic models changed with evidence.
steps.practice: Put 4 models in order, from Dalton to Thomson to Rutherford to Bohr, with the experiment behind each change.
steps.detail: Each model fixed what the last one could not explain. Rutherford found the tiny dense nucleus by firing alpha particles at gold foil.
steps.proof: A timeline of 4 models with 1 key experiment each.
steps.pitfall: Treating the Bohr model as the final picture.

problems.prompt: Who discovered the electron in 1897?
What did most alpha particles do in the Rutherford gold foil test?
What did Bohr add to the model in 1913?

steps.title: Ionic Bonds
steps.mastery: Show electron transfer between a metal and a nonmetal.
steps.practice: Draw dot and cross diagrams for NaCl and MgO, showing the electrons moved and the charges.
steps.detail: The metal gives electrons to the nonmetal. The opposite ions attract in a giant lattice.
steps.proof: Na+ Cl- with 1 electron moved, Mg2+ O2- with 2 moved.
steps.pitfall: Drawing a shared pair between Na and Cl.

problems.prompt: Electrons moved to form \(\mathrm{CaO}\)?
Formula of the compound of \(\mathrm{Mg}^{2+}\) and \(\mathrm{Cl}^{-}\)?
Does \(\mathrm{NaCl}\) conduct electricity as a solid at 25 degrees C?
problems.answer: No, only when melted or dissolved.

steps.title: Covalent Bonds
steps.mastery: Show shared electron pairs between nonmetals.
steps.practice: Draw dot and cross diagrams for H2, H2O, CO2 and N2, marking single, double and triple bonds.
steps.detail: Nonmetals share pairs so each reaches a full shell. Sharing 2 or 3 pairs makes double or triple bonds.
steps.proof: H2 single, H2O 2 singles, CO2 2 doubles, N2 a triple.
steps.pitfall: Leaving out lone pairs on O and N.

problems.prompt: Shared pairs in \(\mathrm{N_{2}}\)?
Lone pairs on O in \(\mathrm{H_{2}O}\)?
Bonds between C and each O in \(\mathrm{CO_{2}}\)?

steps.title: Metallic Bonds
steps.mastery: Explain metals as ions in a sea of electrons.
steps.practice: Explain in 3 sentences why copper conducts, bends without breaking and has a high melting point of about 1085 degrees C.
steps.detail: Metal ions sit in a lattice surrounded by free electrons. The moving electrons carry current and let layers slide.
steps.proof: 3 sentences tied to the electron sea model.
steps.pitfall: Saying metals conduct because their ions move.

problems.prompt: What carries current in a 1 m copper wire?
Why can Al be hammered into foil 0.02 mm thick?
problems.answer: Layers of ions slide over each other.

problems.prompt: Stronger metallic bond, Na with 1 outer electron or Mg with 2?

steps.title: Electronegativity and Polarity
steps.mastery: Use electronegativity differences to rank bond polarity.
steps.practice: Rank the 4 bonds H-H, H-Cl, H-O and Na-Cl from nonpolar to ionic using Pauling electronegativity values.
steps.detail: Unequal sharing makes a polar bond. A very large difference means electrons are transferred, giving an ionic bond.
steps.proof: H-H, H-Cl, H-O, Na-Cl.
steps.pitfall: Calling every bond between different atoms ionic.

problems.prompt: Most electronegative element in all 118?
Difference for H 2.2 and Cl 3.2?
Is a C-H bond with a difference of 0.4 polar or nearly nonpolar?

steps.title: Bonding and Properties
steps.mastery: Link bond type to melting point, solubility and conduction.
steps.practice: Predict melting point and conduction for NaCl, diamond, Cu and CH4 and match each to its bonding.
steps.detail: Giant ionic, giant covalent and metallic solids melt high. Simple molecules melt low because only weak forces hold molecules together.
steps.proof: A table of 4 substances with predictions and bond types.
steps.pitfall: Saying CH4 boils low because its covalent bonds are weak.

problems.prompt: Why does \(\mathrm{CH_{4}}\) boil at -162 degrees C?
Does diamond conduct electricity, with 4 bonds per C?
Does graphite conduct, with 3 bonds per C?

steps.title: Galvanic Cells
steps.mastery: Build a cell from 2 half cells.
steps.practice: Sketch a Zn and Cu cell with 1 M solutions and a salt bridge, labeling the anode, cathode and electron flow.
steps.detail: Oxidation happens at the anode and reduction at the cathode. Electrons flow through the wire and ions through the salt bridge.
steps.proof: A labeled cell with Zn as the anode.
steps.pitfall: Sending electrons through the salt bridge.

problems.prompt: Anode in a Zn/Cu cell?
Electron flow in the Zn/Cu cell, which way?
Job of the salt bridge filled with \(\mathrm{KNO_{3}}\)?
problems.answer: Let ions flow to keep charges balanced.

steps.title: Standard Potentials
steps.mastery: Compute cell voltage from E values.
steps.practice: Find E for a Zn/Cu cell with E(Zn2+/Zn) = -0.76 V and E(Cu2+/Cu) = +0.34 V.
steps.detail: E cell = E cathode - E anode. A positive value means the reaction runs on its own.
steps.pitfall: Multiplying E values by the number of electrons.

problems.prompt: E for Ag+/Ag 0.80 and Cu2+/Cu 0.34?
Is E cell = -0.3 V spontaneous?
Reference electrode at 0.00 V?

steps.title: Free Energy and Cells
steps.mastery: Link cell voltage to delta G.
steps.practice: Compute delta G for the Zn/Cu cell with n = 2, F = 96,485 C/mol and E = 1.10 V.
steps.detail: delta G = -nFE. A positive voltage gives a negative delta G, so the reaction is spontaneous.
steps.proof: About -212 kJ/mol.
steps.pitfall: Dropping the minus sign.

problems.prompt: delta G for \(n = 1\), \(E = 1.00\) V?
Sign of delta G when \(E = + 0.5\) V?
Value of F to 3 figures?

steps.title: Electrolysis
steps.mastery: Predict products when current drives a reaction.
steps.practice: Predict the products of electrolyzing molten NaCl and of brine, aqueous NaCl.
steps.detail: In electrolysis the cathode is negative and reduces, the anode oxidizes. In water, H2 may form instead of a reactive metal.
steps.proof: Molten: Na and Cl2. Brine: H2, Cl2 and NaOH.
steps.pitfall: Expecting Na metal from aqueous NaCl.

problems.prompt: Product at the cathode for molten \(\mathrm{PbBr_{2}}\)?
Product at the anode for molten \(\mathrm{NaCl}\)?
Gas at the cathode for dilute \(\mathrm{H_{2}SO_{4}}\)?

steps.title: Faraday Calculations
steps.mastery: Find mass deposited from current and time.
steps.practice: Find the mass of Cu plated by 2.0 A for 965 s from Cu2+, with Cu = 63.5 g/mol.
steps.detail: Charge Q = It, moles of electrons = Q/F, then use the half equation ratio to get moles of metal.
steps.proof: 1930 C, 0.02 mol e-, 0.01 mol Cu, about 0.635 g.
steps.pitfall: Forgetting that Cu2+ needs 2 electrons per atom.

problems.prompt: Charge from 3 A for 100 s?
Moles of e- in 9650 C?
Moles of Cu from 0.1 mol of electrons, in \(\mathrm{Cu}^{2+} + 2e^{-} \to \mathrm{Cu}\)?

steps.title: Shells 2, 8, 8
steps.mastery: Write simple shell configurations for the first 20 elements.
steps.practice: Write the shell configuration for C, Na, Cl, Ar and Ca using the 2, 8, 8, 2 pattern.
steps.detail: Shells fill from the nucleus outward. The outer shell count matches the group number for main groups.
steps.pitfall: Putting more than 2 electrons in the first shell.

problems.prompt: Shells for O, atomic number 8?
Shells for Mg, atomic number 12?
Outer electrons in P, atomic number 15?

steps.title: Subshells s, p, d
steps.mastery: Fill 1s, 2s, 2p and beyond in the right order.
steps.practice: Write full configurations for N, Na, Fe and Br in 1s2 2s2 2p6 notation.
steps.detail: Fill in the order 1s 2s 2p 3s 3p 4s 3d 4p. Each s subshell holds 2, each p holds 6 and each d holds 10.
steps.proof: N 1s2 2s2 2p3, Na [Ne]3s1, Fe [Ar]4s2 3d6, Br [Ar]4s2 3d10 4p5.
steps.pitfall: Filling 3d before 4s.

problems.prompt: Configuration of O, 8 electrons?
How many electrons fit in a 3d subshell?
Short form for K, 19 electrons?

steps.title: Orbital Boxes
