steps.detail: A relation on a set is a set of pairs. 'Divides' on {1, 2, 3, 4} includes (1, 2), (2, 4) and (3, 3). You can write it as pairs, a table or a diagram. Each view is good at showing something different.
steps.proof: 1 list and 1 drawing.
steps.pitfall: Thinking a relation needs a formula.

problems.prompt: Does 2 divide 4? Answer yes or no.
Is (4, 2) in 'divides' on {1, 2, 3, 4}? Answer yes or no.
How many pairs does 'divides' have on {1, 2, 3, 4}?

steps.title: Test the Properties
steps.mastery: Test a relation for the 3 big properties and find a counterexample if one fails.
steps.practice: Test 'less than' and 'equals' on the integers for 3 properties.
steps.detail: Reflexive means everything relates to itself. Symmetric means a to b gives b to a. Transitive means a to b and b to c gives a to c. Test each one, and look for a single counterexample if you think one fails.
steps.proof: A table of 6 answers.
steps.pitfall: Confusing symmetric with reflexive.

problems.prompt: Is \(5 < 5\) true? Answer yes or no.
Is 'less than' transitive on the integers? Answer yes or no.
Is 'equals' symmetric? Answer yes or no.

steps.title: Use Equivalence Relations
steps.mastery: Identify equivalence relations and classes.
steps.practice: Show that 'same remainder mod 3' is an equivalence relation, and list its 3 classes on 0 to 8.
steps.detail: A relation with all 3 properties sorts things into groups, called classes. Same remainder mod 3 gives 3 classes. Every element is in exactly one. It's how we treat different things as the same, for some purpose.
steps.proof: 1 proof and 3 classes.
steps.pitfall: Forgetting to check all 3 properties.

problems.prompt: 'Same remainder mod 3' splits the numbers 1 to 10 into classes. How many classes are there, and how big is the biggest?
problems.answer: 3 classes, and the biggest is {1, 4, 7, 10}, with 4 numbers.

problems.prompt: Are 2 and 8 in the same class mod 3? Answer yes or no.
Name the 3 properties of an equivalence relation.

steps.title: Use Partial Orders
steps.mastery: Spot a partial order and draw a Hasse diagram.
steps.practice: Draw the Hasse diagram of 'divides' on {1, 2, 3, 6}.
steps.detail: A partial order is reflexive, antisymmetric and transitive. Not everything has to be comparable, such as 2 and 3 under 'divides'. A Hasse diagram leaves out the obvious links and just draws upward steps. It's a good view of dependencies.
steps.proof: 1 diagram.
steps.pitfall: Assuming that any 2 items can be compared.

problems.prompt: Are 2 and 3 comparable under 'divides'? Answer yes or no.
Is 'divides' a partial order on positive integers? Answer yes or no.
Name the minimum of 'divides' on {1, 2, 3, 6}.

steps.title: Compose Relations
steps.mastery: Combine relations step by step.
steps.practice: Compose 'parent of' with itself on a family of 5 and name the new relation.
steps.detail: R then S connects a to c if a reaches b by R, and b reaches c by S. 'Parent of' with itself gives 'grandparent of'. It's the same idea as joining tables in a database, or matrix multiplication on an adjacency matrix.
steps.proof: 1 answer.
steps.pitfall: Reading the order backward.

problems.prompt: Compose 'parent of' with 'parent of'. Name it.
R = {(1, 2)} and S = {(2, 3)}. What's R then S?
R = {(1, 2)} and S = {(3, 4)}. How many pairs are in R then S?

steps.title: Use Set Notation
steps.mastery: Read and write sets and membership.
steps.practice: List the elements of {x in Z : 0 < x < 5} and write 2 membership statements.
steps.detail: A set is a collection with no order and no repeats. {1, 2, 2} is just {1, 2}. Builder notation describes a rule. Keep 'is an element of' apart from 'is a subset of', as they aren't the same thing.
steps.proof: 1 list and 2 statements.
steps.pitfall: Thinking that order or repeats matter.

problems.prompt: How many elements does {1, 2, 2, 3} have?
List {x in Z : 0 < x < 5}.
Is 2 an element of {1, {2}}? Answer yes or no.

steps.title: Combine Sets
steps.mastery: Combine 2 groups by union, overlap and what's left over.
steps.practice: For A = {1, 2, 3} and B = {2, 3, 4}, compute A ∪ B, A ∩ B and A - B.
steps.detail: Union means in either, intersection means in both, and difference means in the first but not the second. A Venn diagram of 2 circles helps you check. Complements depend on what the whole universe is, so say what it is.
steps.proof: 3 sets.
steps.pitfall: Mixing up union and intersection.

problems.prompt: A = {1, 2, 3}, B = {2, 3, 4}. How many elements are in A ∪ B?
Same sets. How many elements are in A ∩ B?
Same sets. List \(A - B\).

steps.title: Count with Inclusion-Exclusion
steps.mastery: Count a union without double counting.
steps.practice: Count the numbers from 1 to 100 divisible by 2 or 5 using |A| + |B| - |A ∩ B|.
steps.detail: |A ∪ B| = |A| + |B| - |A ∩ B|. Adding both counts the overlap twice, so take it back once. From 1 to 100, 50 are even and 20 are multiples of 5, and 10 are both, for 60 in total.
steps.proof: 1 count.
steps.pitfall: Adding the two sizes and stopping.

problems.prompt: How many of 1 to 100 are divisible by 2 or 5?
In a class of 30, 20 play soccer, 15 play chess and 8 do both. How many play neither?

steps.title: Use Subsets and Power Sets
steps.mastery: Find how many subsets a group of n things has.
steps.practice: List all 8 subsets of {a, b, c} and check that the count is 2^3.
steps.detail: A set with n elements has 2^n subsets, since each element is either in or out. That includes the empty set and the set itself. The power set is the set of all of these. It's a good model for yes-or-no choices.
steps.proof: 8 subsets.
steps.pitfall: Forgetting the empty set.

problems.prompt: How many subsets does {a, b, c} have?
How many subsets does a 5 element set have?
Is the empty set a subset of {1, 2}? Answer yes or no.

steps.title: Prove Set Claims
steps.mastery: Prove that one set is inside another.
steps.practice: Prove A ∩ B is a subset of A by taking any element x, in 3 lines.
steps.detail: To show A is a subset of B, take any x in A and show it's in B. To show two sets are equal, show both directions. Use words like 'let x be', so the reader can follow. Venn diagrams guide you but don't prove things.
steps.proof: 1 short proof.
steps.pitfall: Giving one example as if it proved the claim.

problems.prompt: To prove \(A = B\), how many subset directions must you show?
\(x\) is in A ∩ B. Must \(x\) be in A? Answer yes or no.
Is 1 example enough to prove 'A is a subset of B'? Answer yes or no.

steps.title: Define a Tree
steps.mastery: Recognize trees and their properties.
steps.practice: Draw all 3 different trees with 5 vertices and count their edges.
steps.detail: A tree is connected with no cycles. It has n - 1 edges, and there's one path between any two vertices. Remove an edge and it splits apart. Add an edge and you get a cycle. These facts are all equivalent to each other.
steps.proof: 3 trees.
steps.pitfall: Thinking a tree needs a root.

problems.prompt: How many edges does a tree with 8 vertices have?
Add 1 edge to a tree. Is it still a tree? Answer yes or no.
How many paths are there between 2 vertices in a tree?

steps.title: Use Rooted Trees
steps.mastery: Read depth, height and leaves.
steps.practice: Draw a rooted tree with 7 nodes, and label height, depth and leaves.
steps.detail: Rooting a tree gives parents and children. Depth counts from the root, and height is the deepest level. Leaves have no children. File systems and HTML are rooted trees. Code usually moves through them with recursion.
steps.proof: 1 labeled tree.
steps.pitfall: Confusing height with depth.

problems.prompt: What's the depth of the root?
Count the leaves of a full binary tree of height 2.
A full binary tree has height 2. How many nodes?

steps.title: Search Binary Trees
steps.mastery: Use a binary search tree.
steps.practice: Insert 5, 3, 8, 1, 4 into a BST and search for 4, counting the 3 comparisons.
steps.detail: Left is smaller, and right is larger. Each step cuts the search. Balanced trees have height about log n, so searches are quick. Sorted inserts make a bad tree that's really just a line, which is why balanced versions exist.
steps.proof: 1 tree.
steps.pitfall: Inserting sorted data and expecting it to be fast.

problems.prompt: Insert 5, 3, 8. Which node is the root?
Height of a balanced BST with 1023 nodes?
Insert 1, 2, 3, 4 into a BST. What's its height?

steps.title: Traverse a Tree
steps.mastery: Walk a tree in a set order.
steps.practice: Write preorder, inorder and postorder for a 5 node tree.
steps.detail: Preorder visits a node first, inorder visits it between its children, and postorder visits it last. Inorder on a BST gives you sorted order. Postorder fits deleting or adding up sizes, because children come first. Practice on small trees.
steps.proof: 3 orders.
steps.pitfall: Mixing up pre and post.

problems.prompt: Root 2, left 1, right 3. Give the inorder walk.
Same tree. Give the preorder walk.
Same tree. Give the postorder walk.

steps.title: Count Trees
steps.mastery: Count spanning trees and Catalan structures.
steps.practice: Use Cayley's formula to count labeled trees on 4 vertices, then list the first 5 Catalan numbers.
steps.detail: Cayley's formula gives n^(n - 2) labeled trees. Catalan numbers count binary trees, balanced brackets and more: 1, 1, 2, 5, 14. Many problems that look unrelated turn out to be the same count, which is a joy of this subject.
steps.proof: 2 answers.
steps.pitfall: Assuming labeled and unlabeled counts are the same.

problems.prompt: How many labeled trees are on 4 vertices?
Give the 5th Catalan number, in the list 1, 1, 2, 5, 14.
How many balanced strings have 3 pairs of brackets?

steps.title: Find Missing Values
steps.mastery: Count missing values in each column and decide how to handle them.
steps.practice: Run df.isna().sum() on a dataset and write a plan for each column with any missing values.
steps.detail: Missing values can be dropped, filled or kept as their own category. The right choice depends on why they are missing. Always count them before deciding.
steps.proof: Each column with missing values has a plan.
steps.pitfall: Filling every missing value with 0 without thinking.

problems.prompt: A column of 200 rows has 30 missing. What percent is missing?
Which call counts missing values per column of 'df'?
Why can filling missing 'income' with 0 distort the mean?
problems.answer: 0 is a real value that drags the mean down. Missing does not mean zero.

steps.title: Remove Duplicates
steps.mastery: Find and remove exact and near-duplicate rows.
steps.practice: Count duplicate rows with df.duplicated().sum() and drop them, then check the new shape.
steps.detail: Exported data often repeats rows. Decide which columns define a duplicate, such as order_id, and keep the first or latest copy.
steps.proof: The shape drops by exactly the number of duplicates.
steps.pitfall: Dropping duplicates on all columns when 2 rows differ only by a timestamp.

problems.prompt: A table has 1000 rows and 40 duplicates. How many after dropping them?
Which method on 'df' removes duplicate rows?
2 rows share an 'order_id' but differ in 'updated_at'. Which do you usually keep?

steps.title: Fix Inconsistent Labels
steps.mastery: Standardize categories written several ways into one spelling.
steps.practice: Clean a 'state' column holding 'NY', 'ny', 'New York' and ' NY ' into one value.
steps.detail: Strip spaces, fix case, then map known variants to a standard. value_counts before and after shows whether it worked.
steps.proof: value_counts shows one 'NY' entry.
steps.pitfall: Fixing case but not trailing spaces.

problems.prompt: What does ' NY '.strip() return?
What does 'ny'.upper() return?
A column has 'NY' x 50, 'ny' x 10 and 'New York' x 5. After cleaning, how many 'NY'?

steps.title: Convert Types
steps.mastery: Convert text columns to numbers and dates so they behave correctly.
steps.practice: Convert a 'price' column like '$1,200' to a number and a 'date' column like '03/04/2026' to a datetime.
steps.detail: Strip symbols and commas before pd.to_numeric. Give pd.to_datetime an explicit format so March 4 is not read as April 3. Use errors='coerce' to spot values that fail.
steps.proof: The dtypes show float and datetime.
steps.pitfall: Letting the date parser guess day and month order.

problems.prompt: After removing '$' and ',', what number is '$1,200' times 3?
Read with format '%m/%d/%Y', which month is '03/04/2026'?
What does errors='coerce' do to a value that cannot convert?

steps.title: Handle Outliers
steps.mastery: Find extreme values and decide whether they are errors or real.
steps.practice: Use a box plot or the 1.5 x IQR rule to flag outliers in a 'height_cm' column, then check each one.
steps.detail: An outlier might be a typo (a height of 1800 cm) or a real rare case. Fix typos, keep real values, and record what you did.
steps.proof: Each flagged value is labeled as error or real.
steps.pitfall: Deleting every outlier automatically.

problems.prompt: Q1 = 160 and Q3 = 180. What is the IQR?
With that IQR, what is the upper fence at Q3 + 1.5 x IQR?
A height of 1800 cm is most likely what kind of outlier?

steps.title: Compute Correlation
steps.mastery: Compute and interpret the Pearson correlation coefficient.
steps.practice: Compute df['hours'].corr(df['score']) for a dataset and describe its strength and direction.
steps.detail: r runs from -1 to 1. Its sign shows direction and its size shows how tightly points follow a straight line. Around 0.7 or more is strong.
steps.proof: You report r and describe it in words.
steps.pitfall: Reading r = 0.3 as a strong relationship.

problems.prompt: Give the lowest and then the highest value Pearson's r can take.
r = -0.8: strong or weak, and which direction?
r = 0.05: is there a strong straight-line relationship? Answer yes or no.

steps.title: Plot Before Trusting
steps.mastery: Plot data before trusting a correlation, since different shapes give the same r.
steps.practice: Plot Anscombe's 4 datasets and note that each has r of about 0.82.
steps.detail: Anscombe's quartet shows a line, a curve, an outlier and a single far point, all with the same r. Only a plot shows which you have.
steps.proof: You describe each of the 4 shapes.
steps.pitfall: Reporting r without looking at a scatter plot.

problems.prompt: How many datasets are in Anscombe's quartet?
Can a U-shaped relationship have r near 0? Answer yes or no.
1 extreme outlier can do what to r?
problems.answer: Inflate or flip it, even when the other points have no relationship.

steps.title: Correlation Is Not Causation
steps.mastery: Explain why a correlation alone does not show cause.
steps.practice: List 2 explanations other than cause for the correlation between ice cream sales and drownings.
steps.detail: A third variable (hot weather) can drive both. The direction can also run backward, or it can be chance. Only experiments or careful designs establish cause.
steps.proof: You name hot weather and 1 other explanation.
steps.pitfall: Claiming one variable causes another from r alone.

problems.prompt: Ice cream sales and drownings both rise in July. Name the likely third variable.
A variable that drives both 'X' and 'Y' is called what?
Name 1 study design that can show cause.

steps.title: Rank Correlation
steps.mastery: Use Spearman correlation for monotonic but non-linear relationships.
steps.practice: Compute both Pearson and Spearman for a dataset where y = x^3 and compare them.
steps.detail: Spearman uses ranks, so any steadily increasing relationship scores 1 even if it is curved. It is also less sensitive to outliers.
steps.proof: Spearman is 1 and Pearson is lower.
steps.pitfall: Using Pearson on a curved but monotonic relationship and calling it weak.

problems.prompt: For \(y = x^{3}\) on x = 1 to 10, what is Spearman's correlation?
Which correlation uses ranks: Pearson or Spearman?
Name 1 advantage of Spearman with 1 extreme outlier.
problems.answer: It is less affected by the outlier.

steps.title: Correlation Matrix
steps.mastery: Build a correlation matrix and read it carefully.
steps.practice: Compute df.corr() for 5 numeric columns and list the 2 strongest relationships.
steps.detail: A matrix shows every pair at once, and a heatmap makes it scannable. Look for surprising pairs and for near-duplicate columns with r near 1.
steps.proof: You list the 2 strongest pairs with their r values.
steps.pitfall: Reading the diagonal of 1s as findings.

problems.prompt: A correlation matrix of 5 columns has how many cells?
What value is always on the diagonal of a 5 x 5 correlation matrix?
Two columns correlate at 0.99. What might that mean?
problems.answer: They measure almost the same thing (near-duplicate).

steps.title: Define One Row
steps.mastery: Say in one sentence what a single row of a dataset represents.
steps.practice: Write one sentence that defines a row for 3 datasets: a store's sales export, a class roster and a weather log.
steps.detail: Every analysis question depends on the unit of observation. A sales export might have one row per item sold, not per order, so counting rows counts items. Write the definition before computing anything.
steps.proof: Each dataset has a one-sentence row definition.
steps.pitfall: Counting rows and calling it orders when each row is a line item.

problems.prompt: A table has 1 row per student per class. Alice takes 4 classes. How many rows is she?
An orders file has 3 rows for order 1001 (3 items). How many orders are in those rows?
A weather log has 1 row per hour. How many rows cover 2 days?

steps.title: Variables and Types
steps.mastery: Know which kind of value each column holds, because that decides what you can compute.
steps.practice: List the 6 columns of a sample dataset and label each as numeric, categorical, date or text.
steps.detail: Types decide which operations make sense: you can average a numeric column but not a ZIP code, even though it holds digits. A date stored as text needs converting before you can sort it by time.
steps.proof: Every column has a type and one sentence on what it means.
steps.pitfall: Treating ID numbers or ZIP codes as numbers to be averaged.

problems.prompt: Is a column of ZIP codes like 02139 numeric or categorical?
Can you take the mean of a 'color' column with values red, blue and green? Answer yes or no.
A 'signup_date' column holds text like '2026-03-04'. What must happen before sorting it by time?
problems.answer: Convert it to a date type.

steps.title: Shape of a Dataset
steps.mastery: Report a dataset's number of rows and columns and what each dimension means.
steps.practice: Load a CSV with pandas and print df.shape, then write what the 2 numbers mean.
steps.detail: shape gives (rows, columns). Checking it after every load and transform is the quickest way to catch a filter that removed too much or a join that duplicated rows.
steps.proof: You report the shape and the meaning of each number.
steps.pitfall: Never checking the shape after a transform.

problems.prompt: A table loads with shape (500, 8). Read off the number of rows.
df.shape is (500, 8). How many columns?
After a filter, the shape went from (500, 8) to (120, 8). How many rows were removed?

steps.title: Tidy Data
steps.mastery: Recognize tidy data: one variable per column, one observation per row.
steps.practice: Reshape a table with columns 'jan', 'feb' and 'mar' into 2 columns, 'month' and 'value'.
steps.detail: In tidy data, months spread across columns become values in a single month column. pandas melt does this. Tidy tables make grouping and plotting simple.
steps.proof: The reshaped table has 3 times as many rows and 2 value columns.
steps.pitfall: Keeping one column per month, which makes time comparisons awkward.

problems.prompt: A table has 10 rows and columns 'jan', 'feb' and 'mar'. After melting into 'month' and 'value', how many rows?
Which function, 'pivot' or 'melt', turns wide columns into rows?
Is a table with columns 'name', 'test1', 'test2' and 'test3' tidy for comparing tests? Answer yes or no.
problems.answer: No, the tests should be values in one column.

steps.title: Data Dictionary
steps.mastery: Write a short data dictionary listing each column's meaning, type and units.
steps.practice: Write a data dictionary for 5 columns, including units such as kg, USD or seconds.
steps.detail: A data dictionary saves every future reader from guessing. Units matter: a 'price' column in cents instead of dollars changes every result by 100 times.
steps.proof: Each column has a meaning, type and unit.
steps.pitfall: Leaving units implied, so someone averages cents as dollars.

problems.prompt: A 'price' column is in cents and averages 1250. What is that in dollars?
A 'duration' column is in seconds and a value is 5400. How many hours?
Name the 3 things to list per column in a data dictionary.

steps.title: Mean and Median
steps.mastery: Compute the mean and median and explain when they differ.
steps.practice: Compute the mean and median of incomes 30, 35, 40, 45 and 300 (thousands) and explain the gap.
steps.detail: The mean is pulled by extreme values and the median is not. When they differ a lot, the data is skewed and the median usually describes a typical value better.
steps.proof: Mean 90 and median 40, with the gap explained by the 300.
steps.pitfall: Reporting the mean income of a skewed sample as typical.

problems.prompt: What is the mean of 2, 4 and 9?
What is the median of 2, 4, 9 and 11?
The mean is 90 and the median is 40. Is the data right- or left-skewed?

steps.title: Spread
steps.mastery: Measure spread with range, standard deviation and the interquartile range.
steps.practice: Compute the range, IQR and standard deviation of 4, 8, 6, 5 and 7.
steps.detail: Spread says how far values sit from the center. The IQR ignores extremes. The standard deviation uses all values and is in the data's units.
steps.proof: Range 4, and you compute the IQR and a standard deviation of about 1.41.
steps.pitfall: Reporting a mean without any measure of spread.

problems.prompt: What is the range of 3, 9, 4 and 12?
What is the population standard deviation of 2, 4, 4, 4, 5, 5, 7 and 9?
Q1 is 10 and Q3 is 25. What is the IQR?

steps.title: Quantiles
steps.mastery: Use percentiles to describe where a value sits in a distribution.
steps.practice: Compute the 25th, 50th and 90th percentiles of a column with df.quantile([0.25, 0.5, 0.9]).
steps.detail: The 90th percentile is the value 90% of the data sits below. Percentiles are robust to outliers and easy to explain.
steps.proof: You report 3 percentiles.
steps.pitfall: Confusing a percentile (a value) with a percentage (a share).

problems.prompt: The median sits at which percentile: 25th, 50th or 75th?
A score is at the 80th percentile in a class of 50. About how many scores are below it?
Write the pandas call for the 95th percentile of column 'x'.

steps.title: Summaries by Group
steps.mastery: Compare summary statistics across groups.
steps.practice: Compute the median and IQR of 'time_on_task' for 3 user groups and write which group is most variable.
steps.detail: Comparing groups is where summaries become useful. Report center and spread together, or a group with one extreme user can look different for the wrong reason.
steps.proof: You name the most variable group with numbers.
steps.pitfall: Comparing only means across groups with different spreads.

problems.prompt: Group A median 12 and IQR 4, Group B median 12 and IQR 15. Which is more variable?
Means 20 and 25 with sample sizes 3 and 3000. Which mean is more trustworthy?
Which pandas call computes a median per 'group'?

steps.title: Five-Number Summary
steps.mastery: Report the minimum, Q1, median, Q3 and maximum and read a box plot from them.
steps.practice: Write the 5-number summary of 2, 4, 5, 7, 9, 11 and 20 and sketch the box plot.
steps.detail: The 5 numbers show center, spread and skew at once, and a box plot draws exactly them. A long upper whisker shows a right tail.
steps.proof: Min 2, Q1 4, median 7, Q3 11, max 20 (using the median-of-halves method).
steps.pitfall: Mixing up the median with the mean when drawing the box.

problems.prompt: What is the median of 2, 4, 5, 7, 9, 11 and 20?
In a box plot of 100 scores, what does the line inside the box show?
A box plot's upper whisker is 3 times longer than the lower one. What does that suggest?

steps.title: Normal Shape
steps.mastery: Recognize a normal distribution and use the 68-95-99.7 rule.
steps.practice: Use the 68-95-99.7 rule to find the range holding 95% of heights with mean 170 cm and standard deviation 8.
steps.detail: In a normal distribution, about 68% of values fall within 1 standard deviation, 95% within 2, and 99.7% within 3.
steps.proof: 95% fall between 154 and 186 cm.
steps.pitfall: Assuming every dataset is normal.

problems.prompt: Mean 100 and SD 15: give the low end, then the high end, of the range that holds about 68%.
What percent of a normal distribution lies more than 2 SD above the mean?
A value has z = 3. Is it unusual? Answer yes or no.
problems.answer: Yes, only about 0.15% are that high.

steps.title: Z-Scores
steps.mastery: Standardize a value with z = (x - mean) / SD to compare across scales.
steps.practice: Compute z-scores for a test score of 85 (mean 75, SD 5) and 90 (mean 80, SD 10) and say which is more impressive.
steps.detail: A z-score says how many standard deviations a value sits from its mean. It lets you compare scores on different tests.
steps.proof: z = 2 for the 85 and z = 1 for the 90, so the 85 is more impressive.
steps.pitfall: Comparing raw scores from tests with different spreads.

problems.prompt: Value 60, mean 50, SD 5: what is z?
Value 40, mean 50, SD 10: what is z?
z = 1.5 with mean 200 and SD 20. What is the value?

steps.title: Skewed Data
steps.mastery: Recognize skewed distributions and choose robust summaries for them.
steps.practice: Plot a histogram of 1000 incomes and decide whether to report the mean or the median.
steps.detail: Incomes, house prices and website visits usually have long right tails. The median and percentiles describe them better than the mean.
steps.proof: You choose the median and give a reason.
steps.pitfall: Reporting the mean of a long-tailed variable as typical.

problems.prompt: For 1000 right-skewed incomes, which is usually larger: the mean or the median?
Name 2 real variables that are usually right-skewed.
Which transform often makes right-skewed data more symmetric: 'log' or 'square'?

steps.title: Discrete Distributions
steps.mastery: Use the binomial distribution for counts of successes in fixed trials.
steps.practice: Calculate the probability of exactly 2 heads in 3 fair coin flips with the binomial formula.
steps.detail: Binomial: n trials, each with success probability p. P(k) = C(n, k) p^k (1 - p)^(n - k). The expected count is n x p.
steps.pitfall: Using a binomial when trials are not independent.

problems.prompt: 10 trials with p = 0.3: what is the expected number of successes?
What is C(4, 2)?
What is the probability of 0 heads in 2 fair flips?

steps.title: Check the Shape
steps.mastery: Check whether data looks normal before using methods that assume it.
steps.practice: Make a histogram and a Q-Q plot of 200 values and decide whether a normal assumption is reasonable.
steps.detail: On a Q-Q plot, normal data falls near a straight line. Curves at the ends show heavy tails or skew. With large samples, mild departures often do not matter.
steps.proof: You state yes or no with a reason from the plots.
steps.pitfall: Running a normality test on 10000 rows and panicking at tiny departures.

problems.prompt: On a Q-Q plot of 200 values, what pattern suggests normal data?
problems.answer: Points close to a straight line.

problems.prompt: Points curve upward at the right end. What does that suggest?
problems.answer: A heavy right tail or right skew.

problems.prompt: With n = 5000, does a tiny departure from normality usually matter for a mean? Answer yes or no.

steps.title: Consent and Purpose
steps.mastery: Check that data is used only for purposes people agreed to.
steps.practice: Write the original purpose of 1 dataset you use and 2 uses that would go beyond it.
steps.detail: Data collected for one purpose is not automatically fine for another. Using health data for marketing, for example, breaks trust and often law.
steps.proof: You list the purpose and 2 out-of-scope uses.
steps.pitfall: Assuming any data you can access is fine to use.

problems.prompt: Name 1 law that governs personal data in the EU.
Data was collected to deliver orders. Is using it to train an unrelated ad model clearly allowed? Answer yes or no.
problems.answer: No, it may go beyond the purpose.

problems.prompt: Before reusing 2024 order data for a new purpose, what should you check?
problems.answer: Whether consent and policy cover the new use.

steps.title: Re-identification Risk
steps.mastery: Recognize how 'anonymous' data can identify people.
steps.practice: List 3 columns in a dataset that could identify someone when combined, such as ZIP code, birth date and gender.
steps.detail: Removing names is not enough. A famous study found ZIP code, birth date and gender identify most Americans. Aggregate or coarsen such fields.
steps.proof: You list 3 risky columns and a fix for each.
steps.pitfall: Publishing 'anonymized' rows with exact birth dates and ZIP codes.

problems.prompt: Name 3 fields that together can identify most Americans.
problems.answer: ZIP code, birth date and gender.

problems.prompt: Coarsen a birth date of 2008-04-17 to reduce risk.
Is removing the 'name' column enough to anonymize data? Answer yes or no.

steps.title: Fairness Across Groups
steps.mastery: Compare a model's errors across groups to find unequal harm.
steps.practice: Compute a model's false-positive rate separately for 2 groups and compare them.
steps.detail: A model can be accurate overall and still fail one group much more. Check error rates by group, and look at who bears the cost of each error type.
steps.proof: You report 2 group error rates and the gap.
steps.pitfall: Reporting only overall accuracy.

problems.prompt: False positives are 5% in group A and 15% in group B. What is the gap?
Can a model be 95% accurate overall and unfair to one group? Answer yes or no.
Name 1 source of unfairness in training data.
problems.answer: Historical bias or underrepresentation of a group.

steps.title: Minimize Data
steps.mastery: Collect and keep only the data you need.
steps.practice: Review 1 dataset's 15 columns and mark the ones your analysis does not need, then drop them.
steps.detail: Data you do not hold cannot leak. Minimization reduces risk and often simplifies analysis. Set deletion dates for data you keep.
steps.proof: Unneeded columns are removed and a retention date is set.
steps.pitfall: Keeping every field forever just in case.

problems.prompt: A table has 15 columns and you need 6. How many can you drop?
Name 1 benefit of data minimization.
problems.answer: Less damage if there is a breach (also simpler analysis).

problems.prompt: Should personal data have a retention limit? Answer yes or no.

steps.title: Think About Harm
steps.mastery: Ask who could be harmed by an analysis or model before releasing it.
steps.practice: Write 2 ways a school dropout prediction model could harm students and 1 safeguard for each.
steps.detail: Predictions can label people, decide resources or invade privacy. Safeguards include human review, explaining results and letting people appeal.
steps.proof: Two harms with a safeguard each.
steps.pitfall: Assuming a model is neutral because it is math.

problems.prompt: Name 1 harm of a dropout prediction model.
problems.answer: Labeling a student as likely to fail, which can lower expectations.

problems.prompt: Name 1 safeguard for an automated decision.
problems.answer: Human review (or a way to appeal).

problems.prompt: Is a model neutral just because it uses math? Answer yes or no.
problems.answer: No, it reflects its data and design choices.

steps.title: Randomize Assignment
steps.mastery: Assign units to groups at random so the comparison is fair.
steps.practice: Randomly assign 200 users to 2 groups with a fixed seed and check the groups have similar ages.
steps.detail: Randomization balances everything, measured or not, on average. That is what lets a difference be called caused by the treatment.
steps.proof: Both groups have about 100 users and similar mean ages.
steps.pitfall: Letting users choose their group.

problems.prompt: 200 users split evenly at random: how many per group?
Why not let users opt in to the new feature for an A/B test?
problems.answer: Volunteers differ from others, so differences are not due to the feature.

problems.prompt: With 200 users randomized, which traits balance on average: measured, unmeasured, or both?

steps.title: Choose a Metric
steps.mastery: Pick 1 primary metric before running an experiment.
steps.practice: Write 1 primary metric, its definition and the minimum change worth acting on for a checkout redesign test.
steps.detail: Choosing the metric in advance prevents hunting for any number that moved. A secondary list catches side effects.
steps.proof: You have 1 primary metric with a definition and threshold.
steps.pitfall: Deciding which metric matters after seeing the results.

problems.prompt: Name 1 primary metric for a checkout redesign.
Why choose the metric before the 2-week test starts?
problems.answer: To avoid picking whichever metric happened to move.

problems.prompt: Conversion is 4% and the smallest change worth acting on is 0.4 points. What target is that?

steps.title: Plan Sample Size
steps.mastery: Estimate how many users a test needs before starting.
steps.practice: Use an online calculator to find the sample size per group for detecting a lift from 10% to 12% at 80% power.
steps.detail: Smaller effects need larger samples. Deciding the size in advance stops you ending the test the moment it looks good.
steps.proof: You have a per-group sample size written down.
steps.pitfall: Running a test for 2 days and calling it.

problems.prompt: Detecting a 1% lift instead of a 5% lift needs bigger or smaller samples?
What does 80% power mean?
problems.answer: An 80% chance of detecting the effect if it is real.

problems.prompt: You need 4000 per group and get 1000 users a day split evenly. How many days?

steps.title: Avoid Peeking
steps.mastery: Avoid stopping a test early because the result looks good.
steps.practice: Write a rule for your test: analyze only after reaching the planned sample size of 4000 per group.
steps.detail: Checking daily and stopping at the first p < 0.05 inflates false positives a lot. Fix the sample size or use a method designed for sequential checks.
steps.proof: The rule is written before the test starts.
steps.pitfall: Stopping on day 3 because p dipped below 0.05.

problems.prompt: Does checking 10 times and stopping at the first p < 0.05 keep a 5% false-positive rate? Answer yes or no.
Name 1 way to monitor a test safely.
problems.answer: A sequential testing method with adjusted thresholds.

problems.prompt: Planned size is 4000 per group and you have 1500. Should you conclude yet? Answer yes or no.

steps.title: Read the Result
steps.mastery: Report the lift, its uncertainty and the decision.
steps.practice: Report an A/B result: control 10.0% and treatment 11.2% conversion, with a 95% interval for the difference.
steps.detail: Give the absolute and relative lift, the interval and the decision. An interval that includes 0 means the effect is not clear.
steps.proof: You state lift, interval and decision.
steps.pitfall: Reporting only that the test won.

problems.prompt: Control converts at 10.0% and treatment at 11.2%. What is the absolute lift, in percentage points?
Express a rise from 10.0% to 11.2% as a percent of the starting rate.
The 95% interval for the lift is -0.3 to 2.7 points. Is the effect clearly positive? Answer yes or no.

steps.title: First Look
steps.mastery: Inspect the first rows, the types and a summary of every new dataset.
steps.practice: Run df.head(), df.info() and df.describe() on a new dataset and write 3 things you noticed.
steps.detail: These 3 calls show values, types, missing counts and ranges. Surprises like a negative age or a column of all zeros show up here before they spoil an analysis.
steps.proof: You list 3 observations.
steps.pitfall: Starting modeling before looking at the data.

problems.prompt: Which call shows the first 5 rows?
df.describe() shows age min = -3. What does that suggest?
Which call on 'df' shows column types and non-null counts?

steps.title: Check Ranges
steps.mastery: Compare each column's minimum and maximum with what is possible.
steps.practice: List the min and max of 5 numeric columns and mark any impossible values.
steps.detail: A percent above 100, a date in the future or a price of 0 are all clues. Knowing what is possible is half of exploratory analysis.
steps.proof: Every impossible value is marked.
steps.pitfall: Accepting summary statistics without asking whether they make sense.

problems.prompt: A 'percent_complete' max is 140. Is that possible? Answer yes or no.
An 'age' column ranges from 0 to 212. Which value is suspicious?
A 'signup_date' max is in the year 2091. What does that suggest?

steps.title: Count Categories
steps.mastery: Count the values in each categorical column to spot rare and odd categories.
steps.practice: Run value_counts() on 3 categorical columns and note categories with fewer than 5 rows.
steps.detail: Rare categories are often typos. Very common ones dominate results. Both matter before grouping.
steps.proof: Rare categories are listed and checked.
steps.pitfall: Grouping without checking for typo categories first.

problems.prompt: Counts are 'red' 50, 'blue' 45 and 'Red' 2. What is likely wrong?
Which method counts the values in column 'color'?
A category has 3 rows out of 10000. What share is that?

steps.title: Look at Distributions
steps.mastery: Plot histograms of numeric columns to see shape, skew and gaps.
steps.practice: Plot histograms of 3 numeric columns with 30 bins each and describe each shape in a few words.
steps.detail: A histogram shows whether values are symmetric, skewed or have 2 peaks. The shape decides which summary statistics make sense.
steps.proof: Each histogram has a 1-line description.
steps.pitfall: Using too few bins and hiding a second peak.

problems.prompt: A histogram of 1000 incomes has a long tail to the right. Is it right-skewed or left-skewed?
A histogram shows 2 peaks. What is that called?
With 1000 values and 30 bins, about how many values per bin on average?

steps.title: Check Relationships
steps.mastery: Look at pairs of variables with scatter plots and cross-tabs before testing anything.
steps.practice: Make a scatter plot of 2 numeric columns and a crosstab of 2 categorical columns, and describe each.
steps.detail: A quick look at pairs shows obvious links, clusters and outliers. It also suggests which questions are worth testing formally.
steps.proof: You describe 1 relationship from each plot.
steps.pitfall: Jumping to correlation numbers without plotting.

problems.prompt: On a scatter of 'hours' against 'score', points rise from lower left to upper right. Positive or negative?
Which pandas function builds a table of counts for 2 categories?
A scatter plot shows 2 separate clusters. Name 1 thing to check next.
problems.answer: Whether a third variable (like group or region) separates them.

steps.title: Ratios and Rates
steps.mastery: Create ratio features that compare quantities fairly.
steps.practice: Create 'revenue_per_visit' from 'revenue' and 'visits' and compare it across 3 stores of different sizes.
steps.detail: Raw totals favor big units. A rate like revenue per visit compares fairly. Guard against division by 0.
steps.proof: Each store has a per-visit figure.
steps.pitfall: Comparing raw totals between stores of very different sizes.

problems.prompt: Revenue 5000 and visits 250. What is revenue per visit?
Store A earns 10000 from 1000 visits, B earns 6000 from 300. Which earns more per visit?
What should a ratio feature do when visits = 0?
problems.answer: Set it to missing or handle it explicitly, not divide by 0.

steps.title: Date Parts
steps.mastery: Split dates into useful parts like weekday, month and hour.
steps.practice: Create 'weekday' and 'hour' columns from a 'timestamp' column with the pandas .dt accessor.
steps.detail: Many patterns repeat by weekday or hour. df.timestamp.dt.dayofweek gives 0 for Monday through 6 for Sunday.
steps.proof: Both new columns have sensible values.
steps.pitfall: Treating dates as raw numbers or strings.

problems.prompt: In pandas, what dayofweek number is Monday?
Name 1 feature from a date useful for predicting store traffic.
problems.answer: Weekday (or month, or whether it is a holiday).

steps.title: Encode Categories
steps.mastery: Turn categorical columns into numbers a model can use.
steps.practice: One-hot encode a 'color' column with 3 values using pd.get_dummies and check the new columns.
steps.detail: One-hot encoding makes a 0/1 column per category. Do not encode categories as 1, 2, 3, which invents an order. Rare categories can be grouped as other.
steps.proof: You get 3 indicator columns.
steps.pitfall: Encoding red, green and blue as 1, 2 and 3.

problems.prompt: A color column has red, green, blue and black, and a size column has S, M and L. Keeping every category, how many columns does one-hot encoding both make?
Why is encoding sizes as 1, 2, 3 fine but colors as 1, 2, 3 not?
problems.answer: Sizes have a real order and colors do not.

problems.prompt: Which function, 'get_dummies' or 'melt', one-hot encodes?

steps.title: Scale Features
steps.mastery: Standardize numeric features so different units do not dominate.
steps.practice: Standardize 'income' and 'age' with (x - mean) / SD and compare their new ranges.
steps.detail: Many models are sensitive to scale. Standardizing puts features on similar footing. Fit the scaler on training data only.
steps.proof: Both columns have mean about 0 and SD about 1.
steps.pitfall: Fitting the scaler on all data, leaking test information.

problems.prompt: Age 40, mean 30, SD 10. What is the standardized value?
After standardizing, what is a column's mean?
Should the scaler be fit on training data only? Answer yes or no.

steps.title: Test a Feature
steps.mastery: Check whether a new feature improves a model on held-out data.
steps.practice: Compare a model's validation score with and without 1 new feature, using the same split.
steps.detail: A feature earns its place only if it helps on data the model has not seen. Training scores always improve with more features.
steps.proof: You report 2 validation scores.
steps.pitfall: Judging a feature by training accuracy.

problems.prompt: Validation accuracy goes from 0.82 to 0.85 with a feature. What is the gain?
Training accuracy rises but validation falls. What is happening?
Why use the same 80/20 split for both comparisons?
problems.answer: So the difference comes from the feature, not the data split.

steps.title: State the Hypotheses
steps.mastery: Write a null and an alternative hypothesis for a question.
steps.practice: Write H0 and H1 for whether a new tutoring program raises mean test scores.
steps.detail: The null hypothesis says no effect, such as equal means. The alternative says there is an effect. The test asks how surprising the data would be if the null were true.
steps.proof: H0: the means are equal. H1: the tutored mean is higher.
steps.pitfall: Writing the hypothesis you hope for as the null.

problems.prompt: What does H0, the null hypothesis, usually say: an effect or no effect?
Write H0 for 'coin is fair' using p for the chance of heads.
Is 'the new drug changes recovery time' a one-sided or two-sided H1?

steps.title: Read a p-value
steps.mastery: Interpret a p-value correctly and know what it does not say.
steps.practice: Write a correct one-sentence reading of p = 0.03 for a test comparing 2 groups.
steps.detail: A p-value is the probability of data at least this extreme if the null were true. It is not the probability the null is true, and it says nothing about how big the effect is.
steps.proof: Your sentence mentions 'if there were no difference'.
steps.pitfall: Saying p = 0.03 means a 3% chance the null is true.

problems.prompt: p = 0.03 with alpha = 0.05: reject the null? Answer yes or no.
A second study gets p = 0.20. At the 0.05 level, is the result significant?
Does p = 0.001 mean the effect is large? Answer yes or no.
problems.answer: No, only that it is unlikely under the null.

steps.title: Run a t-Test
steps.mastery: Compare 2 group means with a t-test and report the result.
steps.practice: Run scipy.stats.ttest_ind on 2 groups of 30 scores and report t, p and the mean difference.
steps.detail: A t-test compares means relative to their variability. Report the difference in means alongside p, since that is what readers care about.
steps.proof: You report the difference, t and p.
steps.pitfall: Reporting only that p was below 0.05.

problems.prompt: Which scipy function compares 2 independent group means?
Group means are 72 and 78. What is the difference?
Besides 'p = 0.03', what extra number should a report give?
problems.answer: The effect size, such as the mean difference.

steps.title: Effect Size
steps.mastery: Report how big a difference is, not just whether it is significant.
steps.practice: Compute Cohen's d for means 75 and 80 with a pooled SD of 10.
steps.detail: Cohen's d is the mean difference divided by the SD. Values near 0.2 are small, 0.5 medium and 0.8 large. Large samples make tiny effects significant.
steps.proof: d = 0.5, a medium effect.
steps.pitfall: Calling a significant but tiny effect important.

problems.prompt: Means 100 and 103, SD 15. What is Cohen's d?
Is d = 0.2 usually called small, medium or large?
With n = 1000000, a difference of 0.01 SD is significant. Is it important? Answer yes or no.
problems.answer: No, usually not. The effect is tiny, even though it's significant.

steps.title: Multiple Tests
steps.mastery: Know why running many tests produces false positives, and correct for it.
steps.practice: Calculate how many false positives to expect from 20 tests at alpha = 0.05 when nothing is real, then apply a Bonferroni correction.
steps.detail: Each test has a 5% false-positive chance, so 20 tests give about 1 by luck. Bonferroni divides alpha by the number of tests.
steps.proof: Expect 1 false positive, and the corrected alpha is 0.0025.
steps.pitfall: Running 50 tests and reporting the 3 that hit p < 0.05.

problems.prompt: 100 tests at alpha 0.05 with no real effects: expected false positives?
Bonferroni alpha for 10 tests at 0.05?
You tested 30 features and found 2 significant at 0.05. Should you trust them? Explain.
problems.answer: Not yet, about 1.5 false positives are expected by chance.

steps.title: Pick the Key
steps.mastery: Identify the column that links 2 tables and check it is unique where it should be.
steps.practice: Check that 'customer_id' is unique in a customers table with df['customer_id'].is_unique before joining.
steps.detail: A join matches rows on a key. If the key repeats on the side that should be unique, rows multiply. Check before, not after.
steps.proof: is_unique returns True.
steps.pitfall: Joining on 'name', which repeats and changes.

problems.prompt: A customers table of 500 rows has 500 unique IDs. Is the key unique? Answer yes or no.
Why is 'customer_name' a poor join key?
problems.answer: Names repeat and can be spelled differently.

problems.prompt: Which pandas property checks uniqueness of column 'id'?

steps.title: Inner and Left Joins
steps.mastery: Choose between an inner and a left join and predict the row count.
steps.practice: Join 100 orders to 80 customers with how='left' and how='inner' and compare the row counts.
steps.detail: An inner join keeps only matches. A left join keeps every left row and fills missing matches with NaN. Choose by whether unmatched rows matter.
steps.proof: The left join has 100 rows and the inner has the matched count.
steps.pitfall: Using an inner join and silently dropping orders with no customer record.

problems.prompt: 100 orders, 90 match a customer. How many rows from an inner join (unique customer keys)?
Same tables, a left join from orders. How many rows?
In a left join of 100 orders, what fills the customer columns for orders with no match?

steps.title: Check Row Counts
steps.mastery: Compare row counts before and after every join to catch duplication.
steps.practice: Record len(df) before and after a join and explain any change.
steps.detail: A many-to-many join can multiply rows. If a left join returns more rows than the left table had, the right key is not unique.
steps.proof: The row count is as expected.
steps.pitfall: Never checking and reporting doubled totals.

problems.prompt: Left table 200 rows, after a left join 260. What does that suggest?
problems.answer: Duplicate keys on the right side.

problems.prompt: Which 'merge' argument raises an error if keys are not one-to-one?
Sales totaled $10,000 before a join and $15,000 after. What likely happened?

steps.title: Find Unmatched Rows
steps.mastery: Use an indicator column to see which rows matched in a join.
steps.practice: Run a merge with indicator=True and count 'left_only', 'right_only' and 'both'.
steps.detail: The indicator column shows where each row came from. Unmatched rows often reveal ID formatting problems like leading zeros.
steps.proof: You report the 3 counts.
steps.pitfall: Assuming every row matched.

problems.prompt: Counts are both 950, left_only 50, right_only 0. How many left rows had no match?
IDs '007' and '7' fail to match. What is a likely cause?
problems.answer: One side was stored as text with leading zeros.

problems.prompt: Which merge argument adds a '_merge' column?

steps.title: Stack Tables
steps.mastery: Append tables with the same columns using concat.
steps.practice: Combine 12 monthly CSV files with the same columns into 1 table with pd.concat and add a 'month' column.
steps.detail: concat stacks rows. Make sure the columns match in name and type, and add a column recording each row's source.
steps.proof: The combined table has the sum of the 12 row counts.
steps.pitfall: Concatenating files with different column names and getting misaligned columns.

problems.prompt: 12 files of 1000 rows each: how many rows after concat?
Is concat a join on a key? Answer yes or no.
Why add a 'month' column while stacking 12 files?
problems.answer: To know which file each row came from.

steps.title: Run Top to Bottom
steps.mastery: Make a notebook that runs cleanly from the first cell to the last.
steps.practice: Restart the kernel and run all cells of 1 notebook, fixing each error until it finishes.
steps.detail: Running cells out of order creates results that cannot be reproduced. Restart and Run All is the test. If it fails, so would anyone else's run.
steps.proof: Restart and Run All finishes without errors.
steps.pitfall: Relying on a variable defined in a cell you later deleted.

problems.prompt: A notebook has 12 cells and fails at cell 7 after a restart. How many cells ran successfully?
Name the Jupyter menu action that tests reproducibility.
Why can a notebook that works now fail after 'Restart and Run All'?
problems.answer: It relied on state from cells run out of order or deleted.

steps.title: Load From Raw
steps.mastery: Start every analysis from the raw file, not from a hand-edited copy.
steps.practice: Write the first cell to read the raw CSV and do all cleaning in code below it.
steps.detail: If cleaning happens by hand in a spreadsheet, nobody can repeat it. Code that goes from raw file to result is the analysis.
steps.proof: Deleting every intermediate file and rerunning recreates the results.
steps.pitfall: Fixing typos by hand in Excel before loading.

problems.prompt: A hand-edited CSV has 5 fixes nobody wrote down. How many of them can a colleague reproduce?
Where should a typo fix like 'Nwe York' to 'New York' live?
Name 1 benefit of reading the raw file in cell 1.
problems.answer: Anyone can rerun the whole analysis from the original data.

steps.title: Pin Your Environment
steps.mastery: Record package versions so the notebook runs the same later.
steps.practice: Write a 'requirements.txt' with the versions of pandas and numpy you used.
steps.detail: A library update can change results or break code. Pinning versions with pip freeze or an environment file lets someone rebuild your setup.
steps.proof: requirements.txt lists exact versions.
steps.pitfall: Assuming 'latest' will behave the same next year.

problems.prompt: Which 'pip' command lists installed package versions?
What does 'pandas==2.2.2' in requirements.txt mean?
Why pin versions for a report rerun in 12 months?
problems.answer: So library changes cannot alter or break the results.

steps.title: Set Random Seeds
steps.mastery: Fix random seeds so sampling and model results repeat exactly.
steps.practice: Set np.random.seed(42) or pass random_state=42 to every sampling call, then run twice and compare.
steps.detail: Random samples and splits change each run unless the seed is fixed. Fixed seeds make results checkable.
steps.proof: Two runs give identical numbers.
steps.pitfall: Setting a seed in one cell but sampling in an earlier one.

problems.prompt: Two runs of df.sample(5) without a seed: are they likely identical? Answer yes or no.
Which argument fixes a pandas sample: random_state or seed_value?
You set random_state=42 in 3 sampling calls. Will reruns match? Answer yes or no.

steps.title: Explain in Markdown
steps.mastery: Add short markdown notes that explain each step and each decision.
steps.practice: Add a 1-sentence markdown cell above each of your 5 main steps explaining why it is there.
steps.detail: A notebook is read by people. A sentence like 'Dropping 12 rows with negative ages, all entry errors' turns code into an explanation.
steps.proof: Each main step has a markdown note.
steps.pitfall: Leaving a notebook of code with no explanation of choices.

problems.prompt: You dropped 12 of 400 rows. What percent is that?
Write a 1-sentence note for dropping duplicates.
problems.answer: For example: Dropped 40 duplicate orders from a double export.

problems.prompt: Above a cell that drops 12 rows, should the note explain what the code does or why?
problems.answer: Why, mostly. The code already shows what it does.

steps.title: Map the Steps
steps.mastery: Draw the steps from raw source to final table.
steps.practice: Draw a 4-box diagram for a daily pipeline: extract from the API, clean, aggregate and load to a table.
steps.detail: Naming the steps shows where things can fail and what each step's input and output are. Keep each step small and testable.
steps.proof: Your diagram has 4 steps with inputs and outputs.
steps.pitfall: Writing 1 giant script that does everything at once.

problems.prompt: Name the 3 letters for extract, transform, load.
A pipeline has 4 steps. If step 2 fails, which steps do not run?
Why split a pipeline into 4 small steps?
problems.answer: So a failure is easy to find and that step can be rerun.

steps.title: Make Steps Rerunnable
steps.mastery: Write steps that give the same result when run twice.
steps.practice: Change a load step that appends rows into one that replaces the day's partition, then run it twice.
steps.detail: Idempotent steps can be retried safely. Appending twice duplicates data, while replacing a day's slice does not.
steps.proof: Running twice gives the same row count.
steps.pitfall: Appending on every run so a retry doubles the data.

problems.prompt: A step appends 1000 rows and is retried once by mistake. How many rows land?
A step gives the same result whether run 1 or 2 times. What is it called?
Name 1 way to make a daily load rerunnable.
problems.answer: Delete and replace that day's partition.

steps.title: Validate the Data
steps.mastery: Add checks that stop a pipeline when the data looks wrong.
steps.practice: Add 3 checks to a pipeline: row count above 0, no missing 'id' and 'amount' at least 0.
steps.detail: Failing loudly on bad data beats publishing wrong numbers. Checks on counts, nulls and ranges catch most upstream problems.
steps.proof: A broken input file stops the pipeline with a clear message.
steps.pitfall: Letting a half-empty file silently update the dashboard.

problems.prompt: Yesterday 50000 rows and today 120. What should a check do?
problems.answer: Fail or alert, since the drop is suspicious.

problems.prompt: Name 3 basic data checks.
problems.answer: Row count, missing values and value ranges.

problems.prompt: Should a pipeline publish data that fails a check? Answer yes or no.

steps.title: Schedule and Monitor
steps.mastery: Run a pipeline on a schedule and get alerted when it fails.
steps.practice: Schedule a daily 6 am run and add an alert if it has not succeeded by 7 am.
steps.detail: Schedulers like cron or Airflow run steps on time. Alerts on failure or lateness mean someone finds out before the readers do.
steps.proof: A missed run triggers an alert.
steps.pitfall: Discovering a week later that the pipeline stopped.

problems.prompt: A cron expression '0 6 * * *' runs when?
Name 1 tool for scheduling pipelines.
The run should finish by 7 am but it is 9 am with no success. What should happen?

steps.title: Log and Backfill
steps.mastery: Keep logs of each run and know how to backfill missed days.
steps.practice: Write a backfill plan to rerun 3 missed days in date order and check each day's row count.
steps.detail: Logs show what ran, how many rows and how long it took. A backfill reruns the steps for past dates, which only works if steps are idempotent.
steps.proof: The plan lists 3 dates and a check for each.
steps.pitfall: Backfilling with steps that append, creating duplicates.

problems.prompt: 3 missed days rerun 1 at a time: how many runs?
Name 2 things a run log should record.
problems.answer: Row counts and run duration (also start time and status).

problems.prompt: Why must steps be 'idempotent' before a backfill?

steps.title: Fit a Line
steps.mastery: Fit a simple linear regression and read the slope and intercept.
steps.practice: Fit score = a + b x hours on a dataset and write what b means in one sentence.
steps.detail: The slope says how much y changes per 1-unit increase in x. The intercept is the predicted y at x = 0, which may not mean anything real.
steps.proof: Your sentence says how many points each extra hour adds.
steps.pitfall: Reading the intercept literally when x = 0 is outside the data.

problems.prompt: y = 50 + 5x. What is the predicted y at x = 4?
In y = 50 + 5x, how much does y change per 1-unit increase in x?
In y = 50 + 5x, what is y at x = 0?

steps.title: Read R-squared
steps.mastery: Interpret R-squared as the share of variation explained.
steps.practice: Fit a model and write a sentence explaining its R-squared of 0.64.
steps.detail: R-squared of 0.64 means the model explains 64% of the variation in y. A low R-squared can still have a useful, real slope.
steps.proof: Your sentence says 64% of the variation is explained.
steps.pitfall: Thinking R-squared measures whether the model is causal.

problems.prompt: R-squared = 0.25. What percent of the variation is left unexplained?
r = 0.8 in simple regression. What is R-squared?
Does a high R-squared prove x causes y? Answer yes or no.

steps.title: Multiple Regression
steps.mastery: Read coefficients in a model with several inputs as effects holding the others fixed.
steps.practice: Fit price ~ size + bedrooms and write what the 'bedrooms' coefficient means.
steps.detail: Each coefficient is the change in y for 1 unit of that input with the others held constant. That is why a coefficient can flip sign when another variable is added.
steps.proof: Your sentence includes holding size constant.
steps.pitfall: Reading a coefficient as the total effect, ignoring the other inputs.

problems.prompt: price = 50000 + 200 x size + 10000 x bedrooms. Predict price for size 100 and 2 bedrooms.
In that model, how much does 1 extra bedroom add with size fixed?
Why might the 'bedrooms' coefficient turn negative once 'size' is included?
problems.answer: Because at a fixed size, more bedrooms means smaller rooms.

steps.title: Check Residuals
steps.mastery: Plot residuals to check whether a linear model fits.
steps.practice: Plot residuals against fitted values for 1 model and describe any pattern.
steps.detail: Residuals are actual minus predicted. A random cloud is good. A curve suggests a missing non-linear term and a funnel suggests changing variance.
steps.proof: You describe the residual pattern and what it implies.
steps.pitfall: Skipping residual plots and trusting the fit.

problems.prompt: Actual 80, predicted 74. What is the residual?
Residuals form a U shape. What does that suggest?
problems.answer: A curved relationship the line misses.

problems.prompt: Residuals spread wider as fitted values grow. What is that called?

steps.title: Predict Responsibly
steps.mastery: Make predictions within the range of the data and state the uncertainty.
steps.practice: Predict y for 3 new x values, 2 inside the data range and 1 far outside, and explain why the last is risky.
steps.detail: A model is only checked where there is data. Extrapolating far outside assumes the pattern continues, which often fails. Report prediction intervals.
steps.proof: You flag the out-of-range prediction.
steps.pitfall: Predicting a 10-year-old's height at age 40 from a growth line.

problems.prompt: Data covers x from 1 to 10. Is predicting at x = 50 extrapolation? Answer yes or no.
Growth of 6 cm per year from age 5 to 12. Why not predict height at age 30 with it?
problems.answer: Growth stops, so the line no longer applies.

problems.prompt: Which is wider: a confidence interval for the mean or a prediction interval for 1 new point?

steps.title: Population and Sample
steps.mastery: Distinguish the population you care about from the sample you have.
steps.practice: Write the population and the sample for a survey of 200 students at 1 school about all teens' sleep.
steps.detail: The sample can only speak for the population it was drawn from. 200 students at 1 school speak for that school, not all teens.
steps.proof: You name both and the gap between them.
steps.pitfall: Generalizing from a convenient sample to everyone.

problems.prompt: A poll of 500 voters in 1 city: what population can it describe best?
Is a sample of 1000 from a biased source better than 300 from a random one? Answer yes or no.
problems.answer: No, bias does not shrink with size.

problems.prompt: Name the population for 'all US high-school seniors' studies.

steps.title: Random Sampling
steps.mastery: Draw a simple random sample so every member has an equal chance.
steps.practice: Use df.sample(n=50, random_state=1) to draw 50 rows from 1000 and compare the sample mean with the full mean.
steps.detail: A random sample avoids choosing based on anything related to the outcome. Its mean will be close to the population's, with error that shrinks as the sample grows.
steps.proof: The 2 means are close.
steps.pitfall: Taking the first 50 rows, which may be sorted by date or region.

problems.prompt: 50 of 1000 rows: what fraction is sampled?
Why is taking the first 50 rows risky?
problems.answer: The file may be sorted, so the first rows are not typical.

problems.prompt: Does a larger random sample usually give a closer estimate? Answer yes or no.

steps.title: Selection Bias
steps.mastery: Spot when the way people entered the data skews the result.
steps.practice: List 3 ways an online product-review dataset differs from all customers.
steps.detail: Who chooses to be measured matters. Reviewers are often unusually happy or unhappy. Survivors are counted while those who dropped out are not.
steps.proof: You list 3 concrete differences.
steps.pitfall: Treating volunteers' answers as representative.

problems.prompt: A gym surveys members who have stayed 2 years. What group is missing?
In WWII, analysts studied only planes that returned. What is that bias called?
Online reviews average 4.5 stars. Name 1 reason this may overstate satisfaction.
problems.answer: Happy customers or prompted reviews are overrepresented (and the unhappy often leave silently).

steps.title: Response and Measurement Bias
steps.mastery: Recognize bias from how questions are asked and how values are measured.
steps.practice: Rewrite the leading question "Don't you agree homework is too long?" as a neutral one.
steps.detail: Wording, order and who asks all shape answers. Self-reported numbers like sleep or exercise are often overestimated.
steps.proof: Your question has no suggested answer.
steps.pitfall: Trusting self-reported exercise hours as exact.

problems.prompt: Rewrite "How much do you love our app?" neutrally.
problems.answer: For example: How would you rate our app from 1 to 5?

problems.prompt: People report 8 hours of sleep but trackers show 6.5. What is the gap?
Name 1 source of measurement bias in a bathroom-scale weight survey.

steps.title: Sample Size
steps.mastery: Know how the margin of error shrinks with larger samples.
steps.practice: Calculate the approximate margin of error 1 / sqrt(n) for samples of 100, 400 and 1600.
steps.detail: Margin of error shrinks with the square root of n, so 4 times the sample halves the error. Bias does not shrink at all.
steps.pitfall: Thinking a huge biased sample beats a modest random one.

problems.prompt: Approximate margin of error for n = 400?
Margin of error is 1 / sqrt(n). To halve it, by what factor must n grow?
Approximate margin of error for n = 10000?

steps.title: SELECT and WHERE
steps.mastery: Write SQL that selects columns and filters rows.
steps.practice: Write a query returning 'name' and 'score' from 'students' where 'score' is at least 90.
steps.detail: SELECT picks columns, FROM picks the table, WHERE filters rows. Text values need single quotes, numbers do not.
steps.proof: Your query returns only students scoring 90 or more.
steps.pitfall: Using double quotes for text values in SQL.

problems.prompt: Write a query for all columns of 'orders'.
Which clause filters rows: SELECT, WHERE or ORDER BY?
Write a filter for 'city' equal to Boston.

steps.title: Aggregate in SQL
steps.mastery: Use GROUP BY with COUNT, SUM and AVG.
steps.practice: Write a query that counts orders and sums 'amount' per 'region' from 'orders'.
steps.detail: GROUP BY collapses rows to one per group. Every selected column must be grouped or aggregated. HAVING filters groups after aggregating.
steps.proof: The result has 1 row per region with a count and a sum.
steps.pitfall: Selecting a non-aggregated column that is not in GROUP BY.

problems.prompt: Which SQL function counts rows per group?
Which clause filters groups with SUM(amount) > 1000: WHERE or HAVING?
A table has 3 regions and 4 product types, with every pairing present. How many rows does GROUP BY region, product return?

steps.title: Joins in SQL
steps.mastery: Join 2 tables in SQL on a shared key.
steps.practice: Write a query joining 'orders' to 'customers' on 'customer_id' and returning order id and customer name.
steps.detail: JOIN ... ON matches rows. LEFT JOIN keeps unmatched left rows. Alias tables (o, c) to keep queries short.
steps.proof: Each order shows its customer's name.
steps.pitfall: Forgetting the ON clause and producing every combination of rows.

problems.prompt: Which SQL join keeps all orders even with no customer match?
A join with no ON condition on tables of 10 and 20 rows returns how many rows?
Write the ON clause matching 'orders' and 'customers' on 'customer_id', aliased o and c.

steps.title: Limit and Order
steps.mastery: Return the top rows of a query with ORDER BY and LIMIT.
steps.practice: Write a query for the 10 highest-scoring students using ORDER BY score DESC LIMIT 10.
steps.detail: ORDER BY sorts and LIMIT trims. Fetching only what you need is faster and kinder to a shared database.
steps.proof: The query returns exactly 10 rows in descending order.
steps.pitfall: Downloading 5 million rows to look at the top 10.

problems.prompt: Which keyword sorts largest first: ASC or DESC?
Write the clause that returns at most 5 rows.
Why use LIMIT when exploring a 50-million-row table?
problems.answer: So the query returns quickly and does not load everything.

steps.title: Push Work to the Database
steps.mastery: Do filtering and aggregation in SQL before loading data into pandas.
steps.practice: Rewrite a script that loads a whole table into pandas and filters it, so the WHERE and GROUP BY run in SQL.
steps.detail: Databases are built to filter and aggregate large tables. Bringing back a summary instead of raw rows saves memory and time.
steps.proof: The script loads only the summary rows.
steps.pitfall: Loading 10 GB into memory to compute 1 average.

problems.prompt: A query returns 12 monthly totals instead of 3 million rows. How many rows reach pandas?
Name 2 operations best pushed into SQL.
Which pandas function runs a SQL query and returns a DataFrame?

steps.title: Lead With the Finding
steps.mastery: Open a report with the main finding and its implication in plain words.
steps.practice: Write a 2-sentence opening for an analysis: what you found and what should happen next.
steps.detail: Busy readers may read only the first lines. Put the answer first, then the evidence. Skip how you cleaned the data.
steps.proof: Your opening states 1 finding and 1 recommended action.
steps.pitfall: Opening with methods and burying the finding on page 4.

problems.prompt: Rewrite "We analyzed 3 months of data" as a finding-first opening.
problems.answer: For example: Returning customers spend 40% more, so retention should be the Q3 priority.

problems.prompt: How many main findings should an opening state: 1 or 10?
In a 2-page report, where should methods details go?

steps.title: State Uncertainty
steps.mastery: Say how sure you are in words and numbers.
steps.practice: Rewrite "sales will rise 12%" as an estimate with a range and a confidence word.
steps.detail: Ranges and phrases like 'likely' set honest expectations. Overconfidence costs trust when the number misses.
steps.proof: Your sentence includes a range.
steps.pitfall: Reporting a single precise number as certain.

problems.prompt: Rewrite "churn is 8%" with a range.
problems.answer: For example: churn is about 8% (likely between 6% and 10%).

problems.prompt: Is "between 9% and 15%" more honest than "exactly 12%" for a forecast? Answer yes or no.
Name 1 phrase that signals moderate confidence.

steps.title: One Chart, One Point
steps.mastery: Choose 1 chart per point and title it with the message.
steps.practice: Pick the 3 charts that support your 3 key points and give each a title that states the point.
steps.detail: Each chart should earn its place by showing 1 thing. A title like 'Mobile users convert 2x better' tells readers what to see.
steps.proof: Three charts with message titles.
steps.pitfall: Pasting 15 charts with default titles.

problems.prompt: Rewrite the title 'Conversion by device' as a message.
problems.answer: For example: Mobile converts at twice the desktop rate.

problems.prompt: You have 3 key points and 1 chart for each. You cut the weakest point. How many main charts remain?
Why title a chart 'Mobile converts 2x better' instead of 'Conversion by device'?
problems.answer: So readers know what to look for.

steps.title: Know Your Audience
steps.mastery: Adjust detail and language for who will read the work.
steps.practice: Write the same finding twice: once for an engineer team and once for a 1-minute executive update.
steps.detail: Executives want the decision and the risk. Analysts want the method. Same facts, different emphasis and length.
steps.proof: Two versions with different lengths and detail.
steps.pitfall: Sending a notebook to someone who needs a 1-line answer.

problems.prompt: Which audience usually wants the method details: the CEO or the analytics team?
How long should a 1-minute executive update be: 2 sentences or 2 pages?
Name 2 things an executive summary must include.
problems.answer: The finding and the recommended action.

steps.title: Recommend an Action
steps.mastery: End with a specific, testable recommendation.
steps.practice: Write 1 recommendation with an owner, an action and a way to measure it, such as a test of the new email in May.
steps.detail: An analysis is done when someone can act on it. Specific recommendations with a measurement plan close the loop.
steps.proof: Your recommendation names who, what and how it will be measured.
steps.pitfall: Ending with 'more research is needed' and nothing else.

problems.prompt: Rewrite "improve retention" as a specific action.
problems.answer: For example: send a day-7 welcome email to new users in May and compare 30-day retention.

problems.prompt: Name 3 parts of a good recommendation.
problems.answer: An owner, an action and a measure.

problems.prompt: Is 'more research is needed' a complete recommendation? Answer yes or no.

steps.title: Filter Rows
steps.mastery: Keep only the rows that match a condition using column comparisons.
steps.practice: Use pandas to keep rows where 'score' is at least 80 and 'year' is 2025, then count them.
steps.detail: Filtering uses a boolean mask: df[(df.score >= 80) & (df.year == 2025)]. Use & and | with brackets around each condition, not the words and and or.
steps.proof: You get the count of matching rows.
steps.pitfall: Writing and between conditions, which raises an error in pandas.

problems.prompt: Which symbol combines 2 conditions with AND in a pandas filter: and, & or &&?
A 'score' column holds 70, 85, 90 and 60. How many rows pass score >= 80?
Why must each condition sit in brackets, like (df.a > 1) & (df.b < 5)?
problems.answer: Because & binds more tightly than the comparisons.

steps.title: Select Columns
steps.mastery: Choose just the columns you need and rename them clearly.
steps.practice: Select 3 columns from a 20-column table and rename 'amt_usd' to 'amount'.
steps.detail: Working with only the needed columns makes output readable and catches typos early. df[['a', 'b']] selects, and df.rename(columns={'old': 'new'}) renames.
steps.proof: Your table has 3 clearly named columns.
steps.pitfall: Carrying 20 columns through every step.

problems.prompt: How many brackets surround a list of column names in df[['a', 'b']]?
problems.answer: 2 pairs: one for indexing and one for the list.

problems.prompt: Write the rename that changes 'amt' to 'amount'.
A table has 20 columns and you select 3. How many are dropped from view?

steps.title: Group and Aggregate
steps.mastery: Group rows by a category and compute a summary for each group.
steps.practice: Group sales by 'region' and compute total and mean 'amount' for each region.
steps.detail: groupby splits the table, the aggregate summarizes each piece, and the results combine into one row per group. Name each output column so the result explains itself.
steps.proof: You get one row per region with 2 summary columns.
steps.pitfall: Grouping by a column with typos, so one region appears as 2 groups.

problems.prompt: Sales of 10 and 30 in 'North' and 20 in 'South'. What is the North total?
What is the North mean?
A groupby over region and year has 4 distinct regions and 3 distinct years, with every pairing present. How many rows does it return?

steps.title: Sort and Rank
steps.mastery: Sort a table by one or more columns and take the top rows.
steps.practice: Sort products by 'revenue' descending and show the top 5 with df.nlargest or sort_values.
steps.detail: sort_values(ascending=False) puts the biggest first. Sorting by 2 columns breaks ties. Taking the top N after grouping answers which group was largest.
steps.proof: The top 5 products show in descending order.
steps.pitfall: Forgetting ascending=False and showing the bottom 5.

problems.prompt: Revenues 50, 90, 20 and 70 sorted descending: what is second?
Which 'sort_values' argument sorts from largest to smallest?
2 products tie at 90 revenue. How do you decide their order?
problems.answer: Sort by a second column, such as name or units.

steps.title: Add Computed Columns
steps.mastery: Create new columns from existing ones with whole-column arithmetic.
steps.practice: Add a 'unit_price' column equal to 'revenue' divided by 'units' for every row at once.
steps.detail: Whole-column arithmetic like df['unit_price'] = df.revenue / df.units is faster and clearer than a loop. Check for division by 0 and missing values afterward.
steps.proof: Every row has a unit price and no row has inf.
steps.pitfall: Looping over rows with iterrows to do arithmetic.

problems.prompt: Revenue 120 and units 4: what is the unit price?
What does pandas give for 10 / 0 in a column?
Why is column arithmetic preferred over a Python loop over 1 million rows?
problems.answer: It runs much faster and is shorter to read.

steps.title: Plot Over Time
steps.mastery: Plot a time series and describe its trend and repeating patterns.
steps.practice: Plot 2 years of daily sales and write 1 sentence on the trend and 1 on any weekly or yearly pattern.
steps.detail: A line plot over time shows trend, season and noise. Resampling to weekly or monthly can make the trend clearer.
steps.proof: You write 2 sentences from the plot.
steps.pitfall: Shuffling time-ordered rows before analysis.

problems.prompt: Daily data for 2 years has about how many points?
Which method turns 730 daily rows into weekly totals?
Sales peak every December. What kind of pattern is that?

steps.title: Moving Averages
steps.mastery: Smooth a noisy series with a rolling mean.
steps.practice: Compute a 7-day rolling mean of daily visits with rolling(7).mean() and plot both lines.
steps.detail: A rolling mean averages each point with its neighbors, smoothing noise. A 7-day window removes weekly cycles.
steps.proof: The smoothed line shows the trend clearly.
steps.pitfall: Using a window so wide it hides real changes.

problems.prompt: Values 10, 12, 14: what is their 3-day mean?
How many leading NaN values does rolling(7).mean() produce?
Why use a 7-day window for daily web visits?
problems.answer: It averages out the weekly cycle.

steps.title: Lags and Change
steps.mastery: Create lagged values and period-over-period changes.
steps.practice: Add 'sales_lag1' with shift(1) and a 'pct_change' column, then read the change on 3 dates.
steps.detail: Yesterday's value often predicts today's. shift moves values down by rows. pct_change gives growth rates.
steps.proof: You read 3 percent changes correctly.
steps.pitfall: Using future values as features by shifting the wrong way.

problems.prompt: Sales go from 200 to 250. What is the percent change?
What does shift(1) put in row 5?
Why is shift(-1) dangerous as a predictive feature?
problems.answer: It uses the future value, leaking information.

steps.title: Decompose a Series
steps.mastery: Split a series into trend, season and remainder.
steps.practice: Run seasonal_decompose on 3 years of monthly data with period=12 and describe each component.
steps.detail: Decomposition separates the long-term trend, the repeating season and what is left. Large remainders mark unusual events.
steps.proof: You describe trend, season and remainder.
steps.pitfall: Picking the wrong period, like 7 for monthly data.

problems.prompt: Monthly data repeats each year. What 'period' do you pass?
Daily data repeats each week. What 'period' do you pass?
