If the wall at row 1, column 1 were removed, would the shortest route from S to E in the maze get shorter?
problems.answer: No. It is still 6 moves, since Manhattan distance is 6.

steps.title: When A* Pays Off
steps.mastery: Estimate how much work a good heuristic saves, and keep its guarantee in mind.
steps.practice: On an open 100 by 100 grid with the goal 10 cells away, estimate how many cells BFS and A* each look at.
steps.detail: BFS spreads in every direction, so it explores roughly a disc around the start. A* with a good heuristic heads toward the goal and looks at a thin band. With an admissible and consistent h, A* still returns a shortest path.
steps.proof: BFS around 200 cells, A* around 10 to 20.
steps.pitfall: Expecting A* to help when the heuristic is close to 0 everywhere.

problems.prompt: On an open grid, the goal is 10 steps away. Roughly how many cells does BFS explore before reaching it?
problems.answer: About 200, every cell within 10 steps, a diamond of \(2 \times 10^{2} + 2 \times 10 + 1 = 221\).

problems.prompt: Does A* with an admissible heuristic always return a shortest path? Answer for a grid with 50 walls.
What does it mean for a heuristic to be consistent? Write the inequality for an edge u→v with cost c.
problems.answer: \(h(u) \le c + h(v)\), so the estimate never drops by more than the step costs.

steps.title: Relax Every Edge
steps.mastery: Run Bellman-Ford by relaxing every edge in rounds until distances stop changing.
steps.practice: Run Bellman-Ford from S on the 5-vertex figure graph, relaxing all 6 edges per round, until a round changes nothing.
steps.detail: Set dist[S] = 0 and the rest to ∞. In each round, relax every edge once in a fixed order. A shortest path has at most V - 1 edges, so V - 1 rounds are always enough, and you can stop early when a round makes no change.
steps.pitfall: Stopping after 1 round because nothing obvious is left.

problems.prompt: For a graph with 6 vertices, how many rounds does Bellman-Ford need at most?
Find the shortest distance from S to every vertex in the figure graph.
Why are V - 1 rounds always enough when there is no negative cycle?
problems.answer: A shortest path visits each vertex at most once, so it has at most V - 1 edges, and round k fixes every path of k edges.

steps.title: Trace One Round
steps.mastery: Trace a single Bellman-Ford round in a given edge order and see how order changes progress.
steps.practice: Relax the 6 figure edges once in the order S→A, S→B, B→A, A→C, C→D, B→D, and write dist after each one.
steps.detail: Within a round, a distance updated early can feed edges later in the same round, so the edge order changes how much one round achieves. The final answer is the same either way, only the number of rounds differs.
steps.pitfall: Using only distances from the start of the round, then being surprised the trace differs from code.

problems.prompt: After 1 round in the order S→A, S→B, B→A, A→C, C→D, B→D, what is dist[A]?
After that same round, what is dist[D]?
If the edges were relaxed in the reverse order, would round 1 give the same distances?
problems.answer: Not always. Fewer updates feed each other, but after enough rounds the final distances are the same.

steps.title: Find a Negative Cycle
steps.mastery: Detect a negative cycle with 1 extra round of Bellman-Ford.
steps.practice: Add the edge C→B with weight -6 to a small graph, run V - 1 rounds, then a V-th round, and see whether anything still changes.
steps.detail: If a V-th round still lowers a distance, some cycle has a negative total, and shortest paths through it do not exist: going round again always gets cheaper. Report the cycle instead of a distance.
steps.proof: The V-th round still improves, so there is a negative cycle.
steps.pitfall: Returning distances anyway when the extra round still changes something.

problems.prompt: Edges A→B 1, B→C -3 and C→A 1. Is there a negative cycle?
How does Bellman-Ford tell you a negative cycle is reachable from the start?
problems.answer: An extra V-th round still lowers some distance.

problems.prompt: Why does "shortest path" stop making sense when a negative cycle sits on the route?
problems.answer: You can go round the cycle again and again, and the cost keeps dropping without limit.

steps.title: Bellman-Ford or Dijkstra
steps.mastery: Choose between Bellman-Ford and Dijkstra from the edge weights and the graph size.
steps.practice: Estimate the work for V = 1,000 and E = 10,000 with each algorithm, then say which you would use with and without negative edges.
steps.detail: Bellman-Ford is O(VE), slow but simple, and works with negative edges. Dijkstra is O((V + E) log V) and needs every weight to be 0 or more. Use Dijkstra unless negatives force your hand.
steps.proof: Bellman-Ford about 10 million steps, Dijkstra about 110,000.
steps.pitfall: Reaching for Bellman-Ford on every problem just to be safe, and timing out.

problems.prompt: What is the running time of Bellman-Ford?
With V = 1,000 and E = 10,000, roughly how many relax steps does Bellman-Ford do at worst?
A map of 200,000 roads has only positive travel times. Which algorithm, and why?
problems.answer: Dijkstra. No negative edges, and it is far faster than \(O(VE)\) at that size.

steps.title: Early Exit and Currency Loops
steps.mastery: Stop Bellman-Ford early when a round changes nothing, and use it to spot currency loops that make money.
steps.practice: Turn the exchange rates 0.9, 0.9 and 1.25 into weights of -log(rate), and check whether the loop is negative.
steps.detail: If a whole round updates nothing, later rounds cannot either, so stop. For currencies, a loop whose rates multiply to more than 1 makes money. Taking -log of each rate turns products into sums and that loop into a negative cycle.
steps.proof: The rates multiply to 1.0125, and the -log weights sum to a negative number.
steps.pitfall: Using log instead of -log, which turns the money loop into a positive cycle.

problems.prompt: Why is it safe to stop Bellman-Ford after a round with no updates?
problems.answer: Each round only uses the current distances, so if none changed, the next round would do the same nothing.

problems.prompt: USD→EUR is 0.9, EUR→GBP is 0.9 and GBP→USD is 1.25. What do the rates multiply to, to 4 decimal places?
Does that currency loop make money, and what would Bellman-Ford find with -log weights?
problems.answer: Yes, 1.25% per trip. It finds a negative cycle.

steps.title: Run BFS with a Queue
steps.mastery: Run breadth-first search by hand, keeping the queue and the visited set on paper.
steps.practice: Run BFS from A on a 6-vertex graph, taking neighbors in alphabetical order, and write the queue after each step.
steps.detail: Put the start in a queue and mark it seen. Repeatedly take the front vertex and add each unseen neighbor to the back, marking it as you add it. Because the queue is first in, first out, vertices come out in order of distance.
steps.proof: BFS from A visits A, B, D, C, E, F.
steps.pitfall: Taking from the back of the queue, which turns BFS into DFS.

problems.prompt: Give the BFS order from A for the graph in the figure, taking neighbors alphabetically.
problems.answer: A, B, D, C, E, F

problems.prompt: In the same BFS, what is in the queue right after A has been taken out and its neighbors added?
Why does BFS use a queue rather than a stack?
problems.answer: A queue serves vertices in the order they were found, so every vertex 1 step away comes out before any vertex 2 steps away.

steps.title: Distances in Hops
steps.mastery: Read the shortest number of edges from the start to every vertex off a BFS.
steps.practice: Label each vertex of the figure graph with its BFS distance from A, then list the vertices at each distance.
steps.detail: The start has distance 0. When BFS finds v from u, dist[v] = dist[u] + 1. Since nothing at distance k is processed before everything at k - 1, this is the fewest edges possible when every edge counts the same.
steps.pitfall: Updating a distance after the vertex has already been seen.

problems.prompt: What is the BFS distance from A to F in the figure?
Which vertices are exactly 2 edges from A?
When all edges cost the same, why is the BFS distance the shortest path?
problems.answer: BFS reaches every vertex at distance k before any at distance k + 1, so the first time it finds a vertex is by the fewest edges.

steps.title: Rebuild the Path
steps.mastery: Store a parent for each vertex during BFS and walk back from the target to get the actual route.
steps.practice: Run BFS from A storing parent[v] when v is found, then walk parents back from F and reverse the list.
steps.detail: Distances tell you how far, parents tell you how. Set parent[v] = u at the moment u discovers v. To get the path, start at the target and follow parents until you reach the start, then reverse.
steps.proof: A-B-C-F.
steps.pitfall: Forgetting to reverse, so the path comes out backward.

problems.prompt: Using BFS from A with alphabetical neighbors, what is the path to F?
In that BFS, which vertex is the parent of E?
There are 2 shortest paths from A to E in the figure graph. Name both.

steps.title: Mark Seen When Enqueued
steps.mastery: Mark a vertex as seen when it enters the queue, so no vertex is added twice.
steps.practice: Trace BFS on a square 1-2-3-4 with the diagonal 1-3, once marking on enqueue and once on dequeue, and count queue entries.
steps.detail: If you only mark a vertex when it comes out of the queue, 2 neighbors can both add it before then, and it gets processed twice. Marking it when it goes in keeps the total work at O(V + E).
steps.proof: Marking on enqueue gives 4 entries; marking on dequeue gives more.
steps.pitfall: Marking on dequeue, which can add the same vertex many times on a dense graph.

problems.prompt: If you mark vertices only when they leave the queue, how many times can 1 vertex enter it?
problems.answer: More than once, up to once per neighbor.

problems.prompt: BFS runs on a graph with 1,000 vertices and 5,000 edges. Roughly how many steps does it take?
problems.answer: About 6,000, since BFS is \(O(V + E)\). With undirected edges each one is looked at twice, so up to about 11,000.

problems.prompt: This BFS adds vertices twice: "for v in g[u]: if v not in seen: q.append(v)". Fix it in 1 line.

steps.title: Many Starts at Once
steps.mastery: Run BFS from several start vertices together to get the distance to the nearest one.
steps.practice: Put both A and F in the starting queue at distance 0, run BFS, and label every vertex.
steps.detail: Multi-source BFS loads all the starts first, each at distance 0. The result is the distance from each vertex to its nearest start. It is the same as adding a fake vertex joined to every start and subtracting 1.
steps.pitfall: Running a separate BFS from each start and keeping the last result instead of the minimum.

problems.prompt: A fire starts at A and F at minute 0 and spreads 1 edge a minute. Which vertex catches fire last, and when?
problems.answer: All 4 of B, C, D and E catch fire at minute 1, together.

problems.prompt: With both A and F in the starting queue, what is the distance to C?
Why does multi-source BFS give the same answers as adding 1 super source?
problems.answer: A super source joined to every start puts them all at distance 1, which is the same as starting them all at 0 and adding 1.

steps.title: Two-Color a Graph
steps.mastery: Decide whether a graph is bipartite by coloring it with 2 colors so no edge joins matching colors.
steps.practice: Try to 2-color a 6-cycle, a triangle and a tree on 5 vertices, and say which ones work.
steps.detail: A graph is bipartite if its vertices split into 2 groups with every edge going between the groups. That is the same as a 2-coloring. It works exactly when the graph has no cycle of odd length.
steps.proof: The 6-cycle and the tree work, the triangle does not.
steps.pitfall: Thinking any graph with a cycle cannot be bipartite.

problems.prompt: Is the 6-cycle in the figure bipartite?
problems.answer: Yes. Alternate colors round the cycle: 1, 3, 5 in one group and 2, 4, 6 in the other.

problems.prompt: Is a triangle on vertices 1, 2 and 3 bipartite?
problems.answer: No. It is a cycle of length 3, which is odd.

problems.prompt: State the rule that tells you from cycles alone whether a graph is bipartite. Is a 5-cycle bipartite?
problems.answer: A graph is bipartite exactly when it has no cycle of odd length, so a 5-cycle is not.

steps.title: Check with BFS
steps.mastery: Test bipartiteness in code by BFS coloring and watching for an edge inside 1 color.
steps.practice: Write a BFS that gives the start color 0 and each new neighbor the opposite color, and returns False on a clash.
steps.detail: Color the start 0. Each time BFS finds a new vertex, give it the other color from its parent. If it ever sees an edge between 2 vertices of the same color, the graph is not bipartite. Run it from every uncolored vertex to cover all components.
steps.proof: A clash means an odd cycle.
steps.pitfall: Only checking the first component.

problems.prompt: BFS colors vertex A with color 0. What color do A's neighbors get?
During that BFS you find an edge between 2 vertices that both have color 1. What does that mean?
problems.answer: The graph is not bipartite, since there is an odd cycle.

problems.prompt: Is every tree with at least 2 vertices bipartite? Why?
problems.answer: Yes. A tree has no cycles at all, so no odd ones.

steps.title: Find a Matching
steps.mastery: Find a largest matching: pairs joined by edges with no vertex used twice.
steps.practice: Match the 3 people in the figure to the 3 jobs they can do, using each person and job at most once, and make as many pairs as possible.
steps.detail: A matching is a set of edges with no shared endpoints. In a bipartite graph it pairs one side with the other, like people with jobs. A perfect matching uses every vertex, which needs both sides the same size.
steps.proof: 3 pairs.
steps.pitfall: Giving one job to 2 people.

problems.prompt: What is the largest number of pairs you can match in the figure?
Give 1 largest matching for the figure.
4 workers and 3 jobs: can there be a perfect matching? Why?
problems.answer: No. A perfect matching needs every vertex used, and 1 worker would always be left.

steps.title: Grow with Augmenting Paths
steps.mastery: Make a matching bigger by finding an augmenting path and flipping its edges.
steps.practice: Start with only Ann-X matched in the figure and find a path from an unmatched person to an unmatched job that alternates unmatched and matched edges.
steps.detail: An augmenting path starts and ends at unmatched vertices and alternates between edges outside and inside the matching. Flipping every edge on it adds 1 pair. When no augmenting path exists, the matching is as big as it gets.
steps.proof: Ben-X-Ann-Y flips to Ben-X and Ann-Y.
steps.pitfall: Starting the path at a vertex that is already matched.

problems.prompt: A matching has 2 pairs and you find an augmenting path. How many pairs after flipping it?
Where must an augmenting path start and end, if 2 of 6 vertices are unmatched?
problems.answer: At 2 vertices that are both unmatched, one on each side.

problems.prompt: What is the running time of Kuhn's augmenting path algorithm on a bipartite graph with V vertices and E edges?

steps.title: Model Problems as Matching
steps.mastery: Spot assignment problems that are bipartite matching in disguise.
steps.practice: Model 5 students and 4 project slots, each student listing 2 slots, as a bipartite graph, and say what the largest matching means.
steps.detail: When things on one side each pair with at most 1 thing on the other, and some pairings are not allowed, draw it as a bipartite graph. The largest matching is the most assignments possible. Hall's condition says a group of k needs at least k options between them.
steps.proof: The matching size is the number of students who get a slot.
steps.pitfall: Forgetting that a slot can only take 1 student.

problems.prompt: 3 students all list only Project X and Project Y. Can all 3 get a project?
problems.answer: No. 3 students share only 2 projects, which breaks Hall's condition.

problems.prompt: Placing rooks on a chessboard with no 2 in the same row or column is which graph problem?
problems.answer: Bipartite matching between rows and columns.

problems.prompt: Shifts need 1 nurse each. Nurse Kim can do Monday or Tuesday, Lee only Monday. What is the most shifts covered?
problems.answer: 2: Lee on Monday and Kim on Tuesday.

steps.title: Count the Pieces
steps.mastery: Count the connected components of a graph by looking for groups with no edges between them.
steps.practice: Draw 8 vertices with edges 1-2, 2-3, 4-5, 6-7, 7-8 and 6-8, then circle each piece and count them.
steps.detail: A connected component is a largest group where every vertex can reach every other. A single vertex with no edges is a component on its own. Every vertex belongs to exactly 1.
steps.pitfall: Forgetting isolated vertices, which are components too.

problems.prompt: How many connected components does the graph in the figure have?
A graph has 10 vertices and 3 edges, and no 2 edges share a vertex. How many components does it have?
problems.answer: 7. Each edge joins 2 vertices into 1 piece, so 10 - 3 = 7.

problems.prompt: List the components of the figure graph as sets.

steps.title: One Search per Piece
steps.mastery: Find all components with a loop that starts a new search from every unvisited vertex.
steps.practice: Write a loop over vertices 1 to n that starts a DFS from each unseen vertex and counts how many it starts.
steps.detail: Each search marks one whole component. Starting a new one from the next unseen vertex means you never count a component twice, and the number of searches started is the answer. The total work is still O(V + E).
steps.proof: The number of searches started equals the number of components.
steps.pitfall: Starting a search from every vertex, seen or not, which overcounts.

problems.prompt: A loop starts a DFS from each unseen vertex of a 12-vertex graph and starts 4 searches. How many components are there?
What is the total running time of counting components with 1 search per piece?
Your component counter returns 8 for the figure graph. What is the likely bug?
problems.answer: It starts a search from every vertex without checking seen, so it counts each vertex.

steps.title: Label Each Component
steps.mastery: Give every vertex the id of its component so later questions are a lookup.
steps.practice: Fill comp[v] for the 8-vertex graph by numbering searches 0, 1, 2, then answer "are 3 and 8 connected?" from the array.
steps.detail: Pass a label into the search and write it into comp[v] for every vertex it reaches. After that, "are u and v connected?" is just comp[u] == comp[v], which is instant for any number of questions.
steps.proof: comp = [0, 0, 0, 1, 1, 2, 2, 2], so 3 and 8 are not connected.
steps.pitfall: Rerunning a full search for every connected-or-not question.

problems.prompt: With comp = [0, 0, 0, 1, 1, 2, 2, 2] for vertices 1 to 8, are 2 and 3 connected?
How long does each "are u and v connected?" question take once comp is filled?
With comp = [0, 0, 0, 1, 1, 2, 2, 2], how big is the largest component?

steps.title: Components on a Grid
steps.mastery: Count islands on a grid by treating land cells as vertices joined to their land neighbors.
steps.practice: Count the islands of '#' in a 4 by 5 grid, moving only up, down, left and right, then again with diagonals allowed.
steps.detail: Loop over every cell. When you find unvisited land, count an island and flood fill it so you do not count it again. Whether diagonal neighbors join islands changes the answer, so read the question.
steps.proof: The count drops when diagonals are allowed.
steps.pitfall: Counting land cells instead of islands.

problems.prompt: How many islands of '#' does the grid hold, moving only up, down, left and right?
If diagonal neighbors also join land, how many islands does the grid have?
Your island counter loops over 1,000 by 1,000 cells. Roughly how much work is that?
problems.answer: About 1,000,000 cells, each looked at a constant number of times, so O(rows × cols).

steps.title: Join the Pieces
steps.mastery: Find the fewest new edges needed to connect a graph from its component count.
steps.practice: For the 8-vertex figure graph, count the components and add the fewest edges to connect it, drawing them.
steps.detail: A graph with k components needs exactly k - 1 new edges to become connected: join one vertex of each piece to the next. This shows up as "how many roads to build" questions.
steps.proof: 3 components, so 2 new edges.
steps.pitfall: Answering k instead of k - 1.

problems.prompt: How many new edges are needed to connect the figure graph?
A road map has 6 towns split into 4 groups that cannot reach each other. How many roads must be built at least?
A network of 50 computers has 49 cables and is fully connected. How many components does removing 1 cable make?
problems.answer: 2. A connected graph with V - 1 edges is a tree, and removing any tree edge splits it.

steps.title: Spot a Cycle
steps.mastery: Find a cycle in a drawing, and know that a connected graph with V - 1 edges has none.
steps.practice: Draw 5 vertices joined as a tree, then add 1 more edge and trace the cycle it makes.
steps.detail: A cycle is a path that returns to its start without reusing an edge. A connected graph with V vertices and exactly V - 1 edges is a tree and has no cycle. Every extra edge creates at least 1.
steps.proof: The new edge plus the tree path between its ends is the cycle.
steps.pitfall: Calling going back and forth along 1 edge a cycle.

problems.prompt: Does the graph in the figure have a cycle? If so, name one.
A connected graph has 9 vertices and 8 edges. Can it have a cycle?
Add 3 new edges to a tree on 9 vertices. At least how many cycles appear?

steps.title: Undirected Cycle Check
steps.mastery: Detect a cycle in an undirected graph with DFS by skipping the edge back to the parent.
steps.practice: Run DFS on a triangle 1-2-3 and on a path 1-2-3, passing the parent each call, and say where each one finds a seen neighbor.
steps.detail: In undirected DFS, every vertex sees its parent as a neighbor, which is not a cycle. Any other neighbor that is already seen closes a loop. Pass the parent as an argument so you can skip it.
steps.proof: Triangle: vertex 3 sees 1, a cycle. Path: no cycle.
steps.pitfall: Flagging the parent as a cycle, so every graph with an edge looks cyclic.

problems.prompt: DFS on the path 1-2-3 is at vertex 2 and sees vertex 1, already seen. Is that a cycle?
DFS on the triangle 1-2-3 goes 1, 2, 3, then 3 sees 1. Cycle or not?
problems.answer: Cycle, since 1 is seen and is not 3's parent.

problems.prompt: Besides DFS, name another structure that detects undirected cycles while adding edges 1 at a time.
problems.answer: Union-Find: an edge whose 2 ends already share a set closes a cycle.

steps.title: Directed Cycle Check
steps.mastery: Detect a directed cycle with 3 colors: unvisited, in progress, and done.
steps.practice: Color vertices white, gray and black while running DFS on edges 1→2, 2→3, 3→1, and say when the cycle shows.
steps.detail: Gray means on the current DFS path. Reaching a gray vertex means a path leads back to itself, a cycle. Reaching a black vertex is fine, that branch is finished. A plain seen set cannot tell these apart.
steps.proof: At 3, the edge to 1 hits a gray vertex.
steps.pitfall: Using one seen set, which flags harmless cross edges as cycles.

problems.prompt: Directed edges 1→2, 1→3, 2→3. DFS from 1 visits 2, then 3, finishes, then 1 looks at 3 again. Is there a cycle?
Directed edges A→B, B→C, C→A. Where does the 3-color DFS from A spot the cycle?
problems.answer: At C, when the edge C→A reaches A, which is still gray.

problems.prompt: Why does a directed graph need 3 colors when an undirected one needs only seen and parent?
problems.answer: In a directed graph you can reach a finished vertex by another route without a cycle, so finished and in-progress must be told apart.

steps.title: Cycles in Dependencies
steps.mastery: Read a cycle in a dependency graph as a plan that can never start.
steps.practice: List 4 courses with prerequisites where 1 cycle sneaks in, draw the arrows, and find it.
steps.detail: If A needs B, B needs C and C needs A, none of them can go first. Build tools and package managers reject such plans. Finding the cycle and printing it is more useful than just saying "cycle".
steps.proof: The cycle is the loop of prerequisites.
steps.pitfall: Blaming the course that was read last instead of printing the loop.

problems.prompt: Calculus needs Algebra, Algebra needs Arithmetic, Arithmetic needs Calculus. Can any course be taken first?
How would you print the cycle once DFS hits a gray vertex v?
problems.answer: Walk back from the current vertex through parents until you reach v, then print that list.

problems.prompt: In the directed figure graph, is there a cycle?
problems.answer: No. Every arrow goes left to right.

steps.title: Cycles and Edge Counts
steps.mastery: Use edge counts and DFS together to answer cycle questions quickly.
steps.practice: Take 3 graphs: 6 vertices with 5 edges connected, 6 vertices with 6 edges, and 6 vertices with 4 edges. Say what you can conclude about cycles from counts alone.
steps.detail: For a connected undirected graph, E = V - 1 means no cycle and E ≥ V means at least 1. If the graph might be disconnected, count components first: no cycle exactly when E = V - k for k components.
steps.proof: No cycle; at least 1 cycle; not connected, so count components.
steps.pitfall: Using E = V - 1 on a graph that is not connected.

problems.prompt: An undirected graph has 8 vertices, 6 edges and 2 components. Does it have a cycle?
problems.answer: No. 8 - 2 = 6 edges is exactly a forest.

problems.prompt: Keep 8 vertices and 6 edges, but split them into 3 components. Cycle or not?
problems.answer: Yes. A forest with 3 trees would have only 5 edges.

problems.prompt: Can a directed graph with 4 vertices and 3 edges have a cycle?
problems.answer: Yes, for example 1→2, 2→3, 3→1 with vertex 4 alone.

steps.title: Run DFS by Hand
steps.mastery: Trace depth-first search by going as deep as possible and backing up only at dead ends.
steps.practice: Run DFS from A on the 6-vertex figure graph with neighbors in alphabetical order, writing the visit order and each backtrack.
steps.detail: From the current vertex, go to the first unseen neighbor and repeat. When none are left, back up to the vertex you came from and try its next neighbor. The order depends on the neighbor order, so state it.
steps.proof: DFS from A visits A, B, C, F, E, D.
steps.pitfall: Visiting all neighbors of a vertex before going deeper, which is BFS.

problems.prompt: Give the DFS order from A for the graph in the figure, taking neighbors alphabetically.
problems.answer: A, B, C, F, E, D

problems.prompt: What replaces the call stack when you write DFS without recursion?
problems.answer: An explicit stack: push the start, then pop a vertex and push its unseen neighbors.

problems.prompt: Run DFS from 1 on the graph in the figure, neighbors in increasing order. What is the visit order?

steps.title: Write Recursive DFS
steps.mastery: Write a short recursive DFS and know where it breaks on deep graphs.
steps.practice: Write def dfs(u) in Python with a seen set, then run it on a path of 5 vertices and print the order.
steps.detail: Recursive DFS is 4 lines: mark u, then call dfs(v) for each unseen neighbor. Python stops at about 1,000 nested calls, so on a long path either raise the limit with sys.setrecursionlimit or use a stack.
steps.proof: It prints 0, 1, 2, 3, 4.
steps.pitfall: Marking v as seen inside the loop and also at the top, which is harmless, or not at all, which loops forever on a cycle.

problems.prompt: Fill the blank: "def dfs(u): seen.add(u); for v in g[u]: if v not in seen: ____"
Recursive DFS in Python runs on a path of 100,000 vertices. What happens by default?
problems.answer: It raises RecursionError, since the default limit is about 1,000 calls.

problems.prompt: Write the main loop of an iterative DFS using a list called stack.
problems.answer: while stack: u = stack.pop(); if u in seen: continue; seen.add(u); stack.extend(v for v in g[u] if v not in seen)

steps.title: Discovery and Finish Times
steps.mastery: Record when DFS first reaches each vertex and when it finishes with it.
steps.practice: Run DFS from 1 on the 4-vertex figure graph with a counter, writing discovery and finish times as d/f.
steps.detail: Tick a clock when DFS enters a vertex and again when it leaves. A vertex finishes only after everything reachable below it. These times are what topological sort and strongly connected components are built on.
steps.pitfall: Giving a vertex its finish time as soon as its first child is done.

problems.prompt: Run DFS from 1 on the figure graph, neighbors in increasing order. Which vertex finishes first?
In that same DFS, give the discovery and finish times of vertex 1.
During DFS on an undirected graph you meet an already-seen vertex that is not your parent. What does that tell you?

steps.title: DFS Tree and Edge Types
steps.mastery: Split the edges of a graph into DFS tree edges and the rest.
steps.practice: Run DFS from A on the 6-vertex figure graph, draw the tree edges bold, then list every edge that is not in the tree.
steps.detail: A tree edge is one DFS used to reach a new vertex. In a connected graph with V vertices there are V - 1 of them. In an undirected graph every other edge is a back edge, joining a vertex to one of its ancestors.
steps.proof: Tree edges: A-B, B-C, C-F, F-E, E-D.
steps.pitfall: Counting an edge twice because it appears in 2 adjacency lists.

problems.prompt: How many tree edges does a DFS from A on the figure graph have?
After that DFS, how many of the 7 edges are left over as back edges?
Name the back edges in the DFS from A with alphabetical neighbors.

steps.title: Flood Fill a Grid
steps.mastery: Use DFS on a grid to find and size a region of matching cells.
steps.practice: Take a 5 by 5 grid of letters, flood fill from the top-left cell over same-letter neighbors up, down, left and right, and count the cells.
steps.detail: Each cell is a vertex and its 4 neighbors are its edges, as long as they are inside the grid and match. A DFS from a cell marks its whole region. This is how the paint bucket tool works.
steps.proof: The count is the size of the top-left region.
steps.pitfall: Forgetting the bounds check and reading off the edge of the grid.

problems.prompt: Flood fill from the top-left cell of the grid, moving up, down, left and right over 'A' cells. How many cells fill?
How many separate same-letter regions does the grid have?
If moves can also go diagonally, how many cells does the 'B' region starting at the top right hold?

steps.title: Settle the Nearest Vertex
steps.mastery: Run Dijkstra by hand, each time settling the unsettled vertex with the smallest distance so far.
steps.practice: Run Dijkstra from A on the 6-vertex figure graph, writing the distance table after each vertex is settled.
steps.detail: Start with A at 0 and every other vertex at ∞. Pick the unsettled vertex with the smallest distance, settle it, and update its neighbors. With no negative edges, nothing found later can beat a settled distance, because every other route starts from something at least as far.
steps.pitfall: Settling vertices in the order they were discovered, like BFS.

problems.prompt: Running Dijkstra from A on the figure graph, which vertex is settled right after A?
Give the order in which Dijkstra from A settles all 6 vertices of the figure graph.
problems.answer: A, C, B, D, E, F

problems.prompt: With every weight 0 or more, why can a settled distance never improve later?
problems.answer: Any other route must leave through an unsettled vertex whose distance is already at least as big, and adding edges of weight 0 or more cannot make it smaller.

steps.title: Relax an Edge
steps.mastery: Relax an edge by checking whether going through it gives a shorter distance.
steps.practice: Relax the edge C→B of weight 1 when dist[C] = 2 and dist[B] = 4, then the edge B→D of weight 5.
steps.detail: Relaxing u→v with weight w means: if dist[u] + w < dist[v], set dist[v] = dist[u] + w and parent[v] = u. Dijkstra is just relaxing every edge out of each vertex as it gets settled.
steps.proof: dist[B] becomes 3, then dist[D] becomes 8.
steps.pitfall: Updating dist[v] even when the new route is longer.

problems.prompt: dist[u] = 7, the edge u→v costs 3, and dist[v] = 12. What is dist[v] after relaxing?
dist[C] = 2, edge C→B costs 1 and B's estimate is 4. What does relaxing C→B change?
problems.answer: dist[B] drops to 3 and parent[B] becomes C.

problems.prompt: Write the relax step as 2 lines of Python.
problems.answer: if dist[u] + w < dist[v]: dist[v] = dist[u] + w; parent[v] = u (then push (dist[v], v) on the heap).

steps.title: Dijkstra with a Heap
steps.mastery: Write Dijkstra with a binary heap and skip the stale entries it leaves behind.
steps.practice: Write Dijkstra in Python with heapq, pushing (dist, vertex) pairs, then run it on the 6-vertex figure graph.
steps.detail: Push (0, start). Pop the smallest pair. If its distance is bigger than dist[u], it is stale from before a better route was found, so skip it. Otherwise relax every edge out of u and push improved neighbors.
steps.proof: O((V + E) log V) with a binary heap.
steps.pitfall: Processing stale heap entries, which repeats work and can give wrong parents.

problems.prompt: Which Python module gives Dijkstra its priority queue?
You pop (9, "D") but dist["D"] is already 8. What should the code do, and why?
problems.answer: Skip it. It is a stale entry pushed before the better route to D was found.

problems.prompt: What is the running time of Dijkstra with a binary heap, for V vertices and E edges?

steps.title: Rebuild the Shortest Path
steps.mastery: Store a parent each time a distance improves, then walk back from the target to get the route.
steps.practice: Run Dijkstra from A on the 6-vertex figure graph with a parent table, then write the shortest route to F and its cost.
steps.detail: Each successful relax sets parent[v] = u. After Dijkstra finishes, start at the target and follow parents to the start, then reverse. The cost is dist[target], and it should equal the sum along the route.
steps.proof: A-C-B-D-E-F, cost 13.
steps.pitfall: Forgetting to update parent when a distance improves a second time.

problems.prompt: What is the shortest path from A to F in the figure graph?
What does the shortest path from A to F in the figure cost?
In Dijkstra from A on that graph, what is the parent of D?

steps.title: Where Dijkstra Fails
steps.mastery: Show with a 3-vertex example why Dijkstra can be wrong once an edge is negative.
steps.practice: Run Dijkstra from A on A→B 2, A→C 5, C→B -4, and compare dist[B] with the true shortest distance.
steps.detail: Dijkstra settles B at 2 before it looks at C. The route A-C-B costs 1, but B is already settled and never revisited. Adding a constant to every weight does not fix it, because longer routes get penalized more. Use Bellman-Ford.
steps.proof: Dijkstra says 2, the truth is 1.
steps.pitfall: Shifting all weights up to make them positive, which changes which path is shortest.

problems.prompt: What does Dijkstra from A give for dist[B] in the figure, and what is the true value? Give Dijkstra's first.
problems.answer: Dijkstra says 2. The true shortest is 1, along A-C-B.

problems.prompt: Can you fix negative edges by adding 4 to every weight? Explain with 1 example.
problems.answer: No. A path with 3 edges gains 12 while a 1-edge path gains only 4, so the shortest path can change.

problems.prompt: Some edges weigh -2 or -5, but no cycle is negative. Which algorithm should you use?

steps.title: Union and Find
steps.mastery: Use union and find to merge groups and ask whether 2 items share a group.
steps.practice: Start with 6 items alone, apply union(1, 2), union(3, 4), union(2, 3), and answer find(1) == find(4) and find(5) == find(6).
steps.detail: Each group is a tree, and find walks up to its root. union joins 2 roots. Two items are in the same group exactly when their roots match. Start with parent[i] = i, every item alone.
steps.proof: Yes for 1 and 4, no for 5 and 6.
steps.pitfall: Joining the 2 items themselves instead of their roots.

problems.prompt: After union(1, 2), union(3, 4) and union(2, 3), are 1 and 4 in the same group?
8 items start alone. Then 4 calls merge 1 with 2, 3 with 4, 2 with 3, and 5 with 6. How many groups now?
Write find(x) without any speedups, using a parent list.
problems.answer: while parent[x] != x: x = parent[x]; return x

steps.title: Path Compression
steps.mastery: Flatten trees during find so later finds take only a step or 2.
steps.practice: Draw the chain 5→4→3→2→1, run find(5) with path compression, and redraw the tree.
steps.detail: On the way back from the root, point every vertex you passed straight at the root. The next find from any of them takes 1 step. In Python: if parent[x] != x: parent[x] = find(parent[x]); return parent[x].
steps.proof: Afterward 5, 4, 3 and 2 all point straight at 1.
steps.pitfall: Only updating the vertex you started from.

problems.prompt: The parent chain is 5→4→3→2→1. After find(5) with path compression, what is the parent of 5?
Following on from the chain 5→4→3→2→1, where does 3 point once that compressed lookup is done?
Write find(x) with path compression in Python.
problems.answer: def find(x): if parent[x] != x: parent[x] = find(parent[x]); return parent[x]

steps.title: Union by Size
steps.mastery: Attach the smaller tree under the larger one to keep trees shallow.
steps.practice: Merge a group of size 3 into a group of size 7 by size, and say which root ends on top and the new size.
steps.detail: Keep size[root] for each group. When merging, hang the smaller root under the larger and add the sizes. With path compression too, each operation costs about α(n), which is at most 4 for any practical n.
steps.proof: The size 7 root stays on top, new size 10.
steps.pitfall: Always attaching the first argument under the second, which can build a long chain.

problems.prompt: You merge a group of size 3 with a group of size 7, by size. Which root becomes the root of both?
problems.answer: The root of the size 7 group.

problems.prompt: Why does union by size keep trees shallow, even for 1,000,000 items?
problems.answer: A vertex only gets deeper when its group at least doubles in size, so its depth is at most \(\log_{2} n\).

problems.prompt: With both path compression and union by size, about how long does each operation take for n = 1,000,000?
problems.answer: Nearly constant, about \(\alpha (n)\), which is under 5.

steps.title: Detect Cycles with Union-Find
steps.mastery: Detect a cycle as edges arrive by checking whether both ends already share a group.
steps.practice: Add the edges 1-2, 2-3, 3-4, 4-1 one at a time to a union-find, and say which edge closes a cycle.
steps.detail: For each new undirected edge u-v, if find(u) == find(v), u and v are already connected, so this edge closes a cycle. Otherwise, union them. This is exactly the check Kruskal uses.
steps.proof: The edge 4-1 closes the cycle.
steps.pitfall: Calling union before checking find, which hides the cycle.

problems.prompt: Edges arrive in the order 1-2, 2-3, 3-4, 4-1. Which edge closes a cycle?
Edges arrive as 1-2, 3-4, 2-3, 5-6, 6-4. Does any edge close a cycle?
problems.answer: No. Each edge joins 2 different groups.

problems.prompt: Which MST algorithm relies on this exact check?

steps.title: Count Groups as You Go
steps.mastery: Keep a running count of groups that drops by 1 on each successful union.
steps.practice: Start with 10 people as 10 groups, apply 6 friendships where 2 are already friends of friends, and track the count.
steps.detail: Start with n groups. Each union that actually merges 2 different groups lowers the count by 1. A union inside 1 group changes nothing. This answers "how many groups now?" after every step in O(1).
steps.proof: 10 - 4 = 6 groups.
steps.pitfall: Lowering the count on every union call, even when both items share a group.

problems.prompt: 10 items start alone and 4 unions each join 2 different groups. How many groups are left?
union(3, 7) is called but 3 and 7 are already in the same group. How does the group count change?
A class of 30 has friendship pairs coming in. When does the group count reach 1?
problems.answer: When everyone is connected through friends, after at least 29 merging unions.

steps.title: Degrees Decide It
steps.mastery: Decide whether an Euler path or circuit exists by counting odd-degree vertices.
steps.practice: Write the degree of each vertex of the 5-vertex figure graph, count the odd ones, and say whether a path or circuit exists.
steps.detail: In a connected graph, an Euler circuit uses every edge once and returns to the start; it exists when every degree is even. An Euler path that does not return exists when exactly 2 vertices are odd, and it must start at one of them.
steps.proof: Odd vertices: A, C. A path exists, a circuit does not.
steps.pitfall: Checking degrees but forgetting the graph must be connected.

problems.prompt: Which vertices of the figure graph have odd degree?
Does the figure graph have an Euler path, an Euler circuit, or neither?
problems.answer: An Euler path, starting at A or C, but no circuit.

problems.prompt: A connected graph has 4 vertices of odd degree. How many pen strokes does it take to draw every edge once?

steps.title: The Bridges of Königsberg
steps.mastery: Explain why the 7 bridges of Königsberg cannot be crossed exactly once each.
steps.practice: Draw Königsberg as 4 land masses joined by 7 bridges, write each degree, and explain the answer from the counts.
steps.detail: Euler turned the city into a graph: land masses are vertices and bridges are edges. The 4 degrees are 5, 3, 3 and 3. All 4 are odd, but a walk needs at most 2 odd vertices, so no such walk exists.
steps.proof: Degrees 5, 3, 3, 3: all odd, so it is impossible.
steps.pitfall: Trying routes by hand instead of counting degrees.

problems.prompt: In the figure, what are the degrees of the 4 land masses of Königsberg?
Why can no walk in Königsberg cross each of the 7 bridges exactly once?
problems.answer: All 4 land masses have odd degree, and a walk allows at most 2.

problems.prompt: What is the fewest bridges Königsberg would need to add for an Euler path to exist?
problems.answer: 1, joining 2 of the odd land masses.

steps.title: Hierholzer's Algorithm
steps.mastery: Build an Euler circuit by following unused edges and splicing in loops.
steps.practice: Run Hierholzer from C on the bowtie graph, triangles A-B-C and C-D-E sharing C, writing the stack as you go.
steps.detail: Walk from the start along unused edges until you are stuck, which only happens back at the start. Then back up to the first vertex with unused edges and walk a loop from there, splicing it in. A stack does the splicing. It runs in O(E).
steps.proof: One circuit is C-A-B-C-D-E-C.
steps.pitfall: Deleting an edge from only 1 adjacency list in an undirected graph.

problems.prompt: What is the running time of Hierholzer's algorithm on E edges?
Starting an Euler path in the figure graph, which 2 vertices may you start from?
problems.answer: A and C, the 2 odd vertices. Either one works.

problems.prompt: Give an Euler path through every edge of the figure graph exactly once.

steps.title: Directed Euler Paths
steps.mastery: Check for directed Euler circuits and paths from in-degree and out-degree.
steps.practice: For the directed edges 1→2, 2→3, 3→1, 1→3, write each in and out degree and decide what exists.
steps.detail: A directed Euler circuit needs in = out at every vertex. A directed Euler path needs 1 vertex with out = in + 1, where it starts, 1 with in = out + 1, where it ends, and the rest equal. The edges must also be connected.
steps.proof: Vertex 1 has out 2 and in 1, vertex 3 has in 2 and out 1, so a path exists from 1 to 3.
steps.pitfall: Using undirected odd-degree rules on a directed graph.

problems.prompt: Directed edges 1→2, 2→3, 3→1, 1→3. Which vertex must an Euler path start from?
problems.answer: 1, because its out-degree is 1 more than its in-degree.

problems.prompt: What must be true of every vertex for a directed Euler circuit?
In a directed graph, vertex 4 has in-degree 3 and out-degree 1. Can an Euler path exist?
problems.answer: No. In and out may differ by at most 1.

steps.title: Euler Paths in Practice
steps.mastery: Recognize puzzles that are Euler paths in disguise, from drawing figures to street sweeping.
steps.practice: Decide whether the envelope shape with 5 corners can be drawn in 1 stroke, then name 2 real problems that are Euler paths.
steps.detail: Drawing without lifting the pen, a mail carrier covering every street once, and building DNA sequences from fragments are all Euler path problems. Counting odd degrees answers whether it is possible in seconds.
steps.proof: Yes, starting from 1 of the 2 bottom corners.
steps.pitfall: Confusing Euler paths, which use every edge once, with Hamiltonian paths, which visit every vertex once.

problems.prompt: An Euler path uses every edge once. What does a Hamiltonian path use once?
A street sweeper must cover all 12 streets of a district without repeats and end where it began. Which condition must the map meet?
problems.answer: Every intersection must have an even number of streets, and the streets must be connected.

problems.prompt: Which of these is easy to check, an Euler path or a Hamiltonian path?
problems.answer: An Euler path. Counting degrees settles it, while no fast test for Hamiltonian paths is known.

steps.title: Capacities and Flow
steps.mastery: Check that a flow respects every capacity and keeps flow in equal to flow out at each middle vertex.
steps.practice: Put a flow of 5 on S→A, A→C and C→T, then check every capacity and every vertex balance.
steps.detail: Each edge has a capacity, the most it can carry. A valid flow never exceeds a capacity, and at every vertex except the source and sink, flow in equals flow out. The value of the flow is the total leaving the source.
steps.proof: Valid, with value 5.
steps.pitfall: Letting flow pile up at a middle vertex.

problems.prompt: An edge has capacity 7 and carries 9 units. Is that allowed?
problems.answer: No. Flow can never exceed capacity.

problems.prompt: 12 units flow into a middle vertex. 7 leave by 1 edge and x by the other. What is x?
A flow sends 6 units out of the source and 2 of them come back into it. What is the flow value?

steps.title: Find the Max Flow
steps.mastery: Find the maximum flow from source to sink by pushing flow along paths until none has room left.
steps.practice: Push flow along S-A-C-T, then S-A-D-T, then S-B-D-T in the 6-vertex figure, writing the room left on each edge.
steps.detail: Pick any path from S to T with spare capacity, push as much as its tightest edge allows, and repeat. Keep a note of the flow on each edge. When no path has room, you have the maximum, as long as you also allow undoing flow (next step).
steps.proof: Max flow 11.
steps.pitfall: Stopping early because the first path you picked blocked others.

problems.prompt: What is the maximum flow from S to T in the figure?
Along S-A-C-T in the figure, how much flow can you push at most?
Which edge into T is full at the maximum flow in the figure?
problems.answer: D→T, carrying 7 of 7. C→T carries only 4 of its 10.

steps.title: Cuts and the Min Cut
steps.mastery: Measure an s-t cut and use the max-flow min-cut theorem to check a flow is the best.
steps.practice: Split the figure vertices into {S, A} and the rest, add the capacities of edges crossing from the S side, then try other splits.
steps.detail: A cut splits the vertices with S on one side and T on the other. Its capacity is the sum of capacities on edges from the S side to the T side. Every flow is at most every cut, and the max flow equals the smallest cut.
steps.proof: The {S, A} cut is 17. The smallest cut is 11.
steps.pitfall: Adding edges that cross backward, from the T side to the S side.

problems.prompt: What is the capacity of the cut with {S, A} on one side in the figure?
State the max-flow min-cut theorem in 1 sentence.
problems.answer: The largest flow from s to t equals the smallest capacity of any cut separating them.

problems.prompt: Find a cut in the figure whose capacity equals the max flow.
problems.answer: {S, A, B, D} against {C, T}: A→C 4 + D→T 7 = 11.

steps.title: The Residual Graph
steps.mastery: Build the residual graph, with room left forward and flow you can undo backward.
steps.practice: For an edge of capacity 10 carrying 6, draw its residual edges, then explain how a backward edge lets a later path reroute flow.
steps.detail: Each edge u→v with capacity c and flow f becomes a forward edge with c - f room and a backward edge v→u with f. Pushing along a backward edge cancels earlier flow. Ford-Fulkerson stops when the residual graph has no path from s to t.
steps.proof: Forward 4, backward 6.
steps.pitfall: Leaving out backward edges, which can get stuck below the maximum.

problems.prompt: An edge has capacity 10 and carries 6. Give its residual forward capacity, then its backward one.
Why does the residual graph include backward edges? Use an edge carrying 6 units as the example.
problems.answer: The backward edge with room 6 lets a later path cancel up to 6 units an earlier path sent the wrong way.

problems.prompt: When does the Ford-Fulkerson method stop, and what does that prove?
problems.answer: When the residual graph has no s-t path. The flow is then maximum, since the reachable vertices form a cut it fills.

steps.title: Model Problems as Flow
steps.mastery: Turn matching and capacity problems into flow networks and pick an algorithm.
steps.practice: Turn the 3-person, 3-job matching from earlier into a flow network with a source and a sink, and state every capacity.
steps.detail: Add a source joined to every left vertex and a sink joined from every right vertex, all with capacity 1, and give the middle edges capacity 1. The max flow is the max matching. A vertex limit becomes an in-copy and an out-copy joined by an edge.
steps.proof: Every capacity is 1, and the max flow is the matching size.
steps.pitfall: Giving the middle edges capacity ∞, which lets 1 job take 2 people.

problems.prompt: When you model a 3-person, 3-job matching as flow, what capacity does every edge get?
A warehouse can handle 50 units a day. How do you put that limit on a vertex in a flow network?
problems.answer: Split it into an in-vertex and an out-vertex joined by an edge of capacity 50.

problems.prompt: What is the running time of Edmonds-Karp, which picks shortest augmenting paths with BFS?

steps.title: The Triple Loop
steps.mastery: Write Floyd-Warshall as 3 nested loops with k, the middle vertex, on the outside.
steps.practice: Write Floyd-Warshall in Python for a 4-vertex graph, with d[i][j] = min(d[i][j], d[i][k] + d[k][j]).
steps.detail: After the round for k, d[i][j] is the best path that only passes through vertices 1 to k in the middle. That is why k must be the outer loop. Start with d[i][i] = 0, edge weights where there are edges, and ∞ elsewhere.
steps.proof: for k: for i: for j: d[i][j] = min(d[i][j], d[i][k] + d[k][j]).
steps.pitfall: Putting k in the inner loop, which gives wrong answers.

problems.prompt: In Floyd-Warshall, which of the 3 loop variables must be the outermost?
Floyd-Warshall runs on 400 vertices. About how many inner steps is that?
How much memory does Floyd-Warshall need for V = 400 vertices?

steps.title: Trace One Round
steps.mastery: Trace one k round by hand and see which entries improve.
steps.practice: Start the 4-vertex figure table, run the round for k = 2, and circle the entries that change.
steps.detail: For the round k, check every pair (i, j): is going i to k, then k to j, cheaper than the current d[i][j]? Only entries whose route can use k change. Rows and columns for k itself never change in its own round.
steps.proof: d[1][3] drops from 7 to 5 in round k = 2.
steps.pitfall: Updating with d[i][k] + d[k][j] before both values are filled in.

problems.prompt: In the figure graph, what is d[1][3] after the round for k = 2?
Before any rounds, what is d[2][1] in the figure graph?
Once every round is done, how cheap is the trip from 2 back to 1 in the figure?

steps.title: Read the All-Pairs Table
steps.mastery: Read shortest distances between any 2 vertices off a finished Floyd-Warshall table.
steps.practice: Finish Floyd-Warshall on the 4-vertex figure graph and fill the whole 4 by 4 table.
steps.detail: Row i, column j holds the shortest distance from i to j. In a directed graph the table is usually not symmetric. Keep a next[i][j] table too if you need the actual routes.
steps.proof: The finished table matches the answer figure.
steps.pitfall: Reading row and column the wrong way round in a directed graph.

problems.prompt: From the finished table for the figure graph, what is the shortest distance from 3 to 2?
Going from 4 to 3 in the figure graph, what is the cheapest total?
Is the finished table for the figure graph symmetric? Why or why not?
problems.answer: No. The edges are one-way, so going from i to j can cost differently from j to i.

steps.title: Negative Cycles in the Table
steps.mastery: Spot a negative cycle in Floyd-Warshall from a negative number on the diagonal.
steps.practice: Add an edge with weight -10 to the 4-vertex figure graph so a cycle goes negative, rerun, and check the diagonal.
steps.detail: d[i][i] starts at 0. If it ends up negative, there is a cycle through i with a negative total, and distances that can reach it are not well defined. Negative edges alone are fine, only negative cycles break things.
steps.proof: A negative entry appears on the diagonal.
steps.pitfall: Treating any negative edge as a problem.

problems.prompt: After Floyd-Warshall, d[3][3] = -2. What does that tell you?
problems.answer: There is a negative cycle through vertex 3.

problems.prompt: Does Floyd-Warshall work with negative edges but no negative cycles?
The figure graph has a cycle 1-2-3-4-1. What is its total weight?

steps.title: When to Use It
steps.mastery: Choose Floyd-Warshall, repeated Dijkstra or BFS from the graph size and what is being asked.
steps.practice: For 3 inputs, V = 100 all pairs, V = 100,000 one source, and V = 2,000 all pairs, pick an algorithm and estimate the work.
steps.detail: Floyd-Warshall is O(V³), so it is good up to a few hundred vertices and is short to write. For 1 source use Dijkstra or BFS. For all pairs on big sparse graphs, run Dijkstra from every vertex.
steps.proof: Floyd-Warshall, Dijkstra, and Dijkstra from each vertex.
steps.pitfall: Using O(V³) on 100,000 vertices.

problems.prompt: V = 100 and you need every pair of distances. Which algorithm, and roughly how many steps?
V = 100,000 with 300,000 edges and 1 source. Which algorithm?
problems.answer: Dijkstra (or BFS if every edge costs the same).

problems.prompt: Why is Floyd-Warshall a bad fit for V = 5,000?
problems.answer: \(5{,}000^{3}\) is 125 billion steps, far too many.

steps.title: Cells as Vertices
steps.mastery: Count the vertices and edges of a grid graph, with 4-direction moves.
steps.practice: Count the vertices and edges of a 3 by 4 grid where each cell links to its up, down, left and right neighbors.
steps.detail: Each cell is a vertex. With 4-direction moves, a cell links to up to 4 neighbors, fewer on the border. An R by C grid has R(C - 1) horizontal links and C(R - 1) vertical ones.
steps.proof: 12 vertices and 17 edges.
steps.pitfall: Counting each link twice, once from each cell.

problems.prompt: How many vertices does a 5 by 7 grid graph have?
With 4-direction moves, how many neighbors does a corner cell of a 6 by 6 grid have?
How many edges does a 3 by 3 grid graph have with 4-direction moves?

steps.title: Neighbors in Code
steps.mastery: Write the neighbor loop for a grid with a direction list and a bounds check.
steps.practice: Write a Python loop over the 4 direction pairs that yields the in-bounds, open neighbors of cell (r, c).
steps.detail: Keep the directions in a list like [(0, 1), (1, 0), (0, -1), (-1, 0)] and add each to (r, c). Check 0 ≤ nr < R and 0 ≤ nc < C before reading the cell, and skip walls. For 8 directions add the 4 diagonals.
steps.proof: for dr, dc in dirs: nr, nc = r + dr, c + dc; if 0 <= nr < R and 0 <= nc < C and grid[nr][nc] != "#": yield nr, nc.
steps.pitfall: Reading grid[nr][nc] before the bounds check, which wraps around with -1 in Python.

problems.prompt: Write the 4 direction pairs for up, down, left and right moves.
Write the bounds check for a neighbor (nr, nc) in a grid with R rows and C columns.

accept: nr >= 0 and nr < R and nc >= 0 and nc < C

problems.prompt: In a 5 by 5 grid with rows and columns from 0, list the 4-direction neighbors of (2, 3).

steps.title: Shortest Path in a Maze
steps.mastery: Find the fewest moves through a maze with BFS over its open cells.
steps.practice: Run BFS by hand on the 5 by 5 maze, writing each open cell's distance from S, and read off the distance at E.
steps.detail: Every move costs 1, so BFS finds the fewest moves. Write distances in the cells as the search spreads, like a wave. Keep parents if you need the route itself, not just its length.
steps.proof: 8 moves.
steps.pitfall: Counting cells on the route, including S, which is 1 more than the moves.

problems.prompt: What is the fewest number of moves from S to E in the maze? '#' is a wall.
How many open cells can be reached from S in the maze, counting S?
BFS on a 1,000 by 1,000 grid: roughly how many cells does it touch at most?
problems.answer: 1,000,000, since each cell is visited once.

steps.title: Count Regions and Rooms
steps.mastery: Count separate open regions of a grid by flood filling from each unvisited open cell.
steps.practice: Count the rooms of '.' cells in a 4 by 4 floor plan where '#' is a wall, flood filling each new room.
steps.detail: Loop over every cell. When you hit an open cell not yet visited, count a room and flood fill it. The count at the end is the number of rooms. Size each room by counting cells as you fill.
steps.proof: The count is the number of flood fills started.
steps.pitfall: Starting a flood fill from cells already visited.

problems.prompt: How many separate rooms of '.' does the floor plan have, moving up, down, left and right?
What is the size of the largest room in that floor plan?
A grid has 40 open cells in 5 rooms of equal size. How many cells does each flood fill visit?

steps.title: Cells to Numbers
steps.mastery: Turn a cell (r, c) into a single id with r × C + c, and back again.
steps.practice: Number every cell of a 3 by 5 grid with r × 5 + c, then turn ids 7 and 14 back into (r, c).
steps.detail: Graph code that expects vertices 0 to n - 1 works on grids once each cell has one number. The id is r × C + c, where C is the number of columns. Back again: r = id // C and c = id % C.
steps.pitfall: Multiplying by the number of rows instead of columns.

problems.prompt: With 5 columns, what id does cell (2, 3) get?
With 5 columns, which cell is id 17?
Why turn cells into single numbers like 13 before running graph code?
problems.answer: So the grid fits array-based code: a dist list of length \(R \times C\), adjacency by id, and union-find over 0 to n - 1.

steps.title: Root the Tree
steps.mastery: Pick a root and read off parents, depths and leaves.
steps.practice: Root the 7-vertex figure tree at 1, then write each vertex's parent and depth and list the leaves.
steps.detail: Choose a root, then every other vertex has exactly 1 parent: its neighbor on the path to the root. Depth is the number of edges from the root. Leaves are vertices with no children.
steps.proof: Leaves: 4, 6 and 7. Depth of 7 is 3.
steps.pitfall: Treating the root as a leaf because it is at the edge of the drawing.

problems.prompt: With the figure tree rooted at 1, what is the parent of 7?
What is the depth of vertex 7, with the root at depth 0?
List the leaves of the figure tree when it is rooted at 1.

steps.title: LCA by Climbing
steps.mastery: Find the lowest common ancestor by lifting the deeper vertex up, then lifting both together.
steps.practice: Find LCA(4, 5), LCA(6, 7) and LCA(2, 7) by climbing parents in the figure tree.
steps.detail: First climb the deeper vertex until both are at the same depth. Then climb both together until they meet. The meeting point is the LCA. A vertex counts as its own ancestor, so LCA(5, 7) is 5.
steps.pitfall: Forgetting a vertex can be its own ancestor.

problems.prompt: Climbing from 4 and from 7 in the figure, where do the 2 routes first meet?
Which vertex is the lowest shared ancestor of 7 and 6?
Asked for the lowest common ancestor of 5 and 7, which vertex do you give, and why?
problems.answer: 5, because 5 is an ancestor of 7 and counts as its own ancestor.

steps.title: Distance Through the LCA
steps.mastery: Count the edges between any 2 nodes in a tree with 1 formula.
steps.practice: Compute dist(4, 7) and dist(7, 6) in the figure tree with depth[u] + depth[v] - 2 × depth[LCA].
steps.detail: The only path between 2 vertices in a tree goes up to their LCA and back down. So the number of edges is depth[u] + depth[v] - 2 × depth[lca]. Once LCA is fast, every distance question is fast.
steps.proof: 3 and 5.
steps.pitfall: Adding the 2 depths and forgetting to subtract the shared part.

problems.prompt: What is the distance between 4 and 7 in the figure tree?
How many edges separate 7 and 6 in the figure tree?
Why does the distance formula subtract 2 × depth[LCA]?
problems.answer: Both depths count the edges from the LCA up to the root, which the path between u and v never uses, so they come off twice.

steps.title: Binary Lifting
steps.mastery: Answer ancestor questions in O(log n) with a table of 2ᵏ-th ancestors.
steps.practice: Fill up[v][0] and up[v][1] for every vertex of the figure tree, then find the 3rd ancestor of 7 using 3 = 2 + 1.
steps.detail: up[v][0] is the parent and up[v][k] = up[up[v][k - 1]][k - 1], the ancestor 2ᵏ steps up. To jump n steps, follow the bits of n. LCA uses the same table to lift both vertices together in about log n jumps.
steps.proof: The 3rd ancestor of 7 is 1.
steps.pitfall: Filling the table in the wrong order so up[v][k - 1] is not ready yet.

problems.prompt: In binary lifting, what does up[v][k] store?
problems.answer: The ancestor of v that is 2ᵏ steps up.

problems.prompt: In the figure tree, what is up[7][1], the ancestor 2 steps above 7?
For n = 100,000 vertices, about how many entries does the binary lifting table hold?

steps.title: Entry and Exit Times
steps.mastery: Answer "is u an ancestor of v?" in O(1) with DFS entry and exit times.
steps.practice: Run DFS on the figure tree from 1, record tin and tout for each vertex, then test whether 2 is an ancestor of 7 and of 6.
steps.detail: u is an ancestor of v exactly when tin[u] ≤ tin[v] and tout[v] ≤ tout[u], because v is entered and left while u is still open. The subtree of u is the slice of vertices entered between tin[u] and tout[u].
steps.proof: 2 is an ancestor of 7 but not of 6.
steps.pitfall: Comparing only entry times, which also matches vertices visited later in other branches.

problems.prompt: Write the test for "u is an ancestor of v" using tin and tout.
How many vertices are in the subtree of 2 in the figure tree, counting 2?
Is 3 an ancestor of 7 in the figure tree?

steps.title: What a Spanning Tree Is
steps.mastery: Recognize a spanning tree: every vertex joined, no cycles, exactly V - 1 edges.
steps.practice: Draw 3 different spanning trees of a 5-vertex graph, check each has 4 edges, and total their weights.
steps.detail: A spanning tree keeps every vertex connected using the fewest edges, which is always V - 1. Add any edge and you make a cycle, remove any and you split it. The minimum spanning tree is the one with the smallest total weight.
steps.proof: Each has 4 edges.
steps.pitfall: Calling a set of edges a spanning tree when it leaves a vertex out.

problems.prompt: How many edges does a spanning tree of a 6-vertex graph have?
Does the bold set of edges in the figure form a spanning tree? Say why.
problems.answer: No. It has a cycle A-B-D-A and leaves C and F out.

problems.prompt: Why can a minimum spanning tree never contain a cycle? Use a 3-edge cycle to explain.
problems.answer: Dropping the heaviest edge of the cycle keeps everything connected and lowers the total, so a cycle is never minimal.

steps.title: Kruskal's Algorithm
steps.mastery: Build an MST by taking edges from lightest to heaviest and skipping any that would close a cycle.
steps.practice: Sort the 8 figure edges by weight and run Kruskal, writing take or skip next to each one.
steps.detail: Sort all edges by weight. Go down the list: if an edge joins 2 different pieces, take it. If its ends are already connected, skip it, because it would make a cycle. Stop once you have V - 1 edges.
steps.proof: Takes C-F, A-D, A-B, B-E, B-C, total 15.
steps.pitfall: Taking an edge because it is light without checking for a cycle.

problems.prompt: List the edges Kruskal takes on the figure graph, in the order it takes them.
What is the total weight of the minimum spanning tree in the figure?
Which is the first edge Kruskal skips on the figure graph, and why?
problems.answer: B-D (weight 6). Its ends are already connected.

steps.title: Prim's Algorithm
steps.mastery: Build an MST by growing one tree outward, always adding the cheapest edge that reaches a new vertex.
steps.practice: Run Prim from A on the 6-vertex figure graph, writing which vertex joins at each step and the edge it joins by.
steps.detail: Start with one vertex. Look at every edge from the tree to a vertex outside it, and add the cheapest. Repeat until every vertex is in. With a heap this runs in O(E log V), like Dijkstra.
steps.proof: Vertices join in the order A, D, B, E, C, F.
steps.pitfall: Picking the cheapest edge anywhere in the graph, which is Kruskal, not Prim.

problems.prompt: Running Prim from A on the figure graph, which edge is added first?
In what order do the vertices join the tree when Prim starts at A?
problems.answer: A, D, B, E, C, F

problems.prompt: Do Prim and Kruskal always give the same total weight on 1 graph?
problems.answer: Yes. Both give a minimum spanning tree, so the totals match even if the edges differ when weights tie.

steps.title: Union-Find Inside Kruskal
steps.mastery: Use union-find to make the cycle check in Kruskal fast.
steps.practice: Run Kruskal on the figure graph again, keeping a union-find, and write find(u) and find(v) for each edge before deciding.
steps.detail: Each piece of the forest is a set. An edge u-v closes a cycle exactly when find(u) == find(v). Otherwise take it and union the 2 sets. Sorting the edges is the slow part, O(E log E).
steps.proof: Each skip is an edge whose ends share a root.
steps.pitfall: Running a full DFS for every edge to check for a cycle.

problems.prompt: In Kruskal, what does find(u) == find(v) tell you about the edge u-v?
problems.answer: u and v are already connected, so the edge would make a cycle.

problems.prompt: What is the running time of Kruskal with union-find on E edges?
Why does Kruskal sort the edges before doing anything else?
problems.answer: So it always tries the lightest remaining edge first, which is what makes the result minimal.

steps.title: Using a Minimum Spanning Tree
steps.mastery: Apply MSTs to cabling and network problems and know what they do not answer.
steps.practice: Cable 6 buildings using the figure costs in thousands of dollars, find the cheapest total, then name 1 thing an MST does not minimize.
steps.detail: An MST is the cheapest way to connect everything. It is not the shortest path between any 2 points, and it does not make the longest link short. If all weights are different, there is exactly 1 MST.
steps.proof: 15 thousand dollars.
steps.pitfall: Reading the MST path between 2 buildings as their shortest route.

problems.prompt: Using the figure costs in thousands of dollars, what is the cheapest way to connect all 6 buildings?
Is the path between 2 vertices inside an MST always their shortest path in the graph? Give a reason.
problems.answer: No. The MST minimizes the total, not each pair, so a direct edge can be shorter than the tree route.

problems.prompt: A graph has 12 edges, all with different weights. How many minimum spanning trees does it have?

steps.title: Read a Graph Drawing
steps.mastery: Count the vertices and edges in a drawing and read off the degree of any vertex.
steps.practice: Draw a graph with 5 vertices and 6 edges, then write the degree of each vertex and check they add to 12.
steps.detail: A vertex is a dot and an edge is a line between 2 dots. The degree of a vertex is how many edges touch it. Every edge has 2 ends, so the degrees always add up to twice the number of edges, a fast check on any count.
steps.proof: The degrees add to 12.
steps.pitfall: Counting an edge once in the degree total instead of once at each end.

problems.prompt: How many vertices and how many edges does the graph in the figure have? Give the vertices first.
What is the degree of vertex B in the figure?
A graph has 7 edges. What do all its degrees add up to, and why?
problems.answer: 14, because each edge adds 1 to the degree of both of its ends.

steps.title: Adjacency Lists
steps.mastery: Write an adjacency list, one list of neighbors per vertex, for directed and undirected graphs.
steps.practice: Write the adjacency list for edges 1-2, 1-3, 2-3 and 3-4, then for the directed edges 1→2, 2→3, 3→1.
steps.detail: Each vertex gets a list of the vertices it connects to. In an undirected graph, the edge u-v goes in both lists. In a directed graph, u→v only goes in u's list. In Python this is a dict of lists or a list of lists.
steps.pitfall: Adding an undirected edge to only one of its 2 lists.

problems.prompt: Write the adjacency list for the graph in the figure.
A directed graph has edges 1→2, 2→3, 3→1 and 1→3. List the out-neighbors of vertex 1.
An undirected graph has 7 edges. How many entries are there across all its adjacency lists?

steps.title: Adjacency Matrix
steps.mastery: Write and read an adjacency matrix, where row u, column v is 1 when there is an edge u to v.
steps.practice: Write the 4 by 4 matrix for edges 1-2, 1-3, 2-3 and 3-4, then check it is symmetric.
steps.detail: An n-vertex graph gets an n by n grid of 0s and 1s, or weights. For an undirected graph the grid is symmetric across its diagonal. The diagonal is 0 unless a vertex has an edge to itself.
steps.pitfall: Putting 1s on the diagonal for every vertex.

problems.prompt: Write row 3 of the adjacency matrix for the graph in the figure.
Why is the adjacency matrix of an undirected graph always symmetric? Use the edge 1-2 as your example.
problems.answer: The edge 1-2 puts a 1 at both (1, 2) and (2, 1), and every edge does the same.

problems.prompt: How many edges does the undirected graph with this matrix have?

steps.title: Lists or a Matrix
steps.mastery: Choose between a list and a matrix from the size of the graph and the questions you will ask it.
steps.practice: Estimate the memory for 100,000 vertices with 500,000 edges stored as lists and as a matrix, then pick one.
steps.detail: A matrix costs n² cells whatever the edge count, and answers "is there an edge u-v" instantly. Lists cost about n + 2m entries and make "walk my neighbors" fast. Most real graphs are sparse, so lists are the default.
steps.proof: Lists: about 1.1 million entries. Matrix: 10 billion cells. Use lists.
steps.pitfall: Using a matrix for a big sparse graph and running out of memory.

problems.prompt: How many cells does an adjacency matrix for 10,000 vertices need?
How long does it take to check whether edge (u, v) exists with a matrix, and with lists?
A social network has 1,000,000 users with about 200 friends each. Lists or a matrix? Give rough sizes.
problems.answer: Lists: about 200 million entries. A matrix would need \(10^{12}\) cells, far too many.

steps.title: Read Graph Input
steps.mastery: Turn the usual "n m, then m lines of u v w" input into an adjacency list in code.
steps.practice: Write Python that reads "4 5" and then 5 lines of "u v w" into a list of lists for an undirected weighted graph.
steps.detail: Make n empty lists first. For each line, append (v, w) to u's list and, if undirected, (u, w) to v's list. Watch whether vertices are numbered from 0 or 1, and subtract 1 if the input is 1-based.
steps.proof: g = [[] for _ in range(n)], then g[u].append((v, w)) and g[v].append((u, w)).
steps.pitfall: Forgetting to convert 1-based input to 0-based indexes.

problems.prompt: An undirected input line reads "2 5 7". Which 2 entries does it add to the lists?
problems.answer: (5, 7) in vertex 2's list and (2, 7) in vertex 5's list.

problems.prompt: Input vertices go from 1 to n, and your list has indexes 0 to n - 1. What do you do with the line "3 4"?
problems.answer: Subtract 1 from each: add an edge between indexes 2 and 3.

problems.prompt: Store the weighted graph in the figure as an edge list of (u, v, w) triples.

steps.title: What an SCC Is
steps.mastery: Split a directed graph into its mutually reachable groups by checking paths both ways.
steps.practice: Circle the strongly connected components of the 7-vertex figure graph, checking each pair can reach each other both ways.
steps.detail: In a directed graph, u and v are strongly connected when there is a path from u to v and from v to u. The graph splits into strongly connected components. A vertex in no cycle is a component by itself.
steps.pitfall: Merging 2 cycles because one arrow joins them, when you cannot get back.

problems.prompt: How many strongly connected components does the figure graph have?
Can {1, 2, 3, 4} count as 1 group here? Why?
problems.answer: No. 4 cannot get back to 1, 2 or 3.

problems.prompt: A directed graph with 9 vertices has one cycle through 4 of them and no other cycles. How many SCCs does it have?
problems.answer: 6: the 4-vertex cycle is one SCC, and each of the other 5 vertices is its own.

steps.title: Kosaraju's Two Passes
steps.mastery: Find SCCs with 2 DFS passes: 1 for finish order, and 1 on the reversed graph.
steps.practice: Run DFS on the figure graph and list finish order, reverse every edge, then DFS again in decreasing finish order.
steps.detail: The first pass orders vertices so a component that can reach another is handled first. Reversing the edges traps each search in its own component, so every search in the second pass outlines exactly 1 SCC.
steps.proof: Each second-pass search is 1 component.
steps.pitfall: Running the second pass on the original graph instead of the reversed one.

problems.prompt: In Kosaraju's algorithm, what graph does the second DFS pass run on?
problems.answer: The reversed graph, with every edge turned around.

problems.prompt: In what order does Kosaraju's second pass pick its start vertices?
problems.answer: Decreasing finish time from the first pass.

problems.prompt: What is the running time of Kosaraju's algorithm on V vertices and E edges?

steps.title: The Condensation Graph
steps.mastery: Shrink each SCC to 1 vertex and read the result as a DAG.
steps.practice: Shrink each SCC of the figure graph to 1 dot, draw the arrows between dots, and confirm there is no cycle.
steps.detail: After merging each component into a single vertex, the graph left over has no cycles, because a cycle between components would have merged them. You can then topologically sort it or run DAG dynamic programming.
steps.proof: The condensation has 3 vertices and 2 edges.
steps.pitfall: Expecting the condensation to have cycles.

problems.prompt: How many vertices does the condensation of the figure graph have?
Why is the condensation graph always a DAG?
problems.answer: A cycle between 2 components would mean each reaches the other, so they would be 1 component.

problems.prompt: In the condensation of the figure graph, which component has no incoming edges?

steps.title: Tarjan's Low-Link
steps.mastery: Follow how Tarjan finds every SCC in 1 DFS pass using low-link values and a stack.
steps.practice: Run Tarjan on the cycle 1→2→3→1 by hand, writing tin and low for each vertex, and say when the component pops off the stack.
steps.detail: Each vertex gets an entry time tin and a low value, the earliest tin reachable through its subtree and 1 back edge to the stack. When low[v] == tin[v], v is the root of a component, and everything above it on the stack is that component.
steps.proof: All 3 get low 1, and the component pops at vertex 1.
steps.pitfall: Updating low through edges to vertices already popped into another component.

problems.prompt: In Tarjan's algorithm, what does low[v] == tin[v] mean?
problems.answer: v is the root of a strongly connected component, so pop it and everything above it off the stack.

problems.prompt: How many DFS passes does Tarjan's algorithm need, compared with Kosaraju's 2?
For the cycle 1→2→3→1, what are low[2] and low[3] after Tarjan's DFS from 1?

steps.title: Using SCCs
steps.mastery: Apply SCCs to reachability questions, such as whether every city can reach every other.
steps.practice: Model 5 one-way streets between 4 neighborhoods and decide whether you can drive from any neighborhood to any other.
steps.detail: Every vertex can reach every other exactly when the whole graph is 1 SCC. More generally, to fix a graph into 1 SCC you need max(sources, sinks) new edges in the condensation, unless it is already 1 component.
steps.proof: You can when there is exactly 1 SCC.
steps.pitfall: Checking only that every vertex can reach vertex 1.

problems.prompt: A city has 50 intersections with one-way streets. What must be true of its SCCs for every place to reach every other?
problems.answer: It must be 1 strongly connected component.

problems.prompt: In the figure graph, can vertex 7 reach vertex 1?
Which logic problem, written as clauses like (x OR y), is solved with SCCs of an implication graph?

steps.title: Order the Dependencies
steps.mastery: Write an order of tasks where every arrow points from earlier to later.
steps.practice: Take the 6-task figure graph and write an order where each task comes after all the tasks pointing to it.
steps.detail: A topological order lines up the vertices so every edge goes left to right. It exists exactly when the directed graph has no cycle. There are usually many valid orders, so check yours edge by edge.
steps.proof: One valid order: A, B, C, D, E, F.
steps.pitfall: Putting a task before one of its prerequisites.

problems.prompt: Give a topological order of the figure graph, choosing alphabetically when you have a choice.
problems.answer: A, B, C, D, E, F

problems.prompt: Is B, A, D, C, E, F also a valid order for the figure graph?
problems.answer: Yes. Every edge still goes left to right.

problems.prompt: Why can a graph with the cycle 1→2→3→1 never be ordered this way?
problems.answer: In a cycle each vertex must come before the next, so the first must come before itself.

steps.title: Kahn's Algorithm
steps.mastery: Topologically sort by repeatedly taking a vertex with no incoming edges left.
