problems.prompt: From 1 to 6, which string number is the thickest?
What note is string 3?
Is string 1 the highest in pitch, or the lowest?

steps.title: One Fret, One Half Step
steps.mastery: Know that each fret raises a string by one half step, so 12 frets make an octave.
steps.practice: Play the 5th string open, then at frets 1 through 12, naming each note until you reach A again.
steps.detail: Each fret is a half step, so the notes climb chromatically: A, A#, B, C and on. Remember there's no sharp between B and C or between E and F. At fret 12, you're back at the open string's note an octave up.
steps.proof: A, A#, B, C, C#, D, D#, E, F, F#, G, G#, A.
steps.pitfall: Putting a sharp between B and C.

problems.prompt: What note is the 5th string at fret 2?
What note is the 6th string at fret 12?
What note is the 1st string at fret 3?

steps.title: Find Notes on the Low E
steps.mastery: Name any fret on the low E string quickly, using the dots on the neck as landmarks.
steps.practice: Play E F G A B C D E on the 6th string at frets 0 1 3 5 7 8 10 12, then call out random notes and find them.
steps.detail: The 6th string's notes are worth learning cold, since they're the roots of many barre chords. The dots on most necks at frets 3, 5, 7 and 12 help: G, A, B and E. From those landmarks, step up or down to the rest.
steps.proof: Random notes found on the 6th string in under 3 seconds each.
steps.pitfall: Counting frets from the nut every time.

problems.prompt: Your finger is on the 5th fret of the low E. Which note is it?
Which fret of the thickest of the 6 strings gives C?
Name the note at fret 10 of string 6.

steps.title: Find Notes on the A String
steps.mastery: Find any natural note on the 5th string, which works the same way starting from A.
steps.practice: Play A B C D E F G A on the 5th string at frets 0 2 3 5 7 8 10 12, then quiz yourself on 10 notes.
steps.detail: With the 6th and 5th strings learned, you can find the root of almost any chord shape. The 5th string's dots give C at 3, D at 5 and E at 7. Practice naming notes in both directions.
steps.proof: 10 notes found correctly on the 5th string.
steps.pitfall: Learning only the 6th string and guessing on the 5th.

problems.prompt: On string 5, which fret gives C?
On string 5, fret 7 sounds which note?
Where on string 5 do you find G?

steps.title: Octave Shapes
steps.mastery: Find the same note an octave higher with the shape that goes 2 strings up and 2 frets up.
steps.practice: Play the 6th string at fret 3, which is G, then find its octave on the 4th string at fret 5, and repeat for 5 other notes.
steps.detail: From the 6th or 5th string, skip a string and move up 2 frets to find the octave. When the shape crosses onto the B string, add one more fret, because the G and B strings are tuned a 3rd apart instead of a 4th.
steps.proof: 6 notes each played with their octave.
steps.pitfall: Forgetting the extra fret when the shape crosses the B string.

problems.prompt: The 6th string at fret 5 is A. At which fret is the A an octave up on the 4th string?
The 5th string at fret 3 is C. At which fret is its octave on the 3rd string?
Why does the octave shape shift when it crosses onto the 2nd string?
problems.answer: The G and B strings are tuned a 3rd apart instead of a 4th.

steps.title: Keep the Arm Moving
steps.mastery: Keep the strumming hand moving down and up in steady 8th notes, even when it doesn't hit the strings.
steps.practice: Strum muted strings in down-up 8th notes for 2 minutes at 70 BPM, saying '1 and 2 and' aloud.
steps.detail: The hand moves down on every beat and up on every 'and', like a pendulum. Strum patterns come from choosing which passes hit the strings and which miss. Keeping the motion constant is what keeps the rhythm steady.
steps.proof: 2 minutes of even down-up motion, counted aloud.
steps.pitfall: Stopping the hand between strums, so the timing wanders.

problems.prompt: In 8th-note strumming, which way does the hand move on a beat number like '2'?
In 8th-note strumming, which way does the hand move on the 'and' of 3?
Why keep the arm moving even when you skip 1 strum?
problems.answer: It holds the timing, like a pendulum.

steps.title: Down Down Up Up Down Up
steps.mastery: Play the common pattern D D U U D U, keeping the arm moving all the way through.
steps.practice: Strum D D U U D U on a G chord for 16 bars at 70 BPM, missing the strings on the beat 3 downstroke.
steps.detail: The pattern is down on 1, down on 2, up on the 'and' of 2, a missed down on 3, up on the 'and' of 3, then down on 4 and up on the 'and' of 4. The missed stroke is what makes it groove. Keep the hand moving through it.
steps.proof: 16 bars of the pattern at 70 BPM with no stops.
steps.pitfall: Stopping the hand on beat 3 instead of swinging past the strings.

problems.prompt: In 'D D U U D U', on which beat does the hand miss the strings going down?
How many strums are in 1 bar of D D U U D U?
Which count is the first U of 'D D U U D U' on?

steps.title: Accents and Dynamics
steps.mastery: Accent chosen strums, like beats 2 and 4, to give the rhythm a groove.
steps.practice: Strum 8 bars of steady 8ths on C, accenting beats 2 and 4, then 8 bars accenting only beat 1.
steps.detail: Accents turn a steady strum into a groove. Hitting 2 and 4 harder gives the backbeat of rock and pop. A faster stroke through the strings makes a strum louder, while a lighter, slower one keeps the in-between strums quiet.
steps.proof: 16 bars with clearly different accent patterns.
steps.pitfall: Strumming every 8th at the same volume, so nothing grooves.

problems.prompt: Accenting beats 2 and 4 is called what in rock and pop?
How do you make the strum on beat 2 louder: a faster stroke or a tighter grip?
problems.answer: A faster stroke through the strings.

problems.prompt: In 8 bars of strumming, should every strum be the same volume?
problems.answer: No. Accents give the rhythm shape.

steps.title: Add Muted Strums
steps.mastery: Add percussive muted strums by relaxing the fretting hand, or by slapping the strings with the strumming palm.
steps.practice: Strum G for 8 bars with a muted 'chuck' on beats 2 and 4, made by lifting the fretting fingers slightly.
steps.detail: A chuck is a strum with no pitch, just a click, like a snare drum. Relax the fretting fingers so they touch the strings without pressing, strum, then press again. It adds drive to acoustic playing without a drummer.
steps.proof: 8 bars with a clean chuck on every 2 and 4.
steps.pitfall: Letting go of the neck completely, so the open strings ring.

problems.prompt: What is a strum 'chuck'?
How do you mute the strings with a 3-finger chord without letting go?
problems.answer: Ease the pressure so the fingers touch but don't press.

problems.prompt: On which of the 4 beats does a chuck usually land in pop strumming?

steps.title: Match the Song's Feel
steps.mastery: Choose a strumming pattern that fits a song's feel, tempo and time signature.
steps.practice: Pick a strum pattern for a 3/4 waltz and one for a 4/4 rock song, and play each for 8 bars.
steps.detail: A pattern has to fit the bar: 3 beats for a waltz, 4 for most pop, and 2 big beats for 6/8. Slow, quiet songs often want simple downstrokes, and upbeat songs want busier 8ths or 16ths. Listen to the original to match it.
steps.proof: 2 patterns, each played for 8 bars and fitting its meter.
steps.pitfall: Using the same busy pattern for every song.

problems.prompt: A song is in 3/4. How many beats per bar should your pattern cover?
Which suits a slow ballad at 60 BPM: busy 16ths or simple downstrokes?
A song in 6/8 feels like how many big beats per bar?

steps.title: Pickups and Picking Spot
steps.mastery: Use the pickup selector and where you pick to change the tone: the neck pickup is warm and the bridge pickup is bright.
steps.practice: Play the same lick on the neck pickup, then the bridge pickup, then picking near the neck and near the bridge, 4 versions in all.
steps.detail: The neck pickup hears the string where it moves most, giving a round, warm sound. The bridge pickup sounds thinner and brighter, and it cuts through a band. Where you pick changes things the same way, even on an acoustic.
steps.proof: 4 versions of the lick, each one sounding different.
steps.pitfall: Leaving the selector in one place forever.

problems.prompt: Of the 2 main pickups, which sounds warmer: neck or bridge?
Does picking within 2 cm of the bridge make the tone brighter or warmer?
A solo needs to cut through a 4-piece band. Which pickup helps?

steps.title: Amp Basics
steps.mastery: Set gain, bass, middle and treble on an amp, starting flat and adjusting by ear.
steps.practice: Set every amp knob to 5, play a chord, then change 1 knob at a time and note what it does.
steps.detail: Gain sets how much distortion you get, and volume sets loudness. The 3 tone knobs cut or boost lows, mids and highs. Starting with everything in the middle and moving one knob at a time teaches you what each one really does.
steps.proof: A note for each knob describing its effect.
steps.pitfall: Turning every knob at once and not knowing which one helped.

problems.prompt: On a 1 to 10 dial, what does the gain knob mainly control?
Your guitar disappears in the band mix. Which 1 knob often helps?
Why start with every knob at 5?
problems.answer: A flat starting point lets you hear what each knob changes.

steps.title: Clean, Crunch and Lead
steps.mastery: Set 3 basic sounds, clean, crunch and lead, and know when each one fits.
steps.practice: Write down 3 amp settings, clean at gain 2, crunch at 5 and lead at 7, and play the same riff through each.
steps.detail: Most songs need one of three sounds. Clean suits strumming, ballads and funk. Crunch, a light distortion, suits rock rhythm. Lead has more gain for sustain on solos. Too much gain turns chords to mud.
steps.proof: 3 settings written down, with the riff played through each.
steps.pitfall: Using full gain for everything.

problems.prompt: Which sound fits a strummed ballad: clean at gain 2 or lead?
Which sound gives solos more sustain, at about gain 7?
Too much gain, like 10, makes chords sound how?

steps.title: Effects That Matter
steps.mastery: Know the few effects most players use, overdrive, delay, reverb and chorus, and what each one does.
steps.practice: Try 4 effects, overdrive, delay, reverb and chorus, on the same 4-bar part, and write 1 word for each sound.
steps.detail: Overdrive adds grit, delay repeats notes like an echo, reverb adds the sound of a room, and chorus makes one guitar sound shimmery and doubled. Most great tones use only a couple of these, set lightly.
steps.proof: 4 effects tried, each with a word describing it.
steps.pitfall: Stacking every effect at once until the guitar disappears.

problems.prompt: Of these 4, which effect repeats your notes like an echo?
Of the same 4, which effect sounds like a big room?
Name 1 effect that adds distortion.

steps.title: Tone Is in the Hands
steps.mastery: Get most of your tone from how you play, pick attack, muting and vibrato, before buying gear.
steps.practice: Play 1 riff 3 ways, soft attack, hard attack and with palm muting, on the same settings, and record all 3.
steps.detail: Two players on the same guitar and amp sound different because of their hands. Attack, muting, vibrato and where you pick shape the sound more than most pedals. Work on those first, then add gear for what's left.
steps.proof: 3 recordings of the same riff that sound clearly different.
steps.pitfall: Buying gear to fix a sound that comes from technique.

problems.prompt: Name 2 things in the hands that shape tone.
You want a better sound. What should you try before buying a $200 pedal?
problems.answer: Change your attack, muting and amp settings.

problems.prompt: Why do 2 players sound different on the same guitar and amp?

steps.title: Standard Tuning
steps.mastery: Know standard tuning, E A D G B E from the thickest string to the thinnest.
steps.practice: Say the 6 open string names from the 6th string to the 1st 5 times, then play each string while naming it.
steps.detail: Standard tuning from the thickest string is E, A, D, G, B, E. Both E strings are E, two octaves apart. A phrase like Eddie Ate Dynamite, Good Bye Eddie helps you remember the order.
steps.proof: E, A, D, G, B, E named correctly 5 times.
steps.pitfall: Mixing up the order of G and B.

problems.prompt: Which note is the 5th string in standard tuning?
Of the 2 E strings, which number is the high one?
Name all 6 open strings from the 6th to the 1st.
problems.answer: E, A, D, G, B, E.

steps.title: Use a Tuner
steps.mastery: Tune with a clip-on or app tuner, bringing each string up to pitch from slightly below.
steps.practice: Detune all 6 strings a little, then tune each one with a clip-on tuner, always tuning up to the note.
steps.detail: Pluck the string, read the note and the needle, and turn the peg until the needle sits in the center. If you go past, drop below and come up again. Tuning up keeps the string from slipping flat as the gear settles.
steps.proof: All 6 strings showing the right note, centered.
steps.pitfall: Tuning the 4th string to C# because the tuner showed the nearest note.

problems.prompt: A tuner shows the 4th string at C#. What note should it be?
Why tune up to the note from 1 note below?
problems.answer: It keeps the string from slipping flat as the gear settles.

problems.prompt: The tuner needle sits 10 cents left of center. Is the string sharp or flat?

steps.title: Tune by Ear With Fret 5
steps.mastery: Tune each string to the one below it by matching the 5th fret, except the B string, which uses the 4th.
steps.practice: Tune the 5th string to the 6th string's 5th fret, and carry on up, using the 4th fret of the G string for B.
steps.detail: Fret the lower string and play it with the next open string, then turn the open one until they match. The G to B pair is the odd one, a 3rd apart instead of a 4th, so use fret 4 there. Errors add up, so recheck from the bottom.
steps.proof: All 6 strings matched to each other by ear.
steps.pitfall: Using the 5th fret for the B string and ending up out of tune.

problems.prompt: Which fret on the 6th string matches the open 5th string?
Which fret on the 3rd string matches the open 2nd string?
You tune by ear and the 1st string ends up off. Which string should you check first?
problems.answer: The 2nd, since each string was tuned from the one before.

steps.title: Hear the Beats
steps.mastery: Hear the wobble, called beats, when 2 strings are close but not matched, and tune until it stops.
steps.practice: Play the 6th string at fret 5 and the open 5th string together, and turn the 5th string's peg slowly until the wobble disappears.
steps.detail: Two pitches that are almost the same make a slow pulsing sound. The pulse rate equals the difference in their frequencies. As you get closer, the wobble slows down, and when it stops, they match.
steps.proof: The wobble slowed and then stopped.
steps.pitfall: Turning the peg fast and missing the point where the wobble stops.

problems.prompt: 2 notes are almost in tune and you hear a slow wobble. What does it mean?
problems.answer: They're slightly apart, and it stops when they match.

problems.prompt: The wobble gets faster as you turn the 5th string's peg. Are you getting closer or farther?
A wobble of 2 per second means the 2 notes differ by how many hertz?

steps.title: Keep It in Tune
steps.mastery: Check the tuning at the start of every session, and after big temperature changes or new strings.
steps.practice: Check your tuning at the start of 5 sessions this week, and note which strings drift the most.
steps.detail: Guitars drift with temperature and humidity, and new strings stretch for several days. A minute of tuning at the start of each session saves you from practicing out of tune, and it trains your ear to notice when something's off.
steps.proof: 5 tuning checks logged, with the drifting strings noted.
steps.pitfall: Practicing out of tune because it was fine yesterday.

problems.prompt: Why do new strings go out of tune for the first 3 days?
Name 1 thing that makes a guitar drift out of tune.
problems.answer: Temperature or humidity changes, or new strings stretching.

problems.prompt: Should you tune before each of your 5 sessions?
problems.answer: Yes. It takes a minute and trains your ear.

steps.title: Tell Primary from Secondary
steps.mastery: Sort sources by how close they are to the events.
steps.practice: Sort 8 sources on the Civil War into primary and secondary.
steps.detail: A primary source comes from the time, like a letter from a soldier. A secondary source looks back, like a historian's book. A source can be both, depending on your question. A 1950s book on Lincoln is a primary source about the 1950s.
steps.proof: 8 sorted sources.
steps.pitfall: Assuming primary means true.

problems.prompt: A letter from a soldier in 1863 is which type?
A 2010 textbook on 1863 is which type?
When might a 1950s biography of Lincoln be primary?
problems.answer: When you're studying how people saw him in the 1950s.

steps.title: Ask Who Wrote It
steps.mastery: Question the source's author, audience and purpose.
steps.practice: Answer 5 questions on a 1776 pamphlet: who, when, for whom, why and what's left out.
steps.detail: Every source was made by someone, for a reason. Ask who wrote it, who they wrote to and what they wanted. Thomas Paine's 'Common Sense' was written to convince, so read it as persuasion, not as a neutral report.
steps.proof: 5 answers.
steps.pitfall: Treating a source as a window onto what happened.

problems.prompt: What did Thomas Paine want from 'Common Sense' in 1776?
problems.answer: To convince colonists to break from Britain.

problems.prompt: Name 3 questions to ask of any letter from 1800.
problems.answer: Who wrote it, for whom and why.

problems.prompt: A general reports a 1812 battle to his king. Name 1 reason to doubt him.

steps.title: Read for What's Missing
steps.mastery: Notice the voices that a source leaves out.
steps.practice: Read a page of a plantation record and write 3 things that enslaved people don't get to say.
steps.detail: Archives keep what the powerful thought was worth keeping. Enslaved people may appear only as numbers in a ledger. Ask who's silent. You can read against the grain, looking for traces of those who didn't get to write the record.
steps.proof: 3 notes.
steps.pitfall: Concluding that people didn't matter since they left little writing.

problems.prompt: A ledger from 1840 lists enslaved people with prices only. Whose voice is missing?
What's 'reading against the grain' in 1 line?
problems.answer: Looking for what a source didn't mean to show.

problems.prompt: Why do fewer letters survive from poor people in 1700?
problems.answer: Fewer could write, and fewer records were kept.

steps.title: Cross-Check Sources
steps.mastery: Compare accounts to work out what probably happened.
steps.practice: Compare 2 accounts of the Boston Massacre of 1770, and list 3 differences.
steps.detail: Two witnesses rarely agree. Colonists called 1770 a massacre, and British soldiers said they were attacked. Compare them, and ask why they differ. What they both agree on is often safest, especially if they have reasons to disagree.
steps.proof: 3 differences.
steps.pitfall: Picking the source you like and ignoring the other.

problems.prompt: Paul Revere's 1770 print shows soldiers firing in a line. Why be careful with it?
problems.answer: It was propaganda against the British.

problems.prompt: 2 opposing sources agree on 1 fact. Why does that help?
problems.answer: Neither has a reason to invent it.

problems.prompt: Who defended the British soldiers at trial in 1770?

steps.title: Quote and Cite a Source
steps.mastery: Use source material in your own writing accurately.
steps.practice: Write 3 sentences using 1 short quote from a 1776 letter, and add a citation.
steps.detail: Say who said it and when. Quote only the words you need. Don't change the meaning by trimming. Say how you know, and give a citation so that someone else can find it. Abigail Adams writing 'Remember the Ladies' works as a short quote.
steps.proof: 3 sentences.
steps.pitfall: Dropping in a long quote with no context.

problems.prompt: Who wrote 'Remember the Ladies' in 1776?
Name 2 details to give when you quote a letter from 1776.
Why shouldn't you cut 'not' from a quote of 10 words?

steps.title: Read an Object
steps.mastery: Use an object as evidence for how people thought.
steps.practice: Pick 1 object from the British Museum's online set and write 5 things it shows.
steps.detail: Objects are sources too. A coin shows who ruled, what they valued and how far trade went. Ask who made it, for whom, and how it was used. 'A History of the World in 100 Objects' is a good example of the idea.
steps.proof: 5 notes.
steps.pitfall: Using objects only as pretty pictures.

problems.prompt: Name 3 things a Roman coin can show.
problems.answer: Who ruled, what they valued and how far trade went.

problems.prompt: Which museum is behind 'A History of the World in 100 Objects'?
Name 1 question to ask about any object from 1500.
problems.answer: Who made it and for whom?

steps.title: Understand Mentalities
steps.mastery: Try to see the past through its own beliefs.
steps.practice: Read about Natalie Zemon Davis's 'The Return of Martin Guerre' and note 3 beliefs of the village.
steps.detail: People in the past didn't think like us. Cultural history asks what made sense to them. Why would a village accept a false husband for years? Natalie Davis asked that of Martin Guerre in 1500s France. Understanding isn't the same as agreeing.
steps.proof: 3 beliefs.
steps.pitfall: Calling people stupid for what they believed.

problems.prompt: Who wrote 'The Return of Martin Guerre' in 1983?
Why try to see witch trials of 1692 from inside their beliefs?
problems.answer: It helps explain why they made sense to people.

problems.prompt: Does understanding a belief mean you agree with it? Answer yes or no.

steps.title: Follow a Book
steps.mastery: Trace how an idea spread through print.
steps.practice: Trace how Luther's 95 Theses of 1517 spread, noting 3 steps.
steps.detail: Ideas need carriers. Luther's theses spread quickly thanks to printing and cheap pamphlets. Ask who read, who heard it read aloud, and who could afford it. Spreading isn't the same as being understood, so check how people used it.
steps.proof: 3 steps.
steps.pitfall: Assuming an idea spread just because it was true.

problems.prompt: In what year did Luther post the 95 Theses?
Which 1450s invention helped them spread?
Many in 1520 couldn't read. How did they hear of Luther?
problems.answer: They heard the pamphlets read aloud.

steps.title: Read Popular Culture
steps.mastery: Use songs, festivals and games as evidence.
steps.practice: Explain 1 festival, such as carnival in Venice in 1600, and what it let people do.
steps.detail: Festivals, songs and games show what people cared about. Carnival let people mock rulers for a few days, then go back to normal. Historians debate if that let off steam or helped change things. Look at who took part, and who disapproved.
steps.proof: 1 paragraph.
steps.pitfall: Thinking culture only means high art.

problems.prompt: What did carnival let ordinary people do in 1600?
problems.answer: Mock their rulers for a few days.

problems.prompt: Name 2 kinds of popular culture a historian of 1800 can use.
What's 1 debate about a festival like this over 400 years?
problems.answer: Whether it let off steam or helped change things.

steps.title: Watch Meanings Shift
steps.mastery: See how a symbol or practice changes over time.
steps.practice: Trace 1 symbol, like the Statue of Liberty from 1886, through 3 changing meanings.
steps.detail: Symbols don't stay still. The Statue of Liberty was meant to honor friendship and freedom, and then became a welcome for immigrants after Emma Lazarus's poem caught on. Ask who was using it and what for at each stage.
steps.proof: 3 meanings.
steps.pitfall: Thinking that a symbol has one true meaning.

problems.prompt: Who wrote the poem on the Statue of Liberty, from 1883?
Which country gave the statue in 1886?
Name 1 way the meaning of a flag can shift over 100 years.
problems.answer: New groups use it for new causes.

steps.title: Use Internal Clues
steps.mastery: Date a document from what's inside it.
steps.practice: Find 3 clues in a sample letter that place it within 10 years.
steps.detail: Documents give themselves away. A letter that mentions a president or a new invention can't be older than that thing. A reference to 'the late war' suggests a date. Look for spelling, handwriting and the shape of the paper, too.
steps.proof: 3 clues.
steps.pitfall: Trusting the date at the top with no other check.

problems.prompt: A letter mentions the telephone. Can it date from 1850? Answer yes or no.
A document dated 1700 mentions a 1750 event. What does that suggest?
What clue does 'the late king' give you for a letter about George III?
problems.answer: It was written after his death in 1820.

steps.title: Know Scientific Dating
steps.mastery: Understand radiocarbon dating and tree rings.
steps.practice: Compute how much carbon-14 remains after 2 half-lives of 5,730 years.
steps.detail: Carbon-14 decays with a half-life of about 5,730 years, which dates things that were once alive. Tree rings count years directly. Each method has limits, such as carbon dating not working on stone, or dates older than about 50,000 years.
steps.proof: 1 worked answer.
steps.pitfall: Thinking radiocarbon dates a stone tool itself.

problems.prompt: After 2 half-lives, what fraction of the carbon-14 remains?
How many years are 2 half-lives of 5,730 years?
Can carbon-14 directly date a 3,000 year old stone tool? Answer yes or no.

steps.title: Spot a Forgery
steps.mastery: Check a document for signs that it's fake.
steps.practice: Read about the 1983 Hitler Diaries and list 3 clues that exposed them.
steps.detail: In 1983, a magazine printed diaries said to be Hitler's. Tests found that the paper and ink were too modern. Good checks look at materials, handwriting and facts. Be most careful when a find is exactly what you hoped for.
steps.proof: 3 clues.
steps.pitfall: Trusting a thrilling find because you want it to be true.

problems.prompt: In what year were the Hitler Diaries exposed?
Name 2 things tests found wrong with the Hitler Diaries.
problems.answer: The paper and the ink were too modern.

problems.prompt: Why be most careful when 1 new find fits your thesis perfectly?
problems.answer: You want it to be true.

steps.title: Date with Layers
steps.mastery: Use layers in the ground to put finds in order.
steps.practice: Draw 4 soil layers and label which is oldest, using coin finds to date 2 of them.
steps.detail: In undisturbed soil, lower layers are older. This is stratigraphy. A coin of 200 CE in a layer means that layer can't be earlier than 200. Pits and animal burrows can mix things up, which is why archaeologists record so carefully.
steps.proof: A labeled drawing.
steps.pitfall: Forgetting that later digging can mix up layers.

problems.prompt: In undisturbed ground, which is older: a lower layer or an upper 1?
A layer holds a coin from 200 CE. Can it be from 100 CE? Answer yes or no.
problems.answer: No, it's from 200 CE or later.

problems.prompt: What's the name for the study of layers, starting with 's'?

steps.title: Weigh Evidence
steps.mastery: Say how sure you are and why.
steps.practice: Write 3 claims about 1 event, each labeled certain, likely or possible.
steps.detail: Historians should say how sure they are. 'Certainly' needs strong proof, and 'perhaps' is honest when there's little to go on. More independent sources mean more confidence. Showing doubt makes your work more believable, not less.
steps.proof: 3 labeled claims.
steps.pitfall: Writing every claim in the same confident tone.

problems.prompt: 3 independent sources agree on a date. Which label fits best: certain or possible?
1 later rumor from 100 years on supports a story. Which label fits: likely or possible?
Why does the phrase 'perhaps' help you in a 5 page essay?

steps.title: Read Prices and Wages
steps.mastery: Use prices to compare living standards over time.
steps.practice: Compute how many hours a worker earning $0.25 an hour in 1910 needed for a $1 item.
steps.detail: An old price means nothing alone. A loaf for 5 cents sounds cheap until you see what people made. Compare price to wage to get hours of work. It's a better measure than nominal dollars, and easy to use.
steps.proof: 1 worked sum.
steps.pitfall: Saying that things were cheap back then because the numbers were small.

problems.prompt: A worker earns $0.25 an hour and a shirt costs $1. How many hours is that?
A loaf is 5 cents and wages are 10 cents an hour. How many minutes of work per loaf?
Why not just compare a price of $1 in 1910 with $1 in 2020?
problems.answer: Money was worth far more then.

steps.title: Follow a Commodity
steps.mastery: Trace how one product linked distant places.
steps.practice: Trace sugar from a Caribbean plantation to a London table in 1750 in 4 steps.
steps.detail: One product can hold a whole world together. Sugar tied enslaved labor in the Caribbean to tea drinkers in London. Sidney Mintz wrote about it in 'Sweetness and Power'. Follow who grew it, who shipped it and who got rich.
steps.proof: 4 steps.
steps.pitfall: Treating trade as just goods with no people behind it.

problems.prompt: Who wrote 'Sweetness and Power' in 1985?
Who worked the sugar plantations of the Caribbean in 1750?
Name 1 other product with a similar story, from 1800 to 1860, in the US South.

steps.title: Explain the Industrial Revolution
steps.mastery: Name causes of early industry in Britain.
steps.practice: List 4 causes for Britain industrializing first by 1800, ranked with reasons.
steps.detail: Why Britain? Cheap coal, high wages that made machines worth building, colonies and banks are all argued. Robert Allen stresses wages and coal, and others stress ideas and institutions. It's still debated, so weigh them.
steps.proof: 4 ranked causes.
steps.pitfall: Naming one cause, like steam, as if that explained it.

problems.prompt: Name 2 things Robert Allen stresses for Britain's early industry.
Who improved the steam engine in the 1760s and 70s?
Is 'steam' alone a full answer for why Britain went first by 1800? Answer yes or no.

steps.title: Read a Crash
steps.mastery: Trace a financial crisis from cause to effect.
steps.practice: Write 5 links in a chain from the 1929 crash to mass unemployment in 1933.
steps.detail: The 1929 crash didn't do it alone. Banks failed, credit dried up, spending fell and factories closed. Bad policy made it worse. Show how each link led to the next, and where another choice might have changed things.
steps.proof: 5 links.
steps.pitfall: Saying the crash of October 1929 caused all of it in one step.

problems.prompt: In which month of 1929 did the US stock market crash?
Name 2 links between the 1929 crash and job losses.
Name the 1930 US tariff often blamed for making things worse.

steps.title: Ask Who Benefits
steps.mastery: Link economic change to who gained and lost.
steps.practice: Make a table of 3 winners and 3 losers from cotton mills in Lancashire in 1830.
steps.detail: Growth isn't shared evenly. Mills brought cheap cloth and big fortunes, along with long hours and child labor. Average numbers hide who paid. Ask who gained and who lost, then and later, as both can be true at once.
steps.proof: A 2 column table.
steps.pitfall: Using a growth number as if it answers everything.

problems.prompt: Name 1 group who gained from Lancashire mills in 1830.
Name 1 group who lost out in the same mills in 1830.
GDP rises 5% but real wages fall for 20 years. What's hidden?

steps.title: Explain Why Empires Grow
steps.mastery: Name motives and tools behind expansion.
steps.practice: List 3 motives and 3 tools for the British in India from 1757 to 1857.
steps.detail: Empires want trade, land and prestige. Tools include guns, ships and local allies. In India, the East India Company was a business with an army. After 1857 the British state took over directly. Ask who gained on both sides.
steps.proof: 6 items.
steps.pitfall: Saying that empires just happened because one side was advanced.

problems.prompt: Which company ruled much of India before 1858?
Name 2 tools of empire in 1800.
Which event of 1857 led to direct British rule?

steps.title: Tell the Encounter from Both Sides
steps.mastery: Compare how both sides saw first contact.
steps.practice: Compare a Spanish account and a Nahua account of Tenochtitlan in 1519.
steps.detail: Spanish writers told a story of conquest. Nahua accounts, like those in the Florentine Codex, tell a different story of fear and politics. Cortes also had thousands of native allies. Reading both complicates the idea of a few men beating an empire.
steps.proof: 2 accounts compared.
steps.pitfall: Reading only the winners' letters.

problems.prompt: Who led the Spanish to Tenochtitlan in 1519?
Name the 1500s work holding Nahua accounts of the conquest.
Why is '600 Spaniards beat the Aztecs' misleading for 1521?
problems.answer: They had thousands of native allies.

steps.title: Weigh Disease
steps.mastery: Assess disease's role in the conquest of the Americas.
steps.practice: Compare 2 estimates of population loss in Mexico from 1519 to 1600.
steps.detail: Smallpox and other diseases killed huge numbers, as people in the Americas had no immunity. Estimates vary widely. Disease mattered, but it doesn't erase violence and forced labor, which made things worse. Be careful with any single number.
steps.proof: 2 estimates.
steps.pitfall: Using disease to explain away what people did.

problems.prompt: Which disease hit Tenochtitlan in 1520?
Mexico's population falls from 20 million to 2 million. What percent was lost?
Why doesn't disease alone explain losses in Mexico by 1600?
problems.answer: Violence and forced labor made it worse.

steps.title: Read Resistance
steps.mastery: See resistance beyond open rebellion.
steps.practice: List 3 forms of resistance in colonial Haiti from 1750 to 1804.
steps.detail: People under empire pushed back in many ways: slow work, running away, keeping up religions and, at times, open war. Haiti's revolution, begun in 1791, ended with independence in 1804. Don't look only for big revolts.
steps.proof: 3 forms.
steps.pitfall: Assuming there was none because the records don't show it.

problems.prompt: In what year did Haiti become independent?
Who led the early Haitian Revolution from 1791?
Name 2 quiet ways enslaved people resisted in 1780.

steps.title: Judge an Empire's Legacy
steps.mastery: Argue about what an empire left behind.
steps.practice: Write 150 words on 2 legacies of British rule in India, 1 lasting harm and 1 mix.
steps.detail: Empires leave behind borders, languages, railways and deep harm. The 1947 partition of India killed perhaps a million people along lines drawn in weeks. Avoid the balance sheet that adds up good and bad. Ask who paid, and who got to decide.
steps.proof: 150 words.
steps.pitfall: Adding up roads against deaths, as if they were on one scale.

problems.prompt: In what year was India partitioned?
About how many people died in partition: about 1 million or about 100?
Why is a 'balance sheet' of 200 years of empire a weak method?
problems.answer: It weighs things that can't be compared.

steps.title: Follow a Trade Route
steps.mastery: Trace how goods and ideas crossed regions.
steps.practice: Map the Silk Road from Xi'an to Constantinople with 5 stops and 3 goods.
steps.detail: Long before modern trade, routes linked Asia, Africa and Europe. The Silk Road carried silk, spices and religion. Few traders went the whole way, as goods moved in short stages. Ideas and disease traveled along them, too.
steps.proof: A map of 5 stops.
steps.pitfall: Picturing one merchant walking the whole road.

problems.prompt: Name 1 city at each end of the Silk Road, around 800.
Name 2 things other than silk that moved along it.
Did most traders go the whole 4,000 mile route? Answer yes or no.
problems.answer: No, goods moved in short stages.

steps.title: Track the Columbian Exchange
steps.mastery: Explain how crops and diseases crossed the Atlantic after 1492.
steps.practice: Make a 2 column list of 4 crops or animals that crossed the Atlantic each way after 1492.
steps.detail: Alfred Crosby named it the Columbian Exchange. Potatoes and maize went to Europe and Asia, and horses and wheat to the Americas. Disease came with it. Potatoes fed Europe's growing population. Imagine Italy before tomatoes, which is a surprise.
steps.proof: 2 columns of 4.
steps.pitfall: Telling 1492 only as a story of Spain.

problems.prompt: Who coined 'Columbian Exchange' in 1972?
Name 2 crops that went from the Americas to Europe after 1492.
Name 2 things that came to the Americas after 1492.

steps.title: Follow Silver
steps.mastery: See how one flow of money linked continents.
steps.practice: Trace silver from Potosi to China in 1600 in 4 steps.
steps.detail: Silver mined at Potosi by forced labor went by ship to Europe and across the Pacific to Manila, then on to China. China's tax system wanted silver. One mountain in Bolivia touched economies on 3 continents, an early global market.
steps.proof: 4 steps.
steps.pitfall: Thinking that global trade only began in recent times.

problems.prompt: Which mine in what's now Bolivia produced huge silver in 1600?
Which Pacific port linked Spanish silver to China?
Why did China want so much silver in 1600?
problems.answer: Its taxes were paid in silver.

steps.title: Write Connected History
steps.mastery: Tell a story across borders.
steps.practice: Rewrite 1 paragraph on the Black Death of 1347 so that it covers 3 regions.
steps.detail: National stories can hide what crosses borders. The Black Death moved from Asia to Europe and North Africa on trade routes. Telling it this way shows links you'd otherwise miss. Connected history asks what moved, and what it changed on arrival.
steps.proof: 1 paragraph.
steps.pitfall: Writing the story of one country and adding a line about others.

problems.prompt: Roughly when did the Black Death reach Europe?
Name 3 regions hit by the Black Death by 1350.
Why does the Black Death fit a story of 3 regions better than 1 country?
problems.answer: It moved along trade routes that crossed borders.

steps.title: Question 'Rise of the West'
steps.mastery: Test big claims about why Europe got rich.
steps.practice: Summarize Kenneth Pomeranz's 'The Great Divergence' in 4 lines.
steps.detail: Why did Europe pull ahead? Kenneth Pomeranz said parts of China and England looked alike until about 1800. Coal and colonies made the gap. Others point to institutions and culture. Avoid telling a story in which Europe's win was always coming.
steps.proof: 4 lines.
steps.pitfall: Assuming that today's wealth gap has always been there.

problems.prompt: Who wrote 'The Great Divergence' in 2000?
Until about what year did he say parts of China matched England?
Name 2 factors he stresses for England's lead after 1800.

steps.title: Separate History from Memory
steps.mastery: Tell how the past is remembered from what happened.
steps.practice: Compare a textbook and a family story about 1 event from 1945.
steps.detail: Memory is how people keep the past alive, and it serves the present. History tries to check it against evidence. They shape each other. A family's story of a war may leave out what's painful. Neither is pure, so ask what each one is doing.
steps.proof: 1 comparison.
steps.pitfall: Treating all memory as false and all history as true.

problems.prompt: Name 1 thing a family story of 1945 might leave out.
Does a history book get it right every time? Answer yes or no.
problems.answer: No, it has its own biases too.

problems.prompt: Name 1 thing memory does for a nation after a war, in 1 line.
problems.answer: It gives people a shared story.

steps.title: Read a Monument
steps.mastery: Ask what a statue says about the people who built it.
steps.practice: Look up 1 Confederate statue, note when it was built, and say what this reveals.
steps.detail: Monuments tell you about when they were built. Many Confederate statues went up around 1910, decades after the war, at the height of Jim Crow. They say more about 1910 than 1865. Ask who paid for it, and who was absent.
steps.proof: 1 note.
steps.pitfall: Saying that a statue is simply history itself.

problems.prompt: Many Confederate statues went up decades after 1865. What was happening around 1910?
Name 2 questions to ask about a statue built in 1910.
problems.answer: Who paid for it and who's left out.

problems.prompt: A statue shows a general. What does it mostly say about?
problems.answer: The people who built it, and when.

steps.title: Compare National Memories
steps.mastery: See how countries remember the same event differently.
steps.practice: Compare how Japanese and Chinese school texts treat 1937 in Nanjing, using 2 secondary sources.
steps.detail: The Nanjing Massacre of 1937 is remembered very differently in China and Japan, and it still affects politics today. Germany's approach to its past, with memorials to the victims, is often compared with others. Ask what each country needs to remember.
steps.proof: 2 sources.
steps.pitfall: Treating one nation's memory as simply correct.

problems.prompt: Which city's 1937 massacre is a major dispute between China and Japan?
Name 1 way Germany remembers the victims of 1933 to 1945.
Why might 2 countries' school books differ about 1937?
problems.answer: Each country has its own needs and politics.

steps.title: Study Forgetting
steps.mastery: Notice what a society chooses to forget.
steps.practice: Read about the Tulsa massacre of 1921 and write why it was left out for decades.
steps.detail: What's left out tells you a lot. The Tulsa massacre of 1921 was largely missing from school books for decades. Forgetting can be active. People change records, or avoid speaking of it. Ask who gains from the silence, and what brought it back.
steps.proof: 1 paragraph.
steps.pitfall: Assuming what isn't remembered didn't matter.

problems.prompt: In what year was the Tulsa massacre?
Name 1 thing that made Tulsa fall out of public memory.
problems.answer: It was left out of school books.

problems.prompt: Which 2019 TV series brought Tulsa to wide attention?

steps.title: Handle Living Memory
steps.mastery: Work carefully with memories of recent events.
steps.practice: Interview 1 person about a past event and compare 1 detail with a 1 newspaper from the time.
steps.detail: People remember what mattered, not always what happened. Details shift over time, as they retell it. That doesn't make them liars. Memory also shows how they've come to understand it. Cross-check facts, and treat the rest with respect.
steps.proof: 1 note on 1 detail.
steps.pitfall: Correcting elderly people's memories in the interview.

problems.prompt: A person's date for a 1969 event is off by 2 years. Does that make them a liar? Answer yes or no.
Name 1 source to cross-check a memory of 1969.
What can a wrong detail in a story from 1969 still tell you?
problems.answer: How they've come to understand it.

steps.title: Know the Schools
steps.mastery: Name major ways of writing history.
steps.practice: Write 1 line each on Ranke, the Annales, Marxist history and social history.
steps.detail: History changes as a field. Leopold von Ranke wanted to write it as it really was, from archives. The French Annales school looked at long time spans and climates. Marxists looked at class, and later, others looked at gender and culture.
steps.proof: 4 lines.
steps.pitfall: Thinking history is only facts, with no theories behind it.

problems.prompt: Who said to show the past 'as it really was', in the 1800s?
Name the French school founded in 1929, known for long time spans.
Who wrote 'The Making of the English Working Class' in 1963?

steps.title: Read a Debate
steps.mastery: Follow how historians argued over one question.
steps.practice: Summarize 3 views on the causes of the US Civil War of 1861 in 1 line each.
steps.detail: Historians argue. On the Civil War, the Lost Cause myth denied slavery was the reason, and later writers said economics. Today most stress slavery, and the secession papers say so. Who wrote what, and when, shapes the view.
steps.proof: 3 lines.
steps.pitfall: Treating the newest view as simply true.

problems.prompt: Which factor do most historians now stress for the war of 1861?
What's the name of the myth that denied that slavery was the cause, in 2 words?
Name 1 primary source against that myth, from 1860 and 1861.

steps.title: Spot Bias in a Historian
steps.mastery: Read a historian's work in its own time.
steps.practice: Find 2 assumptions in 1 history written in 1900 and say why they fit that time.
steps.detail: Historians are shaped by when and where they write. A British history from 1900 may take empire for granted. Writing in the Cold War shaped how Russia got described. Bias isn't only a flaw, as we've got our own. Say what yours might be.
steps.proof: 2 assumptions.
steps.pitfall: Thinking that only old historians have bias.

problems.prompt: A British book from 1900 praises empire throughout. What might it assume?
problems.answer: That empire is a good thing.

problems.prompt: How might the Cold War of 1950 shape a book on Russia?
problems.answer: It might push a hostile view.

problems.prompt: Do you have biases writing in 2026? Answer yes or no.

steps.title: Think Counterfactually
steps.mastery: Use 'what if' carefully to test claims of cause.
steps.practice: Answer in 100 words: what if Franz Ferdinand's car hadn't stalled in 1914?
steps.detail: Counterfactuals test how important a cause really is. If removing it changes nothing, it wasn't key. Stay close to what was possible, and don't go further than one step. Some historians dislike them, but careful ones can be useful.
steps.proof: 100 words.
steps.pitfall: Spinning a fantasy with a long chain of guesses.

problems.prompt: What's a 'what if' claim about history called?
You remove a cause and the outcome of 1914 stays the same. What does this suggest?
Why not go 10 steps past 1 change in a 'what if'?

steps.title: Say What You're Doing
steps.mastery: Explain your own approach as a historian.
steps.practice: Write 150 words saying which approach you're using on 1 topic, and why.
steps.detail: Being clear about your method helps your reader judge you. Say what sources you've used, what they miss, and what you're assuming. There's no neutral view. That doesn't mean that anything goes: evidence still decides, and some claims are wrong.
steps.proof: 150 words.
steps.pitfall: Using 'all history is opinion' as an excuse for sloppy work.

problems.prompt: Name 3 things to state about your method in a 10 page paper.
problems.answer: Your sources, what they miss and what you assume.

problems.prompt: Is 'it's all just opinion' a fair view of the Holocaust's facts? Answer yes or no.
problems.answer: No, evidence decides, and some claims are false.

problems.prompt: Why state what your sources miss in 1 line?
problems.answer: Readers can judge how far to trust you.

steps.title: Choose a Beginning
steps.mastery: Pick a start that frames the story.
steps.practice: Write 2 openings for a history of the French Revolution, in 1789 and in 1774.
steps.detail: Where you start is an argument. Starting a revolution with the storming of the Bastille stresses the crowd. Starting with debts from earlier wars stresses money. Each one makes other things look natural. Ask what your start assumes.
steps.proof: 2 openings.
steps.pitfall: Starting with the beginning of time because everything matters.

problems.prompt: Name 1 event of 14 July 1789.
What does starting a story of 1789 with royal debts stress?
Why is it a problem to start a 5 page essay on 1789 with ancient Rome?
problems.answer: It's too far back to help.

steps.title: Build from Causes
steps.mastery: Connect events so that the story explains, and doesn't just list.
steps.practice: Rewrite 5 lines with 'and then' from a list of events using 'so' or 'because'.
steps.detail: A chronicle says this happened, then that. A narrative says this happened, so that followed. E.M. Forster's example: 'The king died and then the queen died' lists. 'The queen died of grief' tells a story. Show the link.
steps.proof: 5 linked lines.
steps.pitfall: Writing one thing after another with no reasons.

problems.prompt: Rewrite in 1 line with a link: 'Prices rose in 1789. People rioted.'
problems.answer: Prices rose in 1789, so people rioted.

problems.prompt: Who gave the 'king died' example, in a book from 1927?
Which explains more: 'and then' or 'because' in a 1 page story?

steps.title: Zoom In and Out
steps.mastery: Mix big trends and a single person's life.
steps.practice: Write 3 sentences on the Great Depression: 1 big number, 1 town and 1 person.
steps.detail: Strong history moves between scales. A national number says what happened at large, while one farmer's letter makes you feel it. Use a person to show the trend, but don't let one story stand in for all of it without saying so.
steps.proof: 3 sentences.
steps.pitfall: Staying so high that no real people appear.

problems.prompt: What share of US workers were out of work in 1933: about 25% or 75%?
Why pair a figure like 25% with a single farmer's letter from 1933?
problems.answer: The person lets you feel the number.

problems.prompt: Name 1 risk of telling 1933 through 1 family alone.
problems.answer: One family may not stand for everyone.

steps.title: Avoid Hindsight
steps.mastery: Write as if the outcome wasn't yet known.
steps.practice: List 3 choices that people faced in June 1914, without assuming the war that followed.
steps.detail: We know how it ended, but they didn't. In summer 1914 many people expected a short crisis. Writing as if the end was fated hides real choices. Ask what looked possible then, and write with that uncertainty in mind.
steps.proof: 3 choices.
steps.pitfall: Saying it was inevitable because it happened.

problems.prompt: In August 1914, many expected the war to be over by when?
What's the mistake called when you assume people then knew what we know, in 1 word?
Why not say that World War 2 was 'inevitable' in 1919?
problems.answer: It hides real choices made later.

steps.title: End with a Point
steps.mastery: Close a narrative with a claim and not just a stop.
steps.practice: Write 2 endings for a 500 word story of the Berlin Wall, 1 that stops and 1 that argues.
steps.detail: A good ending says why it all mattered. Don't just say 'the Wall fell in 1989'. Say what that changed, and what it didn't. Stories don't really end, so your ending is a choice, and it's your final argument.
steps.proof: 2 endings.
steps.pitfall: Ending with 'and that was how it happened'.

problems.prompt: In what year did the Berlin Wall fall?
Rewrite 'and so the Wall fell in 1989' to make a point, in 1 line.
problems.answer: The Wall fell in 1989, but the split between East and West lasted for decades.

problems.prompt: Why is an ending a choice in a 500 word story?
problems.answer: The past goes on, so you choose where to stop and why.

steps.title: Plan an Interview
steps.mastery: Prepare research and questions before speaking with someone.
steps.practice: Write 10 open questions for a person who lived through 1 event in 1970.
steps.detail: Oral history gets at what written records miss. Do your homework on the event first. Write open questions starting with 'tell me about'. Start with easy parts of life, and let them talk. Your list is a guide, and not a script.
steps.proof: 10 questions.
steps.pitfall: Asking only yes or no questions.

problems.prompt: Make this open: 'Was 1970 hard for you?'
problems.answer: Tell me about what 1970 was like for you.

problems.prompt: Why start with easy questions about childhood in a 1 hour talk?
Name 1 thing to read up on before you talk about 1970.
problems.answer: The main events of that time.

steps.title: Get Consent
steps.mastery: Treat the person as a partner in the record.
steps.practice: Write a 1 page consent form covering use, storage and the right to withdraw.
steps.detail: People should know how their words will be used and where they'll be kept. Let them read the transcript and take things back. Be careful with trauma, and let them stop. It's their life. The Oral History Association has good guidelines.
steps.proof: 1 form.
steps.pitfall: Publishing a story someone told you in confidence.

problems.prompt: Name the US group with guidelines for oral history, founded in 1966.
Name 2 things a consent form should cover.
problems.answer: How it's used and where it's kept.

problems.prompt: A person cries during a hard part of their story. Name 1 thing to do in 1 moment.
problems.answer: Offer a break, and let them decide.

steps.title: Record Well
steps.mastery: Get a usable audio or video record.
steps.practice: Record 5 minutes in 1 quiet room and listen back on headphones for noise.
steps.detail: Sound quality decides if anyone can use it later. Pick a quiet room and put the mic close. Test first, as you can't redo a life story. Note the date, place and who's there at the start. Keep copies in 2 places.
steps.proof: A 5 minute test.
steps.pitfall: Assuming the phone in the middle of the table will do.

problems.prompt: Name 3 things to say at the start of a recording.
problems.answer: The date, the place and who's there.

problems.prompt: Why keep copies in 2 places?
A fridge hums in a 5 minute test. Name 1 fix.
problems.answer: Switch it off, or move rooms.

steps.title: Listen and Follow
steps.mastery: Let the person's story lead you.
steps.practice: Practice with a friend for 10 minutes, asking only follow-ups to what they've just said.
steps.detail: Your best question comes from what they've just said. 'What did you mean by...?' Hold back your own stories. Silence gives them room to think. Notice what's skipped, and come back later with care. Avoid correcting people as they talk.
steps.proof: A 10 minute practice.
steps.pitfall: Sticking to your list while they try to tell you something else.

problems.prompt: They mention 'the bad winter' in passing. What's a good follow-up in 1 line?
Why stay silent for 5 seconds after an answer?
problems.answer: It gives them time to think and go on.

problems.prompt: A person gets a 1962 date wrong. Should you correct them during the talk? Answer yes or no.
problems.answer: No, note it and check later.

steps.title: Use What You Recorded
steps.mastery: Transcribe and quote oral sources carefully.
steps.practice: Transcribe 5 minutes of a recording and note where you trimmed anything.
steps.detail: Transcribe accurately, and mark what you've cut. Don't tidy up someone's words so that they sound like you. Use memories with other sources, and say what it is: one person's view, told years later. Give it back to them or their family.
steps.proof: 5 minutes of text.
steps.pitfall: Treating a single interview as a proof of what happened.

problems.prompt: About how long does it take to transcribe 1 hour of talk: 4 hours or 10 minutes?
You trim 1 line from a quote. How should you mark it?
Why not use 1 interview alone to prove what happened in 1962?
problems.answer: It's one person's view, told years later.

steps.title: Learn the Big Labels
steps.mastery: Know common period names and rough dates.
steps.practice: Fill in rough dates for 5 periods, from Antiquity to Early Modern.
steps.detail: Period names are shortcuts. In Europe, Antiquity runs to around 500, then the Middle Ages to about 1500, then Early Modern to about 1800. They give you a map, but dates vary and they don't work the same way everywhere.
steps.proof: 5 periods with dates.
steps.pitfall: Treating these as exact dates when people lived through them.

problems.prompt: Roughly when do the European Middle Ages end: 1500 or 1800?
Did people in 1200 call themselves 'medieval'? Answer yes or no.
Which of 2 periods comes first: Early Modern or Middle Ages?

steps.title: Ask Who Named It
steps.mastery: See how a label carries a judgment.
steps.practice: Look up who coined 'Dark Ages' and 'Renaissance' and write 1 line on what each one implies.
steps.detail: Labels are arguments. 'Dark Ages' was coined by people who thought their own time was bright. 'Renaissance' means rebirth, and suggests that what came before was dead. Medieval people would have been surprised by both.
steps.proof: 2 lines.
steps.pitfall: Using 'Dark Ages' as if it were a plain fact.

problems.prompt: What does 'Renaissance' mean in 1 word?
What does 'Dark Ages' suggest about the time from 500 to 1000?
Who first called those centuries dark, the people then or writers like Petrarch later?

steps.title: Fit Periods to Places
steps.mastery: See where a European label doesn't work elsewhere.
steps.practice: List 3 events from China from 960 to 1279 and explain why 'medieval' fits badly.
steps.detail: 'Medieval' means middle, between Rome and the Renaissance, which only makes sense in Europe. Song China had printing and paper money in those centuries. Other places have their own schemes, like dynasties. Use local periods first.
steps.proof: 3 events with a note.
steps.pitfall: Calling Song China 'medieval' as if it had the same history as France.

problems.prompt: Which Chinese dynasty ran from 960 to 1279?
Name 2 things Song China used before most of Europe.
Why does 'medieval' fit badly in Japan in 1200?
problems.answer: It's named for a European gap between Rome and the Renaissance.

steps.title: Find the Turning Points
steps.mastery: Argue where one period ends and another begins.
steps.practice: Give 2 possible start dates for the modern era and defend 1 in 100 words.
steps.detail: There's rarely a clean break. The modern era might start with 1492, 1789 or the steam engine, and each choice stresses something different. Picking a date is really picking what you think matters most. Say why.
steps.proof: 100 words.
steps.pitfall: Acting like one date is simply the right one.

problems.prompt: Name 2 possible start dates for modern history.
Choosing 1789 as a start stresses what kind of change?
Choosing the 1780s steam engine stresses what kind of change?

steps.title: Use Labels with Care
steps.mastery: Write sentences that use period labels precisely.
steps.practice: Rewrite 3 sentences that use 'medieval' as an insult, using dates and places.
steps.detail: 'That's so medieval' is a slur on a thousand years. Be specific: say 'in 12th century France'. Keep labels when they help, and add dates when they might mislead. Your reader will trust you more if you're precise.
steps.proof: 3 rewritten sentences.
steps.pitfall: Using a period name as a stand-in for bad or backward.

problems.prompt: Rewrite 'medieval people thought the earth was flat' in 1 line with care.
problems.answer: Most educated people in 12th century Europe knew the earth was round.

problems.prompt: Why add '12th century France' to a claim about 'medieval' life?
problems.answer: A thousand years and many places differ.

problems.prompt: Is 'medieval' a fair insult for a modern law from 2020? Answer yes or no.
problems.answer: No, it uses a period as a slur.

steps.title: Map Who Holds Power
steps.mastery: Work out who makes decisions in a given system.
steps.practice: Draw the power structure of 1 system, such as Rome in 50 BCE, with 4 boxes.
steps.detail: Political history asks who decides, and how. Rome in 50 BCE had consuls, a Senate and assemblies, with generals getting too strong. Official titles and real power may differ. Follow who controls money and soldiers.
steps.proof: A chart of 4 boxes.
steps.pitfall: Reading only the official rules and missing where power really lies.

problems.prompt: Which body advised consuls in Rome in 50 BCE?
Name 2 things to follow to find real power in 1 state.
Rome's Senate looked strong in 50 BCE. Who actually held the soldiers?

steps.title: Trace How Rule Changes
steps.mastery: Explain how power moves between groups.
steps.practice: Write 5 steps in how England's Parliament gained power from 1215 to 1689.
steps.detail: Power shifts in steps. The Magna Carta of 1215 limited a king. Civil war and the 1689 Bill of Rights moved power toward Parliament. Look for the moments when rulers needed money or soldiers, since that's when they gave things up.
steps.proof: 5 steps.
steps.pitfall: Thinking democracy simply grew because people became enlightened.

problems.prompt: In what year was the Magna Carta sealed?
Which 1689 act moved power toward England's Parliament?
Why did kings in the 1600s need Parliament so much?

steps.title: Read Political Language
steps.mastery: See how words like 'liberty' have changed.
steps.practice: Find 'liberty' in 2 texts from 1776 and 1860 and write how the meaning differs.
steps.detail: Words change over time. 'Liberty' in 1776 could sit beside slavery in the same mouth. By 1860 it was what both sides claimed. Don't assume a word meant then what it means now. Ask what it did for those who were using it.
steps.proof: 2 uses compared.
steps.pitfall: Reading old words with their modern meanings.

problems.prompt: Both the North and South claimed which word in 1860?
Why be careful with 'democracy' in a text from 400 BCE?
Who said 'all men are created equal' in 1776 and also owned slaves?

steps.title: Follow Elections and Crowds
steps.mastery: Compare formal politics with protest and pressure.
steps.practice: Name 3 ways people without the vote pressured rulers in Britain before 1832.
steps.detail: Those without a vote aren't powerless. Petitions, riots and boycotts all put pressure on rulers. Before Britain's 1832 Reform Act, few men could vote. Crowds still mattered. Look for politics outside the official room.
steps.proof: 3 ways.
steps.pitfall: Thinking politics only happens among voters and leaders.

problems.prompt: Which British act of 1832 widened the vote?
Name 2 ways people without the vote applied pressure in 1820.
What was the 1819 attack on a crowd in Manchester called?

steps.title: Judge a Leader
steps.mastery: Weigh a leader's role against the larger forces around them.
steps.practice: Write 150 words on whether Napoleon made events or events made Napoleon.
steps.detail: Did a leader cause the change, or did the times make the leader? Thomas Carlyle stressed great men, and others stress wider forces. Napoleon was gifted, but the Revolution opened that door. Say which is which, using evidence.
steps.proof: 150 words.
steps.pitfall: Giving all the credit or blame to one person.

problems.prompt: Who wrote about 'great men' in 1841?
Which event opened the door for a poor Corsican soldier in 1790?
Name 1 risk of explaining all of 1933 to 1945 through Hitler alone.
problems.answer: It hides the many people who helped and went along.

steps.title: Read a Museum
steps.mastery: See how a museum makes an argument.
steps.practice: Visit 1 museum or website and write 3 choices the curators made.
steps.detail: A museum isn't neutral. Someone chose what's shown and what to say in 50 words on a label. Ask what's missing, whose voice it is, and what you're supposed to feel. Follow where the objects came from, as some were taken.
steps.proof: 3 choices.
steps.pitfall: Thinking an exhibit simply presents the facts.

problems.prompt: Roughly how many words should a museum label use: 50 or 500?
Name 1 question to ask about objects in a British museum.
Which Greek marbles in London are in a long dispute with Greece?

steps.title: Write for Non-Experts
steps.mastery: Explain history clearly without talking down.
steps.practice: Rewrite 1 academic paragraph of 150 words into 50 words for a museum label.
steps.detail: Most people will spend a few seconds on your work. Lead with what's interesting. Use short sentences and everyday words, and connect to something they know. You can still be honest about doubt. A sign doesn't need jargon to be correct.
steps.proof: 50 words.
steps.pitfall: Cutting nuance so far that it's no longer true.

problems.prompt: You have 50 words for a sign. What goes first?
Rewrite 'socio-economic stratification' in 2 or 3 plain words.
Can you still show doubt in 50 words? Answer yes or no.
problems.answer: Yes, 'we think' or 'probably' will do it.

steps.title: Work with Communities
steps.mastery: Share authority with those whose history it is.
steps.practice: List 3 ways to include a neighborhood in a project about it, in a 1 page plan.
steps.detail: Those whose past you're telling should have a say. Ask them first, and share the decisions, not just the credit. Native groups in the US gained rights to ask for ancestors' remains under a 1990 law. Listen before you plan.
steps.proof: 1 plan.
steps.pitfall: Showing up with your finished project and asking people for a nod.

problems.prompt: Name the 1990 US law on returning Native American remains.
Name 1 way to include a neighborhood before you start a project in 2026.
problems.answer: Ask them what story they want told.

problems.prompt: Is thanking people in a footnote the same as sharing decisions? Answer yes or no.
problems.answer: No, they should have a say.

steps.title: Tell Hard Histories
steps.mastery: Present painful pasts without shock or comfort.
steps.practice: Pick 1 slavery site tour from 2 sites and write how each frames the past.
steps.detail: Some sites gloss over slavery with stories of pretty gowns. Others, like the Whitney Plantation, center the enslaved. Tell the truth, and think about who's in the room. People may be descended from those involved. Avoid horror for its own sake.
steps.proof: 2 frames.
steps.pitfall: Leaving out the hard parts to keep visitors comfortable.

problems.prompt: Which Louisiana site centers enslaved people in its tours?
A tour talks about gowns for 60 minutes and leaves out slavery. What's the problem?
problems.answer: It hides the people who made that wealth.

problems.prompt: Why think about who's in the room on a tour of 20 people?
problems.answer: Some may be descended from those involved.

steps.title: Reach People Online
steps.mastery: Use podcasts and social media without losing accuracy.
steps.practice: Plan a 5 minute podcast from 1 source, with 3 points and links to the evidence.
steps.detail: People get a lot of history online, often with wrong claims. Try a short, honest format. Link your sources. Correct what you get wrong in public. You don't need to go viral, and one person's trust is worth more than a big, false hit.
steps.proof: A plan with 3 points.
steps.pitfall: Dropping the sources to make it punchier.

problems.prompt: A viral post says Vikings wore horned helmets, from 1 opera in 1876. What's the truth?
problems.answer: There's no good evidence they wore them.

problems.prompt: You got 1 date wrong in a podcast. Name 1 honest fix.
Name 1 thing to add to a 5 minute podcast's notes.

steps.title: Read a Historical Table
steps.mastery: Find trends in population and price data.
steps.practice: Compute growth from 1 million to 3 million between 1800 and 1900 as a percent.
steps.detail: Numbers let you see what no diary could show. Learn to compute a percent change and a rate. Check what the table covers and who collected it. England's population roughly tripled in the 1800s, and that's a huge thing to grasp.
steps.proof: 1 worked answer.
steps.pitfall: Assuming a table is neutral because it's numbers.

problems.prompt: Population goes from 1 million to 3 million. What's the percent increase?
A price falls from 20 to 15. What's the percent drop?
A census of 1850 didn't count enslaved people by name. Name the risk.

steps.title: Average with Care
steps.mastery: Use means and medians for skewed historical data.
steps.practice: Compute the mean and median of wages 10, 10, 12, 14 and 100.
steps.detail: A few rich people can pull up an average. The median is often closer to a typical life. Life expectancy of 40 in 1800 doesn't mean that people died at 40. It was mostly pulled down by many deaths of children.
steps.proof: 2 worked answers.
steps.pitfall: Reading a low life expectancy as everyone dying young.

problems.prompt: Wages are 10, 10, 12, 14 and 100. What's the mean?
Which middle value would you report for 5 sorted wages topped by 100, with 12 in the center?
Life expectancy is 40 in 1800. Did most adults die at 40? Answer yes or no.
problems.answer: No, many deaths of children pull it down.

steps.title: Adjust for Inflation
steps.mastery: Compare money across time using a price index.
steps.practice: Convert $10 in 1913 to 2013 dollars using an index going from 10 to 233.
steps.detail: A dollar's value changes. Divide the later index by the earlier one, and multiply. With an index of 10 in 1913 and 233 in 2013, $10 is worth $233. Say which index you've used, as there's more than one way to do this.
steps.proof: 1 worked answer.
steps.pitfall: Comparing wages from different years with no adjustment.

problems.prompt: Index 10 in 1913 and 233 in 2013. What's $10 from 1913 in 2013 dollars?
Index goes from 50 to 100. What's $20 worth in later dollars?
A wage goes from $5 to $10 while prices triple. Did real pay rise? Answer yes or no.

steps.title: Build a Small Dataset
steps.mastery: Turn records into rows you can count.
steps.practice: Enter 20 rows from a ship's list into a spreadsheet with 5 columns.
steps.detail: Quantitative history often starts by typing. Take a passenger list or a parish book, and turn it into rows and columns. Decide on your rules first. Note what's missing, rather than guessing. A little table can answer questions a big one doesn't ask.
steps.proof: 20 rows.
steps.pitfall: Making up values for the gaps, so you can get a tidy table.

problems.prompt: A list has 20 people and 5 columns. How many cells is that?
3 ages are missing in a list of 20. What should you do?
Name 1 kind of record from 1850 to turn into a table.

steps.title: Link Numbers to Claims
steps.mastery: Use numbers honestly in a historical argument.
steps.practice: Write 2 sentences using 1 number from a table for a claim about 1900, and give its source.
steps.detail: A number supports a claim, but doesn't make one. Say what's being counted, for where and for when, and how solid it is. Be careful with small samples. Fogel and Engerman's 'Time on the Cross' from 1974 shows how numbers can provoke big fights.
steps.proof: 2 sentences.
steps.pitfall: Quoting a number without saying where it's from.

problems.prompt: Who wrote 'Time on the Cross' in 1974?
A sample of 10 people out of 100,000 is used for a claim. What's the risk?
problems.answer: It may not stand for the rest.

problems.prompt: Name 3 things to say about a number from 1900.
problems.answer: What it counts, where and when.

steps.title: Frame a Question
steps.mastery: Turn a broad interest into a question you can answer.
steps.practice: Narrow 'World War 2' to 1 question in 3 steps, with a place and years.
steps.detail: Good research starts small. 'World War 2' is too big. 'How did rationing change meals in Leeds from 1940 to 1945?' can be answered, and it may surprise you. Ask how or why, not just what. Check that sources exist first.
steps.proof: 1 question.
steps.pitfall: Picking a topic so huge that you can only summarize.

problems.prompt: Narrow 'the Roman Empire' to 1 question, in under 15 words.
problems.answer: How did the grain supply feed Rome from 50 to 150?

problems.prompt: Why ask 'how' or 'why' over 'what' in a 20 page paper?
problems.answer: It gets you an argument and not just a summary.

problems.prompt: Name 1 check to do before you pick a question for 3 months' work.

steps.title: Work in an Archive
steps.mastery: Find and record primary sources methodically.
steps.practice: Plan 1 day at an archive, listing 5 boxes and how you'll note each item.
steps.detail: Archives have rules, so read them ahead of time. Use finding aids. Photograph where it's allowed. Note the exact location of each item, or you'll never find it again. Plan a day, since you won't get through as much as you'd hope.
steps.proof: A plan of 5 boxes.
steps.pitfall: Taking notes with no box number, then losing the source.

problems.prompt: What's the guide to an archive's holdings called, in 2 words?
Name 3 details to write for each item in 1 box.
problems.answer: The archive, box number and date.

problems.prompt: Why plan for 5 boxes in 1 day over 50?
problems.answer: You'll go slower than you hope.

steps.title: Organize Your Notes
steps.mastery: Keep sources and ideas searchable.
steps.practice: Set up Zotero with 10 sources and 3 tags for your project.
steps.detail: You'll have hundreds of notes soon. Zotero or a simple spreadsheet will save you months. Keep what a source said apart from what you think of it. Note the page numbers now. Back up, as a stolen laptop has ended many projects.
steps.proof: 10 sources and 3 tags.
steps.pitfall: Copying quotes with no page numbers.

problems.prompt: Name 1 free tool for keeping track of 200 sources.
Why keep what 1 source says apart from your view of it, in your notes?
problems.answer: So you don't mix the two later.

problems.prompt: You've lost a page number for a 1 line quote. What's it cost you?
problems.answer: A trip back, or dropping the quote.

steps.title: Write the Argument
steps.mastery: Move from notes to a draft that makes a claim.
steps.practice: Write a 1 page argument summary before drafting your 20 page paper.
steps.detail: Don't wait until you've read it all. Write early, to find out what you think and what's missing. Say your claim on one page, then build. Each section needs a job. Use sources as evidence for your points, instead of walking through them one by one.
steps.proof: 1 page.
steps.pitfall: Writing up everything you found, in the order you found it.

problems.prompt: When should you start writing, after 1 week or after reading it all?
Why summarize your argument on 1 page before you draft 20 pages?
problems.answer: It shows you the claim and the gaps.

problems.prompt: Why not go source by source in a 20 page paper?
problems.answer: It reads like a list and not an argument.

steps.title: Share and Respond
steps.mastery: Present your work and use feedback.
steps.practice: Give a 10 minute talk on your research to 3 people and write down 3 objections.
steps.detail: A paper gets stronger when others poke at it. Present early. Listen to objections and don't rush to answer. Ask a historian who works near your topic to read it. Then revise, and publish or post it, as research that nobody sees helps no one.
steps.proof: 3 objections.
steps.pitfall: Hiding your work until it's perfect.

problems.prompt: Name 1 good way to test a paper of 20 pages before finishing it.
problems.answer: Give a short talk on it.

problems.prompt: You get 3 objections you hadn't thought of. What should you do?
problems.answer: Write them down and deal with them.

problems.prompt: Why not wait until the work of 2 years is perfect to share it?
problems.answer: It never will be, and feedback comes too late.

steps.title: Name the Preconditions
steps.mastery: List long-term tensions before a revolution.
steps.practice: List 4 long-term causes of the French Revolution by 1789.
steps.detail: Revolutions don't come from nowhere. France by 1789 had huge debts, bad harvests, an unfair tax system and new ideas. Long-term causes set the stage. A short-term trigger, like calling the Estates-General, sets it off.
steps.proof: 4 causes.
steps.pitfall: Mixing up the spark with the fuel.

problems.prompt: Name 2 long-term causes of the French Revolution.
problems.answer: Debt and an unfair tax system.

problems.prompt: Which meeting was called in May 1789?
Is a bad harvest in 1788 a long-term cause or a trigger?

steps.title: Track the Stages
steps.mastery: Follow how a revolution moves through phases.
steps.practice: Chart the French Revolution from 1789 to 1799 in 5 phases.
steps.detail: Crane Brinton noted a pattern: moderates, then radicals, then terror, then a reaction. France went from reform in 1789 to the Terror in 1793 and then to Napoleon in 1799. Test whether the pattern fits other revolutions, too.
steps.proof: A chart of 5.
steps.pitfall: Thinking that revolutions always go in one straight line.

problems.prompt: Who wrote 'The Anatomy of Revolution' in 1938?
In which year did the Terror begin in France, roughly?
Who took power in France in 1799?

steps.title: Compare Two Revolutions
steps.mastery: Compare revolutions and say what differs.
steps.practice: Make a 2 column table for the American Revolution of 1776 and the Russian of 1917.
steps.detail: Comparing makes each clearer. The US revolt was mostly about self-rule by elites. Russia in 1917 tore up class and land, and happened during a world war. Ask what each wanted to change, and who led.
steps.proof: A table of 5 rows.
steps.pitfall: Treating them all as one kind of thing.

problems.prompt: Name the party that took power in Russia in October 1917.
Which world war was going on during the Russian Revolution of 1917?
Name 1 big difference between 1776 and 1917.
problems.answer: Russia tore up land and class, and the US mostly kept them.

steps.title: Ask Who's Included
steps.mastery: See who a revolution's promises left out.
steps.practice: Read 'The Rights of Woman' by Olympe de Gouges from 1791 and write 2 points.
steps.detail: Revolutions promise rights, then quarrel over who gets them. The 1789 Declaration didn't mean women, and Olympe de Gouges answered with her own in 1791. Haiti forced the question of slavery. Look at who claimed these words next.
steps.proof: 2 points.
steps.pitfall: Taking the promises at face value.

problems.prompt: Who wrote 'The Rights of Woman' in 1791?
France's 1789 Declaration left out which 2 big groups in practice?
Which colony forced France to deal with slavery in the 1790s?

steps.title: Judge the Outcome
steps.mastery: Decide what a revolution really changed.
steps.practice: Write 100 words on 2 things that changed and 2 that didn't in Russia from 1917 to 1953.
steps.detail: Ask what's different, and for whom. Russia's tsar was gone, but one-man rule returned in Stalin, and rural life stayed hard. Historians ask if revolutions break with the past or continue it. Compare before and after using real figures.
steps.proof: 100 words.
steps.pitfall: Using only what the revolution's leaders said about itself.

problems.prompt: Who ruled the Soviet Union until 1953?
Name 1 thing that stayed similar from the tsars to 1953.
Why not judge 1917 only from what Lenin claimed?
problems.answer: Leaders have reasons to make it look good.

steps.title: Study Everyday Life
steps.mastery: Ask how ordinary people lived, worked and ate.
steps.practice: Write 5 details of a day for a farm family in 1300 using 1 book or article.
steps.detail: Social history looks beyond kings to ordinary people. What did they eat, and how long did they work? Evidence comes from wills, court records and tools. Peasants didn't write diaries, so you've got to piece their lives together.
steps.proof: 5 details.
steps.pitfall: Treating history as only rulers and wars.

problems.prompt: Name 2 sources for the lives of peasants in 1300.
Did most peasants in 1300 keep diaries? Answer yes or no.
Name 1 thing social history asks about, besides kings, in 1 line.
problems.answer: What ordinary people ate and did.

steps.title: Read Class
steps.mastery: See how wealth shaped what people could do.
steps.practice: List 3 differences between a mill owner and a mill hand in Manchester in 1840.
