steps.detail: Class affects how long you live, what you eat and what's expected of you. In 1840 Manchester, workers lived far shorter lives than the rich did. Friedrich Engels wrote about it in 1845. Look for the numbers behind the experience.
steps.proof: 3 differences.
steps.pitfall: Using 'people back then' as if everyone lived the same way.

problems.prompt: Who wrote about Manchester workers in 1845?
Name 1 thing that class changed in 1840 Manchester.
Why is 'people in 1840 lived like this' a weak claim?
problems.answer: It ignores big differences by class.

steps.title: Bring in Gender
steps.mastery: Ask how women's and men's lives differed.
steps.practice: Pick 1 setting from 1800 and list 3 things women could and couldn't legally do.
steps.detail: Laws and customs set limits. In 1800, married women in England usually couldn't own property. Women still ran shops and farms in practice. Compare the law with real lives, as there's often a gap, and that's where it gets interesting.
steps.proof: A list of 3.
steps.pitfall: Adding one famous woman and thinking gender is now covered.

problems.prompt: In England in 1800, could a married woman normally own property in her own name? Answer yes or no.
What's the gap to look for between 1800 law and daily life?
problems.answer: Women often did more than the law allowed.

problems.prompt: Why isn't adding 1 queen enough for a gender history?
problems.answer: It doesn't show how most women lived.

steps.title: Study Migration
steps.mastery: Trace why people move and what they change.
steps.practice: Map 1 migration such as Ireland to Boston in 1847 and write 2 pushes and 2 pulls.
steps.detail: People leave because something pushes them, and go where something pulls them. Over 1 million people left Ireland during the famine of the 1840s. Migrants change the places they reach. Look at both ends of the journey.
steps.proof: A map with notes.
steps.pitfall: Telling it only from the point of view of those who were there first.

problems.prompt: About how many people left Ireland during the famine of the 1840s: 1 million or 100 million?
Name 1 push and 1 pull for Irish migrants in 1847.
problems.answer: Hunger pushed them and jobs pulled them.

problems.prompt: Why look at both ends of a migration in 1847?

steps.title: Use Numbers and Lives
steps.mastery: Combine census data with personal stories.
steps.practice: Compare 1 census record from 1900 with 1 diary entry from the same town.
steps.detail: Numbers show patterns and diaries show what it felt like. A census might say 20% of children worked. A diary says what that was like. Put them together, and notice that each tells you what the other one can't.
steps.proof: 1 comparison.
steps.pitfall: Using only stories or only tables.

problems.prompt: A 1900 census counts every home on a street. What can it reveal?
What can 1 diary entry about a hard week add to a table?
A diary says 'all children here work'. A census for 1900 says 20%. What do you do?
problems.answer: Check who the diary writer knew and how far it applies.

steps.title: Trace an Invention
steps.mastery: Show how an invention spread and changed over time.
steps.practice: Trace printing from China around 800 to Gutenberg around 1450 in 4 steps.
steps.detail: Inventions don't belong to a single person. China printed from woodblocks centuries before Gutenberg's press around 1450. Spread and use matter more than who was first. Ask why it took off in one place, and why it didn't elsewhere.
steps.proof: 4 steps.
steps.pitfall: Telling it as a lone genius story.

problems.prompt: Roughly when did Gutenberg's press appear in Europe?
Which country printed from woodblocks centuries earlier, around 800?
Why does 'who was first' matter less than spread over 500 years?
problems.answer: What changes the world is who used it and how.

steps.title: Avoid Determinism
steps.mastery: Show people shaped how technology got used.
steps.practice: Pick 1 technology, such as the radio in 1930, and name 2 ways that it could've gone differently.
steps.detail: Technology doesn't decide things on its own. Radio could've been a two-way medium, but business and states shaped it as broadcast. Ask who funded it, who used it and what laws applied. Other choices were possible at each step.
steps.proof: 2 alternatives.
steps.pitfall: Saying the machine caused the change, with no people involved.

problems.prompt: Radio in 1920 could've gone 2 ways. Name them.
What's it called when you claim technology alone drives history, in 2 words?
Name 2 forces that shaped radio by 1930.

steps.title: Follow Unintended Effects
steps.mastery: Trace surprising results of a new technology.
steps.practice: List 3 unintended effects of the cotton gin of 1793 on slavery in the US.
steps.detail: New tools can have effects nobody planned. The cotton gin of 1793 cut hand labor for cleaning cotton, yet it made growing cotton so profitable that slavery expanded hugely. Look for such ironies, and don't assume that a machine saves anyone.
steps.proof: 3 effects.
steps.pitfall: Assuming a labor-saving machine always cuts labor.

problems.prompt: Who patented the cotton gin in 1794?
Did slavery shrink or grow in the US after the 1793 cotton gin?
Why did cotton cleaning by machine lead to more field labor in 1820?

steps.title: Link Tech and Power
steps.mastery: See who benefits from technological change.
steps.practice: Write 100 words on how the telegraph helped Britain run its empire by 1870.
steps.detail: Tools serve those who control them. The telegraph let London send orders to India in hours in place of months. Railways moved soldiers as well as goods. Ask who could afford it, who controlled it, and who was watched by it.
steps.proof: 100 words.
steps.pitfall: Treating new tools as equally helpful for everyone.

problems.prompt: A message by ship to India took months in 1850. How long by telegraph in 1870, roughly?
Name 2 things railways moved in India in 1860.
Who benefits most when 1 state controls a telegraph line?
problems.answer: Those in power at the center.

steps.title: Compare Past and Present
steps.mastery: Use past changes carefully to think about today's.
steps.practice: Compare the printing press of 1450 with the internet in 3 ways, and name 1 limit of the comparison.
steps.detail: It's tempting to say the internet is the new printing press. That has some truth: cheap spread, and fights over who's right. But speed and scale differ. Analogies help you ask questions. They don't prove anything, so say where one breaks.
steps.proof: 3 ways and 1 limit.
steps.pitfall: Using history to predict the future with false confidence.

problems.prompt: Name 1 way the internet resembles the printing press of 1450.
Name 1 way the comparison breaks down in 2020.
Can a comparison from 1450 prove what will happen by 2050? Answer yes or no.
problems.answer: No, it can only raise questions.

steps.title: Read a Time Line
steps.mastery: Place events in order and see what overlapped.
steps.practice: Draw a time line from 1400 to 1600 with 5 events, spaced to scale.
steps.detail: Chronology is the first tool in history. You can't talk about cause if you don't know what came first. Spacing a time line to scale shows gaps and overlaps that a plain list hides, and those are often the surprises.
steps.proof: 1 time line to scale.
steps.pitfall: Writing events in a list with equal gaps, so that centuries look the same as weeks.

problems.prompt: Which came first: the printing press of about 1450 or Columbus's voyage of 1492?
How many years from 1492 to 1776?
The Aztec empire fell in 1521 and Luther's theses came in 1517. How many years apart?

steps.title: Count BCE and CE
steps.mastery: Do date arithmetic across the year 1.
steps.practice: Convert 5 BCE dates to their distance from 2000 CE, noting there's no year 0.
steps.detail: BCE years count down toward year 1, and CE years count up. There's no year 0. So from 44 BCE to 14 CE is 57 years, not 58. Getting this wrong throws off ages and lengths of reigns by one year.
steps.proof: 5 worked sums.
steps.pitfall: Adding across the line and forgetting there's no year 0.

problems.prompt: Caesar died in 44 BCE. How many years later is 2000 CE?
From 44 BCE to 14 CE is how many years?
Which is earlier: 300 BCE or 100 BCE?

steps.title: Name the Century
steps.mastery: Convert between years and the name of the century.
steps.practice: Name the century for 8 years, such as 1215, 1789 and 1900.
steps.detail: The 1700s are the 18th century, since the first century was years 1 to 100. Add one to the first two digits. The year 1900 is technically the end of the 19th century. It's a small thing that readers notice when you slip.
steps.proof: 8 answers.
steps.pitfall: Calling the 1700s the 17th century.

problems.prompt: Which century is 1789 in?
Which century is 1215 in?
Name the century of the year 1900.

steps.title: Line Up Parallel Events
steps.mastery: Compare what's happening in different places at one time.
steps.practice: Make a 3 column chart for 1500 to 1550 with Europe, the Americas and Asia.
steps.detail: Time lines usually follow one country, and that hides a lot. Around 1520, the Aztecs fell, the Ottomans rose under Suleiman and Luther split the Church. Lining them up shows who was busy, and breaks the idea of one main story.
steps.proof: A 3 column chart.
steps.pitfall: Assuming the rest of the world stood still while Europe acted.

problems.prompt: Name the Ottoman ruler who rose to power in 1520.
Which empire fell to Cortes in 1521?
Name 1 thing a 3 column chart for 1520 shows that a list for 1 country hides.
problems.answer: That many big events happened at the same time.

steps.title: Sort Sequence from Cause
steps.mastery: Tell apart events that merely came first from ones that caused others.
steps.practice: Pick 3 pairs of events from 1914 to 1918 and write whether 1 caused the other.
steps.detail: Just because something came first doesn't mean it caused the next thing. This error even has a Latin name, post hoc. To claim a cause, you've got to show a link. A shooting in June 1914 led to a war only through alliances and choices.
steps.proof: 3 pairs with reasons.
steps.pitfall: Treating every 'before' as a 'because'.

problems.prompt: What's the Latin name of the 'after it, so because of it' error?
Franz Ferdinand was shot in June 1914. What linked that to a wider war?
A king dies in 1500 and a crop fails in 1501. Is that enough to claim a cause? Answer yes or no.
problems.answer: No, you need to show a link.

steps.title: Explain Why Wars Start
steps.mastery: Separate long causes from triggers.
steps.practice: Sort 6 causes of World War 1 into long-term causes and triggers.
steps.detail: Alliances, arms races, nationalism and empire built pressure over decades. The shooting at Sarajevo in June 1914 was a trigger. Christopher Clark's 'The Sleepwalkers' argues that leaders drifted in. Other historians blame Germany more. Weigh them.
steps.proof: 6 sorted causes.
steps.pitfall: Blaming one assassination for it all.

problems.prompt: Where was Franz Ferdinand shot in June 1914?
Who wrote 'The Sleepwalkers' in 2012?
Is an arms race from 1900 to 1914 a long-term cause or a trigger?

steps.title: Read a Soldier's View
steps.mastery: Use letters to see what fighting was like.
steps.practice: Read 2 letters from a trench in 1916 and list 3 things censors might have cut.
steps.detail: Soldiers wrote home, but censors read their letters, and they often hid things from family. So letters show as well as hide. Compare with memoirs, photos and medical records, to fill in what they couldn't or wouldn't say.
steps.proof: A list of 3.
steps.pitfall: Taking a brave letter home as a full account.

problems.prompt: Who read soldiers' mail in 1916, besides the family?
Why might a son of 19 hide the worst from his mother?
Name 1 source to check a soldier's letter from the Somme in 1916.

steps.title: See the Home Front
steps.mastery: Show how war changed life at home.
steps.practice: List 4 ways World War 2 changed life for women in the US by 1945.
steps.detail: War reaches far past the battlefield. Rationing, factory work and bombing changed daily life. Many American women took new jobs by 1945, though many were pushed out after. Ask who got new chances, and who suffered, like the Japanese Americans.
steps.proof: 4 ways.
steps.pitfall: Treating war as only battles and generals.

problems.prompt: What's the nickname of US women who did war factory work in the 1940s?
Which group of Americans was forced into camps in 1942?
Why might women's job gains from 1945 not have lasted?
problems.answer: Many were pushed out after the war.

steps.title: Study the Peace
steps.mastery: Examine how a war's ending shapes what follows.
steps.practice: Summarize the Treaty of Versailles of 1919 in 5 points and say what each one caused.
steps.detail: Endings matter. Versailles blamed Germany and took land and money, and some say it helped lead to another war. Others say it wasn't that harsh. After 1945, things went differently, with the Marshall Plan. Compare the two.
steps.proof: 5 points.
steps.pitfall: Saying Versailles caused World War 2 with no other reasons.

problems.prompt: In what year was the Treaty of Versailles signed?
Name the US aid plan for Europe that started in 1948.
Why is 'Versailles caused World War 2' too simple for 1939?
problems.answer: The Depression and later choices mattered too.

steps.title: Remember the Aftermath
steps.mastery: Follow what war leaves behind in people and places.
steps.practice: List 3 lasting effects of the Vietnam War on Vietnam or the US after 1975.
steps.detail: War goes on after peace. Veterans live with what they saw. Land is mined or poisoned, like the Agent Orange areas in Vietnam. Refugees rebuild elsewhere. Follow the costs for a long time, since they don't end at the treaty.
steps.proof: 3 effects.
steps.pitfall: Ending your story at the last battle.

problems.prompt: In what year did the Vietnam War end?
Name the chemical sprayed in Vietnam, with effects for decades.
Name 1 lasting cost for US veterans after 1975.

steps.title: Create and Use an ArrayList
steps.mastery: Create an ArrayList, and use add, get, set, remove and size.
steps.practice: Make an ArrayList<String> of 3 names, add a 4th, change the 2nd with set, remove the 1st, and print size().
steps.detail: add puts an item at the end, or at an index if you give one, shifting the rest right. get and set read and replace by index. remove takes an item out and shifts the rest left. size() is the current count, and it changes as you go.
steps.proof: The list ends with 3 names, and size() prints 3.
steps.pitfall: Using .length on an ArrayList. That's for arrays.

problems.prompt: ArrayList<Integer> a holds [5, 8]. After a.add(3), what is a.size()?
a holds [5, 8, 3]. What does a.get(1) return?
a holds [5, 8, 3]. After a.add(1, 9), what is a?

steps.title: Wrapper Types
steps.mastery: Use Integer and Double in ArrayLists, since an ArrayList can't hold primitives directly.
steps.practice: Declare ArrayList<Integer> nums, add 4 ints, and sum them with a for-each loop, letting Java unbox each one.
steps.detail: Generic lists hold objects, so ints go in as Integer objects. Java converts automatically: autoboxing when you add, unboxing when you read. Watch remove: with an int argument it removes by index, not by value.
steps.proof: The loop adds each Integer as an int and prints the total.
steps.pitfall: Calling nums.remove(10) to remove the value 10, which removes index 10 instead.

problems.prompt: Can you write ArrayList<int>?
Java turns an int into an Integer automatically when you add it. What is that called?
nums holds [10, 20]. What does nums.remove(0) remove?
problems.answer: The element at index 0, which is 10.

steps.title: Remove While Looping
steps.mastery: Remove items during a loop without skipping any, by looping backward or adjusting the index.
steps.practice: Remove every even number from [2, 4, 5, 6, 7] with a forward loop, see the bug, then fix it by looping backward.
steps.detail: When you remove at index i, everything after it shifts left, so the next item lands at i. A forward loop then moves on to i + 1 and skips it. Looping backward avoids this, because the shifted items are ones you've already checked.
steps.proof: The forward loop leaves [4, 5, 7], skipping the 4. Looping backward gives [5, 7].
steps.pitfall: Removing inside a for-each loop, which throws an exception.

problems.prompt: A forward loop removes every "x" from [x, x, y]. What is left?
Why does looping backward from size() - 1 avoid skipping?
problems.answer: Removing shifts only items you've already checked.

problems.prompt: Can you call remove inside a for-each loop over an ArrayList?

steps.title: Array or ArrayList
steps.mastery: Choose an array when the size is fixed and an ArrayList when it changes.
steps.practice: Pick array or ArrayList for 12 monthly totals, a growing to-do list and 64 chess squares, and say why for each.
steps.detail: Arrays are fixed in size, hold primitives directly and use [] and length. ArrayLists grow and shrink, hold objects and use get, set and size(). If you know the count in advance and it won't change, an array is simpler.
steps.proof: Arrays for the 12 months and 64 squares, and an ArrayList for the to-do list.
steps.pitfall: Mixing the syntax, like list[0] or arr.size().

problems.prompt: How do you get the size of an ArrayList: .length or .size()?
Which fits a shopping list that grows as you think of things: an array or an ArrayList?
Which is fixed in size once created: int[] or ArrayList<Integer>?

steps.title: Common List Algorithms
steps.mastery: Write the standard ArrayList algorithms: find, insert in order, and remove duplicates.
steps.practice: Write a method that inserts 7 into the sorted list [2, 5, 9, 12] so it stays sorted.
steps.detail: To insert in order, walk the list until you find the first item bigger than the new one, then add at that index. To remove duplicates, build a new list and add each item only if it isn't there yet. indexOf finds an item or returns -1.
steps.proof: 7 goes at index 2, giving [2, 5, 7, 9, 12].
steps.pitfall: Appending and then sorting the whole list, which works but wastes effort.

problems.prompt: Insert 4 into the sorted list [1, 3, 6]. At what index does it go?
A remove-duplicates pass keeps first copies. What does it leave from [3, 1, 3, 2, 1]?
list.indexOf("cat") returns -1. What does that mean?

steps.title: Create and Index
steps.mastery: Create arrays, read and write their elements, and use length.
steps.practice: Create int[] scores = {90, 85, 77, 92}, change the third score to 80, and print scores.length.
steps.detail: An array has a fixed size set when it's made. Indexes run from 0 to length - 1, so the third element is at index 2. length is a field, written without parentheses. Reading outside the range throws ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException.
steps.proof: scores becomes {90, 85, 80, 92}, and length prints 4.
steps.pitfall: Writing scores.length() with parentheses, which is the String form.

problems.prompt: int[] a = {4, 8, 15}; What is a[2]?
What is a[a.length - 1] for int[] a = new int[6];?
problems.answer: 0. A new int array starts filled with zeros.

problems.prompt: int[] a = {1, 2, 3}; What does a[3] do?

steps.title: Know the Default Values
steps.mastery: Know the default values in a new array: 0, 0.0, false and null.
steps.practice: Create new int[3], new double[2], new boolean[2] and new String[2], and print one element of each.
steps.detail: A new array is filled with defaults: 0 for int, 0.0 for double, false for boolean and null for any object type. A null String isn't an empty string, and calling a method on it throws NullPointerException.
steps.proof: 0, 0.0, false and null.
steps.pitfall: Calling words[0].length() on a new String array and crashing on null.

problems.prompt: int[] a = new int[5]; What is a[0]?
String[] s = new String[3]; What is s[1]?
boolean[] f = new boolean[4]; What is f[3]?

steps.title: Sum, Max and Count
steps.mastery: Track a running total, a largest value and a tally together, updating all 3 inside a single loop.
steps.practice: Write one loop over {3, 9, 2, 9, 5} that finds the sum, the max and how many 9s there are.
steps.detail: Set up the accumulators before the loop: sum at 0, count at 0, and max at the first element. Then update all three in the same loop. Starting max at a[0] works even when every value is negative.
steps.proof: Sum 28, max 9 and two 9s.
steps.pitfall: Starting max at 0, which fails on an all-negative array.

problems.prompt: What is the sum of {4, -2, 7}?
Why start max at a[0] instead of 0 for {-5, -2, -8}?
problems.answer: Every value is negative, so 0 would be wrong.

problems.prompt: A loop counts values over 10 in {12, 7, 15, 10, 30}. What's the count?

steps.title: Use Enhanced for Loops
steps.mastery: Use for-each loops to read every element, and know they can't change the array or give the index.
steps.practice: Rewrite a standard for loop that sums {2, 4, 6} as a for-each loop.
steps.detail: for (int x : arr) hands you each element in turn, which is shorter and avoids index mistakes. But x is a copy, so assigning to x leaves the array alone, and there's no index. When you need either, use a standard for loop.
steps.proof: int sum = 0; for (int x : arr) sum += x; gives 12.
steps.pitfall: Trying to set elements to 0 inside a for-each loop.

problems.prompt: 'for (int x : arr) x = 0;' runs on {1, 2}. What is arr afterward?
problems.answer: {1, 2}. Changing x doesn't change the array.

problems.prompt: Can a loop like 'for (int x : arr)' tell you an element's index?
problems.answer: No. Use a standard for loop for that.

problems.prompt: Write a for-each loop header that visits each String w in words.

steps.title: Shift and Reverse
steps.mastery: Reverse or shift an array in place using a temp variable.
steps.practice: Reverse {1, 2, 3, 4, 5} in place by swapping a[i] and a[a.length - 1 - i] up to the middle.
steps.detail: Swapping needs a temp variable: save one value, overwrite it, then put the saved value in the other spot. To reverse, swap pairs from the outside in and stop at the middle, or you'll swap everything back. Shifting moves each element over and handles the end separately.
steps.proof: {5, 4, 3, 2, 1} after 2 swaps.
steps.pitfall: Looping all the way to the end, which reverses the array twice.

problems.prompt: How many swaps reverse an array of 6 elements?
Write the 3 lines that swap a[0] and a[1].
{1, 2, 3, 4} is shifted left by 1, with the first element moving to the end. What is it now?

steps.title: Fields and Constructors
steps.mastery: Write a class with private fields and a constructor that sets them.
steps.practice: Write class Student with fields name and grade and a constructor that sets both, then make 2 students.
steps.detail: Fields hold each object's data. The constructor has the class's name and no return type, and runs when you write new. this.name means the field when a parameter has the same name. If you write any constructor, Java stops supplying the default no-argument one.
steps.proof: new Student("Ana", 11) and new Student("Ben", 10) each hold their own name and grade.
steps.pitfall: Giving the constructor a return type like void, which turns it into a method.

problems.prompt: What does 'this.name = name;' do in a constructor?
problems.answer: Sets the field to the parameter with the same name.

problems.prompt: A class Dog has no constructor written. Can you still call new Dog()?
problems.answer: Yes. Java gives a default no-argument constructor.

problems.prompt: You wrote only Dog(String n). Does new Dog() compile?
problems.answer: No. Writing any constructor removes the default one.

steps.title: Instance Methods
steps.mastery: Write methods that use and change an object's own fields.
steps.practice: Give a Counter class a field count and methods increment() and getCount(), then call increment 3 times.
steps.detail: An instance method runs on one object and can read or change that object's fields directly. Two objects of the same class have separate fields, so changing one leaves the other alone. Calls look like c.increment().
steps.proof: getCount() returns 3.
steps.pitfall: Making count static by mistake, so every Counter shares one value.

problems.prompt: Counter c = new Counter(); c.increment(); c.increment(); What is c.getCount()?
2 Counter objects each call increment() once. What is each one's count?
Why does a method like getCount() need no parameters?
problems.answer: It reads the object's own field.

steps.title: Write toString
steps.mastery: Write a toString method so printing an object shows its data.
steps.practice: Add toString() to Student so System.out.println(s) prints 'Ana, grade 11'.
steps.detail: println calls toString on any object. The default prints the class name and a hash code, which tells you nothing. Override it with public String toString() and build a string from the fields. It makes debugging much easier.
steps.proof: It returns name + ", grade " + grade, which prints Ana, grade 11.
steps.pitfall: Printing inside toString instead of returning the string.

problems.prompt: Without toString, what does printing a Student show?
Write a toString for Point, with fields x and y, that returns '(x, y)'.
problems.answer: public String toString() { return "(" + x + ", " + y + ")"; }

problems.prompt: What return type must toString() have?

steps.title: Static and Instance
steps.mastery: Tell static members, shared by the whole class, from instance members, one per object.
steps.practice: Add a static int count to Student that goes up in the constructor, then make 3 students and print Student.count.
steps.detail: A static field belongs to the class, so all objects share one copy. A static method runs without an object, which means it can't touch instance fields directly. Math.sqrt is static, which is why you call it on the class.
steps.proof: Student.count prints 3.
steps.pitfall: Calling an instance method from main without making an object first.

problems.prompt: A static counter goes up in every constructor. You make 5 objects, then 2 more. What is the counter?
problems.answer: 7. Every object shares the one static counter.

problems.prompt: Can a 'static' method use an instance field directly?
problems.answer: No. It has no object to read it from.

problems.prompt: Math.sqrt(16) is called on the class Math. Is sqrt static?

steps.title: Design a Class
steps.mastery: Design a class from a description: choose its fields, constructor and methods.
steps.practice: Design a BankAccount class from 'it holds an owner and a balance, and can deposit and withdraw', writing the header of each member.
steps.detail: Nouns in the description usually become fields, and verbs become methods. Decide what the constructor must be given and what can start at a default. Keep fields private, and give each method one clear job.
steps.proof: Fields owner and balance, a constructor taking the owner, and deposit, withdraw and getBalance.
steps.pitfall: Making every field public to save writing methods.

problems.prompt: A Book has a title and a page count. Which 2 fields fit?
problems.answer: private String title; private int pages;

problems.prompt: Should withdraw(double amt) on BankAccount return void or boolean?
problems.answer: boolean works well, true if it succeeded.

problems.prompt: Name 1 method a Rectangle class with width and height should have.

steps.title: Branch With if and else
steps.mastery: Write if, else if and else chains, and predict which branch runs.
steps.practice: Write a chain that prints "freezing" below 0, "cold" below 15 and "warm" otherwise, then test it with 0, 14 and 15.
steps.detail: Java checks each condition in order and runs only the first true branch. Without braces, an if controls just the next statement, which is a common source of bugs, so always use braces. Separate ifs, not chained with else, are each checked on their own.
steps.proof: 0 and 14 print cold, and 15 prints warm.
steps.pitfall: Writing two separate ifs when you meant else if, so both can run.

problems.prompt: int t = 0; The chain is 'if (t < 0)' then 'else if (t < 15)'. Which branch runs?
int x = 5; if (x > 3) x = 1; if (x > 3) x = 2; What is x?
What does 'if (false) System.out.print(1); System.out.print(2);' print?

steps.title: Boolean Logic
steps.mastery: Evaluate &&, || and !, and use De Morgan's laws to rewrite a condition.
steps.practice: Rewrite !(a && b) and !(x > 5 || y == 0) using De Morgan's laws.
steps.detail: && is true only if both sides are true, and || if at least one is. De Morgan's laws flip the operator when you push a ! inside: !(a && b) is !a || !b. Java also short-circuits: && stops at the first false and || at the first true.
steps.pitfall: Pushing ! inside without flipping && to ||.

problems.prompt: What does the Java expression 'true && !false' give?
Rewrite !(a || b) with De Morgan's law.
int x = 0; Does 'x != 0 && 10 / x > 1' crash?
problems.answer: No. && stops at the first false, so 10 / x never runs.

steps.title: Write while Loops
steps.mastery: Write while loops that end, and count how many times they run.
steps.practice: Write a while loop that doubles n = 1 until it reaches at least 1000, and count the passes.
steps.detail: A while loop checks its condition before every pass, so it may run zero times. Something in the body must move toward making the condition false. To count passes, trace a table of the variable's values, or add a counter while you test.
steps.proof: 10 passes, ending at 1024.
steps.pitfall: Forgetting to change the loop variable, which loops forever.

problems.prompt: int n = 10; while (n > 0) n -= 3; What is n after the loop?
int k = 1; while (k < 50) k *= 2; What is k after the loop?
How many times does 'int i = 5; while (i < 5) i++;' run its body?

steps.title: for Loops and Off-by-One
steps.mastery: Write for loops with the right bounds, and spot off-by-one errors.
steps.practice: Write 3 for loops that print 1 to 10, 10 down to 1, and the even numbers 0 to 20, then count each loop's passes.
steps.detail: A for loop's header holds the start, the condition and the step. < stops one before the end and <= includes it. To count passes, use (last - first) / step + 1, then check the edges by hand. Most loop bugs are one pass too many or too few.
steps.proof: 10, 10 and 11 passes.
steps.pitfall: Using <= with an array's length, which reads past the end.

problems.prompt: How many times does 'for (int i = 0; i < 10; i++)' run?
How many times does 'for (int i = 1; i <= 10; i += 3)' run?
Count the passes of a loop that starts at i = 10 and runs while i >= 0, subtracting 1 each time.

steps.title: Trace Nested Loops
steps.mastery: Trace nested loops and count the total passes of the inner body.
steps.practice: Write nested loops that print a 4 by 5 grid of stars, and count how many stars print.
steps.detail: The inner loop runs completely for every pass of the outer one. If both bounds are fixed, multiply. If the inner bound depends on the outer variable, add up the inner counts row by row. A small table of i and j values makes this quick.
steps.proof: 20 stars in 4 rows of 5.
steps.pitfall: Multiplying when the inner loop's bound changes with the outer variable.

problems.prompt: An outer loop runs 3 times and the inner loop runs 4 times each pass. How many inner passes in total?
How many stars print from 'for (int i = 1; i <= 4; i++) for (int j = 1; j <= i; j++) print("*")'?
i runs from 0 to 2 and j runs from i to 2, both inclusive. How many inner passes?

steps.title: Make Fields Private
steps.mastery: Make fields private so only the class's own methods can change them.
steps.practice: Change Student's public grade field to private, then fix the code in main that set it directly.
steps.detail: A private field can't be touched from outside the class, so every change goes through a method you wrote. That lets the class reject bad values and change how it stores data later. Public fields let any code break the object.
steps.proof: main now calls s.setGrade(12) instead of writing s.grade = 12.
steps.pitfall: Leaving fields public because it's quicker to write.

problems.prompt: Can main write s.grade = 12 when grade is private?
Why make fields 'private'?
problems.answer: So the class controls every change and can reject bad values.

problems.prompt: Which keyword lets any class read a field: 'public' or 'private'?

steps.title: Write Getters
steps.mastery: Write getter methods that return a field's value without exposing the field itself.
steps.practice: Write getName() and getGrade() for Student, and use them to print a student's info.
steps.detail: A getter is a public method that returns a private field. Naming it getX is the convention. It lets other code read the value without being able to change it. A getter shouldn't change anything.
steps.proof: s.getName() and s.getGrade() print the student's name and grade.
steps.pitfall: Giving a getter a parameter, or making it change the field.

problems.prompt: Write a getter for a private int field 'age'.
What type should getName() return if name is a String?
Does calling getAge() change the object?

steps.title: Write Setters With Checks
steps.mastery: Write setters that check a new value and refuse bad ones.
steps.practice: Write setGrade(int g) that only accepts 9 to 12, and test it with 10 and 15.
steps.detail: A setter is where the class guards itself. Check the value, store it only if it's valid, and otherwise leave the field alone or throw an exception. That way no object can end up in a nonsense state like grade 15.
steps.proof: setGrade(10) works, and setGrade(15) leaves the grade unchanged.
steps.pitfall: Writing a setter that stores anything, which is a public field with extra steps.

problems.prompt: setGrade(15) runs on a setter that only accepts 9 to 12. What is grade afterward?
Write a setter for 'age' that refuses negative values.
problems.answer: public void setAge(int a) { if (a >= 0) age = a; }

problems.prompt: Why is 'setAge' safer than a public age field?
problems.answer: It can check the value before storing it.

steps.title: Keep Some Fields Read-Only
steps.mastery: Decide which fields should have no setter, and use final for values that never change.
steps.practice: Give Student a final int id set in the constructor with no setter, and try assigning it later to see the error.
steps.detail: Not every field should be changeable. An id or a birth date is set once. Leave out the setter and mark it final, and the compiler stops any later change. For a balance, use deposit and withdraw rather than a raw setter.
steps.proof: Assigning id after the constructor gives a compile error.
steps.pitfall: Writing a setter for every field out of habit.

problems.prompt: Can you assign to a 'final' field after the constructor runs?
Should a BankAccount have setBalance(double b)?
problems.answer: No. Use deposit and withdraw so every change is checked.

problems.prompt: Which field of a Student should usually be read-only: id or nickname?

steps.title: Hide the Details
steps.mastery: Keep helper methods private, so other classes see only what they need.
steps.practice: Move a validation helper in BankAccount into a private method, and check that main can't call it.
steps.detail: Public methods are a promise to other code. Private helpers are details you can change at any time without breaking anyone. Keeping that line clear lets you rewrite the inside of a class while everything outside keeps working.
steps.proof: main gets a compile error calling the private helper, and deposit still works.
steps.pitfall: Making helpers public just in case, which ties other code to them.

problems.prompt: Can main call a private helper isValid() in another class?
Why hide helper methods like isValid()?
problems.answer: You can change them later without breaking other code.

problems.prompt: A BankAccount class switches its balance from a double to cents in an int. If its fields are private, what else must change?
problems.answer: Only that class. Other code uses the methods.

steps.title: Read the Question
steps.mastery: Read the whole free-response question, and mark what the method must return and what you're given.
steps.practice: Take 1 released FRQ part and underline the return type, the parameters and every precondition before writing code.
steps.detail: Preconditions tell you what you don't need to check, which saves time and clutter. The method header is given, so copy it exactly. Later parts often say you may assume earlier ones work, which is a hint to call those methods.
steps.proof: Return type, parameters and preconditions underlined before any code.
steps.pitfall: Writing checks for cases the preconditions already rule out.

problems.prompt: An FRQ says 'precondition: arr.length > 0'. Do you need to handle an empty array?
problems.answer: No. The precondition rules it out.

problems.prompt: The header 'public int countMatches(String s)' is given. Should you change it?
problems.answer: No. Use it exactly as given.

problems.prompt: Part (b) says you may assume part (a) works. Should you call your part (a) method?

steps.title: Write Java on Paper
steps.mastery: Write clean Java by hand, with braces matched, semicolons in and indentation clear.
steps.practice: Write a method that returns how many values in an int array are above 50, by hand, in under 6 minutes.
steps.detail: Graders follow your logic, so neat indentation helps them give credit. Small slips like a missing semicolon usually aren't penalized, but wrong loop bounds or a missing return are. Practice on paper weekly so your hand knows the syntax.
steps.proof: A short method with a counter, a loop and a return, written in under 6 minutes.
steps.pitfall: Practicing only in an IDE and freezing when there's no autocomplete.

problems.prompt: Write the loop header that visits every index of int[] arr.
Graders usually forgive 1 missing semicolon. Do they forgive a wrong loop bound?
problems.answer: No. That's a logic error and costs points.

problems.prompt: You run out of room mid-method on page 3. What should you do?
problems.answer: Keep writing on the next page and label it clearly.

steps.title: The Class Question
steps.mastery: Write a complete class from a description: private fields, a constructor and the methods asked for.
steps.practice: Write a Ticket class from 'holds a row and seat number and a price, with getPrice() and a method that raises the price by a percent'.
steps.detail: Read the description for nouns and verbs: nouns become private fields and verbs become methods. Write the header exactly as the question names it. Use this.field = field in the constructor when names match, and return the right type from every method.
steps.proof: A class with 3 private fields, a constructor, getPrice() and raise(double pct).
steps.pitfall: Making the fields public, which loses points on most class questions.

problems.prompt: In a 'Ticket' class FRQ, should the fields be public or private?
raise(10) should add 10% to a price of 50. What is the new price?
A constructor parameter is named row, and so is the field. What do you write to set the field?

steps.title: Array and ArrayList Questions
steps.mastery: Solve the classic array and ArrayList patterns: count, find, remove and build a new list.
steps.practice: Write removeShort(ArrayList<String> words, int n) that removes every word shorter than n, looping backward.
steps.detail: Most list questions are one of a few patterns. Counting and finding walk the list once. Removing loops backward. Building creates a new list and adds to it, leaving the original alone unless the question says otherwise.
steps.proof: A backward loop from words.size() - 1 to 0 that removes each short word.
steps.pitfall: Removing while looping forward and skipping words.

problems.prompt: For words ["hi", "hello", "yo"] and n = 3, what does removeShort leave?
Why loop backward when removing from an ArrayList?
problems.answer: Removing shifts later items left, so a forward loop skips one.

problems.prompt: Should a method named 'buildList' change the original list?
problems.answer: No, unless the question says to.

steps.title: The 2D Array Question
steps.mastery: Write 2D array methods that walk rows or columns and handle the edges.
steps.practice: Write a method that returns the row index with the largest sum in an int[][] grid.
steps.detail: Loop over rows, sum each one with an inner loop, and keep the best sum and its index. Start the best at row 0 rather than at 0, so negative grids work. Name your loop variables r and c so the indexes stay clear.
steps.proof: A method that tracks bestSum and bestRow and returns bestRow.
steps.pitfall: Starting bestSum at 0, which fails when every row's sum is negative.

problems.prompt: For {{1, 2}, {5, 0}, {3, 3}}, which row index has the largest sum?
Write the header of a static method that returns the sum of column c of an int[][] grid.
problems.answer: public static int colSum(int[][] grid, int c)

problems.prompt: Your method uses grid[0].length for the number of columns. When is that safe?
problems.answer: When every row has the same length, which AP grids do.

steps.title: Create and Index a Grid
steps.mastery: Create a 2D array and read an element with [row][col].
steps.practice: Create int[][] g = new int[3][4], set g[2][1] = 7, and print g.length and g[0].length.
steps.detail: A 2D array is an array of rows. g.length is the number of rows, and g[0].length is the number of columns in row 0. The first index picks the row and the second picks the column, both starting at 0.
steps.proof: g.length is 3 and g[0].length is 4.
steps.pitfall: Swapping the indexes and writing [col][row].

problems.prompt: For g = new int[4][7], what is g.length?
A grid is built with new int[5][8]. What is grid[0].length?

steps.title: Row-Major Traversal
steps.mastery: Walk a 2D array row by row with nested loops, rows in the outer loop and columns in the inner one.
steps.practice: Print every element of {{1, 2}, {3, 4}, {5, 6}} in row-major order with nested for loops.
steps.detail: Row-major order finishes a whole row before moving down. The outer loop runs r over the rows and the inner loop runs c over the columns of that row. Using grid[r].length for the inner bound works even when rows differ in length.
steps.proof: It prints 1 2 3 4 5 6.
steps.pitfall: Using grid.length for the inner loop, which only works for square grids.

problems.prompt: In row-major order, which element comes right after the last one in row 0?
Write the outer loop header for the rows of 'grid'.
Write the inner loop header for the columns of 'grid'.

steps.title: Column-Major Traversal
steps.mastery: Walk a 2D array column by column by putting the column loop on the outside.
steps.practice: Walk {{7, 8, 9}, {1, 2, 3}} down each column in turn, and write the 6 numbers in the order you visit them.
steps.detail: Swap the loops: the outer loop runs over columns and the inner one over rows, still reading grid[r][c]. This order is what you need for column sums or a column's largest value. Use grid[0].length for the number of columns.
steps.proof: You visit 7, 1, 8, 2, 9 and then 3.
steps.pitfall: Swapping the loops and also swapping the indexes, which reads the wrong cells.

problems.prompt: What is the column-major order of {{1, 2}, {3, 4}}?
In column-major traversal of a 3 by 4 grid, which loop runs over the rows: the outer or the inner?
Find the sum of column 1 in {{1, 2}, {3, 4}, {5, 6}}.

steps.title: Grid Algorithms
steps.mastery: Find a row sum, a column's largest value and a count of matches in a 2D array.
steps.practice: For {{3, 8, 1}, {9, 2, 7}}, find each row's sum, the largest value in column 0 and how many values are over 5.
steps.detail: Each of these is a one-dimensional algorithm aimed at a row, a column or the whole grid. Fix the row and loop over columns for a row sum. Fix the column and loop over rows for a column max. Loop over everything for a count.
steps.proof: Row sums 12 and 18, column 0 max 9, and 3 values over 5.
steps.pitfall: Resetting the row sum outside the outer loop, so it keeps growing across rows.

problems.prompt: What is the sum of row 0 in {{3, 8, 1}, {9, 2, 7}}?
How many values are even in {{1, 2}, {4, 7}}?
What is the sum of the main diagonal of {{1, 2, 3}, {4, 5, 6}, {7, 8, 9}}?

steps.title: Neighbors and Bounds
steps.mastery: Check a cell's neighbors without going out of bounds.
steps.practice: Write a method that counts how many of a cell's 4 neighbors hold a 1, checking each index is in range first.
steps.detail: A neighbor is one step up, down, left or right. Before reading grid[r - 1][c], check that r - 1 >= 0, and do the same for every edge. Put the range check first in an && so Java never reaches the bad index.
steps.proof: Edge and corner cells skip the neighbors that would fall off the grid.
steps.pitfall: Reading the neighbor first and checking the bounds after, which crashes at the edges.

problems.prompt: How many neighbors, counting up, down, left and right, does the corner cell [0][0] have?
In a 5 by 5 grid, how many neighbors does the center cell [2][2] have?
Write the check that row r - 1 is a valid row.

steps.title: Extend a Class
steps.mastery: Make a subclass with extends, and know that it inherits the parent's public methods.
steps.practice: Write class Animal with speak() returning "...", then class Dog extends Animal, and call speak() on a Dog.
steps.detail: extends says one class is a kind of another. The subclass gets every public method of the parent without rewriting it. Java allows only one parent class. The parent's private fields exist inside the object, but the child can only reach them through the parent's methods.
steps.proof: Dog inherits speak(), so new Dog().speak() returns "...".
steps.pitfall: Copying the parent's methods into the child instead of inheriting them.

problems.prompt: class B extends A. Does B get A's public methods?
Can a Java class extend 2 classes at once?
problems.answer: No. Java allows one parent class.

problems.prompt: Can a subclass use its parent's private fields, like 'name', directly?
problems.answer: No. It can only reach them through the parent's methods.

steps.title: Call super in Constructors
steps.mastery: Call the parent's constructor with super(...) as the first line of the child's constructor.
steps.practice: Give Animal a constructor taking a name, then write Dog(String name, String breed) that calls super(name) first.
steps.detail: The parent's part of the object has to be set up before the child's. So super(...) must come first. If you leave it out, Java inserts super() with no arguments, which fails to compile when the parent has no such constructor.
steps.proof: Dog's constructor starts with super(name), then sets its own breed.
steps.pitfall: Setting the parent's private fields directly from the child constructor.

problems.prompt: Where must super(name) go in a child constructor?
A parent has only Animal(String n). The child constructor doesn't call super. Does it compile?
problems.answer: No. Java inserts super(), which doesn't exist.

problems.prompt: Can 1 constructor call both this(...) and super(...)?
problems.answer: No. Only one, and it must be first.

steps.title: Override Methods
steps.mastery: Override a parent method with the same signature, and use @Override to catch mistakes.
steps.practice: Override speak() in Dog to return "Woof", add @Override, then misspell it as speek() and read the error.
steps.detail: An override has the same name and parameter list as the parent's method. The child's version replaces the parent's for that object. @Override asks the compiler to confirm you're really overriding, which catches typos that would otherwise make a new method silently.
steps.proof: With @Override, speek() gives a compile error, and speak() returns Woof.
steps.pitfall: Changing the parameter list and calling it an override. That's overloading.

problems.prompt: Animal a = new Dog(); Dog overrides speak to return "Woof". What does a.speak() return?
What does @Override do?
problems.answer: Makes the compiler check that you really are overriding a parent method.

problems.prompt: A subclass method has the same name and parameters as the parent's. Overloading or overriding?

steps.title: Call the Parent's Version
steps.mastery: Use super.method() to build on the parent's version of a method instead of replacing it.
steps.practice: Make Dog's toString return super.toString() + ", breed: lab".
steps.detail: Sometimes the child wants the parent's behavior plus a little more. super.method() runs the parent's version, and you add to its result. That avoids copying code, so a fix in the parent reaches the child too.
steps.proof: Dog's toString shows the Animal info followed by the breed.
steps.pitfall: Calling this.toString() inside toString, which calls itself forever.

problems.prompt: Animal's describe() returns "animal". Dog's returns super.describe() + " dog". What does Dog's return?
When should an override call super.method()?
problems.answer: When you want to add to the parent's behavior, not replace it.

problems.prompt: Can a subclass call super.super.method()?

steps.title: Design a Hierarchy
steps.mastery: Design a small class hierarchy with shared code in the parent and the differences in the children.
steps.practice: Design Shape with 3 subclasses, Circle, Rectangle and Triangle, and decide which fields and methods go in the parent.
steps.detail: Use inheritance for 'is a' relationships: a Circle is a Shape. Put what every child shares in the parent, and what differs in each child. If one thing merely has another, like a car with an engine, use a field, not extends.
steps.proof: Shape holds a name and declares area(), and each child holds its own sizes and overrides area().
steps.pitfall: Using extends for 'has a' relationships.

problems.prompt: Should Student extend Person, or Person extend Student?
problems.answer: Student extends Person. Every student is a person.

problems.prompt: Is a Car a kind of Engine, so 'Car extends Engine' makes sense?
problems.answer: No. A car has an engine, so use a field.

problems.prompt: All 3 shapes have area(). Where should its header go?
problems.answer: In Shape, overridden by each subclass.

steps.title: Trace With a Table
steps.mastery: Trace code on paper with a table that records every variable's value after each line.
steps.practice: Trace int a = 3, b = 5; a = a + b; b = a - b; a = a - b; in a 3-column table and give a and b at the end.
steps.detail: Write one column per variable and one row per line or loop pass. Update only what the line changes. It feels slow, but it's faster than guessing and redoing, and it catches the off-by-one and integer division traps the exam is built around.
steps.proof: a goes 3, 8, 5 and b goes 5, 3, so the two values swapped.
steps.pitfall: Tracing in your head and losing track after 3 lines.

problems.prompt: int x = 4; x = x * x - 3; What is x?
int a = 2, b = 7; a = b; b = a; What is b?
int s = 0; for (int i = 1; i <= 4; i++) s += i * i; What is s?

steps.title: Watch Integer Division
steps.mastery: Spot the integer division and casting traps the multiple choice section loves.
steps.practice: Work out 10 / 4, 10 / 4.0, (double) 10 / 4 and (int) (10 / 4.0) before checking any of them.
steps.detail: Java works left to right with the usual precedence, and each operation's type depends only on its two sides. So 1 / 2 * 4.0 is 0 * 4.0, not 2.0. Look for two ints meeting at a / and slow down there.
steps.pitfall: Assuming a double anywhere in the line makes every division decimal.

problems.prompt: What is 1 / 2 * 4.0 in Java?
double d = 3.0 * 5 / 2; What is d?
int avg = (90 + 85) / 2; What is avg?

steps.title: Eliminate Choices
steps.mastery: Eliminate wrong answers by testing edge cases, like empty arrays or the first and last index.
steps.practice: For 5 practice questions, cross off at least 2 choices each by testing an edge case before solving.
steps.detail: Wrong choices are usually wrong at the edges: they skip the first element, run past the last, or fail on an empty list. Test those first. Two choices that differ only in < versus <= are telling you exactly where to look.
steps.proof: 5 questions, each with 2 or more choices crossed off and a reason noted.
steps.pitfall: Testing only the middle of the array, where every choice looks right.

problems.prompt: A method should return the last element of arr. Choice A uses arr[arr.length]. Keep or eliminate?
problems.answer: Eliminate. That index is out of bounds.

problems.prompt: A loop should visit every index. Choice B uses i <= arr.length. Keep or eliminate?
problems.answer: Eliminate. It runs one past the end.

problems.prompt: 2 choices differ only in < versus <=. What should you test?
problems.answer: The boundary value, where the two give different answers.

steps.title: Pace the Section
steps.mastery: Pace the section at about 2 minutes per question, and skip slow ones to come back to.
steps.practice: Answer 10 practice questions in 22 minutes, marking any that take over 3 minutes to come back to.
steps.detail: The section has around 40 questions in 90 minutes. Every question is worth the same, so one stubborn trace shouldn't cost you three easy ones. Mark it, make a guess, move on and return if there's time. Check your pace every 10 questions.
steps.proof: 10 questions done in 22 minutes, with the slow ones marked.
steps.pitfall: Spending 8 minutes on one question while easy ones wait.

problems.prompt: If 42 questions take 90 minutes, about how many minutes is that each, to 1 decimal?
You're stuck after 3 minutes on question 12. What should you do?
problems.answer: Mark it, guess, move on and come back if there's time.

problems.prompt: Is there a penalty for wrong guesses on AP multiple choice?

steps.title: Learn From Mistakes
steps.mastery: Keep a log of missed questions by topic, and drill the topics that show up most.
steps.practice: Log every wrong answer from 2 practice sets with its topic and the reason, then count which topic appears most.
steps.detail: A log turns a vague feeling of being bad at Java into a list like 'six misses on 2D arrays'. Note whether each miss was a content gap, a misread or a careless slip, because each one has a different fix. Drill the biggest group first.
steps.proof: A tally by topic, with the top one picked for next week's drill.
steps.pitfall: Redoing whole practice tests without looking at why you missed anything.

problems.prompt: Your log shows 6 misses on 2D arrays and 1 on strings. What should you drill?
You missed a question because you misread 'not'. What kind of error is that?
problems.answer: A reading error, not a content gap.

problems.prompt: You got 31 of 40 questions right. What percent is that, to the nearest whole number?

steps.title: Write a Method
steps.mastery: Write a static method with parameters and a return type, and call it from main.
steps.practice: Write static int square(int n) and call it with 7 from main, printing the result.
steps.detail: The header gives the return type, the name and each parameter's type and name. return hands back a value of that type and ends the method. A void method returns nothing. Calling it runs the body with the arguments copied into the parameters.
steps.proof: square(7) returns 49, which main prints.
steps.pitfall: Printing inside a method that's supposed to return the value.

problems.prompt: What does 'static int twice(int x) { return x * 2; }' return for twice(9)?
What return type fits a method like printBanner() that only prints?
Write the header for a static method avg that takes 2 doubles and returns a double.
problems.answer: static double avg(double a, double b)

steps.title: Parameters Are Copies
steps.mastery: Explain that primitive parameters are copies, so changing one inside a method leaves the caller's variable alone.
steps.practice: Write static void bump(int x) { x++; }, call it on n = 5, print n, and explain the result.
steps.detail: Java passes every argument by value. For a primitive, the method gets a copy of the number. For an object or array, it gets a copy of the reference, so it can change the object's contents but can't make the caller's variable point somewhere else.
steps.proof: n is still 5, because bump changed only its own copy.
steps.pitfall: Writing a swap method for two ints and expecting it to work.

problems.prompt: int n = 3; change(n); where change sets its parameter to 10. What is n afterward?
An array is passed to a method that sets arr[0] = 9. Does the caller see the change?
problems.answer: Yes. The method gets a copy of the reference to the same array.

problems.prompt: Why doesn't 'static void swap(int a, int b)' swap the caller's variables?
problems.answer: It only swaps its own copies.

steps.title: Overload a Method
steps.mastery: Overload a method with different parameter lists, and predict which version gets called.
steps.practice: Write 2 versions of area, one taking a side and one taking width and height, and call each one.
steps.detail: Methods can share a name if their parameter lists differ in number or types. Java picks the version that matches the arguments most closely. An int argument can widen to a double, but not the other way. Return type alone can't tell two versions apart.
steps.proof: area(5) gives 25 and area(3, 4) gives 12.
steps.pitfall: Writing two versions that differ only in return type, which won't compile.

problems.prompt: Can 2 methods named max differ only in return type?
problems.answer: No. The parameter lists must differ.

problems.prompt: max(int, int) and max(double, double) both exist. Which runs for max(3, 4)?
With those 2 versions, which runs for max(3, 4.5)?
problems.answer: max(double, double), since 3 widens to a double.

steps.title: Follow the Scope
steps.mastery: Tell which variables a block can see, and why a loop variable disappears after the loop.
steps.practice: Declare int i inside a 'for' loop, try to print i after the loop, read the error, and fix it.
steps.detail: A variable exists from its declaration to the closing brace of its block. A loop variable declared in the header lives only inside the loop. Each method has its own locals, so two methods can reuse a name without clashing.
steps.proof: The error is 'cannot find symbol'. Declaring i before the loop fixes it.
steps.pitfall: Declaring a variable inside an if block and trying to use it after.

problems.prompt: A variable is declared inside a 'for' loop's braces. Can you use it after the loop?
Can 2 different methods each have a local variable named count?
problems.answer: Yes. Each one is local to its own method.

problems.prompt: Which error does using an out-of-scope variable give: 'cannot find symbol' or 'missing return'?

steps.title: Return Early and Test
steps.mastery: Use early returns for special cases, and test a method with normal and edge inputs.
steps.practice: Write static boolean isPrime(int n) with an early return for n < 2, and test it on 1, 2, 9 and 13.
steps.detail: Handle the odd cases at the top and return right away, which keeps the main logic simple. Every path through a non-void method must return something, or it won't compile. Test with a normal case, the edges and anything that should fail.
steps.proof: false, true, false and true.
steps.pitfall: Forgetting a return at the end of the method, after the loop.

problems.prompt: isPrime(1) should return what?
Name 3 good test inputs for a method absolute(int x).
problems.answer: A positive number, a negative number and 0.

problems.prompt: What's wrong if a non-void method like getMax() has a path with no return?
problems.answer: It won't compile: missing return statement.

steps.title: Declared and Actual Types
steps.mastery: Tell a variable's declared type from the actual type of the object it holds.
steps.practice: Write Animal a = new Dog(); then name the declared type and the actual type, and try calling a Dog-only method.
steps.detail: The declared type is on the left, and it decides which methods the compiler lets you call. The actual type is what new built, and it decides which version of a method runs. A parent-type variable can hold any child object, but not the other way round.
steps.proof: Declared type Animal, actual type Dog, and the Dog-only call won't compile.
steps.pitfall: Expecting Dog-only methods to be callable through an Animal variable.

problems.prompt: In Animal a = new Cat(); what is the declared type?
Shape s = new Circle(2); Whose area() runs when you call s.area()?
Can you write Dog d = new Animal();?
problems.answer: No. An Animal isn't necessarily a Dog.

steps.title: Predict Which Method Runs
steps.mastery: Predict which overridden method runs: Java picks the actual object's version at run time.
steps.practice: Make an Animal array holding a Dog and a Cat, loop over it calling speak(), and predict each line.
steps.detail: Two checks happen. At compile time, Java checks that the declared type has the method. At run time, it calls the version belonging to the real object. That's why one loop over Animals can make each one speak its own way.
steps.proof: The loop prints Woof, then Meow.
steps.pitfall: Predicting the parent's version because the variable's type is Animal.

problems.prompt: Animal[] a = {new Dog(), new Cat()}; Dog says Woof and Cat says Meow. What does a[1].speak() print?
Animal a = new Dog(); a.fetch(); fetch exists only in Dog. Does it compile?
problems.answer: No. The compiler checks the declared type, Animal.

problems.prompt: How do you call fetch() on a, declared as Animal but holding a Dog?

steps.title: Cast Objects Safely
steps.mastery: Cast a reference down to its actual type, and check first with instanceof.
steps.practice: Loop over an Animal array and call fetch() only on the Dogs, using instanceof and a cast.
steps.detail: A downcast tells the compiler to treat the reference as the child type. If the object isn't really that type, the program crashes with ClassCastException. instanceof checks first, so the cast only runs when it's safe.
steps.proof: Each Dog fetches and the Cats are skipped, with no exception.
steps.pitfall: Casting without checking and crashing on the first Cat.

problems.prompt: What does 'a instanceof Dog' return when a holds a Cat?
Animal a = new Cat(); Dog d = (Dog) a; What happens at run time?
Why check 'instanceof' before casting?
problems.answer: So the cast can't fail at run time.

steps.title: Abstract Classes
steps.mastery: Use an abstract class for a parent that shouldn't be created on its own, with abstract methods the children must fill in.
steps.practice: Make Shape abstract with abstract double area(), then write Circle and Square that implement it.
steps.detail: An abstract method has a header and no body, and every concrete child must provide one. You can't create an object of an abstract class, but you can declare variables of its type. It can still hold fields and normal methods for the children to share.
steps.proof: new Shape() fails, while new Circle(2).area() works.
steps.pitfall: Giving an abstract method a body, which won't compile.

problems.prompt: Shape is abstract. Can you write new Shape()?
Circle extends the abstract Shape but doesn't write area(). What happens?
problems.answer: It won't compile, unless Circle is also abstract.

problems.prompt: Can an abstract class also have regular methods, like toString()?

steps.title: Use Interfaces
steps.mastery: Use an interface to promise a set of methods across classes that aren't related.
steps.practice: Write interface Scorable with int score(), and make both Player and Team implement it.
steps.detail: An interface lists method headers that a class promises to provide. A class can implement many interfaces but extend only one class. Comparable is the one you'll see most: implementing compareTo lets objects be sorted.
steps.proof: Player and Team both have score(), and a Scorable list can hold either one.
steps.pitfall: Writing extends for an interface instead of implements.

problems.prompt: A class can extend 1 class. How many interfaces can it implement?
Which keyword makes a class use an interface: 'extends' or 'implements'?
Comparable<Student> needs which method?

steps.title: Pick a Project
steps.mastery: Choose a Java project that uses classes and lists and fits in about 2 weeks.
steps.practice: List 3 project ideas, like a text adventure, a grade tracker or a card game, and pick one that uses at least 2 classes.
steps.detail: A good first project uses what you know, classes, lists and loops, plus one new thing. Something you'd use or play yourself keeps you going and gets tested properly. Giant ideas stall, so pick one you can finish and then grow.
steps.proof: One idea chosen, with 2 or more classes named.
steps.pitfall: Starting a full 3D game and quitting a week in.

problems.prompt: Which is a better 2-week project: a full 3D game engine or a Blackjack game?
problems.answer: A Blackjack game. It's finishable and uses classes and lists.

problems.prompt: Name 2 classes a Blackjack game might have.
problems.answer: Card and Deck, or Hand and Player.

problems.prompt: Why pick a project like a 'grade tracker' you'd actually use?
problems.answer: You'll test it more and want to fix its bugs.

steps.title: Plan the Classes
steps.mastery: Sketch the classes, their fields and their methods, before writing code.
steps.practice: Draw a class diagram for a library app with Book, Member and Library, listing 2 fields and 2 methods for each.
steps.detail: Decide which class owns each piece of data, and put the methods that use that data in the same class. A quick sketch shows problems, like two classes both tracking whether a book is out, before you've written 300 lines around them.
steps.proof: A diagram of 3 boxes, each with its fields and methods.
steps.pitfall: Putting everything in one giant class with dozens of methods.

problems.prompt: A Library holds many Books. Which field fits?
Which class should know whether a Book is checked out: Book or Member?
problems.answer: Book, with a field like checkedOut.

problems.prompt: Why sketch 3 classes before coding them?
problems.answer: It shows which class owns which data before you're deep in code.

steps.title: Build and Test in Steps
steps.mastery: Build one class at a time and test it in main before moving on.
steps.practice: Write the Card class, test toString on 3 cards in main, then start Deck only once Card works.
steps.detail: Testing each class alone means a bug can only be in the code you just wrote. Write a few lines in main that create objects and print results, and check them against what you expect. Then build the next class on top.
steps.proof: Card prints correctly for all 3 test cards before Deck exists.
steps.pitfall: Writing every class first and testing the whole program at the end.

problems.prompt: You finished Card. What should you do before writing Deck?
problems.answer: Test Card in main with a few examples.

problems.prompt: A standard Deck should hold how many cards?
Deck.deal() is called 53 times on a fresh deck. What should the 53rd call do?
problems.answer: Return null or throw an exception, since the deck is empty.

steps.title: Use the Standard Library
steps.mastery: Use Java's standard library, like Random, Scanner and Collections, instead of writing it yourself.
steps.practice: Shuffle a 52-card ArrayList with Collections.shuffle and read the player's choice with Scanner.
steps.detail: The standard library already has well-tested tools for common jobs. Random makes random numbers, Scanner reads input, Collections sorts and shuffles lists, and Math has the usual functions. Check the docs for what each method returns.
steps.proof: The deck comes out in a different order each run, and the player's typed choice is read.
steps.pitfall: Writing your own shuffle and getting an uneven one.

problems.prompt: Which call shuffles an ArrayList named deck?
Write the line that makes a Scanner reading from the keyboard.
rand.nextInt(6) returns which values?

steps.title: Go Beyond the Exam
steps.mastery: Take Java further with a desktop app, an Android app or a Minecraft mod.
steps.practice: Pick 1 path, JavaFX, Android Studio or a Minecraft Forge mod, and finish its official first tutorial.
steps.detail: The AP course covers the core language. Real projects add a framework on top: JavaFX for windows and buttons, Android for phone apps, Forge or Fabric for Minecraft. Each has a beginner tutorial that ends with something running.
steps.proof: One tutorial finished, with a window, an app or a mod running.
steps.pitfall: Trying all three at once and finishing none.

problems.prompt: Which tool do most people use to build Android apps?
Minecraft Java Edition mods are written in which language?
Name 1 thing a library like JavaFX adds over printing to the console.
problems.answer: Windows and buttons the user can click.

steps.title: Base Case and Recursive Case
steps.mastery: Write a recursive method with a base case that stops it and a recursive case that moves toward that stop.
steps.practice: Write factorial(n) with the base case n == 0, and trace factorial(4) by hand.
steps.detail: Every recursive method needs a case it can answer directly, and a case that calls itself on a smaller problem. Each call must get closer to the base case, or the calls never end. Then the answers pass back up the chain.
steps.proof: factorial(4) is 4 * 3 * 2 * 1 * 1, which is 24.
steps.pitfall: Forgetting the base case, so the method calls itself until the stack overflows.

problems.prompt: What is factorial(5)?
What happens if factorial(n) has no base case?
problems.answer: It recurses forever and throws StackOverflowError.

problems.prompt: For sum(n) = n + sum(n - 1), what's a good base case?

steps.title: Trace the Calls
steps.mastery: Trace recursive calls as a stack, writing each call and the value it returns.
steps.practice: Trace mystery(3), where mystery(n) returns 1 if n == 1, and n * 2 + mystery(n - 1) otherwise, writing every call.
steps.detail: Write the calls going down one per line, then fill in the returns going back up. Each call waits for the one below it to finish. This is exactly how the computer does it, and it's the fastest reliable way to answer recursion questions on paper.
steps.proof: mystery(3) = 6 + mystery(2) = 6 + 4 + mystery(1) = 11.
steps.pitfall: Adding the values on the way down, before the deeper calls have returned.

problems.prompt: f(n) returns 0 if n == 0, and 2 + f(n - 1) otherwise. What is f(4)?
g(n) returns 1 if n <= 1, and g(n - 1) + g(n - 2) otherwise. What is g(5)?
How many calls does f(4) make in total, counting f(4) itself?

steps.title: Recurse on Strings
steps.mastery: Recurse on strings by handling the first character and recursing on the rest.
steps.practice: Write reverse(s) that returns reverse(s.substring(1)) + s.charAt(0), with an empty-string base case, and trace "abc".
steps.detail: s.substring(1) is everything after the first character, so each call works on a shorter string. The empty string is the natural base case. Counting, reversing and checking palindromes all follow this pattern.
steps.proof: reverse("abc") = reverse("bc") + a = "cb" + a = "cba".
steps.pitfall: Using s.length() == 1 as the only base case, which crashes on an empty string.

problems.prompt: What does reverse("hey") return?
count(s) adds 1 if s.charAt(0) is 'a', then recurses on s.substring(1). What is count("banana")?
What base case suits a method that recurses on s.substring(1)?

steps.title: Recursion That Prints
steps.mastery: Predict the output when a print comes before or after the recursive call.
steps.practice: Trace 2 versions of countdown(3), one printing before the recursive call and one printing after it, and write each output.
steps.detail: A print before the call happens on the way down, so values come out in call order. A print after the call waits until the deeper calls finish, so values come out reversed. With prints on both sides, the output mirrors itself.
steps.proof: Before prints 3 2 1, and after prints 1 2 3.
steps.pitfall: Assuming the print always runs first no matter where it sits.

problems.prompt: p(n): if n > 0, print n and then call p(n - 1). What does p(3) print?
Now swap the order: q(n) calls q(n - 1) before printing n, for n >= 1. What appears for q(4)?
r(n): if n > 0, print n, call r(n - 1), then print n. What does r(2) print?

steps.title: Recursion or a Loop
steps.mastery: Decide when recursion is clearer than a loop, and rewrite a simple recursive method as a loop.
steps.practice: Rewrite recursive sum(n) as a for loop, then say which version reads better and which is safer for n = 100000.
steps.detail: Simple counting recursion is usually clearer as a loop, and a loop can't overflow the stack. Recursion shines when a problem splits into smaller copies of itself, like walking a tree or merge sort. The AP exam mostly asks you to trace it.
steps.proof: The loop version is safer for 100000, since recursion that deep overflows the stack.
steps.pitfall: Using recursion for everything because it looks clever.

problems.prompt: Write a loop version of factorial(n).
problems.answer: int r = 1; for (int i = 2; i <= n; i++) r *= i; return r;

problems.prompt: Why might recursive sum(100000) crash?
problems.answer: Too many calls overflow the stack.

problems.prompt: Name 1 task where recursion is usually clearer than a loop, like the one in merge sort.
problems.answer: Walking a tree, or splitting a list in merge sort.

steps.title: Linear Search
steps.mastery: Write a linear search that returns the index of a target, or -1 if it isn't there.
steps.practice: Write linearSearch(int[] a, int t) and test it on {4, 9, 2, 7} with the targets 2 and 5.
steps.detail: Check each element from the start until you find the target, and return its index. If the loop finishes, return -1. It works on any array, sorted or not, but in the worst case it checks every element.
steps.proof: It returns 2 for the target 2 and -1 for 5.
steps.pitfall: Returning -1 inside the loop on the first mismatch.

problems.prompt: How many comparisons does linear search make to find 7 in {4, 9, 2, 7}?
At most how many comparisons does binary search make on a sorted array of 1000?
problems.answer: 10, since each comparison halves what's left and 2^10 = 1024.

problems.prompt: Does linear search on {5, 2, 9} need the array sorted first?

steps.title: Binary Search
steps.mastery: Run binary search on a sorted array, halving the range at each step.
steps.practice: Trace binary search for 23 in {2, 5, 8, 12, 16, 23, 38, 56, 72, 91}, writing low, high and mid at each step.
steps.detail: Look at the middle. If it's the target, stop. If the target is bigger, search the right half, and if smaller, the left half. Each step halves what's left, so even a million items take only about 20 steps. The array must be sorted.
steps.proof: mid 4 holds 16, then mid 7 holds 56, then mid 5 holds 23, found in 3 steps.
steps.pitfall: Running binary search on an unsorted array.

problems.prompt: Each step of binary search halves the range. How many halvings take 1024 items down to 1?
Can binary search work on {5, 2, 9, 1}?
problems.answer: No. The array must be sorted first.

problems.prompt: In {1, 3, 5, 7, 9}, with low = 0 and high = 4, what is the first mid index?

steps.title: Selection Sort
steps.mastery: Trace selection sort, which swaps the smallest remaining item into place on each pass.
steps.practice: Trace selection sort on {29, 10, 14, 37, 13}, writing the array after each pass.
steps.detail: On pass i, find the smallest item from index i to the end and swap it into index i. After each pass, one more item is in its final place at the front. It always takes about n squared comparisons, even on sorted input.
steps.pitfall: Swapping every time a smaller item is found, instead of once per pass.

problems.prompt: After 1 pass of selection sort on {5, 3, 8, 1}, what is the array?
How many passes does selection sort need for 6 items?
For n = 1000 items, does selection sort take about n or about n squared steps?

steps.title: Insertion Sort
steps.mastery: Trace insertion sort, which slides each new item left into the sorted part.
steps.practice: Trace insertion sort on {7, 3, 5, 1}, writing the array after each insertion.
steps.detail: The left part is always sorted. Take the next item, shift bigger items in the sorted part one place right, and drop it into the gap. On nearly sorted data it's very fast, since few shifts are needed.
steps.pitfall: Confusing it with selection sort, which swaps the minimum into place.

problems.prompt: After 2 insertions on {4, 2, 6, 1}, what is the array?
On an already sorted array like {1, 2, 3, 4, 5}, is insertion sort fast or slow?
How many shifts does inserting 1 into the sorted part {2, 4, 6} take?

steps.title: Merge Sort
steps.mastery: Explain merge sort's split and merge steps, and why it runs in about n log n.
steps.practice: Split {38, 27, 43, 3} down to single items, then merge back up, writing each merged list.
steps.detail: Split the list in half again and again until each piece has one item. Then merge pairs of sorted pieces by taking the smaller front item each time. There are about log n levels of splitting and each level does about n work, giving n log n.
steps.pitfall: Merging by sticking the lists end to end without comparing.

problems.prompt: Merge the sorted lists {2, 7} and {3, 5}.
How many times can 8 items be split in half before each piece has 1 item?
Which is faster for 100,000 items: selection sort or merge sort?

steps.title: Install the JDK
steps.mastery: Install a JDK and confirm it works with java -version and javac -version.
steps.practice: Install JDK 21, then run 'java -version' and 'javac -version' and write down both numbers.
steps.detail: The JDK is the kit for writing Java: the compiler, javac, plus the runtime that runs your programs. If either command says it isn't found, the JDK's bin folder isn't on your PATH. Reopen the terminal after installing, since an open one won't see the change.
steps.proof: Both commands print 21 and some build details.
steps.pitfall: Installing only a JRE, which can run Java but has no compiler.

problems.prompt: Which command compiles Hello.java: 'javac Hello.java' or 'java -version'?
What does a JDK include that a plain runtime doesn't?
problems.answer: The compiler, javac, and other developer tools.

problems.prompt: Right after installing, 'javac' isn't recognized. What's the likely fix?
problems.answer: Add the JDK's bin folder to your PATH and reopen the terminal.

steps.title: Write a main Method
steps.mastery: Write a class with a public static void main(String[] args) method that prints a line.
steps.practice: Write Hello.java with a class Hello and a main method that prints 'Hello, Java', then compile and run it.
steps.detail: Every Java program starts in main. A public class must live in a file with exactly its name, so Hello goes in Hello.java. Statements end with semicolons, and braces mark where each block starts and ends. Case matters everywhere.
steps.proof: The terminal prints Hello, Java.
steps.pitfall: Naming the file hello.java when the class is Hello.

problems.prompt: A file holds 'public class Greeter'. What must the file be named?
Write the 1 line that prints Hi and moves to a new line.
What is missing from 'System.out.println("x")' inside main?

steps.title: Compile, Then Run
steps.mastery: Explain the 2 steps: javac turns source into bytecode, and java runs that bytecode on the JVM.
