Why might 'a chipped mug' say more than 'a poor house' in a 2 page scene?
problems.answer: A detail shows it instead of telling you.

steps.title: Read the Mood
steps.mastery: Say how a setting makes a reader feel.
steps.practice: Write 1 word for the mood of 3 opening paragraphs from 3 novels.
steps.detail: Atmosphere is how the place feels. Fog in 'Bleak House' fits a legal system that hides things. Writers choose words that all pull in one direction, so look for clusters of cold, dark or soft words.
steps.proof: 3 words with examples.
steps.pitfall: Naming the plot event when asked about the mood.

problems.prompt: 'Fog everywhere' opens which novel by Charles Dickens?
Words like 'damp', 'gray' and 'silent' appear 3 times in a page. What mood do they build?
What's the difference between a setting and a mood, in 1 line?
problems.answer: Setting is the place, and mood is how it feels.

steps.title: Link Place to Theme
steps.mastery: Show how a setting carries a book's ideas.
steps.practice: Explain in 1 paragraph how the Valley of Ashes works in 'The Great Gatsby'.
steps.detail: Places can stand for ideas. The Valley of Ashes sits between rich and poor, and shows what wealth leaves behind. The moors in 'Wuthering Heights' are as wild as the people on them. Ask what this place argues.
steps.proof: 1 paragraph.
steps.pitfall: Calling everything a symbol with no proof from the text.

problems.prompt: What lies between West Egg and New York in 'The Great Gatsby'?
The moors in 'Wuthering Heights' are wild. What do they match?
problems.answer: The wild passions of the characters.

problems.prompt: A house in 1 novel slowly falls apart as a family does. What's this technique called?

steps.title: Track Change in Place
steps.mastery: See how a move from one place shows a change in a character.
steps.practice: Map 3 places in 'Jane Eyre' and write how each 1 marks a stage in her life.
steps.detail: Many novels are built around moves. Jane Eyre goes from Gateshead to Lowood to Thornfield and beyond, and each place marks a stage in her growth. Note the moment someone leaves or returns, and how the same place looks different.
steps.proof: A map of 3 places.
steps.pitfall: Treating a change of place as just plot with no meaning.

problems.prompt: Name the school in 'Jane Eyre', from 1847.
A hero returns to his hometown after 20 years and it looks small. What has changed?
Why does Gatsby's mansion feel empty at the end of the 9 chapters?
problems.answer: The people came only for the parties.

steps.title: Write with Atmosphere
steps.mastery: Write a short passage that builds a clear mood.
steps.practice: Write a 100 word description of 1 room in 2 versions, one tense and one calm.
steps.detail: You learn a lot by trying it yourself. Change a few details and verbs, and the same room feels different. A clock that ticks can be cozy or scary. Avoid naming the mood, and let the details do the work.
steps.proof: 2 versions of 100 words.
steps.pitfall: Writing 'it was scary' in place of giving details that scare.

problems.prompt: Rewrite 'the room was scary' with 1 detail.
problems.answer: The door behind her clicked shut by itself.

problems.prompt: Which should you do in 100 words: name the mood or show it?
A clock ticks in 2 scenes. How can it feel calm in 1 and tense in the other?
problems.answer: It depends on what's around it and what's about to happen.

steps.title: State a Theme as a Claim
steps.mastery: Write a theme as a full sentence that makes a claim.
steps.practice: Rewrite 5 one word topics like 'love' as full claims about love.
steps.detail: 'Love' is a topic. 'Love can make people cruel' is a theme, since it says something you could disagree with. A theme is a claim about life that the book as a whole makes. Keep it specific, and don't moralize.
steps.proof: 5 claims.
steps.pitfall: Writing a one word answer or a moral like 'be nice'.

problems.prompt: Is 'power' on its own a theme or a topic? Pick 1.
Rewrite the topic 'death' as a 1 sentence theme.
problems.answer: Knowing we'll die can make the small things matter more.

problems.prompt: Why is 'be nice to others' a weak theme for a 300 page novel?
problems.answer: It's a moral, and too simple.

steps.title: Back It with Scenes
steps.mastery: Support a theme with specific moments from the text.
steps.practice: Choose 1 theme in 'Lord of the Flies' and find 3 scenes that support it.
steps.detail: A theme claim needs proof. Find moments where it appears, and also ones that push back. In 'Lord of the Flies' the killing of Piggy shows how fast order fails. Use the text, not your general feeling about it.
steps.proof: 3 scenes with page numbers.
steps.pitfall: Using plot summary as proof with no specific moment.

problems.prompt: Which moment in 'Lord of the Flies' shows order failing near the end?
How many scenes should you find for a short theme claim: 1 or 3?
You find 1 scene that pushes back on your theme. What do you do?
problems.answer: Deal with it, and refine the claim.

steps.title: Find Tensions
steps.mastery: See how a book pulls between two ideas.
steps.practice: List 3 pairs of opposing ideas in 'Frankenstein' such as creation and responsibility.
steps.detail: Rich books don't just preach, they argue with themselves. 'Frankenstein' pulls between the thrill of discovery and the duty to what you've made. Look for pairs that keep colliding, and ask where the book finally lands.
steps.proof: 3 pairs.
steps.pitfall: Forcing one neat lesson onto a book that doesn't give one.

problems.prompt: Name 1 pair of opposing ideas in 'Frankenstein', from 1818.
A novel keeps pitting duty against love for 400 pages and never decides. Is that a flaw? Answer yes or no.
problems.answer: No, that tension can be the point.

problems.prompt: Who pays for Victor's discovery in the 1818 novel?
problems.answer: The people he loves, and the creature.

steps.title: Compare Two Treatments
steps.mastery: Compare how two works handle the same theme.
steps.practice: Compare ambition in 'Macbeth' and 'The Great Gatsby' in 200 words.
steps.detail: Same theme, different claim. Ambition destroys Macbeth because of what he does for it. Gatsby's ruins him because the dream itself was empty. Comparing shows how a theme isn't a single answer, and shows each writer's real stance.
steps.proof: 200 words.
steps.pitfall: Listing facts about each book side by side and never connecting them.

problems.prompt: Name the theme shared by 'Macbeth' and 'The Great Gatsby', in 1 word.
What destroys Macbeth in the end of Act 5?
problems.answer: What he did to get power.

problems.prompt: How does comparing 2 books sharpen a theme?
problems.answer: It shows each writer's specific claim.

steps.title: Avoid Easy Readings
steps.mastery: Test a theme claim against what a critic might say.
steps.practice: Write 1 objection to your theme claim for a 200 page novel and then answer it.
steps.detail: If nobody could disagree, the claim isn't saying much. Try to knock it down yourself. Ask who it leaves out and which scene doesn't fit. A claim that survives this will make for a much better essay, with some real thinking in it.
steps.proof: 1 objection and 1 reply.
steps.pitfall: Taking the first theme you think of and never testing it.

problems.prompt: Your claim is 'war is bad'. Why's that weak in a 400 page novel?
problems.answer: Nobody would disagree, so it says little.

problems.prompt: Name 1 way to test a claim about 'Hamlet', with its 5 acts.
problems.answer: Find a scene that doesn't fit it.

problems.prompt: What should you do with an objection you can't answer?

steps.title: Try a Feminist Reading
steps.mastery: Read a work for how it treats gender and power.
steps.practice: Read 'The Yellow Wallpaper' and write 3 lines on who has power over whom.
steps.detail: A feminist reading asks who gets to speak and decide. In 'The Yellow Wallpaper', a husband's medical care is also control. Look at what's allowed, who's silenced and what the story assumes about women. Back it with the text.
steps.proof: 3 lines with quotes.
steps.pitfall: Just counting how many women are in the book.

problems.prompt: Who holds power over the narrator of 'The Yellow Wallpaper' from 1892?
Name 1 question a feminist reading asks of a 300 page novel.
problems.answer: Who gets to speak and decide?

problems.prompt: Is counting the 2 women in a novel enough for a feminist reading? Answer yes or no.
problems.answer: No, it needs to look at power and voice.

steps.title: Try a Marxist Reading
steps.mastery: Read a work for class and money.
steps.practice: Note every mention of money in 3 chapters of 'The Great Gatsby' and say whom it serves.
steps.detail: A Marxist reading looks at class and who gains. In 'The Great Gatsby', old money sneers at new, and the poor pay for the rich's carelessness. Ask who works, who owns, and what the book takes for granted about wealth.
steps.proof: A list of mentions.
steps.pitfall: Saying only that it's a book about rich people.

problems.prompt: Who pays for Tom and Daisy's actions in the last 2 chapters of 'The Great Gatsby'?
Name 2 things a Marxist reading looks at.
How do old money and new money clash in the 1925 novel?
problems.answer: Tom's set looks down on Gatsby.

steps.title: Try a Postcolonial Reading
steps.mastery: Read a work for empire and who gets a voice.
steps.practice: Read Chinua Achebe's essay on 'Heart of Darkness' and write 2 points he makes.
steps.detail: A postcolonial reading looks at empire. Chinua Achebe argued that 'Heart of Darkness' turns Africans into a backdrop for a white man's crisis. Ask who gets a voice, and which places are treated as just scenery.
steps.proof: 2 points.
steps.pitfall: Thinking this only applies to books set in colonies.

problems.prompt: Who wrote a famous 1975 critique of 'Heart of Darkness'?
What was his main charge about Africans in the novel of 1899?
problems.answer: They're treated as a backdrop with no voice.

problems.prompt: Why might 'Jane Eyre' from 1847 draw a postcolonial reading?
problems.answer: Bertha comes from the colonies and is silenced.

steps.title: Try Psychoanalytic Reading
steps.mastery: Read characters for hidden desire and fear.
steps.practice: Write 1 paragraph on Hamlet's delay using Sigmund Freud's idea of repressed desire.
steps.detail: This approach, from Freud, looks for what people hide from themselves. It's why Hamlet's delay gets read as something he can't face. Dreams, slips and repeating patterns are all clues. Treat it as a question to try, not a final proof.
steps.proof: 1 paragraph.
steps.pitfall: Diagnosing a fictional person as if they were a patient.

problems.prompt: Who founded psychoanalysis around 1900?
Which of Hamlet's 2 problems gets a famous Freudian reading: his delay or his height?
Name 1 kind of clue this approach looks for in a 200 page novel.

steps.title: Choose and Combine
steps.mastery: Choose the lens that opens up the most in a given text.
steps.practice: Read 1 short story through 3 lenses and pick the 1 that says the most new.
steps.detail: No lens is the right one for everything. A lens that works should show you something you didn't see. Try a few, and pick the one that does the most. Don't use theory to replace reading, because the text must still come first.
steps.proof: 1 page with a choice.
steps.pitfall: Using theory words to sound smart, without saying anything new.

problems.prompt: How do you judge a lens on a short story of 10 pages?
problems.answer: By what new things it shows.

problems.prompt: Name 3 lenses you could use on 'Frankenstein', from 1818.
A lens says nothing new about a poem. What should you do?

steps.title: Place a Movement
steps.mastery: Name the main literary periods and when they happened.
steps.practice: Make a time line of 5 movements from Romanticism to Postmodernism with 1 writer each.
steps.detail: Movements are labels that help us see patterns. Romanticism loved feeling and nature around 1800. Realism looked at ordinary life. Modernism broke form after World War 1. Dates are rough, and many writers don't fit.
steps.proof: A time line of 5.
steps.pitfall: Treating these dates as hard walls.

problems.prompt: Roughly when did Romanticism peak: 1800 or 1950?
Which movement grew after World War 1: Realism or Modernism?
Name 1 Romantic poet from around 1800.

steps.title: Read Against the Times
steps.mastery: Explain how a work reacts to what came before.
steps.practice: Compare 1 page each of George Eliot and Virginia Woolf on a character's thoughts.
steps.detail: Movements are often arguments. The Modernists felt that the old realist novel couldn't capture how thought feels, so Woolf tried to write the moving mind. You understand the change by reading both, side by side.
steps.proof: 1 paragraph.
steps.pitfall: Learning a list of traits without reading a page.

problems.prompt: What did Virginia Woolf try to capture, instead of a plain plot, in 1925?
Name the term for prose that follows a mind's flow, in 3 words.
George Eliot's 'Middlemarch' from 1871 belongs to which movement?

steps.title: Trace an Influence
steps.mastery: Follow how one work echoes in a later one.
steps.practice: Find 3 echoes of 'The Odyssey' in James Joyce's 'Ulysses' using a guide.
steps.detail: Writers read each other. Joyce sets his modern Dublin day against Homer's epic, so a small day takes on a huge shape. Look for borrowed plots, lines and names, then ask what the new writer changes and why.
steps.proof: 3 echoes with notes.
steps.pitfall: Calling every similarity an influence, with no evidence.

problems.prompt: Which ancient epic shapes James Joyce's 'Ulysses' from 1922?
'West Side Story' reworks which play from about 1595?
Name 1 thing to check before saying A influenced B in 1 essay.
problems.answer: That B could have read A.

steps.title: Know Key Traditions
steps.mastery: See that traditions exist beyond one country.
steps.practice: Read 1 poem each from the Tang dynasty and the Harlem Renaissance and note 1 feature of each.
steps.detail: There's no one tradition. Tang poets like Du Fu wrote brief, exact poems on loss. The Harlem Renaissance in the 1920s brought Black American voices like Langston Hughes to the center. Each has its own rules.
steps.proof: 2 poems with notes.
steps.pitfall: Assuming 'tradition' means only European books.

problems.prompt: Who wrote 'I, Too' in the Harlem Renaissance of the 1920s?
Name 1 poet of China's Tang dynasty.
Why might an 8th century Chinese poem read differently from a Romantic one?
problems.answer: It comes from other forms and values.

steps.title: Question the Label
steps.mastery: Point out when a movement label doesn't fit.
steps.practice: Choose 1 writer who doesn't fit a label and argue it in 150 words.
steps.detail: Labels get made after the fact, and they can hide things. Was Emily Dickinson a Romantic? She doesn't quite fit. Women and writers of color were often left out when labels were made. Use a label as a start, then push on it.
steps.proof: 150 words.
steps.pitfall: Forcing a writer into a box to finish the essay.

problems.prompt: Why is it hard to label Emily Dickinson from the 1860s?
problems.answer: Her style doesn't match any group of the time.

problems.prompt: Of 2 groups, writers of the time or later critics, who usually names a movement?
Name 1 risk of learning 5 labels and nothing else.
problems.answer: You read the label and not the book.

steps.title: Compare Two Translations
steps.mastery: See how translations of one text differ.
steps.practice: Compare the first 5 lines of 2 translations of 'The Odyssey', such as Fagles and Wilson.
steps.detail: Every translation is an interpretation. Emily Wilson opens 'The Odyssey' with 'Tell me about a complicated man', and it changes how we see Odysseus. Reading two side by side shows you what's the writer and what's the translator.
steps.proof: 2 passages with notes.
steps.pitfall: Assuming there's a single correct version.

problems.prompt: Who translated 'The Odyssey' in 2017 with 'Tell me about a complicated man'?
Why is every translation of a 2,000 year old work an interpretation?
problems.answer: The translator has to make choices.

problems.prompt: Name 1 thing to compare in 2 versions of 5 lines.

steps.title: Weigh Literal and Free
steps.mastery: Weigh closeness to the original against how it reads.
steps.practice: Translate 1 idiom literally and freely, such as 'it's raining cats and dogs'.
steps.detail: A literal version stays close to the words, but can sound odd. A free one reads well but moves away from the source. Translators keep deciding. Idioms make it clear, because a word-for-word version may mean nothing in the other language.
steps.proof: 2 versions.
steps.pitfall: Thinking literal always means faithful.

problems.prompt: What's lost if 'raining cats and dogs' goes word for word into French?
problems.answer: The sense, since it means nothing there.

problems.prompt: Name the 2 poles translators weigh.
Does literal always mean more faithful? Answer yes or no.
problems.answer: No, it can lose the meaning.

steps.title: Spot What Can't Carry
steps.mastery: Notice what's lost in translation.
steps.practice: Find 3 puns or rhymes in 1 Shakespeare scene and say what a Spanish version loses.
steps.detail: Puns, rhyme and wordplay hardly ever carry over. Neither do social cues like the French 'tu' and 'vous'. A translator might add a note or swap in a new joke. Knowing what's lost helps you read with more care.
steps.proof: 3 examples.
steps.pitfall: Blaming a translator for what no one could do.

problems.prompt: What cue do 'tu' and 'vous' in French carry that 'you' in English doesn't?
problems.answer: How formal or close they are.

problems.prompt: Name 2 things that hardly ever carry over in 1 line of verse.
What can a translator do with a joke that fails in 1 language?
problems.answer: Swap in a new one or add a note.

steps.title: Value the Translator
steps.mastery: Treat the translator as a writer whose choices matter.
steps.practice: Find 1 translator's note in a novel and write 2 lines on what it reveals.
steps.detail: Translators have often gone unnamed on the cover. Edith Grossman's version of 'Don Quixote' is hers as well as his. Read the notes. Ask who chose this book and why. Look at who gets translated, which also shapes who gets read.
steps.proof: 2 lines.
steps.pitfall: Saying 'I read Tolstoy' as if there was no translator.

problems.prompt: Who wrote a well known 2003 English 'Don Quixote'?
Where can you often read about a translator's choices in a 500 page novel?
Name 1 thing a translator affects, besides the words, in 1 book.

steps.title: Read in the Original
steps.mastery: Use even basic language skill to check a translation.
steps.practice: Read 1 short Spanish poem with a dictionary and compare it with 1 English version.
steps.detail: Even a little knowledge of a language lets you see choices. Take a short poem and work through it word by word. Then see what a translator did. You'll notice how much sound and order get lost, and what's been added.
steps.proof: 1 poem with notes.
steps.pitfall: Waiting to be fluent before you try anything.

problems.prompt: Do you need to be fluent to compare 1 short poem with a translation? Answer yes or no.
problems.answer: No, a dictionary can get you started.

problems.prompt: Name 2 things in a Spanish poem an English version often changes.
Why start with a poem of 10 lines over a 500 page novel?
problems.answer: You can actually finish and look closely.

steps.title: State a Clear Claim
steps.mastery: Write a thesis that takes a debatable position.
steps.practice: Rewrite 3 weak thesis statements, such as "Phones are interesting", into debatable claims.
steps.detail: A strong claim can be argued against. "Schools should ban phones during class" is debatable, while "Phones exist" is not.
steps.proof: All 3 claims are debatable and specific.
steps.pitfall: Writing a fact or a topic instead of a claim.

problems.prompt: Is "Many students own phones." a debatable claim? Answer yes or no.
Turn the topic "phones at school" into a claim someone could argue against.
problems.answer: For example: Schools should ban phones during class.

problems.prompt: What makes a thesis 'debatable'?
problems.answer: A reasonable person could disagree with it.

steps.title: Give Reasons and Evidence
steps.mastery: Support a claim with 2 or 3 reasons, each backed by evidence.
steps.practice: Outline an argument with 1 claim, 3 reasons and 1 piece of evidence for each reason.
steps.detail: Reasons answer why the claim is true. Evidence shows each reason is true. Without evidence, a reason is just another claim.
steps.proof: Your outline has 3 reasons, each with evidence.
steps.pitfall: Listing reasons with no evidence.

problems.prompt: 3 reasons with 1 piece of evidence each is how many pieces of evidence?
Is "because it is better" a strong reason? Answer yes or no.
Name 1 kind of evidence for "Later school start times help students."
problems.answer: A study showing improved sleep or grades after a later start.

steps.title: Address the Counterargument
steps.mastery: Present the strongest opposing view and respond to it.
steps.practice: Write a 4-sentence paragraph that states the strongest objection to your claim and answers it.
steps.detail: Acknowledging the other side builds trust. Use phrases like "Some argue that..." and then explain why your position still holds.
steps.proof: The paragraph fairly states and answers 1 objection.
steps.pitfall: Ignoring the other side or attacking a weak version of it.

problems.prompt: Start a counterargument sentence for "Schools should ban phones".
problems.answer: For example: Some argue that phones help students research in class.

problems.prompt: What is it called when you argue against a weak, twisted version of the 'other side'?
Why include 1 counterargument paragraph?
problems.answer: It shows fairness and makes your argument more convincing.

steps.title: Spot Logical Fallacies
steps.mastery: Recognize common fallacies in arguments.
steps.practice: Name the fallacy in 5 statements, such as "Everyone is buying it, so it must be good."
steps.detail: Common fallacies: bandwagon (everyone does it), ad hominem (attack the person), false dilemma (only 2 options), slippery slope (one step leads to disaster).
steps.proof: All 5 fallacies are named correctly.
steps.pitfall: Using fallacies in your own arguments without noticing.

problems.prompt: Name the fallacy: "Everyone is buying it, so it must be good."
Name the fallacy: "You can't trust his math, he's only 15."
Name the fallacy: "Either we ban cars or the planet is doomed."

steps.title: Conclude Persuasively
steps.mastery: End an argument by restating the claim and its importance.
steps.practice: Write a 3-sentence conclusion that restates your claim in new words, sums up the reasons and gives a call to action.
steps.detail: A conclusion reminds readers what you proved and why it matters. Do not introduce brand-new evidence.
steps.proof: The conclusion has 3 sentences with a call to action.
steps.pitfall: Ending with a new argument the essay never supported.

problems.prompt: Should a conclusion introduce new evidence? Answer yes or no.
Name 3 parts of a strong conclusion.
problems.answer: A restated claim, a summary of reasons and a call to action.

problems.prompt: Write a call to action for an essay titled "Schools Should Recycle".
problems.answer: For example: Ask your principal to add recycling bins this semester.

steps.title: Know When to Cite
steps.mastery: Cite quotations, paraphrases, data and ideas that are not common knowledge.
steps.practice: Mark which of 8 sentences in a draft need a citation and which are common knowledge.
steps.detail: Cite direct quotes, paraphrased ideas and specific facts or numbers from a source. Widely known facts, like the year World War II ended, do not need one.
steps.proof: All 8 are marked correctly.
steps.pitfall: Citing only direct quotes and not paraphrased ideas.

problems.prompt: Does a paraphrased idea from an article need a citation? Answer yes or no.
Does "Water boils at 100 degrees Celsius at sea level" need a citation? Answer yes or no.
Does a statistic like "62% of teens" from a survey need a citation? Answer yes or no.

steps.title: MLA In-Text Citations
steps.mastery: Write MLA in-text citations with author and page.
steps.practice: Add MLA in-text citations to 3 quotes from a book by Smith on pages 12, 45 and 88.
steps.detail: MLA uses the author's last name and page number in parentheses, with no comma: (Smith 45). If the author is named in the sentence, give only the page.
steps.proof: All 3 citations are formatted correctly.
steps.pitfall: Writing (Smith, page 45) in MLA.

problems.prompt: Write the MLA in-text citation for page 45 of a book by Smith.
The sentence says "Smith argues...". What citation follows the quote from page 12?
Is there a comma between author and page in MLA in-text citations? Answer yes or no.

steps.title: APA In-Text Citations
steps.mastery: Write APA in-text citations with author and year.
steps.practice: Add APA in-text citations for a 2021 article by Lee and a 2019 article by Park and Kim.
steps.detail: APA uses the author and year: (Lee, 2021). For 2 authors use '&' in parentheses: (Park & Kim, 2019). Add a page for direct quotes.
steps.proof: Both citations are formatted correctly.
steps.pitfall: Leaving out the year, which APA requires.

problems.prompt: Write the APA in-text citation for a 2021 article by Lee.
Write it for a 2019 article by Park and Kim.
What does APA add for a direct quote from page 7 of Lee 2021?

steps.title: Works Cited Lists
steps.mastery: Build a correctly ordered works cited or reference list.
steps.practice: Write a works cited list for 4 sources in MLA format, in alphabetical order by author.
steps.detail: Entries go in alphabetical order by the first author's last name. Use a hanging indent. Every in-text citation needs a matching entry.
steps.proof: 4 entries in alphabetical order with hanging indents.
steps.pitfall: Ordering entries by the order you used them.

problems.prompt: Order these authors: Park, Adams, Lee.
What indent style do MLA works cited entries use?
You cited 5 sources in the text. How many works cited entries should there be?

steps.title: Avoid Plagiarism
steps.mastery: Use quotes, paraphrase and citation to keep others' work clearly marked.
steps.practice: Check a 300-word draft against its 3 sources and fix any copied phrase of 4 or more words.
steps.detail: Plagiarism includes copying without quotes, close paraphrase and missing citations. When in doubt, quote and cite.
steps.proof: No uncited or unquoted copied phrases remain.
steps.pitfall: Changing a few words of a sentence and not citing it.

problems.prompt: A sentence copies 6 words from a source without quotes. Is that plagiarism? Answer yes or no.
Name 2 ways to use a source's words honestly.
problems.answer: Quote it with quotation marks and a citation, or paraphrase with a citation.

problems.prompt: Is submitting your own old essay again without permission ever a problem? Answer yes or no.
problems.answer: Yes, it can count as self-plagiarism.

steps.title: Annotate the Text
steps.mastery: Mark a passage with notes on word choice, questions and patterns.
steps.practice: Annotate a 1-page poem or passage with at least 8 marginal notes on word choice, images and questions.
steps.detail: Annotation is thinking on paper. Circle striking words, underline key lines, write questions in the margin. Patterns appear when you mark as you read.
steps.proof: The page has 8 or more notes.
steps.pitfall: Highlighting whole paragraphs without writing anything.

problems.prompt: A page has 8 notes over 4 paragraphs. How many notes per paragraph on average?
Name 2 things worth circling while annotating.
Why write 8 margin notes instead of only highlighting?
problems.answer: Writing forces you to think about why it matters.

steps.title: Word Choice
steps.mastery: Explain why an author chose a specific word over a similar one.
steps.practice: Compare 3 word choices in a passage, such as 'stumbled' against 'walked', and explain the effect of each.
steps.detail: Connotation is the feeling a word carries beyond its dictionary meaning. 'Slender' and 'skinny' mean similar things but feel different.
steps.proof: Each comparison explains a different effect.
steps.pitfall: Saying a word was chosen 'to make it interesting'.

problems.prompt: Which word sounds more positive: 'slender' or 'skinny'?
What feeling does 'stumbled' add compared with 'walked'?
What term names the warm feeling 'home' carries that 'house' does not?

steps.title: Imagery and Figurative Language
steps.mastery: Identify similes, metaphors and personification and explain their effect.
steps.practice: Find 1 simile, 1 metaphor and 1 example of personification in a poem and explain what each suggests.
steps.detail: A simile compares using 'like' or 'as'. A metaphor says one thing is another. Personification gives human traits to non-human things. Always ask what the comparison suggests.
steps.proof: Each device is named and its effect explained.
steps.pitfall: Naming the device without explaining its effect.

problems.prompt: Is "Her smile was sunshine" a simile or a metaphor?
Is "The wind whispered" a simile or personification?
What does "as cold as ice" suggest about a person's manner?
problems.answer: That they are unfriendly or distant.

steps.title: Structure and Shifts
steps.mastery: Notice how a text is organized and where its tone or focus shifts.
steps.practice: Mark the shift in a 14-line sonnet and explain how the poem's tone changes after it.
steps.detail: Structure carries meaning. A shift (often marked by 'but' or 'yet') can turn a poem from problem to answer. In many sonnets it comes around line 9 or line 13.
steps.proof: You mark the line of the shift and describe the change.
steps.pitfall: Reading the poem as having one unchanging tone.

problems.prompt: How many lines does a Shakespearean sonnet have?
Name 2 words that often signal a shift.
Around which line does the turn often come in a Petrarchan sonnet?

steps.title: Write a Close Reading
steps.mastery: Write a paragraph that makes a claim about a passage and supports it with quoted details.
steps.practice: Write a 150-word paragraph claiming how 2 word choices in a passage create a mood, quoting both.
steps.detail: State a claim, quote short evidence, and explain how the words create the effect. Quote phrases, not whole paragraphs.
steps.proof: The paragraph has a claim, 2 quotes and explanations.
steps.pitfall: Summarizing the plot instead of analyzing language.

problems.prompt: In a 150-word close reading, should you quote whole paragraphs or short phrases?
A 150-word paragraph quotes 2 words. How many explanations should follow?
Is "The story is about a boy who gets lost" analysis or summary?

steps.title: Cut Wordiness
steps.mastery: Remove unnecessary words without losing meaning.
steps.practice: Cut a 300-word draft by 20% by removing filler phrases like 'in order to' and 'the fact that'.
steps.detail: Most first drafts carry about one fifth extra words. 'Due to the fact that' becomes 'because'. 'In order to' becomes 'to'.
steps.proof: The draft is 240 words or fewer with the same meaning.
steps.pitfall: Cutting so hard that meaning is lost.

problems.prompt: 20% of a 300-word draft is how many words?
Shorten "due to the fact that".
Shorten "at this point in time".

steps.title: Active Voice
steps.mastery: Rewrite passive sentences in active voice when the actor matters.
steps.practice: Change 5 passive sentences, such as "The ball was kicked by Sam", to active voice.
steps.detail: Active voice puts the actor first and is usually shorter and clearer. Passive voice is useful when the actor is unknown or unimportant.
steps.proof: All 5 are in active voice.
steps.pitfall: Using passive voice to hide who did something.

problems.prompt: Rewrite "The ball was kicked by Sam." in active voice.
Is "Mistakes were made." active or passive?
How many words shorter is "Sam kicked the ball" than "The ball was kicked by Sam"?

steps.title: Reorder for Clarity
steps.mastery: Rearrange sentences and paragraphs so the argument flows.
steps.practice: Cut a 5-paragraph essay into pieces and rearrange the paragraphs in the most logical order.
steps.detail: Order matters: general to specific, or least to most important. Moving a paragraph can fix a confusing argument without rewriting a word.
steps.proof: The new order has a clear reason you can state.
steps.pitfall: Keeping the order you happened to write in.

problems.prompt: Name 2 common logical orders for paragraphs.
problems.answer: Chronological, and least to most important.

problems.prompt: Your strongest reason is in paragraph 2 of 4. Where might it go for impact?
problems.answer: Last, in the final body paragraph.

problems.prompt: 5 paragraphs can be arranged in how many orders?

steps.title: Read Aloud
steps.mastery: Read your draft aloud to catch awkward phrasing and errors.
steps.practice: Read a 1-page draft aloud and mark every place you stumble or run out of breath, then revise those spots.
steps.detail: Your ear catches what your eye skips: missing words, repeated words and sentences that are too long.
steps.proof: Every marked spot is revised.
steps.pitfall: Silently skimming your own writing and missing errors.

problems.prompt: You stumbled 6 times on 1 page. How many spots need revising?
Name 2 problems reading aloud catches.
problems.answer: Missing words and overly long sentences.

problems.prompt: Running out of breath on 1 sentence suggests what?

steps.title: Final Proofread
steps.mastery: Proofread the final draft for spelling, grammar and formatting.
steps.practice: Proofread a 1-page final draft backward, sentence by sentence from the end, and fix every error.
steps.detail: Reading backward stops you following the meaning, so you see each sentence fresh. Check names, numbers and formatting last.
steps.proof: No errors remain on a final check.
steps.pitfall: Proofreading only on screen right after writing.

problems.prompt: Why proofread a 1-page draft backward?
problems.answer: You focus on each sentence instead of the flow.

problems.prompt: You found 5 errors in a 500-word draft. How many per 100 words?
Name 2 things to check last when proofreading.

steps.title: Active Listening
steps.mastery: Show and practice attention with eye contact, nods and follow-up questions.
steps.practice: During a 5-minute conversation, ask 2 follow-up questions about what the other person said.
steps.detail: Active listening means following the speaker's meaning, not planning your reply. Follow-up questions prove and deepen understanding.
steps.proof: You asked 2 relevant follow-up questions.
steps.pitfall: Thinking about your answer while the other person is still speaking.

problems.prompt: Name 1 nonverbal sign of active listening.
Write a follow-up question to "I had a tough week."
problems.answer: For example: What made it tough?

problems.prompt: In a 5-minute talk you asked 2 questions. Is that active listening? Answer yes or no.

steps.title: Paraphrase the Speaker
steps.mastery: Restate what someone said in your own words to check understanding.
steps.practice: In a discussion, restate 3 classmates' points with "So you're saying..." before responding.
steps.detail: Paraphrasing catches misunderstandings early and shows respect. If you get it wrong, the speaker can correct you.
steps.proof: 3 paraphrases are confirmed as accurate by the speakers.
steps.pitfall: Restating a twisted version of the point to argue against it.

problems.prompt: Complete a paraphrase of "I think tests cause too much stress."
problems.answer: So you're saying tests make students too stressed?

problems.prompt: Why say "So you're saying" before responding?
A speaker corrects your paraphrase. What does that tell you?

steps.title: Take Listening Notes
steps.mastery: Note the main points and evidence from a talk you hear once.
steps.practice: Listen to a 10-minute podcast segment once and write its main claim and 3 supporting points.
steps.detail: Without a text to reread, listen for signposts like 'first' and 'the key point is'. Write phrases, not sentences.
steps.proof: Your notes have 1 claim and 3 points.
steps.pitfall: Writing so much that you miss the next point.

problems.prompt: Name 2 signpost phrases that flag key points.
problems.answer: First and the key point is.

problems.prompt: A 10-minute segment has 3 main points. How many minutes per point on average?
Should notes on a 10-minute podcast be full sentences or short phrases?

steps.title: Steelman a View
steps.mastery: Restate the strongest version of a view you disagree with.
steps.practice: Write the strongest 3-sentence case for a position you oppose, as its supporters would put it.
steps.detail: If you can state the other side so well that its supporters agree, you understand the debate. This is the opposite of a straw man.
steps.proof: A supporter of that view would accept your summary.
steps.pitfall: Arguing against the weakest version of the other side.

problems.prompt: What is the opposite of a "straw man" argument called?
Why make the 'steelman' case before arguing against a view?
problems.answer: It shows you understand it and makes your response stronger.

problems.prompt: A supporter reads your summary of their view and says "That's not what we think." What went wrong?
problems.answer: You missed their strongest version, so redo it.

steps.title: Listen for Bias
steps.mastery: Notice loaded language and missing perspectives in what you hear.
steps.practice: Listen to 2 news clips on the same story and list 3 differences in word choice.
steps.detail: Loaded words like 'scheme' versus 'plan' push a view. Noticing them helps you separate facts from framing.
steps.proof: You list 3 word-choice differences.
steps.pitfall: Accepting the framing along with the facts.

problems.prompt: Which word is more loaded: 'plan' or 'scheme'?
Name 1 sign a source may be biased.
problems.answer: Loaded language (or only one side quoted).

problems.prompt: 2 clips describe 1 event as a 'protest' and a 'riot'. What does that show?
problems.answer: Different framing of the same event.

steps.title: Cornell Notes
steps.mastery: Set up and use the Cornell note format during a lesson.
steps.practice: Divide a page into 3 parts (notes, cues and a summary) and take Cornell notes in your next class.
steps.detail: Notes go in the right column during class. Afterward, write questions or cues on the left and a 2 or 3 sentence summary at the bottom. Covering the notes and answering the cues is built-in review.
steps.proof: The page has notes, at least 5 cues and a summary.
steps.pitfall: Filling the page and skipping the cues and summary.

problems.prompt: How many sections does a Cornell page have?
Where do the cue questions go on a Cornell page: left column or bottom?
How long should the bottom summary be: 2 or 3 sentences or a full page?

steps.title: Write Less, Mean More
steps.mastery: Capture key ideas in short phrases instead of copying sentences.
steps.practice: Take notes on a 10-minute talk in no more than 15 lines using abbreviations and phrases.
steps.detail: Copying everything leaves no attention for thinking. Short phrases in your own words force you to process the ideas.
steps.proof: Your notes fit in 15 lines and cover the main points.
steps.pitfall: Trying to write down every word the speaker says.

problems.prompt: Abbreviate 'because' and 'without' in notes.
Shorten "The French Revolution began in 1789 when angry crowds stormed the Bastille prison" to a note of 6 words or fewer.
A 10-minute talk gave you 4 pages of notes. What should change?
problems.answer: Write shorter phrases and only key points.

steps.title: Organize with Structure
steps.mastery: Use headings, bullets and indentation so notes show how ideas connect.
steps.practice: Rewrite 1 page of messy notes as an outline with 3 headings and indented sub-points.
steps.detail: Structure shows which ideas are main and which support them. An outline is easy to review and turn into a study guide.
steps.proof: Your outline has 3 headings and sub-points under each.
steps.pitfall: Writing everything as one long paragraph.

problems.prompt: In an outline with 3 headings, does a sub-point go under or beside its main point?
Your notes have 3 main topics. How many top-level headings?
Name 1 benefit of outlined notes for review.
problems.answer: You can see how ideas connect at a glance.

steps.title: Review Within a Day
steps.mastery: Review and fill gaps in your notes within 24 hours.
steps.practice: Spend 10 minutes within 24 hours of each class rereading your notes and adding anything missing.
steps.detail: Memory fades fast in the first day. A short review the same evening keeps much more and catches gaps while you still remember the lesson.
steps.proof: Notes from 5 classes are reviewed within a day.
steps.pitfall: Reading notes for the first time the night before the test.

problems.prompt: 10 minutes after each of 5 classes is how many minutes a week?
When should the first review happen: within 24 hours or after a week?
Why add missing details within 24 hours?
problems.answer: You still remember the lesson, so gaps are easy to fill.

steps.title: Turn Notes into Questions
steps.mastery: Convert notes into practice questions for self-testing.
steps.practice: Write 5 questions from today's notes and answer them tomorrow without looking.
steps.detail: Testing yourself is one of the most effective ways to learn. Questions turn passive notes into active practice.
steps.proof: You answer the 5 questions the next day and check them.
steps.pitfall: Rereading notes passively and calling it studying.

problems.prompt: Turn the note "Mitochondria = energy for the cell" into a question.
problems.answer: What does the mitochondria do for the cell?

problems.prompt: You answered 3 of 5 correctly. What percent is that?
Which works better for a test in 1 week: rereading or self-testing?

steps.title: Write a Topic Sentence
steps.mastery: Start a body paragraph with a sentence that states its one main idea.
steps.practice: Write topic sentences for 3 paragraphs about the pros of school uniforms.
steps.detail: The topic sentence tells the reader what the paragraph will prove. Everything after it should support that one idea.
steps.proof: Each topic sentence states 1 clear idea.
steps.pitfall: Opening with a fact that does not say what the paragraph argues.

problems.prompt: Is "Uniforms come in many colors." a strong topic sentence for an argument? Answer yes or no.
Write a stronger topic sentence linking uniforms to "focus".
problems.answer: For example: Uniforms reduce distractions, helping students focus.

problems.prompt: How many main ideas should 1 paragraph have?

steps.title: Support with Evidence
steps.mastery: Back up the topic sentence with 2 or 3 pieces of specific evidence.
steps.practice: Add 2 pieces of evidence, a fact and an example, to support "Exercise improves mood."
steps.detail: Evidence can be facts, numbers, quotes or examples. Specific beats general: "a 2019 study of 1000 adults" beats "studies show".
steps.proof: The paragraph has 2 specific pieces of evidence.
steps.pitfall: Repeating the topic sentence in different words instead of supporting it.

problems.prompt: Which is more specific: "studies show" or "a 2019 study of 1000 adults"?
Name 3 kinds of evidence.
A paragraph has a topic sentence and 1 vague sentence. How many more pieces of evidence should you add?

steps.title: Explain the Evidence
steps.mastery: Explain how each piece of evidence supports the paragraph's point.
steps.practice: After each piece of evidence in a paragraph, add 1 sentence starting with "This shows" that links it to your point.
steps.detail: Evidence does not speak for itself. Explaining it shows your thinking and is often what earns the marks.
steps.proof: Each piece of evidence has an explanation sentence.
steps.pitfall: Dropping a quote and moving on without comment.

problems.prompt: Complete the link: "Students with uniforms reported 20% fewer distractions. This shows..."
problems.answer: that uniforms can help students focus.

problems.prompt: A paragraph has 2 quotes and no explanation. How many explanation sentences should you add?
Why add a "This shows" sentence instead of just quoting?
problems.answer: To show how it proves your point.

steps.title: Transitions
steps.mastery: Use transition words to connect sentences and paragraphs.
steps.practice: Add 4 transitions such as 'however', 'for example' and 'as a result' to a paragraph and check each fits the logic.
steps.detail: Transitions signal the relationship: contrast (however), example (for instance), result (therefore), addition (also). The wrong transition misleads.
steps.proof: Each transition matches the logical relationship.
steps.pitfall: Using 'however' where there is no contrast.

problems.prompt: Which transition shows contrast: 'therefore' or 'however'?
Which transition introduces an example: 'for instance' or 'in contrast'?
Fill in: "It rained all day. ___, the game was canceled."

steps.title: Conclude the Paragraph
steps.mastery: End a paragraph with a sentence that wraps up its point and leads onward.
steps.practice: Write closing sentences for 3 body paragraphs that restate each point without copying the topic sentence.
steps.detail: A closing sentence reminds the reader why the paragraph mattered and can bridge to the next one.
steps.proof: Each closing sentence restates the point in new words.
steps.pitfall: Copying the topic sentence word for word.

problems.prompt: Topic sentence: "Exercise improves mood." Is "Exercise improves mood." a good closing sentence? Answer yes or no.
problems.answer: No, it repeats it word for word.

problems.prompt: Write a better closing sentence for the "Exercise improves mood" paragraph.
problems.answer: For example: A daily walk may be one of the simplest ways to feel better.

problems.prompt: Besides summarizing, what can the 1 closing sentence of a paragraph do?

steps.title: Nouns and Verbs
steps.mastery: Identify nouns and verbs by what they do in a sentence.
steps.practice: Underline the nouns and circle the verbs in 5 sentences, such as "The coach blew the whistle."
steps.detail: Nouns name people, places, things or ideas. Verbs show actions or states. The same word can be either: 'run' is a verb in 'I run' and a noun in 'a long run'.
steps.proof: All nouns and verbs are marked correctly.
steps.pitfall: Labeling a word by its usual meaning instead of its job in the sentence.

problems.prompt: In "The coach blew the whistle", what are the 2 nouns?
In "She went for a run", is 'run' a noun or a verb?
Name the verb in "The cat seems tired."

steps.title: Adjectives and Adverbs
steps.mastery: Tell adjectives from adverbs and use each correctly.
steps.practice: Fix 5 sentences that misuse adjectives and adverbs, like "She sings good."
steps.detail: Adjectives describe nouns. Adverbs describe verbs, adjectives or other adverbs, and often end in -ly. 'Good' is an adjective and 'well' is its adverb.
steps.proof: All 5 sentences use the right form.
steps.pitfall: Writing 'He runs quick' instead of 'He runs quickly'.

problems.prompt: Correct "She sings good."
In "a very tall tree", which word is an adverb?
Is 'quickly' in "He ran quickly" an adjective or an adverb?

steps.title: Pronouns
steps.mastery: Use pronouns that clearly match the noun they replace.
steps.practice: Rewrite 3 sentences with unclear pronouns, such as "When Sam met Joe, he smiled."
steps.detail: A pronoun needs a clear antecedent. If 'he' could mean 2 people, name the person again. Subject pronouns (I, she) and object pronouns (me, her) are not interchangeable.
steps.proof: Each rewritten sentence has 1 possible meaning.
steps.pitfall: Writing "Me and him went" instead of "He and I went".

problems.prompt: Correct "Me and Jo went to the store."
problems.answer: Jo and I went to the store.

problems.prompt: Who does 'he' refer to in "When Sam met Joe, he smiled"?
problems.answer: It is unclear, so the sentence should name Sam or Joe.

problems.prompt: Correct "Give the book to Sara and I."
problems.answer: Give the book to Sara and me.

steps.title: Prepositions and Conjunctions
steps.mastery: Use prepositions to show relationships and conjunctions to join ideas.
steps.practice: Circle the prepositions and box the conjunctions in 5 sentences, such as "We stayed inside because it rained on Monday."
steps.detail: Prepositions (in, on, under, after) link a noun to the rest of the sentence. Conjunctions (and, but, because) join words or clauses. FANBOYS lists the coordinating ones: for, and, nor, but, or, yet, so.
steps.proof: All are marked correctly.
steps.pitfall: Confusing 'because' (a conjunction) with a preposition.

problems.prompt: How many coordinating conjunctions does FANBOYS name?
In "The keys are under the mat", what is the preposition?
In "I was tired, so I slept", what is the conjunction?

steps.title: Label a Whole Sentence
steps.mastery: Label the part of speech of every word in a sentence.
steps.practice: Label every word in "The small dog barked loudly at the mail carrier" with its part of speech.
steps.detail: Labeling every word builds the vocabulary to discuss sentences. Work from the verb out: find what is acting, then what describes it.
steps.proof: Every word has a correct label.
steps.pitfall: Skipping articles like 'the', which are adjectives (determiners).

problems.prompt: In that sentence, what part of speech is 'loudly'?
What part of speech is 'at' in it?
What part of speech is 'barked'?

steps.title: Commas in Lists
steps.mastery: Use commas correctly in lists and after introductory phrases.
steps.practice: Add commas to 6 sentences, including "After dinner we washed dried and stacked the plates."
steps.detail: Separate items in a list with commas. Put a comma after an introductory phrase. The comma before 'and' in a list (the Oxford comma) is a style choice, so be consistent.
steps.proof: All 6 sentences are punctuated correctly.
steps.pitfall: Using commas inconsistently in lists across one essay.

problems.prompt: Punctuate "I bought eggs milk and bread."
problems.answer: I bought eggs, milk, and bread. (or eggs, milk and bread)

problems.prompt: Punctuate "After the game we ate pizza."
problems.answer: After the game, we ate pizza.

problems.prompt: What is the comma before 'and' in a list called?

steps.title: Apostrophes
steps.mastery: Write owners and shortened words with the mark in the right spot.
steps.practice: Fix 8 apostrophe errors, including "The dog's are barking" and "Its' raining".
steps.detail: Add 's for singular possession (the dog's bone) and s' for plural (the dogs' bones). Contractions mark missing letters (don't). Plain plurals never take an apostrophe.
steps.proof: All 8 are fixed.
steps.pitfall: Writing "apple's for sale" as a plural.

problems.prompt: Correct "The dog's are barking."
Write the possessive for the bikes belonging to 3 boys.
Correct "Its' raining."

steps.title: Semicolons and Colons
steps.mastery: Pick between ; and : correctly in your own writing.
steps.practice: Write 2 sentences using a semicolon and 2 using a colon.
steps.detail: A semicolon joins 2 complete sentences that are closely related. A colon follows a complete sentence and introduces what explains or lists it.
steps.proof: All 4 sentences use the marks correctly.
steps.pitfall: Putting a colon after an incomplete phrase like "My favorites are:".

problems.prompt: Correct use? "I studied hard; I passed." Answer yes or no.
Correct use? "My favorite foods are: pizza and tacos." Answer yes or no.
problems.answer: No, the colon follows an incomplete clause.

problems.prompt: Rewrite "My favorite foods are: pizza and tacos." so the colon is correct.
problems.answer: I have 2 favorite foods: pizza and tacos.

steps.title: Quotation Marks
steps.mastery: Punctuate quotations correctly, with commas and periods in the right place.
steps.practice: Punctuate 5 sentences with dialogue, such as: she said I will be late.
steps.detail: In American English, commas and periods go inside closing quotation marks. Capitalize the first word of a full quoted sentence.
steps.proof: All 5 are punctuated correctly.
steps.pitfall: Putting the period outside the closing quotation mark.

problems.prompt: Punctuate the 6 words: she said I will be late
In American English, does the comma go inside or outside the closing quotation mark?
Punctuate the 6 words: I love this song he shouted

steps.title: Edit for Punctuation
steps.mastery: Proofread a page specifically for punctuation errors.
steps.practice: Read a 300-word draft aloud once, only checking commas, apostrophes and end marks, and fix every error.
steps.detail: One pass for one type of error catches more than a general reread. Reading aloud helps you hear where pauses belong.
steps.proof: Your draft has no comma splices or apostrophe errors.
steps.pitfall: Proofreading for everything at once and missing small marks.

problems.prompt: A 300-word draft had 6 punctuation errors. About how many per 100 words?
Why read aloud when checking the commas in a 300-word draft?
problems.answer: You can hear where natural pauses fall.

problems.prompt: Name the 2 punctuation errors most readers notice.

steps.title: Preview Before Reading
steps.mastery: Skim headings, the first paragraph and the last paragraph before reading a chapter closely.
steps.practice: Preview a 10-page chapter in 3 minutes, then write 1 sentence predicting its main point.
steps.detail: Previewing gives your brain a frame to hang details on. Read the title, headings, bold words, the first and last paragraphs, and any summary box. Then read properly with the frame in mind.
steps.proof: Your 1-sentence prediction matches the chapter's main point afterward.
steps.pitfall: Starting on page 1 and reading every word at the same speed.

problems.prompt: A chapter has 6 headings. How many should you read during a preview?
You preview for 3 minutes and read for 27. What share of the time was preview?
Name 2 parts of a chapter to read during a preview besides headings.
problems.answer: The first and last paragraphs (also bold terms or a summary box).

steps.title: Read in Phrases
steps.mastery: Take in groups of words at a time instead of decoding each one.
steps.practice: Read a 300-word passage aloud in phrase chunks marked with slashes, like "The old man / walked slowly / to the shore".
steps.detail: Fluent readers see phrases, not single words. Marking chunks trains your eyes to jump in groups, which frees attention for meaning.
steps.proof: You read the passage smoothly with pauses only at the slashes.
steps.pitfall: Pointing at every word and sounding out words you already know.

problems.prompt: How many chunks are in "The old man / walked slowly / to the shore"?
Where does the 1st slash go in "After lunch the class went outside to play"?
Why does reading in 3-word phrases improve comprehension?
problems.answer: Attention moves from decoding single words to the meaning of each group.

steps.title: Measure Your Speed
steps.mastery: Measure reading speed in words per minute and check comprehension at the same time.
steps.practice: Time yourself reading a 600-word article, answer 3 questions about it, and compute your words per minute.
steps.detail: Speed without understanding is useless, so always pair it with questions. Many students read 200 to 250 words per minute. Track it monthly.
steps.proof: You have a words-per-minute figure and a comprehension score.
steps.pitfall: Skimming fast and calling it reading.

problems.prompt: 600 words in 3 minutes is how many words per minute?
900 words in 4 minutes is how many words per minute?
You read 250 words per minute but answered 1 of 4 questions correctly. What should change?
problems.answer: Slow down and focus on understanding.

steps.title: Reread Hard Parts
steps.mastery: Notice when you have stopped understanding and reread that section on purpose.
steps.practice: Mark every spot in a 5-page reading where you lost the thread with a ?, then reread just those spots.
steps.detail: Good readers notice confusion quickly. A mark shows where to look again. Rereading one paragraph beats rereading the whole chapter.
steps.proof: Each ? has a short note on what it means now.
steps.pitfall: Reading to the end of the chapter while confused from page 1.

problems.prompt: You marked 4 spots in 5 pages. How many paragraphs should you reread at minimum?
Name 1 sign you have stopped understanding.
problems.answer: You cannot say what the last paragraph said.

problems.prompt: Why reread 1 paragraph instead of the whole 20-page chapter?
problems.answer: It targets the confusion and saves time.

steps.title: Read Every Day
steps.mastery: Build reading stamina with a daily reading habit of a fixed length.
steps.practice: Read for 20 minutes every day for 2 weeks and log the minutes and pages each day.
steps.detail: Fluency grows with volume. Choose books slightly below your hardest level for daily reading, so it feels smooth.
steps.proof: You log 14 days of reading.
steps.pitfall: Reading only when assigned.

problems.prompt: 20 minutes a day for 14 days is how many minutes?
Write 280 minutes as hours and minutes.
At 25 pages a day, how many pages in 14 days?

steps.title: Search Effectively
steps.mastery: Use specific keywords and search operators to find relevant sources.
steps.practice: Search for sources on teen sleep using 3 keyword variations and quotation marks for an exact phrase.
steps.detail: Specific terms beat questions. Quotation marks find exact phrases, and adding 'site:.gov' or 'site:.edu' targets institutional sources.
steps.proof: You find 5 relevant sources.
steps.pitfall: Searching a vague question and using the first result.

problems.prompt: What do quotation marks around "teen sleep" do in a search?
What does 'site:.gov' limit a search to?
Rewrite "why are teens tired" as better keywords.
problems.answer: For example: teen sleep deprivation school start times.

steps.title: Judge Credibility
steps.mastery: Evaluate a source's author, date, purpose and evidence.
steps.practice: Rate 3 sources on 4 criteria (author, date, purpose and evidence) from 1 to 3 each.
steps.detail: Ask who wrote it and what qualifies them, when it was published, why it exists, and whether it cites evidence. A sales page has a reason to persuade.
steps.proof: Each source has 4 ratings and an overall judgment.
steps.pitfall: Trusting a source because it looks professional.

problems.prompt: A health article from 2004 for a 2026 paper: what concern?
Name 1 reason a company's website may be biased about its product.
problems.answer: It wants to sell the product.

problems.prompt: 4 criteria rated 1 to 3: what is the maximum total score?

steps.title: Primary and Secondary
steps.mastery: Tell primary sources from secondary sources and use each well.
steps.practice: Label 6 sources, such as a diary, a textbook and a research study, as primary or secondary.
steps.detail: Primary sources are original evidence: letters, data, interviews. Secondary sources interpret them: textbooks, reviews. Strong research uses both.
steps.proof: All 6 are labeled correctly.
steps.pitfall: Calling a textbook a primary source.

problems.prompt: Is a 1944 soldier's letter primary or secondary?
Is a 2020 biography of Lincoln primary or secondary?
Is the 1953 Watson and Crick paper reporting DNA's structure primary or secondary?

steps.title: Track Your Sources
steps.mastery: Record source details at the moment you find them.
steps.practice: Keep a source log with author, title, date, URL and the page or paragraph of each fact you take.
steps.detail: Recording sources later wastes hours and risks accidental plagiarism. A log or a citation tool keeps every fact traceable.
steps.proof: Every note links to a logged source.
steps.pitfall: Copying facts and planning to find the source later.

problems.prompt: Name 4 details to log for a web source.
Why log the page number, like p. 45, of a quote?
problems.answer: So you can cite it and find it again.

problems.prompt: Name 1 free citation manager.

steps.title: Synthesize Sources
steps.mastery: Combine several sources to support one point.
steps.practice: Write 1 paragraph that uses 3 sources together to support a single claim.
steps.detail: Synthesis shows how sources agree, add to each other or disagree. It is stronger than a list of one source per paragraph.
steps.proof: Your paragraph cites 3 sources supporting 1 claim.
steps.pitfall: Summarizing one source per paragraph with no connections.

problems.prompt: A paragraph cites 3 sources for 1 claim. Is that synthesis or a list?
Name 1 phrase that connects 2 sources.
2 sources disagree. What should your paragraph do?
problems.answer: Explain the disagreement and which is better supported.

steps.title: Subject and Predicate
steps.mastery: Find the subject and the main verb of any sentence.
steps.practice: Mark the subject and main verb in 6 sentences, including "After the long game, the tired players sat down."
steps.detail: The subject is who or what the sentence is about. The predicate is what it does or is. Opening phrases like 'After the long game' are neither.
steps.proof: Subject and verb are marked correctly in all 6.
steps.pitfall: Taking a word in an opening phrase as the subject.

problems.prompt: In "The tired players sat down", what is the subject?
What is the main verb in "My brother and I baked bread"?
In "Running every day keeps him fit", what is the subject?

steps.title: Fix Fragments
steps.mastery: Turn sentence fragments into complete sentences.
steps.practice: Fix 5 fragments, such as "Because the bus was late.", by joining or completing them.
steps.detail: A fragment lacks a subject, a verb, or a complete thought. A clause starting with 'because' or 'when' needs a main clause attached.
steps.proof: All 5 are complete sentences.
steps.pitfall: Leaving a 'because' clause standing alone.

problems.prompt: Is "Because the bus was late." a complete sentence? Answer yes or no.
Fix "Because the bus was late."
problems.answer: For example: I missed class because the bus was late.

problems.prompt: Is "Running down the hall." complete? Answer yes or no.
problems.answer: No, it has no subject or main verb.

steps.title: Fix Run-Ons
steps.mastery: Fix run-on sentences and comma splices with a period, semicolon or conjunction.
steps.practice: Fix 5 run-ons, such as "I studied all night, I still failed.", in 3 different ways each.
steps.detail: A comma alone cannot join 2 complete sentences. Use a period, a semicolon, or a comma plus a conjunction like 'but'.
steps.proof: Each run-on has 3 correct fixes.
steps.pitfall: Joining 2 sentences with only a comma.

problems.prompt: Is "I was tired, I went to bed." correct? Answer yes or no.
problems.answer: No, it is a comma splice.

problems.prompt: Join those 2 sentences with the conjunction 'so'.
problems.answer: I was tired, so I went to bed.

problems.prompt: Join those 2 sentences with a semicolon instead.
problems.answer: I was tired; I went to bed.

steps.title: Combine Sentences
steps.mastery: Combine short choppy sentences into smoother ones.
steps.practice: Combine "The dog was old. The dog was gray. It slept by the fire." into 1 sentence.
steps.detail: Combining removes repetition and shows how ideas relate. Use relative clauses (who, which), adjectives and conjunctions.
steps.proof: Your sentence keeps all 3 facts and reads smoothly.
steps.pitfall: Combining into one long, tangled sentence.

problems.prompt: Combine "Maria won. Maria was happy."
problems.answer: Maria was happy that she won (or: Maria won and was happy).

problems.prompt: Combine "I like tea. I do not like coffee." with 'but'.
problems.answer: I like tea, but I do not like coffee.

problems.prompt: Combine "The book was long. It was worth reading." with 'although'.
problems.answer: Although the book was long, it was worth reading.

steps.title: Vary Sentence Length
steps.mastery: Mix short and long sentences on purpose for rhythm and emphasis.
steps.practice: Count the words in each sentence of a 150-word paragraph you wrote, then revise so lengths vary between 5 and 25 words.
steps.detail: Many sentences of the same length sound flat. A short sentence after long ones lands with force.
steps.proof: Your revised paragraph has at least 1 sentence under 8 words and 1 over 18.
steps.pitfall: Writing every sentence at 15 words.

problems.prompt: Sentences of 14, 15, 15 and 16 words: is the length varied? Answer yes or no.
Why might a 4-word sentence follow 3 long ones?
Your sentences average 30 words. What should you try?

steps.title: Structure a Short Talk
steps.mastery: Give a short talk that listeners can follow from start to finish.
steps.practice: Prepare a 2-minute talk on a topic you know, with 1 opening line, 3 points and a 1-sentence close.
steps.detail: Listeners cannot reread, so structure helps them follow. Tell them the points, make them, then sum up.
steps.proof: Your talk runs about 2 minutes and hits all 3 points.
steps.pitfall: Rambling with no clear points.

problems.prompt: At about 130 words per minute, how many words is a 2-minute talk?
How many main points suit a 2-minute talk: 3 or 10?
Name the 3 parts of a short talk.
problems.answer: An opening, the main points and a close.

steps.title: Make Your Point First
steps.mastery: State your main point in the first sentence when answering a question.
steps.practice: Answer 5 discussion questions by stating your answer in the first sentence, then giving 1 reason.
steps.detail: Leading with the point makes you easier to follow and harder to interrupt. Details come after.
steps.proof: Each answer opens with the point.
steps.pitfall: Building up slowly so the point arrives at the end, if at all.

problems.prompt: Rewrite "Well, there are many things, and I think maybe..." to lead with a point.
problems.answer: For example: I think homework should be limited, because...

problems.prompt: 5 answers each with 1 point and 1 reason: how many reasons?
Why state the point in the 1st sentence of a discussion answer?
problems.answer: Listeners know what you mean right away.

steps.title: Build on Others
steps.mastery: Respond to what someone said before adding your own idea.
steps.practice: In a discussion, start 3 contributions with phrases like "Building on what Ana said..."
steps.detail: Linking to the previous speaker shows you listened and keeps the discussion connected rather than a series of separate speeches.
steps.proof: 3 contributions reference a previous speaker.
steps.pitfall: Waiting for your turn and ignoring what was just said.

problems.prompt: Name 1 phrase that builds on a classmate's point.
Name 1 phrase that politely disagrees.
Why say "Building on what Ana said" before your own idea?
problems.answer: It shows listening and keeps the discussion connected.

steps.title: Change Your Mind Well
steps.mastery: Update your view in public when given a good reason.
steps.practice: Write 1 sentence you could say when a classmate's evidence changes your view, and use it in the next discussion.
steps.detail: Saying "That changes my mind" builds credibility. Explain what convinced you so others learn too.
steps.proof: You use the sentence once in discussion.
steps.pitfall: Defending a position you no longer believe.

problems.prompt: Complete: "I hadn't thought of that. Given ___, I now think..."
problems.answer: For example: Given the data on sleep, I now think start times should be later.

problems.prompt: Does changing your mind for good reasons lose credibility? Answer yes or no.
When you say "That changes my mind", what should you explain next?

steps.title: Delivery Basics
steps.mastery: Speak with clear volume, steady pace and eye contact.
steps.practice: Record a 1-minute talk on video and rate your volume, pace and eye contact from 1 to 5.
steps.detail: Most nervous speakers talk too fast. Pausing after key points and looking at the audience makes you seem confident.
steps.proof: You rate all 3 and improve 1 in a second recording.
steps.pitfall: Reading word for word from notes without looking up.

problems.prompt: A 1-minute talk with 200 words is too fast or about right at 130 words per minute?
Name 3 delivery skills to rate.
In a 1-minute talk, when should you pause?

steps.title: Learn the Common Patterns
steps.mastery: Use common spelling patterns like 'i before e except after c' and know their exceptions.
steps.practice: Sort 12 words like 'receive', 'believe', 'weird' and 'ceiling' into rule-followers and exceptions.
steps.detail: English spelling has many patterns. Learn the rule, then memorize the handful of exceptions. 'Weird' and 'seize' break the ie rule.
steps.proof: Every word is sorted correctly.
steps.pitfall: Trusting a rule without knowing its exceptions.

problems.prompt: Spell the word that means to get: 'recieve' or 'receive'?
Does 'weird' follow 'i before e except after c'? Answer yes or no.
Which spelling is correct: 'beleive' or 'believe'?

steps.title: Adding Suffixes
steps.mastery: Apply the rules for doubling consonants and dropping a final e when adding suffixes.
steps.practice: Add '-ing' to 'run', 'make', 'begin' and 'visit' and explain each change.
steps.detail: Double the final consonant after a short stressed vowel (run to running). Drop a silent e before a vowel suffix (make to making). Do not double when the stress is not on the last syllable (visit to visiting).
steps.proof: running, making, beginning and visiting.
steps.pitfall: Writing 'makeing' or 'begining'.

problems.prompt: Add '-ing' to 'hop'.
Add '-ing' to 'hope'.
Add '-ed' to 'prefer'.

steps.title: Homophones
steps.mastery: Choose correctly between words that sound alike, such as their, there and they're.
steps.practice: Fill in 10 blanks using their, there, they're, your, you're, its and it's.
steps.detail: They're and you're are short for they are and you are. It's means it is. Its shows possession. Say the full form aloud to check.
steps.proof: All 10 blanks are correct.
steps.pitfall: Using 'it's' for possession.

problems.prompt: Fill the blank: "___ going to the game." (their, there, they're)
Fill the blank: "The dog wagged ___ tail." (its, it's)
Fill the blank: "___ late again." (your, you're)

steps.title: Plurals
steps.mastery: Form plurals correctly, including -es, -ies and irregular plurals.
steps.practice: Write the plurals of 'box', 'city', 'leaf', 'child' and 'tomato'.
steps.detail: Add -es after s, x, z, ch and sh. Change y to ies after a consonant. Some f words become ves. Irregular plurals like children must be learned.
steps.proof: boxes, cities, leaves, children, tomatoes.
steps.pitfall: Writing 'citys' or 'childs'.

problems.prompt: What is the plural of 'church'?
What is the plural of 'baby'?
What is the plural of 'mouse'?

steps.title: Keep a Spelling List
steps.mastery: Track the words you personally misspell and test them weekly.
steps.practice: Collect every word you misspelled in 2 weeks of writing and quiz yourself on the list every Friday.
steps.detail: Everyone has their own problem words. A personal list targets them directly. Remove a word after 3 correct weekly tests.
steps.proof: Your list has fewer words each week.
steps.pitfall: Relying on spellcheck, which misses wrong but real words.

problems.prompt: Your list has 12 words and 3 graduate after 3 correct tests. How many remain?
Name 1 error spellcheck usually misses.
problems.answer: A real word used wrongly, like 'there' for 'their'.

problems.prompt: In this method, a word leaves the list after how many correct Friday tests?

steps.title: Imitate a Sentence
steps.mastery: Copy the structure of a sentence you admire with your own content.
steps.practice: Pick 3 sentences from an author you like and write your own sentence in the same structure for each.
steps.detail: Imitation is how writers learn rhythm and structure. Keep the shape, change every word of content.
steps.proof: 3 imitations keep the original structure.
steps.pitfall: Copying the content instead of the structure.

problems.prompt: Imitate the shape of "The rain fell, the river rose, the town waited."
problems.answer: For example: The bell rang, the doors opened, the hall filled.

problems.prompt: When imitating a sentence by Hemingway, do you keep the content or the structure?
How many clauses does "The rain fell, the river rose, the town waited" have?

steps.title: Rhythm and Emphasis
steps.mastery: Use sentence length and placement to control emphasis.
steps.practice: Rewrite 1 paragraph so its most important idea sits in a sentence of under 8 words at the end.
steps.detail: The end of a sentence or paragraph is the strongest position. A short sentence after long ones adds punch.
steps.proof: The key idea ends the paragraph in a short sentence.
steps.pitfall: Burying the key idea in the middle of a long sentence.

problems.prompt: Which position in a 20-word sentence is usually most emphatic: the middle or the end?
In "The long war was finally over", which word gets the end emphasis?
A paragraph has sentences of 22, 25 and 4 words. Which is likely the emphasis?

steps.title: Concrete Detail
steps.mastery: Use specific sensory details instead of general statements.
steps.practice: Rewrite 3 general sentences, like "The room was messy", with 2 concrete details each.
steps.detail: Concrete details let readers see for themselves. "Three pizza boxes and a sock on the lamp" shows messy without saying it.
steps.proof: Each rewrite has 2 specific details.
steps.pitfall: Stacking adjectives instead of showing specifics.

problems.prompt: Rewrite "The room was messy" with concrete detail.
problems.answer: For example: Three pizza boxes sat on the bed and a sock hung from the lamp.

problems.prompt: Is "It was very very nice" concrete? Answer yes or no.
Name the 5 senses a writer can draw details from.
problems.answer: Sight, sound, smell, taste and touch.

steps.title: Trust the Reader
steps.mastery: Leave some meaning implied instead of explaining everything.
steps.practice: Cut every sentence in a 300-word story that explains what a character feels when the action already shows it.
steps.detail: Readers enjoy working things out. If a character slams a door, you do not need to add "She was angry".
steps.proof: No sentence explains a feeling the action already shows.
steps.pitfall: Explaining every emotion after showing it.

problems.prompt: After "She slammed the door", is "She was angry" needed? Answer yes or no.
What 3-word writing rule names this principle?
Rewrite "He was nervous." to show it.
problems.answer: For example: He tapped his pen and checked the clock 3 times.

steps.title: Develop Your Voice
steps.mastery: Notice your own patterns and keep the ones that sound like you.
steps.practice: Read 3 pieces you wrote and list 3 habits, like favorite words or sentence shapes, then decide which to keep.
steps.detail: Voice comes from consistent choices. Keep the habits that are clear and yours, and cut tics like repeating 'very' or 'just'.
steps.proof: Your list has 3 habits marked keep or cut.
steps.pitfall: Copying another writer's voice permanently.

problems.prompt: Name 1 common writing tic to cut.
You used 'just' 14 times in 500 words. About how often per 100 words?
Where does a writer's voice come from?
problems.answer: Consistent choices in words, rhythm and structure.

steps.title: Find the Main Idea
steps.mastery: Identify the main idea of a text before summarizing it.
steps.practice: Write the main idea of a 2-page article in 1 sentence of 25 words or fewer.
steps.detail: The main idea is what the whole text is about, not one detail. Headings, the opening and the conclusion usually point to it.
steps.proof: Your sentence covers the whole article in 25 words or fewer.
steps.pitfall: Choosing an interesting detail instead of the main idea.

problems.prompt: An article is about why bees matter to farms. Is "Bees have 5 eyes" its main idea? Answer yes or no.
Write a main-idea sentence for the bee article in 25 words or fewer.
problems.answer: For example: Bees pollinate many crops, so farms depend on healthy bee populations.

problems.prompt: Name 2 places in a text where the main idea often appears.
problems.answer: In the opening and the conclusion.

steps.title: Cut the Details
steps.mastery: Leave out examples and minor details when summarizing.
steps.practice: Summarize a 600-word article in 60 words by keeping only the main idea and 2 or 3 key points.
steps.detail: A summary keeps the skeleton and drops the examples. Aim for about one tenth of the original length.
steps.proof: Your summary is about 60 words and includes no examples.
steps.pitfall: Retelling the article in order with every detail.

problems.prompt: One tenth of a 600-word article is how many words?
Should a summary include the author's examples? Answer yes or no.
problems.answer: Usually no, only the main points.

problems.prompt: A 2000-word chapter summarized at one tenth is how many words?

steps.title: Use Your Own Words
steps.mastery: Paraphrase the author's points without copying their sentences.
steps.practice: Read 1 paragraph, close the source, write its point in your own words, then compare the 2 versions.
steps.detail: Writing with the source closed forces real paraphrase. Changing a word or 2 is not paraphrasing and can count as plagiarism.
steps.proof: No phrase of 4 or more words matches the source.
steps.pitfall: Swapping a few synonyms into the author's sentence.

problems.prompt: Paraphrase "The rapid growth of cities has increased traffic congestion."
problems.answer: For example: As cities grow quickly, roads get more crowded.

problems.prompt: Is replacing 2 words with synonyms enough to paraphrase? Answer yes or no.
What should you do with the source while writing your 1st paraphrase?

steps.title: Stay Neutral
steps.mastery: Report the author's ideas without adding your own opinion.
steps.practice: Remove every opinion word, such as 'amazing' or 'wrong', from a 100-word summary you wrote.
steps.detail: A summary reports what the author said. Signal verbs like 'argues' and 'claims' attribute ideas without judging them.
steps.proof: Your summary has no opinion words.
steps.pitfall: Adding praise, as in "The author makes the excellent point that".

problems.prompt: Rewrite "The author wrongly says homework is useless." neutrally.
problems.answer: The author argues that homework is not useful.

problems.prompt: Name 2 neutral signal verbs.
problems.answer: Argues and explains (also states or claims).

problems.prompt: Does "brilliantly" belong in a neutral summary? Answer yes or no.

steps.title: Test Your Understanding
steps.mastery: Use a 3-sentence summary to check whether you understood a text.
steps.practice: Summarize each section of a 3-section chapter in 3 sentences, then check against the chapter for gaps.
steps.detail: If you cannot summarize it, you did not understand it. Gaps in your summary show exactly what to reread.
steps.proof: Each section has a 3-sentence summary with no major gaps.
steps.pitfall: Assuming you understood because the reading felt easy.

problems.prompt: 3 sections with 3 sentences each is how many summary sentences?
You cannot summarize section 2. What should you do?
Why is a 3-sentence summary a good test of understanding?
problems.answer: It requires you to know the main points without the text.

steps.title: Keep One Tense
steps.mastery: Keep verb tense consistent within a paragraph unless time changes.
