steps.practice: Rewrite a 6-sentence story paragraph that switches between past and present so it stays in the past tense.
steps.detail: Shifting tense without a reason confuses the timeline. Choose past or present for a narrative and stick to it.
steps.proof: Every verb in the paragraph is in the past tense.
steps.pitfall: Switching tense mid-sentence, as in "I walked in and she says hello".

problems.prompt: Fix the tense: "I walked in and she says hello."
problems.answer: I walked in and she said hello.

problems.prompt: What tense is 'will finish'?
Fix: "Yesterday we go to the park."
problems.answer: Yesterday we went to the park.

steps.title: Subject-Verb Agreement
steps.mastery: Make verbs agree with their subjects in number.
steps.practice: Fix 6 agreement errors, such as "The list of names are long."
steps.detail: Find the true subject, ignoring phrases in between. 'The list of names' has the singular subject 'list', so it takes 'is'.
steps.proof: All 6 are corrected.
steps.pitfall: Matching the verb to the nearest noun instead of the subject.

problems.prompt: Correct "The list of names are long."
problems.answer: The list of names is long.

problems.prompt: Correct "Each of the students have a book."
problems.answer: Each of the students has a book.

problems.prompt: Is "The team are winning" standard American usage? Answer yes or no.
problems.answer: No, American English uses 'the team is'.

steps.title: Irregular Verbs
steps.mastery: Use the correct past and past participle forms of common irregular verbs.
steps.practice: Write the past and past participle of 10 irregular verbs, such as go, see, write and choose.
steps.detail: Irregular verbs do not add -ed. They must be learned. The past participle follows 'have': 'I have written', not 'I have wrote'.
steps.proof: All 20 forms are correct.
steps.pitfall: Writing 'I have went' or 'I seen'.

problems.prompt: What is the past tense of 'go'?
Correct "I have wrote 3 pages."
What is the past participle of 'choose'?

steps.title: Perfect Tenses
steps.mastery: Use present perfect and past perfect to show order of events.
steps.practice: Write 3 sentences using 'had finished' to show one past event happened before another.
steps.detail: Past perfect (had + participle) marks the earlier of 2 past events. Present perfect (have + participle) links the past to now.
steps.proof: Each sentence shows a clear order of events.
steps.pitfall: Using past perfect when there is no second past event.

problems.prompt: Which happened first in "I had eaten when she arrived"?
Complete with present perfect: "I ___ (live) here for 5 years."
Complete with past perfect: "The movie ___ (start) before we got there."

steps.title: Pronoun Agreement
steps.mastery: Make pronouns agree with their antecedents in number.
steps.practice: Fix 5 sentences such as "Every student should bring their book" in 2 accepted ways each.
steps.detail: Singular 'they' is widely accepted today. In formal writing you can also make the antecedent plural, as in "Students should bring their books".
steps.proof: Each sentence has 2 correct versions.
steps.pitfall: Mixing singular and plural in one sentence, like "A student lost their books and he left".

problems.prompt: Make the antecedent plural: "Every student should bring their book."
Correct "The company changed their logo" for formal American usage.
What pronoun agrees with 'Neither of the boys' in formal writing: his or their?

steps.title: Identify Tone
steps.mastery: Say what attitude a writer takes and back it up with their own words.
steps.practice: Name the tone of 3 short passages and underline 2 words in each that create it.
steps.detail: Tone is the writer's attitude: formal, playful, angry, hopeful. Word choice, sentence length and punctuation all signal it.
steps.proof: Each passage has a tone word and 2 underlined words.
steps.pitfall: Confusing tone (the writer's attitude) with mood (the reader's feeling).

problems.prompt: What tone does "Kindly submit the form by Friday." have: formal or casual?
What tone does "Hey! Grab the form by Friday!" have?
Is tone the writer's attitude or the reader's feeling?

steps.title: Formal and Informal
steps.mastery: Rewrite a message for a formal and an informal audience.
steps.practice: Rewrite the text "cant make it tmrw sry" as an email to a teacher.
steps.detail: Formal writing uses full words, complete sentences and polite phrases. Informal writing allows contractions and slang. Match the reader.
steps.proof: Your email is polite, complete and error-free.
steps.pitfall: Writing to a teacher the way you text a friend.

problems.prompt: Rewrite "cant make it tmrw sry" formally.
problems.answer: For example: I am sorry, but I will not be able to attend tomorrow.

problems.prompt: Is "gonna" appropriate in a college application? Answer yes or no.
Name 2 features of formal writing.
problems.answer: Complete sentences and no slang (also polite phrases).

steps.title: Audience and Purpose
steps.mastery: Choose register based on who will read and why.
steps.practice: Write the same 50-word update for 2 audiences: a younger sibling and a school principal.
steps.detail: The same facts land differently depending on the reader. Adjust vocabulary, detail and formality to the audience and purpose.
steps.proof: The 2 versions differ in vocabulary and formality.
steps.pitfall: Using one style for every reader.

problems.prompt: Which audience suits simple words and short sentences: a 7-year-old or a principal?
Name 2 things to adjust for a new audience.
Is a cover letter for a summer job at the City Library formal or informal?

steps.title: Avoid Unintended Tone
steps.mastery: Spot phrases that sound rude, sarcastic or cold by accident.
steps.practice: Rewrite 3 blunt sentences from emails, such as "Do this now.", so they stay clear but polite.
steps.detail: Written text loses tone of voice, so bluntness reads as rudeness. 'Please', 'could you' and a reason soften requests without making them vague.
steps.proof: Each rewrite is clear and polite.
steps.pitfall: Adding so much softening that the request disappears.

problems.prompt: Rewrite "Send me the file." politely.
problems.answer: For example: Could you please send me the file by 3 pm?

problems.prompt: Can all-caps words read as shouting in email? Answer yes or no.
Name 1 word that softens a request.

steps.title: Consistent Voice
steps.mastery: Keep tone consistent throughout a piece.
steps.practice: Mark any sentence in a 300-word essay where the tone suddenly becomes much more casual or formal, and revise it.
steps.detail: A sudden shift, like slang in a formal essay, jars the reader. Read the whole piece aloud to hear shifts.
steps.proof: No sudden tone shifts remain.
steps.pitfall: Dropping one slang phrase into a formal essay.

problems.prompt: Does "The data clearly indicates, like, a huge trend" keep a consistent tone? Answer yes or no.
Rewrite "The results are, like, totally huge" for a formal essay.
Why read a 300-word essay aloud to check tone?
problems.answer: You hear shifts more easily than you see them.

steps.title: Learn Words in Context
steps.mastery: Work out a new word from the sentence around it and keep that sentence with the word.
steps.practice: Collect 5 unfamiliar words from your reading this week and copy each with its full original sentence.
steps.detail: A word in context shows its meaning, tone and grammar. A list of definitions alone is quickly forgotten.
steps.proof: You have 5 words, each with its sentence and a short meaning.
steps.pitfall: Memorizing definitions with no example sentence.

problems.prompt: In "The arid desert saw no rain for months", what does 'arid' mean?
In "She was elated by the news and could not stop smiling", what does 'elated' mean?
In "His terse reply of 2 words ended the talk", what does 'terse' mean?

steps.title: Use Word Parts
steps.mastery: Use prefixes, roots and suffixes to work out unfamiliar words.
steps.practice: List the prefix, root and suffix of 5 words such as 'transportation' and 'unbelievable', with each part's meaning.
steps.detail: Many English words are built from Latin and Greek parts. 'Port' means carry, 'trans' means across, so 'transport' is carry across. Knowing 20 common parts unlocks hundreds of words.
steps.proof: Each word is split into parts with meanings.
steps.pitfall: Guessing a word's meaning from how it sounds.

problems.prompt: What does the prefix 'un-' mean in 'unhappy'?
The root 'bio' means life. What does 'biology' mean?
Using 'tele' (far) and 'scope' (look), what does 'telescope' mean?
problems.answer: An instrument for looking at far things.

steps.title: Use New Words
steps.mastery: Use each new word in your own writing or speech within a few days.
steps.practice: Write 1 original sentence for each of 5 new words and use 2 of them in conversation this week.
steps.detail: Words become yours when you produce them. Writing your own sentence checks whether you understood the meaning and the grammar.
steps.proof: Five sentences are written and 2 words used aloud.
steps.pitfall: Recognizing words but never using them.

problems.prompt: Write a sentence using 'meticulous'.
problems.answer: For example: She kept meticulous notes, dating every page.

problems.prompt: Is "He was very meticulous about being late" a correct use? Answer yes or no.
problems.answer: No, meticulous means careful and precise.

problems.prompt: Write a sentence using 'reluctant'.
problems.answer: For example: He was reluctant to speak first in class.

steps.title: Review on a Schedule
steps.mastery: Review vocabulary at growing intervals so it sticks.
steps.practice: Review your new words after 1, 3, 7 and 14 days using flashcards with the word on one side and your sentence on the other.
steps.detail: Spaced review targets words just before you would forget them. Each successful review lets the next gap grow.
steps.proof: You complete all 4 reviews for each word.
steps.pitfall: Cramming 50 words the night before a test.

problems.prompt: Reviews on days 1, 3, 7 and 14: how many reviews per word?
What is the gap between the day-7 and day-14 reviews?
Why do 4 spaced reviews beat a single long session?
problems.answer: Each review happens just before forgetting, which strengthens memory more.

steps.title: Choose Precise Words
steps.mastery: Replace vague words with precise ones in your own writing.
steps.practice: Replace 'very good', 'nice' and 'a lot' in a 200-word paragraph you wrote with more exact words.
steps.detail: Precise words carry more meaning in fewer words. 'Very big' becomes 'enormous', 'walked slowly' becomes 'strolled'. Check that the new word fits the tone.
steps.proof: The paragraph has no 'very', 'nice' or 'a lot'.
steps.pitfall: Swapping in fancy words that do not fit the meaning.

problems.prompt: Give a precise replacement for 'very tired'.
Give a precise replacement for 'said loudly'.
Replace 'very small' in "a very small ant".

steps.title: Letters as Numbers
steps.mastery: Read an expression with letters in it and say what each letter stands for.
steps.practice: Evaluate 3a - 2b when a = 5 and b = 4, then again when a = -1 and b = 0.
steps.detail: A letter beside a number means multiplication with the sign left out. Substitute with brackets around the value, 3(-1) - 2(0), and the sign errors disappear. The same expression gives a different answer for every pair of values, which is the whole point of writing it with letters.
steps.proof: 7 the first time and -3 the second.
steps.pitfall: Reading 3a as 'three then a' rather than as 3 multiplied by a.

problems.prompt: Evaluate \(3a - 2b\) when \(a = 5\) and \(b = 4\).
What is \(3a - 2b\) when \(a = - 1\) and \(b = 0\)?
If \(a = 2\) and \(b = 3\), what is the value of \(3a - 2b\)?
problems.answer: 0. Here 3a means 3 times a, which is 6, not the digits 3 and a.
problems.hint: Remember that juxtaposition of a number and a letter denotes multiplication.

steps.title: Collect Like Terms
steps.mastery: Simplify an expression by combining only the terms of the same kind.
steps.practice: Simplify 5x + 3y - 2x + 7y - 4, then simplify 2a^2 + 3a - a^2.
steps.detail: Two terms are alike only if their letters and powers match exactly. Underline each kind in a different color on the first few, then add the coefficients and leave the letter part untouched. A lone number is its own kind and cannot join anything.
steps.pitfall: Adding x and x^2 together because both involve x.

problems.prompt: Simplify \(4y - 2y\).
Simplify \(5x + 3y - 2x + 7y - 4\).

problems.hint: Only combine terms that have the same exponent on the same variable.

steps.title: Expand a Bracket
steps.mastery: Multiply a bracket by what sits outside it, term by term.
steps.practice: Expand 4(2x - 3) and -2(5 - x), then expand and simplify 3(x + 2) - 2(x - 1).
steps.detail: Every term inside gets multiplied, and the sign in front of the bracket travels with the multiplier. Draw the arrows the first dozen times. When two expansions are subtracted, expand both fully before collecting anything.
steps.pitfall: Multiplying only the first term inside the bracket and copying the rest across.

problems.prompt: Expand and simplify \(4(2x - 1) - 3(x + 5)\).
problems.hint: Distribute each term then combine like terms.

problems.prompt: Expand and simplify \(-2(3x - 4) + 7(x + 2)\).
problems.hint: Watch the signs when distributing.

steps.title: Factor Out a Common Term
steps.mastery: Pull the largest shared factor out of every term in an expression.
steps.practice: Factorize 12x + 18, then 5a^2 - 15a, then 6xy + 9x.
steps.detail: Find the highest number dividing every coefficient, and the lowest power of each letter appearing in every term. Take both out together. Expand your answer back to check, it must return the original exactly, not something close.
steps.pitfall: Taking out a factor that only divides some of the terms.

problems.prompt: Factor the greatest common factor from \(8m + 12\).
Factor the greatest common factor from \(9p^{2} - 6p\).
Factor the expression \(14ab + 21a\).
problems.hint: Find the largest factor common to both terms.
Factor out the highest power of each variable that appears in all terms.

steps.title: Rearrange a Formula
steps.mastery: Make a named letter the subject of a formula without changing what it says.
steps.practice: Rearrange v = u + at to make a the subject, then make t the subject of s = vt.
steps.detail: Whatever you do to one side, do to the other. Peel operations off the letter you want in reverse order: undo the addition before the multiplication. Substitute a number set back into both the original and your rearrangement, they must agree.
steps.proof: a = (v - u) / t, and t = s / v.
steps.pitfall: Moving a term across without reversing its operation, so a subtraction stays a subtraction.

problems.prompt: Solve for a in the equation \(a + 3 = 9\).
Rewrite the equation \(5b - 2 = 13\) to isolate b.
Make a the subject of \(v = u + at\).
problems.hint: Subtract u from both sides, then divide by t.

problems.prompt: Make t the subject of \(s = vt\), where \(s = 20\) and \(v = 4\).
problems.hint: Divide both sides by v.

problems.prompt: Given the equation \(3c + 7 = 2c - 5\), rearrange to solve for c.
problems.hint: Move 2c to the left and 7 to the right, then simplify.

steps.title: Turn Words into Algebra
steps.mastery: Write an expression or equation from a situation described in a sentence.
steps.practice: Write an expression for the cost of n tickets at 8 each plus a 3 booking fee, then find n when the total is 59.
steps.detail: Write down what the letter means before anything else: 'let n be the number of tickets'. Translate the sentence clause by clause in the order it is written. Check the finished expression against a case you can count by hand.
steps.proof: 8n + 3, and n = 7.
steps.pitfall: Defining the letter loosely, so 'tickets' means the count in one line and the cost in the next.

problems.prompt: Write an expression for the cost of \(n\) tickets at $8 each plus a $3 booking fee.
If each apple costs $2 and you buy a bags of apples, write the total cost expression.
The total cost of \(n\) tickets is $59. Write an equation and solve for \(n\).
A cinema charges a $5 booking fee plus $10 per ticket. If the total charge is $85, how many tickets were bought? Write the equation and solve.
A school fundraiser sells bracelets for $4 each and collects a $20 donation. If they raised $156 total, how many bracelets were sold? Write the equation and find the number.

steps.title: Times Tables to Twelve
steps.mastery: Recall any product up to 12 x 12 without counting up to it.
steps.practice: Write out the 7 and 8 times tables, then answer 6 x 9, 7 x 8 and 12 x 4 cold.
steps.detail: Say them out loud rather than reading them. The pairs people stall on are almost always 6x7, 7x8, 8x9 and 12x7, so give those four their own pass. A table you can recite forwards but not answer at random is still being computed.
steps.proof: The three answers are 54, 56 and 48, and none of them took a pause.
steps.pitfall: Rebuilding 7 x 8 from 7 x 7 every time, which is recall you have not actually got.

problems.prompt: Answer these three without pausing: \(6 \times 9\), \(7 \times 8\), \(12 \times 4\).
Write out the 7 times table from \(7 \times 1\) to \(7 \times 12\), then cover it and answer \(7 \times 6\) and \(7 \times 11\).
problems.hint: The table ends 77, 84, count back one step from 84 for \(7 \times 11\).

problems.prompt: Answer \(12 \times 7\), \(8 \times 9\), \(6 \times 7\) and \(11 \times 12\) in under 20 seconds total.

steps.title: Long Multiplication
steps.mastery: Multiply two multi-digit numbers on paper and get the same answer twice.
steps.practice: Multiply 347 x 28 by hand, then check it by computing 347 x 30 - 347 x 2.
steps.detail: Set the digits in columns and keep the carries above the line where you can see them. The second row is the tens digit, so it starts one column left. The subtraction check is worth doing every time: it uses different arithmetic, so it catches errors a re-run of the same method repeats.
steps.proof: Both routes give 9716.
steps.pitfall: Losing the place-value zero on the second row, which shifts the whole answer by a factor of ten.

problems.prompt: Multiply \(43 \times 12\) by hand.
Multiply \(218 \times 43\) by hand, then verify with \(218 \times 40 + 218 \times 3\).
Multiply \(526 \times 407\) by hand.
problems.answer: 214,082. The tens digit of 407 is 0, so the middle row is all zeros.

steps.title: Short Division
steps.mastery: Divide a multi-digit number by a single digit, carrying remainders correctly.
steps.practice: Divide 4728 by 6, then multiply your answer back by 6 to check.
steps.detail: Work left to right, carrying what is left over into the next digit. When the divisor does not fit, the quotient digit is 0 and it must be written down. Multiplying back is the check that costs ten seconds and catches nearly everything.
steps.proof: 788 exactly, and 788 x 6 returns 4728.
steps.pitfall: Dropping a digit when the divisor does not go into it, instead of writing a zero.

problems.prompt: Divide 96 by 4.
Divide 4728 by 6 and check by multiplying back.
Divide 6035 by 7 and give the quotient and remainder.
problems.hint: 7 does not go into 6, so the first quotient digit sits over the 0.

steps.title: Estimate Before You Compute
steps.mastery: State the rough size of an answer before working it out exactly.
steps.practice: Estimate 612 x 39 by rounding to 600 x 40, then compute it exactly and compare.
steps.detail: Round each number to one significant figure and multiply those. If the exact answer lands far from the estimate, one of the two is wrong and it is usually the exact one. Rounding one number up and the other down keeps the estimate honest.
steps.proof: The estimate is 24000, the exact answer is 23868, and they agree to within 1%.
steps.pitfall: Rounding both numbers the same way, which pushes the estimate off in one direction rather than bracketing it.

problems.prompt: Estimate \(39 \times 21\) by rounding each to one significant figure.
Round 612 and 39 to one significant figure and multiply. The exact product is 23,868. What is the percentage error of your estimate, to 2 decimal places?
Estimate \(\frac{4870}{61}\) to one significant figure.
problems.answer: About 80. The exact value is 79.8, so the estimate is slightly high because 61 was rounded down to 60.

steps.title: Catch a Wrong Answer
steps.mastery: Spot that a result is impossible from its size, sign or last digit alone.
steps.practice: Decide without computing which of 43 x 27 = 1161, 43 x 27 = 1160 and 43 x 27 = 11610 can be right.
steps.detail: Three cheap tests catch most errors. The magnitude: roughly how many digits should the answer have. The last digit: it is fixed by the last digits of the inputs. The sign: two negatives make a positive. Run all three on every answer that matters.
steps.proof: Only 1161 survives: the last digit of 3 x 7 must be 1, and 11610 is ten times too big.
steps.pitfall: Trusting a calculator answer that is off by a factor of ten because a key was mistyped.

problems.prompt: Without computing, which of 1161, 1160 or 11610 can be \(43 \times 27\)?
problems.answer: 1161. The last digit must be 1 and the answer must have four digits.

problems.prompt: A calculator gives \(18 \times 24 = 4320\). Say what went wrong.
problems.answer: It is ten times too big; the answer is 432.

problems.prompt: Someone reports that \(0.4 \times 0.3 = 1.2\). Give the right answer and name the error.
problems.answer: 0.12. They counted one decimal place instead of two.

steps.title: Multiply the Choices
steps.mastery: Count outcomes of a sequence of independent choices by multiplying.
steps.practice: A menu has 4 starters, 6 mains and 3 desserts. Count the possible three-course meals.
steps.detail: When one choice does not restrict the next, the totals multiply. Draw two stages of a tree to see why: each of the 4 starters branches into all 6 mains. Add only when the choices are alternatives rather than stages.
steps.proof: 72, from 4 x 6 x 3.
steps.pitfall: Adding the options instead of multiplying, giving 13.

problems.prompt: A smoothie bar offers 2 fruit bases, 3 milk types, and 4 sweeteners. How many different smoothies can be made?
A restaurant offers 5 appetizers, 7 main courses, and 2 desserts. How many distinct three-course meals can be ordered?
A combo includes choosing one of 3 sauces, one of 4 breads, and one of 5 cheeses. How many possible combos are there?
problems.hint: Multiply the numbers of options for each choice.

steps.title: Factorials and Arrangements
steps.mastery: Count the orderings of a set of distinct objects.
steps.practice: Count the ways to arrange 5 different books on a shelf, then the ways to seat 4 people in a row.
steps.detail: The first position has n choices, the next n-1, and so on, which is n factorial. It grows brutally fast, 10 objects already give over three million arrangements, so a small answer to an arrangement question is usually a wrong one.
steps.pitfall: Reaching for a formula when the question is a plain factorial.

problems.prompt: How many ways can 3 different keys be arranged on a hook?
In how many orders can 4 distinct cards be dealt face up?
How many possible orderings are there for 6 unique trophies on a shelf?
A theater has 5 distinct seats in a row. In how many ways can 5 different audience members be seated?

steps.title: Order Matters: Permutations
steps.mastery: Count selections where the order of what you pick changes the outcome.
steps.practice: Count the ways to award gold, silver and bronze among 8 runners.
steps.detail: Pick r from n with order mattering: n! over (n-r)!. The test is whether swapping two chosen items gives a different outcome. Gold and silver swapped is a different podium, so order matters here.
steps.proof: 336, from 8 x 7 x 6.
steps.pitfall: Dividing by 3 factorial, which would be right only if the medals were identical.

problems.prompt: From 3 runners, how many ways can gold and silver medals be awarded?
How many ordered pairs can be formed by choosing a president and a treasurer from 4 club members?
In a race with 9 participants, how many possible podium finishes (gold, silver, bronze) are there?
If among 8 runners, runner A cannot win gold, how many ways can gold, silver, and bronze be awarded?
problems.hint: First choose gold excluding A, then continue multiplying.

problems.prompt: 8!/3! is the wrong count for awarding gold, silver and bronze medals to 8 runners. What is the right count?
problems.answer: 336. That is 8!/5! = \(8 \times 7 \times 6\). The 8!/3! count orders 5 runners, not 3.
problems.hint: Consider that gold, silver, bronze are different.

steps.title: Order Does Not: Combinations
steps.mastery: Count selections where only the set chosen matters, not its order.
steps.practice: Count the ways to choose a committee of 3 from 8 people.
steps.detail: Combinations are permutations divided by the orderings of the chosen group: n! over r!(n-r)!. Ask the swap test again, two committee members swapped is the same committee, so divide. The two formulas differ by exactly that r! factor.
steps.pitfall: Using the permutation count, which counts the same committee six times over.

problems.prompt: How many ways are there to choose 2 people from a group of 5?
How many different 3-person committees can be formed from 6 candidates?
How many ways can a committee of 4 be chosen from 10 people?
Why does using the permutation formula 10P4 give a wrong count for choosing a 4-person committee from 10 people?
problems.answer: Because permutations count order, each unordered committee is counted \(4! = 24\) times.
problems.hint: Think about what extra factor permutations introduce.

problems.prompt: If a committee must include Alice, how many ways can the remaining 2 members be chosen from the other 7 people?
problems.hint: Fix Alice first, then choose 2 from the remaining 7.

steps.title: Repetition Allowed
steps.mastery: Count selections where the same item may be chosen more than once.
steps.practice: Count the 4-digit PINs using digits 0 to 9 with repeats allowed, then the ones with no repeats.
steps.detail: With repetition the count is n to the power r, because every position has the full n choices. Without it the pool shrinks by one each time. Read the question for the word 'distinct' or 'different' before choosing.
steps.pitfall: Applying a no-repeat formula to a question that never forbade repeats.

problems.prompt: Count the 1-digit codes that can be formed from the digits 0-9 when repeats are allowed.
How many 2-digit PINs can be created using the digits 0-9 with repeats allowed?
Count the 5-digit PINs that can be formed from the digits 0-9 when repeats are allowed.
How many 4-digit PINs can be formed from the digits 0-9 with repeats allowed if the first digit cannot be zero?
problems.hint: Treat the first position separately (9 choices) and the remaining three positions (10 choices each).

problems.prompt: In how many ways can you select 7 scoops of ice-cream from 4 flavors when any flavor may be chosen more than once?
problems.hint: Use stars-and-bars: choose 3 dividers among 10 positions.

steps.title: Count the Complement
steps.mastery: Count what you want by counting what you do not and subtracting.
steps.practice: Count the 5-letter strings from A to Z that contain at least one vowel.
steps.detail: 'At least one' is nearly always easier as everything minus none. Count the whole space, count the cases you do not want, subtract. Direct counting here means splitting into exactly-one, exactly-two and so on, and adding overlaps you will get wrong.
steps.pitfall: Trying to count 'at least one' directly and double-counting strings with two.

problems.prompt: Flip 3 coins. How many of the outcomes have at least 1 head?
Roll 2 dice. How many of the 36 outcomes have at least one 6?
How many 4-digit PINs, with digits 0 to 9, contain at least one 7?
How many 3-letter strings from A to Z contain at least 1 vowel, counting A, E, I, O and U as vowels?
A club has 5 seniors and 4 juniors. How many 3-person committees include at least 1 junior?
How many 6-bit strings contain at least two 1s?
problems.hint: Take out the strings with no 1s and the strings with exactly one.

steps.title: Overlapping Sets
steps.mastery: Count a union without counting the overlap twice.
steps.practice: Of 30 students, 18 take French and 15 take Spanish, and 7 take both. Count those taking at least one.
steps.detail: Inclusion-exclusion: add the sets, subtract the intersection, because everyone in both was counted twice. Draw the two circles and label the three regions, 11, 7 and 8 here, and the arithmetic checks itself against the total.
steps.pitfall: Adding the two groups and reporting 33, which exceeds the class.

problems.prompt: In a group of 10 people, 4 play piano and 3 play violin, with no one playing both. How many play at least one instrument?
In a club of 20 members, 12 like chess and 8 like checkers, with 5 liking both. How many like at least one game?
Of 30 students, 18 take French and 15 take Spanish, and 7 take both. Count those taking at least one language.
In a survey of 50 people, 28 own a cat, 22 own a dog, and 10 own both. How many own at least one pet?
A library has 40 books on history, 30 on science, and 12 are both history and science. How many books are on at least one of these subjects?

steps.title: Choose the Right Count
steps.mastery: Decide, unprompted, which counting method a worded problem needs.
steps.practice: For these three, name the method: seating 6 people in a row; picking 2 of 10 books; 3-letter codes from 26 letters with repeats.
steps.detail: Two questions decide it every time: does order matter, and is repetition allowed. Answer both in writing before picking a formula. Most errors here are not arithmetic, they are answering the wrong one of the four cases.
steps.proof: Factorial, combination, and n to the power r: 720, 45 and 17576.
steps.pitfall: Pattern-matching on the numbers in the question rather than on its structure.

problems.prompt: What counting method counts the number of ways to arrange 5 distinct toys in a line?
What counting method counts the number of ways to choose 3 students from a class of 12?
Name the counting method for picking 2 books out of 10 different books where order does not matter.
Name the counting method for creating 3-letter codes from the 26 letters of the alphabet when letters may be repeated.
Explain why the problem 'How many ways can 6 people be seated around a circular table?' requires a different counting method than 'Seating 6 people in a row.'.
problems.answer: Because rotations are considered identical, we use circular permutations: (6-1)! = 120, not \(6! = 720\).
problems.hint: Consider identical arrangements under rotation.

problems.prompt: A password must be 4 characters long, using the 10 digits, but no digit may appear more than once. Explain which counting method applies and why the simple \(n^{r}\) formula is not suitable.
problems.answer: We use permutations without repetition: \(10 \cdot 9 \cdot 8 \cdot 7 = 5040\), because each choice reduces the available digits, so repetitions are not allowed.
problems.hint: Think about decreasing choices after each position.

steps.title: Plot and Read Points
steps.mastery: Place a coordinate pair on a grid and read one back without swapping the axes.
steps.practice: Plot (3, -2), (-4, 1) and (0, 5), then name the quadrant each falls in.
steps.detail: The first number is always the horizontal one. Quadrants are numbered counterclockwise from the top right. A point with a zero coordinate lies on an axis and belongs to no quadrant, which is worth saying rather than guessing at.
steps.proof: Fourth, second, and on the positive y-axis between the first and second.
steps.pitfall: Reading (3, -2) as three up and two across, which lands in the wrong quadrant.

problems.prompt: What quadrant does the point (2, -3) lie in?
Plot the points (3, -2), (-4, 1) and (0, 5). Name the quadrant of each, in that order, and say "axis" for a point on an axis.
problems.answer: Fourth, second, and (0, 5) is on the positive y-axis, between the first and second quadrants.

problems.prompt: If a point is read as "three up and two across" instead of (3, -2), which quadrant would be incorrectly identified? Explain the error.
problems.answer: It would be placed in the first quadrant, but the correct point (3, -2) is in the fourth quadrant; the mistake is swapping the sign of the y-coordinate.
problems.hint: Consider the sign of the y-value when reading the ordered pair.

steps.title: Distance Between Points
steps.mastery: Compute the straight-line distance between two points from their coordinates.
steps.practice: Find the distance between (1, 2) and (4, 6), then between (-3, 0) and (1, -3).
steps.detail: The distance is Pythagoras on the horizontal and vertical gaps. Subtract in either order, the squaring removes the sign. Sketching the right triangle before computing makes an impossible answer obvious, because the distance must exceed either gap alone.
steps.proof: 5 and 5, both from 3-4-5 right triangles.
steps.pitfall: Forgetting to square the differences, and subtracting the coordinates instead.

problems.prompt: Find the distance between (1, 1) and (4, 5).
Find the distance between (-2, 3) and (1, -1).
Find the distance between (0, 0) and (2, 3).
problems.hint: Square each coordinate difference, add them, then take the square root.

problems.prompt: Find the distance between (-5, -2) and (3, 4).
problems.hint: Compute the differences, square them (signs disappear), sum, and take the square root.

steps.title: Midpoint of a Segment
steps.mastery: Find the point exactly halfway between two given points.
steps.practice: Find the midpoint of (2, 7) and (8, 1), then find B when A is (1, 1) and the midpoint is (4, 5).
steps.detail: Average the x values and average the y values. Going backwards, the midpoint is as far from A as B is from the midpoint, so double the gap. Check by confirming your answer is the same distance from both ends.
steps.pitfall: Subtracting the coordinates rather than averaging them.

problems.prompt: What is the midpoint of (0,0) and (4,6)?
Find the midpoint of (-2, 5) and (6, -1).
Given points \(P(1, 4)\) and \(Q(7, - 2)\), a student subtracts the coordinates to get (6,-6) and claims this is the midpoint. Identify the error and give the correct midpoint.
problems.answer: The midpoint is \((\frac{1 + 7}{2}, \frac{4 + - 2}{2}) = (4, 1)\); the error was using subtraction instead of averaging.

problems.prompt: Point A is (3, -5) and the midpoint of segment AB is (8, 2). Find point B.
problems.hint: Use the midpoint formula solved for the unknown endpoint.

steps.title: Parallel and Perpendicular
steps.mastery: Decide from two gradients whether lines are parallel, perpendicular or neither.
steps.practice: Say how y = 3x + 1 relates to y = 3x - 4, and to y = -x/3 + 2.
steps.detail: Parallel lines share a gradient. Perpendicular gradients multiply to -1, so one is the negative reciprocal of the other. Rearrange both equations into y = mx + c before comparing, or you are comparing coefficients that are not gradients.
steps.proof: Parallel to the first, since both have gradient 3; perpendicular to the second, since 3 x -1/3 is -1.
steps.pitfall: Taking the negative of a gradient as perpendicular without also inverting it.

problems.prompt: Are the lines \(y = 2x + 3\) and \(y = 2x - 5\) parallel, perpendicular, or neither?
Are the lines \(y = - 0.5x + 4\) and \(y = 2x - 1\) perpendicular?
problems.answer: Yes. The slopes \(-\frac{1}{2}\) and 2 multiply to -1.

problems.prompt: Line L_1 has gradient 4. Which gradient makes a line perpendicular to L_1: -4, \(\frac{1}{4}\), \(-\frac{1}{4}\) or 4?
problems.hint: Recall the negative reciprocal rule.

problems.prompt: Two lines have gradients \(m_{1} = 3\) and \(m_{2} = - \frac{1}{3}\). A student says they're parallel because the numbers look alike. Are they parallel, perpendicular, or neither?
problems.answer: Perpendicular. The product \(3 \times (-\frac{1}{3}) = - 1\), which is the test for perpendicular lines.
problems.hint: Check the product of the gradients.

steps.title: The Equation of a Circle
steps.mastery: Read the center and radius from a circle's equation, and write one from them.
steps.practice: State the center and radius of (x - 2)^2 + (y + 3)^2 = 25, then write the circle centered at (0, 4) with radius 6.
steps.detail: The form is (x - h)^2 + (y - k)^2 = r^2. The signs inside flip, so (y + 3)^2 means k is -3. The right-hand side is the radius squared, which is why 25 gives a radius of 5.
steps.proof: Center (2, -3) and radius 5; the second is x^2 + (y - 4)^2 = 36.
steps.pitfall: Reading the right-hand side as the radius rather than as its square.

problems.prompt: What is the center of the circle \((x - 5)^{2} + (y - 2)^{2} = 9\)?
What is the radius of the circle \(x^{2} + y^{2} = 16\)?
State the center and radius of \((x + 1)^{2} + (y - 4)^{2} = 49\).
Write the equation of the circle with center (3, -2) and radius \(\sqrt{13}\).
problems.hint: Square the radius when forming the equation.

problems.prompt: Expand \((x - 2)^{2} + (y + 3)^{2} = 25\), then give the radius of the circle.
problems.answer: 5. Expanded it is \(x^{2} - 4x + 4 + y^{2} + 6y + 9 = 25\), and the radius is \(\sqrt{25} = 5\), not 25.
problems.hint: Remember the RHS is the square of the radius.

steps.title: Where Two Graphs Meet
steps.mastery: Find the intersection of two graphs by solving their equations together.
steps.practice: Find where y = x + 1 meets y = x^2 - 1.
steps.detail: Set the two expressions for y equal, collect everything on one side, and solve. Each solution for x gives a point, so substitute back into whichever equation is simpler. A quadratic and a line meet twice, once or not at all, and the discriminant says which.
steps.proof: At (-1, 0) and (2, 3), from solving x^2 - x - 2 = 0.
steps.pitfall: Solving for x and forgetting to compute the matching y, so the answer is not a point.

problems.prompt: What is \(y\) when \(x = 0\) for the line \(y = x + 1\)?
What is the y-value on the parabola \(y = x^{2} - 1\) when \(x = 2\)?
Find the intersection point(s) of \(y = x + 1\) and \(y = x^{2} - 1\).
Solve for the intersection of \(y = - x + 4\) and \(y = x^{2} - 4x + 3\), and give the exact points.
problems.hint: Set the two expressions equal and solve the resulting quadratic.

problems.prompt: The line \(y = 2x - 1\) meets the parabola \(y = x^{2} - 4\) at two points. Give both points, with their y-values.
problems.answer: (3, 5) and (-1, -3). Solving \(x^{2} - 4 = 2x - 1\) gives \(x = 3\) or -1, and each needs its y-value to be a point.
problems.hint: First solve for \(x\), then substitute back to get \(y\).

steps.title: Prove a Shape from Coordinates
steps.mastery: Use distance and gradient to prove a claim about a shape on the grid.
steps.practice: Show that (0, 0), (4, 0), (4, 3) and (0, 3) form a rectangle, using gradients and lengths.
steps.detail: A drawing suggests; the arithmetic proves. Equal opposite sides give a parallelogram, and one right angle upgrades it to a rectangle. State which fact you are using for each claim rather than computing everything and hoping the conclusion follows.
steps.proof: Opposite sides have equal length 4 and 3, and adjacent gradients are 0 and undefined, so the corners are right angles.
steps.pitfall: Concluding from the drawing that the angles are right rather than showing it from the numbers.

problems.prompt: What is the distance between (0,0) and (3,4)?
What is the gradient of the line through (2,1) and (2,5)?
Using the distance formula, find the length of the side between (0,0) and (4,0).
problems.hint: \(\Delta x = 4\), \(\Delta y = 0\)

problems.prompt: Show that the gradient of the line through (0,0) and (4,3) is \(\frac{3}{4}\).
problems.hint: Gradient = \(\frac{\Delta y}{\Delta x}\)

problems.prompt: Prove that the quadrilateral with vertices (0,0), (4,0), (4,3), (0,3) is a rectangle by demonstrating both that opposite sides are equal in length and that adjacent sides are perpendicular using gradients.
problems.answer: Opposite sides: (0,0)-(4,0) length 4 and (4,3)-(0,3) length 4; (4,0)-(4,3) length 3 and (0,0)-(0,3) length 3. Gradients: horizontal sides have gradient 0, vertical sides have undefined gradient. Since a horizontal line is perpendicular to a vertical line, each corner is a right angle. With equal opposite sides and right angles, the shape is a rectangle.
problems.hint: Compute lengths of each side then the gradients of each side.

problems.prompt: Given points \(A(0, 0)\), \(B(4, 0)\), \(C(4, 3)\), \(D(0, 3)\), prove that diagonal AC is equal in length to diagonal BD and use this to confirm the shape is a rectangle.
problems.answer: AC length = \(\sqrt{(4 - 0)^{2} + (3 - 0)^{2}} = 5\); BD length = \(\sqrt{(0 - 4)^{2} + (3 - 0)^{2}} = 5\). The diagonals are equal. Combined with the fact that one adjacent pair of sides (e.g., AB and BC) are perpendicular (gradient 0 and undefined), the quadrilateral satisfies the definition of a rectangle.
problems.hint: Find both diagonals using the distance formula.

steps.title: Three Ways to Write It
steps.mastery: Convert freely between a fraction, a decimal and a percentage.
steps.practice: Fill the row for 3/8, then for 0.45, then for 12%, giving all three forms each time.
steps.detail: A percentage is a fraction with a denominator of 100, so per cent to decimal is a division by 100 and the point moves two places left. Fraction to decimal is just the division the bar was always asking for. Build the table rather than memorizing pairs.
steps.pitfall: Moving the decimal point the wrong way, turning 12% into 1.2 rather than 0.12.

problems.prompt: Write \(\frac{1}{2}\) as a decimal and then as a percentage.
Give \(\frac{3}{8}\) as a decimal and then as a percentage.
Give 12% as a decimal and as a fraction in lowest terms.

steps.title: Decimal Arithmetic
steps.mastery: Add, subtract and multiply decimals with the point in the right place.
steps.practice: Compute 12.4 + 3.75, then 2.5 x 0.4, then 0.6 x 0.03.
steps.detail: For addition, line up the points and pad with zeros so every number has the same number of places. For multiplication, ignore the points entirely, multiply as whole numbers, then count the total decimal places in both inputs and put that many in the answer.
steps.pitfall: Lining up the right-hand digits instead of the decimal points when adding.

problems.prompt: Compute \(2.5 \times 0.4\).
Compute \(0.6 \times 0.03\), placing the decimal point by counting places.
problems.answer: 0.018. It needs three places, because the inputs have one and two.

steps.title: Percentage Of
steps.mastery: Find a stated percentage of a quantity, and go back the other way.
steps.practice: Find 15% of 240, then find the number whose 30% is 72.
steps.detail: Turn the percentage into a decimal and multiply. Reversing it is a division by that same decimal, not by the percentage itself. Writing the sentence as an equation first, 0.3 x n = 72, makes which operation is needed obvious rather than remembered.
steps.proof: 36, and 240, the second is 72 divided by 0.3.
steps.pitfall: Dividing by the percentage rather than by the decimal, so 30% becomes a division by 30.

problems.prompt: Find 10% of 240.
Find 15% of 240.
Find the number whose 30% is 72.

steps.title: Percentage Change
steps.mastery: Compute a change as a percentage of the original, in either direction.
steps.practice: A price goes from 80 to 92. Find the percentage increase, then take 92 back down by the same percentage.
steps.detail: Change divided by the original, times 100. The original is the number you started from, and swapping it for the final value is the error. That a rise and an equal fall do not return you to the start is not a trick, the base moved, and the second percentage is of the larger number.
steps.proof: A 15% increase, and 92 reduced by 15% is 78.2, not 80.
steps.pitfall: Believing a 15% rise and a 15% fall cancel, because the two are percentages of different numbers.

problems.prompt: A price rises from 80 to 92. Find the percentage increase.
80 grew by 15% to 92. Now take 92 down by 15%. What do you get?
problems.answer: 78.2, so you don't get back to 80. The base has moved.

problems.prompt: A value falls 20% then rises 20%. What percentage of the original value is it now?

steps.title: Reverse a Percentage
steps.mastery: Recover an original value from a figure that already includes a change.
steps.practice: A jacket costs 66 after a 12% discount. Find the original price.
steps.detail: After a 12% discount the price is 88% of the original, so the original is the price divided by 0.88. Write the multiplier first, 0.88 for a 12% cut, 1.12 for a 12% rise, and the division follows. Check by applying the change forwards to your answer.
steps.proof: 75, because 66 divided by 0.88 is 75, and 12% of 75 is 9.
steps.pitfall: Adding 12% back onto 66, which gives 73.92 and is not the original.

problems.prompt: A price of 100 is cut by 10%. Give the new price.
A jacket costs 66 after a 12% discount. Find the original price.
problems.hint: 66 is 88% of the original.

problems.prompt: A bill is 141 including 17.5% tax. Find the amount before tax, to the nearest penny.

steps.title: The Index Laws
steps.mastery: Combine powers of the same base by adding, subtracting or multiplying indices.
steps.detail: Multiplying adds the indices, dividing subtracts them, and a power of a power multiplies them. All three need the same base, so 2^3 x 3^2 combines into nothing. Expanding a small case by hand settles which rule applies.
steps.pitfall: Multiplying the indices when the powers are multiplied, so 2^3 x 2^5 becomes 2^15.

problems.prompt: Simplify \(2^{2} \times 2^{3}\).

problems.hint: Multiply the exponents.

problems.prompt: Simplify \(2^{4} \times 2^{-2}\).
problems.hint: Subtract the exponents when a negative exponent appears.

steps.title: Zero and Negative Powers
steps.mastery: Evaluate a power with a zero or negative index without guessing.
steps.detail: Anything non-zero to the power 0 is 1, which follows from dividing a power by itself. A negative index is a reciprocal, not a negative number. A negative index on a fraction flips it, then applies the positive power.
steps.pitfall: Reading 2^-3 as -8, treating the negative index as a negative answer.

problems.prompt: Evaluate \(5^{0}\).
Evaluate \((\frac{3}{4})^{0}\).
Evaluate \(4^{-2}\).
problems.hint: Write as \(\frac{1}{4^{2}}\).
Invert the fraction and raise to the positive exponent.

steps.title: Fractional Powers
steps.mastery: Read a fractional index as a root and evaluate it.
steps.detail: The denominator of the index is the root and the numerator is the power. Take the root first so the numbers stay small: 16^(3/4) is the fourth root of 16, which is 2, then cubed to 8. The other order gives the same answer through far uglier arithmetic.
steps.pitfall: Taking the root of the whole thing after applying the power, which makes the arithmetic much harder than it needs to be.

problems.prompt: Evaluate \(4^{\frac{1}{2}}\).
Evaluate \(27^{\frac{1}{3}}\).
Evaluate \(16^{\frac{3}{4}}\).
Evaluate \(32^{\frac{2}{5}}\).
problems.hint: Take the fifth root then square.

problems.prompt: Evaluate \(81^{\frac{3}{4}}\).
problems.hint: First take the fourth root.

steps.title: What a Logarithm Is
steps.mastery: Rewrite an exponential statement as a logarithm and back again.
steps.practice: Rewrite 2^5 = 32 as a logarithm, then evaluate log base 3 of 81.
steps.detail: A logarithm answers 'what power gives this'. So log base b of n is the exponent you raise b to in order to reach n. Reading every log question back as the exponential it came from is the fastest way to evaluate it.
steps.proof: log base 2 of 32 is 5, and the second is 4.
steps.pitfall: Losing track of which number is the base and which is the answer.

problems.prompt: Rewrite \(3^{2} = 9\) as a logarithm.
What is log base 5 of 125?
Rewrite \(4^{3} = 64\) as a logarithm, then evaluate log base 2 of 16.
Rewrite \(9^{2} = 81\) as a logarithm, then express 81 as \(3^{k}\).
problems.hint: First change to a log, then write 81 as a power of 3.

problems.prompt: Rewrite \(16 = 2^{4}\) as a logarithm, then find log base 4 of 2.
problems.hint: Remember the base is the number you raise to get the argument.

steps.title: The Log Laws
steps.mastery: Split or combine logarithms of products, quotients and powers.
steps.practice: Write log(xy^2) as a sum of simpler logs, then combine log 8 - log 2 into one.
steps.detail: A product becomes a sum, a quotient becomes a difference, and a power comes out as a multiplier. There is no law for the log of a sum. Testing a law on small numbers, log 8 - log 2 against log 4, is the check that catches the invented ones.
steps.proof: log x + 2 log y, and log 4.
steps.pitfall: Turning log(x + y) into log x + log y, which is not a law and is not true.

problems.prompt: Write log base 10 of 20 as a sum of logs of its prime factors.
Combine log base 10 of 50 minus log base 10 of 2 into a single logarithm.
Express log base 10 of \((xy^{2})\) as a sum of simpler logarithms.
Split log base 10 of \((a^{3}b/c^{2})\) into separate logarithms.
Combine log base 10 of 8 + log base 10 of \(4 - 2\) log base 10 of 2 into a single logarithm.

steps.title: Solve With Logs
steps.mastery: Solve an equation where the unknown sits in the exponent.
steps.practice: Solve 3^x = 50, giving the answer to three decimal places.
steps.detail: Take the log of both sides, then bring the exponent down as a multiplier. The base does not matter as long as both sides use the same one. Substitute your answer back into the original to confirm it is close to 50.
steps.proof: x = log 50 / log 3, which is 3.561.
steps.pitfall: Dividing 50 by 3 because the 3 looks like a coefficient.

problems.prompt: Solve \(3^{x} = 50\), give the answer to three decimal places.

problems.hint: Rewrite 125 as \(5^{3}\).

problems.answer: \(x = 4\). Write 32 as \(2^{5}\), so \(x + 1 = 5\). Dividing both sides by 2 doesn't touch the exponent.

steps.title: Growth and Decay
steps.mastery: Model a repeated proportional change and find when it reaches a target.
steps.practice: A population of 200 grows 8% a year. Find its size after 10 years, then the year it passes 500.
steps.detail: Repeated proportional change is a power, not a multiplication: the size is 200 x 1.08^n. Finding the year takes a log. Checking the first two years by hand confirms the multiplier before you trust the formula.
steps.proof: About 432 after 10 years, and it passes 500 during year 12.
steps.pitfall: Adding 8% of the original each year rather than compounding on the new total.

problems.prompt: A colony of 150 bacteria grows 5% in one hour. What is its size after that hour?
A bank account has $500 and earns 3% interest each month, compounded monthly. What is the balance after 2 months? (Round to the nearest cent).
A population of 200 grows 8% per year. What is its size after 10 years? (Round to the nearest whole number).
problems.hint: Use the formula \(P(1 + r)^{t}\).

problems.prompt: A population of 200 grows 8% per year. In which year does the population first become at least 500?
problems.hint: Solve \(200(1.08)^{n} \ge 500\) for the smallest integer \(n\).

problems.prompt: A population starts at 200 and grows 8% per year for the first 5 years, then 5% per year thereafter. In which year does it first exceed 500? (Give the smallest integer year).
problems.hint: First compute the size after 5 years, then apply 5% growth until it reaches 500.

problems.prompt: Why does adding 8% of the original 200 each year give a later year than the correct compounding method for reaching 500?
problems.answer: Because simple addition treats growth as linear, underestimating the true exponential increase, so the population reaches 500 later.

steps.title: Equivalent Fractions
steps.mastery: Scale a fraction up or down without changing the quantity it names.
steps.practice: Write 3/4 with denominators of 8, 20 and 100, then reduce 18/24 to lowest terms.
steps.detail: Multiplying the numerator and denominator by the same number is multiplying by 1, which is why the value holds. Reducing is the same move in reverse: divide both by their highest common factor. Find that factor rather than halving repeatedly and hoping.
steps.proof: 6/8, 15/20, 75/100, and 18/24 reduces to 3/4, all four name the same quantity.
steps.pitfall: Adding to the top and bottom instead of multiplying, which changes the value.

problems.prompt: Write \(\frac{3}{4}\) with a denominator of 8.
Reduce \(\frac{18}{24}\) to lowest terms and name the factor you divided by.
Reduce \(\frac{84}{126}\) to lowest terms.
problems.hint: Both are divisible by 6, then by 7.

steps.title: Add Unlike Denominators
steps.mastery: Add or subtract two fractions whose denominators start out different.
steps.practice: Compute 2/3 + 1/4 and 5/6 - 3/8, giving both answers in lowest terms.
steps.detail: Find a common denominator first, the lowest common multiple keeps the numbers small, but any common multiple works. Rescale both fractions to it, then add only the numerators. The denominator counts what size the pieces are, and it does not change when you count more of them.
steps.pitfall: Adding the denominators together, so 1/2 + 1/3 comes out as 2/5.

problems.prompt: Compute \(\frac{1}{4} + \frac{1}{4}\).
Compute \(\frac{2}{3} + \frac{1}{4}\) in lowest terms.
Compute \(\frac{5}{6} - \frac{3}{8}\) in lowest terms.
problems.hint: The lowest common denominator is 24.

steps.title: Multiply and Divide
steps.mastery: Multiply fractions straight across, and divide by inverting the second one.
steps.practice: Compute 3/5 x 10/9 and 4/7 divided by 2/3, canceling before you multiply.
steps.detail: Multiplication needs no common denominator: tops together, bottoms together. Cancel any factor shared by a numerator and a denominator first, even across the two fractions, and the arithmetic stays small. Division is multiplication by the reciprocal, and only the divisor flips.
steps.pitfall: Inverting the first fraction rather than the second when dividing.

problems.prompt: Compute \(\frac{2}{3} \times \frac{3}{5}\).
Compute \(\frac{7}{8} \times \frac{4}{21}\), canceling common factors before multiplying.
problems.hint: The 4 cancels with the 8 and the 7 cancels with the 21.

problems.prompt: Compute \(\frac{9}{10}\) divided by \(\frac{3}{4}\). Then give what you'd get by wrongly inverting \(\frac{9}{10}\) instead. Give both, in that order.
problems.answer: \(\frac{6}{5}\). Inverting the first instead would give \(\frac{5}{6}\).

steps.title: Mixed Numbers
steps.mastery: Convert between mixed numbers and improper fractions in both directions.
steps.practice: Convert 3 and 2/5 to an improper fraction, then turn 47/6 back into a mixed number.
steps.detail: Going in, multiply the whole number by the denominator and add the numerator. Coming out, divide and keep the remainder on top. Always convert to improper before multiplying or dividing, the mixed form is for reading, not for arithmetic.
steps.pitfall: Leaving a mixed number in place during multiplication, which quietly drops the whole part.

problems.prompt: Convert 3 and \(\frac{2}{5}\) to an improper fraction.
Convert \(\frac{47}{6}\) to a mixed number.
Compute 2 and \(\frac{1}{2}\) multiplied by 1 and \(\frac{1}{3}\), giving a mixed number.
problems.hint: Convert both to improper fractions first: \(\frac{5}{2}\) and \(\frac{4}{3}\).

steps.title: Compare Two Fractions
steps.mastery: Decide which of two fractions is larger without converting to decimals.
steps.practice: Order 5/8, 7/12 and 2/3 from smallest to largest using a common denominator of 24.
steps.detail: Rescale everything to one denominator and compare the numerators. Cross-multiplication is the shortcut for exactly two: a/b beats c/d when ad exceeds bc. Both beat converting to decimals, which rounds and can make two close fractions look equal.
steps.pitfall: Assuming the fraction with the bigger numerator is bigger, regardless of the denominator.

problems.prompt: Which is larger, \(\frac{3}{5}\) or \(\frac{2}{5}\)?
Order \(\frac{5}{8}\), \(\frac{7}{12}\) and \(\frac{2}{3}\) from smallest to largest.
problems.hint: Rescale all three to twenty-fourths.

problems.prompt: Which is larger, \(\frac{7}{9}\) or \(\frac{8}{11}\)? Decide by cross-multiplying.

steps.title: One Input, One Output
steps.mastery: Decide whether a rule or a graph defines a function at all.
steps.practice: Say which of y = x^2, x = y^2 and the circle x^2 + y^2 = 9 define y as a function of x.
steps.detail: A function sends each input to exactly one output. On a graph that is the vertical line test: any vertical line may cross at most once. Two outputs for one input is the only thing that disqualifies a rule, so many-to-one is fine.
steps.proof: Only y = x^2; the other two give two y values for a single x.
steps.pitfall: Applying the vertical line test to the wrong axis and rejecting a perfectly good function.

problems.prompt: Does the equation \(y = 3x + 2\) define \(y\) as a function of \(x\)?
Is the graph consisting of the line \(y = x\) together with the isolated point (0,1) a function \(y(x)\)?
Consider the relation defined by \(x^{2} + y^{2} = 4\). Does it define \(y\) as a function of \(x\)? Explain why.
problems.answer: No, because for many \(x\) values there are two corresponding \(y\) values (positive and negative).
problems.hint: Try the vertical line test.

problems.prompt: The relation \(x = y^{2}\) is given. Does it define \(y\) as a function of \(x\)? Explain the mistake if one applies the vertical line test to \(x\).
problems.answer: No, because for a given \(x\) there are two \(y\) values (±√x); the vertical line test must be applied to vertical lines, not horizontal.
problems.hint: Remember which variable is independent.

steps.title: Function Notation
steps.mastery: Evaluate f(x) at a value, including at an expression rather than a number.
steps.practice: Given f(x) = 2x^2 - 3, compute f(4), f(-1) and f(a + 1).
steps.detail: f(x) names a machine, and whatever sits in the bracket goes everywhere x appears. Substitute with brackets, then expand. Feeding in an expression rather than a number is the same operation and is where the notation starts earning its keep.
steps.pitfall: Reading f(a + 1) as f(a) + 1, which is not what the notation says.

problems.prompt: Given \(f(x) = 2x^{2} - 3\), compute \(f(2)\).

problems.hint: Replace \(x\) by \(3x\).

problems.prompt: Given \(f(x) = 2x^{2} - 3\), evaluate \(f(a + 1)\).
problems.hint: Do not split the parentheses.

steps.title: Domain and Range
steps.mastery: State which inputs a function accepts and which outputs it can produce.
steps.practice: Give the domain and range of f(x) = 1/(x - 2) and of g(x) = sqrt(x + 3).
steps.detail: Two things break a domain: dividing by zero and taking an even root of a negative. Find those first. The range is easier read off a sketch than reasoned about, so draw the graph before answering.
steps.proof: f excludes x = 2 and never outputs 0; g needs x >= -3 and outputs values from 0 upwards.
steps.pitfall: Giving the domain and stopping, when the range is the half people actually get wrong.

problems.prompt: What is the domain of \(f(x) = \frac{1}{x - 2}\)?
What is the range of \(g(x) = \sqrt{x + 3}\)?
State the domain and range of \(h(x) = \frac{1}{x - 2}\).
For the function \(k(x) = \sqrt{x + 3}\), give its domain and range, and explain why the range starts at 0.
problems.answer: Domain: \(x \ge - 3\); Range: \(y \ge 0\), because square roots are never negative.
problems.hint: Consider the output of √.

problems.prompt: The function \(m(x) = \sqrt{9 - x^{2}}\) is defined. Determine its domain and range.
problems.hint: Think of the semicircle of radius 3.

steps.title: Read a Graph
steps.mastery: Extract intercepts, turning points and behavior from the picture of a function.
steps.practice: For y = x^2 - 4x + 3, find both x-intercepts, the y-intercept and the vertex.
steps.detail: The y-intercept is the value at x = 0. The x-intercepts are the roots. For a parabola the vertex sits halfway between the roots, so average them and substitute back. Every one of these is a computation, and the sketch is the check.
steps.proof: Intercepts at x = 1 and x = 3, y-intercept 3, vertex at (2, -1).
steps.pitfall: Reading the vertex off the sketch by eye instead of computing it.

problems.prompt: What is the y-intercept of \(y = x^{2} - 4x + 3\)?
What are the x-intercepts of \(y = x^{2} - 4x + 3\)?
Find the vertex of \(y = x^{2} - 4x + 3\).
For the parabola \(y = x^{2} - 4x + 3\), state the axis of symmetry and whether it opens upward or downward.
problems.hint: Write the quadratic in vertex form to read the axis.

problems.prompt: Reflect \(y = x^{2} - 4x + 3\) over the x-axis. Give the new y-intercept, then the new vertex.
problems.hint: Reflect the y-coordinates of the original intercepts and vertex.

steps.title: Compose Two Functions
steps.mastery: Apply one function to the output of another, in the right order.
steps.practice: With f(x) = x + 3 and g(x) = 2x, compute f(g(5)), g(f(5)) and the rule for f(g(x)).
steps.detail: Work from the inside out: g acts on x, then f acts on that. The two orders give different answers in general, which is the point of the exercise. Write the inner result down before applying the outer function rather than doing both in your head.
steps.pitfall: Applying f first in f(g(x)), when the inner function always runs first.

problems.prompt: If \(f(x) = x + 3\), what is \(f(5)\)?
If \(g(x) = 2x\), what is \(g(5)\)?
With \(f(x) = x + 3\) and \(g(x) = 2x\), find \(f(g(5))\).
Find the formula for (f∘g)(x) given \(f(x) = x + 3\) and \(g(x) = 2x\).
problems.hint: Substitute \(g(x)\) into \(f(x)\).

problems.prompt: With the same functions, compute \(g(f(5))\).

steps.title: Find an Inverse
steps.mastery: Construct the function that undoes another, and say when one exists.
steps.practice: Find the inverse of f(x) = 3x - 5, then explain why f(x) = x^2 has none over all reals.
steps.detail: Swap x and y, then solve for y. An inverse exists only when the function is one-to-one, which on a graph is the horizontal line test. Check by composing: f of its inverse must return x exactly.
steps.proof: The inverse is (x + 5)/3; x^2 has none because 2 and -2 share an output.
steps.pitfall: Confusing the inverse with the reciprocal, so the inverse of 3x is written as 1/(3x).

problems.prompt: What is \(f^{-1}(x)\) for the linear function \(f(x) = 2x + 3\)?
Evaluate the inverse of \(g(x) = - 4x + 7\) at x=5.
Find the inverse function of \(h(x) = 3x - 5\).
State whether the function \(p(x) = x^{2}\) has an inverse on the set of all real numbers, and explain why.
problems.answer: No, because it is not one-to-one; e.g., 2 and -2 give the same output.

problems.prompt: Given \(f(x) = \sqrt{x + 1}\), find its inverse and state its domain.
problems.hint: Set \(y = \sqrt{x + 1}\) and solve for \(x\).

problems.prompt: Explain why the function \(q(x) = x^{3} - 2x\) is invertible over all reals, and write its inverse relation (not an explicit formula).
problems.answer: It is strictly increasing, so it has an inverse; the inverse is the unique real solution \(y\) of \(y^{3} - 2y = x\).
problems.hint: Consider monotonicity.

steps.title: Transform a Graph
steps.mastery: Predict how a graph moves when its equation is altered.
steps.practice: Describe how y = (x - 2)^2 + 1 differs from y = x^2, then sketch y = -x^2 + 3.
steps.detail: Changes inside the bracket act on the input and move the graph the opposite way horizontally. Changes outside act on the output and move it the intuitive way vertically. A minus outside flips it top to bottom. Test one point to settle any doubt.
steps.proof: Two right and one up; the second is the parabola flipped and lifted three.
steps.pitfall: Shifting left for (x - 2) because of the minus sign, when the graph moves right.

problems.prompt: What is the vertex of \(y = (x - 2)^{2}\)?
If \(y = x^{2}\) is shifted up by 4 units, what is the new equation?
Describe how the graph of \(y = (x - 2)^{2} + 1\) differs from \(y = x^{2}\).
problems.answer: It is shifted right 2 units and up 1 unit.

problems.prompt: Write the equation of the parabola obtained by reflecting \(y = x^{2}\) across the x-axis and then shifting it up 3 units.
Sketch the graph of \(y = (x + 3)^{2} - 2\) and list the sequence of transformations applied to \(y = x^{2}\).
problems.answer: Shift left 3 units, then down 2 units.
problems.hint: Remember the sign inside the parentheses moves opposite to the sign.

problems.prompt: Explain why the graph of \(y = - (x - 1)^{2} + 4\) is a parabola opening downwards and locate its vertex.
problems.answer: The negative sign flips it, so it opens down; vertex at (1,4).

steps.title: Angle Facts
steps.mastery: Use the angle rules on a line, at a point and in a triangle to find a missing angle.
steps.practice: Two angles on a straight line are 3x and 2x. Find x, then find both angles.
steps.detail: Angles on a straight line total 180, at a point 360, and in a triangle 180. Write the equation before touching the arithmetic, and say which rule you used. Re-read the question at the end, it usually wants the angles, not x.
steps.proof: x = 36, so the angles are 108 and 72, and they sum to 180.
steps.pitfall: Solving for x and giving that as the angle, when the angle was 3x.

problems.prompt: Two angles on a straight line are 30° and 45°. Find the missing angle.
Two angles on a straight line are 3x° and 2x°. Give \(x\), then the 3x° angle, then the 2x° angle.
Angles on a straight line are 4x° and \((3x + 5)^{\circ}\). Find \(x\).
problems.answer: 25. Then \(7x + 5 = 180\) gives \(x = 25\), and the angles are 100° and 80°, which sum to 180°.
problems.hint: Set up the equation \(4x + (3x + 20) = 180\).

steps.title: Parallel Line Angles
steps.mastery: Name corresponding, alternate and co-interior angles and use them to find one.
steps.practice: A transversal crosses two parallel lines. One angle is 68. Find the co-interior angle and the alternate angle.
steps.detail: Corresponding angles are in matching corners and are equal. Alternate angles sit inside on opposite sides and are equal. Co-interior sit inside on the same side and total 180. Trace the F, Z and C shapes on the diagram before naming anything.
steps.proof: Co-interior is 112, alternate is 68.
steps.pitfall: Calling a co-interior pair equal, when they add to 180 rather than match.

problems.prompt: What is the measure of the co-interior angle when one interior angle formed by a transversal with parallel lines is 70°?
A transversal makes a corresponding angle of 45° with a pair of parallel lines. What is the angle next to it on the same line?
problems.answer: 135°, since angles on a straight line add to 180°.

problems.prompt: A transversal cuts two parallel lines and makes an interior angle of 68°. Give the co-interior angle, then the alternate interior angle.
problems.hint: Co-interior angles are supplementary; alternate interior angles are equal.

problems.prompt: Parallel lines are crossed by a transversal, and one interior angle is 120°. Give its co-interior angle, then its corresponding angle.
problems.hint: Co-interior angles add to 180°, corresponding angles are equal.

steps.title: Triangle Properties
steps.mastery: Classify a triangle and use its properties to find sides or angles.
steps.practice: An isosceles triangle has an apex angle of 40. Find the two base angles.
steps.detail: Equilateral gives three 60s. Isosceles gives two equal base angles opposite the two equal sides. Mark the equal sides on your own sketch before computing, which angles are equal follows from which sides are, and a misread diagram is the usual cause of a wrong answer here.
steps.proof: Both are 70, since 180 - 40 leaves 140 to share equally.
steps.pitfall: Splitting the wrong angle when the diagram is not drawn to scale.

problems.prompt: A triangle has side lengths 5 cm, 5 cm, and 8 cm. What type of triangle is it by sides?
An isosceles triangle has an apex angle of 40°. What are the measures of the two base angles?
In a triangle, two angles measure 30° and 45°. Find the third angle and classify the triangle by its angles.
problems.hint: Angles in a triangle sum to 180°; an angle greater than 90° makes it obtuse.

problems.prompt: A triangle has side lengths 7 cm, 7 cm, and 7 cm and one interior angle measuring 60°. Verify that the triangle is equilateral and determine the measures of the other two angles.
problems.answer: The triangle is equilateral; all angles are 60°, so the remaining angles are 60° each.
problems.hint: In an equilateral triangle all sides and all angles are equal.

steps.title: Area and Perimeter
steps.mastery: Compute area and perimeter for rectangles, triangles, circles and compound shapes.
steps.practice: Find the area of a triangle with base 12 and height 7, then the area of a circle of radius 5 to one decimal place.
steps.detail: Triangle area is half base times perpendicular height, and the height must meet the base at a right angle. Circle area is pi r squared; circumference is 2 pi r. For a compound shape, cut it into pieces you know and add, marking each piece on the sketch.
steps.pitfall: Using the slant side as the height of a triangle instead of the perpendicular one.

problems.prompt: What is the perimeter of a rectangle with length 8 and width 3?
What is the area of a triangle with base 5 and height 4?
Find the area of a triangle with base 12 and height 7.
Find the area of a circle with radius 5, rounded to one decimal place.
problems.hint: Use \(\pi \approx 3.14\).

problems.prompt: A shape consists of a rectangle 6 by 4 attached to a semicircle of radius 2 on one side. What is the total area, rounded to one decimal?
problems.hint: Add rectangle area to half the area of a circle.

steps.title: Pythagoras
steps.mastery: Find any side of a right triangle given the other two.
steps.practice: Find the hypotenuse when the legs are 9 and 12, then find the missing leg when the hypotenuse is 13 and one leg is 5.
steps.detail: The square on the hypotenuse equals the sum of the squares on the other two. Finding the hypotenuse is an addition; finding a leg is a subtraction. Identify the hypotenuse first, it is always opposite the right angle and always the longest side.
steps.pitfall: Adding the squares when finding a leg, where they should be subtracted.

problems.prompt: Find the length of the hypotenuse of a right triangle with legs 9 and 12.
Find the missing leg of a right triangle where the hypotenuse is 13 and one leg is 5.
Find the length of the hypotenuse of a right triangle with legs 8 and 15.
problems.hint: Apply the Pythagorean theorem: \(c = \sqrt{a^{2} + b^{2}}\).

problems.prompt: A ladder 20 ft long leans against a wall, touching the wall 12 ft above the ground. How far is the foot of the ladder from the wall?
problems.hint: Use c² = a² + b² and solve for the missing side.

steps.title: Prove It for Every Case
steps.mastery: Argue a geometric claim from stated reasons rather than from the drawing.
steps.practice: Prove that the angles in any triangle sum to 180, using a line drawn parallel to one side.
steps.detail: Draw a line through one vertex parallel to the opposite side. The two outer angles at that vertex equal two of the triangle's angles by alternate angles, and the three together lie on a straight line. Give a reason for every step; a diagram shows one case and a proof covers all of them.
steps.proof: The two alternate-angle pairs at the parallel line place all three angles on a straight line, which is 180.
steps.pitfall: Measuring the drawing and calling the measurement a proof.

problems.prompt: True or false: measuring the angles of 3 triangles and getting 180 each time proves the angle sum for all triangles.
Lines AB and CD cross at O. Prove angle AOC equals angle BOD, with a reason for each step.
problems.answer: Angles AOC and AOD lie on a straight line, so they add to 180. Angles BOD and AOD also lie on a straight line, so they add to 180. Subtracting angle AOD from both gives angle AOC = angle BOD.

problems.prompt: Prove that an exterior angle of a triangle equals the sum of the 2 remote interior angles.
problems.answer: Let the interior angles be A, B and C, with exterior angle E next to C. E and C lie on a straight line, so \(E = 180 - C\). The triangle's angles add to 180, so \(A + B = 180 - C\). So \(E = A + B\).

problems.prompt: In triangle ABC, AB = AC, and M is the midpoint of BC. Prove angle B equals angle C.
problems.answer: AB = AC is given, BM = CM because M is the midpoint, and AM is shared. So triangles ABM and ACM are congruent by SSS. Matching angles are equal, so angle B = angle C.

problems.prompt: Prove that the angles of any convex quadrilateral ABCD sum to 360, using diagonal AC.
problems.answer: AC splits ABCD into triangles ABC and ACD. Each triangle's angles sum to 180. Together those angles make up exactly the angles of ABCD, because the angles at A and C split along the diagonal. So the sum is \(180 + 180 = 360\).

problems.prompt: In parallelogram ABCD, the diagonals meet at O. Prove that O is the midpoint of each diagonal.
problems.answer: AB is parallel to CD, so angle OAB = angle OCD and angle OBA = angle ODC as alternate angles. Opposite sides give AB = CD. So triangles OAB and OCD are congruent by ASA. Matching sides give OA = OC and OB = OD.

steps.title: Read the Symbols
steps.mastery: Say precisely which values a given inequality allows, endpoints included.
steps.practice: List three values satisfying x > 4 and three satisfying x <= 4, then say whether 4 itself is in either.
steps.detail: The bar under the symbol means the endpoint counts. On a number line an open circle excludes it and a filled one includes it. When a question says 'at least' it is >=, and 'more than' is >.
steps.proof: 4 belongs to the second set only, because <= includes its endpoint and > does not.
steps.pitfall: Treating < and <= as interchangeable, which loses or gains exactly one value.

problems.prompt: Give one integer that satisfies \(x > 4\).
List three integers that satisfy \(x \le 4\).
Is the number 4 included in the solution set of \(x > 4\)? Answer yes or no.
problems.hint: Recall that > does not include its endpoint.

steps.title: Solve Like an Equation
steps.mastery: Solve a one-variable inequality using the same moves as an equation.
steps.practice: Solve 3x + 4 < 19, then solve 2(x - 1) >= x + 5.
steps.detail: Adding, subtracting, and multiplying or dividing by a positive all leave the direction alone. The answer is a set, so it is written as an inequality rather than as x = something. Test one value from inside your range and one from outside.
steps.proof: x < 5, and x >= 7.
steps.pitfall: Writing the answer as a single number rather than as a range.

problems.prompt: Solve \(2x < 6\).
Solve \(x + 5 > 9\).
Solve \(4 - x \le 2\) and give the solution as an inequality.
problems.hint: Subtract 4 then divide by -1, remembering to flip the sign.

problems.prompt: Solve \(3(x - 2) > 9\) and express the answer as a range.
problems.hint: Divide by 3 then add 2; no sign flip is needed.

steps.title: Flip on a Negative
steps.mastery: Reverse the inequality sign whenever both sides are multiplied or divided by a negative.
steps.practice: Solve -2x > 10, then solve 5 - 3x <= 14.
steps.detail: Multiplying by a negative reflects the number line, so the order of every pair of values swaps. The safest habit is to move the variable term to whichever side keeps its coefficient positive, which avoids the flip entirely. Always test one value.
steps.pitfall: Keeping the direction after dividing by a negative, which reverses the meaning of the answer.

problems.prompt: Solve \(-x < 3\).
Solve \(-5 \ge 2y\).
Solve \(-4x \le 8\) and write the solution.
problems.hint: Divide by -4 and flip the inequality sign.

problems.prompt: Solve \(7 - 2z > 1\) and give the inequality for \(z\).
problems.hint: Subtract 7 then divide by -2, flipping the sign.

steps.title: Double Inequalities
steps.mastery: Solve a compound inequality that traps a variable between two bounds.
steps.practice: Solve -3 < 2x + 1 <= 9 and state the range of x.
steps.detail: Whatever you do, do to all three parts at once. Subtract 1 from each, then divide each by 2. The result is a range with an excluded lower end and an included upper one, and the two endpoints keep the strictness they arrived with.
steps.pitfall: Operating on only two of the three parts, which breaks the chain.

problems.prompt: Solve \(-2 < x \le 4\) and state the range of \(x\).
Solve \(1 \le 3y - 2 < 7\) and give the solution for \(y\).
Solve \(-4 < - 2x + 5 \le 2\) and express the solution as an inequality.
problems.hint: Isolate the term with \(x\), then divide by the negative coefficient and flip the inequality signs.

problems.prompt: Solve \(0 < 4 - 2t \le 6\) and write the solution for t as a double inequality.
problems.hint: Apply the same operation to all three parts; when dividing by -2, reverse the inequality signs.

steps.title: Draw the Solution
steps.mastery: Represent a solution set on a number line with the correct endpoint markers.
steps.practice: Draw the number line for x >= -1, then for -4 < x < 2, marking endpoints correctly.
steps.detail: Rewrite the inequality so the variable is on the left before drawing anything, 5 > x is x < 5, and it shades left. Filled circle for <= and >=, open for < and >. The picture is the fastest way to check a compound answer.
steps.proof: A filled circle at -1 shading right; open circles at -4 and 2 with the segment between them shaded.
steps.pitfall: Shading the wrong side because the variable is written on the right of the symbol.

problems.prompt: Mark the solution set for \(x \le 3\) on a number line, indicating the endpoint correctly.
problems.answer: Closed circle at 3 with shading to the left.

problems.prompt: Draw the number line for \(-5 \le x < 1\), marking the endpoints correctly.
problems.answer: Closed circle at -5, open circle at 1, shading the segment between them.

problems.prompt: Represent the solution set of \(-2x \le 6\) on a number line, marking the endpoint correctly.
problems.answer: Closed circle at -3 with shading to the right.
problems.hint: Solve the inequality first, remembering to flip the inequality sign when dividing by a negative number.

steps.title: Inequalities from Words
steps.mastery: Turn a constraint stated in words into an inequality and solve it.
steps.practice: A taxi charges 4 plus 2 per mile and you have 25. Write an inequality for the miles m and solve it.
steps.detail: Define the letter, write the total, then decide which symbol the words demand. 'You have 25' is a ceiling, so it is <=. Finish by asking whether the context allows fractions, money often does, journeys and people do not.
steps.proof: 4 + 2m <= 25, so m <= 10.5, meaning 10 whole miles.
steps.pitfall: Giving 10.5 as the answer when the quantity can only be a whole number.

problems.prompt: A bus fare costs $2 per ride and you have $10. Write an inequality for the number of rides r you can take.
Each plant needs at least 0.5 m² of space and a garden can hold at most 15 m². Write an inequality for the number of plants \(n\) you can grow.
A taxi charges a base fare of $4 plus $2 per mile, and you have $25. Solve \(4 + 2m \le 25\). What is the greatest whole number of miles you can travel?
problems.answer: 10. \(4 + 2m \le 25\) gives \(m \le 10.5\), and the meter counts whole miles.
