problems.prompt: Over C major, a line leaps from C up to F, then steps down to E. What is the F?
Which non-chord tone goes 'step in, leap out'?
Does an appoggiatura more often fall on beat 1 or on the & of 1?

steps.title: Label a Melody
steps.mastery: Label every non-chord tone in a short melody over given chords.
steps.practice: Label each non-chord tone in 4 bars of a Bach chorale melody with P, N, S, A or E.
steps.detail: Spell the chord under each beat first. Any melody note not in that chord is a non-chord tone. Then check how it enters and leaves to name it. Most melody notes in chorales turn out to be chord tones or passing tones.
steps.proof: Every non-chord tone in the 4 bars carries a letter.
steps.pitfall: Labeling a note without checking which chord sits under it at that moment.

problems.prompt: Over C major, the line is C, D, E, F, G. Which notes are non-chord tones?
Over F major, the line is A, Bb, A. What is the Bb?
A line holds C from a C chord into a G chord, then falls to B. What is the C?

steps.title: Label Chords in Major
steps.mastery: Label chords with Roman numerals, capitals for major and lowercase for minor.
steps.practice: In C major, label C, Dm, Em, F, G, Am and Bdim with Roman numerals.
steps.detail: The numeral is the scale degree of the chord's root. The case shows the quality, and a small circle marks diminished. Numerals describe a chord's job in the key, so the same progression looks the same in every key.
steps.proof: I, ii, iii, IV, V, vi and vii°.
steps.pitfall: Writing every numeral in capitals, which hides the quality.

problems.prompt: In G major, what Roman numeral is the C chord?
Bm shows up in a D major song. Which Roman numeral is it?
Label E diminished with its Roman numeral in F major.

steps.title: Label Chords in Minor
steps.mastery: Label chords in minor keys, including the major V that the raised 7th creates.
steps.practice: In A minor, label Am, Bdim, C, Dm, E and F, and note why E is major.
steps.detail: Natural minor gives i, ii°, III, iv, v, VI and VII. Composers almost always raise the 7th in the V chord so it has a leading tone, which turns v into V. So expect a major V in minor keys, with an accidental.
steps.proof: i, ii°, III, iv, V and VI. E is major because G# is the raised 7th.
steps.pitfall: Labeling the dominant as minor v when the music shows the raised 7th.

problems.prompt: In A minor, what Roman numeral is the C chord?
In E minor, spell the 3 notes of the V chord using harmonic minor.
Gm turns up in a D minor piece. Label it with a Roman numeral.

steps.title: Feel the Dominant Pull
steps.mastery: Explain why V goes to I: the leading tone rises a half step and the root falls a fifth.
steps.practice: Play G7 to C in C major and trace where the B and the F move.
steps.detail: The leading tone in V wants to rise to the tonic. In V7 the 7th wants to fall a step. Together with the bass falling a 5th, those pulls make V to I the strongest move in tonal music. Composers use it to end phrases and confirm keys.
steps.proof: B rises to C and F falls to E.
steps.pitfall: Moving the leading tone down, which kills the resolution.

problems.prompt: In C major, which note of G7 is the leading tone?
Where does the 7th of G7, the F, usually move in C major?
What is V7 in E-flat major?

steps.title: Play Common Progressions
steps.mastery: Recognize I IV V I, ii V I and I V vi IV, and play them in any key.
steps.practice: Play ii V I in C, F and B-flat major, naming all 9 chords as you play them.
steps.detail: A progression in numerals is a pattern you can drop into any key. Learn the pattern, then find the chords by counting up the scale. ii V I is the backbone of jazz, and I V vi IV runs through countless pop songs.
steps.proof: Dm G C, then Gm C F, then Cm F Bb.
steps.pitfall: Memorizing a progression in one key only, so it won't move.

problems.prompt: Write the 3 chords of ii V I in G major.
Write I V vi IV in D major.
Write ii7 V7 Imaj7 in F major.

steps.title: Analyze a Short Piece
steps.mastery: Label every chord in an 8-bar passage and mark where the cadences fall.
steps.practice: Take an 8-bar hymn in G major, write a numeral under every chord, and box each V to I.
steps.detail: Name the key first, then go chord by chord. Spell each chord, restack it if needed, find the root and write the numeral. Cadences usually land at bar 4 and bar 8. Patterns like IV V I will start to jump out at you.
steps.proof: A numeral under every chord, with the cadence at bar 8 boxed.
steps.pitfall: Labeling chords before deciding the key.

problems.prompt: A phrase in C major goes C, F, G, C. Write the numerals.
A passage in A major goes A, D, E7, A. Which chord is the dominant seventh?
A phrase in D major ends on an A chord. Which numeral is that last chord?

steps.title: Build Major Scales
steps.mastery: Build any major scale from the step pattern W W H W W W H.
steps.practice: Build D major and E-flat major from the pattern, naming all 8 notes of each.
steps.detail: Start on the tonic and write the next 7 letters in order, one of each. Then adjust each note with sharps or flats until the gaps match the pattern. Using every letter exactly once is what keeps the spelling right.
steps.proof: D E F# G A B C# D, and Eb F G Ab Bb C D Eb.
steps.pitfall: Writing Gb instead of F# in D major, which skips the letter F.

problems.prompt: What is the 4th note of G major?
Name the 3 sharps in A major.
Write the 8 notes of E major.
problems.answer: E, F#, G#, A, B, C#, D#, E.

steps.title: Build Natural Minor
steps.mastery: Build a natural minor scale from W H W W H W W, or from its relative major.
steps.practice: Build A minor and C minor, then check that A minor uses all 7 notes of C major and no others.
steps.detail: Natural minor lowers the 3rd, 6th and 7th of the major scale on the same tonic. Or start on the 6th note of a major scale and play its notes. Both ways give the same answer, and checking one against the other catches spelling slips.
steps.proof: A B C D E F G A, and C D Eb F G Ab Bb C.
steps.pitfall: Lowering only the 3rd and calling it minor.

problems.prompt: What is the 3rd note of D minor?
What is the relative minor of G major, which has 1 sharp?
Write the 8 notes of F natural minor.
problems.answer: F, G, Ab, Bb, C, Db, Eb, F.

steps.title: Harmonic Minor
steps.mastery: Raise the 7th of natural minor to get harmonic minor, with its leading tone.
steps.practice: Build A harmonic minor and D harmonic minor, and name the gap between the 6th and 7th notes.
steps.detail: The raised 7th sits a half step below the tonic, which pulls strongly toward home and makes the V chord major. It also leaves a wide gap of three half steps between the 6th and 7th, the sound people call exotic. The raised note is an accidental, not part of the key signature.
steps.proof: A B C D E F G# A and D E F G A Bb C# D, with an augmented 2nd between 6 and 7.
steps.pitfall: Writing the raised 7th into the key signature.

problems.prompt: In E harmonic minor, which of the 7 notes gets raised?
How many half steps are between the 6th and 7th of harmonic minor?
Write the 8 notes of G harmonic minor.
problems.answer: G, A, Bb, C, D, Eb, F#, G.

steps.title: Melodic Minor
steps.mastery: Raise the 6th and 7th going up in melodic minor, and use natural minor coming down.
steps.practice: Write A melodic minor up and down, all 15 notes, marking the 2 that change with direction.
steps.detail: Going up, the raised 6th smooths over the awkward gap of harmonic minor while keeping the leading tone. Coming down there's no pull toward the tonic, so both go back to natural. Jazz players often use the rising form both ways.
steps.proof: Up: A B C D E F# G# A. Down: A G F E D C B A.
steps.pitfall: Using the raised notes on the way down in a classical exam answer.

problems.prompt: In A melodic minor going up, what are the 6th and 7th?
Going down, which of the 3 forms of minor does melodic minor usually use?
Write the 8 notes of D melodic minor going up.
problems.answer: D, E, F, G, A, B, C#, D.

steps.title: Name the Scale Degrees
steps.mastery: Name the scale degrees: tonic, supertonic, mediant, subdominant, dominant, submediant and leading tone.
steps.practice: Label all 7 degrees of F major with their names and their notes.
steps.detail: The names describe position. Dominant is a 5th above the tonic and subdominant a 5th below it, which lands on the 4th degree. Mediant and submediant sit halfway to each. The leading tone leads up to the tonic, a half step away.
steps.proof: F tonic, G supertonic, A mediant, Bb subdominant, C dominant, D submediant, E leading tone.
steps.pitfall: Calling the 4th degree the dominant because it comes before the 5th.

problems.prompt: What is the dominant, degree 5, of C major?
What is the subdominant, degree 4, of D major?
In B-flat major, which note is the leading tone, degree 7?

steps.title: Learn Solfege
steps.mastery: Give each degree of the major scale its solfege syllable, and sing them in tune.
steps.practice: Sing the C major scale on solfege up and down 3 times, then sing 'do mi sol do'.
steps.detail: Solfege gives each scale degree its own syllable, so you learn how it feels in the key rather than what letter it is. In movable do, do is always the tonic, whatever the key. That makes every major key feel the same to sing.
steps.proof: Three clean scales up and down, then the arpeggio in tune.
steps.pitfall: Using fixed do with letter names, which makes every key feel different.

problems.prompt: Which solfege syllable is the 5th degree?
Which syllable comes just below the top 'do'?
In movable do, which syllable is A in A major, with its 3 sharps?

steps.title: Sing Common Patterns
steps.mastery: Sing patterns like do-mi-sol and stepwise runs until they come without thinking.
steps.practice: Sing 'do mi sol mi do', then 'do re mi fa sol fa mi re do', 5 times each, from a given starting pitch.
steps.detail: Most melodies are built from scale steps and chord outlines. Drilling those few shapes means you'll recognize them on the page and sing them at once. Watch the half steps, mi to fa and ti to do, which singers tend to make too wide.
steps.proof: Both patterns sung 5 times, in tune and on the beat.
steps.pitfall: Singing mi to fa as a whole step, which drags the whole scale sharp.

problems.prompt: Which 3 syllables spell the tonic triad?
Which pair is a half step in the major scale: 'mi-fa' or 're-mi'?
In major, what's the other half step besides 'mi' to 'fa'?

steps.title: Keep the Pulse
steps.mastery: Keep a steady pulse while singing, even when a pitch goes wrong.
steps.practice: Sing 8 bars at sight with a metronome at 72, and keep going past any mistake.
steps.detail: Graders and listeners forgive a wrong note far more easily than a stop. Keep the beat going with your hand or foot, and if you miss a pitch, find the next one and carry on. Practice recovering on purpose, since stopping becomes a habit.
steps.proof: 8 bars sung to the end with no stops.
steps.pitfall: Stopping to fix every wrong note, which wrecks the rhythm.

problems.prompt: You miss a note in bar 3. Should you stop and fix it?
problems.answer: No. Keep the pulse and come back to it after.

problems.prompt: Why conduct or tap while sight-singing 8 bars?
A metronome is at 60 and each beat is a quarter note. How long does one 4/4 bar take?

steps.title: Scan Before You Sing
steps.mastery: Take 30 seconds to scan the key, meter, range and hard leaps before singing.
steps.practice: Before singing a new 8-bar melody, spend 30 seconds naming its key, meter, highest note and biggest leap.
steps.detail: A quick scan prevents most mistakes. Find do from the key signature and the last note, set the tempo from the meter, and spot the leaps and tricky rhythms. Hum the hardest spot once in your head before you start.
steps.proof: Key, meter, top note and biggest leap named before the first note.
steps.pitfall: Starting to sing right away and finding the hard leap halfway through.

problems.prompt: What 2 things should you check first in a new melody?
problems.answer: The key and the time signature.

problems.prompt: A melody has 3 sharps and ends on A. Which note is 'do'?
You spot an octave leap in bar 6 during your scan. How can you prepare for it?
problems.answer: Find the 2 notes and hear them in your head first.

steps.title: Practice Like the Exam
steps.mastery: Practice in AP style: 75 seconds to look, then sing once and record it.
steps.practice: Record 3 sight-singing melodies with 75 seconds of practice each, then score yourself on pitch and rhythm.
steps.detail: Exam conditions feel different from practice, so rehearse them. Use the full prep time to scan and hum, then sing once with no restarts. Listening back shows mistakes you miss while singing, and scoring yourself shows which skill to drill.
steps.proof: 3 recordings, each with a score for pitch and one for rhythm.
steps.pitfall: Practicing only with unlimited time and restarts.

problems.prompt: On the AP exam, how many seconds do you get to practice each sight-singing melody?
Why record your AP practice instead of just singing it?
problems.answer: You can hear pitch and rhythm mistakes you miss while singing.

problems.prompt: You sing 4 of 8 bars right on pitch. What fraction of the bars is that?

steps.title: Build Major and Minor Triads
steps.mastery: Build major and minor triads by stacking thirds: major then minor for a major triad, minor then major for a minor one.
steps.practice: Build 6 triads on D, F and A, first as major and then as minor.
steps.detail: Write the root, skip a letter, write the next, skip again. That gives a stack of thirds like D F A. Then fix the middle note: a major 3rd above the root makes it major, and a minor 3rd makes it minor. The outer 5th stays perfect in both.
steps.proof: D F# A and D F A, F A C and F Ab C, A C# E and A C E.
steps.pitfall: Changing the 5th instead of the 3rd to turn major into minor.

problems.prompt: Spell a G major triad, root first, with its 3 notes.
Which 3 notes make an E minor triad?
B-flat is the root of a major triad. Name its 3rd and 5th.

steps.title: Diminished and Augmented
steps.mastery: Build diminished triads from two minor thirds and augmented ones from two major thirds.
steps.practice: Spell B diminished, C augmented and F# diminished.
steps.detail: Diminished is minor with the 5th lowered a half step, and augmented is major with the 5th raised. Keep the letters as a stack of thirds, so C augmented is C E G#, never C E Ab. Diminished chords show up on the 7th degree of every major key.
steps.proof: B D F, C E G# and F# A C.
steps.pitfall: Spelling C augmented as C E Ab, which breaks the stack of thirds.

problems.prompt: Spell a C# diminished triad.
Spell the 3 notes of an F augmented triad.
In C major, which of the 7 triads is diminished?

steps.title: Triads in a Key
steps.mastery: Know the quality of each triad in a major key: major on I, IV and V, minor on ii, iii and vi, diminished on vii.
steps.practice: Write all 7 triads of G major and label each one's quality.
steps.detail: Build a triad on every note of the scale using only notes from the key. The qualities always fall in the same pattern, so learn it once and use it everywhere. In minor keys the pattern shifts, and the raised 7th changes v into V.
steps.proof: G, Am, Bm, C, D, Em and F# diminished.
steps.pitfall: Adding accidentals that aren't in the key to make every chord major.

problems.prompt: What quality is the ii chord, built on degree 2, in any major key?
In F major, spell the IV chord.
In D major, spell the vii chord, built on degree 7.

steps.title: Build Seventh Chords
steps.mastery: Build the four common sevenths: major 7, dominant 7, minor 7 and half-diminished 7.
steps.practice: Build Cmaj7, C7, Cm7 and Cm7b5, and name the interval from the root to the 7th in each.
steps.detail: Add one more third on top of a triad. A major triad with a major 7th is a major 7 chord. A major triad with a minor 7th is a dominant 7, the V7 chord. A minor triad with a minor 7th is a minor 7, and a diminished triad with a minor 7th is half-diminished.
steps.proof: C E G B, C E G Bb, C Eb G Bb and C Eb Gb Bb.
steps.pitfall: Reading C7 as a major 7th chord. Plain 7 means the dominant, with a flat 7th.

problems.prompt: Spell the 4 notes of G7.
Spell Dm7.
Spell Fmaj7.

steps.title: Name Chords on Sight
steps.mastery: Name a chord's root and quality from its notes, even when they're shuffled or inverted.
steps.practice: Name the 3 chords E G C, F A D and B D G F, putting each one in stacked thirds first.
steps.detail: Rearrange the notes until each sits a third above the last. The bottom note of that stack is the root, whatever note was lowest in the original. Then read the quality from the intervals above the root.
steps.proof: C major, D minor and G7.
steps.pitfall: Calling the lowest written note the root without restacking.

problems.prompt: Name the 3-note chord A C F.
Name the 3-note chord G Bb E.
Name the chord D F# A C.

steps.title: Ranges and Spacing
steps.mastery: Keep each of the 4 voices in range, with no more than an octave between neighboring upper voices.
steps.practice: Write a C major chord for SATB with the soprano on E5, then check each voice's range and spacing.
steps.detail: Rough ranges: soprano C4 to G5, alto G3 to C5, tenor C3 to G4 and bass E2 to C4. Soprano and alto, and alto and tenor, should stay within an octave of each other. The bass may sit further below the tenor. Voices shouldn't cross.
steps.proof: All 4 voices sit in range, and the upper pairs are within an octave.
steps.pitfall: Letting the tenor climb above the alto to fill a chord.

problems.prompt: What is the usual top note for an SATB soprano: G5 or C6?
The soprano is on E5 and the alto on C4. Is that spacing allowed?
problems.answer: No. They're more than an octave apart.

problems.prompt: The tenor and bass are 2 octaves apart. Is that allowed?
problems.answer: Yes. The bass may sit more than an octave below the tenor.

steps.title: Double the Right Note
steps.mastery: Double the root of a root-position triad, and never double the leading tone.
steps.practice: Write V to I in C major in 4 parts with the root doubled in both chords.
steps.detail: Four voices and three chord notes means one note gets doubled. In root position, double the root. Never double the leading tone, because both copies want to rise to the tonic, which makes parallel octaves. In first inversion, doubling the soprano note is usually safe.
steps.proof: G B D G goes to C C E G, with no B doubled.
steps.pitfall: Doubling the leading tone to make a chord sound fuller.

problems.prompt: In a root-position C major triad for SATB, which of its 3 notes is usually doubled?
In G major, why shouldn't you double F# in a D chord?
problems.answer: F# is the leading tone, and doubling it forces parallel octaves or a bad resolution.

problems.prompt: In an I6 chord, which note is a safe one to double?
problems.answer: The soprano note, or any note except the leading tone.

steps.title: Avoid Parallel 5ths and Octaves
steps.mastery: Find and fix parallel 5ths and octaves between any two voices.
steps.practice: Check every pair of voices in a 4-chord progression for parallel 5ths and octaves, and fix any you find.
steps.detail: When two voices a 5th or octave apart both move to another 5th or octave in the same direction, they stop sounding independent. Check all 6 pairs of voices at every chord change. Contrary motion, with the voices moving opposite ways, is the usual fix.
steps.proof: Every pair checked, with any parallels rewritten by contrary motion.
steps.pitfall: Checking only soprano and bass and missing parallels in the inner voices.

problems.prompt: How many pairs of voices do you check in SATB writing?
The soprano goes C5 to D5 while the bass goes F3 to G3. Is that a problem?
The bass goes C3 to G2 and the tenor goes C4 to G3. What's wrong?

steps.title: Move Smoothly
steps.mastery: Keep common tones in the same voice and move the other voices by the smallest step.
steps.practice: Connect C major to F major in 4 parts, keeping the shared C in the same voice.
steps.detail: Find the notes the two chords share and hold them still. Move every other upper voice to the nearest note of the next chord. Leave the leaps to the bass. Smooth upper voices are easy to sing and almost never make parallels.
steps.proof: C holds, E moves up to F and G moves up to A.
steps.pitfall: Moving all 4 voices in the same direction, which invites parallels.

problems.prompt: C major and A minor share how many of their 3 notes?
Going from C to G in C major, which of the 3 notes of C can stay in place?
The alto leaps from E4 up to C5 between two chords. What should you try instead?
problems.answer: Keep a common tone, or move by step to a nearer note.

steps.title: Resolve Tendency Tones
steps.mastery: Resolve the leading tone up to the tonic and the 7th of V7 down by step.
steps.practice: Write V7 to I in G major in four parts and show the leading tone rising and the 7th falling.
steps.detail: Tendency tones are the notes that pull hardest. The leading tone rises a half step to the tonic, and the chord 7th falls a step. If you resolve those two first, the rest of the chord falls into place. An inner-voice leading tone may drop to the 5th in some cases.
steps.proof: D F# A C goes to G G B D, with F# rising to G and C falling to B.
steps.pitfall: Resolving the 7th upward, which sounds wrong in a V7 to I.

problems.prompt: In G major, which note of the V7 chord is its 7th?
In that G major V7 to I, where does the C go?
In C major, a V7 with B in the soprano goes to I. Where does the B go?

steps.title: Stack a Major Triad
steps.mastery: Build a major chord from a root by stacking two thirds.
steps.practice: Build major triads on C, G and F, naming all 3 notes of each.
steps.detail: A major third then a minor third: 4 semitones then 3. C gives C E G, G gives G B D, F gives F A C. Every major triad has the same 4-then-3 shape, so the chord is the shape rather than the letters.
steps.proof: C E G, G B D and F A C.
steps.pitfall: Stacking 2 major thirds, which gives an augmented chord rather than a major one.

problems.prompt: Name the 3 notes of a C major triad.
What are the 2 interval sizes in a major triad, in semitones, bottom to top?
Stacking 4 then 3 semitones from F gives which 3 notes?

steps.title: Make It Minor
steps.mastery: Convert a major triad to minor by lowering one note.
steps.practice: Turn C major into C minor and name which of the 3 notes moves, and by how much.
steps.detail: Flatten the middle note by a semitone: C E G becomes C Eb G, so the stack is 3 then 4 rather than 4 then 3. The root and the fifth do not move, which is why major and minor chords on the same root sound related rather than unrelated.
steps.proof: C Eb G, with only the third moved down 1 semitone.
steps.pitfall: Flattening the fifth as well, which gives a diminished chord.

problems.prompt: Name the 3 notes of a C minor triad.
Which 1 of the 3 notes moves when major becomes minor, and how far?
problems.answer: The third, down a half step.

problems.prompt: What are the 2 interval sizes in a minor triad, in semitones, bottom to top?

steps.title: Diminished and Augmented
steps.mastery: Build the two triads made of equal thirds.
steps.practice: Build a diminished and an augmented triad on C, naming the 3 notes of each.
steps.detail: Diminished is 3 then 3, C Eb Gb, and augmented is 4 then 4, C E G#. Both are symmetrical, which is why they sound unsettled: no note is obviously the root when every interval is the same size.
steps.proof: C Eb Gb and C E G#.
steps.pitfall: Calling C Eb Gb a minor chord, which has a perfect fifth rather than a diminished one.

problems.prompt: Name the 3 notes of a C diminished triad.
Name the 3 notes of a C augmented triad.
What do the 2 interval sizes have in common in diminished and augmented triads?

steps.title: Chords of a Key
steps.mastery: Name the triads that a major key produces on each degree.
steps.practice: Build triads on all 7 degrees of C major and label each major, minor or diminished.
steps.detail: Using only the key's own notes gives major on 1, 4 and 5; minor on 2, 3 and 6; diminished on 7. That pattern is the same in every major key, which is why chord numbers transfer between keys and letters do not.
steps.proof: Major on 1, 4, 5; minor on 2, 3, 6; diminished on 7.
steps.pitfall: Making every chord major, which forces 3 notes outside the key.

problems.prompt: Which 3 degrees of a major key carry major triads?
In a major key, which scale degree has the diminished triad? Answer with 1 number.
In C major, what kind of triad sits on degree 2, and what are its notes?

steps.title: Add the Seventh
steps.mastery: Extend a triad to four notes and hear the difference.
steps.practice: Build a G dominant seventh, naming all 4 notes, and say which note wants to resolve.
steps.detail: Add a minor third above the fifth: G B D F. The F is a semitone above E, the third of C major, and that pull is what makes a dominant seventh want to land on C. Play G7 then C to hear it, then G7 alone and notice it does not feel finished.
steps.proof: G B D F, and the F resolves down to E.
steps.pitfall: Adding a major seventh to a dominant chord, which gives F# and removes the pull entirely.

problems.prompt: Name the 4 notes of a G dominant seventh.
Which note turns G into G7, and where does it want to move?
problems.answer: F, falling a half step to E.

problems.prompt: Which interval is added above the fifth of G B D to make a 4-note dominant seventh?

steps.title: Read a Chord Symbol
steps.mastery: Turn a written chord symbol into specific notes.
steps.practice: Name the notes of Am, D7 and Fmaj7-3 symbols.
steps.detail: The letter is the root, m means minor, 7 means a dominant seventh, maj7 means a major seventh. So A C E, D F# A C, and F A C E. The symbols are compact and unambiguous once you know that 7 alone means the flattened one.
steps.proof: A C E, D F# A C, and F A C E.
steps.pitfall: Reading D7 as a D major seventh, which gives C# instead of C.

problems.prompt: Name the 3 notes of Am.
Name the 4 notes of D7.
Name the 4 notes of Fmaj7.

steps.title: Play Them in Time
steps.mastery: Change between chords cleanly at a steady tempo.
steps.practice: Play C, F, G, C at 60 BPM, 1 chord per 2 beats, with no gap at the changes.
steps.detail: The difficulty is the change, not the chord, so practice the join: play the last beat of one chord and the first of the next, 8 times, before running the sequence. A gap at the change is the thing a listener notices and the player does not.
steps.proof: 4 chords in 8 beats at 60 with no audible gap between them.
steps.pitfall: Practicing the 4 chords separately, which leaves every change unpracticed.

problems.prompt: At 60 BPM with 1 chord every 2 beats, how many seconds do 4 chords take?
problems.answer: 8 seconds: 8 beats at 1 beat a second.

problems.prompt: What should be drilled 8 times before running the sequence?
Who notices the gap at 1 of the 4 chord changes first?

steps.title: Start From One Idea
steps.mastery: Write a motif short enough to develop.
steps.practice: Write a 2-bar motif of no more than 6 notes and play it 4 times.
steps.detail: Short ideas are workable and long ones are finished: 6 notes can be inverted, displaced and extended, while a 16-bar tune can only be repeated. Play it 4 times and check it survives repetition without becoming annoying, which is the test it has to pass.
steps.proof: A 2-bar motif of 6 notes or fewer that survives 4 repetitions.
steps.pitfall: Starting with a complete 16-bar melody, which leaves nothing to develop.

problems.prompt: Is the motif 2 bars of up to 6 notes, or 16 bars?
Why is a 16-bar tune a worse starting point than 6 notes?
problems.answer: It's already finished, so there's nothing left to develop.

problems.prompt: What test must the motif pass on the 4th repetition?
problems.answer: It still sounds good and doesn't get annoying.

steps.title: Develop Before Adding
steps.mastery: Extend a piece by transforming what you have.
steps.practice: Write 8 bars using only your 6-note motif and 3 transformations of it.
steps.detail: The instinct when 8 bars are needed is to invent 4 new ideas, which produces a piece that goes nowhere because nothing returns. Transform instead: sequence it up a step, invert it, stretch it to double length. The listener hears development rather than a list.
steps.proof: 8 bars traceable to 1 motif and 3 named transformations.
steps.pitfall: Writing 4 new ideas in 8 bars, which sounds like a list rather than a piece.

problems.prompt: How many transformations fill the 8 bars, and of how many motifs? Give the transformations first.
Name 2 transformations available.
problems.answer: Sequence it up a step, and invert it.

problems.prompt: What does a piece of 4 unrelated ideas sound like?

steps.title: Plan the Shape First
steps.mastery: Decide a piece's sections before writing its notes.
steps.practice: Write a plan for 32 bars as 4 sections of 8, naming the loudest and the quietest.
steps.detail: Four boxes with a dynamic and a function each, state, develop, contrast, return, is enough of a plan. Naming the loudest and quietest sections in advance is what gives the piece a shape rather than a uniform intensity, which is the commonest fault in a first composition.
steps.proof: A 4-box plan with a named peak and trough.
steps.pitfall: Starting to write bar 1 with no plan, which produces 32 bars at 1 intensity.

problems.prompt: How many sections does the 32-bar plan hold, and how many bars is each? Give the sections first.
Which 2 sections are named in advance?
What is the commonest fault in a first 32-bar composition?
problems.answer: The same intensity all the way through, with no shape.

steps.title: Write a Bass Line
steps.mastery: Support a melody with a line that moves independently.
steps.practice: Write a bass line under 8 bars of melody, moving in the opposite direction at least 4 times.
steps.detail: A bass line that follows the melody's contour adds thickness and nothing else. Moving against it creates 2 lines, which is what makes the texture sound composed. Mark the 4 places you moved against the melody so the choice is visible.
steps.proof: A bass line with 4 marked points of contrary motion.
steps.pitfall: Doubling the melody an octave down, which is 1 line played twice.

problems.prompt: How many times must the bass move against the melody in 8 bars?
What does doubling the melody 1 octave down produce?
Why mark the 4 points of contrary motion?
problems.answer: It makes the choice visible and easy to check.

steps.title: Harmonize Your Own Tune
steps.mastery: Choose chords that support a melody you wrote.
steps.practice: Harmonize your 8-bar melody with no more than 5 chords, changing at most once per bar.
steps.detail: Fewer chords, changed less often, almost always sounds better than more: a chord per beat leaves no room for the melody to be the subject. Five chords across 8 bars is a reasonable ceiling for a first attempt, and the cadence is the 1 place worth spending an extra change.
steps.proof: 8 bars harmonized with 5 chords or fewer.
steps.pitfall: Changing chord on every beat, which buries the melody under harmony.

problems.prompt: At most, how many chords may the 8 bars use, and how many changes per bar? Give the chords first.
problems.answer: 5 chords, with at most 1 change per bar.

problems.prompt: What happens to the melody when the chord changes on all 4 beats of every bar?
problems.answer: The melody stops being the focus.

problems.prompt: Where in the 8 bars is an extra chord change most worth spending?

steps.title: Write the Ending
steps.mastery: Finish a piece so it sounds finished rather than stopped.
steps.practice: Write 2 endings for the same 8 bars, 1 cadencing and 1 fading, and choose between them.
steps.detail: An ending is a decision, and the 2 obvious options sound very different: a perfect cadence closes, a fade leaves the piece open. Write both and play them to somebody. The one you keep should be the one that matches the plan, not the one that was easier to write.
steps.proof: 2 written endings and a stated reason for the choice.
steps.pitfall: Stopping when the material runs out, which sounds like an accident.

problems.prompt: Name the 2 endings this step asks for.
What should decide which of the 2 you keep?
problems.answer: The plan, not which one was easier to write.

problems.prompt: What does stopping when the material runs out after 8 bars sound like?

steps.title: Notate It Properly
steps.mastery: Write a score somebody else could read and play.
steps.practice: Notate your 32 bars with key, time signature, tempo, 3 dynamics and 2 articulations.
steps.detail: A score missing its tempo and dynamics is a set of pitches: the performer has to invent the parts you left out, and they will invent something else. Include the tempo as a number, not only a word, and put a dynamic at every section boundary.
steps.proof: A score carrying a numeric tempo, 3 dynamics and 2 articulation marks.
steps.pitfall: Notating only the pitches and rhythms and leaving the interpretation to be guessed.

problems.prompt: Name the 5 things this step requires on the score.
problems.answer: Key, time signature, tempo, 3 dynamics and 2 articulations.

problems.prompt: Why give the tempo as a number as well as a word like Allegro?
problems.answer: A word names a range about 40 BPM wide, and a number is exact.

problems.prompt: Where should a dynamic marking always appear across the 4 sections?
problems.answer: At the start of every section.

steps.title: Get It Played
steps.mastery: Hear your piece performed by somebody who is not you.
steps.practice: Give your score to 1 other player and note 3 places where what you heard differs from what you meant.
steps.detail: Another player reads what is on the page rather than what is in your head, which is the only honest test of a score. Where they play something unintended, the notation is usually at fault, a missing articulation, an ambiguous tempo, and that is fixable.
steps.proof: 3 differences noted, each traced to something on the page.
steps.pitfall: Telling the player what you meant before they read it, which destroys the test.

problems.prompt: How many differences does this step ask you to note, 3 or 10?
A player plays something you didn't mean. Where is the fault usually?
problems.answer: In the notation: a missing or unclear mark.

problems.prompt: Why not explain what you meant to the 1 player before they read your score?
problems.answer: It spoils the test of whether the score says what you meant.

steps.title: Revise From the Recording
steps.mastery: Rewrite a piece after hearing it, rather than after finishing it.
steps.practice: Listen to a recording of your 32 bars and make 3 specific changes to the score.
steps.detail: First drafts are too long, too uniform and too busy in the middle, in roughly that order. Cut before you add: removing 4 bars is more often the right change than writing 4 more. Mark the 3 changes on the score with the bar numbers and play it again.
steps.proof: 3 marked changes with bar numbers, and a second recording.
steps.pitfall: Treating the first version as finished because it is written down.

problems.prompt: Name the 3 usual faults of a first draft, in order.
problems.answer: Too long, too uniform, too busy in the middle.

problems.prompt: Revising a draft, which is more often right: cutting 4 bars or adding 4?
What must each of the 3 changes carry?

steps.title: Read the Dynamic Marks
steps.mastery: Order the common volume markings and say what each means.
steps.practice: Put these 6 in order from quietest to loudest: mf, pp, ff, p, f, mp.
steps.detail: The ladder is pp, p, mp, mf, f, ff, piano is quiet, forte is loud, and m is the middle of each. They are relative to the piece and the instrument rather than absolute, so mf on a flute and mf on a trombone are different sound levels.
steps.proof: pp, p, mp, mf, f, ff in that order.
steps.pitfall: Reading p as loud because piano is an instrument, which inverts half the ladder.

problems.prompt: Put these 6 in order from quietest to loudest: mf, pp, ff, p, f, mp.
problems.answer: pp, p, mp, mf, f, ff.

problems.prompt: Of the 6 markings, which is louder, mp or mf?
Are the 6 dynamic markings from pp to ff exact sound levels or relative ones?
problems.answer: Relative, to the piece and the instrument.

steps.title: Play a Crescendo
steps.mastery: Grow the volume steadily across a stated number of bars.
steps.practice: Play 4 bars of a single repeated note growing from p to f, changing level once per bar.
steps.detail: Divide the range into 4 steps, p, mp, mf, f, one per bar, so the growth is even rather than arriving in the last beat. Recording it is the only reliable check: a crescendo almost always sounds bigger from behind the instrument than in front of it.
steps.proof: A recording where each of the 4 bars is audibly louder than the one before.
steps.pitfall: Staying at p for 3 bars and jumping to f in the last, which is a step rather than a crescendo.

problems.prompt: Name the 4 levels for a bar-by-bar crescendo from p to f.
You stay at p for 3 bars then jump to f. What have you played?
problems.answer: A sudden jump, and that isn't a crescendo.

problems.prompt: Why record the 4 bars rather than judging while playing?
problems.answer: A crescendo sounds bigger to the player than to someone listening in front.

steps.title: Separate and Join Notes
steps.mastery: Play the same notes staccato and legato and hear the difference.
steps.practice: Play a 5-note phrase twice at 70 BPM, once fully detached and once fully joined.
steps.detail: Staccato shortens each note and leaves silence before the next; legato holds each until the next begins, with no gap and no overlap. The pitches and rhythm are identical, so the 2 versions isolate articulation as the only variable.
steps.proof: The 2 recordings differ only in the gaps between the 5 notes.
steps.pitfall: Playing staccato faster than legato, which changes the tempo as well as the articulation.

problems.prompt: What does staccato leave between 2 consecutive notes?
What is the gap between 2 legato notes?
Your staccato version of 5 notes is faster than the legato one. What went wrong?
problems.answer: The tempo changed too, so the comparison isn't fair.

steps.title: Accent One Note
steps.mastery: Make a single note stand out without disturbing the rest.
steps.practice: Play 4 equal crotchets at 70 BPM with an accent on beat 3 only.
steps.detail: An accent is a louder attack on 1 note, not a louder bar. Keep beats 1, 2 and 4 matched and lift only the third, then check by recording: an accent people can hear as an accent rather than as a lurch is a surprisingly small difference in level.
steps.proof: Beat 3 is audibly stronger and the other 3 beats are level with each other.
steps.pitfall: Also lengthening the accented note, which turns it into a rhythmic change rather than a dynamic one.

problems.prompt: Which of the 4 beats carries the accent in this exercise?
What must stay equal while beat 3 is accented?
You lengthen the accented note as well. What have you changed?
problems.answer: The rhythm, not only the dynamic.

steps.title: Shape a Phrase
steps.mastery: Give a phrase a high point and taper either side of it.
steps.practice: Play an 8-note phrase with its loudest note at note 5, growing to it and easing after.
steps.detail: Decide the high point before playing, then work backwards: notes 1 to 4 grow, note 5 peaks, 6 to 8 ease off. A phrase played at 1 level is the default and sounds like an exercise, which is what shaping is for.
steps.proof: A recording where note 5 is the loudest and the shape either side is even.
steps.pitfall: Putting the high point on the last note, which usually sounds like the phrase has stopped rather than arrived.

problems.prompt: In an 8-note phrase peaking at note 5, which notes grow?
What do notes 6 to 8 do?
problems.answer: They ease off from the peak.

problems.prompt: What does an 8-note phrase played at 1 level sound like?

steps.title: Follow a Marked Score
steps.mastery: Play every dynamic and articulation a passage asks for.
steps.practice: Take 8 bars of marked music and list every dynamic and articulation mark in it before playing.
steps.detail: List them first, the p at bar 1, the crescendo over bars 3 to 4, the staccato in bar 6, so you know what the passage asks for rather than discovering it while playing. Then play it and mark the ones you missed. Most players miss about half at first reading.
steps.proof: A list of the marks in the 8 bars, with the ones you missed ticked off after playing.
steps.pitfall: Reading the notes at first sight and adding the dynamics on a later pass, which usually means never.

problems.prompt: Why list the marks in 8 bars before playing them?
problems.answer: So you play the passage as written and don't find the marks halfway through.

problems.prompt: Roughly what share of the marks in 8 bars does a player miss at first reading?
You mark 2 misses after playing. What do those 2 become?
problems.answer: The targets for the next run-through.

steps.title: Match a Pitch
steps.mastery: Sing back a single played note accurately.
steps.practice: Sing back 5 played notes within your range and check each against the instrument.
steps.detail: Sing the note before checking, then play it again to compare. If you are consistently flat or sharp by the same amount, that is easier to fix than random error. Five notes is enough to see which it is.
steps.proof: 5 sung notes checked, with the direction of any consistent error noted.
steps.pitfall: Humming along while the note still sounds, which is matching rather than reproducing.

problems.prompt: You are flat on all 5 notes by about the same amount. Random or systematic error?
problems.answer: Systematic, and that's easier to fix.

problems.prompt: Why sing before playing the note a 2nd time?
problems.answer: Otherwise you're matching a pitch you can hear, not making it from memory.

problems.prompt: Why sing 5 test notes instead of 1 when checking your pitch?
problems.answer: So a pattern in the error shows up, not one lucky or unlucky note.

steps.title: Two Intervals Apart
steps.mastery: Distinguish two well-separated intervals by ear.
steps.practice: Name 10 intervals drawn only from a minor second and a perfect fifth, and score yourself.
steps.detail: Start with 2 intervals that sound nothing alike, 1 semitone against 7. Getting 9 or 10 means the discrimination is reliable and a third interval can join. This is deliberately easy, because the habit of scoring and adding is what makes ear training work.
steps.proof: A score of 9 or 10 out of 10 before any interval is added.
steps.pitfall: Starting with a set of 6 intervals, where a score of 4 gives no information.

problems.prompt: A minor second is 1 semitone. How many semitones is a perfect fifth?
What score out of 10 allows a 3rd interval into the set?
Why not begin with 6 intervals?
problems.answer: A score of 4 out of 10 doesn't tell you which pairs you mix up.

steps.title: Build the Interval Set
steps.mastery: Add intervals to your recognizable set one at a time.
steps.practice: Add a major third to your set of 2 and score 10 more, then decide whether to add a fourth.
steps.detail: One at a time, scoring each round. Note the confusions by pair rather than only the total: mistaking a major third for a perfect fourth is a specific thing to drill, and it disappears from view if you only record 7 out of 10.
steps.proof: A score out of 10 for the set of 3, with the confused pairs written down.
steps.pitfall: Adding 3 intervals at once after a good round, which usually collapses the score.

problems.prompt: Your set of 3 scores 7 of 10 with 3 thirds called fourths. What do you drill?
Are intervals added to the set 1 at a time or 3?
Why record the confused pair rather than just 7 out of 10?
problems.answer: The pair tells you what to practice, and the total doesn't.

steps.title: Hear Major From Minor
steps.mastery: Identify a chord's quality by ear.
steps.practice: Name 10 played triads as major or minor, keeping the root constant.
steps.detail: Keep the root the same so only the quality varies, that isolates what you are listening for. Aim for 9 of 10 before letting the root move, because a moving root adds pitch memory to a problem that was about quality.
steps.proof: 9 or more correct out of 10 with a fixed root.
steps.pitfall: Varying the root from the start, which makes 2 problems out of 1.

problems.prompt: Which 1 of the 3 notes differs between a major and a minor triad?
Why keep the root fixed for the first 10 trials?
problems.answer: It isolates the chord's quality from pitch memory.

problems.prompt: What score out of 10 lets the root start moving?

steps.title: Follow a Bass Line
steps.mastery: Sing the lowest line of a played progression.
steps.practice: Listen to a 4-chord progression 3 times and sing the 4 bass notes back.
steps.detail: The bass is the easiest line to isolate and the one that tells you most about the harmony. Three hearings, then sing; checking against the instrument afterwards usually shows the first and last notes right and the middle 2 approximate, which is normal and improves quickly.
steps.proof: 4 bass notes sung, with the number correct written down.
steps.pitfall: Trying to hear all 3 notes of every chord before the bass line is reliable.

problems.prompt: Which line of a 4-chord progression is easiest to isolate?
You get bass notes 1 and 4 right and 2 and 3 approximate. Normal or not?
problems.answer: Normal. The ends are easiest and the middle comes with practice.

problems.prompt: How many hearings before singing the 4 notes?

steps.title: Name a Progression
steps.mastery: Identify a common progression from a small set by ear.
steps.practice: Name 10 played progressions drawn from 1-4-5-1 and 1-5-6m-4, and score yourself.
steps.detail: Two progressions, both 4 chords, one cadencing and one looping. Listen for whether it closes: a 1-4-5-1 arrives and a 1-5-6m-4 does not. That single question answers most of the trials without identifying any individual chord.
steps.proof: A score out of 10, with the deciding cue written in 1 line.
steps.pitfall: Trying to name each chord in turn, which is slower and less reliable than hearing whether it closed.

problems.prompt: Which of the 2 progressions closes rather than loops?
What single question decides most of the 10 trials?
problems.answer: Whether the progression closed or not.

problems.prompt: Which is more reliable: naming 4 chords in turn, or hearing the shape?

steps.title: Transcribe a Short Phrase
steps.mastery: Write down a melody you have only heard.
steps.practice: Transcribe a 4-bar melody from a recording, 1 bar at a time, and check it by playing it back.
steps.detail: Work bar by bar and get the rhythm before the pitches, a correct rhythm with 2 wrong notes is closer than the reverse. Playing your transcription against the recording is the check, and any note that clashes is one to redo rather than to argue about.
steps.proof: 4 written bars that play back against the recording without clashing.
steps.pitfall: Transcribing pitches first and fitting the rhythm afterwards, which usually needs starting again.

problems.prompt: Which comes first in transcribing 4 bars: the rhythm or the pitches?
How do you check the 4 bars?
problems.answer: Play your transcription along with the recording and listen for clashes.

problems.prompt: Is a correct rhythm with 2 wrong pitches closer than correct pitches with a wrong rhythm?

steps.title: Keep a Weekly Score
steps.mastery: Track ear training numerically so progress is visible.
steps.practice: Record your scores for 3 exercise types each week and compare 4 weeks of figures.
steps.detail: Ear training improves slowly and invisibly, which is why most people stop. Three numbers a week, intervals, chord quality, progressions, turns that into a line you can see. A score that has not moved in 4 weeks means the set is wrong, not that you cannot do it.
steps.proof: 4 weeks of 3 scores each, with any flat line identified.
steps.pitfall: Practicing without scoring, which leaves no way to tell progress from familiarity.

problems.prompt: How many numbers does this step record each week, 1 or 3?
A score has not moved across 4 weeks. What does that indicate?
problems.answer: The exercise set is wrong. It doesn't mean your ability is fixed.

problems.prompt: Practicing without a score across 4 weeks makes what impossible to tell?
problems.answer: Real progress from just getting used to the material.

steps.title: Find the Phrases
steps.mastery: Divide a piece into its natural units.
steps.practice: Mark the phrase endings in 16 bars and say how many bars each phrase runs.
steps.detail: Listen for where the line breathes: a cadence, a rest, a repeated rhythm starting again. Most phrases are 4 or 8 bars, and 16 bars usually divides into 4 of 4. Where a phrase is 5 bars, that irregularity is usually the most interesting thing on the page.
steps.proof: Phrase endings marked, with the bar count of each written in.
steps.pitfall: Marking phrases at bar lines rather than at cadences, which finds 16 phrases in 16 bars.

problems.prompt: 16 bars most often divides into how many phrases of what length?
Name 2 signals of a phrase ending.
problems.answer: A cadence, and a rest or breath in the line.

problems.prompt: A phrase runs 5 bars where the others run 4. Is that an error?
problems.answer: No, it is usually the most interesting moment in the passage.

steps.title: Label What Repeats
steps.mastery: Use letters to record a piece's sections and repeats.
steps.practice: Label a 32-bar piece with letters, giving the same letter to sections that repeat.
steps.detail: Call the first section A, and use A again only when the material returns. AABA is the commonest 32-bar shape, 8 bars each, and writing the letters takes 2 minutes and tells you most of what there is to know about the architecture.
steps.proof: A letter per 8-bar section, with repeats sharing a letter.
steps.pitfall: Giving a new letter to a section that returns with small changes, which hides the return.

problems.prompt: What is the commonest 32-bar form, in letters?
A section returns with a small variation. Same letter or new one?
problems.answer: The same letter, maybe with a prime mark like A', since the material came back.

problems.prompt: How many bars does each section of AABA hold in a 32-bar piece?

steps.title: Binary and Ternary
steps.mastery: Tell a two-part form from a three-part one.
steps.practice: Label 2 short pieces as AB or ABA and say what makes each what it is.
steps.detail: Binary is a statement and a contrast; ternary adds a return, which changes how the piece feels far more than the extra section suggests. The return is what makes ternary sound resolved and binary sound like it stopped.
steps.proof: 1 piece labeled AB and 1 ABA, with the return identified.
steps.pitfall: Calling any 3-section piece ternary, when ABC is 3 sections and no return.

problems.prompt: Which of AB and ABA has a return?
Is a piece in 3 sections labeled ABC ternary?
problems.answer: No, ternary needs the return, not just 3 sections.

problems.prompt: What does the return do to how an ABA piece of 3 sections ends?
problems.answer: It sounds finished, not just stopped.

steps.title: Verse and Chorus
steps.mastery: Identify the sections of a popular song form.
steps.practice: Map a 3-minute song into verse, chorus and bridge, with a bar count for each section.
steps.detail: The chorus repeats with the same words, the verse repeats with new ones, and the bridge appears once. Counting bars usually shows 8 or 16 per section and a chorus that arrives sooner than you remember, often inside the first 60 seconds.
steps.proof: A map of the song with a bar count against every section.
steps.pitfall: Labeling by intensity rather than by repetition, which calls any loud section a chorus.

problems.prompt: In a 3-minute song, what distinguishes a verse from a chorus?
problems.answer: The chorus repeats with the same words, and the verse comes back with new ones.

problems.prompt: How many times does a bridge usually appear in a 3-minute song?
Why is loudness a poor test for a chorus in a 3-minute song?
problems.answer: Form is about repetition, not loudness.

steps.title: Follow a Sonata Exposition
steps.mastery: Identify the two theme areas and the key change between them.
steps.practice: Mark where the 2nd theme of a sonata exposition starts and name the key it arrives in.
steps.detail: The first theme is in the home key; the second arrives in the dominant, or in the relative major if the piece is minor. Finding the key change is easier than finding the theme: look for the new key signature's accidentals appearing consistently, then look 2 bars earlier.
steps.proof: The second theme marked, with its key named and justified by the accidentals.
steps.pitfall: Looking for the theme by its tune, when the key change is the reliable signal.

problems.prompt: In a major-key sonata, which key does the 2nd theme usually arrive in?
In a minor-key sonata, which key is the 2nd theme likely to arrive in?
Which is the more reliable signal of the 2nd theme, the tune or the key change?

steps.title: Track a Theme's Return
steps.mastery: Notice how returning material has been changed.
steps.practice: Compare a theme's first and last appearance and list 3 differences.
steps.detail: Returns are rarely literal: the key, the instrumentation, the accompaniment or the ending may differ. Listing 3 differences is what turns listening into analysis, and the change at the end is usually the most deliberate one, a return that has not changed has not gone anywhere.
steps.proof: 3 named differences between the 2 appearances.
steps.pitfall: Hearing a return as identical because the tune is the same, and missing the changed harmony under it.

problems.prompt: Name 3 things that commonly change when a theme returns.
problems.answer: The key, the instruments and the accompaniment.

problems.prompt: A theme comes back for the 3rd and last time. Which part of it is most often rewritten?
problems.answer: The ending, so it can close the piece instead of leading on.

problems.prompt: The tune is identical on both appearances. What should you check?
problems.answer: The harmony and accompaniment under it.

steps.title: Map a Whole Piece
steps.mastery: Produce a one-page diagram of a piece's architecture.
steps.practice: Diagram a 5-minute piece on 1 page, with sections, bar numbers and keys marked.
steps.detail: Boxes for sections, bar numbers under them, keys above, arrows for returns. On 1 page the proportions become visible, a development twice the length of the exposition, a coda that is a third of the piece, and those proportions are what a listener actually experiences.
steps.proof: 1 page showing every section with its bars and key.
steps.pitfall: Writing a list of sections rather than a diagram, which loses the proportions.

problems.prompt: What 3 things are marked on each box of the diagram?
problems.answer: The section, its bar numbers and its key.

problems.prompt: What does a diagram show that a list of 6 sections does not?
problems.answer: The proportions: how long each section is next to the others.

problems.prompt: How are returns shown on the 1-page diagram?
problems.answer: With arrows back to the earlier section.

steps.title: Build a Form Yourself
steps.mastery: Write a short piece to a plan you chose in advance.
steps.practice: Plan 24 bars as ABA with 8 bars each, then write it and check the return is recognizable.
steps.detail: Write the plan before the notes: 8 bars of A, 8 of contrasting B, then A again with 1 deliberate change. Deciding the architecture first is what stops a piece wandering, and the deliberate change in the return is what stops it being a repeat.
steps.proof: 24 bars in ABA with the return carrying 1 intentional change.
steps.pitfall: Composing forwards until it feels finished, which usually produces 40 bars of A with no shape.

problems.prompt: How many bars does each section of a 24-bar ABA hold?
What does the returning A of 8 bars carry that the first A did not?
What usually happens to 24 bars written straight through with no plan?
problems.answer: It wanders: lots of A and no shape.

steps.title: Hear Two Lines at Once
steps.mastery: Follow two independent melodies sounding together.
steps.practice: Play 4 bars of a 2-part piece, then play each line alone and sing 1 while playing the other.
steps.detail: Separating the lines is the skill: play the upper alone, then the lower, then sing the upper while playing the lower. Singing 1 part while playing another is where the independence becomes real rather than theoretical.
steps.proof: Both lines played alone, and the upper sung while the lower is played.
steps.pitfall: Hearing the 2 parts as a chord sequence, which loses the horizontal motion that is the point.

problems.prompt: What are the 3 passes over the 4 bars?
problems.answer: The upper line alone, the lower line alone, then sing one while you play the other.

problems.prompt: What is lost by hearing 2 parts as a chord sequence?
problems.answer: How each line moves on its own.

problems.prompt: Which of the 3 passes makes the independence of 2 lines real?
problems.answer: Singing 1 part while you play the other.

steps.title: Move by Step
steps.mastery: Write a second line that moves mostly stepwise.
steps.practice: Write a lower line under an 8-note melody using steps of 1 or 2 semitones wherever possible.
steps.detail: Stepwise motion is what makes a line singable and audible as a line rather than as a series of notes chosen for their chords. Allow a leap when the harmony demands it, then step back in the opposite direction afterwards, which is how a leap stops sounding like a mistake.
steps.proof: A lower line where most intervals are 1 or 2 semitones.
steps.pitfall: Writing the lower line as the root of each chord, which leaps constantly and sings badly.

problems.prompt: What interval size should most of the 8 steps be?
You need a leap of 7 semitones for the harmony. What follows it?
What is wrong with using each chord's root as the lower line?
problems.answer: It jumps all the time and doesn't sing as a line.

steps.title: Contrary Motion
steps.mastery: Make two lines move in opposite directions.
steps.practice: Write 4 bars where the upper line rises 5 notes while the lower falls, and mark each pair.
steps.detail: Two lines moving apart sound independent; 2 moving in parallel sound like 1 line thickened. Contrary motion is the cheapest way to make a texture sound like counterpoint, and marking the direction under each pair is how you check it actually happened.
steps.proof: 5 pairs marked, each with the 2 lines moving in opposite directions.
steps.pitfall: Writing both lines in the same direction throughout, which is a single line in disguise.

problems.prompt: 2 lines both rising across 5 notes sound like what?
What is the cheapest way to make 2 lines sound independent?
problems.answer: Contrary motion: move them in opposite directions.

problems.prompt: How do you check the direction of all 5 pairs?
problems.answer: Mark each line's direction under every pair.

steps.title: Avoid the Parallel Fifths
steps.mastery: Spot and fix consecutive perfect fifths between two lines.
steps.practice: Find the 2 parallel fifths in a given 4-bar exercise and rewrite them using contrary motion.
steps.detail: Two lines a fifth apart moving in the same direction fuse into 1 sound, which is why the convention exists, it is a description of what the ear does rather than an arbitrary rule. The fix is usually to move 1 line in the opposite direction or to change its interval.
steps.proof: 2 parallel fifths found and rewritten so the lines separate.
steps.pitfall: Treating the rule as arbitrary and ignoring it, then wondering why 2 parts sound like 1.

problems.prompt: 2 lines a perfect fifth apart move up together. What does the ear hear?
Name 2 fixes for a parallel fifth.
problems.answer: Move 1 line the other way, or change the interval between them.

problems.prompt: How many semitones is the perfect fifth these 2 lines move in?

steps.title: Resolve the Tension
steps.mastery: Place a dissonance and take it to a consonance by step.
steps.practice: Write a 4th above the bass on beat 1 and resolve it down by step on beat 2, in 2 bars.
steps.detail: Dissonance is not an error, it is the thing that makes the resolution mean something, what matters is that it resolves, by step, and soon. A dissonance left hanging or leapt away from sounds like a mistake even when it was intentional.
steps.proof: 2 bars where the dissonance on beat 1 steps down to a consonance on beat 2.
steps.pitfall: Leaping away from a dissonance, which makes it sound unintended.

problems.prompt: A dissonance on beat 1 resolves how, and when?
problems.answer: By step, on the next beat.

problems.prompt: What happens when a dissonance on beat 1 is leapt away from?
problems.answer: It sounds like a mistake, not planned tension.

problems.prompt: Is dissonance an error in 2-part writing?
problems.answer: No, it creates the tension the resolution releases.

steps.title: Write Four Parts
steps.mastery: Harmonize a melody in four voices with sensible spacing.
steps.practice: Harmonize a 4-note melody in 4 parts, keeping the upper 3 voices within an octave of each other.
steps.detail: The bass may sit low, but gaps between the upper 3 make the chord sound hollow. Double the root when a triad has to fill 4 voices, and avoid doubling the third, which thickens the chord's quality more than it needs.
steps.proof: 4 chords in 4 parts with the upper 3 voices inside an octave.
steps.pitfall: Leaving a tenth between the 2 upper voices, which sounds like 2 separate textures.

problems.prompt: Which of the 4 voices may sit far from the others?
Filling 4 voices from a 3-note triad, which note do you double?
In 4-part writing, which note of a major triad do you usually avoid doubling?
problems.answer: The third. Doubling it overweights the chord's color, and a doubled leading tone has nowhere good to go.

steps.title: Analyze Eight Bars
steps.mastery: Label the harmony of a passage in numerals.
steps.practice: Take 8 bars of a chorale and write the numeral for each chord, marking any 2 inversions.
steps.detail: Identify the bass note, then the chord above it, then the numeral and inversion. Working bass-first is faster and less error-prone than looking at the whole stack. The point of the labels is to see the pattern: most chorale phrases turn out to use 5 or 6 chords.
steps.proof: A numeral under every chord in the 8 bars, with the inversions marked.
steps.pitfall: Naming chords from the top note down, which misidentifies every inversion.

problems.prompt: Which note of a 4-note stack do you identify first when labeling it?
Why is working from the top note of 4 downwards unreliable?
Roughly how many distinct chords does a chorale phrase of 8 bars usually use?

steps.title: Hear Your Own Writing
steps.mastery: Play back what you wrote and correct what the page hid.
steps.practice: Play your 4-part harmonization of 4 chords and list 2 things you would change.
steps.detail: Writing that looks correct often sounds thin, muddy or static, and only playing it reveals which. List 2 specific changes, a doubled third, a gap between voices, a bass that leapt, rather than a general impression, then make them and play it again.
steps.proof: 2 specific changes listed and applied, with the passage played before and after.
steps.pitfall: Accepting writing that follows the rules without ever hearing it.

problems.prompt: Name 2 faults that look fine on the page and sound wrong.
problems.answer: A doubled third, and a gap between the upper voices.

problems.prompt: How many changes does this step ask you to list, 2 or 10?
What is the final check on 4-part writing?

steps.title: Improvise on Three Notes
steps.mastery: Make music from a deliberately tiny set of pitches.
steps.practice: Improvise 8 bars over a C drone using only C, D and E, varying rhythm rather than pitch.
steps.detail: Three notes removes the choice of what to play and leaves the choice of when, which is where most of the interest is anyway. Vary length, rests and accent. Eight bars on 3 notes that holds attention is a better exercise than 8 bars of scale running.
steps.proof: 8 bars using only 3 pitches, with the rhythm audibly varied.
steps.pitfall: Adding more notes when it starts to feel limited, which is the moment the exercise begins working.

problems.prompt: Which pitches does the 3-note, 8-bar exercise allow?
If the 3 pitches cannot vary, what does?
problems.answer: The rhythm, length, rests and accents.

problems.prompt: You want a 4th note at bar 5. What is the instruction?
problems.answer: Stay with 3. The limit is the point of the exercise.

steps.title: Play a Motif and Answer It
steps.mastery: State a short idea and reply to it.
steps.practice: Improvise a 2-bar motif, then answer it with 2 bars that share its rhythm but end differently.
steps.detail: Call and response is the smallest complete musical shape. Keep the rhythm of the answer identical and change only where it lands, so the relationship is audible. A solo made of unrelated 2-bar fragments is what improvising without this sounds like.
steps.proof: 4 bars where the answer's rhythm matches the call and its ending differs.
steps.pitfall: Making the answer a completely new idea, which sounds like starting again rather than replying.

problems.prompt: Are the call and the answer 2 bars each or 4?
In a 2-phrase question and answer, what stays the same, and what changes?
problems.answer: The rhythm stays, and the ending changes.

problems.prompt: A completely new idea in bars 3 and 4 sounds like what?

steps.title: Improvise Over Two Chords
steps.mastery: Change your note choices when the harmony changes.
steps.practice: Improvise 8 bars over 2 bars each of C and F, landing on a chord tone at every change.
steps.detail: The change is the only moment that must be right: hit a note from the new chord on its first beat and the rest follows. Practice the changes alone, play only the first beat of each chord for 8 bars, before improvising through them.
steps.proof: 4 chord changes, each met with a note belonging to the arriving chord.
steps.pitfall: Playing a C scale through the F bars, which sounds fine until the B lands.

problems.prompt: Which beat of a new chord must carry a chord tone, the 1st or the 4th?
Over a C major chord, which note of the 7-note C major scale clashes most when you hold it?
problems.answer: F, a half step above the chord's E.

problems.prompt: What do you practice before improvising through 4 changes?
problems.answer: Landing on the first beat of each chord, alone.

steps.title: Use Space
steps.mastery: Leave silence inside an improvisation on purpose.
steps.practice: Improvise 8 bars where at least 2 full bars are silent, placed deliberately.
steps.detail: Silence is what makes a phrase a phrase, and the reflex under pressure is to fill everything. Decide in advance which 2 bars are empty. Recording is the check: 2 bars of rest almost always sound shorter in the room than they look on the plan.
steps.proof: A recording with 2 audibly empty bars in 8.
steps.pitfall: Filling the planned silence because it felt too long while playing.

problems.prompt: How many of the 8 bars are silent?
When is the placement of the 2 silent bars decided?
How does 2 bars of silence feel while playing, against how it sounds?
problems.answer: It feels longer while you play than it sounds on the recording.

steps.title: Develop One Idea
steps.mastery: Take a single motif through several transformations.
steps.practice: Take a 1-bar motif and play 6 variations: louder, slower, higher, rhythmically displaced, inverted, fragmented.
steps.detail: Six versions of 1 idea is a solo; 6 unrelated ideas is a warm-up. Name the transformation before playing each, so the variation is a decision rather than a drift. Displacement and inversion are the 2 that most people never try.
steps.proof: 6 named variations of the same 1-bar motif.
steps.pitfall: Playing 6 different ideas and calling them variations.

problems.prompt: How many variations of the 1-bar motif does this step ask for?
Name 2 transformations most players never try.
What is the difference between 6 variations and 6 ideas?
problems.answer: Variations grow 1 idea. 6 ideas is just a warm-up.

steps.title: Improvise in a Mode
steps.mastery: Use a mode's characteristic note deliberately while improvising.
steps.practice: Improvise 8 bars in D Dorian over a D drone, landing on the B natural at least 4 times.
steps.detail: The characteristic note is what makes the mode audible, and under pressure it is the note people avoid because it feels exposed. Counting the landings forces the issue: 4 in 8 bars is enough that a listener hears Dorian rather than D minor.
steps.proof: 8 bars with the B natural landed on 4 times or more.
steps.pitfall: Avoiding the characteristic note, which leaves the improvisation sounding like plain D minor.

problems.prompt: Improvising in D Dorian, which note makes the mode audible?
What does avoiding it leave the 8 bars sounding like?
Why do players avoid the B natural under pressure in 8 bars of Dorian?
problems.answer: It feels exposed, since it's the note that defines the mode.

steps.title: Trade Four Bars
steps.mastery: Improvise in dialogue with another player.
steps.practice: Trade 4-bar phrases with 1 other player for 32 bars, answering what they just played.
steps.detail: Listen to their 4 bars and take something from them, a rhythm, a shape, the last note, into yours. Trading without listening is 2 people soloing alternately. Thirty-two bars is 4 exchanges each, which is long enough to develop something.
steps.proof: 8 phrases traded, each carrying something from the one before.
steps.pitfall: Planning your 4 bars while they play theirs, which is not listening.

problems.prompt: Trading 4-bar phrases with a partner for 32 bars, how many phrases do you play between you?
Name 2 things you can take from their phrase into yours.
problems.answer: A rhythm, or the last note.

problems.prompt: Two players trade 4 bars each without listening to each other. What does it sound like?
problems.answer: Two people taking turns to solo, not a conversation.

steps.title: Record and Listen Back
steps.mastery: Judge your own improvisation from a recording.
steps.practice: Record 32 bars of improvisation and list 2 things that worked and 2 that did not.
steps.detail: Playing and judging cannot happen at once, which is why recording is the only real feedback. Expect the recording to be less busy than it felt and the silences to be shorter. Name 4 specific moments with bar numbers rather than an overall impression.
steps.proof: 4 named moments with bar numbers, 2 good and 2 not.
steps.pitfall: Listening back for an overall verdict, which produces a mood rather than something to work on.

problems.prompt: Reviewing a 32-bar recording, why name 2 moments that worked as well as 2 that didn't?
problems.answer: So you keep doing what works, not just fix mistakes.

problems.prompt: What should each of the 4 carry?
Why can't you judge 32 bars while you play them?
problems.answer: Your attention is busy playing, so judging has to wait.

steps.title: Improvise Inside a Form
steps.mastery: Solo over a repeating structure without losing your place.
steps.practice: Improvise over a 12-bar blues for 2 choruses, and say which bar you are in at any point.
steps.detail: Count the form while playing, bar 5 is where the harmony moves, bar 9 is the turnaround. Losing the place is the standard failure, and the cure is to mark those 2 bars with something deliberate so the structure is audible in your own playing.
steps.proof: 2 choruses of 12 bars with the chord changes met in the right bars.
steps.pitfall: Playing 11 or 13 bars and arriving at the turnaround in the wrong place.

problems.prompt: How many bars is 2 choruses of a 12-bar blues?
In a 12-bar blues, which 2 bars bring the big chord changes worth marking? Give the earlier one first.
problems.answer: Bars 5 and 9. Bar 5 moves to the IV chord and bar 9 to the V.

problems.prompt: What is the standard failure when soloing over 2 choruses of a repeating form?
problems.answer: Losing your place and reaching the turnaround in the wrong bar.

steps.title: Count the Size
steps.mastery: Name an interval's number by counting letters inclusively.
steps.practice: Name the size of C to G, D to A, and E to C, counting the start note as 1.
steps.detail: Count both end notes: C to G is C D E F G, so a fifth. E to C is E F G A B C, a sixth. Counting the steps between rather than the letters inclusive gives a number one too small, which is the single most common interval error.
steps.proof: A fifth, a fifth and a sixth.
steps.pitfall: Counting gaps instead of letters, which calls C to G a fourth.

problems.prompt: Counting C as 1, what size is C up to G?
Counting E as 1, what size is E up to C?
Counting the 4 gaps rather than the 5 letters gives what error on C to G?

steps.title: Add the Quality
steps.mastery: Distinguish major from minor by counting semitones.
steps.practice: Count the semitones in C to E and in C to Eb, then name both of the 2 intervals.
steps.detail: C to E is 4 semitones, a major third; C to E flat is 3, a minor third. The size comes from the letters and the quality from the semitone count, which is why both notes keep the letter E, the size is a third either way.
steps.proof: 4 semitones is a major third and 3 is a minor third.
steps.pitfall: Calling C to E flat a second because the note was altered, when the letter distance is unchanged.

problems.prompt: Is C up to E 3 semitones or 4, and what interval is that?
Is C up to Eb 3 semitones or 4?
Does flattening the upper note change the interval's size or its quality?
problems.answer: Its quality only. A third is still a third.

steps.title: The Perfect Intervals
steps.mastery: Identify the intervals that are called perfect rather than major.
steps.practice: Give the semitone counts for a perfect fourth, a perfect fifth and an octave, 3 numbers.
steps.detail: 5, 7 and 12 semitones. Unisons, fourths, fifths and octaves are perfect rather than major or minor, which is a naming convention with acoustic roots: these are the intervals whose frequency ratios are simplest. Altering one gives diminished or augmented rather than minor.
steps.proof: 5, 7 and 12 semitones, and none of the 3 is called major.
steps.pitfall: Calling a fifth major, which is not a category a fifth has.

problems.prompt: Is a perfect fifth 7 semitones or 8?
Is a perfect fourth 5 semitones or 6?
Which 4 interval sizes are called perfect?

steps.title: Invert an Interval
steps.mastery: Work out what an interval becomes when the notes swap.
steps.practice: Invert C up to E and C up to G, and give the 2 new intervals.
steps.detail: The 2 sizes always sum to 9: a third inverts to a sixth, a fifth to a fourth. Major becomes minor and perfect stays perfect, so C to E major third inverts to E to C minor sixth. That rule saves learning the large intervals separately.
steps.proof: A minor sixth and a perfect fourth, and both pairs of sizes sum to 9.
steps.pitfall: Expecting the sizes to sum to 8, which is the octave rather than the inversion rule.

problems.prompt: A major third of 4 semitones inverts to which interval?
What do the 2 sizes of an interval and its inversion always sum to?
A perfect fifth of 7 semitones inverts to what?

steps.title: Sing Then Check
steps.mastery: Produce an interval with your voice and verify it.
steps.practice: Sing a perfect fifth above 3 given notes, then check each against an instrument.
steps.detail: Sing first and check second, otherwise you are copying rather than producing. Use a reference for the starting note only. A fifth is the easiest to hold, which is why it comes first; being within a semitone on all 3 is a reasonable first standard.
steps.proof: All 3 sung fifths land within a semitone of the instrument.
steps.pitfall: Playing the target interval first, which turns the exercise into imitation.

problems.prompt: You sing a fifth above C. Which note are you aiming at?
Why sing all 3 before checking any?
problems.answer: Playing first turns it into copying, not making the pitch yourself.

problems.prompt: What is a reasonable first standard for accuracy across 3 sung fifths?

steps.title: Name What You Hear
steps.mastery: Identify a played interval by ear from a small set.
steps.practice: Name 10 intervals played at random from major third, perfect fifth and octave, keeping score.
steps.detail: Three well-separated intervals first, not all 12: the point is to build 3 reliable anchors rather than to guess among many. Keep score, 8 of 10 is the threshold to add a fourth interval to the set, and below 6 means dropping back to 2.
steps.proof: A score out of 10, with the confusions noted by pair.
steps.pitfall: Starting with all 12 intervals, where a 30 per cent score teaches nothing about which are confused.

problems.prompt: You score 8 of 10 on 3 intervals. What is the next step?
problems.answer: Add a 4th interval to the set.

problems.prompt: You score 5 of 10. What do you do?
problems.answer: Drop back to 2 intervals that sound far apart.

problems.prompt: Why start with 3 intervals rather than all 12?
problems.answer: A low score across 12 doesn't tell you which pairs you mix up.

steps.title: Move the Bottom Note Up
steps.mastery: Produce the first inversion of a triad.
steps.practice: Invert C major once by moving C up an octave, and name the resulting 3 notes bottom to top.
steps.detail: C E G becomes E G C. The chord is still C major, same 3 notes, but the lowest sounding note is now E. That distinction between the chord and its bass is the whole subject, and it is why a chord symbol sometimes carries a slash.
steps.proof: E G C, still a C major chord.
steps.pitfall: Calling E G C an E minor chord, which would need E G B.

problems.prompt: Name the 3 notes of C major in first inversion, bottom to top.
Which of the 3 notes is in the bass?
Is E G C, with its 3 notes in that order, a C chord or an E chord?
problems.answer: A C chord: C major, with E in the bass.

steps.title: Second Inversion
steps.mastery: Produce and recognize a triad with its fifth in the bass.
steps.practice: Write C major in second inversion, naming the 3 notes, and say which degree is lowest.
steps.detail: Move E up too and you get G C E, with the fifth in the bass. A triad has 3 positions, root, first and second inversion, because it has 3 notes, and after 3 moves you are back where you started an octave up.
steps.proof: G C E, with the fifth in the bass.
steps.pitfall: Expecting a third inversion of a triad, which does not exist, only a 4-note chord has one.

problems.prompt: Name the 3 notes of C major in second inversion.
Not counting root position, how many inversions does a 4-note seventh chord have?
Which chord size is needed for a third inversion, 3 notes or 4?

steps.title: Read the Slash Notation
steps.mastery: Interpret a chord symbol that names its own bass note.
steps.practice: Name the notes of C/E and G/D, 2 symbols, and say which inversion each is.
