steps.proof: 3 urgent tasks batched or handed off.
steps.pitfall: Dropping deep work every time someone pings you.

problems.prompt: 6 quick requests come in by 11 am. What's a better plan than replying to each right away?
A coworker can do a task as well as you. What can you do?
Why are many of the 10 daily pings low priority for you?

steps.title: Pick Your 1 Thing
steps.mastery: Name the single most important task each day.
steps.practice: For 5 mornings, star 1 task that would make the day a win if it got done.
steps.detail: When everything feels important, nothing is. One starred task gives focus. Ask "If I only got 1 thing done today, what would it be?" Do that first if you can.
steps.proof: 5 days, each with 1 starred task and whether it got done.
steps.pitfall: Starring 4 tasks, which defeats the point.

problems.prompt: Write the question that finds your 1 thing.
problems.answer: "If I only got 1 thing done today, what would it be?"

problems.prompt: You starred 3 tasks. What's wrong?
problems.answer: It defeats the focus. Star only 1.

problems.prompt: Your starred task got done 4 of 5 days. How did it go?

steps.title: Name What You're Avoiding
steps.mastery: Find the feeling behind putting off a task.
steps.practice: For 3 tasks you're avoiding, write the feeling behind each: bored, anxious, confused or overwhelmed.
steps.detail: Procrastination is usually avoiding a feeling. Laziness is rarely the real cause. Bored, anxious, confused and overwhelmed each need a different fix. Naming the right one is half the work.
steps.proof: 3 tasks, each with a feeling named.
steps.pitfall: Calling it laziness, which points to no fix.

problems.prompt: You keep putting off a form because you don't know what 2 boxes mean. Which feeling?
You put off calling the doctor because you fear bad news. Which feeling?
You've put off 3 tasks for a week. Is that usually just laziness?
problems.answer: No. It's usually avoiding a feeling.

steps.title: Fix Confusion
steps.mastery: Clear up an unclear task so you know the first step.
steps.practice: For 1 confusing task, write 3 questions you need answered and ask 1 person today.
steps.detail: Unclear tasks get avoided because there's no obvious first move. List what you don't know. Ask a teacher, coworker or friend. Once you know the first step, starting is easy.
steps.proof: 3 questions written and at least 1 answered today.
steps.pitfall: Staring at a task you don't understand and hoping it clears up.

problems.prompt: You don't know what format the report needs. Write 1 question to ask.
problems.answer: "Do you want the report as slides or a doc?"

problems.prompt: Should you write 3 questions or 30?
Name 2 people you could ask about a confusing school task.

steps.title: Fix Fear
steps.mastery: Shrink a scary task down to its real size.
steps.practice: For 1 task you dread, write the worst case, how likely it is from 1 to 10, and what you'd do if it happened.
steps.detail: Fear makes tasks look huge. Writing the worst case shows it's usually unlikely and survivable. Then shrink the first step so it's small enough to take today.
steps.proof: 1 dreaded task with worst case, likelihood and plan written.
steps.pitfall: Avoiding the task until the deadline makes it worse.

problems.prompt: You rate the worst case 2 out of 10 likely. What does that tell you?
After writing the worst case, what's next?
problems.answer: Shrink the first step and take it.

problems.prompt: You dread asking for an extension. What's a tiny first step?

steps.title: Fix Boredom
steps.mastery: Make a dull task easier to get through.
steps.practice: For 1 boring task, add a timer, music or a small reward, and work for 25 minutes.
steps.detail: Boring tasks won't become fun, so add some help. A timer turns it into a race. Music lifts the mood. A small reward afterward gives a reason. Pick 1 or 2.
steps.proof: 1 boring task worked for 25 minutes with 1 helper.
steps.pitfall: Waiting for a dull task to start feeling interesting.

problems.prompt: Name 2 ways to make filing receipts less dull.
Is the boring task session 25 minutes or 3 hours?
Write a small reward for after 25 minutes of filing.

steps.title: Fix Overwhelm
steps.mastery: Break a huge task into steps small enough to start.
steps.practice: For 1 overwhelming task, write 5 small steps and finish the first one today.
steps.detail: Big tasks feel impossible because you see all of it at once. Small steps feel doable. Write them down so your head can let go, then focus only on step 1.
steps.proof: 1 big task split into 5 steps with step 1 done.
steps.pitfall: Thinking about the whole thing at once and freezing.

problems.prompt: Split "Move apartments" into 2 first steps.
problems.answer: Get 10 boxes, then pack the bookshelf.

problems.prompt: Why write the 5 steps down?
problems.answer: So your head can let go and focus on step 1.

problems.prompt: You finished step 1 of 5. How should that feel?
problems.answer: Like progress. The task is 20% done.

steps.title: Spot Your Pattern
steps.mastery: Notice which feeling causes most of your procrastination.
steps.practice: For 14 days, log each time you put something off and the feeling behind it.
steps.detail: A pattern usually shows up. Maybe anxiety drives most of it, or confusion. Then you know which fix to reach for first.
steps.proof: A 14 day log with your top feeling named.
steps.pitfall: Treating each delay as a one-off.

problems.prompt: Anxiety shows up 8 of 12 times. What does that tell you?
What 2 things do you log each time?
Your top feeling is confusion. Which fix comes first?

steps.title: List Every Project
steps.mastery: Find everything you're doing that takes more than one step.
steps.practice: Write a list of every project you have going, aiming for at least 10.
steps.detail: A project is anything that needs more than 1 action, like planning a trip, fixing a bike or applying for a job. Most people have 10 to 30 and only think of 4. The rest hide as tasks that never get done.
steps.proof: A list of 10 or more projects.
steps.pitfall: Calling "Plan trip" a task and wondering why it never gets ticked off.

problems.prompt: Is "Plan birthday party" a task or a project?
Is "Text Sam the address" a task or a project?
You listed 4 projects in 5 minutes. What helps you find more?
problems.answer: Go area by area: school, home, money, health, people.

steps.title: Define Done
steps.mastery: Write what finished looks like for each project.
steps.practice: Write a 1 line done statement for 5 projects, like "Party held on May 3 with 10 friends."
steps.detail: Projects without an end drag on. A done line tells you when to stop and what to aim for. Make it something you could check off, with a date if it has one.
steps.proof: 5 projects with 1 line done statements.
steps.pitfall: Leaving projects open-ended so they never finish.

problems.prompt: Write a done line for "Fix bike."
problems.answer: "Bike rides with working brakes and gears by Saturday."

problems.prompt: Write a done line for "Job applications."
Why does a 1 line done statement help?
problems.answer: You know when to stop and what to aim for.

steps.title: Break Into Steps
steps.mastery: Split a project into steps small enough to finish in one sitting.
steps.practice: Break 1 project into 8 steps, each taking 1 hour or less.
steps.detail: Big projects stall because they're hard to start. Steps make them doable. Each one should be a single action, like "Book venue" or "Make guest list." Order them roughly so step 1 is obvious.
steps.proof: 1 project split into 8 ordered steps.
steps.pitfall: Leaving "Plan party" as one giant step.

problems.prompt: Name 3 steps for "Plan party."
problems.answer: Make a guest list, book a venue, send invites.

problems.prompt: Is "Organize everything" a good step?
problems.answer: No. It's too big and vague.

problems.prompt: Should each of the 8 steps take 1 hour or less, or a full week?

steps.title: Give Each Project a Next Action
steps.mastery: Make sure every active project has one clear thing to do next.
steps.practice: Write 1 next action beside each of your 10 projects.
steps.detail: A stalled project almost always has no next action. When every project has one, you can act on any of them in a spare 20 minutes. If you can't think of a next action, the project might need a done line first.
steps.proof: 10 projects, each with a next action.
steps.pitfall: Projects sitting for weeks because nobody knows the next step.

problems.prompt: Project "Bike repair" has no next action. Write one.
problems.answer: "Look up the brake pad size for my bike."

problems.prompt: You can't think of a next action for a project. What might be missing?
You have 20 free minutes. How does a next action list help?
problems.answer: You can pick one and act right away.

steps.title: Check Projects Weekly
steps.mastery: Look at every project in the weekly review to keep them moving.
steps.practice: Review your project list in 4 weekly reviews and update next actions.
steps.detail: Projects drift without a weekly look. In the review, check each one: is the next action still right, done, or stuck? Write a new next action wherever the old one is finished.
steps.proof: 4 weekly reviews with all projects checked.
steps.pitfall: Only looking at projects when something goes wrong.

problems.prompt: A next action from last week is done. What do you write?
A project hasn't moved in 3 weeks. What do you check first?
problems.answer: Whether the next action is clear and doable.

problems.prompt: Should you look at all 10 projects weekly or yearly?

steps.title: Close Finished and Dead Projects
steps.mastery: Close projects that are done or no longer wanted so the list stays honest.
steps.practice: Close 2 projects this week: 1 that's finished and 1 you've quietly given up on.
steps.detail: A list full of dead projects makes the live ones harder to see. Mark finished projects done and celebrate a little. Move dead ones to someday or delete them. Closing on purpose feels better than letting them rot.
steps.proof: 2 projects closed.
steps.pitfall: Keeping a dead project on the list for 6 months out of guilt.

problems.prompt: A project hasn't been touched in 6 months and you don't care anymore. What do you do?
problems.answer: Close it, or move it to someday.

problems.prompt: Why close 2 finished projects instead of just ignoring them?
problems.answer: So the list shows only live work.

problems.prompt: You closed 2 projects. What should the list look like now?

steps.title: Write a Weekly Look Back
steps.mastery: Write a short reflection on how the week went.
steps.practice: Every Friday for 4 weeks, answer 3 questions in writing: what worked, what didn't, what to change.
steps.detail: Without reflection, you repeat the same week with more effort. Three questions keep it short. Write, don't just think, because writing forces clear answers. Ten minutes is enough.
steps.proof: 4 weekly reflections with 3 answers each.
steps.pitfall: Thinking it over in your head, where it stays vague.

problems.prompt: Name the 3 reflection questions.
problems.answer: What worked, what didn't and what to change.

problems.prompt: Why write the 3 answers instead of just thinking them?
Your reflection takes 45 minutes. What's the risk?
problems.answer: It feels like a chore, and you'll stop doing it.

steps.title: Find What Worked
steps.mastery: Pull out the choices that made good days good.
steps.practice: Look at your 3 best days this month and write 1 thing each had in common.
steps.detail: People study bad days and ignore good ones. Good days hold clues, like an early start, a short task list or a walk at lunch. Find what they share and do more of it.
steps.proof: 3 best days with 1 shared factor named.
steps.pitfall: Only studying what went wrong.

problems.prompt: Your 3 best days all started with a 7 am walk. What's the lesson?
Why study your 3 best days, not only the bad ones?
Name 1 common factor good days might share.
problems.answer: A short task list, for example.

steps.title: Spot Repeated Problems
steps.mastery: Notice problems that keep showing up across weeks.
steps.practice: Read 4 weeks of reflections and circle any problem that appears 2 or more times.
steps.detail: One bad day is noise. The same problem 3 weeks in a row is a pattern. Patterns are where small changes pay off most. Circle them and pick 1 to tackle.
steps.proof: 4 weeks read with repeated problems circled.
steps.pitfall: Treating every problem as a one-off.

problems.prompt: "Ran out of time Thursday" shows up 3 of 4 weeks. What is it?
A problem shows up in 1 of 4 weeks. Is it a pattern yet?
You found 4 patterns. How many should you tackle first?

steps.title: Make 1 Small Change
steps.mastery: Turn each reflection into one concrete change for next week.
steps.practice: Write 1 change for next week from your reflection and put it on your calendar.
steps.detail: Reflection without change is just a diary. Pick 1 small, specific change, like "Start Thursday's report on Wednesday." Put it on the calendar so it happens.
steps.proof: 1 change written and scheduled.
steps.pitfall: Writing 6 vague changes like "be better" that never happen.

problems.prompt: Rewrite "Manage time better" as 1 change.
problems.answer: "Start Thursday's report on Wednesday at 3 pm."

problems.prompt: Why put the 1 change on the calendar?
Should you make 1 change per week or 6?

steps.title: Check Last Week's Change
steps.mastery: See whether last week's change worked before choosing a new one.
steps.practice: Start each reflection by rating last week's change from 1 to 5 for how well it worked.
steps.detail: Changes need checking. Some work, some don't. Rate it. Keep what scores 4 or 5, adjust what scores 3, drop what scores 1 or 2.
steps.proof: 4 weeks of changes rated.
steps.pitfall: Making new changes without checking old ones.

problems.prompt: Last week's change scored 5. What do you do?
It scored 2. What do you do?
problems.answer: Drop it, and try something else.

problems.prompt: Why rate last week's change from 1 to 5 before choosing a new one?

steps.title: Look Back Each Quarter
steps.mastery: Reflect on a whole season to see bigger trends.
steps.practice: Every 3 months, spend 30 minutes reading your weekly reflections and write a 5 line summary.
steps.detail: Weekly reflections show small patterns. A quarterly look shows the big ones, like how your goals moved or which habits stuck. Five lines is enough.
steps.proof: A 5 line quarterly summary.
steps.pitfall: Never looking past the current week.

problems.prompt: Should the bigger look back happen every 3 months or every 3 years?
Should the quarterly summary be 5 lines or 5 pages?
Name 1 big trend you might spot.

steps.title: Book the Review
steps.mastery: Set a fixed weekly slot for reviewing your whole system.
steps.practice: Book 1 hour at the same time each week, like Friday at 3 pm, and call it Weekly Review.
steps.detail: Without a fixed slot, the review gets skipped when weeks get busy, which is when it matters most. Pick a time with low energy demands. Friday afternoon or Sunday evening are common.
steps.proof: A repeating 1 hour Weekly Review in your calendar.
steps.pitfall: Doing the review "when there's time," which is never.

problems.prompt: Name 2 common times for a weekly review.
Your week is packed. Should you skip the review?
problems.answer: No. Busy weeks need it most.

problems.prompt: Why hold the review at the same time all 52 weeks?
problems.answer: It becomes a habit instead of a decision.

steps.title: Empty Every Inbox
steps.mastery: Clear all capture spots so nothing is hiding.
steps.practice: In the review, empty 4 places: your capture inbox, email inbox, notes app and bag or desk papers.
steps.detail: Things pile up in more places than you think: loose papers, voice memos, screenshots, texts to yourself. Go through each and move items to lists, calendar or trash. The goal is zero untouched items.
steps.proof: 4 capture places at zero after the review.
steps.pitfall: Clearing the task inbox and ignoring the pile of papers in your bag.

problems.prompt: Name 3 places things hide besides your main inbox.
problems.answer: Bag papers, screenshots and texts to yourself.

problems.prompt: A receipt in your bag needs a refund claim. Where does it go?
problems.answer: A task on your list, like "Submit refund for 45 dollars."

problems.prompt: Your inbox had 23 items. When is it at zero?
problems.answer: When every item has been moved, done or deleted.

steps.title: Look at Every Project
steps.mastery: Check that each active project has a clear next action.
steps.practice: Read your project list and make sure all 5 or more projects have 1 next action written.
steps.detail: A stalled project is almost always one with no next action. Go down the list. If a project has none, write one now. If a project is no longer wanted, move it to someday or drop it.
steps.proof: Every active project with 1 next action.
steps.pitfall: Letting projects sit for weeks with nothing to do next.

problems.prompt: Project "Plan trip" has no next action. Write one.
A project hasn't moved in 4 weeks. What's the likely cause?
problems.answer: It has no clear next action.

problems.prompt: You no longer care about project 6. What do you do?
problems.answer: Move it to someday, or drop it.

steps.title: Check the Calendar Both Ways
steps.mastery: Look back and ahead on the calendar to catch loose ends and prep needs.
steps.practice: Look at the past 7 days and the next 14 days, and write any task each event creates.
steps.detail: Past events leave follow-ups: thank-you notes, notes to file, promises made. Future events need prep: a gift, a form, a booking. Two weeks ahead gives time to act.
steps.proof: Follow-up and prep tasks written from 21 days of calendar.
steps.pitfall: Seeing a birthday on the calendar the morning of it.

problems.prompt: Last week you met a mentor. Name 1 follow-up task.
A trip is on day 12 of the next 14. Name 1 prep task.
problems.answer: Book a ride to the airport.

problems.prompt: Why look 14 days ahead instead of 2?

steps.title: Pick Next Week's Focus
steps.mastery: Choose the few outcomes that matter most for the coming week.
steps.practice: Write 3 outcomes you want by next Friday and block time for each.
steps.detail: The review isn't only cleanup. It's where you steer. Pick 3 outcomes instead of 20 tasks. Then put time on the calendar for each so they don't get buried.
steps.proof: 3 outcomes written, each with time blocked.
steps.pitfall: Ending the review with a list of 40 tasks and no focus.

problems.prompt: Rewrite "work on essay" as an outcome for Friday.
problems.answer: "Full draft of the essay done by Friday."

problems.prompt: Should you pick 3 outcomes for the week or 20?
Why block time on the calendar for all 3 outcomes?
problems.answer: So they don't get buried by other tasks.

steps.title: Keep a Checklist
steps.mastery: Use a fixed checklist so the review takes about an hour every time.
steps.practice: Write a 6 item review checklist and use it for 3 weeks in a row.
steps.detail: A checklist makes the review faster and stops you skipping steps. A common list: empty inboxes, review projects, check calendar back, check calendar ahead, review someday list, pick weekly focus.
steps.proof: A 6 item checklist used in 3 reviews.
steps.pitfall: Making up the review from scratch each week.

problems.prompt: Name 3 items for a review checklist.
problems.answer: Empty inboxes, review projects and check the calendar.

problems.prompt: Your review took 2.5 hours. What might help?
problems.answer: A checklist to keep it focused.

problems.prompt: After 3 weeks, 1 step always feels useless. What do you do?

steps.title: Count Your Yeses
steps.mastery: See how many commitments you've taken on before adding another.
steps.practice: List every commitment you agreed to in the last 30 days and mark which ones you wanted.
steps.detail: Most overload comes from small yeses that each seemed fine. Writing them all down shows the real load. Mark each one: wanted, fine, or regret. The regret column shows where a no would have helped.
steps.proof: A 30 day list of commitments, each marked wanted, fine or regret.
steps.pitfall: Judging each new request alone, without looking at the pile it lands on.

problems.prompt: You count 14 yeses in 30 days and regret 6. What does that tell you?
problems.answer: Almost half were yeses you didn't want.

problems.prompt: Name the 3 marks for each commitment.
Why look at 30 days instead of 1 request?
problems.answer: The load only shows when you see them all together.

steps.title: Ask What It Costs
steps.mastery: Weigh a request against what it pushes out.
steps.practice: For the next 3 requests, write what you'd have to drop or delay to say yes.
steps.detail: Every yes is a no to something else, often your own work or rest. Before agreeing, name the cost. "If I help with the fundraiser Saturday, my essay slips to Sunday night." Seeing the trade makes the choice honest.
steps.proof: 3 requests, each with its cost written down.
steps.pitfall: Saying yes as if your time were empty.

problems.prompt: A friend asks for 4 hours of help Saturday. Your essay is due Monday. What's the cost?
problems.answer: Less time for the essay, likely a late Sunday night.

problems.prompt: Why write the cost down for all 3 requests?
Finish the sentence: every 1 yes is a no to...
problems.answer: Something else, often your own work or rest.

steps.title: Use a Holding Line
steps.mastery: Buy time before answering so you don't agree on reflex.
steps.practice: Answer the next 5 requests with a holding line, like "Let me check and get back to you by tomorrow."
steps.detail: Reflex yeses happen in the moment. A holding line gives you a few hours to check your calendar and the cost. Always give a time for your real answer so people aren't left hanging.
steps.proof: 5 requests answered first with a holding line.
steps.pitfall: Saying "sure!" before you've looked at your week.

problems.prompt: Write a holding line for a request made at 3 pm.
problems.answer: "Let me check my week and get back to you by tonight."

problems.prompt: Why say "by 6 pm" in your holding line?
problems.answer: So the other person isn't left waiting.

problems.prompt: You used a holding line and then forgot to answer for 4 days. What went wrong?
problems.answer: You needed a reminder to reply by the time you promised.

steps.title: Decline in 1 or 2 Sentences
steps.mastery: Say no clearly and kindly without a long excuse.
steps.practice: Write 3 short no's you'd actually say and use 1 this week.
steps.detail: A clear no now is kinder than a yes you deliver late or badly. Keep it short. Thank them, decline, and offer something smaller only if you want to. Long excuses invite people to solve them for you.
steps.proof: 3 short no's written and 1 used.
steps.pitfall: Giving 4 reasons, which the other person then argues with.

problems.prompt: Write a 1 sentence no to "Can you lead the club fundraiser?"
problems.answer: "Thanks for thinking of me, but I can't take that on this term."

problems.prompt: You want to help a little. Write a no with a smaller offer.
problems.answer: "I can't run it, but I can help set up for 1 hour."

problems.prompt: Why avoid listing 4 reasons?

steps.title: Say It Early
steps.mastery: Decline at the start instead of agreeing and backing out later.
steps.practice: Spot 1 commitment you're dreading this month and tell the person within 48 hours that you can't do it.
steps.detail: Backing out early is far easier for everyone than backing out late. If you already know a yes was a mistake, say so now while there's time to find someone else. Apologize once, briefly, and don't over-explain.
steps.proof: 1 dreaded commitment ended within 48 hours.
steps.pitfall: Waiting until the day before, when nobody can cover for you.

problems.prompt: You agreed to help on the 20th but know it's too much. It's the 5th. When should you say so?
problems.answer: Now, by the 7th at the latest.

problems.prompt: Why is backing out 15 days ahead kinder than 1 day ahead?
problems.answer: They have time to find someone else.

problems.prompt: Write a 1 sentence message to back out of helping on the 20th.
problems.answer: "I'm sorry, I overcommitted and can't help on the 20th after all."

steps.title: Keep a No List
steps.mastery: Decide some answers ahead so you don't weigh them every time.
steps.practice: Write a no list of 5 things you'll decline by default, like weeknight events after 9 pm.
steps.detail: Some requests come up again and again. Deciding once saves you the stress each time. A no list might include late weeknights, extra committees or lending money. You can still make exceptions, but the default is no.
steps.proof: A 5 item no list written.
steps.pitfall: Agonizing over the same kind of request every week.

problems.prompt: Name 2 items that might go on a no list.
problems.answer: Weeknight events after 9 pm, and joining another committee.

problems.prompt: A request matches your no list. What's your default answer?
Your no list says no events after 9 pm. Can you still make an exception?
problems.answer: Yes, but no is the default.

steps.title: Shrink the First Step
steps.mastery: Make the first move so small it feels almost silly to skip.
steps.practice: For 3 tasks you're avoiding, write a first step that takes under 2 minutes, like "open the file."
steps.detail: Most avoidance lives in the first 2 minutes. Shrink the opening move until it's easy: open the doc, write the title, put on running shoes. Once you've started, carrying on is far easier than starting was.
steps.proof: 3 tiny first steps written, and at least 1 done.
steps.pitfall: Waiting until you feel ready, which can take weeks.

problems.prompt: Shrink "Write essay" to a first step under 2 minutes.
problems.answer: "Open the doc and type the title."

problems.prompt: Shrink "Go for a run" to a first step.
Why does a 2 minute step work when "write essay" doesn't?
problems.answer: It's easy to start, and starting is the hard part.

steps.title: Use a 10 Minute Timer
steps.mastery: Promise yourself only ten minutes on a task you're dodging.
steps.practice: Set a timer for 10 minutes and work on 1 avoided task, with permission to stop when it rings.
steps.detail: Ten minutes feels doable even on a bad day. Often you'll keep going past the timer. If you stop, you still made real progress, and the task is no longer untouched.
steps.proof: 3 avoided tasks started with a 10 minute timer.
steps.pitfall: Planning a 3 hour session and never starting it.

problems.prompt: The timer rings at 10 minutes and you're on a roll. Do you have to stop?
problems.answer: No. Keep going if you want.

problems.prompt: You stop at 10 minutes. Was it worth it?
problems.answer: Yes. The task moved forward and is easier to restart.

problems.prompt: Why does a 3 hour plan often fail to start?
problems.answer: It feels too big to begin.

steps.title: Set Up the Night Before
steps.mastery: Get everything ready ahead of time so starting takes no effort.
steps.practice: For 3 nights, set out what tomorrow's first task needs, like the open file or a packed gym bag.
steps.detail: Setup is a hidden barrier. Hunting for the book or the charger eats your fresh start. Lay things out the night before. In the morning you sit down and begin.
steps.proof: 3 nights of setup done.
steps.pitfall: Spending the first 20 minutes looking for things.

problems.prompt: Name 2 things to set out the night before.
problems.answer: The book you need, and a packed gym bag.

problems.prompt: You spent 20 minutes at 8 am finding notes. What would have helped?
problems.answer: Setting them out the night before.

problems.prompt: Your first task is a run at 6 am. What do you set out?
problems.answer: Shoes, clothes and water by the door.

steps.title: Start at a Set Minute
steps.mastery: Tie starting to the clock instead of to a feeling.
steps.practice: Pick a start time for 1 task on 5 days and begin at that exact minute.
steps.detail: Waiting until you feel like it often means never. A set time removes the choice. When the clock hits 9:00, you start, even if it's just the 2 minute step.
steps.proof: 5 days of starting at the set time.
steps.pitfall: Telling yourself you'll start when you feel ready.

problems.prompt: Your start time is 9:00. It's 9:00 and you don't feel like it. What do you do?
Why does a set time like 9:00 help?
You waited for motivation 3 days in a row. What likely happened?

steps.title: Allow a Messy Start
steps.mastery: Begin without needing the work to be good yet.
steps.practice: Write a rough first draft of 1 task in 15 minutes with no editing.
steps.detail: Perfectionism blocks starting. Give yourself permission to be messy. A bad draft can be fixed later. A blank page can't. Turn off spellcheck if it distracts you.
steps.proof: 1 rough draft done in 15 minutes.
steps.pitfall: Rewriting the first sentence 10 times.

problems.prompt: You've rewritten 1 sentence 10 times in 20 minutes. What's going on?
Should you edit during the 15 minute draft?
Why is a bad draft better than 0 words?
problems.answer: You can improve a draft. A blank page gives you nothing.

steps.title: Count Your Starts
steps.mastery: Track starts so you can see the skill growing.
steps.practice: For 7 days, make a tally mark each time you start a task you'd been avoiding.
steps.detail: Starting is the skill this node trains, so count starts rather than finishes. Watching the tally grow shows that it's getting easier, even on days you don't finish much.
steps.proof: A 7 day tally of starts.
steps.pitfall: Counting only finished tasks and feeling like nothing changed.

problems.prompt: You started 9 avoided tasks in 7 days. Good week?
Why tally 9 starts instead of only 2 finishes?
problems.answer: Starting is the skill being trained.

problems.prompt: Week 1 had 4 starts and week 2 had 9. What does it show?

steps.title: Check Capture Holds Up
steps.mastery: Confirm that everything you need to remember lands in your inbox.
steps.practice: For 7 days, note every time you remember something that wasn't in your system.
steps.detail: A trusted system catches everything. Every miss shows a gap, like a promise in a hallway or an idea in the shower. Fix each gap with a capture tool in that spot.
steps.proof: 7 days of misses noted, each with a fix.
steps.pitfall: Accepting misses as normal.

problems.prompt: You remember a promise at 11 pm that wasn't captured. What's the fix?
Ideas come in the shower. Name 1 fix.
problems.answer: A waterproof notepad, or capturing right after.

problems.prompt: Your log shows 0 misses for 7 days. What does that mean?

steps.title: Run Every Habit for a Month
steps.mastery: Keep capture, daily planning and the weekly review going for a full month.
steps.practice: Run capture daily, plan each evening and hold 4 weekly reviews in the next 30 days.
steps.detail: A system you trust is built by running it. Track all 3 habits for 30 days. Missing 1 day is fine. Missing a weekly review is the one that breaks trust fastest.
steps.proof: 30 days with capture, daily plans and 4 weekly reviews.
steps.pitfall: Skipping the weekly review, which lets everything drift.

problems.prompt: Name the 3 habits.
problems.answer: Capture, daily planning and the weekly review.

problems.prompt: Of the 3 habits, which breaks trust fastest when skipped?
You missed 2 evening plans in 30 days. Is the system broken?

steps.title: Test the Quiet Head
steps.mastery: Notice whether your mind feels clear when you work.
steps.practice: During 3 focused sessions, write a tally each time an unrelated task pops into your head.
steps.detail: The point of a trusted system is a quiet head. If tasks keep popping up, something isn't captured. Write each one down in the inbox and keep working.
steps.proof: 3 sessions with tallies.
steps.pitfall: Ignoring the pop-ups and losing focus.

problems.prompt: You get 8 pop-ups in 1 session. What does it suggest?
During a session you get 8 pop-ups. What do you do with each one?
problems.answer: Write it in the inbox and keep working.

problems.prompt: Your tallies drop from 8 to 2 over 3 weeks. What changed?

steps.title: Fix the Weak Link
steps.mastery: Find the part of the system that fails most and fix it.
steps.practice: Pick the 1 habit you skip most and change 1 thing about it this week.
steps.detail: Every system has a weak link. Find it and fix 1 thing: move the review time, simplify the inbox, set a reminder. Small fixes beat a new system.
steps.proof: 1 weak link named and 1 fix made.
steps.pitfall: Throwing out the whole system because 1 part fails.

problems.prompt: You skip the Friday review 3 weeks in a row. Name 1 fix.
problems.answer: Move it to a better time, like Sunday at 6 pm.

problems.prompt: 1 habit keeps failing. Is a brand new system the best fix?
Should you change 1 thing this week or 5?

steps.title: Handle a Busy Week
steps.mastery: Keep the system alive when life gets hectic.
steps.practice: Write a minimum version of each habit for busy weeks, like a 10 minute review.
steps.detail: Busy weeks are when systems break. A minimum version keeps it alive: 1 minute capture, 5 minute plan, 10 minute review. Then build back up.
steps.proof: Minimum versions written for 3 habits.
steps.pitfall: Dropping everything during busy weeks.

problems.prompt: What's a minimum weekly review?
Why have a 10 minute minimum review?
You used the minimums for 6 busy days. When do you return to the full version?

steps.title: Recover After a Break
steps.mastery: Restart the system after time away.
steps.practice: After any break of 3 or more days, run a full weekly review before starting normal work.
steps.detail: Breaks happen: travel, illness, holidays. A review on return catches everything that piled up. Then you're back on track.
steps.proof: A review done after a break.
steps.pitfall: Jumping back in without catching up.

problems.prompt: You're back from 5 days away. What do you do first?
Why run a full review after 5 days away?
Does a 1 day break need a full review, or 3 days or more?

steps.title: Trust It
steps.mastery: Give a single task your full attention, trusting the lists to hold everything else.
steps.practice: For 3 days, work on your top task for 90 minutes without checking anything else.
steps.detail: Trust means you can focus. If the system works, nothing is forgotten while you're busy. Notice the calm.
steps.proof: 3 days of 90 minute focus blocks.
steps.pitfall: Checking lists every 10 minutes.

problems.prompt: What's the sign you trust your system?
Should each focus block be 90 minutes or 9?
You check lists every 10 minutes. What does it suggest?
problems.answer: You don't trust the system yet.

steps.title: Find the Next Action
steps.mastery: Turn a vague topic into the very next physical step.
steps.practice: Rewrite 5 vague tasks on your list as next actions, like "Find the renewal email" for "Sort out insurance."
steps.detail: "Sort out insurance" is a topic. It has no first move, so it sits. A next action is something you could do right now: find, call, email, write, buy. Ask "what's the very first thing I'd do?" and write that.
steps.proof: 5 vague tasks rewritten as physical next actions.
steps.pitfall: Writing topics like "taxes" that give you nothing to start on.

problems.prompt: Rewrite "Taxes" as a next action.
problems.answer: "Find last year's W-2 in the email."

problems.prompt: Rewrite "Birthday party" as a next action.
problems.answer: "Text 6 friends to ask if Saturday works."

problems.prompt: Is "Think about college" a next action?
problems.answer: No. Something like "List 5 colleges to look up" is.

steps.title: Start With a Verb
steps.mastery: Write every task so it begins with a clear verb.
steps.practice: Edit your task list so each of the first 15 items starts with a verb like call, email, buy or write.
steps.detail: A verb tells you what to do. "Dentist" could mean book, cancel or pay. "Call dentist to book a cleaning" is clear. Good task verbs are physical: call, email, buy, print, draft, ask, fill out.
steps.proof: 15 tasks, each starting with a verb.
steps.pitfall: Using fuzzy verbs like "handle" or "deal with" that hide the real action.

problems.prompt: Rewrite "Dentist" with a clear verb.
problems.answer: "Call the dentist to book a cleaning."

problems.prompt: Why is "Deal with email" weak?
problems.answer: Deal with hides what you'll actually do.

problems.prompt: Name 4 good physical task verbs.

steps.title: Add the Context
steps.mastery: Include enough detail that future you can act without thinking.
steps.practice: Add 1 key detail to 10 tasks, like a phone number, a link or a name.
steps.detail: A task should be doable without detective work. "Email Ms. Lee re: field trip form" beats "email teacher." Add the who, the what or the link. Future you is busy and will skip anything that needs figuring out.
steps.proof: 10 tasks with a name, number or link added.
steps.pitfall: Writing tasks so short that you can't remember what they meant.

problems.prompt: Improve "Email teacher."
problems.answer: "Email Ms. Lee about the field trip form."

problems.prompt: You wrote "Call about the thing" 3 days ago. What went wrong?
problems.answer: It left out the key detail, so it can't be acted on.

problems.prompt: Name 3 kinds of detail to add to a task.
problems.answer: A name, a phone number and a link.

steps.title: Split the Big Ones
steps.mastery: Break tasks that take more than an hour into smaller steps.
steps.practice: Find 3 tasks that would take over 60 minutes and split each into steps of 30 minutes or less.
steps.detail: Big tasks get avoided because they're hard to start. "Write essay" becomes "Write 3 bullet outline," "Draft intro," "Draft body paragraph 1." Each step should feel doable in 1 sitting.
steps.proof: 3 big tasks each split into steps under 30 minutes.
steps.pitfall: Leaving "Write essay" on the list for 2 weeks.

problems.prompt: Split "Clean garage" into 3 steps.
problems.answer: "Bag trash," "Sort tools into 1 box," "Sweep the floor."

problems.prompt: Should each split step take 30 minutes or less, or up to 3 hours?
Is "Study for finals" one task or a project?
problems.answer: A project. Split it into steps.

steps.title: Run the 2 Minute Rule
steps.mastery: Finish tiny tasks right away instead of listing them.
steps.practice: For 1 day, do any task under 2 minutes the moment it comes up, and count how many.
steps.detail: Writing down a 2 minute task and finding it later takes longer than just doing it. Reply to the quick text, file the form, take out the trash. Anything longer goes on the list.
steps.proof: A count of tiny tasks finished on the spot in 1 day.
steps.pitfall: Listing a 30 second reply, then forgetting it for a week.

problems.prompt: A text needs a yes or no. List it or do it?
problems.answer: Do it now. It takes under 2 minutes.

problems.prompt: A form takes 20 minutes. List it or do it now?
Why not list a 1 minute task?
problems.answer: Listing and finding it takes longer than doing it.

steps.title: Pick 3 for Today
steps.mastery: Choose a short list of what must get done today.
steps.practice: For 5 mornings, pick 3 tasks from your list as today's must-dos.
steps.detail: A list of 30 isn't a plan. It guarantees the day ends feeling behind. Pick 3 that matter most. If you finish them, great, take more. The rest of the list waits.
steps.proof: 5 days, each with 3 chosen tasks and how many got done.
steps.pitfall: Picking 12 must-dos and finishing 4.

problems.prompt: Your list has 28 items. How many go on today's must-do list?
You finished your 3 by 1 pm. What now?
Why does a 30 item list feel bad at 6 pm?
problems.answer: You can never finish it, so you always feel behind.

steps.title: Plan the Night Before
steps.mastery: Choose tomorrow's tasks before the day starts.
steps.practice: For 5 nights, spend 5 minutes before bed writing tomorrow's 3 tasks.
steps.detail: Deciding at night means you start the morning knowing what to do. Your brain may even work on it overnight. Look at the calendar too, so you pick tasks that fit the time you have.
steps.proof: 5 nights of 3 tasks chosen in advance.
steps.pitfall: Starting the day by checking email and letting it decide for you.

problems.prompt: You have 3 hours of meetings tomorrow. How does that change your 3 tasks?
problems.answer: Pick smaller tasks that fit the free time.

problems.prompt: Should night planning take 5 minutes or 45?
What's the risk of opening email first at 8 am?
problems.answer: Other people's requests decide your day.

steps.title: Put the Hardest First
steps.mastery: Do the most important or hardest task early, while you're fresh.
steps.practice: For 5 days, start with your toughest of the 3 tasks before email or chat.
steps.detail: Energy and focus are usually best early. If you start with easy stuff, the hard task slides to 4 pm when you're tired. Do it first and the rest of the day feels lighter.
steps.proof: 5 days where the hardest task came first.
steps.pitfall: Clearing 20 small emails first and running out of energy.

problems.prompt: Your 3 tasks are: write report, reply to 2 emails, file receipts. Which comes first?
Why might the hard task fail at 4 pm?
problems.answer: You're tired, and focus is lower.

problems.prompt: You're a night person and sharpest at 8 pm. Does "hardest first" still mean 8 am?
problems.answer: No. Do it in your sharpest hours.

steps.title: Match Tasks to Time
steps.mastery: Fit today's tasks to the hours you actually have free.
steps.practice: Write how many free hours you have today and estimate time for each of your 3 tasks.
steps.detail: People plan as if the day is empty. Check the calendar first. If you have 2 free hours, 3 tasks of 1 hour won't fit. Adjust before you start, not at 5 pm.
steps.proof: 3 tasks with time estimates that fit your free hours.
steps.pitfall: Planning 6 hours of tasks on a day with 2 free hours.

problems.prompt: You have 2 free hours and 3 tasks of 1 hour each. What do you do?
problems.answer: Drop 1, or shrink them so they fit.

problems.prompt: Before picking tomorrow's 3 tasks, what do you check?
Why adjust at 9 am instead of at 5 pm?
problems.answer: You can still choose what to drop.

steps.title: Close the Day
steps.mastery: End each day by checking what got done and setting up tomorrow.
steps.practice: Spend 5 minutes at the end of 5 days ticking off tasks and moving unfinished ones.
steps.detail: A short shutdown helps you stop thinking about work. Tick what's done. Move unfinished tasks to tomorrow or later. Then you can switch off knowing nothing is lost.
steps.proof: 5 end-of-day closes done.
steps.pitfall: Leaving the list a mess, so tomorrow starts with confusion.

problems.prompt: 2 of 3 tasks got done. What happens to the 3rd?
problems.answer: Move it to tomorrow or later.

problems.prompt: Should closing the day take 5 minutes or 1 hour?
Why does closing help you relax at 7 pm?

steps.title: List What You Use
steps.mastery: Take stock of every tool your system relies on.
steps.practice: List every app and notebook you use to plan, capture or track, with how many of the 7 days you open each.
steps.detail: Systems sprawl. A task app, 2 note apps, a planner, sticky notes, a calendar. Write them all down with how often you open each. Tools you rarely open are clutter, and they hide things.
steps.proof: A list of every tool with how often you use it.
steps.pitfall: Adding a new app without checking what you already have.

problems.prompt: You use 3 apps daily and 4 others once a month. Which are clutter?
problems.answer: The 4 you open once a month.

problems.prompt: Why note that 4 of your tools get opened once a month?
problems.answer: Rarely opened tools hide things and add clutter.

problems.prompt: Name 3 kinds of tools to include.
problems.answer: A task app, a notes app and a calendar.

steps.title: Cut to the Core 3
steps.mastery: Shrink your setup to a calendar, a task list and a notes home.
steps.practice: Keep 1 calendar, 1 task list and 1 notes home, and retire every other planning tool this week.
steps.detail: Most people need only 3 tools: a calendar for times, a task list for actions and notes for reference. More tools mean more places to check and more places to forget. Move anything important out of the extras before you retire them.
steps.proof: 3 core tools kept and the rest retired.
steps.pitfall: Running 2 task apps at once, so neither is trusted.

problems.prompt: Name the 3 core tools.
problems.answer: A calendar, a task list and a notes home.

problems.prompt: You have 2 task apps. What do you do?
problems.answer: Pick 1, and move everything from the other into it.

problems.prompt: Before retiring 1 of your 2 note apps, what must you do?
problems.answer: Move anything important out of it.

steps.title: Stop Shopping for Apps
steps.mastery: Notice when tinkering with tools has become a way to avoid work.
steps.practice: Set a rule for 30 days: no new productivity apps and no system redesigns.
steps.detail: Rebuilding your system feels productive, but it's often a polished way to procrastinate. Switching apps has rarely been the real problem. Give your current setup 30 days before you change anything.
steps.proof: 30 days with no new apps or redesigns.
steps.pitfall: Spending a Sunday afternoon setting up a new app instead of doing the work.

problems.prompt: You spent 3 hours setting up a new planner. What might have happened?
problems.answer: It became a way to avoid the real work.

problems.prompt: Should you give your current setup 3 days or 30 before changing it?
You missed 3 deadlines. Is a new app likely to fix that?
problems.answer: Rarely. Habits matter more than tools.

steps.title: Learn 3 Shortcuts
steps.mastery: Get faster at the tools you keep.
steps.practice: Learn 3 shortcuts in your task app or calendar, like quick add or keyboard capture.
steps.detail: Speed makes a tool easier to use, and an easy tool gets used. Quick add, natural language dates like "Fri 3pm" and a keyboard shortcut for capture save seconds every time. Those seconds add up.
steps.proof: 3 shortcuts learned and used 10 times each.
steps.pitfall: Clicking through 4 menus to add a single task.

problems.prompt: Name 2 helpful shortcuts.
problems.answer: Quick add, and natural language dates.

problems.prompt: Why does saving 10 seconds per task matter?
problems.answer: It makes the tool easy, so you keep using it.

problems.prompt: Type a quick-add task for a Friday 3 pm call with Sam.

steps.title: Match the Tool to the Habit
steps.mastery: Pick tools that support habits you already have.
steps.practice: Write which tool supports each of your 3 key habits: capture, daily plan and weekly review.
steps.detail: Tools should serve habits, not the other way around. If you capture on your phone, your inbox must be on your phone. If you plan on paper, a paper planner is fine. Check that each habit has a tool that fits how you work.
steps.proof: 3 habits, each matched to 1 tool.
steps.pitfall: Forcing a desktop-only tool when you capture on the go.

problems.prompt: You capture ideas on the bus. Should your inbox be desktop only?
problems.answer: No. It should be on your phone or in a pocket notebook.

problems.prompt: You love planning on paper. Is a paper planner OK?
Name the 3 key habits to match.
problems.answer: Capture, the daily plan and the weekly review.

steps.title: Review Tools Every 6 Months
steps.mastery: Check your setup twice a year and change only what's broken.
steps.practice: Book a 30 minute tools review every 6 months and change at most 1 thing.
steps.detail: A short review stops tools from drifting. Ask what's working, what's annoying and what's unused. Change only 1 thing per review so your system stays stable.
steps.proof: A 30 minute review in the calendar with 1 change noted.
steps.pitfall: Overhauling everything at once and losing track of tasks.

problems.prompt: Should you review your tools every 6 weeks or every 6 months?
You found 5 annoyances in the review. How many do you change?
Name 3 questions for the review.
problems.answer: What's working, what's annoying and what's unused.

steps.title: Ohm Law
steps.mastery: Use V = IR for a single resistor.
steps.practice: Find the current through a 6 ohm resistor on 12 V and the voltage across 220 ohms carrying 0.05 A.
steps.detail: Current equals voltage over resistance. Higher resistance means less current for the same voltage.
steps.proof: 2 A and 11 V.
steps.pitfall: Dividing the wrong way round.

steps.title: Series and Parallel
steps.mastery: Combine resistors in series and in parallel.
steps.practice: Find the total resistance of 2 ohm and 6 ohm in series and in parallel.
steps.detail: Series resistances add. In parallel the total is smaller than the smallest branch.
steps.proof: 8 ohm and 1.5 ohm.
steps.pitfall: Adding parallel resistances directly.

problems.prompt: 3 resistors of 4 ohm in series?
Two 10 ohm resistors in parallel?
3 ohm and 6 ohm in parallel?

steps.title: Kirchhoff Rules
steps.mastery: Use Kirchhoff junction and loop rules to solve a network.
steps.practice: Solve a circuit with a 12 V battery, a 4 ohm resistor in series with 2 parallel 6 ohm resistors for every current.
steps.detail: Currents into a junction equal currents out, and voltages around any loop sum to zero.
steps.proof: Total 7 ohm, 12/7 A from the battery and 6/7 A in each branch.
steps.pitfall: Losing track of sign when going around a loop.

problems.prompt: 3 A in, 1 A out of 1 branch. Other branch?
Battery 9 V, drops of 4 V and 2 V. Third drop?
Voltage across 2 parallel branches on a 6 V source?

steps.title: Power and Energy
steps.mastery: Compute electrical power and cost.
steps.practice: Find the power of a 2 A kettle on 230 V and the cost of running it 0.1 h at 15 cents per kWh.
steps.detail: P = IV = I^2 R = V^2/R. Multiply power in kW by hours to get kWh, then by the price per kWh to get the cost.
steps.proof: 460 W and about 0.7 cents.
steps.pitfall: Using watts when the price is per kilowatt hour.

problems.prompt: P for 12 V and 3 A?
P in a 10 ohm resistor with 2 A?
Energy in kWh for 2000 W for 3 h?

steps.title: Real Batteries
steps.mastery: Include internal resistance in a circuit.
steps.practice: Find the terminal voltage of a 9 V battery with 1 ohm internal resistance driving 8 ohms.
steps.detail: Some voltage is lost inside the battery. Terminal voltage = emf - Ir, and it drops as more current is drawn.
steps.proof: I = 1 A, terminal voltage 8 V.
steps.pitfall: Ignoring internal resistance when the load is small.

problems.prompt: emf 6 V, \(r = 0.5\) ohm, \(I = 2\) A. Terminal V?
Short circuit current for 9 V and \(r = 1\) ohm?
Why is a bird on 1 power line safe?
problems.answer: No voltage difference across its body.

steps.title: Charge and Coulomb Law
steps.mastery: Compute the force between 2 charges.
steps.practice: Find the force between 2 charges of 2 microcoulombs each 0.3 m apart with k = 9 x 10^9.
steps.detail: F = k q1 q2/r^2, the same inverse square shape as gravity. Like charges repel and unlike charges attract.
steps.proof: 0.4 N, repulsive.
steps.pitfall: Forgetting to convert microcoulombs to coulombs.

problems.prompt: Halve the distance. Force factor?
Charges of +3 and -3 microcoulombs. Attract or repel?
Charge of 1 electron in C?

steps.title: Electric Field
steps.mastery: Find E from a point charge with E = kq/r^2.
steps.practice: Find the field 0.5 m from a 5 microcoulomb charge and the force on a 2 nC charge placed there.
steps.detail: E = kq/r^2 is the force per unit charge. Multiply by a test charge to get the force on it.
steps.pitfall: Using the test charge to compute the field.

problems.prompt: E from 1 nC at 1 m with \(k = 9 \times 10^{9}\)?
Force on 2 C in a field of 100 N/C?
Direction of E near a -4 microcoulomb charge?

steps.title: Field Lines
steps.mastery: Sketch field patterns for charges and plates.
steps.practice: Sketch field lines for a single + charge, a + and - pair and 2 parallel plates 1 cm apart.
steps.detail: Lines start on + and end on -. Closer lines mean a stronger field, and between plates the field is uniform.
steps.proof: 3 sketches with arrows.
steps.pitfall: Drawing field lines that cross.

problems.prompt: Can 2 field lines cross at 1 point?
Field between plates 0.01 m apart at 100 V?
Field inside a charged metal sphere of radius 1 m?

steps.title: Potential and Voltage
steps.mastery: Relate potential difference to energy per charge.
steps.practice: Find the energy gained by an electron crossing 100 V and its speed if it starts at rest, with m = 9.1 x 10^-31 kg.
steps.detail: Voltage is energy per charge, so W = qV. Converting to kinetic energy gives the speed.
steps.proof: 1.6 x 10^-17 J and about 5.9 x 10^6 m/s.
steps.pitfall: Treating voltage as a force.

problems.prompt: Energy for 2 C across 12 V?
1 eV in joules?
Potential 0.5 m from 1 nC with \(k = 9 \times 10^{9}\)?

steps.title: Capacitors
steps.mastery: Use Q = CV and the energy stored.
steps.practice: Find the charge and energy on a 100 microfarad capacitor at 12 V.
steps.detail: A capacitor stores charge in proportion to the voltage across it. The energy stored is 1/2 CV^2.
steps.proof: 1.2 mC and 7.2 mJ.
steps.pitfall: Using CV^2 without the half.

problems.prompt: Q on 10 microfarads at 5 V?
Energy in 2 F at 3 V?
Double V from 6 to 12 V. Energy factor?

steps.title: The EM Spectrum
steps.mastery: Order the spectrum by wavelength and frequency.
steps.practice: Order 7 regions from radio to gamma by wavelength and give 1 use of each.
steps.detail: All EM waves travel at c in a vacuum. Shorter wavelength means higher frequency and more energy per photon.
steps.proof: Radio, microwave, IR, visible, UV, X-ray, gamma with uses.
steps.pitfall: Thinking radio waves are sound.

problems.prompt: Which has higher frequency, UV or IR, out of the 7 regions?
Speed of 2.45 GHz microwaves in a vacuum?
Wavelength of a 100 MHz FM radio wave?

steps.title: Fields That Regenerate
steps.mastery: Describe EM waves as linked electric and magnetic fields.
steps.practice: Sketch an EM wave with E and B at right angles and explain in 2 sentences why it needs no medium.
steps.detail: A changing E field makes a B field and a changing B field makes an E field. The pair carries itself through empty space.
steps.proof: A sketch with E, B and the direction of travel all at 90 degrees.
steps.pitfall: Drawing E and B parallel.

problems.prompt: Angle between E and B in an EM wave?
Can light cross the 150 million km of vacuum to Earth?
Who predicted EM waves in the 1860s?

steps.title: Speed of Light From Constants
steps.mastery: Compute c from the electric and magnetic constants.
steps.practice: Compute c = 1/sqrt(mu0 epsilon0) with mu0 = 4 pi x 10^-7 and epsilon0 = 8.85 x 10^-12.
steps.detail: Maxwell found that the wave speed comes straight from 2 measured constants. It matched the speed of light.
steps.proof: About 3.00 x 10^8 m/s.
steps.pitfall: Dropping the square root.

problems.prompt: mu0 epsilon0 value, roughly?
Light travel time from the Sun at \(1.5 \times 10^{11}\) m?
Distance light goes in 1 ns?

steps.title: Energy and Intensity
steps.mastery: Use intensity and the inverse square law.
steps.practice: Find the intensity 2 m from a 100 W bulb radiating evenly, then at 4 m.
steps.detail: Power spreads over a sphere of area 4 pi r^2. Doubling distance cuts intensity to a quarter.
steps.proof: About 2.0 W/m^2 and 0.50 W/m^2.
steps.pitfall: Using a circle area instead of a sphere.

problems.prompt: Intensity factor going from 1 m to 3 m?
Sunlight at Earth is about 1360 W/m². At 2 AU?
Area of a sphere of radius 1 m?

steps.title: Polarization
steps.mastery: Use Malus law for polarizers.
steps.practice: Find the intensity through 2 polarizers at 60 degrees when 100 W/m^2 of unpolarized light enters.
steps.detail: The first polarizer halves unpolarized light. Each next one passes I cos^2 theta.
steps.pitfall: Forgetting the first halving.

problems.prompt: Polarized 40 W/m² through a filter at 90 degrees?
At 45 degrees, 40 W/m² becomes?
Can sound waves in air at 340 m/s be polarized?

steps.title: Define Work
steps.mastery: State the definition of mechanical work as a scalar product of force and displacement.
steps.practice: Calculate the work done by a constant 10 N force pushing a crate 3 m horizontally.
steps.detail: Write the force vector and displacement vector. Verify they are collinear; if not, use the component of the force along the displacement. Multiply the magnitude of that component by the distance traveled. Record the result in joules.
steps.proof: Work = 10 N × 3 m = 30 J.
steps.pitfall: Multiplying force and distance without checking that the force is parallel to the displacement.

problems.prompt: What is the work done by a 5 N force moving an object 2 m in the direction of the force?
Calculate the work done by a constant 12 N force pushing a crate 4 m horizontally.
A 8 N force pushes a crate 3 m opposite to the direction of motion. What is the work done by the force?
problems.hint: Remember work = \(F \cdot d \cdot \cos \theta\); opposite direction gives \(\cos \theta = - 1\).

steps.title: Introduce Kinetic Energy
steps.mastery: Relate a moving object's kinetic energy to its mass and speed.
steps.practice: Compute the kinetic energy of a 2 kg ball moving at 4 m/s.
steps.detail: Use the formula KE = ½ mv². Plug in the mass and speed values, square the speed first, then multiply by the mass and ½. Write the answer with the unit joule.
steps.proof: KE = ½ × 2 kg × (4 m/s)² = 16 J.
steps.pitfall: Forgetting to square the speed or omitting the ½ factor.

problems.prompt: What is the kinetic energy of a 1 kg object moving at 2 m/s?
Compute the kinetic energy of a 3 kg ball moving at 5 m/s.
A 0.5 kg projectile has a kinetic energy of 8 J. What is its speed?
problems.hint: Solve KE = ½ m v² for v.

steps.title: Work-Energy Theorem
steps.mastery: Apply the work-energy theorem to equate net work to the change in kinetic energy.
steps.practice: A 1 kg cart accelerates from 2 m/s to 5 m/s. Find the net work done on the cart.
steps.detail: Calculate initial KE with the initial speed, then final KE with the final speed. Subtract initial from final to get ΔKE, which equals net work. Keep units consistent.
steps.proof: ΔKE = ½·1·5² − ½·1·2² = 12.5 J − 2 J = 10.5 J, so net work = 10.5 J.
steps.pitfall: Using final speed for both terms or ignoring the initial kinetic energy.

problems.prompt: A 2 kg cart speeds up from 0 m/s to 3 m/s. What is the net work done on it?
A 1.5 kg sled accelerates from 2 m/s to 6 m/s. Find the net work done.
A 1 kg cart slows down from 4 m/s to 1 m/s. What is the net work done on the cart?
problems.hint: Work equals change in kinetic energy; final minus initial.

steps.title: Potential Energy of Gravity
steps.mastery: Express gravitational potential energy as the product of weight and height.
steps.practice: Find the gravitational potential energy of a 3 kg mass lifted 4 m above ground (g = 9.8 m/s²).
steps.detail: Multiply the mass by the acceleration due to gravity to get weight, then multiply by the vertical displacement. Record the result in joules, rounding if desired.
steps.pitfall: Using mass instead of weight (mg) or forgetting the height factor.

problems.prompt: What is the gravitational potential energy of a 2 kg mass lifted 3 m (g=9.8 m/s²)?
Find the gravitational potential energy of a 5 kg object raised 7 m above ground (use g=9.8 m/s²).
A 10 kg weight is suspended 0.5 m above the floor. What is its gravitational potential energy? (Use g=9.8 m/s²).
problems.hint: Weight = mg; then multiply by height.

steps.title: Conserve Mechanical Energy
steps.mastery: Use conservation of mechanical energy when non-conservative forces are absent.
steps.practice: A 0.5 kg pendulum bob is released from a height 0.6 m above its lowest point. Compute its speed at the bottom.
steps.detail: Set initial potential energy equal to final kinetic energy. Solve for speed by isolating v², then take the square root. Keep significant figures consistent.
steps.pitfall: Including friction or air resistance when the problem states a frictionless system.

problems.prompt: A 0.2 kg pendulum bob is released from 0.3 m height. What is its speed at the lowest point? (g=9.8 m/s²).
A 0.8 kg block slides down a frictionless 2 m high incline. Find its speed at the bottom.
A 0.5 kg pendulum bob reaches a speed of 4 m/s at the bottom of its swing. Assuming no friction, from what height was it released? (g=9.8 m/s²).
problems.hint: Set initial PE = final KE and solve for height.

steps.title: Solve Combined Work-Energy Ramp Problem
steps.mastery: Combine work from gravity and external forces to find final speed using the work-energy theorem.
steps.practice: A 1.5 kg skateboarder starts from rest at the top of a frictionless 2 m high ramp, then rides onto a level section where a constant 5 N push acts for 3 m. Find the speed at the end of the push.
steps.detail: Compute the work done by gravity as the loss of potential energy (mgh). Add the work done by the external push (force × distance). Set the sum equal to the change in kinetic energy, solve for the final speed, and keep units consistent.
steps.proof: Work_gravity = m·g·h = 1.5·9.8·2 = 29.4 J (gain). Work_push = 5 N·3 m = 15 J. Total work = 44.4 J = ΔKE = ½·1.5·v² → v = √(2·44.4/1.5) ≈ 7.68 m/s.
steps.pitfall: Treating the push as opposing motion or forgetting to add the gravitational work to the push work.

problems.prompt: Calculate the gravitational work on a 2.0 kg object that slides down a frictionless 3 m high ramp.
A 1.5 kg skateboarder starts from rest at the top of a frictionless 2 m high ramp and then receives a constant 5 N push along a horizontal 3 m section. What is the speed at the end of the push?
problems.answer: 7.69 m/s. The ramp gives \(1.5 \times 9.8 \times 2 = 29.4\) J and the push adds 15 J, so \(v = \sqrt{2 \times \frac{44.4}{1.5}}\).

problems.prompt: If the same skateboarder receives a constant 5 N force opposite to its motion along the 3 m horizontal section after the ramp, what is its speed at the end of the section?
problems.answer: 4.38 m/s. The ramp gives 29.4 J and the force takes 15 J, so \(v = \sqrt{2 \times \frac{14.4}{1.5}}\).
problems.hint: Subtract the work done by the opposing push from the gravitational work before converting to kinetic energy.

steps.title: Isolate One Object
steps.mastery: Draw a single object alone with its forces.
steps.practice: Draw free-body diagrams for 4 cases: a 2 kg book on a table, a hanging lamp, a box being pushed and a falling ball.
steps.detail: Draw only the chosen object as a dot or box. Every force on it comes from something touching it or from gravity.
steps.proof: 4 diagrams with every force labeled by its source.
steps.pitfall: Adding forces the object exerts on other things.

problems.prompt: Forces on a 2 kg book resting on a table?
problems.answer: Weight down and normal force up.

problems.prompt: Forces on a 3 kg ball in free fall, no air?
Weight of a 2 kg book with \(g = 9.8\) m/s²?

steps.title: Name Every Force
steps.mastery: Label weight, normal, tension, friction and applied forces.
steps.practice: Label each force on a 5 kg crate pulled by a rope at 30 degrees across a rough floor.
steps.detail: Each force gets a name, a direction and a source. A force with no source is not real, like a "force of motion".
steps.proof: 5 forces: weight, normal, tension, friction and none extra.
steps.pitfall: Inventing a forward force that keeps a moving object going.

problems.prompt: Direction of kinetic friction on a crate moving right at 2 m/s?
Force from a rope on a hanging 4 kg mass?
Is there a forward force on a puck sliding at 3 m/s on ice?

steps.title: Components on a Slope
steps.mastery: Split weight into parts along and across an incline.
steps.practice: Split the weight of a 10 kg block on a 30 degree slope into parallel and perpendicular parts.
steps.detail: Tilt the axes to match the slope. Along the slope mg sin theta pulls down and across it mg cos theta presses in.
steps.proof: 49 N along and about 84.9 N into the slope.
steps.pitfall: Swapping sin and cos.

problems.prompt: Parallel part of 100 N on a 30 degree slope?
Perpendicular part of 100 N on a 60 degree slope?
Normal force on a 10 kg block on a 30 degree frictionless slope?

steps.title: Diagram to Equations
steps.mastery: Write Newton second law for each axis from the diagram.
steps.practice: Write sum F = ma along x and y for a 5 kg box pushed with 20 N against 8 N of friction, then solve for a.
steps.detail: Each axis gets its own equation. Forces along the motion go in one equation, balanced forces in the other.
steps.pitfall: Putting the ma term on the diagram as a force.

problems.prompt: Net force from 20 N right and 8 N left?
a for a net 12 N on 5 kg?
A 60 kg person in an elevator going up at 2 m/s² accel. Normal force with \(g = 9.8\)?

steps.title: Systems of Objects
steps.mastery: Draw linked diagrams for connected bodies.
steps.practice: Draw diagrams for 2 blocks of 3 kg and 2 kg joined by a string over a pulley, then find the acceleration.
steps.detail: Draw each block separately. The same tension acts on both, and both share the same acceleration size.
steps.proof: a = 2g/5 = 3.92 m/s^2 with the 2 kg block hanging.
steps.pitfall: Using 1 diagram for both and losing the tension.

problems.prompt: Masses 3 kg on a smooth table and 2 kg hanging. a with \(g = 9.8\)?
Tension in the string joining the 3 kg and 2 kg blocks?
Atwood machine with 5 kg and 3 kg. a with \(g = 9.8\)?

steps.title: Fluid Pressure at Depth
steps.mastery: Compute hydrostatic pressure using density, gravity, and depth.
steps.practice: Calculate the pressure at 5 m depth in freshwater (ρ = 1000 kg/m³).
steps.detail: Write down the formula P = ρ g h. Plug in the given density, the standard gravity 9.81 m/s², and the depth of 5 m. Multiply step-by-step, keeping units consistent (kg·m⁻¹·s⁻² = Pa). Verify the result is a positive pressure value.
steps.pitfall: Forgetting to include the gravitational constant 9.81 m/s².

problems.prompt: Find the water pressure at 12 m depth in fresh water, with \(g = 9.81\) m/s². Give it in kPa.
Seawater has ρ = 1025 kg/m³. Find the gauge pressure 30 m down in kPa, to 1 decimal place.
Adding 101.3 kPa of air pressure, what is the total pressure 10 m down in fresh water, in kPa?

steps.title: Hydrostatic Pressure Difference
steps.mastery: Find pressure differences between two depths in the same fluid.
steps.practice: Find the pressure difference between 2 m and 8 m depth in oil (ρ = 850 kg/m³).
steps.detail: Compute the depth difference Δh = 8 m − 2 m = 6 m. Apply ΔP = ρ g Δh with ρ = 850 kg/m³ and g = 9.81 m/s². Multiply sequentially: 850 × 9.81 = 8338.5, then × 6 = 50031 Pa. Record the answer with appropriate units.
steps.pitfall: Using the deeper pressure alone instead of the difference Δh.

problems.prompt: What is the pressure difference between 1 m and 4 m deep in fresh water, in Pa?
A diver goes from 5 m to 15 m in seawater (ρ = 1025 kg/m³). How much does the pressure rise, in kPa to 1 decimal place?
A mercury manometer (ρ = 13,600 kg/m³) shows a 0.25 m height difference. What pressure difference is that, in kPa to 2 decimal places?

steps.title: Pascal's Principle Force Transfer
steps.mastery: Use equal pressure to relate forces on pistons of different areas.
steps.practice: Determine the force required on a 2 cm² piston to lift a 50 kg load on a 200 cm² piston.
steps.detail: Convert areas to the same units (cm² is fine because they cancel). Compute the ratio A₁/A₂ = 2/200 = 0.01. Multiply the load weight m g = 50 × 9.81 = 490.5 N by the ratio: 0.01 × 490.5 = 4.905 N. This is the minimum input force.
steps.pitfall: Mixing up which area belongs to the input versus the output piston.

problems.prompt: A 1 cm² piston is pushed with 20 N and connects to a 100 cm² piston. What force comes out?
A car lift has a 10 cm² input piston and a 1,000 cm² output piston. What input force holds up a 12,000 N car?
On a 2 cm² and 200 cm² piston pair, the small piston moves down 40 cm. How far does the big one rise, in cm?
problems.hint: The volume of fluid pushed out of one cylinder goes into the other.

steps.title: Buoyant Force on a Sphere
steps.mastery: Calculate buoyant force using displaced fluid volume.
steps.practice: Compute the buoyant force on a steel sphere of radius 0.1 m fully submerged in water (ρ = 1000 kg/m³).
steps.detail: First find the sphere's volume: V = (4/3)πr³. With r = 0.1 m, r³ = 0.001 m³, so V ≈ 4.1888 × 10⁻³ m³. Then apply Archimedes' principle: F_b = ρ g V. Multiply 1000 kg/m³ × 9.81 m/s² = 9810 N/m³, then × 0.0041888 m³ ≈ 41.1 N. Record the force with units of newtons.
steps.pitfall: Using radius instead of volume or forgetting the 4/3 π factor.

problems.prompt: A block of volume 0.002 m³ sits fully under water. Find the buoyant force with \(g = 9.81\) m/s², to 2 decimal places.
A rock weighs 30 N in air and 18 N hanging in water. What is the buoyant force on it?
A wooden block with density 600 kg/m³ floats in water. What fraction of it is under the surface?

steps.title: Continuity in Varying Pipe Diameters
steps.mastery: Apply the continuity equation to relate speeds in different cross-sections.
steps.practice: A pipe narrows from 0.2 m to 0.1 m diameter. If water speed in the wide section is 2 m/s, find the speed in the narrow section.
steps.detail: Compute areas: A₁ = π(0.2)²/4 = 0.0314 m², A₂ = π(0.1)²/4 = 0.00785 m². Ratio A₁/A₂ = 4. Multiply by v₁ = 2 m/s to get v₂ = 8 m/s. Verify that the product A₂v₂ equals A₁v₁.
steps.proof: A₁v₁ = A₂v₂ → v₂ = (A₁/A₂) v₁ = (0.2²/0.1²) × 2 = 8 m/s.
steps.pitfall: Using diameters directly instead of areas (πd²/4).

problems.prompt: Water at 2 m/s in a hose of area 3 cm² goes into a nozzle of area 0.5 cm². How fast does it come out?
A pipe's diameter halves. By what factor does the water speed change?
Water flows at 3 m/s through a pipe of cross-section 0.05 m². What is the flow rate in cubic meters per second?

steps.title: Bernoulli Exit Speed
steps.mastery: Use Bernoulli's equation to find fluid speed from a height difference.
steps.practice: Water at 3 m height in a tank exits a nozzle at ground level. Compute the exit speed ignoring losses.
steps.detail: Write Bernoulli between the surface (point 1) and the nozzle exit (point 2): P₁ + ½ρv₁² + ρgh₁ = P₂ + ½ρv₂² + ρgh₂. With v₁≈0, h₁ = 3 m, h₂ = 0, and P₁ = P₂, solve for v₂: v₂ = √(2gh). Plug g = 9.81 m/s² and h = 3 m, calculate the square root to obtain ≈7.67 m/s.
steps.pitfall: Adding the atmospheric pressure term when it cancels out in the height-only case.

problems.prompt: Water drains through a hole 5 m below the surface of a tank. Find the exit speed to 2 decimal places, with \(g = 9.81\) m/s².
How far below the surface must a hole be for water to leave at 6 m/s? Give meters to 2 decimal places.
Air moves faster over the top of a wing than under it. Use Bernoulli to say what that does to the pressure on top.
problems.answer: Faster flow means lower pressure, so the pressure on top is lower and the wing is pushed up.

steps.title: Design a Simple Hydraulic Lift
steps.mastery: Combine Pascal's principle and force calculations to size a hydraulic system.
steps.practice: Sketch a lift with pistons of 5 cm² and 250 cm². If you press with 10 N on the small piston, calculate the maximum load it can lift.
steps.detail: Draw two cylinders sharing fluid. Label the small piston area A₁ = 5 cm² and the large piston area A₂ = 250 cm². Apply Pascal: F₂ = (A₂/A₁) F₁. Compute the ratio 250/5 = 50, then multiply by the input force 10 N to get F₂ = 500 N. Convert to mass by dividing by g if desired (≈51 kg). Ensure the sketch shows the fluid connection.
steps.pitfall: Forgetting to keep the area ratio dimensionless or mixing N with kg.

problems.prompt: A lift has 4 cm² and 400 cm² pistons. With 25 N pushing on the small one, what is the most it can hold up, in N?
What mass does that 2,500 N load correspond to, with \(g = 9.81\) m/s², to 1 decimal place?
A lift must raise 8,000 N with only 40 N of input on a 3 cm² piston. How big must the output piston be, in square centimeters?

steps.title: Identify Friction Types
steps.mastery: Distinguish static and kinetic friction and state their coefficient symbols and typical values.
steps.practice: Write down the static coefficient μs = 0.4 and kinetic coefficient μk = 0.3 for a rubber-on-concrete surface.
steps.detail: Look up a common material pair (e.g., rubber on concrete) in a textbook or reliable online table. Record the static coefficient as μs and the kinetic coefficient as μk, keeping the decimal format. Remember that static friction is usually larger than kinetic friction, so the numbers should reflect that relationship.
steps.proof: The symbols μs and μk appear correctly with the given numbers.
steps.pitfall: Confusing μs with μk or omitting the subscript, which leads to using the wrong coefficient in calculations.

problems.prompt: Rubber on concrete has \(\mu_{s} = 0.4\). What is the largest static friction on a 50 kg crate resting on it, with \(g = 9.8\) m/s²?
A 2 kg block rests on a rubber-on-concrete surface. Which coefficient, \(\mu_{s}\) or \(\mu_{k}\), is used to determine if it will start moving?
A student writes \(\mu_{s} = 0.3\) for rubber on concrete. Identify the mistake and give the correct static coefficient.
problems.hint: Recall typical values for rubber on concrete.

steps.title: Calculate Static Friction Force
steps.mastery: Compute the maximum static friction force that prevents motion for a given normal force.
steps.practice: Find the maximum static friction force for a 7 kg crate on a horizontal floor with μs = 0.5.
steps.detail: First calculate the normal force: N = m · g (mass times gravity, g ≈ 9.81 m/s²). Then multiply N by the static coefficient μs. Write each intermediate value on paper to avoid arithmetic errors. Verify the final number is reasonable compared with the weight of the crate.
steps.proof: Maximum static friction = μs · m · g = 0.5 × 7 × 9.81 ≈ 34.3 N.
steps.pitfall: Using the kinetic coefficient instead of the static one, which underestimates the force needed to start motion.

problems.prompt: What is the normal force on a 7 kg crate on a horizontal floor (g = 9.81 m/s²)?
Find the maximum static friction force for an 8 kg crate on a horizontal floor with \(\mu_{s} = 0.4\).
A 5 kg block rests on a 20° incline with \(\mu_{s} = 0.5\). What is the maximum static friction force parallel to the surface?
problems.hint: Find normal force using mg \(\cos \theta\) first.

steps.title: Determine Kinetic Friction Force
steps.mastery: Calculate the kinetic friction force acting on an object moving at constant speed.
steps.practice: Compute the kinetic friction force on a 4 kg sled sliding on ice with μk = 0.08.
steps.detail: Use the same normal-force formula as for static friction. Multiply by μk, not μs. Record the calculation steps: N = 4 × 9.81 = 39.24 N, then Fk = 0.08 × 39.24 ≈ 3.1 N. Check that the kinetic force is smaller than the static maximum you computed earlier for a similar mass.
steps.proof: Kinetic friction = μk · m · g = 0.08 × 4 × 9.81 ≈ 3.1 N.
steps.pitfall: Forgetting that the normal force on a horizontal surface equals mg, leading to an incorrect denominator.

problems.prompt: A 20 kg sled slides on ice with \(\mu_{k} = 0.08\). What is the friction force to 1 decimal place, with \(g = 9.8\) m/s²?
Compute the kinetic friction force on a 6 kg sled sliding on ice with \(\mu_{k} = 0.05\).
A 4 kg sled slides on a level surface with \(\mu_{k} = 0.08\) while a 5 N push acts forward. What is the net force to 1 decimal place, with \(g = 9.8\) m/s²?
problems.answer: About 1.9 N forward, since friction is \(0.08 \times 4 \times 9.8 = 3.1\) N.
problems.hint: Subtract kinetic friction from the applied force.

steps.title: Analyze Circular Motion without Friction
steps.mastery: Identify the centripetal acceleration required for uniform circular motion and the net radial force needed.
steps.practice: Calculate the centripetal acceleration for a 2 kg mass moving at 3 m/s around a circle of radius 1.5 m.
steps.detail: Write the formula a_c = v² / r. Substitute v = 3 m/s and r = 1.5 m, then square the speed before dividing. Keep units consistent (meters and seconds). After finding a_c, you may later multiply by mass to get the required net radial force.
steps.pitfall: Using the wrong radius or speed in the v²/r formula, which flips the magnitude of the acceleration.

problems.prompt: What is the centripetal acceleration of an object moving at 2 m/s in a circle of radius 4 m?
Calculate the centripetal acceleration for a 2 kg mass moving at 3 m/s around a circle of radius 1.5 m.
A 0.5 kg object moves in a circle of radius 0.8 m at 4 rad/s. Give the centripetal force in N, then the acceleration in m/s².
problems.hint: Use \(a = \omega^{2} r\).

steps.title: Combine Friction and Centripetal Force
steps.mastery: Determine whether static friction can supply the required centripetal force for a car turning on a flat road.
steps.practice: A 1500 kg car travels at 20 m/s around a curve of radius 50 m. With μs = 0.7, decide if the car can negotiate the turn without skidding.
steps.detail: First compute the needed centripetal force using m v² / r. Then find the maximum static friction using μs · m · g. Compare the two numbers: if the frictional limit is lower, the tires cannot provide enough grip. Write each number on a separate line to keep the comparison clear.
steps.proof: Required centripetal force = m v² / r = 1500 × 400 / 50 = 12 000 N. Maximum static friction = μs · m · g = 0.7 × 1500 × 9.81 ≈ 10 300 N. Since 12 000 N > 10 300 N, the car will skid.
steps.pitfall: Comparing the kinetic friction force instead of the static one, which would incorrectly suggest the car can turn safely.

problems.prompt: What maximum static friction can a 1500 kg car get on a flat road with \(\mu_{s} = 0.7\) and \(g = 9.8\) m/s²? Round to the nearest 100 N.
A 1500 kg car takes a curve of radius 50 m at 20 m/s with \(\mu_{s} = 0.7\). Can it make the turn without skidding?
problems.answer: No. It needs 12,000 N of friction, and the most it can get is about 10,300 N.

problems.prompt: If the road is banked at 10° and \(\mu_{s} = 0.7\), can the same 1500 kg car negotiate the 20 m/s turn on a radius of 50 m without skidding? (Assume \(g = 9.81\) m/s².).
problems.answer: Yes; banking supplies ~2590 N, friction needs ~9410 N which is below the 10 300 N limit.
problems.hint: Resolve forces into radial components.

steps.title: Apply to Real-World Problems
steps.mastery: Set up and solve a friction-in-circular-motion problem from scratch, choosing appropriate coefficients and checking the result.
steps.practice: Design a banked turn for a roller coaster car of mass 800 kg traveling at 12 m/s on a curve of radius 30 m, assuming no reliance on friction (μ = 0). Calculate the required banking angle θ.
steps.detail: When friction is absent, the normal force provides the necessary radial component. Use tan θ = v²/(r g). Compute v² = 144, r g = 30 × 9.81 ≈ 294.3, then divide to get 0.49. Take the arctangent (use a calculator) and convert to degrees. Record the angle to the nearest whole degree.
steps.pitfall: Using the friction formula when μ = 0, or forgetting to convert the angle from radians to degrees when reporting the answer.

problems.prompt: For a car moving at 12 m/s on a curve of radius 30 m, what is the value of v² / (r g)?
