Design a banked turn for a roller-coaster car of mass 800 kg traveling at 12 m/s on a curve of radius 30 m, assuming no friction \((\mu = 0)\). What banking angle \(\theta\) (in degrees) is required?
problems.hint: Use \(\tan \theta\) = v² / (r g).

problems.prompt: If the same roller-coaster car (800 kg, 12 m/s, \(r = 30\) m) were on a banked turn of 26° but the surface had a coefficient of friction \(\mu = 0.2\), what is the maximum speed the car could travel without slipping down the bank? (Give the speed in m/s, rounded to two significant figures.).
problems.hint: Use the banking-with-friction formula: v_max = √[r g (tanθ + μ) / (1 - μ tanθ)].

steps.title: Newton Law of Gravitation
steps.mastery: Compute gravity between 2 masses.
steps.practice: Compute the force between Earth, 6.0 x 10^24 kg, and a 70 kg person at radius 6.4 x 10^6 m with G = 6.67 x 10^-11.
steps.detail: F = G m1 m2 / r^2. The same law that holds you on the ground also holds the Moon in its orbit.
steps.proof: About 684 N, close to 70 x 9.8.
steps.pitfall: Measuring r from the surface instead of the center.

problems.prompt: Double the distance. Force changes by what factor?
Double 1 mass. Force changes by what factor?
Triple the distance from 1 R to 3 R. Factor?

steps.title: Field Strength g
steps.mastery: Find g at different heights and on other planets.
steps.practice: Compute g on the surface of Mars, mass 6.4 x 10^23 kg and radius 3.4 x 10^6 m.
steps.detail: g = GM/r^2. It depends on the planet mass and on how far you are from its center.
steps.proof: About 3.7 m/s^2.
steps.pitfall: Using Earth g everywhere.

problems.prompt: g at 2 Earth radii from the center, with 9.8 at the surface?
Weight of a 50 kg person where \(g = 3.7\)?
Does mass change from 50 kg on the Moon?

steps.title: Circular Orbits
steps.mastery: Set gravity equal to the centripetal force.
steps.practice: Find the orbital speed at 7.0 x 10^6 m from Earth center, using GM = 4.0 x 10^14.
steps.detail: For a circle, GMm/r^2 = mv^2/r, so v = sqrt(GM/r). The satellite mass cancels out completely.
steps.proof: About 7.6 km/s.
steps.pitfall: Thinking a heavier satellite needs to go faster.

problems.prompt: \(v = \sqrt{\frac{GM}{r}}\) with GM = \(4 \times 10^{14}\) and \(r = 1 \times 10^{7}\) m. What is v in km/s, to 1 decimal place?
Does the orbital speed depend on a 500 kg vs 1000 kg satellite?
Higher orbit, r from 7 to \(14 \times 10^{6}\) m. Faster or slower?

steps.title: Kepler Laws
steps.mastery: Use T^2 proportional to r^3.
steps.practice: Use Kepler third law to find the period of a planet at 4 AU from the Sun.
steps.detail: Planets farther out take longer to go around. Measured in years and AU, the rule for anything circling the Sun is simply T^2 = r^3.
steps.proof: T = 8 years.
steps.pitfall: Using T proportional to r.

problems.prompt: Period at 9 AU?
Mars at 1.52 AU. Period?
Where in an elliptical orbit around the Sun is a planet fastest?

steps.title: Escape and Energy
steps.mastery: Use gravitational potential energy to find escape speed.
steps.practice: Compute escape speed from Earth with GM = 4.0 x 10^14 and R = 6.4 x 10^6 m.
steps.detail: Gravitational PE is -GMm/r. To escape, kinetic energy must reach zero total energy, so v = sqrt(2GM/R).
steps.proof: About 11.2 km/s.
steps.pitfall: Using mgh for heights comparable to the radius.

problems.prompt: Escape speed is 11.2 km/s where orbital speed is 7.9 km/s. Their ratio is close to the square root of what whole number?
problems.answer: 2. The ratio is about 1.41, which is \(\sqrt{2}\).

problems.prompt: Sign of GPE far below infinity, at \(r = 2R\)?
Escape speed with \(\frac{2GM}{R} = 1.0 \times 10^{8}\)?

steps.title: First Law
steps.mastery: Use delta U = Q - W for a gas.
steps.practice: Find the change in internal energy when a gas absorbs 500 J and does 200 J of work.
steps.detail: Energy in as heat raises internal energy and work done by the gas lowers it. It is energy conservation for heat.
steps.proof: delta U = 300 J.
steps.pitfall: Mixing up the sign of work done by vs on the gas.

problems.prompt: \(Q = 100\) J in, \(W = 100\) J by gas. delta U?
A gas is compressed with 50 J of work and loses 20 J of heat. What is \(\Delta U\)?

steps.title: Work on PV Diagrams
steps.mastery: Find work as the area under a pressure volume curve.
steps.practice: Find the work done by a gas expanding from 0.01 to 0.03 m^3 at 200,000 Pa.
steps.detail: At constant pressure W = P delta V. On a PV diagram the work is the area under the path.
steps.pitfall: Forgetting that a closed loop does net work equal to its area.

problems.prompt: W at 100,000 Pa from 1 to 3 L?
Work in a constant volume process at \(2 \times 10^{5}\) Pa?
Area of a rectangle loop 100 kPa tall and 0.002 m³ wide?

steps.title: Heat Engines
steps.mastery: Compute efficiency of an engine.
steps.practice: Find the efficiency of an engine taking 1000 J of heat and expelling 700 J.
steps.detail: Efficiency = W/Qh = 1 - Qc/Qh. Some heat must always be dumped, so no engine reaches 100%.
steps.pitfall: Forgetting the heat expelled.

problems.prompt: Qh = 500 J, \(W = 150\) J. Efficiency?
Efficiency 25% and Qh = 800 J. Work?
Heat dumped by the 25% engine taking in 800 J?

steps.title: Carnot Limit
steps.mastery: Find the maximum efficiency between 2 temperatures.
steps.practice: Compute the Carnot efficiency between 600 K and 300 K, and between 500 degrees C and 20 degrees C.
steps.detail: No engine beats 1 - Tc/Th with temperatures in kelvin. Bigger temperature gaps allow higher limits.
steps.proof: 50% and about 62%.
steps.pitfall: Using Celsius in the Carnot formula.

problems.prompt: Carnot limit for 400 K and 300 K?
Can a real engine between 600 and 300 K reach 55%?
Th = 1000 K, limit 70%. Tc?

steps.title: Entropy
steps.mastery: Estimate entropy changes and use the second law.
steps.practice: Compute the entropy change when 3340 J melts ice at 273 K and when 1000 J flows from 400 K to 300 K.
steps.detail: delta S = Q/T at constant temperature. Heat flowing hot to cold always raises total entropy.
steps.proof: 12.2 J/K, and +0.83 J/K total.
steps.pitfall: Thinking entropy can never decrease anywhere.

problems.prompt: delta S for 600 J at 300 K?
Total delta S for 1200 J from 600 K to 300 K?
Can a fridge at 5 degrees C lower its inside entropy?
problems.answer: Yes, by raising it more outside.

steps.title: Magnetic Fields
steps.mastery: Sketch fields around magnets and currents.
steps.practice: Sketch the field of a bar magnet and of a long straight wire carrying 5 A, with directions.
steps.detail: Field lines run from north to south outside a magnet. Around a wire they form circles given by the right hand grip rule.
steps.proof: 2 sketches with arrows.
steps.pitfall: Drawing straight lines out from a wire.

problems.prompt: Unit of magnetic field, named after 1 person?
Field around a wire: lines or circles, for 5 A?
Like poles of 2 magnets attract or repel?

steps.title: Force on a Wire
steps.mastery: Use F = BIL for a current in a field.
steps.practice: Find the force on a 0.2 m wire carrying 3 A at right angles to a 0.5 T field.
steps.detail: A current in a field feels a push across both. Fleming left hand rule gives the direction.
steps.pitfall: Using F = BIL when the wire is parallel to the field.

problems.prompt: Force when the wire runs parallel to a 1 T field?
Double the current from 3 to 6 A. Force factor?

steps.title: Charges in Fields
steps.mastery: Find the radius of a charge circling in a magnetic field.
steps.practice: Find the radius for a proton, 1.67 x 10^-27 kg, moving at 2 x 10^6 m/s in a 0.5 T field.
steps.detail: F = qvB acts as a centripetal force, so r = mv/(qB). Faster or heavier particles curve less.
steps.proof: About 0.042 m.
steps.pitfall: Expecting a magnetic force to speed a charge up.

problems.prompt: Does a magnetic field do work on a moving charge at \(10^{5}\) m/s?
Force on \(1.6 \times 10^{-19}\) C at \(10^{6}\) m/s in 1 T?
Double B from 0.5 to 1 T. Radius factor?

steps.title: Induction
steps.mastery: Use Faraday law of induction.
steps.practice: Find the emf in a 100 turn coil when the flux drops from 0.02 to 0 Wb in 0.1 s.
steps.detail: A changing flux induces an emf equal to N times the rate of change. Lenz law says it opposes the change.
steps.pitfall: Expecting an emf from a steady field.

problems.prompt: Flux 0.5 T through 0.02 m². Phi?
Rod 0.5 m long moving at 4 m/s in 0.2 T. emf?
Magnet held still inside 1 coil. emf?

steps.title: Motors, Generators and Transformers
steps.mastery: Explain motors and generators and use the transformer ratio.
steps.practice: Find the secondary voltage of a transformer with 100 primary and 2000 secondary turns on 12 V AC.
steps.detail: Motors turn current into motion and generators turn motion into current. Transformers scale voltage by the turns ratio.
steps.pitfall: Using a transformer on DC.

problems.prompt: An ideal transformer takes in 10 W and steps down to 12 V. What current comes out, to 2 decimal places?
problems.answer: About 0.83 A, since 10 W divided by 12 V is 0.83 A. An ideal transformer loses no power.

problems.prompt: Why do power lines use 400,000 V?
problems.answer: Lower current means less heat lost.

steps.title: Define Momentum
steps.mastery: State the definition of momentum as the product of mass and velocity and compute it for a given object.
steps.practice: Write the momentum of a 3 kg cart moving at 4 m/s.
steps.detail: Take a piece of paper and write down the formula p = m·v. Identify the mass (3 kg) and the velocity (4 m/s) of the cart. Multiply the numbers, then write the result with the proper unit. Double-check that you have not swapped the numbers or omitted the unit.
steps.proof: p = 3 kg × 4 m/s = 12 kg·m/s.
steps.pitfall: Forgetting to include the correct units (kg·m/s) or mixing up mass and velocity.

problems.prompt: What is the momentum of a 2 kg object moving at 3 m/s?
Calculate the momentum of a 5 kg cart traveling at 7 m/s.
A 4 kg sled moves west at 5 m/s. What is its momentum (include direction)?
problems.hint: Treat direction as part of the answer.

steps.title: Calculate Momentum Change
steps.mastery: Determine the change in momentum when an object's speed varies, using Δp = m·Δv.
steps.practice: Compute the change in momentum when a 2 kg ball slows from 6 m/s to 2 m/s.
steps.detail: Write the initial momentum p_i = m·v_i and the final momentum p_f = m·v_f. Subtract p_i from p_f to get Δp. Remember that a decrease in speed gives a negative Δp, indicating momentum loss. Verify the arithmetic and sign before finalising the answer.
steps.proof: Δp = 2 kg × (2 m/s - 6 m/s) = 2 kg × (-4 m/s) = -8 kg·m/s.
steps.pitfall: Using final minus initial speed incorrectly, leading to a sign error.

problems.prompt: What is the change in momentum of a 1 kg ball that speeds up from 2 m/s to 5 m/s?
A 3 kg crate slows from 8 m/s to 3 m/s. Find \(\Delta p\).
A 2 kg puck goes from 4 m/s east to 2 m/s west. Taking east as positive, what is \(\Delta p\) in kg·m/s?
problems.hint: Remember velocity sign.

steps.title: Impulse and Average Force
steps.mastery: Apply the impulse-momentum theorem (Impulse = Δp) to find average force over a time interval.
steps.practice: Find the average force on a 0.5 kg puck that speeds up from 0 m/s to 3 m/s in 0.2 s.
steps.detail: First calculate the change in momentum using the mass and the velocity change. Then divide that Δp by the time interval (0.2 s) to obtain the average force. Write each step clearly, keep track of units, and confirm that the force magnitude makes sense for a small puck.
steps.proof: Δp = 0.5 kg × 3 m/s = 1.5 kg·m/s;  F_avg = Δp / Δt = 1.5 kg·m/s ÷ 0.2 s = 7.5 N.
steps.pitfall: Dividing by the wrong time interval or forgetting to convert units, which gives an incorrect force.

problems.prompt: What impulse is delivered to a 1 kg ball that speeds up from 0 m/s to 2 m/s?
Find the average force on a 0.8 kg object that changes velocity from 1 m/s to 4 m/s in 0.5 s.
A 0.3 kg puck experiences a force that changes its momentum by -0.9 kg·m/s over 0.3 s. What is the average force?
problems.hint: Impulse = \(\Delta p\).

steps.title: Elastic Collision Conservation
steps.mastery: Use conservation of momentum to solve for final speeds in a perfectly elastic collision.
steps.practice: A 1 kg cart moving at 4 m/s collides elastically with a 2 kg cart at rest. Find the 1 kg cart's speed after the collision.
steps.detail: Write the momentum conservation equation and the kinetic-energy conservation equation for an elastic collision. Solve the two equations simultaneously, or use the shortcut formula for v1'. Keep sign conventions consistent: a negative result means the cart reverses direction. Check the answer by confirming total kinetic energy is unchanged.
steps.proof: With v1' = (m1 - m2)/(m1 + m2) · v1, you get v1' = (1 - 2)/(1 + 2) · 4 m/s = -1.33 m/s, so the 1 kg cart bounces back at 1.33 m/s.
steps.pitfall: Applying the inelastic-collision formula instead of the elastic one, which yields the wrong speed.

problems.prompt: What is the speed of the 2 kg cart after it elastically collides with a 1 kg cart at rest, given the 2 kg cart was moving at 3 m/s?
A 1 kg cart at 5 m/s collides elastically with a 3 kg cart at rest. What is the 1 kg cart's final velocity?
Two carts collide elastically: \(m_{1} = 2\) kg moving at 4 m/s, \(m_{2} = 3\) kg moving at -1 m/s (opposite direction). What is the final velocity of the 2 kg cart?
problems.hint: Use the full elastic-collision formula: \(v_{1}' = \frac{m_{1} - m_{2}}{m_{1} + m_{2}} \cdot v_{1} + \frac{2m_{2}}{m_{1} + m_{2}} \cdot v_{2}\).

steps.title: Inelastic Collision Outcome
steps.mastery: Determine the common final velocity after a perfectly inelastic collision where objects stick together.
steps.practice: Calculate the speed after a 0.8 kg clay ball moving at 5 m/s sticks to a 0.2 kg block initially at rest.
steps.detail: Write the total initial momentum as the sum of each object's momentum. Since the block is at rest, its momentum term is zero but still write it for completeness. Divide the total momentum by the combined mass to get the final velocity. Verify that the result is between the initial speeds, as expected for an inelastic stick-together collision.
steps.pitfall: Adding the masses but forgetting to include the momentum of the stationary object (which is zero, but the term must be present).

problems.prompt: What is the final speed when a 0.5 kg ball moving at 4 m/s sticks to a 0.5 kg block initially at rest?
A 0.7 kg object moving at 6 m/s collides inelastically with a 0.3 kg object at rest and they stick together. What is their common speed after the collision?
A 0.9 kg cart moving at 5 m/s collides and sticks to a 0.1 kg cart moving opposite at 2 m/s. What is the final velocity (including direction) of the combined mass?
problems.hint: Include the momentum of the moving 0.1 kg cart (negative direction) before dividing by the total mass.

steps.title: Momentum Transfer in a Kick
steps.mastery: Apply conservation of momentum to a real-world interaction, solving for the recoil speed of the kicker.
steps.practice: A 0.2 kg soccer ball is kicked to 12 m/s. If the foot (1 kg) was initially at rest, calculate the foot's speed right after the kick assuming an isolated system.
steps.detail: Set the total initial momentum to zero because both foot and ball start at rest. After the kick, write the momentum of the ball (0.2 kg·12 m/s) and the unknown foot momentum (1 kg·v_foot). Solve for v_foot, remembering that the foot's velocity is opposite in direction to the ball's, hence the negative sign. Confirm the magnitude is reasonable for a human foot recoil.
steps.proof: From m_ball · v_ball + m_foot · v_foot = 0, v_foot = -(0.2 kg · 12 m/s)/1 kg = -2.4 m/s, so the foot moves back at 2.4 m/s.
steps.pitfall: Treating the foot as stationary after the kick or forgetting the opposite direction sign, which gives a positive speed for the foot.

problems.prompt: What is the momentum of a 0.2 kg soccer ball moving at 12 m/s?
A 0.2 kg soccer ball is kicked to 12 m/s by a 1 kg foot that was at rest. Treating them as an isolated system, what is the foot's velocity right after?
A 0.5 kg ball is kicked to 8 m/s by a 2 kg foot that was initially at rest. Using conservation of momentum, calculate the foot's recoil speed and state its direction relative to the ball.
problems.hint: Set total momentum to zero and solve for the foot's velocity.

steps.title: Define Position and Displacement
steps.mastery: State the difference between position and displacement and compute displacement on a straight line.
steps.practice: Write the displacement for an object that moves from x = 2 m to x = 9 m on a straight line.
steps.detail: Mark the initial and final positions on a number line. Subtract the initial coordinate from the final coordinate, keeping the sign. Record the result as the vector displacement, not the summed path length.
steps.proof: Displacement = 9 m − 2 m = 7 m.
steps.pitfall: Confusing displacement with total distance traveled when the path changes direction.

problems.prompt: Write the displacement for an object that moves from \(x = 5\) m to \(x = 8\) m on a straight line.
Write the displacement for an object that moves from \(x = - 3\) m to \(x = 4\) m on a straight line.
An object moves from \(x = 2\) m to \(x = 5\) m, then back to \(x = 1\) m on the same line. What is its net displacement?
problems.hint: Displacement = final position, initial position.

steps.title: Calculate Average Velocity
steps.mastery: Find average velocity by dividing total displacement by elapsed time.
steps.practice: Compute the average velocity of the object that moved 7 m in 2 s.
steps.detail: Take the displacement you just calculated and the time interval. Divide displacement by time, preserving the sign to indicate direction. Write the answer with units of meters per second.
steps.proof: Average velocity = 7 m / 2 s = 3.5 m/s.
steps.pitfall: Using total distance instead of displacement when the motion reverses.

problems.prompt: Compute the average velocity of an object that moves 4 m in 2 s.
Compute the average velocity of an object that has a displacement of 10 m over 5 s.
An object travels 6 m forward then 2 m backward in a total time of 4 s. What is its average velocity?
problems.hint: Use net displacement (forward minus backward) divided by total time.

steps.title: Determine Constant Acceleration
steps.mastery: Calculate constant acceleration as the change in velocity divided by the time interval.
steps.practice: Find the acceleration of a car that speeds up from 0 m/s to 20 m/s in 4 s.
steps.detail: Record the initial and final velocities. Subtract the initial velocity from the final velocity, then divide by the elapsed time. Keep the units as meters per second squared.
steps.pitfall: Treating acceleration as a speed rather than a rate of change of velocity.

problems.prompt: Find the acceleration of a car that speeds up from 0 m/s to 10 m/s in 2 s.
Find the acceleration of a vehicle that speeds up from 5 m/s to 25 m/s in 5 s.
A car decelerates from 30 m/s to 10 m/s in 4 s. What is its acceleration?
problems.hint: Acceleration = (final velocity, initial velocity) / time.

steps.title: Apply SUVAT Equation
steps.mastery: Use the equation x = x₀ + v₀t + ½at² to find position under constant acceleration.
steps.practice: Using x = x₀ + v₀t + ½at², calculate the final position after 3 s for an object starting at x₀ = 5 m, v₀ = 2 m/s, a = 4 m/s².
steps.detail: Plug the given numbers into the formula step by step: multiply v₀ by t, compute a·t², halve it, then add all terms to x₀. Verify each arithmetic step before writing the final position.
steps.pitfall: Omitting the ½ factor on the acceleration term, which halves the contribution of the a t² part.

problems.prompt: Find the position after 2 s for \(x_{0} = 0\) m, \(v_{0} = 3\) m/s and \(a = 2\) m/s².
Find the position after 6 s for \(x_{0} = 10\) m, \(v_{0} = - 4\) m/s and \(a = 1\) m/s².
A stone drops from rest at a height of 45 m. Using \(g = 10\) m/s², how long does it take to reach the ground?

steps.title: Solve Multi-Stage Motion Problem
steps.mastery: Combine successive constant-acceleration segments to obtain total displacement.
steps.practice: Find the total displacement of an object that starts from rest, accelerates at 2 m/s² for 5 s, then at -3 m/s² for 4 s.
steps.detail: Compute the distance covered in the first interval using s = ½at². Find the velocity at the end of that interval (v = at) and use it as the initial velocity for the second interval. Apply s = v₀t + ½at² for the second part, then add the two distances.
steps.proof: First stage: s₁ = ½ · 2 · 5² = 25 m and v₁ = 10 m/s. Second stage: s₂ = 10 · 4 + ½ · (-3) · 4² = 40 - 24 = 16 m. Total displacement = 41 m.
steps.pitfall: Resetting the velocity to zero before the second stage instead of carrying over the final velocity from the first stage.

problems.prompt: An object starts from rest and accelerates at 1.5 m/s² for 3 s. What is its displacement?
An object moves with a constant acceleration of -1 m/s² for 5 s, starting with a velocity of 8 m/s. What is its displacement?
An object starts from rest, accelerates at 2 m/s² for 3 s, then at -4 m/s² for 2 s. Find its total displacement.
problems.hint: First find the velocity after the first stage and use it as the initial velocity for the second stage.

problems.prompt: For the motion in the last problem, a student treats the second stage as starting from rest and gets 9 m + \(0.5 \times (-4) \times 2^{2} = 1\) m. What did they get wrong?
problems.answer: The second stage starts at 6 m/s, not from rest, so that velocity has to be carried in. Dropping it leaves out the distance covered by the motion already under way.
problems.hint: Remember the velocity at the end of the first stage is not zero.

steps.title: Identify Net Force on a Box
steps.mastery: Determine the resultant force acting on an object by vector addition of all applied forces.
steps.practice: Calculate the net force on a 5 kg box pushed with 12 N east and pulled with 8 N west.
steps.detail: Place the box on a frictionless surface. Write each force as a signed number along the east‑west axis (east positive, west negative). Add the numbers to get the net force. Verify the sign tells you the direction. This step builds the habit of treating forces as vectors before using Newton's laws.
steps.proof: 12 N − 8 N = 4 N east, which is the correct vector sum.
steps.pitfall: Adding magnitudes without keeping track of direction, especially when forces oppose each other.

problems.prompt: What is the net force on a 2 kg box pushed with 5 N east?
Calculate the net force on a 3 kg box acted on by 10 N north and 4 N south.
A 4 kg crate is pulled 7 N north and simultaneously pushed 9 N south. What is the magnitude and direction of the net force?
problems.hint: Treat opposite directions as opposite signs when adding the forces.

steps.title: Apply Newton's First Law
steps.mastery: Predict that an object with zero net force maintains its current state of motion.
steps.practice: State what happens to a 2 kg puck sliding at 3 m/s on a frictionless ice surface when no horizontal forces act on it.
steps.detail: Recall that the first law (inertia) says motion does not change without net force. Write the initial velocity vector, confirm that all horizontal forces sum to zero, and then state that the velocity remains unchanged for any amount of time. Use the result from step 1 to verify the net force is indeed zero.
steps.proof: The puck continues at 3 m/s in the same direction because the net force is zero.
steps.pitfall: Assuming the object will eventually stop even when friction is absent.

problems.prompt: A 1 kg puck slides at 2 m/s on a frictionless ice surface with no horizontal forces acting. What happens to its motion?
problems.answer: It continues at 2 m/s in the same direction.

problems.prompt: A 2 kg puck slides at 3 m/s on frictionless ice. Does it need a forward force to keep moving?
problems.answer: No. With no net force it keeps its 3 m/s and its direction.

problems.prompt: A 0.5 kg cart moves at 4 m/s on a frictionless track and then travels through a region with no forces for 5 s. What is its speed after this interval?
problems.hint: Use Newton's first law; speed is unchanged when net force is zero.

steps.title: Use Newton's Second Law for Acceleration
steps.mastery: Calculate an object's acceleration by dividing the net force by its mass (F = ma).
steps.practice: Find the acceleration of a 3 kg cart when a net horizontal force of 15 N acts on it.
steps.detail: Take the net force from step 1 (or any given value). Write the formula a = F/m, plug in the numbers, and solve for a. Double‑check that the force is in newtons and mass in kilograms so the result is in meters per second squared. Record the acceleration vector with the same direction as the net force.
steps.proof: a = F/m = 15 N / 3 kg = 5 m/s², which matches the calculation.
steps.pitfall: Confusing mass with weight or forgetting to keep units consistent.

problems.prompt: Find the acceleration of a 2 kg object acted on by a net force of 6 N east.
Find the acceleration of a 3 kg cart when a net horizontal force of 15 N acts on it.
problems.answer: 5 m/s² in the direction of the force.

problems.prompt: A 10 kg sled is pulled with 25 N north and 15 N south. What is its acceleration?
problems.hint: Subtract opposing forces before applying F=ma.

steps.title: Demonstrate Newton's Third Law Pairs
steps.mastery: Identify action‑reaction force pairs and state that they act on different bodies.
steps.practice: When a 10 N hand pushes a wall, write the force the wall exerts on the hand.
steps.detail: Label the hand as object A and the wall as object B. The force from A on B is 10 N forward; the reaction is a 10 N force from B on A backward. Emphasize that the two forces never cancel because they act on different bodies. Sketch a free‑body diagram for each object to visualize the pair.
steps.proof: The wall exerts a 10 N force on the hand opposite to the hand's push, satisfying the third law.
steps.pitfall: Applying the reaction force to the same object that experiences the action force.

problems.prompt: A hand pushes a wall with 5 N. What force does the wall exert on the hand?
A book rests on a table. The Earth exerts a 9.8 N downward force on the book. What force does the book exert on the Earth?
A person of 70 kg pushes a 100 kg crate with a horizontal force of 120 N. State the reaction force and the object on which it acts.
problems.answer: 120 N opposite direction acting on the person.
problems.hint: Action-reaction forces act on different bodies.

steps.title: Solve a Two‑Body Interaction Problem
steps.mastery: Combine all three Newtonian laws to predict motion of interacting objects without assistance.
steps.practice: Two ice skaters, each 60 kg, push off each other with a 30 N force for 2 s. Calculate each skater's final speed.
steps.detail: Use the third law to note each skater experiences a 30 N force in opposite directions. Apply the second law via impulse: Δp = F·t, then Δv = Δp/m. Since initial speeds are zero, the final speed equals Δv. Verify that momentum is conserved (total momentum remains zero). Write the answer as 1 m/s east for skater 1 and 1 m/s west for skater 2.
steps.proof: Impulse = F·t = 30 N·2 s = 60 Ns; Δv = Impulse/m = 60 Ns / 60 kg = 1 m/s for each skater, moving in opposite directions.
steps.pitfall: Adding the forces together instead of treating them as separate action‑reaction pairs on each skater.

problems.prompt: Two 50 kg skaters push off each other with a 20 N force for 1 s. What is the final speed of each skater?
Two 60 kg ice skaters push off each other with a 30 N force for 2 s. Calculate each skater's final speed.
Two astronauts of 80 kg and 120 kg push apart with an average force of 20 N for 3 s. Give the 80 kg astronaut's final speed, then the 120 kg one's.
problems.answer: 0.75 m/s for the 80 kg astronaut and 0.5 m/s for the 120 kg astronaut, opposite directions.
problems.hint: Use the average force to compute impulse, then divide by each mass.

steps.title: Reflection
steps.mastery: Use the law of reflection and plane mirrors.
steps.practice: Draw rays for a light hitting a mirror at 35 degrees to the normal, and locate the image of an object 2 m in front.
steps.detail: The angle of reflection equals the angle of incidence. A plane mirror image sits as far behind as the object is in front.
steps.proof: Reflected at 35 degrees and the image 2 m behind.
steps.pitfall: Measuring angles from the mirror surface instead of the normal.

problems.prompt: Light hits a mirror at 40 degrees from the normal. What angle does the reflected ray make with the mirror's surface?
problems.answer: 50 degrees. The reflected ray is 40 degrees from the normal, and \(90 - 40 = 50\).

problems.prompt: Object 3 m in front of a mirror. Distance to its image?
Mirror height needed to see your full 1.8 m height?

steps.title: Refraction and Snell Law
steps.mastery: Use n1 sin theta1 = n2 sin theta2.
steps.practice: Find the angle in glass, n = 1.5, for light entering from air at 30 degrees.
steps.detail: Light slows in a denser medium and bends toward the normal. Snell law gives the new angle.
steps.proof: sin theta = 0.333, about 19.5 degrees.
steps.pitfall: Bending the ray away from the normal entering glass.

problems.prompt: Speed of light in glass with \(n = 1.5\)?
Light from water, \(n = 1.33\), into air. Toward or away from the normal?
Critical angle for glass with \(n = 1.5\) into air?

steps.title: Lenses
steps.mastery: Use the thin lens equation.
steps.practice: Find the image distance and magnification for an object 30 cm from a converging lens of focal length 10 cm.
steps.detail: 1/f = 1/do + 1/di. A positive di means a real image on the far side, and m = -di/do gives its size.
steps.proof: di = 15 cm and m = -0.5.
steps.pitfall: Mixing up the sign of the focal length for a diverging lens.

problems.prompt: Object at 20 cm, \(f = 10\) cm. di?
Object at 5 cm, \(f = 10\) cm. di?
Power of a lens with \(f = 0.5\) m?

steps.title: Dispersion and Color
steps.mastery: Explain how a prism splits white light.
steps.practice: Explain in 3 sentences why a prism makes a spectrum and why red bends less than violet.
steps.detail: The refractive index depends on wavelength. Violet at about 400 nm slows and bends more than red at about 700 nm.
steps.proof: 3 sentences on dispersion.
steps.pitfall: Thinking the prism adds color to white light.

problems.prompt: Wavelength of red light, roughly, in nm from 1 to 1000?
Which bends more in glass, 400 nm or 700 nm light?
A rainbow forms from dispersion in what, out of 3 options: dust, rain, wind?

steps.title: Interference and Diffraction
steps.mastery: Use the double slit to measure wavelength.
steps.practice: Find the wavelength when slits 0.1 mm apart give fringes 5 mm apart on a screen 1 m away.
steps.detail: Light through 2 slits forms bright and dark fringes. Fringe spacing = lambda L/d.
steps.proof: lambda = 500 nm.
steps.pitfall: Using the slit width instead of the slit spacing.

problems.prompt: \(\lambda = 600\) nm, \(d = 0.2\) mm, \(L = 2\) m. Fringe spacing?
Halve d from 0.2 to 0.1 mm. Fringes get wider or narrower?
Who did the double slit experiment around 1801?

steps.title: Photons
steps.mastery: Compute photon energy with E = hf.
steps.practice: Find the energy of a 500 nm photon with h = 6.63 x 10^-34 and c = 3 x 10^8.
steps.detail: Light comes in lumps of energy hf = hc/lambda. Shorter wavelengths mean more energy per photon.
steps.proof: About 4.0 x 10^-19 J, about 2.5 eV.
steps.pitfall: Using the wavelength in nm without converting to m.

problems.prompt: Energy of a photon at \(10^{15}\) Hz?
More energy per photon: 400 nm or 700 nm?
Photons per second from a 1 W beam of \(4 \times 10^{-19}\) J photons?

steps.title: Photoelectric Effect
steps.mastery: Use KE max = hf - phi for emitted electrons.
steps.practice: Find the max KE of electrons from a metal with work function 2.0 eV under 3.5 eV photons.
steps.detail: Each photon frees at most 1 electron. Below a threshold frequency, no electrons come out however bright the light.
steps.pitfall: Thinking brighter red light can free electrons that blue light frees.

problems.prompt: Work function 4 eV, photon 3 eV. Electrons emitted?
Doubling the intensity at 3.5 eV changes what?
problems.answer: The number of electrons, not their max KE.

problems.prompt: Light of 4.5 eV hits a metal with a work function of 2.3 eV. What is the stopping voltage?
problems.answer: 2.2 V, since the fastest electrons have \(4.5 - 2.3 = 2.2\) eV.

steps.title: Energy Levels
steps.mastery: Find emitted wavelengths from level differences.
steps.practice: Find the photon energy and wavelength for a hydrogen jump from n = 3 to n = 2, with E = -13.6/n^2 eV.
steps.detail: Atoms emit photons equal to the gap between levels. That is why each element shows a unique line spectrum.
steps.proof: 1.89 eV and about 656 nm, red.
steps.pitfall: Using the energy of a single level instead of the difference.

problems.prompt: E of hydrogen level \(n = 1\)?
Energy to ionize hydrogen from \(n = 1\)?
Gap from \(n = 2\) to \(n = 1\)?

steps.title: Matter Waves
steps.mastery: Use the de Broglie wavelength.
steps.practice: Find the de Broglie wavelength of an electron at 10^6 m/s and of a 0.15 kg ball at 40 m/s.
steps.detail: Every particle has lambda = h/p. For everyday objects it is far too small to notice.
steps.pitfall: Thinking only light has a wavelength.

problems.prompt: Momentum giving \(\lambda = 6.63 \times 10^{-10}\) m?
Double the speed from \(10^{6}\) m/s. lambda factor?
Experiment showing electron waves in 1927, by Davisson and Germer?

steps.title: Uncertainty and Probability
steps.mastery: Use the uncertainty principle and probability amplitudes.
steps.practice: Estimate the minimum momentum uncertainty for an electron confined to 10^-10 m using delta x delta p >= h/(4 pi).
steps.detail: Position and momentum cannot both be sharp. Quantum outcomes are probabilities given by squared amplitudes.
steps.proof: About 5.3 x 10^-25 kg m/s.
steps.pitfall: Blaming the uncertainty on bad instruments.

problems.prompt: Amplitude 0.6 for 1 outcome. Probability?
Halve delta x from 2 to 1 nm. Minimum delta p factor?
\(\frac{h}{4\pi}\) to 2 figures?

steps.title: The 2 Postulates
steps.mastery: State the postulates of special relativity.
steps.practice: Write the 2 postulates of Einstein 1905 theory and explain why a 0.5c spaceship still measures light at c.
steps.detail: Physics is the same in every inertial frame, and light always moves at c. Everything else follows from these 2 ideas.
steps.proof: 2 postulates and 1 explanation.
steps.pitfall: Adding velocities to get light faster than c.

problems.prompt: Speed of light measured from a ship at 0.9c?
Year Einstein published special relativity, in the 1900s?
Is a frame accelerating at 2 m/s² inertial?

steps.title: Time Dilation
steps.mastery: Use the Lorentz factor gamma.
steps.practice: Compute gamma at 0.6c and 0.8c, and the time a 10 year trip at 0.8c takes on board.
steps.detail: gamma = 1/sqrt(1 - v^2/c^2). Moving clocks run slow by this factor, as seen from the ground.
steps.proof: 1.25, 1.67 and 6 years.
steps.pitfall: Applying gamma to the wrong frame.

problems.prompt: gamma at 0.6c?
A muon lives 2.2 microseconds at rest. Lifetime at \(\gamma = 10\)?
gamma at 0.99c, roughly?

steps.title: Length Contraction
steps.mastery: Find contracted lengths along the motion.
steps.practice: Find the length of a 100 m ship moving at 0.8c, as measured from the ground.
steps.detail: Lengths along the motion shrink by gamma. Distances across the motion do not change.
steps.pitfall: Contracting lengths perpendicular to motion.

problems.prompt: Ship 50 m at \(\gamma = 2\). Measured length?
Width of a 10 m wide ship at 0.8c?
Distance 4 light years shrinks to what at 0.6c?

steps.title: Mass and Energy
steps.mastery: Use E = mc^2 to trade mass for energy in relativity.
steps.practice: Find the energy in 1 g of mass and the mass lost when 3.2 x 10^-11 J is released in fusion.
steps.detail: Mass and energy are interchangeable. Tiny mass changes in nuclei release large energy.
steps.proof: 9 x 10^13 J and about 3.6 x 10^-28 kg.
steps.pitfall: Forgetting to square c.

problems.prompt: E for 1 kg?
Rest energy of an electron, \(9.1 \times 10^{-31}\) kg, in J?
Mass for \(9 \times 10^{10}\) J?

steps.title: Simultaneity and Spacetime
steps.mastery: Show that simultaneity depends on the observer.
steps.practice: Explain with the train and 2 lightning flashes why events at the same time for 1 observer are not for another.
steps.detail: Light from both ends takes equal time only in the frame where the flashes are equal distances away. A moving observer sees 1 first.
steps.proof: A labeled sketch with a 3 sentence explanation.
steps.pitfall: Thinking the disagreement is just a signal delay.

problems.prompt: Spacetime interval for 5 s and 3 light seconds?
Can 2 observers in relative motion at 0.5c agree on the speed of light?
Can cause and effect swap order for events 1 s apart at the same place?

steps.title: Angular Quantities
steps.mastery: Convert between linear and angular motion.
steps.practice: Convert 3000 rpm to rad/s and find the speed of a point 0.2 m from the axis.
steps.detail: Angles are measured in radians. v = r omega links a point speed to the spin rate.
steps.proof: About 314 rad/s and 62.8 m/s.
steps.pitfall: Using degrees in v = r omega.

problems.prompt: Radians in 1 full turn?
omega for 60 rpm?
v at \(r = 0.5\) m and \(\omega = 4\) rad/s?

steps.title: Torque
steps.mastery: Compute torque as force times lever arm.
steps.practice: Find the torque from 20 N on a 0.3 m wrench at 90 degrees and at 30 degrees to the handle.
steps.detail: Torque = r F sin theta. A longer handle or a more perpendicular push gives more turning effect.
steps.proof: 6 N m and 3 N m.
steps.pitfall: Using the full length when the force is at an angle.

problems.prompt: Torque of 10 N at 0.5 m, perpendicular?
Torque when the force points straight along a 0.4 m wrench?
Force needed for 12 N m on a 0.3 m wrench?

steps.title: Balance a Seesaw
steps.mastery: Use the balance of torques for equilibrium.
steps.practice: Find where a 30 kg child must sit to balance a 45 kg adult sitting 1.0 m from the pivot.
steps.detail: In balance the clockwise torques equal the counterclockwise torques. Heavier people sit closer to the pivot.
steps.proof: 1.5 m from the pivot.
steps.pitfall: Balancing forces instead of torques.

problems.prompt: 20 kg at 2 m balances what mass at 1 m?
A 100 N weight at 0.6 m needs what force at 1.2 m?
Sum of torques on a balanced 4 m beam?

steps.title: Moment of Inertia
steps.mastery: Use I to describe resistance to spinning.
steps.practice: Compute I for a 2 kg point mass at 0.5 m and compare a hoop and a solid disc of 2 kg and radius 0.5 m.
steps.detail: I = sum of mr^2. Mass far from the axis makes something harder to spin up, so a hoop has twice the I of a disc.
steps.pitfall: Using mass alone and ignoring how it is spread.

problems.prompt: I of a 3 kg point at 2 m?
Solid disc, 4 kg, radius 1 m. \(I = \frac{1}{2}MR^{2}\)?
Which rolls down a 30 degree ramp faster, a hoop or a solid disc?

steps.title: Angular Momentum
steps.mastery: Use conservation of L = I omega.
steps.practice: Find a skater spin rate when I drops from 4 to 1 kg m^2 starting at 2 rad/s.
steps.detail: With no outside torque, I omega stays fixed. Pulling arms in shrinks I, so the spin speeds up.
steps.proof: 8 rad/s.
steps.pitfall: Assuming kinetic energy is also conserved here.

problems.prompt: L for \(I = 3\) kg m² and \(\omega = 5\) rad/s?
I doubles from 2 to 4 kg m². New omega from 6 rad/s?
A skater spins with \(L = 8\) kg m²/s and pulls in from \(I = 4\) to \(I = 1\) kg m². Give the kinetic energy before, then after, in J.
problems.answer: 8 J before and 32 J after, since KE = \(\frac{L^{2}}{2I}\).

steps.title: Speed of Sound
steps.mastery: Use sound speed to find distances.
steps.practice: Find the distance to a cliff when an echo returns 2 s after a shout, with sound at 340 m/s.
steps.detail: Sound goes there and back, so halve the total distance. Speed depends on the medium and temperature.
steps.pitfall: Forgetting to halve the echo path.

problems.prompt: Thunder 3 s after lightning. Distance?
Sound in water at 1500 m/s takes 0.2 s each way. Depth?
Is sound faster in steel or in 20 degrees C air?

steps.title: Pitch and Loudness
steps.mastery: Link pitch to frequency and loudness to intensity.
steps.practice: Compute the intensity ratio for a rise from 60 dB to 80 dB.
steps.detail: Pitch follows frequency. Loudness uses decibels, where each 10 dB is a factor of 10 in intensity.
steps.proof: A factor of 100.
steps.pitfall: Thinking 80 dB is only a third louder than 60 dB.

problems.prompt: Intensity factor for +30 dB?
problems.answer: 1000, since every 10 dB is a factor of 10.

problems.prompt: Intensity factor for +30 dB?
Give the low end, then the high end, of human hearing for a 20 year old, roughly, in Hz.

steps.title: Doppler Effect
steps.mastery: Predict the pitch shift from a moving source.
steps.practice: Find the heard frequency of a 500 Hz siren moving toward you at 20 m/s, with sound at 340 m/s.
steps.detail: A source moving toward you squashes the waves, raising the pitch. f heard = f v/(v - vs).
steps.proof: About 531 Hz.
steps.pitfall: Using a plus sign for an approaching source.

problems.prompt: Same siren moving away at 20 m/s. Heard f?
Does a stationary 500 Hz source sound shifted?
Pitch rises or falls as a car passes at 30 m/s?

steps.title: Pipes and Resonance
steps.mastery: Find resonant frequencies of open and closed pipes.
steps.practice: Work out the lowest 2 notes of a 0.85 m flute style tube open at both ends and the same tube capped at 1 end, with v = 340 m/s.
steps.detail: Air in a pipe vibrates at set notes. Open pipes use f = nv/2L, and closed pipes have only odd harmonics with f = nv/4L.
steps.proof: Open: 200 and 400 Hz. Closed: 100 and 300 Hz.
steps.pitfall: Including even harmonics for a closed pipe.

problems.prompt: Fundamental of a 0.5 m open pipe at 340 m/s?
Fundamental of a 0.5 m closed pipe?
Next harmonic of a closed pipe after 170 Hz?

steps.title: Beats and Resonance
steps.mastery: Use beats to tune and resonance to explain shattering glass.
steps.practice: Find the beat frequency of 440 and 444 Hz notes, and explain how a singer can break a glass at 900 Hz.
steps.detail: Two close notes beat at the difference frequency. Driving at a natural frequency builds large vibrations.
steps.proof: 4 beats per second, and resonance explained.
steps.pitfall: Thinking volume alone breaks the glass.

problems.prompt: Beats from 256 and 260 Hz?
A string at 438 Hz beats 2 times a second with 440 Hz. Fix?
problems.answer: Tighten it to raise the pitch.

problems.prompt: Why did the Tacoma Narrows Bridge fail in 1940?

steps.title: Temperature and Scales
steps.mastery: Convert between Celsius, kelvin and Fahrenheit.
steps.practice: Convert 25 degrees C to kelvin and Fahrenheit, and 98.6 F to Celsius.
steps.detail: Kelvin starts at absolute zero, so K = C + 273. Fahrenheit uses F = 9/5 C + 32 instead.
steps.proof: 298 K, 77 F and 37 degrees C.
steps.pitfall: Adding 273 for a temperature change.

problems.prompt: 0 degrees C in K?
100 degrees C in F?
Water at 25 degrees C is what temperature in kelvin, to the nearest whole number?

steps.title: Specific Heat
steps.mastery: Use Q = mc delta T for heating.
steps.practice: Find the heat to warm 2 kg of water from 20 to 80 degrees C with c = 4200 J/kg K.
steps.detail: Some materials need more energy per degree than others. Water has a high specific heat, which is why oceans change temperature slowly.
steps.pitfall: Using grams with a per kilogram value of c.

problems.prompt: Q for 1 kg of water warming 10 K?
Same Q into 1 kg of Cu with \(c = 385\). Temperature rise?
Which heats faster under 1000 W, 1 kg of water or 1 kg of Al?
problems.answer: 1 kg of Al, since aluminum's specific heat is about a fifth of water's.

steps.title: Latent Heat
steps.mastery: Compute energy for changes of state.
steps.practice: Find the energy to melt 0.5 kg of ice at 0 degrees C with L = 334,000 J/kg, then warm it to 20 degrees C.
steps.detail: Q = mL for a change of state with no temperature change. Add mc delta T for each warming stage.
steps.pitfall: Adding a temperature change during melting.

problems.prompt: Energy to boil 1 kg of water at 100 degrees C, \(L = 2.26 \times 10^{6}\)?
Energy to freeze 2 kg of water, \(L = 334{,}000\)?
Why does steam at 100 degrees C burn worse than water at 100?
problems.answer: It releases latent heat as it condenses.

steps.title: Heat Transfer
steps.mastery: Tell conduction, convection and radiation apart.
steps.practice: Name the main transfer in 4 cases: a metal spoon in soup, a room heater, sunlight and a boiling pot of 2 L.
steps.detail: Conduction passes energy through contact, convection moves warm fluid and radiation needs no medium at all.
steps.proof: Conduction, convection, radiation and convection.
steps.pitfall: Saying heat rises, when warm fluid rises.

problems.prompt: How does the Sun heat Earth across 150 million km?
Main transfer in a metal pan handle 20 cm long?
Why are freezer coils near the top of 1 old fridge?
problems.answer: Cold air sinks and sets up convection.

steps.title: Thermal Expansion and Gases
steps.mastery: Use the ideal gas law PV = nRT.
steps.practice: Find the pressure of 2 mol of gas in 0.05 m^3 at 300 K with R = 8.31.
steps.detail: PV = nRT links pressure, volume and temperature in kelvin. Heating a gas in a fixed box raises its pressure.
steps.proof: About 99,700 Pa.
steps.pitfall: Using Celsius in PV = nRT.

problems.prompt: Gas at 300 K heated to 450 K at fixed V. Pressure factor?
Volume of 1 mol at 273 K and 101,000 Pa?
A 10 m steel rail warms 30 K, \(\alpha = 1.2 \times 10^{-5}\). Expansion?

steps.title: Define Vector Quantity
steps.mastery: Identify a vector as a quantity that has both magnitude and direction.
steps.practice: Write the vector representing a displacement of 8 m toward the northeast (45° from the positive x-axis).
steps.detail: Recall that a vector is written as magnitude followed by its direction angle. Choose a standard coordinate system with the positive x-axis to the right and the positive y-axis upward. For a northeast direction, the angle is 45° measured counter-clockwise from the x-axis. Record the vector as "8 m ∠45°" or in component form (5.66 m, 5.66 m) after you compute the components later. This step establishes the notation you will use for all later work.
steps.proof: The answer is 8 m ∠45°, which shows both length and angle.
steps.pitfall: Confusing a vector with a scalar by omitting the direction or angle.

problems.prompt: What is the magnitude and direction of a vector that is 5 m long pointing directly east?
Write the vector representing a displacement of 8 m toward the northeast (45° from the positive x-axis).
A student records the vector as 12 m only. What essential information is missing?
problems.hint: Recall what defines a vector.

steps.title: Represent Vectors Graphically
steps.mastery: Draw vectors to scale with correct direction using arrows.
steps.practice: On graph paper, draw a vector of 6 m at 120° from the positive x-axis, using 1 cm = 1 m.
steps.detail: Place the tail of the vector at the origin. Measure a 120° angle from the positive x-axis using a protractor, then count 6 cm along that line for the head. Add an arrowhead to indicate direction. Label the vector with its magnitude and angle. This visual representation helps you verify component calculations later.
steps.proof: The arrow should be 6 cm long, pointing to the second quadrant, forming a 120° angle with the x-axis.
steps.pitfall: Drawing the arrow too short or pointing in the wrong quadrant, which flips the sign of components.

problems.prompt: On graph paper with a 1 cm = 1 m scale, how many centimeters long should a 3 m vector be?
Draw a vector of 6 m at 120° from the positive x-axis using a 1 cm = 1 m scale. How long in centimeters is the arrow?
If you accidentally draw the 120° vector pointing into the fourth quadrant, which component sign will be incorrect?
problems.answer: The y-component sign (it should be positive but would be negative).
problems.hint: Consider the quadrant where 120° lies.

steps.title: Decompose Vector into Components
steps.mastery: Break any 2-D vector into perpendicular x- and y-components using sine and cosine.
steps.practice: Find the x- and y-components of a 9 N force at 30° above the positive x-axis.
steps.detail: Write the vector as F = (F cosθ, F sinθ). Plug in F = 9 N and θ = 30°. Compute cosine and sine values (cos30°≈0.866, sin30°=0.5). Multiply to obtain the components, then record them as (7.79 N, 4.5 N). Double-check that the signs match the quadrant of the original vector.
steps.proof: x-component = 9 cos30° ≈ 7.79 N, y-component = 9 sin30° = 4.5 N.
steps.pitfall: Using the wrong trigonometric function for each component or mixing up degrees and radians.

problems.prompt: What is the x-component of a 10 N force pointing 60° above the positive x-axis?
Give the x- and then the y-component, in N, of a 9 N force at 30° above the positive x-axis.
A 7 N force points 210° from the positive x-axis. Give its x- and then its y-component, in N.
problems.hint: Use cosine for \(x\) and sine for \(y\); remember the angle is in the third quadrant.

steps.title: Add Vectors Algebraically
steps.mastery: Combine multiple vectors by adding their corresponding components.
steps.practice: Compute the resultant of vectors A = 7 m at 0° and B = 5 m at 90° and C = 10 m at 225°.
steps.detail: Convert each vector to component form: A = (7 cos0°, 7 sin0°) = (7, 0). B = (5 cos90°, 5 sin90°) = (0, 5). For C, angle 225° is in the third quadrant, so both components are negative: C = (10 cos225°, 10 sin225°) = (-7.07, -7.07). Add the x-components (7 + 0 - 7.07 ≈ -0.07) and y-components (0 + 5 - 7.07 ≈ -2.07). Use the Pythagorean theorem and arctangent to find the magnitude and direction of the resultant.
steps.pitfall: Assigning a positive sign to the y-component of the 225° vector, which should be negative because it lies in the third quadrant.

problems.prompt: Vector A has components (3, 0) m. What is its magnitude?
Vector B has components (0, 4) m. What is its direction measured from the positive x-axis?
Add \(D = (6, - 8)\) m and \(E = (-3, 4)\) m. Give the magnitude of the resultant in m, then its direction in degrees.
problems.hint: Add the components to get (3, -4) m, then use the Pythagorean theorem and arctangent.

problems.prompt: Three vectors are \(F = (2, - 5)\) m, \(G = (-2, 5)\) m, and \(H = (0, - 3)\) m. After adding them, on which axis does the resultant lie?
problems.hint: Add the x-components and y-components separately.

steps.title: Resolve Forces on an Incline
steps.mastery: Decompose a force acting on an inclined plane into components parallel and perpendicular to the surface.
steps.practice: Resolve a 20 N force that pushes up a 30° incline into components parallel to the plane and normal to the plane.
steps.detail: Draw the incline with the angle θ = 30° relative to the horizontal. The force is directed up the slope, so its direction coincides with the plane. Resolve the force by projecting it onto axes that are parallel (along the plane) and perpendicular (into the plane). The parallel component is F cosθ and the normal component is F sinθ. Compute using θ = 30°: cos30°≈0.866, sin30°=0.5. Multiply by 20 N to obtain the two components, then label them on your diagram.
steps.proof: Parallel component = 20 cos30° ≈ 17.32 N, Normal component = 20 sin30° = 10 N.
steps.pitfall: Treating the force as if it were aligned with the horizontal, which swaps the sine and cosine values.

problems.prompt: A horizontal 10 N force acts on a block on a 30° incline. Give its component along the incline, then into the incline, in N.
problems.answer: Parallel component = 10 \(\cos 30^{\circ} \approx 8.66\) N, Normal component = 10 \(\sin 30^{\circ} = 5\) N.

problems.prompt: A horizontal 20 N push acts on a block on a 30° incline. Give its component along the incline, then into the incline, in N.
problems.answer: Parallel component = 20 \(\cos 30^{\circ} \approx 17.32\) N, Normal component = 20 \(\sin 30^{\circ} = 10\) N.

problems.prompt: A 30 N force acts down a 30° incline, aimed 20° below the surface. Give its component along the incline, then into the incline, in N.
problems.answer: About 28.19 N down the plane and 10.26 N into it, from \(30\cos 20^{\circ}\) and \(30\sin 20^{\circ}\).
problems.hint: Use the angle between the force direction and the plane (20°) with sine for the normal component and cosine for the parallel component.

steps.title: Wave Vocabulary
steps.mastery: Name amplitude, wavelength, frequency and period.
steps.practice: Label a sketch of a wave with amplitude 3 cm and wavelength 12 cm, and find the period at 5 Hz.
steps.detail: Amplitude is height from rest, wavelength is the repeat distance and frequency counts waves per second.
steps.proof: A labeled sketch and T = 0.2 s.
steps.pitfall: Measuring amplitude from trough to crest.

problems.prompt: Period for 50 Hz?
Frequency for a period of 0.5 s?
Crest to trough is 8 cm. Amplitude?

steps.title: Wave Speed
steps.mastery: Use v = f lambda to link speed and size.
steps.practice: Find the speed of a wave with f = 4 Hz and lambda = 2.5 m, and the wavelength of a 340 m/s sound at 680 Hz.
steps.detail: Speed equals frequency times wavelength. The medium sets the speed, and the source sets the frequency.
steps.proof: 10 m/s and 0.5 m.
steps.pitfall: Thinking higher frequency makes sound travel faster.

problems.prompt: \(v = 3 \times 10^{8}\) m/s, \(f = 1.5 \times 10^{8}\) Hz. lambda?
A wave enters a slower medium at 20 Hz. Which changes, f or lambda?

steps.title: Transverse and Longitudinal
steps.mastery: Tell the 2 kinds of wave apart.
steps.practice: Classify 4 waves, light, sound, a guitar string and a slinky push, as transverse or longitudinal.
steps.detail: Transverse waves wobble across the direction of travel and longitudinal ones push along it.
steps.proof: Light and the string transverse, sound and the push longitudinal.
steps.pitfall: Calling sound transverse because graphs draw it as a curve.

problems.prompt: Can sound travel through a 1 m vacuum?
Is light, with 500 nm wavelength, transverse?
P waves in an earthquake are which type, out of 2?

steps.title: Superposition
steps.mastery: Add 2 waves that overlap at the same point.
steps.practice: Sketch 2 pulses of amplitude 2 cm meeting in phase and out of phase on a rope.
steps.detail: At each point the displacements simply sum. Crest on crest builds a bigger wave, and crest on trough cancels.
steps.proof: 4 cm and 0 cm at the overlap.
steps.pitfall: Thinking the waves bounce off each other.

problems.prompt: Pulses of 3 cm and -1 cm overlap. Result?
Path difference of 1 wavelength. Constructive or destructive?
Path difference of 0.5 wavelength?

steps.title: Standing Waves
steps.mastery: Find harmonics on a string fixed at both ends.
steps.practice: Find the first 3 harmonic frequencies of a 0.65 m string with wave speed 260 m/s.
steps.detail: A string fixed at both ends fits whole numbers of half wavelengths, so lambda = 2L/n and f = nv/2L.
steps.pitfall: Fitting whole wavelengths on the string.

problems.prompt: Fundamental for \(L = 1\) m and \(v = 100\) m/s?
Nodes in the 3rd harmonic, counting both ends?
Shorten the string from 0.65 to 0.325 m. Fundamental change?

steps.title: Follow the Soloist
steps.mastery: Follow the singer or player's tempo and breaths instead of driving your own tempo.
steps.practice: Accompany a recording of a singer for 16 bars, matching every slowdown and breath.
steps.detail: The soloist leads and the accompanist follows. Watch for breaths and know where the phrases end, since that's where they'll stretch. Listening matters more than your own part.
steps.proof: 16 bars where the piano stays with every slowdown.
steps.pitfall: Keeping strict time while the singer slows, so you pull apart.

problems.prompt: The singer slows at bar 12. What should you do?
In a 16-bar song, who usually sets the tempo: the soloist or the accompanist?
How can you see a singer's breath coming at bar 8?
problems.answer: Watch them, and know where the phrase ends.

steps.title: Stay Under the Soloist
steps.mastery: Keep the accompaniment softer than the soloist, especially in their low notes.
steps.practice: Play 8 bars at mp under a singer, and drop to p whenever their line goes below C4.
steps.detail: A piano can easily cover a voice, especially in the singer's low range, which is quieter. Play softer there, thin out the texture, and avoid doubling the melody all the time so the soloist stays in front.
steps.proof: 8 bars where the piano drops whenever the voice goes low.
steps.pitfall: Playing at the same volume as when you play alone.

problems.prompt: A singer's line drops below C4. Should you play louder or softer?
Why do a singer's notes below C4 need more space?
problems.answer: They're quieter, so a loud piano covers them.

problems.prompt: Should the piano's right hand double the melody for all 16 bars?
problems.answer: No. It can thin out or drop the melody, so the voice leads.

steps.title: Introductions and Endings
steps.mastery: Play an intro that sets the key and tempo, and an ending that gives the soloist room to finish.
steps.practice: Write a 4-bar intro for a song in G major that ends on D7, so the singer knows when to come in.
steps.detail: An intro sets the key, the tempo and the mood, and ending it on V points straight to the singer's entry. At the end, follow the soloist's last note and finish with them, not before.
steps.proof: A 4-bar intro ending on D7, played into the singer's entry.
steps.pitfall: Starting so fast or so long that the singer can't find their entry.

problems.prompt: Why end an intro in G on V, the D7 chord?
problems.answer: It points to the key, so the singer's entry feels natural.

problems.prompt: How long is a common song intro: 4 bars or 32 bars?
A singer holds the last note for 4 beats. Should you cut off before or with them?

steps.title: Simplify When Needed
steps.mastery: Simplify a hard accompaniment to keep time and support, rather than playing every note badly.
steps.practice: Take a dense 8-bar accompaniment and write a simpler version that keeps the bass notes and a chord on each beat.
steps.detail: A soloist needs steady time and clear harmony more than every written note. Drop inner notes and fast decorations first, and keep the bass line and the rhythm of the chords. A simple part played well beats a hard one played shakily.
steps.proof: A simplified 8 bars that keeps the bass and the beat.
steps.pitfall: Struggling through every note and dragging the tempo.

problems.prompt: An accompaniment is too hard at 120 BPM. What can you drop first?
problems.answer: Inner notes and fast decorations, keeping the bass and rhythm.

problems.prompt: In 8 bars, which matters most to a soloist: every written note or steady time?
Which 2 parts of the texture should stay when you simplify?
problems.answer: The bass line and the rhythm of the chords.

steps.title: Know When to Drop Out
steps.mastery: Leave space for the soloist by dropping out or thinning out when they need the spotlight.
steps.practice: Mark 2 places in a song where you'll play only single notes or rest, and try it with a singer or recording.
steps.detail: Sometimes the best accompaniment is almost nothing. A quiet, exposed line or a fast run sounds better with space around it. Contrast also makes the full moments feel bigger when you come back in.
steps.proof: 2 marked places where the piano thins out, tried with a soloist.
steps.pitfall: Playing full chords under every note the soloist sings.

problems.prompt: A singer has a quiet, exposed line in bar 20. What can you do?
problems.answer: Play very little, or drop out for a moment.

problems.prompt: Why can less piano in 2 places make a song stronger?
problems.answer: Contrast gives the big moments more weight.

problems.prompt: The soloist has a fast run in bar 8. Should you play busy chords under it?
problems.answer: No. Hold a chord or rest so the run is clear.

steps.title: Play Block Triads
steps.mastery: Play major and minor triads in root position as block chords, with fingers 1, 3 and 5.
steps.practice: Play C, F and G major triads as block chords in the right hand with fingers 1-3-5, 4 times each at 60 BPM.
steps.detail: A root-position triad is the root, the note a 3rd up and the note a 5th up, which on the keys looks like play one, skip one, play one, skip one, play one. All three keys should go down together. Switching between major and minor only moves the middle note.
steps.proof: C E G, F A C and G B D, each played cleanly 4 times.
steps.pitfall: Letting the notes land one after another instead of together.

problems.prompt: Which 3 notes are in an F major triad?
Which right-hand fingers play the 3 notes of a root-position triad?
Change the 3-note C major chord to C minor. Which note moves, and where to?

steps.title: Use Inversions
steps.mastery: Use inversions so chords move to the nearest notes instead of jumping.
steps.practice: Play C to F to G to C in the right hand, using C in root position, F in second inversion and G in first inversion, so no note moves more than a 3rd.
steps.detail: Jumping the whole hand from root position to root position sounds choppy. Inversions rearrange the same notes so the shared or nearby ones stay close. The hand barely moves, and the chords flow into each other.
steps.proof: C E G, then C F A, then B D G, then C E G again, with every note moving a 3rd or less.
steps.pitfall: Playing every chord in root position and leaping the whole hand.

problems.prompt: What are the 3 notes of a C major triad in first inversion, from the bottom?
Which inversion of F major has C4 on the bottom?
Moving from C4 E4 G4 to C4 F4 A4, how many notes change?

steps.title: Left-Hand Chord Patterns
steps.mastery: Accompany with left-hand patterns like block chords, broken chords and root-fifth-octave.
steps.practice: Play a C-G-Am-F progression with the left hand in 3 patterns, block, broken and root-fifth-octave, 2 bars each.
steps.detail: The same chords can feel very different depending on the pattern. Block chords are firm and simple. Broken chords flow and fill space. Root-fifth-octave gives a big, open sound. Pick the pattern that fits the song's mood and tempo.
steps.proof: 6 bars played, 2 in each pattern, with the chords changing in time.
steps.pitfall: Using block chords for everything, which can sound stiff in slow songs.

problems.prompt: A root-fifth-octave pattern on C3 plays which 3 notes?
What is a 3-note broken chord?
problems.answer: A chord played one note at a time.

problems.prompt: Which left-hand pattern fills more space in a ballad at 60 BPM: block or broken?

steps.title: Seventh Chords
steps.mastery: Play dominant, major and minor seventh chords, and hear how each one pulls.
steps.practice: Play G7, Cmaj7 and Am7 in the right hand, then resolve G7 to C 5 times and listen to the pull.
steps.detail: A seventh chord adds one more 3rd on top of a triad. G7 has a tense pull toward C, because its B wants to rise to C and its F wants to fall to E. Major and minor sevenths sound softer and are common in jazz and pop.
steps.proof: 3 sevenths played, and G7 resolving to C each time.
steps.pitfall: Playing Cmaj7 when the chart says C7, which has a Bb.

problems.prompt: Spell the 4 notes of G7.
Spell the 4 notes of Cmaj7.
When G7 resolves to C, which of its 4 notes pulls down to E?

steps.title: Voice for Color
steps.mastery: Spread or rearrange a chord's notes to change its color, like an open voicing split across both hands.
steps.practice: Play C major 3 ways, close in 1 hand, open across 2 hands, and with the 3rd on top, and describe how each one sounds.
steps.detail: Voicing is the order and spacing of a chord's notes. Close voicings sound tight, and open ones sound full and rich. The top note is what the ear hears as the melody. Keep notes spread apart in the low register, where close notes turn muddy.
steps.proof: 3 voicings played, with a word or two on how each one sounds.
steps.pitfall: Stacking close chords low in the bass, which sounds muddy.

problems.prompt: A C chord has E on top. Which note of the chord is in the melody?
Which usually sounds fuller: C-E-G in 1 hand, or C2-G2 plus E4-C5 across 2 hands?
Why avoid a close chord low in the bass, like C2-E2-G2?
problems.answer: Low notes close together sound muddy.

steps.title: Speed, Not Force
steps.mastery: Control volume with how fast the key goes down, not by pushing harder with the arm.
steps.practice: Play C4 10 times, getting a little louder each time by dropping the key faster, with a loose arm.
steps.detail: A piano hammer is thrown at the string, and the speed of the key sets how hard it hits. Once the note sounds, pressing harder does nothing. Loud playing comes from arm weight and a quick drop, with the arm staying loose.
steps.proof: 10 notes rising evenly in volume, with no tension in the arm.
steps.pitfall: Pressing harder into the key after the note sounds.

problems.prompt: What makes 1 note on C4 louder: key speed or how long you hold it?
Your arm goes tense when you play loud at bar 9. What's a better way?
problems.answer: Use arm weight and a faster key drop, staying loose.

problems.prompt: Why does pressing harder 1 second after the note sounds do nothing?
problems.answer: The hammer has already left the string.

steps.title: Use the Whole Range
steps.mastery: Play the full range of dynamics, pp to ff, with 4 or 5 clear levels you can repeat.
steps.practice: Play a C major scale 5 times, at pp, p, mf, f and ff, and record whether each level is clearly different.
steps.detail: Many players only use two volumes, medium and loud. Clear, repeatable levels give music shape and contrast. Practice the soft end most, since playing very quietly while staying even is the hardest part.
steps.proof: 5 recordings, each clearly softer or louder than its neighbor.
steps.pitfall: Playing everything at mf and calling it expressive.

problems.prompt: Which is softer: 'mp' or 'mf'?
What does 'cresc.' tell you to do?
Order these 5 from softest to loudest: f, pp, mf, p, ff.

steps.title: Balance the Hands
steps.mastery: Keep the tune on top while the accompaniment stays soft underneath it.
steps.practice: Play an 8-bar melody at mf in the right hand while the left hand plays block chords at p.
steps.detail: Listeners follow the melody, so it should sit on top of the accompaniment. Each hand needs its own volume at once, which takes practice. Try the accompaniment alone at its soft level first, then add the melody over it.
steps.proof: 8 bars with the melody clearly above the chords.
steps.pitfall: Letting the left hand match the melody's volume and cover it.

problems.prompt: In an 8-bar song, which is usually louder: the melody or the accompaniment?
Name 1 drill for hand balance.
problems.answer: Touch the left-hand keys silently, then add it softly under the melody.

problems.prompt: Why practice the accompaniment alone at 'p' first?
problems.answer: So you learn how soft it can be before adding the melody.

steps.title: Voice the Top Note
steps.mastery: Bring out the top note of a chord in one hand by putting more weight on that finger.
steps.practice: Play 4 chords in the right hand and make the top note ring louder than the other 2, by leaning toward finger 5.
steps.detail: In many pieces the melody is the top note of chords. Tilt the hand slightly toward the pinky and let that finger arrive a touch faster. The other notes go down softer, so the tune sings over them.
steps.proof: 4 chords with the top note clearly loudest.
steps.pitfall: Playing every note of the chord at the same volume, hiding the tune.

problems.prompt: Which finger, 1 to 5, usually plays the top note of a right-hand chord?
Why bring out the top note of a 3-note chord?
A hymn tune sits on top of 4-part chords. Which voice should sound most?

steps.title: Articulation
steps.mastery: Play legato, staccato and accents cleanly, and switch between them on purpose.
steps.practice: Play 2 bars legato, 2 bars staccato and 2 bars with accents on beats 1 and 3, at 80 BPM.
steps.detail: Legato connects notes smoothly, with each key held until the next goes down. Staccato makes them short and separated. Accents stress single notes. Switching cleanly between them is what makes a passage sound alive instead of flat.
steps.proof: 6 bars played, with each kind of touch clearly different.
steps.pitfall: Making staccato so short and stiff that it sounds harsh.

problems.prompt: What does 1 dot over a note mean?
A curved line over 4 notes means what?
problems.answer: Play them legato, smooth and connected.

problems.prompt: What does '>' over a note mean?
problems.answer: An accent, so play it louder.

steps.title: Learn the Finger Numbers
steps.mastery: Number the fingers 1 to 5, from thumb to pinky, in both hands, and read them in music.
steps.practice: Place each finger on its own key from C4 to G4 in the right hand, say its number out loud, then repeat with the left hand from C3 to G3.
steps.detail: Both hands use the same numbers, thumb 1 to pinky 5, so the hands mirror each other. Numbers printed above or below notes tell you which finger to use. Reading them is the first step to good fingering.
steps.proof: Both hands play 5 notes with the right numbers, mirrored.
steps.pitfall: Numbering the left hand from the pinky, as if the hands matched.

problems.prompt: What finger number, from 1 to 5, is the right-hand pinky?
The left hand plays C D E F G starting with its pinky on C. Which finger plays G?
A '3' appears above a note for the right hand. Which finger plays it?

steps.title: Write the Fingering In
steps.mastery: Decide the fingering for tricky spots in advance, and write it on the music.
steps.practice: Pick 4 bars that trip you up, try 2 fingerings for each, and pencil in the one that works.
steps.detail: Fingering chosen on the spot changes from day to day, so the passage never settles. Decide once, write it down, and use it every time. Only mark the places that aren't obvious: shifts, crossings and stretches.
steps.proof: 4 bars with fingering penciled in where it matters.
steps.pitfall: Deciding fresh each time you play, so your hands never learn it.

problems.prompt: Why write fingering in for 4 tricky bars rather than deciding each time?
problems.answer: Using the same fingers every time builds reliable muscle memory.

problems.prompt: You use finger 2 on Monday and finger 3 on Tuesday for the same note. What happens?
problems.answer: The passage never settles, so it keeps tripping you.

problems.prompt: In a 32-bar piece, should you write fingering on every note?
problems.answer: No. Only where it's not obvious, like shifts and crossings.

steps.title: Thumb Under, Finger Over
steps.mastery: Pass the thumb under, or a finger over, to cover more than 5 notes smoothly.
steps.practice: Play C major up 1 octave in the right hand with 1 2 3 1 2 3 4 5 at 60 BPM, keeping the thumb pass smooth.
steps.detail: Five fingers only reach five notes, so longer lines need the thumb to slide under the hand going up, or a finger to cross over going down. Keep the wrist level and move the thumb early, so there's no bump in the sound.
steps.proof: An even scale with no gap at the thumb pass.
steps.pitfall: Lifting the whole hand and jumping instead of passing the thumb.

problems.prompt: Going up 1 octave of right-hand C major, after which finger does the thumb pass under?
Going down 1 octave of right-hand C major, which finger crosses over the thumb?
Why keep the wrist level during a thumb pass at 60 BPM?
problems.answer: A dipping wrist makes a bump in the sound.

steps.title: Fit Fingering to the Hand
steps.mastery: Choose fingering that suits the passage, with strong fingers on accents and the hand kept in one place when possible.
steps.practice: Finger a 2-bar melody 3 ways, and record which one sounds most even at 80 BPM.
steps.detail: Good fingering keeps shifts to a minimum and puts strong fingers on the notes that matter. The thumb is short and suits white keys. Fingers 4 and 5 are weaker, so they need care on important notes.
steps.proof: 3 recordings compared, with the most even fingering chosen.
steps.pitfall: Putting the thumb on a black key in a fast passage.

problems.prompt: Should a black key like F# usually go to the thumb?
problems.answer: Usually not. The thumb is short, so it suits white keys.

problems.prompt: A melody spans 5 notes, C to G. How many hand shifts does it need?
Of fingers 1 to 5, which is usually weakest and needs the most careful practice?

steps.title: Keep It Consistent
steps.mastery: Stick to the chosen fingering every time, even when practicing slowly, so it becomes automatic.
steps.practice: Play your hardest 4 bars 10 times slowly with the written fingering, starting over whenever you use a different finger.
steps.detail: Your hands learn whatever you repeat, including mistakes. Practicing slowly with the real fingering builds the same motions you'll use at speed. If a fingering really doesn't work, change it on purpose and retrain it.
steps.proof: 10 clean runs with the written fingering.
steps.pitfall: Using an easier fingering when slow and switching at full speed.

problems.prompt: You played 10 times and switched fingers 3 times. What should you do?
problems.answer: Slow down until the written fingering is automatic.

problems.prompt: Why practice at 60 BPM with the final fingering, not a simpler one?
problems.answer: Slow practice trains the same motion you'll use at speed.

problems.prompt: Can you change a fingering after 2 weeks of practice?
problems.answer: Yes, but decide once and then retrain it on purpose.

steps.title: Hands Separately First
steps.mastery: Learn each hand alone until it plays without thought, before putting them together.
steps.practice: Play the right hand of 8 bars 5 times without a mistake, then the left hand 5 times, before trying both.
steps.detail: When both hands are new, your attention splits and both fall apart. Get each hand automatic first, so combining them only asks for coordination. Most beginners need extra time on the left hand.
steps.proof: 5 clean runs of each hand before the first try together.
steps.pitfall: Combining hands on day one and practicing the mistakes in.

problems.prompt: How many clean runs of 8 bars per hand is a good target before combining?
Why does hands-separate practice of 8 bars help?
problems.answer: Each hand becomes automatic, so your attention is free for combining.

problems.prompt: Of the 2 hands, which usually needs more solo practice for beginners?

steps.title: Combine Slowly
steps.mastery: Put the hands together at a slow tempo, often half speed, where every note is clean.
steps.practice: Play 4 bars hands together at 50 BPM with a metronome, then raise it by 4 BPM each time it's clean 3 times in a row.
steps.detail: Speed hides mistakes and makes them stick. Start slow enough to be clean, and climb in small steps. If mistakes appear, drop back to the last clean tempo. It feels slow, and it's the fastest route to the real tempo.
steps.proof: A log of tempos, rising 4 BPM at a time.
steps.pitfall: Jumping straight to the target tempo and repeating errors.

problems.prompt: Your target is 100 BPM. What's a good starting tempo for hands together?
You start at 50 BPM and raise it 4 BPM each time. After 5 raises, what is it?
At 66 BPM you make 2 mistakes. What should you do?
problems.answer: Drop back to the last clean tempo.

steps.title: Work in Small Chunks
steps.mastery: Combine the hands in chunks of 1 or 2 bars, overlapping into the next bar.
steps.practice: Practice bars 1 to 2 hands together, then 2 to 3, then 3 to 4, always including the first note of the next bar.
steps.detail: Short chunks keep the challenge small. Overlapping each chunk into the next bar trains the joins, which is where most stumbles happen. Once each chunk is clean, link them into longer runs.
steps.proof: Every overlapping chunk clean, then all 4 bars played through.
steps.pitfall: Practicing chunks that stop dead at the bar line, so the joins never get trained.

problems.prompt: Why include the first note of the next bar in each 2-bar chunk?
problems.answer: It joins chunks, so the seams don't trip you.

problems.prompt: An 8-bar piece is practiced in 2-bar chunks that overlap by 1 bar. How many chunks is that?
You can play every chunk but stumble across bar 4 to 5. What should you practice?
problems.answer: The chunk from bar 4 to bar 5.

steps.title: Find Where the Hands Line Up
steps.mastery: Mark where the hands play together on the beat, and use those spots as anchors.
steps.practice: Circle every beat in 4 bars where both hands play at once, and play just those notes in rhythm first.
steps.detail: The moments where both hands strike together hold the two parts in time. Practicing those first gives you a skeleton. Then add the notes in between, one hand at a time, while keeping the anchors steady.
steps.proof: 4 bars with the together beats circled and played as a skeleton.
steps.pitfall: Treating the two hands as unrelated, so they drift apart.

problems.prompt: Why practice only the together notes in 4 bars first?
problems.answer: They're the anchors that hold the 2 hands in time.

problems.prompt: The left hand plays on beats 1 and 3, the right on every beat. On which beats do they line up?
The right hand plays 2 eighths per beat and the left hand 1 quarter. How many right-hand notes per left-hand note?

steps.title: Play Without Looking Down
steps.mastery: Play hands together with your eyes on the music, finding the keys by touch.
steps.practice: Play 8 bars hands together at a slow tempo while looking only at the music, glancing down no more than 2 times.
steps.detail: Every glance down risks losing your place on the page. Learn hand positions and the feel of the black-key groups so you can find keys by touch. Start with short passages and allow a glance only for big jumps.
steps.proof: 8 bars played with 2 glances down or fewer.
steps.pitfall: Watching your hands the whole time and stalling at each new line.

problems.prompt: You look down 8 times in 8 bars. What should you practice?
problems.answer: Feeling key distances with your eyes on the page.

problems.prompt: Name the 2 black-key groups that help you find your place by touch.
How many glances down in 8 bars is a good target to start with?

steps.title: Spot the Chords
steps.mastery: Find the chord behind each bar of written music by stacking its notes in thirds.
steps.practice: Name the chord in each of 8 bars of a simple piece, writing the letter name above every bar.
steps.detail: Collect the notes from both hands in a bar, drop the repeats, and stack them in thirds. The bottom of the stack is the root. Notes that don't fit are usually passing notes. A bar can hold two chords, so check each beat if the notes don't settle.
steps.proof: A chord name written over each of the 8 bars.
steps.pitfall: Naming the chord from the lowest note alone, which fails on inversions.

problems.prompt: A bar's left hand has G2 and D3, and the right hand has B4. Which chord is it?
Bar 3 holds A, C and E spread over both hands. Which chord is it?
