steps.practice: Find 3 sentences over 30 words in a draft and split each into 2 or 3 shorter ones.
steps.detail: Long sentences make readers hold too much at once. Most clear writing averages 15 to 20 words. Mix in short ones for punch. If a sentence has more than 2 commas, check if it should be split.
steps.proof: 3 long sentences split.
steps.pitfall: Writing 50 word sentences with 4 commas.

problems.prompt: What's a common average sentence length for clear writing?
Your sentence has 4 commas and 45 words. What do you do?
Your sentences all run 18 to 22 words. Why mix in a few short ones?

steps.title: Swap Fancy Words for Plain Ones
steps.mastery: Replace jargon and inflated words with plain ones whenever the reader doesn't need the technical term.
steps.practice: Circle 5 fancy or jargon words in a draft, like "utilize" or "facilitate," and replace each with a plain word.
steps.detail: Inflated words make writing sound stiff and push readers away. "Utilize" means "use." "Facilitate" means "help." "Commence" means "start." Keep a technical term only when your reader knows it and no plain word does the same job. In that case, define it the first time.
steps.proof: 5 words swapped for plain ones in 1 draft.
steps.pitfall: Choosing "utilize" over "use" because it sounds smarter.

problems.prompt: Rewrite "We will commence the meeting at 9."
Rewrite "This tool facilitates communication between 2 teams."
Your readers are new to biology and you need the word "osmosis." What do you do?
problems.answer: Keep it, and define it the first time.

steps.title: Say It Out Loud First
steps.mastery: Check that you can explain your point simply before trusting the written version.
steps.practice: Explain your main point to a friend in 2 sentences without looking at the draft, then compare it with your written opening.
steps.detail: If you can say it simply, you can write it simply. People often explain more clearly out loud than on the page. When your spoken version is clearer than the draft, borrow its words. Record yourself if no friend is around.
steps.proof: A 2 sentence spoken explanation compared with the draft.
steps.pitfall: Keeping a written version you couldn't explain in 2 sentences out loud.

problems.prompt: Your spoken 2 sentences are clearer than your 6 sentence opening. What do you do?
problems.answer: Rewrite the opening using the spoken version.

problems.prompt: No friend is around. Name 1 other way to try this.
You can't explain your point in 2 sentences. What does that suggest?
problems.answer: The point isn't clear yet, even to you.

steps.title: Cut Filler Words
steps.mastery: Remove words that add length but no meaning.
steps.practice: Search a draft for 6 filler words, "very," "really," "just," "actually," "basically" and "quite," and delete or replace each one.
steps.detail: Filler words creep in while drafting. Most can be deleted with no loss. "Very tired" can become "exhausted." "I just wanted to say" can become "I wanted to say." A search for each word makes this a quick mechanical pass.
steps.proof: 1 draft with all 6 filler words checked and most cut.
steps.pitfall: Keeping "really very important" because it feels emphatic.

problems.prompt: Rewrite "It was really very cold."
Rewrite "I just wanted to ask if you're free."
Why use search to find all 6 filler words?
problems.answer: It finds every instance fast and mechanically.

steps.title: Trim Wordy Phrases
steps.mastery: Replace long phrases with shorter ones that mean the same thing.
steps.practice: Find 5 wordy phrases in a draft, like "in order to" or "due to the fact that," and replace each with 1 or 2 words.
steps.detail: Common wordy phrases have short swaps: "in order to" becomes "to," "due to the fact that" becomes "because," "at this point in time" becomes "now," "in the event that" becomes "if." Each swap saves words and reads faster.
steps.proof: 5 wordy phrases shortened.
steps.pitfall: Writing "at this point in time" when "now" works.

problems.prompt: Shorten "due to the fact that."
Shorten "in the event that."
Shorten "We met in order to discuss the plan."

accept: We met to discuss the plan.
We met to discuss the plan

steps.title: Cut 10 Percent
steps.mastery: Shorten a finished draft by a set amount to force tighter writing.
steps.practice: Take a 500 word draft and cut it to 450 words without losing any point.
steps.detail: A target makes cutting concrete. Most drafts can lose 10 percent with no loss of meaning, and they read better for it. Look for repeated points, long warm-ups and filler.
steps.proof: A 500 word draft cut to 450.
steps.pitfall: Cutting key examples while leaving filler.

problems.prompt: A draft is 800 words. What's a 10 percent cut target?
Name 3 places to look for cuts.
problems.answer: Repeated points, long warm-ups and filler.

problems.prompt: You cut an example that made your point clear. Was that a good cut?

steps.title: Say Each Point Once
steps.mastery: State each idea once, in its strongest form and best place.
steps.practice: Highlight every idea that appears 2 or more times in a draft, keep the strongest version, and delete the others.
steps.detail: Drafts circle back. You make a point in paragraph 1, again in 3 and again in 5, each a bit different. Readers notice and lose patience. Pick the clearest wording, put it where it does the most work, and cut the echoes. A short summary at the end of a long report is the one fair exception.
steps.proof: 1 draft with every repeated idea reduced to 1 version.
steps.pitfall: Restating the main point at the end of every paragraph.

problems.prompt: Your main point appears in paragraphs 1, 3 and 5. What do you do?
problems.answer: Keep the strongest version and cut the other 2.

problems.prompt: Your 10 page report ends with a 3 line summary. Is that a repeat to cut?
problems.answer: No. A short summary helps in long pieces.

problems.prompt: Two sentences in paragraph 2 say the same thing in different words. Which do you keep?

steps.title: Trim Paragraph Edges
steps.mastery: Cut the warm-up and wind-down sentences that pad the start and end of paragraphs.
steps.practice: In 3 paragraphs, delete the first and last sentence, reread, and keep each cut only if no meaning is lost.
steps.detail: Paragraphs often open with a vague lead-in and close with a line that just repeats the point. Test cutting both. Often the paragraph starts stronger on its second sentence and ends cleaner on its second to last. Put back anything the paragraph truly needs.
steps.proof: 3 paragraphs tested, with useless edge sentences cut.
steps.pitfall: Ending every paragraph with "This shows how important X is" out of habit.

problems.prompt: A paragraph ends "This shows why sleep matters." The previous sentence already made that clear. Keep it?
You cut a first sentence and the paragraph no longer makes sense. What do you do?
You test 3 paragraphs and 2 improve. How many cuts do you keep?

steps.title: Run a Concision Pass Every Time
steps.mastery: Make cutting a standard step before anything goes out.
steps.practice: Run a 10 minute concision pass on your next 5 pieces before sending them, checking filler words, wordy phrases and repeats.
steps.detail: Concision is a mechanical pass that anyone can learn. The checklist is short: search filler words, swap wordy phrases, cut repeats, trim paragraph edges. Ten minutes usually cuts 10 percent and makes the piece easier to read.
steps.proof: 5 pieces with a logged concision pass and word counts before and after.
steps.pitfall: Skipping the pass when rushed, which is when drafts are wordiest.

problems.prompt: A piece goes from 600 to 540 words after the pass. What percent was cut?
Name 4 checks in the concision pass.
problems.answer: Filler words, wordy phrases, repeats and paragraph edges.

problems.prompt: You're rushed and have 10 minutes before sending. Skip the pass?
problems.answer: No. Rushed drafts need it most.

steps.title: Pick 1 Precise Detail
steps.mastery: Choose one exact detail that does more than several vague ones.
steps.practice: Describe 3 places you know in 1 sentence each, using only 1 specific detail per place.
steps.detail: "The kitchen was messy and old and cluttered" gives the reader nothing to see. "A calendar from 2009 still hung by the fridge" gives them a whole kitchen. One sharp detail lets the reader fill in the rest. Pick the detail only this place would have.
steps.proof: 3 one-sentence descriptions, each built on 1 detail.
steps.pitfall: Stacking 3 vague adjectives in place of 1 real detail.

problems.prompt: Rewrite "The room was old and dusty and sad" with 1 precise detail.
problems.answer: "A clock on the wall had stopped at 4:15 years ago."

problems.prompt: Which is stronger: "a nice car" or "a red 1998 pickup with 1 blue door"?
problems.answer: A red 1998 pickup with 1 blue door.

choices: A red 1998 pickup with 1 blue door
accept: A red 1998 pickup with 1 blue door

problems.prompt: Why does 1 detail beat 3 adjectives?
problems.answer: The reader can picture it and fill in the rest.

steps.title: Use All 5 Senses
steps.mastery: Go past sight and use sound, smell, touch and taste to make a scene real.
steps.practice: Write a 5 sentence description of a place with 1 sentence for each of the 5 senses.
steps.detail: Most writers lean on sight alone. Smell and sound pull readers in fast. The squeak of a gym floor, the smell of chlorine, the cold metal of a bleacher make a pool feel real in a way "it was a big pool" never will.
steps.proof: A 5 sentence description using all 5 senses.
steps.pitfall: Describing only what things look like.

problems.prompt: Write 1 smell for a school cafeteria.
Write 1 sound for a hospital waiting room at 2 am.
problems.answer: "A vending machine humming and a TV on low."

problems.prompt: Of the 5 senses, which do most writers skip?

steps.title: Trade Clichés for Fresh Images
steps.mastery: Replace worn-out phrases with comparisons that feel new.
steps.practice: Find 5 clichés in your writing, like "cold as ice" or "busy as a bee," and replace each with a fresh comparison.
steps.detail: Clichés slide past readers without a picture. "Cold as ice" means nothing anymore. "Cold as the back of a fridge door" makes them feel it. Fresh images come from your own world, so look at what's around you.
steps.proof: 5 clichés replaced with fresh comparisons.
steps.pitfall: Writing "her heart pounded like a drum" without thinking.

problems.prompt: Replace "quiet as a mouse" with a fresh comparison.
problems.answer: "Quiet as a library at 8 am," or something from your own life.

problems.prompt: Why does "cold as ice" fail after 100 years of use?
problems.answer: Readers have seen it so often they don't picture anything.

problems.prompt: Name 1 place to find fresh images.

steps.title: Show With Concrete Nouns
steps.mastery: Choose specific nouns over general ones.
steps.practice: Circle 10 general nouns in a draft, like "tree," "car" or "food," and replace each with a specific one, like "oak," "minivan" or "cold pizza."
steps.detail: General nouns blur the picture. Specific nouns sharpen it with no extra words. "A bird" could be anything. "A crow" brings an image and a mood with it.
steps.proof: 10 nouns made specific.
steps.pitfall: Writing "a flower" when you mean "a dandelion" and losing the picture.

problems.prompt: Make "a dog" specific.
Make "food" specific.
Why swap "bird" for "crow" in 1 sentence?
problems.answer: It sharpens the picture with no extra words.

steps.title: Trim Long Description
steps.mastery: Keep description short enough that it adds to the scene without stalling it.
steps.practice: Take 1 description paragraph of 6 or more sentences and cut it to 2, keeping only the strongest details.
steps.detail: Readers skim long description to get back to the action. Listing every object in a room slows the story and buries the one detail that mattered. Keep 1 or 2 sharp details and trust the reader to build the rest. You can scatter more detail through the action later.
steps.proof: 1 long paragraph cut to 2 sentences with the best details kept.
steps.pitfall: Describing every object in a room before anything happens.

problems.prompt: Your paragraph lists 9 things in a bedroom. How many details might you keep?
You cut 7 details. Where can a few go if you still want them?
Why do readers skim a 9 sentence description?
problems.answer: They want to get back to what's happening.

steps.title: Notice 1 Thing a Day
steps.mastery: Build observation into a daily habit so precise details come easily.
steps.practice: Write 1 sentence describing something you saw, heard or smelled each day for 14 days, using 1 specific detail.
steps.detail: Good description starts with noticing. A daily sentence trains your eye: the man at the bus stop with mismatched gloves, the smell of rain on hot pavement. After 2 weeks you'll have a bank of real details to use in stories.
steps.proof: 14 one-sentence observations in a notebook.
steps.pitfall: Waiting for a big scene before practicing description.

problems.prompt: Write 1 observation sentence from a bus ride.
problems.answer: "The driver hummed the same 3 notes at every red light."

problems.prompt: After 14 days, what do you have besides practice?
problems.answer: A bank of real details to use.

problems.prompt: Should each of the 14 sentences be vague or specific?

steps.title: Write a Messy First Draft
steps.mastery: Get a complete rough version down without stopping to fix it.
steps.practice: Write a 500 word first draft of 1 short piece in 30 minutes without deleting a single sentence.
steps.detail: A first draft only has to exist. Editing while drafting stalls you, because every sentence gets judged before the next one is written. Write straight through. Typos, weak words and gaps are fine. You'll fix them when there's a whole draft to fix.
steps.proof: A 500 word draft written in 30 minutes with no deletions.
steps.pitfall: Rewriting the first paragraph 6 times before writing the second.

problems.prompt: You've spent 25 minutes on your first 2 sentences. What's going wrong?
You spot a typo in sentence 3 while drafting. Fix it now?
problems.answer: No. Keep going and fix it later.

problems.prompt: Why write all 500 words before editing any of them?
problems.answer: You can't shape what doesn't exist yet.

steps.title: Leave Placeholders
steps.mastery: Mark gaps with a placeholder so missing facts or words don't stop the draft.
steps.practice: In your next draft, use [TK] or brackets at least 3 times instead of stopping to look something up or find the right word.
steps.detail: Writers use TK, short for "to come," to mark a gap. A missing date, a better word or a quote to find later all get a bracket. The draft keeps moving. Afterward, search for TK and fill them in one pass.
steps.proof: A draft with at least 3 bracketed placeholders, filled in afterward.
steps.pitfall: Leaving the draft to research a detail and never coming back.

problems.prompt: You can't remember the year a law passed. What do you write?
You want a sharper word than "big." What do you write while drafting?
Your draft has 6 placeholders. How do you find them all later?
problems.answer: Search the document for TK or brackets.

steps.title: Turn Off the Inner Editor
steps.mastery: Quiet the urge to judge sentences while drafting.
steps.practice: Draft for 15 minutes with your screen dimmed or font color set to white, so you can't reread as you go.
steps.detail: If you can't see what you wrote, you can't fix it. Some writers dim the screen or type in white text to stop rereading. It feels strange, but words flow faster. Then turn the color back and look at what you've got.
steps.proof: A 15 minute draft written without rereading.
steps.pitfall: Reading back every sentence as soon as you finish it.

problems.prompt: Why type in white text for 15 minutes?
problems.answer: So you can't reread and edit as you go.

problems.prompt: After 15 minutes of blind drafting, what do you do?
problems.answer: Turn the text color back and read it.

problems.prompt: Name 1 other way to stop rereading while drafting.
problems.answer: Dim the screen or cover the top of the page.

steps.title: Draft in One Sitting
steps.mastery: Finish a short draft in a single session so the thread doesn't break.
steps.practice: Write 1 complete draft of under 800 words, beginning to end, in a single 45 minute session.
steps.detail: Short pieces are easiest to draft in 1 go. Your thinking stays connected and the piece hangs together. Longer pieces can be drafted section by section, each in 1 session.
steps.proof: 1 complete draft under 800 words written in 1 session.
steps.pitfall: Writing 2 paragraphs a day for 2 weeks and losing the thread.

problems.prompt: Why draft short pieces in 1 sitting?
Your piece is 5,000 words. How do you draft it?
problems.answer: Section by section, each in 1 session.

problems.prompt: You run out of time at 600 of 800 words. What do you do?
problems.answer: Write notes for the ending so you can pick up tomorrow.

steps.title: Let It Rest, Then Read
steps.mastery: Step away from a draft before revising so you see it fresh.
steps.practice: Wait at least 24 hours after finishing a draft, then read it once out loud and note 3 things to fix.
steps.detail: Right after writing, you read what you meant rather than what's on the page. A day away fixes that. Reading aloud catches clunky sentences and missing words your eyes skip. Keep the first read to 3 big notes so you fix structure before polishing sentences.
steps.proof: A draft read aloud after 24 hours with 3 notes.
steps.pitfall: Revising the moment you finish, while it's too fresh to see.

problems.prompt: Should a draft rest about 24 hours or 10 minutes before revising?
Why read the 500 words aloud instead of silently?
problems.answer: Your ear catches clunky sentences your eyes skip.

problems.prompt: On the first read, should you note about 3 fixes or 30?

steps.title: Ask in the First 2 Lines
steps.mastery: Put the request and the deadline at the very top of a message.
steps.practice: Rewrite 3 recent emails so the first 2 lines say what you need and by when.
steps.detail: People read the top of a message and decide whether to act. If your ask is in paragraph 3, it gets missed. Lead with the request and the date. Context goes after, for anyone who needs it.
steps.proof: 3 emails rewritten with the ask and deadline in the first 2 lines.
steps.pitfall: Opening with 3 lines of background before getting to the point.

problems.prompt: Rewrite this opening: "Hope you're well. I wanted to touch base about the project we discussed last month..."
problems.answer: "Can you send the final budget by Friday? We need it for the board meeting."

problems.prompt: What 2 things belong in the first 2 lines?
problems.answer: What you need, and by when.

problems.prompt: Your ask is in paragraph 3 of 4. What usually happens?

steps.title: Ask for 1 Thing
steps.mastery: Keep each message to a single clear request so it gets a single clear answer.
steps.practice: Split 1 email that asks for 3 things into separate, shorter messages, or number the asks clearly.
steps.detail: Messages with several asks usually get 1 answered and the rest ignored. If you need 3 things, number them or send separate messages. One clear ask per message gets decisions instead of threads.
steps.proof: 1 multi-ask email split or numbered.
steps.pitfall: Burying 3 questions in 1 long paragraph.

problems.prompt: Your email asks for a budget, a date and a room. Name 2 ways to fix it.
problems.answer: Number the 3 asks, or send 3 short emails.

problems.prompt: You asked 3 things and got 1 answer. Why?
Rewrite "Could you maybe look at the draft sometime and let me know if it seems OK?" as 1 clear ask.
problems.answer: "Could you review the draft and send comments by Thursday?"

steps.title: Write Subject Lines That Work
steps.mastery: Write subject lines that say what the message needs.
steps.practice: Rewrite 5 vague subject lines, like "Quick question," to include the topic and the action, like "Approve budget by Fri."
steps.detail: The subject line is the first thing read and the main thing searched later. A good one names the topic and what's needed. Add a date if there's a deadline.
steps.proof: 5 subject lines rewritten.
steps.pitfall: Using "Hi" or "Update" as a subject line.

problems.prompt: Rewrite the subject "Question."
problems.answer: "Room for Tuesday's meeting: need yes by 3 pm."

problems.prompt: Why put "need yes by 3 pm" in the subject line?
problems.answer: The reader knows what's needed before opening it.

problems.prompt: Is "Update" a good subject line?

steps.title: Keep It to 5 Sentences
steps.mastery: Cut work messages to the length the reader needs to act.
steps.practice: Write your next 5 work emails in 5 sentences or fewer, moving extra detail to an attachment or a link.
steps.detail: Short messages get read and answered. Long ones get skimmed, saved for later and forgotten. Most requests fit in 5 sentences: the ask, the deadline, 1 or 2 lines of context, and thanks. If it truly needs more, attach a doc or suggest a quick call.
steps.proof: 5 emails of 5 sentences or fewer.
steps.pitfall: Sending 10 paragraphs to ask a yes or no question.

problems.prompt: Your email to confirm a meeting time is 12 sentences. What can you cut it to?
problems.answer: About 2 or 3 sentences: the time, a question and thanks.

problems.prompt: The topic needs a long back and forth. What's often better than a 20 line email?
Name 4 parts that fit in a 5 sentence request.
problems.answer: The ask, the deadline, a line of context and thanks.

steps.title: Match Tone to the Reader
steps.mastery: Adjust tone for who's reading while keeping the message clear and polite.
steps.practice: Write the same 3 sentence update twice: once to a manager and once to a coworker you know well.
steps.detail: The facts stay the same. The tone shifts. A manager or new client gets polite and direct. A friendly coworker can get a lighter touch. Clear and polite works with everyone, so start there and loosen up only when you know the reader.
steps.proof: 2 versions of the same update, each fitting its reader.
steps.pitfall: Writing to a new client the way you'd text a friend.

problems.prompt: Rewrite "yo, report's late lol" for a manager.
problems.answer: "The report will be 1 day late. I'll send it Thursday by noon."

problems.prompt: Name 1 tone that works with every reader.
You've worked with a coworker for 2 years. Can the tone be lighter?
problems.answer: Yes, if that's how you usually talk.

steps.title: Follow Up Without Nagging
steps.mastery: Nudge unanswered messages in a short, friendly way.
steps.practice: For 1 email with no reply after 3 working days, send a 2 sentence follow-up that repeats the ask and the date.
steps.detail: Most unanswered emails are just buried. A brief, friendly nudge that repeats the ask brings them back to the top. Reply in the same thread so the history is there. Skip guilt-trip lines like "As per my last email," which put people on the defensive.
steps.proof: 1 two sentence follow-up sent in the original thread.
steps.pitfall: Writing "As per my last email" in a cold tone.

problems.prompt: Write a 2 sentence follow-up for an unanswered budget request.
problems.answer: "Hi Sam, just bumping this up. Could you send the budget by Friday?"

problems.prompt: Should you follow up after about 3 working days or 3 hours?
Why send the follow-up in the same thread as the first 1?
problems.answer: So the history is right there.

steps.title: Pick an Arguable Question
steps.mastery: Start an essay from a real question that thoughtful people disagree about.
steps.practice: Write 3 essay questions that start with "Should" or "Why," and pick the 1 you can find evidence for on both sides.
steps.detail: An essay is an argument made in public. It needs a question with real disagreement, like "Should schools ban phones during class?" If nobody disagrees, there's nothing to argue. Checking that both sides have evidence keeps you honest.
steps.proof: 3 questions written and 1 chosen with evidence on both sides.
steps.pitfall: Arguing something nobody disputes, like "Sleep matters," which leaves nothing to prove.

problems.prompt: Is "Should schools start later?" an arguable question?
Is "Is exercise good for you?" a strong essay question?
Rewrite "Social media" as an arguable question.
problems.answer: "Should kids under 13 be allowed on social media?"

steps.title: Answer With a Claim
steps.mastery: Turn your question into a single claim that the essay will defend.
steps.practice: Answer your chosen question in 1 sentence of 25 words or fewer, with a because clause.
steps.detail: The claim is your answer plus a reason. "Schools should ban phones during class because they cut focus and test scores" gives the reader your position and the shape of the argument in one line.
steps.proof: 1 claim sentence with a because clause.
steps.pitfall: Starting the essay without saying what you think.

problems.prompt: Turn "Should schools start later?" into a claim with a because clause.
problems.answer: "Schools should start at 9 because teens need more sleep to learn."

problems.prompt: Why add a because clause to your 25 word claim?
problems.answer: It shows the reason and shapes the argument.

problems.prompt: Your claim is 40 words with 3 becauses. What's the fix?
problems.answer: Narrow it to the strongest reason.

steps.title: Show the Evidence
steps.mastery: Support each point with evidence the reader can check.
steps.practice: For each of 3 body paragraphs, add 1 fact, 1 example and 1 source the reader could look up.
steps.detail: Readers trust what they can check. A study, a number or a real example is stronger than an opinion. Name the source, like "a 2019 study from the CDC," so the reader can follow it.
steps.proof: 3 body paragraphs each with a fact, an example and a named source.
steps.pitfall: Supporting points with "everyone knows" or "it's obvious" instead of evidence.

problems.prompt: Is "Everyone knows phones are distracting" good evidence?
Name 3 kinds of evidence.
problems.answer: A fact, an example and a source.

problems.prompt: Rewrite "studies show" so a reader can check it.

steps.title: Face the Strongest Objection
steps.mastery: Name the best argument against your claim early and answer it honestly.
steps.practice: Write 1 paragraph that states the strongest objection to your claim in a way its supporters would accept, then answer it.
steps.detail: Readers who disagree are waiting for you to ignore their best point. Naming it fairly, early in the essay, earns trust. Then answer it: show why your claim still holds, or narrow your claim to account for it. Arguing against a weak version of the other side convinces nobody.
steps.proof: 1 counter-argument paragraph that a supporter of the other side would call fair.
steps.pitfall: Picking the silliest objection because it's easy to knock down.

problems.prompt: Your claim is "Phones should be banned in class." Write the strongest objection.
problems.answer: "Phones let students look things up and reach family in an emergency."

problems.prompt: Your essay has 5 paragraphs. Where might the objection go?
The objection is partly right. What can you do with your claim?
problems.answer: Narrow it, like banning phones except for emergencies.

steps.title: End With "So What?"
steps.mastery: Close by showing what changes if the reader agrees.
steps.practice: Write a final paragraph of 3 sentences that answers "So what?" without starting with "In conclusion."
steps.detail: A weak ending repeats the introduction. A strong one shows what the argument means: what should happen next, who it affects or what's at stake. Keep it short and concrete, and end on your strongest line.
steps.proof: A 3 sentence ending that shows why the argument matters.
steps.pitfall: Opening the last paragraph with "In conclusion" and repeating paragraph 1.

problems.prompt: Your last paragraph repeats your 3 points word for word. What's missing?
problems.answer: What it all means, the "so what."

problems.prompt: Name 2 things a "so what" ending can show.
problems.answer: What should happen next, and who it affects.

problems.prompt: Rewrite "In conclusion, phones are bad in class."
problems.answer: "If schools put phones away for 50 minutes a day, students get that focus back."

steps.title: Test It on Someone Who Disagrees
steps.mastery: Check that the essay is fair by giving it to a reader on the other side.
steps.practice: Ask 1 person who disagrees with your claim to read the essay and mark any sentence that feels unfair or misleading.
steps.detail: Friends who agree will miss your blind spots. A reader who disagrees will spot the unfair line, the cherry-picked fact or the weak answer to their side. You don't need to change your claim, but fixing unfair parts makes the essay far more persuasive.
steps.proof: Notes from 1 reader who disagrees, with unfair lines fixed.
steps.pitfall: Only showing the essay to people who already agree.

problems.prompt: Why give the essay to 1 person who disagrees?
problems.answer: They'll spot unfair parts that people who agree would miss.

problems.prompt: Your reader marks 2 lines as unfair. Must you change your claim?
Name 1 kind of unfairness a skeptical reader might catch.

steps.title: Ask Specific Questions
steps.mastery: Get useful feedback by asking readers targeted questions instead of whether they liked it.
steps.practice: Give 1 draft to a reader with 3 written questions, like "Where did you get bored?" and "What's the main point in 1 sentence?"
steps.detail: Vague questions get vague answers. "Did you like it?" gets "Yeah, it was good." Specific questions get usable answers. Ask where they got lost, bored or confused, and what they think the point is. Compare their answer to your intended point.
steps.proof: 3 specific questions sent with a draft and 3 answers back.
steps.pitfall: Asking only "What did you think?" and getting a polite shrug.

problems.prompt: Rewrite "Did you like it?" as a specific question.
Your reader says the main point is X, but you meant Y. What does that tell you?
problems.answer: The point isn't coming through clearly.

problems.prompt: Name 3 useful feedback questions.
problems.answer: Where did you get lost? Where were you bored? What's the main point?

steps.title: Listen Without Defending
steps.mastery: Hear feedback fully before responding, without arguing.
steps.practice: In your next feedback session, say only "thanks" and "tell me more" while the reader talks, and take notes.
steps.detail: Arguing with feedback stops it. The reader's confusion is real, even if you think they shouldn't be confused. Write it down and decide later. Defending your choices teaches readers to stop being honest with you.
steps.proof: 1 feedback session where you only listened and took notes.
steps.pitfall: Explaining what you "really meant" every time a reader is confused.

problems.prompt: A reader says paragraph 3 confused them. You want to explain it. What should you say instead?
Why not explain what you meant in paragraph 3?
problems.answer: The reader won't have you there to explain when they read it.

problems.prompt: Name 2 phrases to use while listening.

steps.title: Trust Where, Doubt How
steps.mastery: Take readers seriously about where the problem is, and use your own judgment on the fix.
steps.practice: For 5 pieces of feedback, write where the reader struck a problem and your own fix, which may differ from theirs.
steps.detail: Readers are reliable about where something went wrong. They're less reliable about how to fix it. If 2 readers stall at paragraph 4, something is wrong there, even if their fix doesn't fit your piece.
steps.proof: 5 notes with problem location and your own fix.
steps.pitfall: Ignoring a problem because you don't like the reader's suggested fix.

problems.prompt: A reader says "Add a joke in paragraph 4 because it drags." What's the reliable part?
3 readers stumble at the same sentence. What does that mean?
problems.answer: That sentence has a real problem.

problems.prompt: You don't like a reader's fix. Should you ignore the problem?

steps.title: Weigh Feedback by Agreement
steps.mastery: Treat comments that several readers share as stronger than one person's taste.
steps.practice: Collect notes from 3 readers on the same draft and mark every comment that 2 or more of them make.
steps.detail: One reader's dislike may just be taste. When 2 or 3 people point at the same spot, it's a pattern worth fixing first. Single comments still deserve a look, but they go lower on the list. This keeps you from rewriting the whole piece for one person.
steps.proof: 3 sets of notes with shared comments marked and fixed first.
steps.pitfall: Rewriting the ending because 1 of 3 readers didn't like it.

problems.prompt: 1 of 3 readers dislikes your ending. Is that a pattern yet?
problems.answer: Not yet. Note it and watch for more.

problems.prompt: All 3 readers say the middle drags. What goes first on your fix list?
2 readers flag paragraph 5 for different reasons. Is it worth a look?
problems.answer: Yes. Something there is catching readers.

steps.title: Close the Loop
steps.mastery: Thank readers and show them their notes mattered, so they'll help again.
steps.practice: After revising, send each reader a short thanks naming 1 change you made because of their notes.
steps.detail: Reading a draft carefully takes time. Readers who see their notes made a difference are far more likely to read for you again. A 2 sentence message is enough: thanks, and here's what changed.
steps.proof: A thank-you sent to each reader with 1 specific change named.
steps.pitfall: Taking notes from 3 people and never replying.

problems.prompt: Write a 2 sentence thank-you to a reader.
problems.answer: "Thanks for reading my essay. I cut the slow middle part you flagged, and it's much tighter now."

problems.prompt: Why name 1 specific change?
Should you send the 3 thank-yous after revising or before reading their notes?

steps.title: Build a Small Reader Group
steps.mastery: Find a few regular readers who know your work and give steady notes.
steps.practice: List 3 people who could read your drafts regularly, then ask 1 of them to read 1 piece a month.
steps.detail: Readers who see many of your drafts learn your habits and spot patterns a stranger misses. Trade reading if you can: you read theirs, they read yours. Start with 1 person and grow it.
steps.proof: 3 names listed and 1 regular reader who agreed.
steps.pitfall: Asking a different stranger each time and starting from scratch.

problems.prompt: Name 1 way to make regular reading fair for both people.
problems.answer: Trade drafts, so you read theirs too.

problems.prompt: After 6 months, why might a regular reader give better notes than a new one?
problems.answer: They know your habits and spot patterns.

problems.prompt: You listed 3 people. How many do you ask first?

steps.title: Link the Ends and Starts
steps.mastery: Hand each paragraph's last idea to the start of the next so the reader never jumps.
steps.practice: In 1 draft, underline the last idea of each paragraph and the first idea of the next, and fix 2 pairs that don't connect.
steps.detail: Writing flows when each paragraph hands something to the next. If paragraph 2 ends on cost and paragraph 3 opens on history, the reader feels a jump. Echo a word or idea from the end of one paragraph at the start of the next.
steps.proof: 1 draft with paragraph ends and starts underlined and 2 gaps fixed.
steps.pitfall: Gluing paragraphs together with "Also" and "Another thing is" instead of real links.

problems.prompt: Paragraph 2 ends on how much bike lanes cost. Paragraph 3 starts "Bike lanes began in Denmark." What's the problem?
problems.answer: The idea jumps without a link.

problems.prompt: Rewrite the start of paragraph 3 to connect to cost.
problems.answer: "That cost has paid off before, starting in Denmark."

problems.prompt: Name 1 way to link 2 paragraphs.
problems.answer: Echo a word or idea from the end of the last one.

steps.title: Fix Order Before Sentences
steps.mastery: Recognize that choppy writing usually comes from paragraph order more than wording.
steps.practice: Cut 1 choppy draft into paragraphs, shuffle them on a table, and rebuild the order before changing any sentences.
steps.detail: When a piece feels choppy, people often rewrite sentences. The real problem is usually order. Lay the paragraphs out and try new sequences. Often a single swap smooths the whole thing.
steps.proof: 1 draft reordered at the paragraph level.
steps.pitfall: Polishing sentences in a piece whose paragraphs are in the wrong order.

problems.prompt: Your draft feels choppy even after you've rewritten every sentence. What should you try?
Why test paragraph order before rewriting any of the 30 sentences?
Name 1 physical way to test paragraph order.
problems.answer: Cut them out and shuffle them on a table.

steps.title: Use Transition Words With Care
steps.mastery: Choose linking words that show the real relationship between ideas.
steps.practice: Circle every transition word in 1 draft, like "however," "so" and "also," and check each one shows the right link.
steps.detail: Transitions signal how ideas connect: contrast (but, however), cause (so, because), addition (and, also) or time (then, later). The wrong one confuses readers. Too many sound stiff. Use them only where the link needs saying.
steps.proof: 1 draft with every transition checked.
steps.pitfall: Starting every paragraph with "Furthermore" or "Moreover" out of habit.

problems.prompt: Which transition shows contrast: "so" or "but"?
Fill in: "It rained all day, ___ the game was canceled."
Every paragraph starts with "Furthermore." What's the problem?
problems.answer: It sounds stiff, and the links may not be real.

steps.title: Lead With Topic Sentences
steps.mastery: Open each paragraph with a sentence that tells the reader what it will show.
steps.practice: Rewrite the first sentence of 4 paragraphs in a draft so each one states that paragraph's main point.
steps.detail: A topic sentence is a signpost. Readers who skim, and most do, read the first line of each paragraph. If those lines alone tell the story of the piece, the structure is working. When a paragraph's point is hidden in sentence 5, move it up.
steps.proof: 4 paragraphs rewritten with clear topic sentences.
steps.pitfall: Burying each paragraph's main point in its middle.

problems.prompt: You read only the first line of all 5 paragraphs and can't tell what the essay argues. What's wrong?
problems.answer: The topic sentences don't state the main points.

problems.prompt: A paragraph's point appears in sentence 5. What do you do?
Write a topic sentence for a paragraph about bike lanes cutting crashes by 30 percent.
problems.answer: "Bike lanes make streets safer for everyone."

steps.title: Read It Out Loud
steps.mastery: Use your ear to find the spots where the writing stumbles.
steps.practice: Read 1 full draft aloud at normal speed and mark every place you stumble, run out of breath or lose the thread.
steps.detail: Your ear catches jumps, missing links and tangled sentences that your eye skips. A stumble usually means a sentence is too long or a link is missing. Mark them all first, then fix them in a second pass.
steps.proof: 1 draft read aloud with every stumble marked and then fixed.
steps.pitfall: Reading silently and missing the rough spots.

problems.prompt: You run out of breath halfway through 1 sentence. What does it suggest?
problems.answer: The sentence is too long. Split it.

problems.prompt: You stumble at the start of paragraph 4. What might be missing?
Should you fix each stumble as you read, or mark all 8 first?

choices: Fix each one as I read

steps.title: Book a Daily Writing Slot
steps.mastery: Set a fixed time to write so starting doesn't depend on feeling inspired.
steps.practice: Pick 1 daily slot of 20 minutes, like 7:00 am or right after dinner, and put it in your calendar for 14 days.
steps.detail: Writers who finish things mostly write at set times. The slot creates the ideas, rather than waiting for ideas to create the slot. Twenty minutes is short enough to keep on busy days. Same time and same place make it automatic.
steps.proof: A 20 minute slot booked in the calendar for 14 days.
steps.pitfall: Waiting to feel inspired before you sit down.

problems.prompt: You plan to write "when an idea comes." In 2 weeks, how often will you likely write?
problems.answer: Rarely. Ideas tend to come after you sit down.

problems.prompt: Name 2 good times for a 20 minute slot.
problems.answer: First thing in the morning, or right after dinner.

problems.prompt: Why only 20 minutes instead of 2 hours?
problems.answer: It's short enough to keep every day.

steps.title: Set a Word Target
steps.mastery: Give each session a small, countable goal so it has a clear finish.
steps.practice: Set a target of 200 words per session and log your count after each of the next 10 sessions.
steps.detail: A word count turns "write" into something you can finish. Two hundred words is about 1 short page, doable in 20 minutes. Count words and ignore quality for now. Bad words still count. Over 10 sessions, that's 2,000 words of raw material.
steps.proof: 10 sessions with word counts logged.
steps.pitfall: Judging sessions only by whether the writing was good.

problems.prompt: 200 words a day for 10 days. How many words?
You wrote 200 words but think they're bad. Does the session count?
You hit 200 words in 12 minutes. What do you do?
problems.answer: Stop happily, or keep going if you want.

steps.title: Track the Streak
steps.mastery: Keep a visible record of writing days to build momentum.
steps.practice: Mark each day you hit your target on a calendar for 30 days.
steps.detail: A streak you can see is motivating. Mark the day right after the session. If you miss, write the next day. Missing 1 day is normal, but missing 2 in a row is how habits fade.
steps.proof: A 30 day calendar with writing days marked.
steps.pitfall: Quitting the habit after 1 missed day.

problems.prompt: You miss Wednesday. What's the rule for Thursday?
problems.answer: Write. Don't miss 2 in a row.

problems.prompt: You wrote 25 of 30 days. Good month?
You finish writing at 7:20 am. When should you mark the calendar?

steps.title: Protect the Slot
steps.mastery: Keep the writing time free of distractions so the 20 minutes actually go to writing.
steps.practice: For your next 7 sessions, turn off Wi-Fi or put your phone in another room before you start.
steps.detail: The internet is the biggest thief of writing time. One check turns into 15 minutes gone. Close the browser, silence the phone and keep only your document open. Look things up after the session, marked with a quick note like TK.
steps.proof: 7 sessions with Wi-Fi off or the phone in another room.
steps.pitfall: Researching a small fact mid-sentence and losing 30 minutes online.

problems.prompt: You need a date you don't know mid-sentence. What do you do?
problems.answer: Write TK or a note and look it up after the session.

problems.prompt: Name 2 ways to protect the slot.
problems.answer: Turn off Wi-Fi, and put the phone in another room.

problems.prompt: You checked email once in 20 minutes and lost 10. What does it tell you?

steps.title: Review After 30 Days
steps.mastery: Look back at a month of writing to see what the habit produced.
steps.practice: After 30 days, add up your total words and pick the 2 best pieces to keep working on.
steps.detail: A month of 200 word sessions can produce 5,000 words or more. Seeing the total shows the habit works. Pick the best bits to develop further, and note which times or places worked best.
steps.proof: A 30 day total and 2 pieces picked to develop.
steps.pitfall: Never looking back and losing track of what you've made.

problems.prompt: You wrote 200 words on 25 days. What's the total?
Your best sessions were all at 7 am. What does that suggest?
Why pick 2 pieces to develop?
problems.answer: So the raw writing turns into finished work.

steps.title: Set a Total and Quota
steps.mastery: Turn a long project into a daily word count with a finish date.
steps.practice: Pick a target length for 1 long project, divide it by the days you have, and write the daily quota on your wall.
steps.detail: Long projects stall when they feel endless. A total and a deadline turn them into simple math. A 50,000 word draft over 100 days is 500 words a day. Track the running total so you always know where you stand.
steps.proof: A target length, a finish date and a daily quota written down.
steps.pitfall: Starting a novel with no target length or end date.

problems.prompt: 60,000 words in 120 days. What's the daily quota?
You can write only 5 days a week. 40,000 words in 20 weeks is how many words per writing day?
Why track a running total across 100 days?
problems.answer: So you always know where you stand.

steps.title: Keep a Project Map
steps.mastery: Hold the shape of a long project in one place you can see at a glance.
steps.practice: Write a 1 page map of your project with 1 line per chapter or section, and update it each week.
steps.detail: Months into a project, it's easy to lose track of what's where. A 1 page map shows the whole shape. Note what each part does and any loose ends. Updating it weekly stops contradictions and repeats from piling up.
steps.proof: A 1 page map with 1 line per section, updated weekly for 4 weeks.
steps.pitfall: Relying on memory for what happened in chapter 3 when you're writing chapter 19.

problems.prompt: Your character's eyes are blue in chapter 2 and brown in chapter 14. What would have caught it?
problems.answer: A project map or notes file.

problems.prompt: Should the project map be about 1 page or 30?
Should you update the map every 7 days or once a year?

steps.title: Keep Momentum Over Polish
steps.mastery: Push through the full draft before going back to fix early parts.
steps.practice: For the next 30 days, write forward only and log any fixes in a "later" list instead of rewriting.
steps.detail: Going back to polish chapter 1 again and again is the most common way long projects die. Momentum matters more than any single day. Keep a list of fixes and handle them in revision once the whole draft exists.
steps.proof: 30 days of forward-only writing with a "later" list.
steps.pitfall: Rewriting chapter 1 for the 6th time while chapters 2 to 20 don't exist.

problems.prompt: You realize chapter 2 needs a new scene while writing chapter 9. What do you do?
problems.answer: Add it to the later list and keep going.

problems.prompt: Why write forward only for 30 days?
Your later list has 12 fixes. When do you handle them?
problems.answer: In revision, after the full draft.

steps.title: Set a Bad Day Minimum
steps.mastery: Keep a long project moving on days when energy or time runs out.
steps.practice: Set a minimum of 100 words for bad days, and use it every time you can't reach your normal quota.
steps.detail: Over months, there will be sick days, busy weeks and flat moods. Skipping completely breaks the thread, and restarting gets harder each day. A tiny minimum keeps the story in your head. Many days, 100 words turns into 400 once you start.
steps.proof: A 100 word minimum written down and used on every low day for 4 weeks.
steps.pitfall: Skipping whole weeks because the full quota feels impossible.

problems.prompt: You've missed your 500 word quota 3 days in a row. What do you do today?
Why does a 100 word day still matter?
problems.answer: It keeps the project in your head.

problems.prompt: Your 100 word session turned into 450. Does the minimum still count as a win?

steps.title: Finish the Draft
steps.mastery: Reach the end of a full draft, even a rough one, before revising.
steps.practice: Write "The End" on your full draft by your deadline, whatever shape it's in, and log the final word count.
steps.detail: A finished rough draft can be revised into something good. An unfinished one, however polished, can't. Getting to the end also shows you what the book or project is really about, which changes how you revise the start.
steps.proof: A complete draft with "The End" and a final word count logged.
steps.pitfall: Stalling at 80 percent because the ending isn't perfect yet.

problems.prompt: You're at 45,000 of 50,000 words and the ending feels weak. What do you do?
problems.answer: Finish it anyway and fix it in revision.

problems.prompt: Why can finishing change how you revise chapter 1?
problems.answer: You learn what the project is really about.

problems.prompt: Name 1 thing to log when you finish.

steps.title: Rest Before Revising
steps.mastery: Step away from a finished long draft so you can revise it as a reader.
steps.practice: Put the finished draft away for at least 14 days, then read it straight through in 1 or 2 sittings, taking notes only.
steps.detail: After months inside a project, you can't see it clearly. Two weeks or more away lets you read it as a reader would. Read it whole and fast, noting big problems, before fixing anything. The first full read shows structure problems you couldn't see while drafting.
steps.proof: 14 days away followed by a full read with notes and no edits.
steps.pitfall: Starting line edits on chapter 1 the morning after finishing.

problems.prompt: You finish the draft on March 1. When is the earliest full read?
On the first full read after 14 days, should you fix typos as you go?
Why read it in 1 or 2 sittings?
problems.answer: To see the whole structure at once.

steps.title: Write the Opening Last
steps.mastery: Draft the body first and come back to the opening once you know what it introduces.
steps.practice: For your next piece, start with a 1 line placeholder opening, draft the body, then write the real opening at the end.
steps.detail: You rarely know what you're introducing until the piece exists. Starting with the body avoids hours spent polishing an opening you'll throw away. A placeholder like "[Intro: about bike lanes]" keeps you moving.
steps.proof: A piece whose opening was written after the body.
steps.pitfall: Spending 2 hours on the first sentence before writing anything else.

problems.prompt: You've rewritten your first line 8 times and have no body yet. What would help?
problems.answer: Use a placeholder and draft the body first.

problems.prompt: Write a placeholder opening for a 600 word essay on school uniforms.
Why write the opening after the other 4 paragraphs?
problems.answer: You only know what you're introducing once the piece exists.

steps.title: Start With Something Concrete
steps.mastery: Open with a specific scene, fact or question that pulls the reader in.
steps.practice: Write 3 different first lines for 1 piece: a scene, a surprising fact and a question.
steps.detail: Openings that start with broad statements like "Since the dawn of time" lose readers. Concrete openings work better: a moment ("At 6 am the bus was already full"), a number ("1 in 3 teens sleeps less than 7 hours") or a sharp question.
steps.proof: 3 first lines in 3 styles for 1 piece.
steps.pitfall: Starting with "Since the dawn of time" or a dictionary definition.

problems.prompt: Rewrite "Throughout history, sleep has been important" as a concrete opening.
problems.answer: "Most teens get 2 hours less sleep than they need."

problems.prompt: Name the 3 opening styles in this step.
problems.answer: A scene, a surprising fact and a question.

problems.prompt: Is "Webster's Dictionary defines courage as..." a strong opening?

steps.title: Get to the Point Fast
steps.mastery: Make sure the opening paragraph tells the reader where the piece is going.
steps.practice: Rewrite 1 opening so your central claim or purpose appears within the first 3 sentences.
steps.detail: Readers decide in seconds whether to keep going. Hook them, then tell them what the piece is about. A long warm-up loses people. Short pieces should get to the point in the first paragraph.
steps.proof: 1 opening with the claim within 3 sentences.
steps.pitfall: Spending 2 paragraphs warming up before saying anything.

problems.prompt: Your claim appears in paragraph 3 of a 5 paragraph essay. What's the fix?
problems.answer: Move it into the first paragraph.

problems.prompt: Should a 500 word piece reach its point within about 3 sentences or 3 paragraphs?
Name the 2 jobs of an opening.
problems.answer: Hook the reader, and say where the piece is going.

steps.title: Cut the Warm-Up Lines
steps.mastery: Delete the sentences at the start of a draft where you were only warming up.
steps.practice: Take 3 old drafts, cross out the first 1 or 2 sentences of each, and decide whether the piece now starts better.
steps.detail: Many drafts begin with the writer clearing their throat: "In this essay I will discuss..." or "There are many views on this topic." Those lines helped you start writing, but the reader doesn't need them. The real opening is often sitting in sentence 2 or 3.
steps.proof: 3 drafts checked, with warm-up lines cut where it helped.
steps.pitfall: Keeping "In this essay I will talk about" as your first line.

problems.prompt: Your first line is "In this essay I will discuss 3 reasons for later start times." What's a stronger start?
problems.answer: Start with the strongest reason or a striking fact about teen sleep.

problems.prompt: You cut sentence 1 and the piece now opens with a vivid scene. What does that tell you?
Is "There are many views on this topic" a useful first line in a 600 word piece?

steps.title: Test It on Readers
steps.mastery: Check whether your opening makes real people want to read on.
steps.practice: Show 3 people only your first paragraph and ask, "Would you keep reading? Why or why not?"
steps.detail: The only test of an opening is whether readers keep going. Show just the first paragraph, so they judge only that. If 2 of 3 say no, try one of your other first lines. Their reasons tell you what to change.
steps.proof: 3 readers' answers about your first paragraph.
steps.pitfall: Assuming the opening works because you like it.

problems.prompt: 2 of 3 readers say they'd stop. What do you do?
problems.answer: Try a different opening and test again.

problems.prompt: 1 reader says "I didn't know what it was about." What should change?
Why show only the first paragraph to all 3 readers?
problems.answer: So they judge the opening alone.

steps.title: Write a 5 Line Outline
steps.mastery: Sketch the order of a piece in a few lines before writing full sentences.
steps.practice: Before your next piece, write a 5 line outline: 1 line for the opening, 3 for the main points and 1 for the ending.
steps.detail: Even a tiny outline prevents the most common structural problem: a piece that only finds its point at the end. Five lines take 5 minutes. Each line is a short phrase. You can change it as you go.
steps.proof: A 5 line outline written before drafting.
steps.pitfall: Starting to draft with no idea where the piece is going.

problems.prompt: Your essay finds its main point in the last paragraph. What would an outline have caught?
problems.answer: That the point should come earlier.

problems.prompt: How long should a 5 line outline take?
Write a 5 line outline for "Why I walk to school."
problems.answer: Opening: the morning walk. Point 1: time to think. Point 2: exercise. Point 3: seeing the town. Ending: why I'll keep doing it.

steps.title: Order the Main Points
steps.mastery: Arrange points so each one sets up the next.
steps.practice: Write your 3 main points on separate sticky notes and try 2 different orders, then pick the one that flows best.
steps.detail: Order changes meaning. Some pieces go from simple to complex. Others go from least to most important. Arguments often put the strongest point last. Moving notes around makes it easy to compare orders.
steps.proof: 2 orders tried and 1 chosen with a reason.
steps.pitfall: Keeping the first order you thought of without testing another.

problems.prompt: You're persuading someone. Where might your strongest point go?
problems.answer: Last, or first if attention is short.

problems.prompt: You're teaching a process. What order makes sense?
Name 1 tool for testing orders.

steps.title: Add Evidence Under Each Point
steps.mastery: List the support for each point before drafting.
steps.practice: Under each of your 3 main points, write 2 pieces of evidence, like a fact, an example or a quote.
steps.detail: A point without support is an opinion. Listing evidence early shows which points are strong and which need research. If a point has nothing under it, you may need to cut it or dig.
steps.proof: 3 points with 2 pieces of evidence each.
steps.pitfall: Discovering mid-draft that a main point has no support.

problems.prompt: Point 2 has no evidence under it. Name 2 options.
problems.answer: Research more, or cut the point.

problems.prompt: Name 3 types of evidence.
problems.answer: A fact, an example and a quote.

problems.prompt: Why list 2 pieces of evidence per point before drafting?
problems.answer: To see which points are strong.

steps.title: Outline Backward From the Ending
steps.mastery: Decide the ending first and plan the path to it.
steps.practice: Write your last sentence first, then outline 4 steps that lead the reader there.
steps.detail: Knowing where you're going makes the path clearer. Write the final point first. Then ask what the reader needs to believe it.
steps.proof: An ending sentence and a 4 step outline leading to it.
steps.pitfall: Hoping an ending appears on its own.

problems.prompt: Why write the last sentence before the first 4 steps?
problems.answer: You know where the piece is going.

problems.prompt: Write the 1 question that helps you outline backward.
problems.answer: What does the reader need to believe the ending?

problems.prompt: Your ending is "So cities should plant more trees." Name 1 step the reader needs first.
problems.answer: Evidence that trees cool streets, for example.

steps.title: Let the Outline Change
steps.mastery: Treat the outline as a guide that can shift during drafting.
steps.practice: After drafting, compare your draft to the outline and note 2 places it changed.
steps.detail: Drafting often turns up better ideas than the outline had. When it does, update the outline so the rest of the draft follows the new plan. The outline exists to help you, so let it change.
steps.proof: 2 changes noted.
steps.pitfall: Forcing the draft to match a weak outline.

problems.prompt: Your draft found a better point 3. What do you do?
Your draft drifted from 2 lines of the outline. Must you force it back?
problems.answer: No. Update the outline if the new direction is better.

problems.prompt: Your new point 3 is stronger than point 2. What might you change in the outline?
problems.answer: Swap their order, or cut the weaker one.

steps.title: Read Poems Out Loud
steps.mastery: Hear a poem's sound and rhythm by reading it aloud.
steps.practice: Read 5 short poems aloud, twice each, and note 1 sound pattern you hear in each, like repeated sounds or a beat.
steps.detail: Poetry is written for the ear. Reading silently misses rhyme, rhythm and repeated sounds. Read slowly, pausing at line ends. The second read usually reveals patterns the first missed.
steps.proof: 5 poems read aloud twice with 1 sound note each.
steps.pitfall: Skimming poems silently like a news article.

problems.prompt: Name 2 sound patterns you might hear in a poem.
problems.answer: Rhyme, and repeated starting sounds, like "silver sea."

problems.prompt: Why read each of the 5 poems twice?
problems.answer: The second read shows patterns the first one missed.

problems.prompt: In "Peter Piper picked a peck," what sound pattern repeats?

steps.title: Compress a Paragraph
steps.mastery: Squeeze prose into a few lines by keeping only the strongest words.
steps.practice: Take a 100 word paragraph you wrote and cut it into a poem of 30 words or fewer.
steps.detail: Poetry packs meaning tight. Cut filler, explanations and most "the" and "and." Keep strong nouns and verbs. Let the reader make connections you'd normally spell out.
steps.proof: A 100 word paragraph turned into a poem of 30 words or fewer.
steps.pitfall: Breaking a full paragraph into short lines without cutting any words.

problems.prompt: Your poem still has 95 words after line breaks. What went wrong?
problems.answer: You didn't cut. You only broke lines.

problems.prompt: Which words usually survive compression: "very," "the," or strong nouns?
Compress "The old dog slowly walked across the frozen yard in the early morning."
problems.answer: "Old dog, slow / across the frozen yard. / Dawn."

steps.title: Break Lines on Purpose
steps.mastery: Choose where lines end so each break adds emphasis or surprise.
steps.practice: Write 1 eight line poem twice with different line breaks, then pick the version where the breaks do more.
steps.detail: The end of a line is a tiny pause, so the last word gets extra weight. Breaking a line in an odd spot can create surprise or a double meaning. Make every break a choice. Don't let the width of the page decide.
steps.proof: 2 versions of 1 poem with a note on which breaks work better.
steps.pitfall: Breaking lines wherever the page runs out.

problems.prompt: In an 8 line poem, which word in each line gets extra weight?
Break "I wanted to leave but I stayed" into 2 lines to stress "leave."
problems.answer: "I wanted to leave / but I stayed."

problems.prompt: Why write 2 versions?
problems.answer: To compare how different breaks change the poem.

steps.title: Use Concrete Images
steps.mastery: Build a poem from things the reader can see, hear or touch.
steps.practice: Write a 6 line poem about a feeling using only concrete images and never naming the feeling.
steps.detail: Abstract words like "love" or "sadness" give readers nothing to picture. Concrete images carry feeling better. A cold cup of coffee on a table says more about loneliness than the word itself.
steps.proof: A 6 line poem with no feeling named.
steps.pitfall: Writing lines like "My sadness is deep and endless" that give readers nothing to see.

problems.prompt: Rewrite "I feel lonely" as a concrete image.
problems.answer: "2 cups on the counter, 1 still clean."

problems.prompt: Why avoid naming the feeling anywhere in the 6 lines?
problems.answer: Images carry it better, and let the reader feel it.

problems.prompt: Name 1 concrete image for joy.
problems.answer: A dog sprinting through sprinklers, for example.

steps.title: Write Inside a Form
steps.mastery: Use a fixed form's rules to push you toward fresher word choices.
steps.practice: Write 1 haiku of 5, 7 and 5 syllables and 1 poem of exactly 14 lines on the same subject.
steps.detail: Constraints help. When you need exactly 5 syllables, the first word that comes to mind often won't fit, so you find a better one. Short forms like haiku train compression. Longer fixed forms, like a 14 line sonnet shape, train you to build and turn an idea.
steps.proof: 1 haiku and 1 fourteen line poem on the same subject.
steps.pitfall: Padding a line with "oh" or "so very" just to hit the count.

problems.prompt: Count the syllables: "An old silent pond."
Your haiku's middle line has 9 syllables. What do you do?
problems.answer: Cut or swap words to reach 7.

problems.prompt: Why can a strict 5, 7, 5 count lead to better words?
problems.answer: The first word often won't fit, so you look harder.

steps.title: Revise by Ear
steps.mastery: Polish a poem by listening for clunky sounds and rhythm.
steps.practice: Read 1 of your poems aloud 3 times on different days and change at least 3 words that sound wrong.
steps.detail: The ear catches what the eye forgives: 2 hard sounds that jam together, a line that runs out of breath, a rhythm that stumbles. Reading on different days gives fresh ears. Swap words until each line sounds the way it should.
steps.proof: 1 poem read aloud on 3 days with 3 or more word changes.
steps.pitfall: Revising only by looking at the page.

problems.prompt: A line reads "the black cat's tracks crept past." What sound problem might you hear?
problems.answer: Lots of hard "k" and "t" sounds jamming together.

problems.prompt: Why read on 3 different days?
A line runs out of breath when read aloud. Name 1 fix.

steps.title: Find 10 Places to Submit
steps.mastery: Build a list of real places that publish the kind of work you write.
steps.practice: List 10 magazines, websites, contests or publishers that accept your kind of writing, with their deadline and word limit.
steps.detail: Submitting starts with a target list. Read what each place publishes before sending, since a great poem sent to a place that only runs essays is wasted. Note word limits, deadlines and whether they pay. Start with a mix of reach targets and likely fits.
steps.proof: A list of 10 places with deadlines and word limits.
steps.pitfall: Sending work to places you've never read.

problems.prompt: A magazine publishes only essays under 1,500 words. Your story is 4,000 words. Should you send it?
Name 3 things to note for each place.
problems.answer: Deadline, word limit and whether they pay.

problems.prompt: Why read a place's work before submitting?
problems.answer: To see if your piece fits what they publish.

steps.title: Follow the Guidelines Exactly
steps.mastery: Submit exactly the way each place asks, so your work gets read.
steps.practice: For your next 3 submissions, check 5 guideline points each: format, length, file type, cover letter and simultaneous submission rules.
steps.detail: Editors get far more work than they can read. Ignoring guidelines is the fastest way to a rejection. Match the format, stay under the word limit, use the file type they ask for and include only what they want.
steps.proof: 3 submissions checked against 5 guideline points.
steps.pitfall: Sending a 3,000 word piece to a place with a 2,000 word limit.

problems.prompt: The guidelines ask for a .docx file. You have a PDF. What do you do?
Name 5 guideline points to check.
problems.answer: Format, length, file type, cover letter and the rules on sending elsewhere at the same time.

problems.prompt: Why follow all 5 guideline points so closely?
problems.answer: Editors often reject work that ignores them.

steps.title: Write a Short Cover Note
steps.mastery: Write a brief, plain cover letter that lets the work speak.
steps.practice: Write a cover note of 3 to 5 sentences: the title and length, 1 line about you, and thanks.
steps.detail: Editors don't need your life story. A short note with the title, word count, a one-line bio and a thank-you is standard. Don't explain or praise the piece. Let it stand on its own.
steps.proof: A cover note of 3 to 5 sentences ready to reuse.
steps.pitfall: Writing a full page explaining what your poem means.

problems.prompt: Name 3 things a cover note includes.
problems.answer: The title, the word count and a short bio.

problems.prompt: Should your 4 sentence cover note explain what the poem means?
Your cover note runs 2 pages. What should it be cut to?

steps.title: Track Every Submission
steps.mastery: Keep a log so nothing gets lost or sent twice.
steps.practice: Set up a tracker with 5 columns: piece, place, date sent, response and next place to send.
steps.detail: Responses can take weeks or months, and with several pieces out it's easy to lose track. A simple spreadsheet keeps you organized. Log every response, including form rejections, and note where each piece goes next so a rejection turns straight into a new submission.
steps.proof: A tracker with 5 columns and all current submissions logged.
steps.pitfall: Losing track of where you sent what.

problems.prompt: Name the 5 columns.
problems.answer: Piece, place, date sent, response and next place.

problems.prompt: You have 8 pieces out at 12 places. Why keep a tracker?
problems.answer: To stay organized and avoid sending the same piece to 1 place twice.

problems.prompt: Do responses usually come in 2 days, or can they take weeks to months?

steps.title: Send It Back Out Fast
steps.mastery: Resubmit a rejected piece quickly so rejection never turns into stalling.
steps.practice: After each rejection, send the piece to the next place on your list within 7 days, and log it.
steps.detail: Rejection is the normal result of submitting, even for strong work. Editors turn down good pieces for reasons that have nothing to do with you: a full issue, a similar piece last month. The habit that matters is sending it out again the same week. Reread it once, fix anything obvious, then send.
steps.proof: Every rejected piece resent within 7 days for a month, logged in the tracker.
steps.pitfall: Letting a piece sit in a drawer for a year after 1 rejection.

problems.prompt: You get a rejection on Monday. By when should the piece go out again?
problems.answer: By the next Monday at the latest.

problems.prompt: A piece has 4 rejections. Is it a bad piece?
Name 1 reason a good piece gets rejected.
problems.answer: The issue was full, or they ran something similar.

steps.title: Set a Yearly Submission Goal
steps.mastery: Aim for a volume of submissions that makes acceptance a numbers game you can win.
steps.practice: Set a goal for submissions this year, like 50, and check your tracker count on the 1st of each month.
steps.detail: Acceptance rates at many places are low, sometimes under 5 percent. The writers who get published usually send a lot. A yearly goal turns that into a habit. Count submissions, since that's the part you control.
steps.proof: A yearly goal written and checked monthly.
steps.pitfall: Sending 2 pieces a year and taking each rejection as final.

problems.prompt: A goal of 50 submissions a year is about how many per week?
Why count your 50 submissions instead of acceptances?
problems.answer: Submissions are the part you control.

problems.prompt: A magazine accepts 3 percent of pieces. If you send there 10 times, is 1 acceptance likely?
problems.answer: Not certain, but it helps. 10 tries at 3% gives about a 26% chance of at least 1.

steps.title: Put the Conclusion First
steps.mastery: Lead a report with the answer, then give the support.
steps.practice: Rewrite the opening of 1 report so the first 2 sentences state the finding and the recommendation.
steps.detail: Reports are skimmed. Many readers stop after the first paragraph. Put the answer up top: what you found and what to do. The details follow for anyone who needs them. This is the reverse of a school essay, which builds up to its point.
steps.proof: 1 report opening with the finding and recommendation in the first 2 sentences.
steps.pitfall: Building suspense through 4 pages before revealing the result.

problems.prompt: Your report's recommendation is on page 3. Where should it go?
Rewrite "This report looks at our bus routes" as a lead with the answer.
problems.answer: "Merging routes 4 and 7 would save 20 minutes a day. We recommend doing it by May."

problems.prompt: Why put the answer in the first 2 sentences?
problems.answer: Many readers stop after the first paragraph.

steps.title: Write a 3 Line Summary
steps.mastery: Sum up a report in a few lines a busy reader can act on.
steps.practice: Write a 3 line summary at the top of your next report: what you looked at, what you found and what you recommend.
steps.detail: A short summary lets a busy reader decide in 30 seconds. Keep each line to 1 sentence. Use numbers where you can. If the summary needs 10 lines, the report's point isn't clear yet.
steps.proof: A 3 line summary at the top of a report.
steps.pitfall: Writing a summary that's as long as a full page.

problems.prompt: Name the 3 lines of the summary.
problems.answer: What you looked at, what you found and what you recommend.

problems.prompt: Your summary is 12 lines. What does it suggest?
problems.answer: The main point isn't clear yet.

problems.prompt: Rewrite "Sales were different" with a number.

steps.title: Use Headings That Say Something
steps.mastery: Write headings that tell the reader the point of each section.
steps.practice: Rewrite 4 headings in a report so each states the section's main point, like "Costs rise 8 percent" instead of "Costs."
steps.detail: Readers navigate reports by headings. "Costs" says what the section is about. "Costs rise 8 percent in Q3" says what it found. Informative headings let skimmers get the story from headings alone.
steps.proof: 4 headings rewritten to state findings.
steps.pitfall: Using 1 word headings like "Background" and "Data" that say nothing.

problems.prompt: Rewrite the heading "Survey."
problems.answer: "80% of students want later start times."

problems.prompt: Why rewrite 4 headings to state findings?
problems.answer: Skimmers get the story from the headings alone.

problems.prompt: Is "Background" an informative heading?

steps.title: Make It Easy to Scan
steps.mastery: Format reports so readers can find what they need fast.
steps.practice: Reformat 1 page of a report with short paragraphs of 3 to 4 sentences, bullet lists for steps and bold key numbers.
steps.detail: Dense pages get skipped. Short paragraphs, lists and clear numbers help readers find things. Use bullets for steps or options, and keep arguments in sentences.
steps.proof: 1 page reformatted for scanning.
steps.pitfall: Writing 1 page as a single block of text.

problems.prompt: Should report paragraphs run about 3 to 4 sentences or 12?
You have 5 steps to list. Should they be bullets or a paragraph?
problems.answer: Bullets or a numbered list, since they're steps.

problems.prompt: Name 1 formatting tool that helps scanning.

steps.title: Write Steps Anyone Can Follow
steps.mastery: Write numbered instructions that a newcomer can follow without asking for help.
steps.practice: Write instructions for 1 task you know well in 6 numbered steps, each starting with a verb and holding 1 action.
steps.detail: Instructions fail when steps hide 2 or 3 actions, skip something obvious to you, or use terms the reader doesn't know. Number the steps. Start each with a verb like "Open," "Click" or "Pour." Say what the reader should see when a step worked, like the light turning green.
steps.proof: 6 numbered steps, each with 1 action and a verb first.
steps.pitfall: Writing "Set up the account and configure settings" as 1 step.

problems.prompt: How many steps should "Log in, open Settings and turn on alerts" become?
Why add "The light turns green" after step 3?
Step 4 says "Configure the router." Why might a newcomer get stuck?
problems.answer: It hides several actions and assumes knowledge.

steps.title: Test It on a Skimmer
steps.mastery: Check that someone skimming for a minute walks away with the main point.
steps.practice: Give your report to 1 person for 60 seconds, take it back, and ask what it recommends and why.
steps.detail: Real readers skim. If someone can't name your recommendation after 60 seconds, the summary, headings or first paragraph aren't doing their job. Fix those and test again with someone new.
steps.proof: A 60 second skim test with the reader's answer written down.
steps.pitfall: Assuming every reader will read every word.

problems.prompt: After 60 seconds, the reader names a minor detail instead of the recommendation. What needs work?
problems.answer: The summary and headings, so the main point stands out.

problems.prompt: The reader names the recommendation but not the reason. What could you add?
problems.answer: A short reason in the summary.

problems.prompt: You fixed the summary. Should you retest with the same reader or a new 1?

steps.title: Revise Big Before Small
steps.mastery: Fix structure and argument before touching word choice and commas.
steps.practice: Make 3 passes on 1 draft in order: first structure, then paragraphs, then sentences, and note what changed in each.
steps.detail: Polishing sentences you later cut is wasted work. Start big: is the order right, is the argument complete, does anything need cutting? Then look at paragraphs. Only then fix words and commas. Each pass has 1 job.
steps.proof: 1 draft revised in 3 ordered passes with notes for each.
steps.pitfall: Fixing commas in a section you end up deleting.

problems.prompt: Put these 3 passes in order: sentences, structure, paragraphs.
You spent 30 minutes polishing a paragraph, then cut it. What went wrong?
Name 2 questions for the structure pass.
problems.answer: Is the order right, and does anything need cutting?

steps.title: Wait a Day
steps.mastery: Put distance between drafting and revising so you can see the draft as a reader.
steps.practice: After finishing a draft, wait at least 24 hours before your structure pass.
steps.detail: Right after drafting, you're attached to every line and read what you meant. A day later you see what's on the page. That's when cutting a section you like becomes possible.
steps.proof: A draft revised after at least 24 hours away.
steps.pitfall: Revising 10 minutes after finishing, when every sentence still feels precious.

problems.prompt: You finish a draft at 9 pm. When is the earliest good time for the structure pass?
Why does 1 day away make cutting easier?
problems.answer: You're less attached and see the page as a reader.

problems.prompt: You have only 2 hours before a deadline. What's a shorter break that helps?
problems.answer: A 30-minute walk away from the draft.

steps.title: Reverse Outline the Draft
steps.mastery: Outline what the draft actually says to find structural problems.
steps.practice: Write 1 line per paragraph summarizing what each paragraph of your draft does, then look for gaps, repeats and bad order.
steps.detail: A reverse outline shows the real structure. Reading 1 line per paragraph makes it easy to spot 2 paragraphs saying the same thing, a missing step or a point in the wrong place.
steps.proof: A reverse outline with 2 or more problems found.
steps.pitfall: Revising sentence by sentence without seeing the whole shape.

problems.prompt: Your reverse outline shows paragraphs 3 and 6 both say "bike lanes save money." What do you do?
Your reverse outline jumps from cause to solution with no evidence. What's missing?
A draft has an opening, 4 body paragraphs and an ending. How many lines does its reverse outline have?

steps.title: Cut a Section You Like
steps.mastery: Cut good writing when it doesn't serve the piece, without losing it for good.
steps.practice: Find 1 section in a draft that you like but that doesn't serve the main point, and move it to a separate cuts file.
steps.detail: The hardest cuts are passages you're proud of. A cuts file makes it painless, since nothing is deleted forever. Many writers find the piece reads better without the favorite part, and the cut passage sometimes becomes the start of something new.
steps.proof: 1 liked section moved to a cuts file and the draft reread without it.
steps.pitfall: Keeping a lovely paragraph that drags the piece off its point.

problems.prompt: A 200 word passage is the best writing in the draft but is off topic. Keep or move to cuts?
Why does a cuts file make cutting a 200 word passage easier?
problems.answer: Nothing is lost, so letting go hurts less.

problems.prompt: Your cuts file has 3 passages on the same side topic. What could they become?
problems.answer: The start of a new piece.

steps.title: Keep the Claim in View
steps.mastery: Revise with the central claim in front of you so drift is easy to spot.
steps.practice: Write your 1 sentence claim on a sticky note, put it beside the screen, and reread the draft marking any part that doesn't support it.
